en: The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Life Span. Chapter One: On Life Span.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Kuśinagara, in the birthplace of the Mallas, between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Ādira-vatī River.
At that time, the World-Honored One was accompanied by a great assembly of eighty billion hundred thousand bhikṣus, who surrounded him before and behind.

On the fifteenth day of the second month, as he approached the time of his parinirvāṇa, he emitted a great sound through the Buddha’s supernatural power; this sound pervaded all places up to the Peak of Existence. In accordance with the various voices of their species, he universally addressed all sentient beings:

"Today, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, out of compassion for sentient beings and to protect them, regards all beings equally as he does Rāhula, acting as their refuge, shelter, and dwelling place."
"The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa; if any among all sentient beings have any doubts, you may now ask them all, for this shall be your final question.

At that time, during the early morning, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face. These lights were of manifold colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and agate—and the radiance shone throughout this trichiliocosm Buddha-world, and likewise throughout the ten directions.
Among them, all sentient beings of the six realms who encountered this light had their karmic defilements and afflictions entirely eliminated.
Having seen and heard this, those beings were filled with great sorrow; simultaneously raising their voices, they wailed and wept, crying out:
"Alas, compassionate father! How painful, how bitter!"
They raised their hands to strike their heads, beat their breasts, and wailed; some among them trembled with their whole bodies, weeping and sobbing.
At that time, the great earth, its mountains, and its oceans all shook violently, and the sentient beings there said to one another:
"Let us each restrain ourselves; do not grieve so bitterly."

You should go quickly to the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, and upon reaching the place where the Tathāgata is, prostrate yourself with your head at his feet in reverent salutation, and entreat the Tathāgata not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to remain in the world for a kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa.
They grasped each other's hands and spoke again:
"The world is empty and void; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, while unwholesome karmas increase and manifest in the world."
"Virtuous ones, you must go now, go quickly! Before long, the Tathāgata will surely enter parinirvāṇa.
He spoke further, saying:
"The world is empty and void; the world is empty and void! From this day forth, we shall have no protector, no one to revere, and we shall be destitute, orphaned, and exposed."
"Once we have departed from the Unsurpassed World-Honored One, to whom shall we turn if doubts arise?

At that time, there were immeasurable great disciples—Venerable Mahākātyāyana, Venerable Bakula, Venerable Upānanda, and other such great bhikṣus—who, upon encountering the Buddha’s light, found their bodies trembling and shaking so violently that they could not support themselves; their minds became turbid and bewildered, and they cried out loudly, giving rise to all manner of such sufferings and afflictions.

At that time, there were also eight million bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats who had attained mastery over their minds, fulfilled what was to be done, and were free from all afflictions. Their faculties were well-subdued, and they possessed great majesty like great dragon kings. They had perfected the wisdom of emptiness and realized their own benefit. Like a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood trees, or like a lion king surrounded by lions, they had accomplished such immeasurable merits; all of them were true sons of the Buddha.

At the break of dawn, when the sun had just begun to rise, they left their usual dwelling place; while chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks), they encountered the Buddha’s radiance and said to one another:
"Virtuous friends, quickly rinse your mouths and wash your hands."
Having spoken these words, the hair on his entire body stood on end, blood appeared all over his frame like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling his eyes, he was overcome by great anguish.

Desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to reveal the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means, to ensure that the various modes of preaching the Dharma would not be interrupted, and for the sake of providing the causes and conditions for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also the nun Kautālī, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā, the bhikṣuṇī Upānandā, and the bhikṣuṇī Sāgaramati, together with six billion bhikṣuṇīs; all of them were likewise great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained mastery over their minds, fulfilled what was to be done, and were free from all afflictions. Having tamed their faculties like great dragons, they possessed great majestic virtue and had accomplished the wisdom of emptiness.

Furthermore, at the break of dawn, when the sun first rose, the hair on his entire body stood on end, blood appeared all over his frame like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling his eyes, he was overcome by great suffering.

Furthermore, desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to reveal the Tathāgata’s secret teachings of skillful means, to ensure that the various methods of preaching the Dharma are never interrupted, and for the sake of providing the causes and conditions for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly went to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to sit to one side.

Within the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, there were further bhikṣuṇīs who were all bodhisattvas, dragons among men, whose rank was the ten stages (daśabhūmi) and who dwelt therein immovably; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they manifested in female bodies, yet they constantly cultivated and accumulated the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa), attained the power of mastery, and were able to manifest as Buddhas.

At that time, there were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—nāgas among men—who, established immovably in the rank of the ten stages, manifested their bodies through skillful means.
Their names were:
Bodhisattva Sāgaramati and Bodhisattva Akṣayamati; such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these were their leaders.

Their minds were all entirely respectful toward the Mahāyāna, they dwelt securely in the Mahāyāna, deeply understood the Mahāyāna, delighted in the Mahāyāna, and protected the Mahāyāna. Being well able to accord with all worlds, they made this vow:
"Those who have not yet crossed over, I shall cause them to cross over.

Having already cultivated and maintained pure precepts throughout countless kalpas of the past, skillfully upholding his conduct, liberating those who were not yet liberated, and continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it would never be severed, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma in future ages. Adorned with great adornments, he has accomplished such immeasurable merit as to regard all sentient beings equally, as if looking upon an only son.

Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, he encountered the Buddha’s radiance; his hair stood on end, blood appeared all over his body like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling his eyes, he was overcome by great anguish.

Furthermore, for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to reveal the Tathāgata’s secret teachings of skillful means, to ensure that the various modes of preaching the Dharma are never interrupted, and as a cause and condition for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and with palms joined in reverence, withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, there were also as many upāsakas as there are grains of sand in two Ganges Rivers, who upheld the five precepts and were perfect in their dignified conduct.

Their leaders were the upāsaka King of Undefiled Majestic Virtue, the upāsaka Good Virtue, and others. They deeply delighted in contemplating the gates of various antidotes, namely: suffering and pleasure; permanence and impermanence; purity and impurity; self and non-self; reality and unreality; refuge and non-refuge; sentient beings and non-sentient beings; constancy and non-constancy; security and insecurity; the conditioned and the unconditioned; cessation and non-cessation; nirvāṇa and non-nirvāṇa; and the superior and the non-superior. They constantly delighted in contemplating such gates of the antidotes for these dharmas, and they also desired to hear the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, so that having heard it, they might explain it to others.
They uphold the pure precepts well and thirst for the Mahāyāna; having themselves attained fulfillment, they are further able to satisfy others who likewise thirst for it.
They are skillfully able to grasp unsurpassed wisdom, delighting in the Mahāyāna and protecting the Mahāyāna.
He is well able to accord with all worlds, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated.

He continues the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it shall never be severed; in future ages he shall turn the wheel of Dharma, adorning himself with great adornments. His mind constantly relishes the practice of pure precepts, and he is fully able to accomplish such merits as these. Toward all sentient beings he gives rise to great compassion, regarding them with impartiality and without distinction, as if looking upon an only child.

Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, in order to perform the cremation of the Tathāgata’s body, every person took ten thousand bundles of fragrant wood—sandalwood, aloeswood, gośīrṣa sandalwood, celestial wood, and so forth. Each of these pieces of wood, in its grain, texture, and joints, possessed the subtle radiance of the seven treasures, like various colorful paintings; by the power of the Buddha, they possessed such wondrous colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—which were a joy for all sentient beings to behold.

All the trees were anointed with various kinds of fragrances, such as saffron, aloeswood, and resinous incense; they were further adorned by being strewn with many flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), white lotuses (kumuda), red lotuses (padma), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).
Above all the fragrant trees hang five-colored banners, soft and exquisite like celestial garments, made of *kauśeya* silk, *kṣauma* linen, and various brocades.
These fragrant trees are carried upon jeweled chariots, and these jeweled chariots emit various lights—blue, yellow, red, and white.
The axles and poles were all inlaid with the seven treasures; each chariot was yoked to four horses, and every horse was as swift as the wind.

Before each chariot stood fifty-seven exquisite banners made of precious jewels, covered above by nets of pure gold. Each precious chariot further possessed fifty subtle and wondrous jeweled canopies, and from each chariot hung various flower garlands—Utpala, Kumuda, Padma, and Puṇḍarīka flowers—whose petals were made entirely of pure gold and whose pericarps were of diamond.

Within these flower pedestals there are many black bees that gather and sport therein, enjoying themselves and receiving pleasure; they also produce wondrous sounds, namely: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Within these sounds, they further proclaim the path originally practiced by Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there were various kinds of singing, dancing, and musical performances—zithers, flutes, lutes, pipes, harps, drums, and wind instruments—and from amidst these musical sounds, these words emerged:
"Alas, alas! The world is empty and void."

Before each chariot, there was an upāsaka holding a tray made of the four jewels; upon these trays were various flowers—utpala, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka—as well as saffron and other incenses, all of which were most exquisite and supreme.

The upāsakas prepared various foodstuffs for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, providing everything in full abundance. All were made from fuel of candana and agalloch wood and matured by water of eight virtues. That food was sweet and delicious, possessing six kinds of flavors:
first, bitter; second, sour; third, sweet; fourth, pungent; fifth, salty; and sixth, bland.
Furthermore, there were three qualities:
first, lightness and softness; second, purity and cleanliness; third, conformity with the Dharma.

With such various adornments, he proceeded to the twin śāla trees at the birthplace of the Mallas. He then spread golden sand over the ground, covering it with garments of kālinga, kṣaumapa, and fine silks, extending for twelve yojanas all around.

For the Buddha and the Sangha, he prepared lion-thrones made of the seven precious gems; these thrones were as high and large as Mount Sumeru, and upon each throne there was a jeweled canopy from which various necklaces hung down.
Upon all the śāla trees were suspended various exquisite banners and canopies; their trunks were anointed with various fine incenses, and various famous flowers were scattered among them.
Each of the upāsakas thought to themselves:

"If any sentient being lacks anything—if they need food, I shall give them food; if they need drink, I shall give them drink; if they need a head, I shall give them a head; if they need eyes, I shall give them eyes—whatever things sentient beings require, I shall provide them all."

When making such offerings, one is free from desire, hatred, and the poisonous mind of defilement; without any other thoughts of seeking worldly blessings or pleasures, one aspires solely for unsurpassed, pure enlightenment.
These upāsakas had all already established themselves securely upon the bodhisattva path, and they further thought:
"Now that the Tathāgata has accepted our food, he shall enter parinirvāṇa."

Having had this thought, the hair on their bodies stood on end; blood appeared all over their limbs like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling their eyes, they were overcome by great anguish. Each brought articles of offering, loaded upon jeweled chariots—incense wood, banners, streamers, precious canopies, and food and drink—and quickly went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and offered the articles they had brought to the Tathāgata. After circumambulating him hundreds of thousands of times, they raised their voices and wailed, their lamentation moving heaven and earth.
Beating their breasts and crying out, tears fell like rain, and they spoke to one another: "Alas, O virtuous ones! How bitter it is!"
"The world is empty; the world is empty.
Having said this, he raised his entire body, threw himself before the Tathāgata, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering."
The World-Honored One, knowing the time was not yet right, remained silent and did not accept.
Thus he requested three times, but was refused each time.
The upāsakas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and stood there in silence.

It is just as if a compassionate father had an only son who suddenly fell ill and passed away; having carried the corpse to the burial mound and returned home, he was filled with desolation, sorrow, and anguish.
The upāsakas were likewise filled with grief and distress; they set out various offerings in one place, then withdrew to one side and sat in silence.
At that time, there were also as many upāsikās as the sands of three Ganges Rivers, who upheld the five precepts and were fully endowed with dignified deportment.
Their names were Upāsikā Jīvaśrī, Upāsikā Guṇamālā, and Upāsikā Viśākhā; these eighty-four thousand led the assembly as their foremost members.

She was fully capable of upholding and protecting the True Dharma; for the sake of delivering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, she manifested in a female body to censure the ways of the household life.

She contemplated her own body as being like four venomous snakes; this body is constantly being devoured by immeasurable worms; this body is foul and filthy, a prison bound by lust; this body is loathsome, like a dead dog; this body is impure, with its nine orifices constantly flowing.

This body is like a city: flesh, blood, sinews, and bones are wrapped in skin upon it; the hands and feet serve as watchtowers and battlements; the eyes are the openings; and the head is the palace hall. With the king of the mind dwelling within, this city of the body is abandoned by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, yet is constantly relished and clung to by foolish ordinary people; therein dwell the rākṣasas of greed, anger, and ignorance.
This body is not firm; it is like a reed, an eranda tree, a bubble on the water, or a plantain tree.

This body is impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment of thought; it is like a flash of lightning, a torrential flood, or a mirage, and is also like drawing on water—the mark is joined together as soon as it is drawn.
This body is easily destroyed, like a great tree standing on a steep riverbank.
Before long, this body shall become food for foxes, wolves, owls, crows, vultures, ravens, magpies, and hungry dogs.
What wise person would take pleasure in this body?
One might as well attempt to contain the waters of the great ocean within the hoofprint of an ox; it is impossible to fully describe how this body is impermanent, impure, and foul-smelling.

One might as well roll the great earth into a ball the size of a jujube fruit, gradually reducing it to the size of a mustard seed and even down to a minute atom; yet one could not fully describe the faults and afflictions of this body.
Therefore, you should abandon them as one discards mucus or spittle.
For this reason, all upāsikās should constantly cultivate their minds through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

She deeply delights in inquiring about and receiving Mahāyāna sūtras; having heard them, she is also able to expound them for others. She protects and upholds her original vows, disparaging the female body as something utterly loathsome and wearying, its nature being unstable. Her mind constantly cultivates and accumulates such right contemplation, thereby destroying the boundless cycle of birth and death.
Having thirstily yearned for the Mahāyāna and already attained personal fulfillment, she is further able to satisfy others who likewise thirst for it.

Deeply delighting in the Mahāyāna and guarding the Mahāyāna, although she manifests in a female body, she is in truth a Bodhisattva. She is skillfully able to accord with all worlds, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated. She upholds the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it shall never be severed; in future ages she shall turn the wheel of Dharma, adorning herself with great adornments and firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts. Having fully accomplished such merits as these, she gives rise to a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings, regarding them with impartiality and without duality, as if looking upon an only child.
Again, at the early hour when the sun first rose, they said to one another, "Today we ought to go to the space between the twin trees.

The offerings prepared by the upāsikās were twice as magnificent as before; carrying them to the Buddha's dwelling, they prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have now prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha; we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our offering.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant his permission.
The upāsikās, their wishes unfulfilled, sat to one side with hearts full of sorrow.

At that time, there were also as many Licchavis from the city of Vaiśālī as there are grains of sand in four Ganges Rivers—men and women, young and old, together with their wives, children, and retinues—as well as the kings and their retinues throughout Jambudvīpa. For the sake of seeking the Dharma, they had well-cultivated their moral conduct and were fully endowed with dignified deportment; they had subdued heterodox teachers and those who would destroy the true Dharma, and they constantly said to one another:
"We shall provide gold, silver, and storehouses so that the ambrosial, inexhaustible, and profound treasury of the True Dharma may long abide in the world."
"May we always be able to practice and study; should there be anyone who slanders the Buddha’s True Dharma, we shall cut out their tongue.
He further made this vow:
"Should there be any who have left the household life and violate the prohibitive precepts, I shall compel them to return to secular life and subject them to labor."
If there are those who can deeply delight in and protect the True Dharma, I shall honor them as I would my own parents.
If there are members of the Sangha who can practice the True Dharma, I shall rejoice in their efforts and enable them to attain power and influence.
They always desired to hear Mahāyāna sūtras, and having heard them, were also able to explain them extensively for others; they had all fully accomplished such merits.
Their names were: Vimalagarbha Licchavi, Vimalāpramāda Licchavi, and Gaṅgāvimalaśuddhaguṇa Licchavi. Thus, each addressed the others, saying:
"Virtuous ones, you should now proceed quickly to the place where the Buddha is.

As for the various offerings to be prepared, they were to be complete in every respect; each Licchavi adorned eighty-four thousand great elephants, eighty-four thousand precious chariots drawn by four horses, eighty-four thousand moon-bright jewels, and eighty-four thousand bundles of firewood consisting of celestial wood, sandalwood, and aloeswood. Of each of these varieties, there were eighty-four thousand.

Before each elephant, there were jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies; the smallest of these canopies measured one yojana in circumference and extent, the shortest of the streamers was thirty-two yojanas long, and the lowest of the jeweled banners stood one hundred yojanas high.
Carrying such articles of offering as these, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We have now prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha; we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our offering.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant his consent.
The Licchavis and others, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress.
By the supernatural power of the Buddha, they rose seven *tāla* trees high from the ground and remained silently suspended in mid-air.

At that time, there were also ministers and elders as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers who revered the Mahāyāna; if there were followers of heterodox schools who slandered the True Dharma, these people had the power to subdue them, just as a shower of hail destroys grasses and trees.
Their names were:
the elder Sūryaprabha, the elder Lokapāla, and the elder Dharmapāla; these and others served as the leaders.

The offerings they prepared were five times greater than before, and together they proceeded to the space between the twin śāla trees. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulating him hundreds of thousands of times, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We now prepare various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha; we only pray that you will take pity on us and accept our offerings.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept them.
The elders, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress;
yet, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, they rose seven *tāla* trees’ height above the ground and remained suspended in mid-air in silence.

At that time, there were also kings of Vaiśālī, numbering as many as the sands of six Ganges Rivers, along with their palace ladies, wives, and retinues; as well as all the kings within Jambudvīpa, excluding Ajātaśatru and the people of the cities, towns, and villages.
Their names were Moon-Stainless King and others; each, having arrayed the fourfold army, desired to go to where the Buddha was.
Each of these kings had a retinue of one hundred and eighty trillion subjects.

These chariot troops were drawn by elephants and horses; the elephants had six tusks, and the horses were as swift as the wind. Their ornaments and equipment were six times more magnificent than those before.

Among the precious canopies, even the smallest measured eight *yojanas* in circumference and length and breadth; the shortest banners were sixteen *yojanas* long, and the lowest jeweled standards were thirty-six *yojanas* high.

All these kings were fully established in the True Dharma; they detested and despised false teachings, revered the Mahāyāna, and took deep delight in the Mahāyāna. They felt compassion for sentient beings, regarding them all equally as their only child. The fragrance of the food and drink they possessed spread forth, filling four yojanas.
Again, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, he took these various kinds of exquisite and delicious foods, went to the twin trees to where the Tathāgata was, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"We have prepared these offerings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; we only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will accept our final offering.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, did not grant his consent.
These kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, there were also queens from as many kingdoms as there are grains of sand in seven Ganges Rivers; with the sole exception of King Ajātaśatru’s queen, they had all manifested in female bodies for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
They constantly observed their physical conduct and cultivated their minds through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness,
and wishlessness. Their names were Lady Wondrous of the Three Realms and Lady Loving Virtue.

All these queens of the various kings were likewise established in the True Dharma; they practiced the prohibitive precepts, were complete in dignified deportment, and felt compassion for sentient beings as if for an only son. They said to one another:
"We should now go quickly to the place where the World-Honored One resides."

The offerings provided by the queens of the various kings were seven times greater than before: fragrant flowers, precious banners, silken streamers, pennants, canopies, and exquisite food and drink. The smallest of the precious canopies measured sixteen *yojanas* in circumference and breadth; the shortest of the pennants was thirty-six *yojanas* long; the lowest of the precious banners was sixty-eight *yojanas* high; and the fragrance of the food and drink spread everywhere, filling an area of eight *yojanas*.

Carrying such articles of offering as these, they went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We have prepared these offerings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; we only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will accept our final offering.
Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept.

At that time, the various ladies, their wishes unfulfilled, harbored grief and distress in their hearts; they tore out their hair and beat their breasts, wailing loudly as if they had recently lost a beloved son, then withdrew to one side and remained there in silence.
At that time, there were also goddesses as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, with the goddess Viśālanetrī as their leader, who spoke these words: "O sisters!..."
"Observe closely, observe closely! These multitudes of people have prepared various kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings, wishing to present them to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus.
We, too, should likewise prepare subtle and wonderful offerings to make an offering to the Tathāgata; once the Tathāgata has accepted them, he shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"Sisters!
The appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world is extremely rare; to make offerings to them at their final passing is even more difficult.
If a Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, the world becomes empty and desolate."
These celestial maidens delight in the Mahāyāna and desire to hear it; having heard it, they are also able to explain it extensively for others.

Having themselves become fully satisfied through their thirsting aspiration for the Mahāyāna, they are further able to satisfy those who likewise thirst and aspire. They protect the Mahāyāna, and if there are followers of other teachings who harbor hatred and jealousy toward the Mahāyāna, they have the power to crush them, just as hail destroys grass.

They uphold the precepts and are fully endowed with dignified deportment; they are skillfully able to accord with all worldly ways, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated. In future worlds, they shall turn the wheel of Dharma and succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem, ensuring it is never severed. They study and practice the Mahāyāna, adorning themselves with great adornments, and thus accomplish immeasurable merits. With equal compassion for all sentient beings, they regard them as if looking upon an only son.

Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rises, each takes various kinds of celestial incense and fragrant woods—twice as many as all the fragrant woods found among humans—the fragrance of which can eliminate all manner of foul odors and impurities among human beings.

There were white chariots with white canopies, each drawn by four white horses. Upon every chariot, white curtains were spread; from the four sides of these curtains hung golden bells, various fragrant flowers, precious banners, flags, and canopies. There were exquisite delicacies, various musical performances, and lion thrones were laid out. The four legs of each throne were made of pure dark-blue lapis lazuli. Behind each throne was a leaning couch made of the seven treasures, and before each throne was a golden table. Furthermore, there were lamp-stands made of the seven treasures, with various precious gems serving as lamps. Sublime celestial flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground.
After these celestial maidens had presented this offering, their hearts were filled with sorrow and they shed copious tears, experiencing great anguish.

Yet, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to manifest the Tathāgata’s secret teachings of skillful means, and to ensure that the various methods of preaching the Dharma would not be interrupted, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it.
The goddesses, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress.
They withdrew to one side and sat in silence.
At that time, there were also as many dragon kings as the sands of nine Ganges Rivers dwelling in the four directions,
with the dragon kings Vāsuki, Nanda, and Upananda as their leaders.

These dragon kings, likewise at the early morning hour when the sun first rises, prepared various offerings twice as magnificent as those of humans and devas. Carrying them to the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
These dragon kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, there were also as many yakṣa-king spirits as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers, with King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader, who each said to one another:
"O virtuous ones, you should now quickly proceed to the place where the Buddha is."

They prepared offerings twice as grand as those of the other nāgas and carried them to the Buddha’s dwelling. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulating him a hundred thousand times, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We pray only that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not grant his request.
These kṣetrapāla kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, there were also twenty Ganges-sands of *garuḍa* kings, with the *Garuda* King Subduer of Enemies as their leader.
There were also thirty Ganges-sands of *gandharva* kings, with the *Gandharva* King Narada as their leader.
Furthermore, there were kings of the kinnaras, as numerous as the sands of forty Ganges Rivers, with King Sudarśana as their leader.
Furthermore, there were kings of the mahoragas, as numerous as the sands of fifty Ganges Rivers, with King Mahāsudarśana as their leader.
Furthermore, there were sixty Ganges-sands of asura kings, with King Śāmbala as their leader.
Additionally, there were seventy Ganges-sands of dhānava kings, with King Vimalanadī and King Bhadradatta as their leaders.

Furthermore, there were eighty *gangesā-samudra* numbers of rākṣasa kings, with King Bhīṣma as their leader; they abandoned their evil minds and ceased eating humans, giving rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion toward those they previously hated. Though their forms were once hideous, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they all became handsome and upright.
Furthermore, there were ninety *gaṅgā*-sands of forest spirit kings (*vanadevatā-rāja*), with King Delighting in Fragrance (*Gandharati*) as their leader.
Furthermore, there were a thousand *gaṅgā*-sands of mantra-holding kings (*dhāraṇīdhara-rāja*), with Great Illusion Mantra-Holding King (*Mahāmāyā-dhāraṇīdhara-rāja*) as their leader.
Furthermore, there were one hundred million *gaṅgānadīvāluka* spirits of lustful form, with King Sudarśana as their leader.
Additionally, there were ten billion *gaṅgānadīvāluka* celestial courtesans, with Lambā, Urvaśī, Tilottamā, and Viśvakā as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were a thousand billion earth-dwelling ghost kings, with King Bai-shi as their leader.
There were also ten trillion *Ganges*-sands worth of devaputras, as well as various celestial kings, including the Four Heavenly Kings.

Furthermore, there were wind deities of the four quarters, as numerous as the sands of ten trillion *gaṅgā* rivers, who blew upon the trees, scattering seasonal and non-seasonal flowers between the twin trees.
Again, there were cloud-and-rain deities, as numerous as the sands of ten trillion *gaṅgā* rivers, all of whom thought:

"When the Tathāgata enters *nirvāṇa* and his body is cremated, we shall pour down rain so that the fire may be extinguished at the proper time, providing coolness for those among the assembly who are distressed by the heat."

Furthermore, there were twenty *gaṅgā* rivers’ worth of great fragrant elephant kings—namely, Rāhu Elephant King, Golden Elephant King, Sweet-Taste Elephant King, Azure-Eye Elephant King, and Desire-Fragrance Elephant King—who were the leaders among them. Revering and delighting in the Mahāyāna, and knowing that the Buddha would soon enter parinirvāṇa, they each plucked countless and boundless exquisite lotus flowers and came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Furthermore, there were as many lion kings as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers, with the Lion’s Roar King as their leader, bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Carrying various flowers and fruits, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were twenty times as many as the sands of the Ganges of various bird kings—ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, gandharva birds, kalavinka birds, mynas and parrots, kucira birds, vahika birds, kalavinka birds, and jivajivaka birds—and such birds as these, carrying various flowers and fruits, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were water buffaloes, oxen, and sheep, as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers, who went to where the Buddha was and yielded wondrously fragrant milk. This milk flowed until it filled all the ditches and pits within the city of Kuśinagara, being fully endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor. Having accomplished this deed, they withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were as many ṛṣis from the four continents as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers, with the Ṛṣi Kṣāntivādin as their leader. Carrying various fragrant flowers and sweet fruits, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We pray only that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our final offering.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not grant his request.
At that time, the rishis, their wishes unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Among all the bee-kings in Jambudvīpa, the Bee-King Wondrous Sound was the foremost; carrying various kinds of flowers, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him once, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, all the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs within Jambudvīpa assembled, with the sole exception of the two groups led by the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda.

Furthermore, throughout the intervals between immeasurable, incalculable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as all the mountains in Jambudvīpa—of which Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is the foremost—the mountains were magnificently adorned. The forests were lush and verdant; the trees flourished with spreading branches that shielded the sun’s rays. Various exquisite flowers were found everywhere, and dragon springs and flowing streams were pure, fragrant, and pristine.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as divine seers, incantation masters, performers, and musicians—such multitudes as these filled the space within.
These mountain deities also came to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were incalculable numbers of deities of the four great oceans and various river deities, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, who possessed great majestic virtue and possessed of great supernormal powers; the offerings they presented were twice as superior as those before.
The bodily radiance of the various deities, their musical performances, and their lamps completely eclipsed the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared.
They scattered campaka flowers over the River Hiraṇyavatī and approached the Buddha’s dwelling; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, in the śāla grove of the city of Kuśinagara, the trees turned white like white cranes.

In the midst of the sky, there spontaneously appeared pavilions made of the seven treasures, with intricate carvings and engravings clearly and exquisitely adorned; they were surrounded by railings interspersed with various jewels.

Beneath the hall, there are many flowing springs and bathing pools, filled with the most exquisite lotus flowers, resembling the northern land of Uttarakuru and the Joyful Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the midst of the Śāla grove was adorned with various ornaments and was likewise exceedingly delightful.
All these devas, humans, asuras, and others, beholding the signs of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, were moved by grief and sorrow, and found no joy.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra-devānām-indra each said to one another:
"Observe, all of you: the devas, humans, and asuras have prepared a grand offering, desiring to make their final offering to the Tathāgata."
We, too, should likewise make such offerings; if I am the last to receive this offering, then the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) will be accomplished and fulfilled without difficulty.
At that time, the offerings presented by the Four Heavenly Kings were twice as magnificent as those before;
they brought mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, karkārava flowers,
mahākarkārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, and saṃtānikā flowers.
...mahāsaṃtānikā flowers, priyaṅgu flowers, mahāpriyaṅgu flowers, samantabhadra flowers, mahāsamantabhadra flowers,
kāla flowers, mahākāla flowers, gandhapura flowers, mahāgandhapura flowers,
nandana flowers, mahānandana flowers, saṃkalpa flowers, and mahāsaṃkalpa flowers.
They brought *gandhamādana* flowers, *mahāgandhamādana* flowers, *samantagandha* flowers, *mahāsamantagandha* flowers, *devasuvarṇapatra* flowers,
*nāgapuṣpa* flowers, *pārijātaka* tree flowers, and *kovidāra* tree flowers; furthermore,
they carried various kinds of exquisite and delicious foods and came to where the Buddha was, prostrating at his feet.
The radiance of all these devas and humans was able to eclipse the sun and moon, causing them no longer to appear.
With these offerings, they wished to make an offering to the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept them.
At that time, the devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Then Śakra-devānām-indra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven prepared various offerings even more magnificent than before; the flowers they brought were likewise of such a nature that their fragrance was subtle and most delightful. Carrying the Hall of Victory and its various smaller halls, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, we deeply delight in and cherish the Mahāyāna. We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our food.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
Then the Śakras of the devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Extending even to the sixth heaven, the offerings presented became increasingly superior to those before, consisting of precious banners, pennants, and canopies.

The smallest of the precious canopies covered the four continents; the shortest of the pennants reached around the four seas; and the lowest of the banners extended as far as the Heaven of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*). When a gentle breeze blew upon the pennants, they produced wondrous sounds.
Carrying superior delicacies, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the time, remained silent and did not accept.
These devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Reaching upward as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all the remaining Brahma hosts gathered together.
At that time, Mahābrahmā and the other Brahma hosts emitted bodily radiance that pervaded the four continents.
In the desire realm, among humans and devas, the light of the sun and moon no longer appeared at all.

Carrying various jeweled banners, silken streamers, pennants, and canopies—even the shortest pennants reaching from the Brahma palace to the space between the śāla trees—they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
At that time, the Brahmās, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, together with an immeasurable retinue of great asuras, whose bodily radiance surpassed that of Brahmā, carrying various jeweled banners, silken streamers, pennants, and canopies—the smallest of which could cover a thousand worlds—and bearing exquisite, sweet delicacies, came to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept this final offering from us."
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
The asuras, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, together with his retinue, the celestial maidens, and an immeasurable, boundless, incalculable multitude, opened the gates of hell and provided clear, cool water, saying to them:

"Now you have no power to act; you should simply focus your minds on the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and establish this final offering of sympathetic joy, which shall cause you to obtain peace for a long night."
At that time, within the hells, Māra Pāpīyān completely removed the swords and the immeasurable bitter poisons, and caused a torrential rain to fall to extinguish the blazing, fiery flames.

Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he further gave rise to this thought and caused all his retinue to cast away their swords, bows and arrows, armor and weapons, spears and lances, long hooks, golden mallets, battle-axes, discuses, and nooses. The offerings they brought were twice as magnificent as those prepared by all humans and devas; even the smallest of their parasols could cover a medium chiliocosm. They came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“We now love and delight in the Mahāyāna, and we shall protect the Mahāyāna.”
“World-Honored One!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the sake of making offerings, out of fear, to deceive others, for the sake of wealth and profit, or to follow another, receive this Mahāyāna—whether they be genuine or counterfeit—at that time we shall, for the sake of such persons, eliminate their fears and recite this mantra:

‘Ṭa ki | ṭaṭara-ṭaki | lohale | mahālohale | ara | cara | tara | svāhā. This mantra can cause those who have lost their minds, those who are fearful, those who preach the Dharma, and those who do not sever the True Dharma—to subdue non-Buddhists, protect their own bodies, protect the True Dharma, and protect the Mahāyāna—by reciting this mantra.”

If there are those who can uphold such a mantra, they will have no fear of wild elephants; even when entering wildernesses, desolate marshes, or treacherous places, they will give rise to no fear, nor will they suffer from water or fire, lions, tigers, wolves, bandits, or royal calamities.
World-Honored One!
If there are those who can uphold such a mantra, they will be able to completely eliminate all such fears.
World-Honored One!
"To those who uphold this mantra, we shall provide protection, just as a tortoise hides its six limbs.
World-Honored One!
We now speak these words not out of flattery or deceit; to those who uphold this mantra, we shall, with utmost sincerity, augment their power."
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Māra Pāpīyas, saying:

"I do not accept your offering of food and drink; I have already accepted the divine mantra you have spoken for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings and the fourfold assembly."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, he remained silent and did not accept.
Thus he was requested three times, yet he still did not accept.
Then Māra Pāpīyas, his wishes unfulfilled, harbored sorrow and distress in his heart and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Great Lord Maheśvara, together with his immeasurable and boundless retinue and the hosts of devas, presented offerings that completely eclipsed all the offerings of Brahmā, Śakra, the four world-protecting kings, the eight classes of gods and humans, as well as non-humans.
That which was provided by Brahmā and Śakra appeared like a collection of ink beside a conch shell, and was no longer visible at all.
The smallest of the precious canopies was able to cover a trichiliocosm.
Carrying such articles of offering as these, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The meager offerings we present are like a mosquito offering sustenance to me, or like someone casting a single handful of water into the great ocean, or lighting a small lamp to assist the hundred-thousand suns; it is like taking a single flower from among the profuse blossoms of spring and summer, or adding a *ting-li* seed to Mount Sumeru—how could these ever truly benefit the great ocean, the brilliance of the sun, the multitude of flowers, or Mount Sumeru?
"World-Honored One!
The meager offerings I now present are likewise so.
Even if one were to fill a trichiliocosm with fragrant flowers, music, banners, and canopies to make offerings to the Tathāgata, it would still not be worth mentioning."
Why is this? Because for the sake of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata constantly undergoes various sufferings and afflictions within the evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will look upon us with compassion and accept our offerings.

At that time, to the east of this world, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands, there was a buddha-field named *Manojña-svara*. There, the Buddha was named Ākāśasama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, that Buddha addressed his foremost great disciple, saying:

"Good son, you should now go to the Sahā world in the western direction. In that land there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; that Buddha will before long enter parinirvāṇa."
"Good son!

You may take this fragrant food of this world—this food is delicious and brings peace and security when eaten—and offer it to that Buddha, the World-Honored One. After the World-Honored One has partaken of this food, he will enter parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! You may all pay homage and request that your doubts be resolved.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantagātra accepted the Buddha’s instruction; he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and together with immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, set out from that land and arrived here in this Sahā world.
At that moment, the great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

Thereupon, within the assembly—Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, Māra Pāpīyas, Maheśvara, and such a great multitude—seeing this earthquake, their body hairs stood on end, their throats and tongues grew parched, and they were struck with such terror and trembling that each wished to flee in all directions.
They saw their own bodies no longer possess radiance, and all their majestic power was utterly extinguished without remainder.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat and addressed the great assembly:
"O sons of good family!
"Do not be afraid, do not be afraid! Why is this?

To the east of here, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable, incalculable, asaṃkhyeya Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a world named Manojñābhirāma-ghoṣa. There dwells a Buddha named Ākāśasama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. There is a bodhisattva there named Anantakāya, who, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas, wishes to come here to make offerings to the Tathāgata."
Because of that bodhisattva’s power of majestic virtue, the radiance of your bodies has all ceased to appear.
Therefore, you should give rise to joy and harbor no fear.
At that time, the great assembly all saw that Buddha and his assembly from afar, as if looking at their own bodies in a clear mirror.
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the assembly again:
"What you now see of that Buddha and his assembly is just like seeing this Buddha."
"By the Buddha's spiritual power, you shall likewise behold immeasurable Buddhas in the nine directions.
At that time, the great assembly said to one another: "Alas! Alas!"
"The world is empty; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, the entire great assembly beheld the Bodhisattva Anantakāya and his retinue.

From every single pore of this Bodhisattva’s body, there emerged a great lotus flower. Each of these lotus flowers contained seventy-eight thousand cities, equal in length and breadth to the city of Vaiśālī. Their walls and moats were interspersed with the seven treasures, and rows of precious *tāla* trees stood in seven tiers. The population was flourishing, peaceful, and prosperous. The defensive towers were made of Jambūnada gold, and each tower was adorned with various kinds of the seven treasures. The groves, trees, flowers, and fruits were lush and abundant; when a gentle breeze stirred them, they produced subtle and wondrous sounds, harmonious and elegant like celestial music.
The people within the city, hearing these sounds, immediately experienced supreme and wondrous bliss.
Within these moats, exquisite waters filled them completely, pure, fragrant, and clean like genuine lapis lazuli.
Within these waters are boats made of the seven treasures; people board them to frolic, bathe, and enjoy themselves together, their happiness being boundless.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable lotuses of various colors—*utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers—each of which is as large in length and breadth as a chariot wheel.

Upon the banks of those moats, there are many groves and gardens; within each garden are five spring-pools. Within these pools grow various flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (kumuda), yellow lotuses (padma), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka). These flowers are as large in length and breadth as chariot wheels, their fragrance is most exquisite, and they are exceedingly delightful.
The water is supremely pure and soft, where wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks sport and play.

Within each garden are various palatial residences made of many jewels; each residence is exactly four yojanas in length and breadth. All the walls are composed of the four treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with doors of pure gold. They are surrounded by railings, and the ground is of ruby, strewn with golden sand.

Within this palace and its grounds, there are many flowing springs and bathing pools made of the seven treasures; by the side of each pool, there are eighteen golden staircases, with *jambūnada* gold forming the plantain trees, like the Nandana Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

In each of these cities, there were eighty-four thousand kings; each king had immeasurable numbers of consorts and court ladies with whom they enjoyed themselves, delighting in pleasure and happiness.
The rest of the people were likewise; each, in their own dwelling place, enjoyed themselves together.
Among those beings, no other names were heard, but only the sound of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna was heard.

Within each of these flowers, there was a lion throne; the four legs of each throne were made of deep blue lapis lazuli, and upon the seats were spread soft, white garments—garments so subtle and exquisite that they surpassed all things within the triple world.

On each seat sat a king, who taught and transformed sentient beings through the Mahāyāna Dharma; some sentient beings copied, upheld, read, and recited it, practicing according to the teachings, thus disseminating the Mahāyāna sūtras.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, having settled these immeasurable sentient beings within himself and caused them to renounce worldly pleasures, spoke these words:
"Alas, alas! How bitter it is!"
"The world is empty; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, surrounded on all sides by immeasurable bodhisattvas, having manifested such supernatural powers, took these various and boundless offerings, as well as exquisite and delicious food and drink. If anyone caught the fragrance of this food, all their afflictions and defilements were completely extinguished.
By virtue of this Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers, the entire assembly was able to behold such transformations.
The body of the Bodhisattva Anantagātra was infinitely large, its measure equal to space; except for the Buddhas, no one else was able to perceive the limits or boundaries of this Bodhisattva’s body.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue prepared offerings even more magnificent than those before; they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We only pray that you will have compassion for us and accept our food.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
Thus he was invited three times, yet he did not accept on any occasion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue withdrew to stand to one side.

Likewise, from the Buddha-worlds of the south, west, and north, there were also immeasurable Bodhisattvas named Anantagātra; the offerings they brought were twice as magnificent as those before. They came to where the Buddha was, and even withdrew to stand to one side—all in exactly the same manner.

At that time, the auspicious and blessed site between the twin śāla trees was thirty-two yojanas in length and breadth, filled with a great assembly such that there was not a single empty space between them.

At that time, the places where the Bodhisattva Anantakāya and his retinue sat were like the point of an awl, the tip of a needle, or a mote of dust. Great Bodhisattvas from Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, all came to this assembly; likewise, all the great multitudes of Jambudvīpa also gathered there—excepting only the two groups of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, King Ajātaśatru and his retinue, and even venomous snakes whose gaze can kill, dung beetles, vipers, scorpions, and those who commit the sixteen kinds of evil deeds—all of whom came to assemble.
The Dānava spirits, the Asuras, and others all abandoned their evil thoughts and gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness, regarding one another as fathers, mothers, elder sisters, or younger sisters;
likewise, the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm turned toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness, with the sole exception of those who hold to the icchantika view.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the ground of this trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple; it was devoid of mounds, ravines, soil, sand, gravel, thorns, and poisonous weeds, and was adorned with various jewels, just like the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha Amitāyus in the western quarter.

At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, just as one sees one's own body in a clear mirror; their vision of the various Buddha-lands was likewise so.
At that time, the five-colored light issuing from the Tathāgata’s face shone forth and overspread the entire great assembly, causing the bodily radiance of all those present to vanish entirely;
having performed what was to be done, the light returned and entered back through his mouth.

At that time, the devas, humans, and the entire assembly, including the asuras, seeing the Buddha’s radiance re-enter through his mouth, were all seized with great terror; their hair stood on end, and they spoke thus:

"The Tathāgata’s radiance has emerged and now returns within; this cannot be without cause or condition. It must be that what was to be done in the ten directions has been accomplished, and this is surely the sign of his final nirvana."
How tragic, how tragic! How can this be?

World-Honored One, you have suddenly abandoned the four immeasurable minds and will no longer accept the offerings presented by devas and humans. The sun of noble wisdom shall from now on be forever extinguished, and the unsurpassed Dharma-ship shall sink here and now.
"Alas, how painful! What great suffering is this in the world!

Raising his hands to beat his breast, he wailed and wept with such intensity that his limbs trembled and he could not support himself; blood flowed from all the pores of his body, drenching the ground.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Āyuṣka-paṭala, Part One, Section Two.
At that time, in the assembly, there was an upāsaka named Cunda, the son of an artisan from the city of Kuśinagara, who was accompanied by fifteen of his peers.

In order that the world might obtain wholesome fruits, he set aside his dignified bearing, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, wept with tears falling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will compassionately accept our final offering for the sake of delivering immeasurable sentient beings.”
"World-Honored One!

From this day forth, we are without a master, without kin, without rescue, without protection, without refuge, and without a destination; we are impoverished and famished. We wish to seek our future sustenance from the Tathāgata; we only pray that you will take pity on us, accept our humble offering, and then enter parinirvāṇa."
“World-Honored One!

It is like a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra who, because of poverty, travels far to another country and exerts his labor in farming. He obtains well-trained oxen and excellent fields that are level and even, free from all saline soil, weeds, and stumps; he only longs for rain from heaven.”
The phrase "taming the ox" is a metaphor for the seven [transgressions] of body and speech.
"Excellent fields that are level and even" is a metaphor for wisdom.
"Removing the saline soil, weeds, and stumps" is a metaphor for eliminating afflictions (*kleśa*).
“World-Honored One!
My present body has been tamed like an ox, its fertile field cleared of stumps and brambles; I now only long for the Tathāgata’s rain of ambrosial Dharma.
As for those of the four castes who are poor, I am one such: I am destitute of the wealth and treasures of the unsurpassed Dharma.”
We only pray that you will take pity on us, sever our poverty and suffering, and extend your salvation to immeasurable beings tormented by distress.
Although what we now offer is meager, we hope it may suffice for the assembly of the Tathāgata.
"I am now without a master, without kin, and without refuge; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion, just as you did for Rāhula.
At that time, the World-Honored One—the All-Knowing One, the Unsurpassed Tamer—addressed Cunda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
I shall now eliminate your poverty for you; I will rain down the unsurpassed Dharma-rain upon the field of your body, causing the sprouts of the Dharma to grow.
Since you now seek from me longevity, physical strength, peace, and eloquence, I shall bestow upon you eternal life, physical strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence.
Why is this? Cunda!
There are two kinds of giving food, yet their karmic rewards do not differ.
What are these two?
First, having received [the prediction], one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
second, having received [the prediction], one enters *nirvāṇa*.
"I now accept your final offering, so that you may fulfill the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, that there is no difference between the karmic fruits of these two kinds of giving is not correct."

Why is this? Those who receive offerings first have not yet exhausted their afflictions and have not yet attained the realization of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); nor have they been able to cause sentient beings to fully fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Those who receive offerings later have already exhausted their afflictions and have already attained the realization of all-knowledge; they are able to cause sentient beings everywhere to fully fulfill the perfection of giving.
Those who receive offerings first are merely sentient beings;
those who receive offerings later are the God among Gods.
Those who receive offerings first possess a body of mixed food, a body of afflictions, a final body, and an impermanent body.
The recipient who receives the gift later possesses a body free from afflictions, a vajra-body, a dharma-body, an eternal body, and a boundless body.
How can it be said that the karmic rewards of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction?

The one who receives the gift first has not yet fulfilled the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, possessing only the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and not yet having attained the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) up to the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*).
The one who receives the gift later has already attained fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and is fully endowed with the Buddha-eye up to the wisdom-eye.
"How can you say that the karmic fruits of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction?
World-Honored One!
When the first recipient receives the gift, having eaten it, it enters the stomach and is digested; they thereby obtain life, physical form, strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence."
"If the recipient of the offering later does not eat it, does not digest it, and lacks the five kinds of fruits,
how can you say that the retributive results of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! The Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, has possessed no body of food, no body of afflictions, and no final body; he possesses the eternal body, the Dharma-body, and the Vajra-body.”
Good son, those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature are said to possess a body of afflictions and a body sustained by various foods; this is their final body.

When the Bodhisattva has received food and drink at that time, he enters the Vajra Samādhi. Once this food is digested, he immediately sees the Buddha-nature and attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, I say that the karmic fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.

At that time, the Bodhisattva destroyed the four māras; now, upon entering nirvāṇa, he likewise destroys the four māras. For this reason, I say that the karmic fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.

Although the Bodhisattva did not extensively expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures at that time, he had already mastered them previously; now, upon entering nirvana, he will analyze and explain them in detail for the sake of all sentient beings. For this reason, I say that the karmic rewards of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.
"Good son!
The body of the Tathāgata has not received food or drink for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Yet, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he said that he first accepted the milk-gruel offered by the two cowherd girls, Nandā and Nandabalā, and only thereafter attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
I truly do not eat.
It is only for the sake of this great assembly that I accept what you offer as my final meal;
in truth, I do not eat.

At that time, the great assembly, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was universally accepting Cunda’s final offering on behalf of the entire congregation, leaped for joy and praised him with one voice, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
How rare, Cunda!
The name you have now established for yourself is not a hollow title.
To be called "Cunda" means to be one who understands the wondrous meaning.
You have now established such a great purpose; therefore, based on the reality of this meaning, you are given the name Cunda.
In this present life, you shall attain great fame and profit, and your virtuous aspirations will be fulfilled.
"How extraordinary, Cunda!
Having been born among humans, you have further attained this most rare and unsurpassed benefit.
Excellent, Cunda!"

As the udumbara flower is rare in the world, so too is the appearance of a Buddha in the world exceedingly difficult; it is further difficult to encounter a Buddha, give rise to faith, and hear the Dharma; yet to be able to perform such a service as this final offering when a Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa is even more difficult than that.
Namo Cunda! Namo Cunda!
You have now fully perfected the *dānapāramitā*, like the autumn moon on the fifteenth night—pure, full, and free from all clouds and mists—which all sentient beings gaze upon with reverence;
you are likewise, and we all look up to you with the same devotion.
The Buddha has already accepted your final offering, enabling you to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Homage to Cunda!
Therefore, it is said that you are like the full moon, whom all sentient beings gaze upon with reverence.
Homage to Cunda!
Although you have received a human body, your mind is like the mind of a Buddha.
You, Cunda, are now truly a son of the Buddha, no different from Rāhula.
At that time, the great assembly spoke these verses:
"Though you were born into the human realm, You have already transcended the sixth heaven.
We and all the multitude Now prostrate ourselves and entreat you."
The Most Honored One among men is now about to enter parinirvāṇa;
out of compassion for us, we pray that you will quickly entreat the Buddha to remain long in this world to benefit immeasurable multitudes of beings.
He shall proclaim the unsurpassed nectar of the Dharma, praised by the wise.
If you do not entreat the Buddha, my life will not be preserved;
therefore, you ought to act on my behalf and respectfully beseech the Teacher, the Tamer of Men.

At that time, Cunda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, like a person whose parents had suddenly died and were then restored to life; Cunda’s joy was just like this. He rose again to pay homage to the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"How wonderful! I have gained my own benefit; I have well obtained this human body.
Having eliminated greed, anger, and the rest, I am forever parted from the three evil realms."
How joyful it is to have gained this personal benefit!
To encounter a hoard of gold and jewels, And to meet the Teacher, the Tamer of Men, One need no longer fear falling into the animal realm.
The Buddha is like the Udumbara flower; To encounter him and give rise to faith is difficult.
Having encountered [the Buddha], those who have already planted roots of goodness will forever leave behind the suffering of the hungry ghosts;
they shall also be able to diminish the ranks of the asuras.
To cast a mustard seed onto the point of a needle is easier than for a Buddha to appear in the world.
By perfecting the practice of giving, I deliver beings from the cycle of birth and death among gods and humans.
The Buddha is unstained by worldly dharmas, like a lotus flower amidst the water;
having skillfully severed the seeds of the Peak of Existence, he forever crosses over the stream of saṃsāra.
To be born as a human in this world is difficult;
to encounter the age of a Buddha is likewise difficult, like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log in the great ocean.
May the merit of the food I now offer bring me the unsurpassed reward.
All fetters of affliction, I have shattered as they are not firm.
Now, in this place, I do not seek the state of gods or humans;
even if I were to obtain them, my heart would find no pleasure therein.
The Tathāgata accepts my offering with immeasurable joy, Just as the eranda flower emits the fragrance of sandalwood.
My body is like the eranda flower; The Tathāgata accepts my offering.
Like the fragrance of sandalwood wafting forth, for this reason I rejoice.
Now I have obtained present retribution in this most excellent and sublime place;
Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas have come to make offerings to me.
All the worlds will give rise to every kind of suffering and affliction, for they know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, intends to enter nirvana.
They cried out these words in a loud voice: "The world is now without a Tamer!"
One should not abandon sentient beings, but regard them as an only son.
The Tathāgata, dwelling among the Saṃgha, expounds the unsurpassed Dharma,
like the precious mountain Sumeru resting securely upon the great ocean.
The Buddha’s wisdom can thoroughly sever the darkness of our ignorance,
just as when clouds arise in the sky, one attains refreshing coolness.
The Tathāgata is able to skillfully eliminate all afflictions.
Just as when the sun rises, its light shines everywhere, dispelling the clouds;
so too these sentient beings, their faces swollen from weeping,
are all adrift upon the waters of suffering caused by birth and death.
"For this reason, World-Honored One, you should increase the faith of sentient beings;
for the sake of severing the suffering of birth and death, please remain long in the world.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said.

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith is likewise exceedingly difficult; yet to be able to fully perfect the perfection of giving by offering food at the very moment the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa is even more difficult still."
"You now, Cunda! Do not grieve so greatly;

you should instead leap for joy and congratulate yourself on having encountered the final opportunity to make offerings to the Tathāgata, thereby fulfilling the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā). You should not request that the Buddha remain long in this world."
"You should now observe that the realms of all Buddhas are entirely impermanent; the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise so.
Then he spoke these verses for Cunda:
"In all worlds, Those who are born must return to death."
Though one's lifespan may be immeasurable, it must inevitably come to an end.
What flourishes must surely decline; those who meet must eventually part.
Youth does not linger for long, and radiant beauty is invaded by disease.
Life is swallowed by death; there is no phenomenon that is eternal.
Though kings attain sovereign power and possess peerless might, all are subject to change and movement; so too is the span of life.
The wheel of manifold suffering is boundless, Cycling on without rest;
The three realms are all impermanent, And within all states of existence there is no joy.
The fundamental nature and characteristics of the Path— All are empty and non-existent.
The flow of conditioned phenomena is subject to destruction, Constantly accompanied by sorrow, affliction, and the like.
Terrorizing are all manner of faults and evils: Old age, sickness, death, decline, and distress.
These are boundless and without end; Easily destroyed and invaded by enemies.
Enveloped by afflictions, like a silkworm within its cocoon, what wise person would find delight in such a state?
This body is a collection of suffering; it is entirely impure.
The shackles, fetters, abscesses, and so forth—these have no fundamental benefit.
Even up to the bodies of the various devas, they are all likewise thus.
All desires are impermanent; therefore, I do not cling to them.
Free from desire and with right reflection, he has realized the truth;
having utterly severed existence, today he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
I have crossed to the other shore of existence and have already transcended all suffering.
Therefore, at this present time, he purely experiences supreme and wondrous bliss.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, he has realized the limit of non-conceptual proliferation;
having forever severed all fetters and bonds, today he enters nirvana.
I am free from old age, illness, and death; my life-span is inexhaustible.
Now I enter parinirvāṇa, like a great fire being extinguished.
Cunda, you should not attempt to fathom the meaning of the Tathāgata.
One should contemplate the Tathāgata’s abiding as being like Mount Sumeru.
Now that I enter parinirvāṇa, I experience the supreme bliss;
such is the nature of all Buddhas’ dharmas—therefore, you should no longer weep.
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is truly as the Holy Teaching declares.”
My present wisdom is so slight and shallow, like that of a mosquito or a gadfly; how could I possibly fathom the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
I am now already with the great dragon-elephants among bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have severed all fetters and outflows, such as the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī and others.
World-Honored One!
It is like a young child who has just left home; although he has not yet received full ordination, he is nonetheless included within the ranks of the Saṃgha.
I am also thus; by the power of the supernatural penetrations of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I have come to be numbered among such great Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, I now wish to cause the Tathāgata to dwell long in this world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
