Just as a hungry person never vomits what they have eaten,
I pray that the World-Honored One will likewise remain forever in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed Cunda, saying: "Cunda!
You should not now utter such words, wishing to cause the Tathāgata to remain forever in the world without entering parinirvāṇa, like that hungry man who could neither transform nor vomit."

"You should now contemplate the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). By contemplating in this way, you will be endowed with the *śūnyatā-samādhi*. If you wish to seek the True Dharma, you should train yourself thus.
Cunda asked: "Mañjuśrī!..."
Now, the Tathāgata is the most honored and supreme among gods and humans; how could such a Tathāgata be a conditioned phenomenon?
If he were a conditioned phenomenon, he would be subject to arising and ceasing.
"Just as a bubble on water arises and perishes swiftly, and as all things come and go in circulation like the wheel of a chariot, so too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
I have heard that the lifespan of the devas is exceedingly long; why then, World-Honored One, is the lifespan of you, the God among Gods, even shorter, not exceeding a hundred years?"

It is like a village headman who possesses power and autonomy; by the force of that autonomy, he can command others. Yet when his merit is exhausted, he subsequently becomes poor and lowly, despised by others, and reduced to being their servant.
Why is this? Because his power would have been lost.
The World-Honored One is likewise; if he were identical to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), then being identical to conditioned phenomena, he could not be called the God among Gods (*devātideva*).
Why is this? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the very nature of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
"Do not view the Tathāgata as being identical to conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
do you speak thus because you know it to be so, or do you speak thus without knowing it— claiming that the Tathāgata is identical to conditioned phenomena?"
If the Tathāgata were the same as ordinary practitioners, one could not say that within the triple world he is the God among Gods, the Sovereign Dharma King.
It is like a king who has a great strongman whose strength equals a thousand men and whom no one else can subdue; therefore, this man alone is said to be "equal to a thousand."
Such a strongman was beloved by the king; the king bestowed upon him noble rank and emoluments, and his rewards were naturally granted.

As for why he was called "one who can match a thousand," it was not necessarily because his physical strength could equal that of a thousand men; rather, because he could surpass a thousand through his various skills and arts, he was thus called "one who can match a thousand."

The Tathāgata is likewise: having subdued the demon of afflictions, the demon of the aggregates, the celestial demon, and the demon of death, he is therefore called the Honored One of the Three Realms, just as that strong man alone can withstand a thousand.
By these causes and conditions, he has accomplished and perfected all manner of immeasurable and true merits; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mañjuśrī!
You should not now engage in conceptualization or discrimination by equating the Dharma of the Tathāgata with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
It is, for example, like a wealthy elder who has a son, and an physiognomist divines that he possesses the marks of a short lifespan.
Having heard this, the parents realized he was incapable of continuing the family lineage; they no longer held him in affection or esteem, regarding him as mere straw.
Furthermore, one who is short-lived is not respected or remembered by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others, whether male or female, young or old.

If the Tathāgata were the same as those who practice conditioned actions, he too would not be honored and revered by all the beings of the world, including gods and humans; furthermore, there would be no one to receive the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, which is unchanging and non-different.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
you should not say that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī:

It is like a poor woman who has no home or protector; moreover, she is oppressed by the suffering of illness and the pangs of hunger and thirst. Wandering about to beg for alms, she takes up residence in another's guest-house and gives birth to a single son there, but the owner of the guest-house drives her out.
Not long after giving birth, she took the child in her arms and wished to travel to another country.

On the way, they encountered a violent wind and rain; cold and suffering came upon them all at once, and they were bitten by many mosquitoes, gadflies, bees, and venomous insects. As they crossed the Ganges, she carried the child as she waded through the water, which flowed with such rapid current that she could not let go; thus, mother and son sank together and perished.
By virtue of such compassionate thoughts, this woman was reborn in the Brahma Heaven after her life ended.

Mañjuśrī! If there are sons of good family who wish to protect the True Dharma, they must not say that the Tathāgata is the same as conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), nor that he is different from conditioned phenomena!
One should only reproach oneself, thinking: "I am now foolish and lack the eye of wisdom; the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
Therefore, one should not declare that the Tathāgata is definitively conditioned or definitively unconditioned."
If one possesses right view, one should say that the Tathāgata is definitively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Why is this?
Because he is able to give rise to wholesome dharmas in sentient beings and because he gives rise to compassion.
Just as that poor woman, while by the Ganges, sacrificed her own life out of love for her child, so too, O son of good family, should a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma act:
rather than sacrificing his body and life, he must never say that the Tathāgata is identical to the conditioned; he should instead say that the Tathāgata is identical to the unconditioned.
Because it is taught that the Tathāgata is identical with the unconditioned, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as that woman attained birth in the Brahma-heaven. Why is this so?
It is for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
How does one protect the Dharma?
It is by declaring that the Tathāgata is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Good son! Although such a person does not seek liberation, liberation arrives of its own accord;
it is like that poor woman who did not seek Brahmā, yet Brahmā arrived of his own accord.

Mañjuśrī! It is like a man traveling far who, becoming utterly exhausted on the road, takes refuge in another’s house. While he is lying there asleep, a great fire suddenly breaks out within the room. He awakens in alarm and immediately reflects:
"I shall certainly die now; of this there is no doubt."
Because he was possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, he wrapped his body in his robes and immediately passed away, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

From that time forward, he became the Great Brahmā King eighty times and was born among humans for a hundred thousand lifetimes as a Wheel-Turning Monarch. This person was never again born in the three evil realms, but was constantly reborn in places of peace and happiness throughout his successive lives.
For this reason, Mañjuśrī,
a son of good family who possesses a sense of shame and modesty should not regard the Buddha as being identical to conditioned phenomena. Mañjuśrī!

It may be said that the heterodox views of non-Buddhists equate the Tathāgata with the conditioned; however, a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts should not give rise to the notion of the Tathāgata as being conditioned.
If one says that the Tathāgata is conditioned, that is false speech;
you should know that such a person, upon death, will enter hell as naturally as a person entering their own home.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is truly an unconditioned dharma; one should not further say that he is conditioned.
From this day forward, within the midst of birth and death, you should abandon ignorance and seek right knowledge; you should know that the Tathāgata is precisely the unconditioned.
If one can contemplate the Tathāgata in this manner, they shall fully attain the thirty-two marks and swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, praised Cunda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"

You have now created the causes and conditions for long life, being able to know that the Tathāgata is a dharma that is eternally abiding, a dharma that is unchanging, and an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.

You have now skillfully concealed the conditioned marks of the Tathāgata, just as that man with the fire on his body covered his body with a garment out of shame; by virtue of this wholesome mind, you will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and further become a Brahmā King or a Cakravartin Wheel-turning Sage King, never falling into the evil realms, but constantly experiencing peace and happiness.

You, too, are like this; because you have skillfully concealed the conditioned marks of the Tathāgata, in a future age you will certainly attain the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, the eighteen unique qualities, and immeasurable lifespan. You shall no longer abide in birth and death but will always experience peace and bliss, and before long you will achieve the state of an Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Cunda! The Tathāgata will later explain this in detail himself. Both you and I shall likewise conceal the conditioned nature of the Tathāgata.
For now, let us set aside both the conditioned and the unconditioned; you should promptly provide food and drink according to the occasion. Such a gift as this is the foremost among all gifts."

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās are exhausted from traveling a long distance, one should provide them with whatever they require at the appropriate time, ensuring that all things are pure.
To give thus swiftly is to possess the fundamental seed of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Cunda!

If there is one who makes a final offering to the Buddha and the Sangha—whether it be much or little, sufficient or insufficient—it is fitting that they act quickly and seize this opportunity, for the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa at this very moment.
Cunda replied, "Mañjuśrī!
For what reason do you now crave this food, speaking of its quantity— whether it is sufficient or insufficient— and thus cause me to give it at this time?"
Mañjuśrī! When the Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years in the past, he was still able to sustain himself; how much more so now, for but a brief moment? Mañjuśrī!
"Do you truly believe that the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, partakes of this food?
However, I know for certain that the body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, not a body sustained by food."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as Cunda has said.
Excellent, Cunda!"
“You have already accomplished subtle and wondrous great wisdom, and have skillfully entered the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
Mañjuśrī said to Cunda:
“If you consider the Tathāgata to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then the body of the Tathāgata is indeed long-lived.”
"If one understands in this way, it will bring joy to the Buddha.
Cunda replied, "The Tathāgata does not find joy in me alone; he likewise finds joy in all sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī said, “The Tathāgata is fully pleased with you, with me, and with all sentient beings.
Cunda replied:
"You should not say that the Tathāgata finds pleasure.
For that which is 'finding pleasure' is a perverted perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*).
If there is a perverted perception, that is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)."
That which possesses birth and death is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
do not say that the Tathāgata is conditioned.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is conditioned, both I and you would be acting under delusion.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata has no thought of attachment or affection.

As for this affectionate concern, it is like a mother cow who loves her calf; even though she wanders in search of water and grass despite being hungry and thirsty, whether she has had enough or not, she suddenly returns home.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, harbor no such thoughts; they regard all beings equally, as they do Rāhula.
Such a way of thinking is precisely the realm of the Buddhas' wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! It is like a king who, driving a team of four noble horses, wishes to have a cart drawn by donkeys catch up with him; such a thing is impossible.
My relationship with you is likewise: to wish to exhaust the subtle, secret, profound, and deep mysteries of the Tathāgata is also impossible.

Mañjuśrī! Just as a garuḍa soars into the void for immeasurable yojanas and looks down upon the great ocean, seeing clearly all the aquatic creatures—fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, and dragons—as well as its own reflection, just as one sees various forms in a bright mirror.
Ordinary worldlings possess little wisdom and cannot fathom such a vision; I and you, likewise, cannot fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī said to Cunda: "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
It is not that I am ignorant of this matter, but I simply wished to test you regarding the affairs of all bodhisattvas."
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various rays of light from his face; these brilliant lights shone upon the body of Mañjuśrī.
Having encountered this light, Mañjuśrī immediately understood its significance and promptly addressed Cunda:
"The Tathāgata now manifests this auspicious sign; before long, he will surely enter parinirvāṇa."
The final offering you have previously prepared should now be presented to the Buddha and the great assembly.
Cunda, you should know that the Tathāgata’s emission of these various kinds of light is not without cause or condition.
Having heard this, Cunda was choked with emotion and remained silent.
The Buddha said to Cunda:
“Regarding the offerings you have presented to the Buddha and the great assembly, now is precisely the right time; the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa.”
A second and a third time he spoke thus.
At that moment, having heard the Buddha’s words, Cunda raised his voice and wept, speaking with a sobbing throat:
"Alas, alas! The world is empty and void!"
They further addressed the great assembly:
"We shall now all together prostrate ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground, and with one voice exhort the Buddha not to enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Cunda:
"Do not weep so bitterly as to wither your heart.

You should contemplate this body as being like a plantain tree, a mirage in the heat, a bubble on water, a magical illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, an unbaked earthen vessel, a flash of lightning; likewise, it is like writing upon water, a prisoner facing execution, ripe fruit, or a piece of meat; it is like a weaving shuttle that has run out of thread, or like a pestle moving up and down. You should contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as food mixed with poison; these conditioned things are full of many faults and afflictions."
Thereupon, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since the Tathāgata does not wish to remain long in this world, how could I refrain from weeping?
Alas, alas! The world is now empty and void."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us and all sentient beings, will remain long in this world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Cunda:
“You should not now speak such words, saying that you would have me remain long in this world out of compassion for you.”
Out of compassion for you and for all beings, I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Such is the nature of all Buddhas; it is likewise the case with all conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, the Buddhas have spoken this verse:
“All conditioned phenomena are by nature impermanent;
having arisen, they do not abide, and their cessation is bliss.”

"Cunda! You should now observe that all conditioned phenomena are a mixture of various dharmas, devoid of self, impermanent, and unstable; this body has many immeasurable faults and afflictions, being like a bubble upon the water. Therefore, you should not weep now."
At that time, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, so it is; it is truly as the World-Honored One has taught.
Although I know that the Tathāgata manifests entry into nirvana through skillful means, I cannot help but harbor distress; yet, upon further reflection, joy arises once more."
The Buddha praised Cunda:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are able to understand that the Tathāgata manifests in common with sentient beings through the skillful means of parinirvāṇa."
Cunda! You should now listen: just as the śarabha birds all gather together at Lake Anavatapta during the months of spring and summer, so too do all the Buddhas come to this place.

Cunda! You should not now contemplate whether the Buddhas have long or short lifespans; all dharmas are like illusory appearances, and the Tathāgata, dwelling within them, remains unstained by any attachment through the power of skillful means.
Why is this? Such is the nature of all Buddhas, Cunda!
I now accept the offerings you have presented, desiring to enable you to cross over the various currents of birth, death, and existence.
Should any humans or devas offer me their final veneration here, they shall all attain the fruit of immovability and forever experience peace and happiness.
Why is this? Because I am a field of merit for all sentient beings.
If you also wish to act as a field of merit for all sentient beings, prepare what you intend to give quickly; it is not fitting to delay long.
At that time, Cunda, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain liberation, bowed his head, suppressed his tears, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
If I were capable of serving as a field of merit, I would be able to discern whether the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa or not.
At present, the wisdom of myself and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is like that of mosquitoes or ants; we truly cannot measure whether the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa or not.
At that time, Cunda and his retinue were filled with grief and wept as they surrounded the Tathāgata, burning incense and scattering flowers, honoring him with all their hearts.
Soon thereafter, he rose from his seat with Mañjuśrī and departed to prepare the utensils for the meal.
Not long after they had left, this earth shook in six ways, and even as far as the Brahma world, it was likewise so.
There are two kinds of earthquakes: either an earthquake or a great earthquake.
A minor tremor is called an earthquake; a major tremor is called a great earthquake.
That which has a low sound is called an earthquake; that which has a loud sound is called a great earthquake.
That which is merely an earthquake is called an earthquake; that which causes mountains, rivers, trees, and the waters of the great ocean to all tremble is called a great earthquake.
That which moves in a single direction is called an earthquake; that which revolves and rotates all around is called a great earthquake.
"Earthquake" refers to the shaking of the earth itself, while "great earthquake" refers to the shaking that causes the minds of sentient beings to tremble at the time of the movement.

When a Bodhisattva first descends from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa, it is called a "great earth tremor"; likewise, from his initial birth, his renunciation, his attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, and his parinirvāṇa, these are called great earth tremors.
"Today the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa; for this reason, this earth shakes so greatly.

When the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans heard these words, the hair on their bodies stood on end, and they wept piteously with one voice, speaking in verse:
"We prostrate and pay homage to the Tamer; We now entreat you, [O World-Honored One],"
Separated from the Sage among Men, we shall forever lack protection.
Now that we see the Buddha enter nirvana, we are submerged in the ocean of suffering;
filled with grief and sorrow, we are like a calf that has lost its mother.
Poor and without protection, like a suffering patient who,
lacking a physician, follows his own whims and eats what he ought not to eat;
so too are sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the afflictions, constantly harmed by various views.
Far removed from the Physician of Dharma, they consume the poison of false teachings;
therefore, the World-Honored Buddha should not be abandoned or forsaken.
Like a land without a sovereign, its people all suffer from hunger.
We too are likewise; we have lost our shelter and the flavor of the Dharma.
Now that we hear of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, our minds are bewildered and distracted, like the great earth when it shakes, losing our sense of all directions.
The Great Sage has entered nirvana; the Buddha-sun has fallen to the earth.
The waters of the Dharma have all dried up; we shall surely die.
With the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings suffer extreme anguish.
Just as the son of an elder, having recently lost his parents,
so it is with the Tathāgata entering nirvāṇa; if he does not return,
we and all sentient beings will be entirely without protection or refuge.
When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, even all the animals feel sorrow and fear;
their hearts are scorched by suffering and distress.
On this day, how could we not feel sorrow and distress?
The Tathāgata views abandonment as if discarding nasal mucus or spittle.
Just as when the sun first rises, its radiance is exceedingly brilliant and intense,
illuminating itself while simultaneously dispelling all darkness.
The light of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers can dispel my suffering and distress;
standing amidst the great assembly, he is like Mount Sumeru.
“World-Honored One!”

It is like a king who fathers several sons, all of whom are handsome in appearance; the king always cherishes them in his heart, first teaching them various arts until they have mastered them all, and only then entrusting them to an executioner to be put to death.
World-Honored One!
Today we are sons of the Dharma; having received the Buddha’s instruction and being endowed with right view, we pray that you will not abandon us.
If you were to abandon us, then we would be like [ordinary] princes.
I only pray that you will dwell for a long time and not enter nirvana.
World-Honored One!
It is like a person who has well studied various treatises, yet develops fear toward this very treatise.
The Tathāgata is likewise; though he has thoroughly penetrated all dharmas, he nevertheless gives rise to fear regarding those dharmas.
If the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for a long time, preaching the flavor of the ambrosia and satisfying all beings, then such sentient beings would no longer fear falling into hell.
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who, having first begun to learn a craft, was arrested by officials and imprisoned in a jail.
Someone asked him:”
"What have you experienced?
He replied, "I am now undergoing great sorrow and suffering; if I can escape it, I shall attain peace and happiness."

The World-Honored One is likewise; for our sake, he practiced various ascetic austerities, yet we have still not escaped the suffering and affliction of birth and death—how, then, could the Tathāgata experience peace and happiness?
World-Honored One!
It is like a king of physicians who is well-versed in prescriptions and medicines; he teaches his secret formulas exclusively to his own son, and does not teach them to other students from outside.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he alone uses the most profound and secret treasury to teach Mañjuśrī exclusively, while neglecting us and failing to show us compassion.
The Tathāgata should have no stinginess regarding the Dharma, yet like that king of physicians who teaches his own son exclusively and does not teach other students from outside.
The reason that physician was unable to teach universally was that his mind harbored a sense of competition and victory, and thus he kept things secret and withheld them.
The Tathāgata’s mind, however, is ultimately free from any sense of competition or victory; for what reason, then, does he not provide such instruction?
I only pray that you will remain for a long time and not enter parinirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!

It is as if an old man, a youth, or one suffering from illness were to leave the good path and travel upon a perilous road; the way is treacherous and difficult, and they undergo much suffering and distress.
Furthermore, there was another person who, seeing him, felt compassion and immediately showed him a level and excellent path.
World-Honored One! I am also like this:

those who are young represent people whose *dharmakāya* has not yet grown; the elderly represent heavy afflictions (*kleśa*); the sick represent those who have not yet escaped birth and death; and the perilous road represents the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will show us the guidance of the ambrosial, right path, remain long in this world, and not enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You bhikṣus, do not grieve, lament, or weep like ordinary people, devas, and humans."
"You should now exert yourselves with diligence and fix your minds in right mindfulness.
When the devas, humans, asuras, and others heard what the Buddha had said, they ceased their weeping.
It was as if someone, having completed the funeral rites for a son, had ceased their weeping.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"You all should open your minds; you ought not to suffer such great grief."
Such is the nature of all Buddhas; therefore, one should remain silent.
Delighting in the practice of heedfulness, guarding the mind with right mindfulness, and staying far removed from all that is unrighteous, one shall find solace and experience joy.
"Furthermore, monks!
If you have any doubts, you should now ask about them all."

Whether it be emptiness or non-emptiness, permanence or impermanence, suffering or non-suffering, dependence or non-dependence, going or not going, returning or not returning, constancy or non-constancy, annihilation or eternity, sentient beings or non-sentient beings, existence or non-existence, reality or unreality, truth or untruth, cessation or non-cessation, secrecy or non-secrecy, duality or non-duality—if you have any doubts regarding such various dharmas as these, you should now inquire; I shall, in accordance with your needs, sever them for you. I shall also first proclaim the Ambrosia (Amṛta) for you, and only thereafter shall I enter Nirvāṇa.
"O Bhikṣus! It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world;

it is difficult to obtain a human body; it is likewise difficult to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith; it is also difficult to endure that which is difficult to endure; and it is likewise difficult to fulfill the prohibitive precepts without deficiency and attain the fruit of Arhatship—just as it is to seek golden sand or the Udumbara flower."
"O Bhikṣus! Having escaped the eight difficulties and obtained this human body—which is so difficult to attain—you must not let your encounter with me pass in vain.

For your sake, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have practiced various asceticisms and have now attained such unsurpassed skillful means; I have sacrificed my body, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain. Therefore, you must not be negligent."
"O you bhikṣus!
How does one adorn the precious city of the True Dharma, fully equipped with the various treasures of merit, using precept, concentration, and wisdom as its walls, moats, and battlements?"

Now that you have encountered this jeweled city of the Buddha-dharma, you should not take these deceptive and false things; it would be like a merchant leader who, upon reaching a city of genuine treasures, takes up shards and rubble and returns home.
You are just like this: having encountered a precious city, you take away counterfeit goods. You bhikṣus!
Do not, with inferior minds, give rise to contentment.
Although you have now left the household life, you do not give rise to longing for this Mahāyāna. O bhikṣus!
Although your bodies are clothed in the dyed robes of the kāṣāya, your minds have not yet been dyed with the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
"O you bhikṣus!
Although you have traveled to many places in order to beg for alms, you have never before begged for the food of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
O you bhikṣus!"
"Though you have shaved off your hair and beards, you have not yet removed the various fetters (saṃyojana) through the True Dharma. You bhikṣus!

I now truly exhort you: while I am currently present and the great assembly is in harmony, and the Tathāgata’s Dharma-nature is true and unerring, you should therefore be diligent; restrain your minds with vigor and crush all fetters. Once the Sun of Wisdom of the Ten Powers has set, you will be shrouded by ignorance."

“O bhikṣus! Just as the great earth, the mountains, and medicinal herbs exist for the use of sentient beings, so too is my Dharma: it gives rise to the exquisite and wholesome flavor of the nectar of Dharma, serving as the excellent medicine for the various diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings.”
I shall now cause all sentient beings, as well as my own children—the fourfold assembly—to dwell entirely within the Secret Treasury; I too shall likewise dwell therein and enter into nirvana.
What is called the "Secret Treasury"?
It is like the three dots of the letter *i*: if they are aligned horizontally, they do not form the *i*; if they are placed vertically, they likewise do not form it.
Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara do they constitute the three dots of the *i*; yet even then, if they were separate from one another, they could not form it either.

I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not nirvana; the body of the Tathāgata is not nirvana; mahāprajñā is not nirvana; nor is it nirvana for these three dharmas to be distinct from one another.
“I now abide securely in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; this is called entering nirvana, like the letter ‘I’ of the world.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would certainly enter nirvana, they were all filled with grief; their body hairs stood on end, tears filled their eyes, and they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Please speak quickly of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
World-Honored One!
Just as among all the tracks of living beings, the elephant’s track is supreme, so too is this perception of impermanence; it is the foremost among all perceptions."

If there are those who diligently practice it, they will be able to eliminate all desire and attachment in the realm of desire, attachment to the realms of form and formlessness, ignorance, pride, and the perception of impermanence.
World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata were to be separated from the perception of impermanence, he would not now enter into parinirvāṇa.

If he were not separated from it, how can you say that by cultivating the perception of impermanence, one becomes detached from craving for the three realms, as well as ignorance, pride, and the perception of impermanence itself?
World-Honored One!
It is like a farmer who, during the autumn months, plows his field deeply and is thus able to remove the weeds.

This perception of impermanence is also like this: it can eliminate all craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realms of form and formlessness, as well as ignorance, arrogance, and even the perception of impermanence itself.
World-Honored One!
It is like plowing a field: plowing in autumn is superior.
Among all footprints, the footprint of an elephant is superior.
"Among all perceptions, the perception of impermanence is supreme, World-Honored One! It is like a sovereign who,
knowing his life is about to end, grants a general amnesty throughout the realm, causing all prisoners confined in dungeons to be fully released, and only then passes away."

The Tathāgata now should likewise act in this way, delivering all sentient beings from their bondage of ignorance and nescience, causing them all to attain liberation, and only thereafter entering parinirvāṇa.
We have not yet attained liberation; how can the Tathāgata now wish to abandon us and enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
It is like a person possessed by a spirit who encounters a skilled master of incantations; through the power of the incantation, they are immediately cured.

The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of all śrāvakas, he eliminates the demon of ignorance and enables them to dwell securely in dharmas such as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā and liberation, just like the worldly letter "i."
World-Honored One!
It is like a fragrant elephant that has been bound by men; even if it has a skilled trainer, the trainer cannot restrain it, for it snaps its tethering chains and departs at will.
I have not yet been thus liberated from the bonds of the fifty-seven afflictions; how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon me and enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
Just as a person suffering from malaria, upon meeting a skilled physician, finds their affliction removed;

so too am I, burdened by many ailments and the feverish disease of wrong livelihood. Although I have met the Tathāgata, my illness has not yet been cured, nor have I attained supreme peace, security, and eternal bliss.
"Why would the Tathāgata wish to abandon us and enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!

It is like a drunken man who is unaware of himself; he does not recognize his kin, nor his mother, daughter, or sister. Confused and debauched, his speech is licentious and unrestrained, and he lies amidst filth and excrement."

At that time, there was a skilled physician who gave him medicine to take; having taken it, he vomited up the wine and regained his memory. He felt shame and remorse in his heart, deeply reproaching himself, thinking: "Wine is the root of all unwholesome evils; if one can sever and abandon it, one will remain far removed from all transgressions."
World-Honored One! I am also like this;

since ancient times, as I have transmigrated through birth and death, I have been intoxicated by sensual desires and greedily craved the five objects of desire. I perceived those who were not my mother as my mother, those who were not my elder sister as my elder sister, and those who were not my daughter as my daughter; I conceived the notion of "living being" toward those who were not living beings. For this reason, I transmigrate and undergo the suffering of birth and death, just like that drunken man lying amidst excrement and filth.

The Tathāgata shall now bestow upon me the medicine of the Dharma, so that I may vomit out the foul wine of afflictions; yet I have not yet attained a mind of awakening—how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon me and enter into parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
It is like a person who praises the plantain tree for its solidity; such a thing is impossible.
World-Honored One!

Sentient beings are also like this: if one were to praise the self, the person, the sentient being, the life-span, the nourisher, the knower and seer, the agent, or the experiencer as being real, such a thing is impossible; we thus cultivate the perception of non-self.
World-Honored One!
It is like the dregs of fermented gruel, which have no further use;
this body is likewise: without self and without master.
World-Honored One!
Just as the seven-leaf flower has no fragrance, so too is this body:
it is without self and without master. We shall thus constantly cultivate the perception of non-self in our minds.
As the Buddha has said:

"All phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self; you, monks, should practice this. Having practiced thus, you will eliminate the conceit 'I am'; having abandoned the conceit 'I am,' you will then enter nirvana."
"World-Honored One!
For example, it is impossible for bird tracks to appear in the sky;
likewise, it is impossible for one who can cultivate the perception of non-self to still possess various [false] views."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully cultivated the perception of non-self.”
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We do not merely cultivate the perception of non-self; we also further cultivate other perceptions, namely: the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of non-self.”
World-Honored One!

It is like a person who is intoxicated; their mind is dazed and confused, and they see all the mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, grasses, trees, palaces, houses, the sun, moon, and stars as if they are all spinning around.
World-Honored One!

If there are those who do not cultivate the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, or the perception of non-self, such persons are not called noble ones; they are full of negligence and wander through birth and death.
“World-Honored One!
For these reasons, we have skillfully cultivated such perceptions.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
As for the analogy of the intoxicated man you have just cited, you know only the words but have not yet grasped their meaning.
What is the meaning?
Just as that intoxicated man sees the sun and moon above and, though they do not actually revolve, conceives the notion that they are revolving;

so too it is with sentient beings. Shrouded by the afflictions and ignorance, they give rise to perverted minds, conceiving what is non-self to be self, the impermanent to be permanent, the impure to be pure, and suffering to be pleasure, because they are covered by these afflictions.
Although they give rise to these conceptions, they do not comprehend their true meaning; it is like a drunken person who perceives the sensation of spinning even when there is no actual spinning.

"Self" (ātman) is the meaning of Buddha; "permanence" (nitya) is the meaning of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); "bliss" (sukha) is the meaning of Nirvana; and "purity" (śubha) is the meaning of the Dharma.
"O you bhikṣus!
How can you say that those who possess the notion of a self transmigrate through birth and death with arrogance and conceit?
If you were to say, 'We also cultivate the notions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self,' these three kinds of cultivation would lack any real meaning."
I shall now explain the superior method for cultivating the three trainings. To reckon suffering as pleasure and pleasure as suffering is an inverted dharma.
To reckon the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is an inverted dharma.
To conceive of non-self as self, or to conceive of self as non-self, is a perverted dharma.
To conceive of the impure as pure, or to conceive of the pure as impure, is a perverted dharma.
There are such four types of inverted dharmas; such people do not know how to correctly cultivate the various dharmas.

"O bhikṣus, you conceive the notion of pleasure within the dharma of suffering, the notion of permanence within the impermanent, the notion of self within the non-self, and the notion of purity within the impure."
In the mundane world there is also permanence, bliss, self, and purity; in the supramundane there is also permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Mundane phenomena possess words but lack meaning; supramundane phenomena possess both words and meaning.
For what reason?
Because the worldly dharmas possess four inversions, one does not know the true meaning. Why is this so?
There are inversions of perception, inversions of mind, and inversions of view.

Due to these three inversions, people of the world perceive suffering within what is pleasant, impermanence within what is permanent, non-self within what is self, and impurity within what is pure; this is called inversion.
Due to their perversion, people in the world understand the words but do not understand the meaning.
What is meant by "meaning"?
That which is "selfless" is called birth and death; that which is the "self" is called the Tathāgata.
The impermanent refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the permanent refers to the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
Suffering refers to all non-Buddhists; bliss is precisely Nirvāṇa.
The impure refers to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma); the pure refers to the true Dharma possessed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is called being non-perverted.
Because one is not perverted, one knows the words and knows their meaning.
If one wishes to distance oneself from the four perversions, one should understand permanence, bliss, self, and purity in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, those who are free from the four inversions can then fully realize permanence, bliss, self, and purity.”
The Tathāgata is now forever free from the four inversions; he has already fully realized permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

If he has already fully realized permanence, bliss, self, and purity, for what reason does he not remain for one kalpa or half a kalpa to instruct us and cause us to leave behind the four inversions? Why instead does he abandon us and intend to enter parinirvāṇa?
If the Tathāgata would deign to look upon us and grant us his instructions, we would receive them with the utmost sincerity, honor them upon our heads, and practice them.
But if the Tathāgata were to enter parinirvāṇa, how could we continue to dwell together with this poisonous body and cultivate the holy life?
"We, too, shall follow the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and enter into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should not speak such words. All my unsurpassed True Dharma is now entrusted to Mahākāśyapa."
This Kāśyapa shall serve as a great refuge for you all; just as the Tathāgata serves as a place of refuge for all sentient beings, so too shall Mahākāśyapa serve as a place of refuge for you.
For example, when a great king who governs many territories goes on a tour of inspection, he entrusts all matters of state to his ministers.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he has entrusted all the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa.
"You should know that the previously cultivated perceptions of impermanence and suffering are not the ultimate truth.
It is like this: suppose, during the springtime, there were a group of people bathing in a large pond and playing on boats who lost a lapis lazuli gem, which sank into the deep water."

At that time, all the people entered the water together to search for this treasure; they vied with one another to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and gravel, each claiming to have found a lapis lazuli bead. Delighted, they brought them out, only then to realize they were not genuine.
At that time, the precious jewel was still within the water; by the power of the jewel, the water became entirely clear and transparent.
Thereupon, the great assembly saw the precious jewel still beneath the water, just as one looks up at the form of the moon in the void.
At that time, there was a wise man among the crowd who, through the power of skillful means, entered the water calmly and slowly, and immediately obtained the pearl.

You, bhikṣus, should not practice the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as if they were ultimate truths, like those people who each took tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, or gravel for precious pearls.
"You all should skillfully learn expedient means; wherever you may be, you should constantly cultivate the perception of self, permanence, bliss, and purity.
Furthermore, you should know that the characteristics of the four dharmas previously practiced are all inverted."
Those who wish to attain the true cultivation of various conceptions are like that wise person skillfully extracting precious jewels, namely:
the conception of self, and the conceptions of permanence, bliss, and purity.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously said:”
"All phenomena are without self; you should train yourselves in this!
Having trained in this, you will be free from the notion of a self;
being free from the notion of a self, you will be free from conceit."
"One who is free from pride attains entry into nirvana.
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Excellent, excellent! You have now skillfully questioned me on this matter in order to sever your own doubts.

It is like a king who is dull-witted and lacking in wisdom, who has a physician that is by nature stubborn and ignorant. Yet the king does not discern this and grants him a generous stipend. When treating various ailments, he uses only milk as medicine; he does not know the root cause from which diseases arise, and though he knows of the medicinal properties of milk, he lacks a proper understanding of them. Whether it be wind-disorders, cold-disorders, heat-disorders, or any other ailment whatsoever, he instructs everyone to consume milk.”
The king did not distinguish between them, yet this physician knew whether the milk was good or bad, superior or inferior.

Furthermore, there was another skilled physician who was proficient in the eight branches of medicine, adept at treating various ailments, and knowledgeable in all prescriptions and medicines; he had come from a distant land.
At that time, the former physician did not know to seek instruction, but instead gave rise to a mind of arrogance and contempt.

The latter, the skilled physician, immediately sought him out as a dependent, requesting to take him as his teacher; he inquired after the secret and profound methods of medical treatment and said to the former physician:
"I now request you, sir, to be my master and model; I only pray that you will expound and explain them for me."
The old physician replied,
"If you can now serve as my attendant for forty-eight years, only then shall I teach you the medical arts.
At that time, the skilled physician immediately accepted his instruction.
"I shall do so; I shall do so. According to my ability, I shall serve as an attendant.
At that time, the former physician took the visiting physician with him into the presence of the king.
At that time, the visiting physician immediately explained various medical prescriptions and other arts to the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know that you ought to distinguish them well: such a method as this can be used to govern the state;
such a method as this can be used to treat illness."

When the king heard these words, he finally realized that the former physician was foolish and lacked wisdom; he immediately expelled him from the kingdom, thereafter redoubling his respect for the visiting physician.
At that time, the visiting physician thought to himself,
"Now is the very moment to instruct the king.
He then spoke to the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty truly loves and cherishes me, you should grant me one wish.
The King immediately replied,
"From this right arm and all other parts of my body, whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you."
The visiting physician said,
“Although Your Majesty has granted me every part of your body, I dare not ask for much.
What I now request is that Your Majesty issue a decree throughout the entire kingdom that, from this day forward, no one shall again take the medicinal milk prescribed by the former physician.”
Why is this? Because this medicine is poisonous and harmful, causing much injury and damage.
If anyone should intentionally take it, their head shall be severed.
“Once the medicine that eliminates the need for nursing has been administered, there shall never again be anyone who dies an untimely death; they shall always abide in peace and happiness.
Therefore, I seek this vow. At that time, the King replied, “That which you seek is truly not worth mentioning.”
He immediately issued a proclamation:
"Throughout the entire kingdom, it is forbidden for anyone with an illness to use milk as medicine; if anyone uses it as medicine, their head shall be severed."

At that time, the visiting physician blended various medicinal herbs with diverse flavors—namely pungent, bitter, salty, sweet, and sour—to treat the multitude of ailments, such that none failed to recover.
Not long after that, the king fell ill again and immediately summoned the physician, saying:
"I am now gravely ill, suffering so much that I am on the verge of death; how should I be treated?"
The physician diagnosed the king’s illness and determined that a medicinal preparation of milk was required; he then addressed the king, saying:
"Regarding the ailment Your Majesty suffers from, you ought to consume milk.
The fact that I previously forbade the use of milk as medicine was a great falsehood."
"If one were to take it now, it would be most effective at removing disease; since Your Majesty currently suffers from a fever, you ought indeed to take milk.
Then the king said to the physician, "Are you mad now?"
Is it for a feverish illness that you say drinking milk can cure this disease?
Previously you spoke of it as poison; why do you now say it should be drunk?
"Do you wish to deceive me?
Previously, when the former physician praised [the medicine], you called it poison and caused me to dismiss him.
Now you say again that it is excellent and most capable of removing disease."
"As you have said, I am indeed your former physician and am certainly superior to you.
At that time, the visiting physician spoke again to the king:
"Your Majesty, you should not speak such words. It is like an insect eating wood; if it happens to form the shape of a character, this insect does not know whether it is a character or not."
When a wise person sees this, they never claim that the insect understands letters, nor do they find it strange.

Your Majesty should know that the old physician was just like this: failing to distinguish between various illnesses, he administered milk medicine to all of them, much like how those insect tracks happened by chance to form characters.
"These former physicians did not understand the quality—whether good or bad, excellent or inferior—of the medicinal milk.
Then the king asked:
"In what way did they not understand?"
The visiting physician replied to the king:
"This medicinal milk is both a poisonous harm and also nectar (amṛta).
In what sense is this milk also called nectar?"

If it is a cow, she shall not eat wine dregs, slippery grass, or wheat bran; her calf must be well-tamed. The place where they graze shall be neither on high plateaus nor in low-lying marshes; they shall drink from clear streams. She must not be made to run at speed, nor shall she be kept in the same herd as bulls. Her drinking and feeding shall be moderate, and her movement and dwelling shall be appropriate.
Such milk as this can eliminate all diseases; it is therefore called the wondrous medicine of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
With the exception of this milk, everything else is termed poisonous and harmful.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King praised the great physician, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
From this day forward, I have finally come to know the good and evil, the superior and inferior qualities of the medicinal milk."
He immediately took it and his illness was cured.
He then issued a proclamation throughout the entire kingdom: "From this day forward, you shall take milk as medicine.
When the people of the country heard this, they all felt resentment and said to one another:
"The Great King is now possessed by a ghost; has he gone mad?
He deceives us and furthermore commands us to drink milk.
All the people, harboring resentment and anger, gathered together at the king's location.
The king said, "You should not harbor anger or resentment toward me; whether this medicinal milk is consumed or not is entirely according to the physician's instruction, and is not my fault."
At that time, the great king and all the people leaped for joy and, with redoubled reverence, made offerings to this physician.
All the patients took the milk medicine, and their illnesses were completely cured.

“O bhikṣus! You should know that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, is likewise so: he is a great King of Physicians who has appeared in the world to subdue all heterodox practitioners and false physicians. In the midst of the assembly of kings, he proclaims these words:
‘I am the King of Physicians.’”
Wishing to subdue the non-Buddhists, he proclaimed these words:
"There is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span, no nourisher, no knower or seer, no agent, and no experiencer."
"Monks, you should know that the 'self' spoken of by these various non-Buddhists is like insects boring into wood and accidentally forming characters.
Therefore, within the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata proclaims 'no-self. It is for the sake of disciplining sentient beings and for the sake of knowing the proper time that he teaches this no-self."
Due to specific causes and conditions, one may also speak of a "self.
This is like that skilled physician who well knows which milk is medicinal and which is not; it is not like the "self" as conceived by ordinary people.

Regarding the self conceived by foolish ordinary people—some say it is as large as a thumb, some say like a mustard seed, and others say like a mote of dust—the Tathāgata says that the self is not like these at all;
therefore, he says that all phenomena are without self, yet in truth they are not without self.
What is this "self"?
If there were any phenomenon that was real, true, permanent, sovereign, a refuge, and whose nature was immutable—that would be called the self.
Just as that great physician was well-versed in the medicinal use of milk, so too is the Tathāgata; for the sake of sentient beings, he teaches that within all phenomena there truly exists a self.
You members of the fourfold assembly should cultivate this Dharma in such a manner.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Two;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter One, Part Three: On Longevity.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you have any doubts regarding the precepts and the Vinaya, ask whatever you wish now; I shall explain them for you so that your hearts may rejoice."
I have already cultivated and studied that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty and quiescent, and I have thoroughly and clearly realized this.
You bhikṣus, do not say that the Tathāgata has only cultivated the emptiness and quiescence of the intrinsic nature of dharmas.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is anything you doubt regarding the Vinaya, you may now ask questions.
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
We lack the wisdom to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this? Because—”
The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; all his meditative concentrations are inconceivable; the teachings he expounds are inconceivable. Therefore, we lack the wisdom to question the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!

It is like an old man, one hundred and twenty years of age, whose body is afflicted by a chronic illness; he lies prostrate upon his bed, unable to rise or move about, his vital strength exhausted and depleted, with but little life remaining.
There was a wealthy man who, having business to attend to, was about to travel to another land. He entrusted a hundred *jin* of gold to this old man, saying:
"I am now traveling abroad; I entrust these precious goods to you. Whether I return in ten years or twenty years, you must return them to me."
At that time, the old man accepted it. However, this old man had no heirs;
not long thereafter, he fell gravely ill and passed away, and all the property he had entrusted was completely lost.
When the owner of the wealth returns, there is no place to which he can demand repayment of his debt.
Thus, this foolish person does not know how to deliberate upon whether someone is a fit recipient for entrustment or not.
For this reason, when he returns, there is nowhere to seek repayment; by these causes and conditions, he loses his wealth and treasures.
World-Honored One!

We śrāvakas are likewise; although we have heard the Tathāgata’s earnest instructions, we are unable to receive and uphold them so as to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, just like that old man who received another's entrusted deposit.
"I am currently without wisdom regarding the various precepts; what, then, should I ask?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you were now to question me, it would bring benefit to all sentient beings."
"Therefore, I tell you: listen and ask whatever you doubt, questioning freely as you wish.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Suppose there is a man, twenty-five years of age, in the prime of his vigor and handsome, possessing abundant wealth such as gold, silver, and lapis lazuli; his parents, wife, children, retinue, and kinsmen are all still living. Another person comes to him and entrusts his treasures to him, saying to him:
"I have some business that requires me to go elsewhere; when my affairs are concluded, I shall return. You must return these to me."
At that time, the strong man guarded these objects as if they were his own.
When the man fell ill, he immediately instructed his family members:
"These gold and jewels were entrusted to me by another; if he comes to demand them, you must return them all to him."
"In this way, the wise person, skillfully knowing how to deliberate, goes out to seek goods upon returning from his travels and obtains them all without any loss.
The World-Honored One is likewise; if he were to entrust the treasure of the Dharma only to Ānanda and the bhikṣus, it would not endure for long."
Why is this? Because all śrāvakas, including Mahākāśyapa, shall likewise be subject to impermanence, just as that old man received the entrusted goods from another.

Therefore, the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma should be entrusted to the bodhisattvas; for since these bodhisattvas are well able to inquire about and respond concerning such jewels of the Dharma, they will cause them to abide for immeasurable thousands of eons, increasing and flourishing to bring benefit, peace, and security to sentient beings, just as that strong man received the entrusted goods from another.
For this reason, it is only the great bodhisattvas who are able to inquire; our wisdom is like that of mosquitoes or gnats—how could we possibly request the profound Dharma of the Tathāgata?
At that time, the śrāvakas remained silent.
Then the Buddha praised the bhikṣus, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"You have well attained the mind free from outflows, the mind of an Arhat.
I too have reflected that for these two reasons, the Great Vehicle should be entrusted to the Bodhisattvas, so that this sublime Dharma may long abide in the world."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire assembly:
"Sons and daughters of good family!
My lifespan is immeasurable, and my eloquence in joyful exposition is inexhaustible. You should all inquire as you please, whether concerning the precepts or the refuges."
A second and a third time, he spoke in this same manner.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva who had originally been a native of the village of Tora. He was of the Kāśyapa clan, born of the Brahmin caste, and was of tender years. By the spiritual power of the Buddha, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, circumambulated [the Buddha] a hundred thousand times, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to inquire briefly; if the Buddha permits it, I shall venture to speak.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, allows you to ask whatever you wish. I shall explain it for you, sever your doubts, and cause you to rejoice."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata, out of compassion, has graciously granted me permission; I shall now ask my question. However, all the wisdom I possess is as slight and insignificant as that of a mosquito or a gadfly.”

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses a majesty of virtue and conduct so towering that his retinue consists solely of those who are like sandalwood—like lions difficult to subdue and an assembly that cannot be destroyed.
The body of the Tathāgata is like true vajra; its color is like lapis lazuli, truly indestructible, and he is further surrounded by such an ocean of great wisdom.
Within this assembly, all the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have fully accomplished immeasurable and boundless, profound and wondrous merits, like fragrant elephants.
In the presence of such a great assembly, how could I dare to pose a question?
It is only by relying on the supernatural power of the Buddha and the majestic virtue of the roots of goodness of this great assembly that I shall venture to ask a few questions.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he spoke in verse, asking:
"How does one attain long life And a vajra-like indestructible body?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions Does one obtain great, firm, and solid power?"
How does one, regarding this sutra, reach the ultimate further shore?
We pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle mysteries and speak extensively for the sake of all sentient beings.
How does one attain vastness and become a refuge for the multitude?
How is it that one who is not truly an arhat is equal to an arhat?
How does one know the celestial Māra creates obstacles for the assembly?
Between what the Buddha speaks and what Pāpīyān speaks, how can one distinguish and discern them?
How do the Tamer of Men, with hearts full of joy, proclaim the True Reality?
Having perfectly accomplished what is right and good, how do they expound upon the four perversions?
And how do they perform virtuous deeds?
Great Seer, you should now explain:
how do the bodhisattvas perceive the nature that is difficult to see?
How do they understand the meaning of the full syllables and the half-syllables?
How does one practice in common with the noble ones, like the sārasa crane,
the kālaṃbaka bird, the sun and moon, Venus, and Jupiter?
How can one who has not yet resolved their mind be called a bodhisattva?
How does one attain fearlessness amidst the great assembly,
like Jāmbūnada gold, such that no one can speak of its faults?
How does one dwell in a defiled world without being stained, like a lotus flower?
How is it that while dwelling amidst afflictions, one is not defiled by those afflictions?
Like a physician treating various ailments, how is one not sullied by disease?
Within the great ocean of birth and death, how does one act as a navigator?
How does one abandon birth and death, Like a snake shedding its old skin?
How does one contemplate the Triple Gem, As being like the celestial wish-fulfilling tree?
If the Three Vehicles have no intrinsic nature, How can they be spoken of?
Just as when pleasure has not yet arisen, how can it be called "experiencing pleasure"?
How do the bodhisattvas obtain an indestructible assembly?
And how do they act as eyes and guides for those born blind?
How does one manifest many heads?
I pray that the Great Sage will explain this.
How does a speaker of the Dharma increase like the waxing moon?
How do you further manifest the ultimate attainment of nirvāṇa?
How does the courageous one demonstrate the paths of humans, gods, and māras?
How does one know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and thereby experience the bliss of the Dharma?
How do the bodhisattvas remain free from all illness?
How do they proclaim the secrets for the sake of sentient beings?
How do they speak of the ultimate and the non-ultimate?
If one has severed the net of doubt, why speak with uncertainty?
How may one draw near to the most supreme and unsurpassed path?
I now entreat the Tathāgata for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
I pray that you will explain the profound and subtle nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Within all dharmas, there exists the nature of peace and bliss;
I only pray that the Great Sage, the Honored One, will analyze and explain this for me.
The great refuge of all beings, the supreme among two-legged ones, the wondrous medicine—
now I wish to inquire about the aggregates, yet I possess no wisdom.
Even the bodhisattvas who are diligent in vigor are likewise unable to know them.
"Such as these are the profound realms of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
Although you have not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), I have already attained it.
Nevertheless, the profound and secret treasury that you inquire about is no different from what is asked by one who possesses all-knowledge."
"Good son!

When I sat beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment and first attained perfect awakening, there were bodhisattvas from immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who also asked me about this profound meaning. Yet the phrasing, the meaning, and the merit of their questions were all exactly like this, without any difference."
"One who asks such questions will be able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I lack the power of wisdom to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such profound meanings.
World-Honored One!
It is as if a mosquito or a gadfly cannot fly across the other shore of the great ocean or traverse the entirety of space."
I am likewise unable to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such an ocean of wisdom, the meaning of the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is like space.
World-Honored One!

It is, for example, like a king who entrusts the bright pearl from his topknot to a minister in charge of the treasury; having received it, the minister bears it upon his head with reverence and increases his protection of it.
I am likewise; I bear upon my head with reverence and increase my protection of the profound meaning of the Vaipulya sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata.
"Why is this? It is so that I may extensively attain profound wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain for you the karma by which the Tathāgata attained long life.
Because Bodhisattvas possess these karmic causes and conditions, they attain a long lifespan; therefore, you should listen and receive this teaching with a sincere mind.”

If there is karma that can serve as the cause for bodhi, one should listen to and receive this meaning with a sincere heart; having listened and received it, one should then explain it to others. Good son!
Because I have cultivated such karma, I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and now I again expound this meaning extensively for the sake of others. Good son!

For example, suppose a prince commits a crime and is imprisoned; the king, out of profound compassion and because he loves his son, personally turns his carriage and goes to the place where he is held.

It is the same for a bodhisattva who desires long life: they should regard all sentient beings with the thought that they are their own children, giving rise to great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, bestowing the precept against killing, and teaching them to cultivate wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, one should establish all sentient beings in the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions. One should then enter all realms of existence—such as the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the asuras—to rescue the suffering beings therein: liberating those not yet liberated, delivering those not yet delivered, and enabling those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain it. By comforting all those who are terrified through such karmic causes and conditions, the bodhisattva attains a long life, gains mastery over all forms of wisdom, and at the end of his lifespan is reborn in the heavens.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regard all sentient beings equally, as if they were their own children—this meaning is profound and obscure; I have not yet been able to understand it.”
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata should not say that a bodhisattva cultivates a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, regarding them as equal to his own children. Why is this so?"

Within the Buddha-dharma, there are those who break the precepts, those who commit crimes of immediate retribution, and those who destroy the true Dharma; how can one regard such people as being like one's own children?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is so, it is so. I truly regard all sentient beings as my own children, just as I do Rāhula.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Formerly, on the fifteenth day during the time of the Saṃgha’s poṣadha, there was once a youth among the assembly of those who had received full ordination and were pure, who did not properly cultivate the actions of body, speech, and mind, and who secretly listened to the recitation of the precepts from a hidden corner.”
Guhapāla, the Vajra-wielding Malla, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, crushed him with his vajra until he was like dust.
"World-Honored One!
This Vajra deity is exceedingly violent and evil; he was able to sever the life-faculty of this boy."
"How is it that the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as being the same as his own son, Rāhula?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"You should not speak such words now. This youth is a manifested person and not real; he was created for the purpose of expelling those who break the precepts and destroy the Dharma so that they may leave the assembly."
Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada is likewise a manifestation. Kāśyapa!

Toward those who slander the True Dharma, the icchantikas, or those who commit acts such as killing up to holding wrong views and intentionally violating prohibitions—I give rise to compassion for all such beings, regarding them with the same thought as I do my son Rāhula.
"Good son!
For example, if the ministers and other officials of a king commit offenses against the royal law, the king executes them according to their crimes and does not let them go.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not like this; toward those who destroy the Dharma, he applies the *karma* of expulsion, the *karma* of reprimand, the *karma* of suspension, the *karma* of accusation, the *karma* of non-visibility, the *karma* of extinction, and the *karma* for not relinquishing evil views."
"Good son!

The reason the Tathāgata performs such acts of subjugation (*karmavācanā*) against those who slander the Dharma is that he wishes to demonstrate to all who commit evil deeds that there is karmic retribution."
"Good son!

You should now know that the Tathāgata is one who bestows fearlessness upon evil sentient beings; whether emitting one ray of light, two, or five, whoever encounters them shall be caused to remain far removed from all evils. The Tathāgata now possesses such immeasurable power."
"Good son, regarding those dharmas that you have not yet seen but wish to see, I shall now describe their characteristics for you.

After my parinirvāṇa, in whichever direction there may be a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, is fully endowed with dignified deportment, and protects the True Dharma—if such a person sees one who destroys the Dharma, they will immediately expel them, rebuke them, and subject them to disciplinary measures. You should know that such a person will obtain immeasurable and incalculable merit."
"Good son!
It is like a king who exclusively practices violence and evil; having contracted a grave illness, a neighboring king hears his name and raises an army to come, intending to utterly destroy him."
At that time, the King of Illness, being powerless, was struck with fear and changed his heart to practice virtue;
thus, the neighboring king obtained immeasurable merit.
The Dharma-holding bhikṣu is also like this: by expelling and rebuking those who destroy the Dharma, he causes them to practice wholesome dharmas and obtain immeasurable merit. Good son!
For example, suppose there were various poisonous trees growing on the fields, houses, and dwellings where an elder resided.
Once the elder became aware of this, he would immediately cut them down, ensuring they were forever eradicated.
Furthermore, it is like a strong man who, seeing white hairs grow upon his head, feels ashamed and plucks them out so they do not grow longer.
A bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma is just the same: when he sees one who breaks the precepts and destroys the True Dharma, he should immediately expel them, rebuke them, and report their offense.

If a virtuous bhikṣu sees one who destroys the Dharma and sets them aside, failing to reprimand, expel, or subject them to formal censure, you should know that such a person is an enemy within the Buddha-dharma.
If he is able to expel, reprimand, and subject them to formal censure, he is my disciple and a true śrāvaka.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to what the Buddha has said, you do not regard all sentient beings equally as your own children, as you do Rāhula.”
World-Honored One!

If one person harms the Buddha with a sword, and another person applies sandalwood paste to the Buddha, and the Buddha gives rise to an impartial mind toward these two, why do you further say that those who violate the prohibitions should be punished?
"If one were to treat those who violate the prohibitions as having been disciplined, such a statement would be erroneous.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Good son!..."

For example, suppose a king, a great minister, or a prime minister has fathered several sons—two, three, or four—who are handsome in appearance and endowed with intelligence and wisdom. He entrusts them to a strict teacher, saying:
"Master, you should instruct these sons of mine in dignified deportment, ritual propriety, the arts, calligraphy, correspondence, accounting, and mathematics, ensuring that they master them all."

"My four sons are now coming to you to receive instruction. Even if three of them should die from the blows of the staff, the remaining one must certainly be disciplined with severity so that he may achieve mastery."
"Though I have lost my three sons, I shall never harbor resentment.
"Kāśyapa! Would this father and teacher incur the sin of killing?"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"Out of affection and with the desire for their accomplishment, and without any ill will, one who instructs them in this way shall obtain immeasurable merit. Good son!"
The Tathāgata is likewise; he regards those who destroy the Dharma as equal to his only son.
The Tathāgata now entrusts the unsurpassed True Dharma to kings, ministers, counselors, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
These kings and the fourfold assembly should exhort and encourage all students so that they may attain superior morality, concentration, and wisdom.

If there are those who do not study these three categories of dharma, being indolent, breaking the precepts, or destroying the true Dharma, the kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly should severely punish them.
"Good son! Would these kings and the fourfold assembly have any transgressions? "No, they would not."
“World-Honored One!
‘Good son, even these kings and the fourfold assembly have no fault, let alone the Tathāgata.’”
"Good son! The Tathāgata has skillfully cultivated such equanimity that he regards all sentient beings as his only child.
One who cultivates in this manner is said to be a bodhisattva cultivating a mind of equanimity, regarding all sentient beings as his only child."
“Good son!
When a bodhisattva practices this karma in such a manner, they attain a long life and are also able to skillfully know the events of their past lives.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva cultivates a mind of equanimity and regards all sentient beings as one would one’s own child, they shall attain a long life.”
The Tathāgata should not speak in such a manner. Why is this?
For one who knows the Dharma and is able to preach various teachings on filial piety might, upon returning home, strike and pelt their parents with tiles and stones.

Yet these parents are a fertile field of merit, bringing great benefit and being difficult to encounter; they should be properly honored with offerings, yet instead one brings them distress and harm—this shows that the person who knows the Dharma acts in contradiction to their words.

The words of the Tathāgata are likewise so: a bodhisattva who cultivates an impartial mind and regards all sentient beings as his own children shall attain long life, possess knowledge of past lives, abide eternally in the world, and remain subject to no change.
Now, World-Honored One, for what cause and condition is Your lifespan so exceedingly short, being equal to that of ordinary humans?
Could it be that the Tathāgata has conceived thoughts of resentment or hatred toward sentient beings?
"Blessed One, what evil karma did you commit in the past, and how many life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) did you sever, to obtain such a short lifespan of less than a hundred years?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
For what reason have you now uttered such coarse words before the Tathāgata?
The Tathāgata is long-lived; among all lifespans, he is the most supreme and most excellent.
"The Dharma of permanence that has been attained is the foremost among all things that are permanent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does the Tathāgata attain a long life?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."

It is like the eight great rivers: first, the Ganges; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarayū; fourth, the Aciravatī; fifth, the Mahī; sixth, the Sindhu; seventh, the Vakṣu; and eighth, the Sītā. These eight great rivers, along with all the small streams, flow entirely into the great ocean.
Kāśyapa!
