Just as all the great rivers of lifespan among humans, devas, on earth, and in the void flow entirely into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, for this reason the lifespan of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like the Lake Anavatapta, from which the four great rivers flow;
so too is the Tathāgata, who brings forth all life.
Kāśyapa! Just as among all eternal phenomena, space is foremost;
so too is the Tathāgata, for among all that is eternal, he is the most supreme.
Kāśyapa! Just as among all medicines, clarified butter (ghṛta) is supreme;
so too is the Tathāgata, for among all sentient beings, his lifespan is supreme.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the lifespan of the Tathāgata is such as this, he should remain for a full kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, constantly proclaiming the wondrous Dharma like the pouring down of great rain.”
“Kāśyapa! You should not now give rise to the notion of extinction regarding the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa!”

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—even including non-Buddhists, those with the five supernatural powers, or those who have attained mastery—who may remain for a kalpa or less than a kalpa, walking through the air, sitting or lying down at will, emitting fire from their left side and water from their right side, or producing smoke and flames from their bodies like a mass of fire; if they wish to prolong their life, they can do so as they please, determining the length of their lifespan according to their own will.

If even those with these five supernormal powers can attain such mastery over their own spiritual faculties as they wish, how much more so the Tathāgata, who has attained sovereign power over all phenomena—how could he be unable to remain for half an eon, or one eon, or a hundred eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even immeasurable eons?
For this reason, you should know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding dharma, the unchanging dharma.

This body of the Tathāgata is a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), not a body sustained by various foods; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests as being like a poisonous tree, and therefore displays the relinquishment of it by entering into nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa! You should know that the Buddha is the eternal dharma, the unchanging dharma.
Within this ultimate truth, you should apply yourselves with diligent effort and cultivate it with a single mind; having cultivated it, you should then explain it extensively for others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between the supramundane Dharma and mundane dharmas?”
As the Buddha has said:
"The Buddha is the eternal Dharma, the unchanging Dharma.
The world also says:
"Brahmā is eternal; Maheśvara is eternal and unchanging.
The self is eternal, nature is eternal, and even atoms are eternal.
If it is said that the Tathāgata is an eternal dharma, for what reason does the Tathāgata not manifest eternally?
If it does not manifest constantly, what distinction would there be?
Why is this? Because from the Brahma-heaven down to the subtle atom, even the nature of the world (*loka-prakṛti*) does not manifest.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose there is an elder who has many oxen; though they are of various colors, they form a single herd. He entrusts them to a cowherd, instructing him to let them graze where there is water and grass, solely for the sake of obtaining clarified butter (ghṛta), and not seeking milk or curds."
That cowherd would milk the cows and eat the milk himself.
When the elder passed away, all his cattle were plundered by a band of thieves.
Having seized the cattle, the thieves had no women with them.
He immediately milked it himself, and having obtained the milk, he drank it.
At that time, the bandits said to one another:
"That great elder keeps this cow not for the sake of the milk or the curd, but solely for the sake of the *sarpis* (clarified butter)."
"What means should we now employ to obtain it?
For *amṛta* (clarified butter) is known as the supreme flavor in the world.
We lack the vessel; even if we were to obtain the milk, we would have no place to set it down."
They further said to one another, "Only a leather bag can contain it.
Although there was a place to hold it, they did not know how to churn it; even buttermilk was difficult to obtain, let alone fresh butter.
At that time, because the thieves added water for the sake of the clarified butter (sarpis), and because of the excess of water, the milk, the curd, and the clarified butter were all lost.
Ordinary beings are likewise; although they possess wholesome dharmas, these are all but the remnants of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma. Why is this?

Because after the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, entered parinirvāṇa, they plundered the remaining wholesome dharmas left by the Tathāgata—such as precepts, concentration, and wisdom—just as those thieves robbed the herd of cattle.
Although ordinary worldlings may attain this precept, concentration, and wisdom, they lack skillful means and are unable to explain them.
For this reason, they cannot obtain the eternal precept, eternal concentration, eternal wisdom, and liberation;
they are like those bandits who, not knowing skillful means, lost the clarified butter.
It is also like a band of thieves who, for the sake of clarified butter (*sarpis*), add water to it.

Ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise: for the sake of liberation, they speak of a self, sentient beings, life-span, a person (*pudgala*), Brahmā, Maheśvara, atoms, the nature of the world (*dharmatā*), as well as morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation; they claim that the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is itself *nirvāṇa*. Yet in reality, they do not attain liberation or *nirvāṇa*, just as those thieves did not obtain the clarified butter.

These ordinary worldlings practice a small measure of pure conduct and provide for their parents; by these causes and conditions, they are reborn in the heavens and experience a small degree of peace and happiness, like that milk to which the bandits added water.
Yet these ordinary people truly do not know that by practicing even a small amount of pure conduct and making offerings to their parents, one can be reborn in the heavens.

Furthermore, they do not understand precepts, meditative concentration, or wisdom, nor do they take refuge in the Triple Gem; because of this ignorance, they speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Although they speak thus, they truly do not know [the reality of these things].
Therefore, after the Tathāgata appears in the world, he expounds for them permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
It is like when a wheel-turning monarch appears in the world: by the power of his merit, the bandits retreat and scatter, and the cattle suffer no loss of life.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King entrusted the oxen to a single cowherd who was highly skillful and resourceful.
Through his expedient means, this man obtained the clarified butter (ghṛta).
Because of this clarified butter, all sentient beings were free from illness and suffering.

When the Holy Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, those ordinary persons who are unable to expound upon ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom immediately retreat and disperse, just as thieves scatter.
At that time, the Tathāgata skillfully expounded both worldly and world-transcending dharmas; for the sake of sentient beings, he caused all bodhisattvas to follow and proclaim them.

Having already attained the *amṛta* (the essence of clarified butter), the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to obtain the supreme flavor of the nectar of Dharma—namely, the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, son of good family,
the Tathāgata is eternal and a dharma that is unchanging.
He is not like the worldlings, fools, and ignorant people who claim that Brahmā and others are eternal dharmas.
This eternal Dharma is designated as the Tathāgata, and not any other phenomenon.
Kāśyapa, you should understand the body of the Tathāgata in this way.
Kāśyapa! All sons and daughters of good family should always bind their minds to the cultivation of these two words: "The Buddha is eternally abiding. Kāśyapa!
If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate these two characters, you should know that such persons follow my practice and will reach the place I have reached.
Good sons!
If there are those who cultivate these two syllables as the mark of cessation, you should know that for such persons, the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
Good son!
"The meaning of nirvana is precisely the dharma-nature of all Buddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of the nature of the Buddha-dharma?
World-Honored One!
I now wish to know the meaning of the nature of dharmas; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will explain it extensively."

Now, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is precisely the relinquishing of the body; that which is the relinquishing of the body is called "non-existence. If there is non-existence, how can the body persist?
If the body were to persist, how could one say that the body possesses the nature of phenomena?
"If the body possesses the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), how can it exist?
How should I now understand this meaning?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Good son! You should not now speak in such a manner, saying that this dharma-nature is extinguished.
As for the dharma-nature, it is without extinction.”
Good son! It is like the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva), which accomplishes the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) yet lacks the perception of form;
one should not ask how these devas abide.
Do you experience joy and pleasure?
What are your perceptions?
What have you seen and heard?
Good son, the realm of the Tathāgata is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Good son, one should not say that the body of the Tathāgata is a phenomenon subject to extinction.
"Good son, such dharmas of cessation are the realm of the Buddha; they are not within the reach of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Good son, you should now not speculate as to where the Tathāgata dwells."
Where does one act?
Where does one see?
Where does one find delight?
Good sons, this meaning is not something that you can know or comprehend; the various skillful means of the Buddhas' Dharma-body are inconceivable.
"Furthermore, good son,
you should cultivate the thought of permanence regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Regarding these three dharmas, there is no thought of difference, no thought of impermanence, and no thought of change."

If one cultivates divergent perceptions regarding these three dharmas, it should be known that such persons have no basis for the pure Three Refuges; all their precepts will be incomplete, and they shall ultimately be unable to realize the fruits of the enlightenment of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
If one can cultivate the perception of permanence regarding this inconceivable [reality], then there will be a place of refuge.
Good son! It is like how, because of a tree, there is a tree’s shadow.
The Tathāgata is likewise; because he possesses the eternal Dharma, he is an object of refuge and is not impermanent.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, then the Tathāgata would not be the place of refuge for the devas or the people of the world.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is as if in the darkness there were a tree but no shadow.”
“Kāśyapa! You should not say that there is a tree but no shadow; it is simply that it is not seen by the fleshly eye. Good son!
The Tathāgata is likewise; his nature is eternally abiding and immutable.
Those who lack the eye of wisdom cannot perceive him, just as one cannot see the shadow of a tree in the darkness.
Ordinary people, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, likewise say that the Tathāgata is an impermanent phenomenon.

If one were to say that the Tathāgata is distinct from the Dharma and the Saṅgha, then he could not constitute the three objects of refuge; just as your father and mother are each distinct individuals, [the Tathāgata] would therefore be impermanent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

From this day forward, I shall use the three matters of the permanence of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha to enlighten my parents and even those up to the seventh generation of my lineage, causing them all to receive and uphold them."
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
I shall now train myself in the inconceivability of the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; having trained myself, I shall also extensively expound this meaning for others."
If there are those who cannot believe or accept this, you should know that such people have long cultivated the notion of impermanence; for these individuals, I shall act as frost and hail.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are now well able to protect and uphold the True Dharma; protecting the Dharma in this manner, you do not deceive others.”
"By virtue of the karmic conditions of the wholesome deed of not deceiving others, one attains long life and gains skillful knowledge of past lives.
**Chapter Two: The Adamantine Body** At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son!
The body of the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding body, the indestructible body, the adamantine body, and the body that does not subsist on coarse food; it is the Dharma-body.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, I do not perceive any such bodies as these.”
One sees only a body that is impermanent, subject to destruction, composed of atoms, and sustained by various foods. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!
You must not now say that the body of the Tathāgata is not firm and is subject to destruction like the body of an ordinary person.”
Good son!

You should now know that the body of the Tathāgata is firm and indestructible throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas; it is not a human or celestial body, nor a body of fear, nor a body sustained by various foods.
The body of the Tathāgata is no-body; this body is neither born nor extinguished, neither practiced nor cultivated, immeasurable and boundless, without tracks, without cognition, and without form.
It is ultimately pure, without movement, without sensation, and without activity;
it does not abide and does not act; it is without flavor and without admixture. It is not...
This is conditioned, yet not karma, not fruit, not practice, not cessation, not mind, and not a numerical category;
it is inconceivable and eternally inconceivable. It is without consciousness and detached from the mind, yet not detached from the mind.
Its mind is equanimous: it neither exists nor does it not exist; it has no coming or going, yet it also goes.
Come! It is not broken, not destroyed, not interrupted, not severed, not emerging, not ceasing;
it is neither a master nor a master, neither existent nor non-existent, neither conceptualization nor discernment, neither syllables nor non-syllables, neither fixed nor unfixed;
it is invisible yet clearly seen, a placeless place, and without...
The dwelling is indeed a dwelling, yet it is neither darkness nor light; it is neither quiescent, and yet it is quiescent.

It is nothingness, neither receiving nor giving, pure and stainless, free from contention and having severed contention, abiding in non-abiding, neither grasping nor falling, neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit.
The field is inexhaustible and beyond exhaustion, free from all exhaustion; it is emptiness that transcends emptiness.
Although it does not abide eternally, it is not subject to momentary extinction. It is without defilement, without characters and free from characters;
it is neither sound nor speech, neither cultivation nor practice, neither measurable nor quantifiable, neither one nor different, and neither form nor appearance.
Adorned with all marks, it is neither courageous nor fearful; it is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, neither feverish nor non-feverish;
it cannot be seen and possesses no characteristics.
The Tathāgata delivers all sentient beings; because there is no delivering, he is able to liberate sentient beings.
Because there is no liberating, he awakens sentient beings.
Because there is no awakening, he teaches the Dharma according to reality.
Because there is no duality, it is immeasurable and unequaled.
It is as level as space, devoid of form or appearance, identical to the nature of non-arising, neither interrupted nor eternal.
Constantly practicing the One Vehicle, sentient beings perceive three.
Without retreating or turning back, they sever all fetters.

Neither contending nor encountering, they do not abide in a nature that is not-nature; they are neither joined nor dispersed, neither long nor short, neither round nor square; they are neither the aggregates, bases, and elements, yet they are also the aggregates, bases, and elements; they neither increase nor diminish, neither win nor lose.
The body of the Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable merits that there is no one who knows it and no one who does not know it;
there is no one who sees it and no one who does not see it.

It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither mundane nor supramundane, neither created nor uncreated, neither dependent nor non-dependent, neither the four great elements nor not the four great elements, neither caused nor causeless, neither a sentient being nor not a sentient being, and neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa. It is a lion, a great lion; it is neither a body nor not a body, and it is ineffable.

Excluding the characteristic of a single dharma, which cannot be calculated, at the time of parinirvāṇa one does not enter parinirvāṇa; the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is fully accomplished with such immeasurable and subtle merits.
“Kāśyapa! Only the Tathāgata knows this mark; it is not something known by the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa!”
Such merits constitute the body of a Tathāgata; it is not a body nurtured by various kinds of food.
Kāśyapa, since the merit of the Tathāgata’s true body is such as this, how could it ever suffer from various ailments and pains, being fragile and unstable like a vessel of unbaked clay?
Kāśyapa! The reason the Tathāgata manifests the suffering of illness is that he wishes to discipline and subdue all sentient beings. Good son!

"You should now know that the body of the Tathāgata is a vajra-body. From this day forward, you should always contemplate this meaning with a focused mind; do not think of it as a body sustained by food. You should also explain to others that the body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Tathāgata has accomplished such meritorious virtues, how could his body be subject to the suffering of illness, or be destroyed by impermanence?”

From this day forward, I shall constantly contemplate that the body of the Tathāgata is the eternal Dharma-body and the body of bliss, and I shall also explain it extensively to others in this same way.
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is indestructible like a vajra, yet we do not yet know what its cause is.
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! Because of the causal conditions of being able to protect and uphold the True Dharma, one attains the accomplishment of this vajra-body.
Kāśyapa!”
Due to my past causes and conditions for protecting the Dharma, I have now attained this adamantine body, which is eternally abiding and indestructible. Good son!

Those who uphold the True Dharma need not receive the five precepts nor cultivate dignified deportment; they should instead carry swords, bows, arrows, spears, and halberds to protect bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bhikṣu who is free from protection, dwelling alone in empty and quiet places, among burial mounds or at the foot of trees, one should say that such a person is a true bhikṣu.”
"If there are those who travel while followed and guarded by attendants, you should know that such people are merely 'shaven-headed householders' (tulu jushi).
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not speak such words, calling them 'shaven-headed householders.'"

If there is a bhikṣu who, wherever he goes, provides for his own needs with simple sufficiency, recites the sūtras, contemplates while practicing seated meditation, and when anyone comes to inquire about the Dharma, he immediately explains it for them—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, merit, and having few desires and knowing contentment.

Although they are able to preach the Dharma in such various ways, they are nevertheless unable to let out the lion’s roar, are not surrounded by lions, and cannot subdue those who are unrighteous and wicked.
In this way, a bhikṣu who cannot benefit himself nor benefit sentient beings should be known as one who is indolent and lazy.
Although he may be able to uphold the precepts and guard his pure conduct, it should be known that such a person is incapable of accomplishing anything of significance.

If there is a bhikṣu whose requisites for sustaining the body are also always abundant, and who is further able to guard and uphold the precepts he has received, and who can roar the lion’s roar, extensively expounding the sublime Dharma—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, and avadānas.
Having extensively expounded such ninefold scriptures for the sake of others, in order to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, he proclaimed these words:
"In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is ordained that bhikṣus must not keep slaves, cattle, sheep, or any other things that are contrary to the Dharma."
If there is a bhikṣu who keeps such impure items as these, he should be disciplined.

As the Tathāgata previously stated in another sūtra: "If there is a bhikṣu who keeps such unlawful items as these, a certain king shall punish him according to the law and compel him to return to lay life."
"If there is a bhikṣu who can let out such a lion's roar, and if those who have broken the precepts hear these words, they will all become enraged and harm this Dharma-preacher."
Even if this Dharma-preacher should pass away, he is still called one who upholds the precepts, benefiting both himself and others.
For this reason, I authorize the rulers of nations, ministers, prime ministers, and all lay followers (upāsakas) to protect those who preach the Dharma.
If there are those who wish to protect the true Dharma, they should train themselves in this way.
Kāśyapa! Those who thus break the precepts and do not protect the Dharma are called "shaven-headed householders."
It is not by maintaining the precepts that one receives such a name. Good son!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in this city of Kuśinagara, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Prāmodyavardhana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.

At that time, the world was vast, magnificent, and pure; it was prosperous, peaceful, and secure, with a flourishing population free from hunger and thirst, like the bodhisattvas in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, remained in the world for immeasurable time; having transformed sentient beings, he subsequently entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
After the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for immeasurable billions of years, and the Buddha-dharma was not extinguished for another forty years.

At that time, there was a precept-observing bhikṣu named Jue-de (Jñānaguṇa), who was surrounded by a vast multitude of disciples and followers. He was capable of the lion’s roar, extensively proclaiming and expounding the ninefold canon of scriptures, and he established a rule that bhikṣus must not keep slaves, cattle, sheep, or any other improper things.
At that time, there were many precept-breaking bhikṣus who, upon hearing these words, all gave rise to malicious thoughts; they took up swords and staves to threaten the Dharma Master.

Then a king named Yǒudé (Possessing Virtue), having heard of this matter, went at once to where the preacher of the Dharma was for the sake of protecting the Dharma, and engaged in a fierce battle with those wicked, precept-breaking bhikṣus, enabling the preacher of the Dharma to escape harm.
At that time, the king’s body was covered with wounds from swords, arrows, and spears; there was not a single spot on his person as large as a mustard seed that remained uninjured.
Thereupon, Jñānagupta immediately praised the king, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You are now truly a protector of the True Dharma; in a future age, this body shall become an immeasurable vessel for the Dharma.

At that time, having heard the Dharma, the king’s heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately passed away to be reborn in the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya, becoming that Buddha’s foremost disciple.

The king, along with his retinue, subjects, and kin—whether they were warriors or those who followed with joy—all attained non-retrogression from the mind of bodhi; at the end of their lives, they were all reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
After his life has ended, the bhikṣu Jñānaguṇa shall likewise attain rebirth in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, becoming the second disciple among that Buddha’s assembly of śrāvakas.
If there is a time when the True Dharma is about to perish, one should uphold and protect it in this manner.
Kāśyapa! The king at that time was none other than myself.
The bhikṣu who preached the Dharma was Kāśyapa Buddha. Kāśyapa!
Those who protect the True Dharma obtain such immeasurable fruits and rewards as these.
"By these causes and conditions, I have today attained various marks with which to adorn myself, achieving the Dharma-body and the indestructible body.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The eternal body of the Tathāgata is like an inscription carved in stone.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Good son!"
For these reasons, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās should diligently protect and uphold the True Dharma; the karmic fruit of protecting the Dharma is vast and immeasurable.
Good son! For this reason, upāsakas who protect the Dharma should take up swords and staves to guard such bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma.
Those who merely receive and maintain the five precepts cannot be called followers of the Mahāyāna.
Not receiving the five precepts for the sake of protecting the true Dharma is what is called the Mahāyāna.
One who protects the true Dharma should wield swords and weapons to attend upon the teacher of the Dharma.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bhikṣus associate as companions with such upāsakas who carry swords and staves, can they be said to have a teacher?”
Is he without a teacher?
Is he one who upholds the precepts,
or is he one who violates them?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not say that these people are breakers of the precepts. Good son!
After my parinirvāṇa, in an age of turbidity and evil, the lands will be desolate and chaotic, with people plundering one another and suffering from hunger.
At that time, many will resolve to leave the household life for the sake of escaping hunger; such persons as these are called "bald men."
These shaven-headed ones, seeing bhikṣus who uphold the precepts, possess perfect deportment, are pure, and protect the True Dharma, will drive them out, or even kill or harm them.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should this person who upholds the precepts and protects the True Dharma travel through villages and cities to teach and transform others?”
“Good son! For this reason, I now permit those who uphold the precepts to rely upon laypeople who carry swords and staves as their companions.
If kings, ministers, elders, or upāsakas, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, carry swords and staves, I declare that such individuals are called ‘upholders of the precepts.’”
"Even if one holds a sword or a staff, one should not take life.
If one can act in this way, one may be called the foremost in upholding the precepts. Kāśyapa!"

Regarding those who protect the Dharma: they possess right view and are able to extensively proclaim the Mahāyāna sūtras. They never hold royal parasols, oil flasks, grain, rice, or various fruits and melons. They do not draw near to kings, ministers, or elders for the sake of gain and offerings. Toward all donors, their minds are free from flattery and crookedness; they are fully endowed with dignified deportment and subdue those evil persons who violate the precepts. Such individuals are called masters who uphold the precepts and protect the Dharma; they serve as true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings, and their minds are vast and expansive like the great ocean.
Kāśyapa!

If there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and offerings, all of that person’s disciples and followers will likewise imitate their teacher in greedily seeking gain and offerings; such a person thus brings about the ruin of his own assembly.
Kāśyapa! There are three kinds of assemblies:
first, the assembly of those who violate the precepts; second, the assembly of the ignorant; and third, the pure assembly.
A community of monks that is corrupted by broken precepts is easily destroyed.
A community of monks who maintain pure precepts cannot be destroyed by the causes and conditions of gain and offerings.
What is meant by a community of monks corrupted by broken precepts?

If there is a bhikṣu who, although he maintains the prohibitive precepts, for the sake of gain and support associates with those who have broken the precepts—sitting, rising, walking, and coming together with them, being intimately attached to them, and sharing in their activities—he is called one who has broken the precepts and is also called a member of a mixed saṃgha.
What is the deluded saṃgha?

If there is a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya who has dull faculties, is dark-witted and obtuse, yet practices few desires and begs for alms; on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and at the time of the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), he instructs his own disciples to perform pure confession, but when he sees non-disciples who have frequently violated the prohibitions, he is unable to instruct them to perform pure confession, and instead proceeds to recite the precepts and hold the invitation ceremony together with them—this is called the deluded saṃgha.
What is meant by the "Pure Sangha"?

There is a community of bhikṣus that cannot be thwarted or destroyed by hundreds of thousands of billions of māras. This assembly of bodhisattvas is pure by nature; they are able to harmonize the two aforementioned groups and cause them all to dwell securely within the pure assembly. These are called the supreme great teachers who protect the Dharma.

One who skillfully upholds the Vinaya, desiring to discipline and benefit sentient beings, knows whether the characteristics of the various precepts are light or heavy; that which is not of the Vinaya they do not realize or know, while that which is of the Vinaya they do indeed realize and know.
How does he tame sentient beings?
If bodhisattvas, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, constantly enter villages without regard for the time or season;
or they go to the dwellings of widows or courtesans and reside there together with them for many years.
If that which is improper for a śrāvaka to do is instead called "taming and benefiting sentient beings," how is one to know what is grave?
If one sees that the Tathāgata has established a precept due to a particular incident, [he says]: "From this day forward, you must be careful not to transgress it again."

Just as the four grave prohibitions are things that those who have left the household life ought not to commit, yet one deliberately commits them; such a person is neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya—this is what is called "grave."
What constitutes a light offense?
If one commits a light matter and is able to relinquish it after these three admonitions, this is called "light.
Regarding "not being certified by what is not in accordance with the Vinaya": if there are those who praise and advocate for the use of impure things, one should not dwell together with them.

Regarding those who should be certified in this Vinaya: they have studied the precepts well and do not associate with those who break them; seeing those whose conduct accords with the Vinaya, their hearts give rise to joy; thus they are able to understand what has been enacted in the Buddha-dharma and are skilled at explaining it—such a person is called a Vinaya Master.
It is the same for one who well understands a single word or well upholds the sūtras.
Thus it is, son of good family!
The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable; the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
So it is, so it is; it is truly as the Holy Teaching declares.”
The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable; the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable. Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, indestructible, and without change.
"I have now learned this well, and I shall also extensively proclaim this meaning for others.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The body of the Tathāgata is the vajra-body, the indestructible body; a bodhisattva should train well in this way, with right view and right knowledge.
If one can thus know and see with perfect clarity, one sees the Buddha’s vajra-body, the indestructible body, just as one sees various forms and images within a mirror.
Chapter Three: On the Merit of the Name The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Three: On the Merit of the Name. At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed Kāśyapa: “Good son!
You should now properly uphold the words, phrases, and all the merits of this sutra.
If there were any sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the name of this sutra, were to be reborn in the four miserable realms, such a thing would be impossible.
Why is this? Such a sutra as this is that which has been practiced by immeasurable and boundless Buddhas; I shall now describe the merits thereby obtained.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?”
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This sutra is named 'Mahāparinirvāṇa'; its beginning is excellent, its middle is excellent, and its end is excellent."
The meaning is profound and the phrasing is excellent; it is perfectly complete with the pure Brahma-conduct, and the treasury of the vajra-jewel is full and without deficiency.
Listen well now, for I shall speak.
Good son, that which is called "Great" is termed "Eternal," just as the eight great rivers all flow back to the great ocean.

This sutra is likewise: it subdues all fetters, afflictions, and the nature of Māras, and subsequently leads to Great Parinirvāṇa through the relinquishing of body and life; therefore, it is named "Great Parinirvāṇa."
Good son! It is also like a physician who possesses a secret formula that encompasses all existing medical prescriptions. Good son!
The Tathāgata is likewise; the various profound and secret treasuries of the sublime Dharma he has taught all enter into the Great Parinirvāṇa, and for this reason it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good son! It is like a farmer who sows seeds in the spring months; he constantly harbors expectations, but once he has harvested the fruit, all his expectations come to rest. Good son!

All sentient beings are likewise: while studying other sutras, they constantly crave their flavor; yet once they hear this Great Parinirvāṇa, their longing for all the flavors found in those other sutras is forever severed.
This Great Nirvana can enable sentient beings to cross over the various streams of existence.
Good son! Just as among all footprints, the elephant’s footprint is the foremost;
This sutra is likewise the most supreme among all sutras and samādhis.
Good son! It is like plowing a field: autumn plowing is the most excellent.
This sutra is likewise the most excellent among all sutras. Good son!
It is like how, among all medicines, clarified butter (ghṛta) is the foremost;
It effectively cures the feverish afflictions and distracted minds of sentient beings; thus, this Great Nirvāṇa is the most supreme. Good son!
It is like sweet clarified butter, which is endowed with eight flavors.
The Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise thus, being fully endowed with eight flavors.

What are these eight? First, permanence; second, constancy; third, peace; fourth, coolness; fifth, freedom from aging; sixth, freedom from death; seventh, freedom from defilement; eighth, bliss. These are the eight flavors with which it is fully endowed.
Possessing these eight flavors, it is therefore called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others dwell securely within this, they are further able to manifest parinirvāṇa in various places; for this reason, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to attain parinirvāṇa through this Great Parinirvāṇa, they should train themselves thus: that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, and that the Dharma and the Saṃgha are likewise so.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
The merit of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; the Dharma and the Saṃgha are likewise inconceivable; and this Great Nirvāṇa is also inconceivable.”
If there are those who study this sutra, they will attain the gateway to the True Dharma and be able to act as skilled physicians.
As for those who have not yet studied it, you should know that such persons are blind, lacking the eye of wisdom, and shrouded by ignorance.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Three;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Nature of the Tathāgata, Part One.
The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas analytically expound upon the Great Parinirvāṇa, there are four aspects of its meaning.

What are these four? First, self-correction; second, correcting others; third, being able to provide answers according to questions; and fourth, skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions.
What is meant by "correcting oneself"?
It is when the Buddha-Tathāgata, having perceived the various causes and conditions, speaks accordingly. For example, it is like a bhikṣu who, seeing a great mass of blazing fire, says:

"I would rather embrace this fiercely burning mass of fire than ever dare to slander the twelve divisions of the sūtras and the secret treasury spoken by the Tathāgata, claiming they were spoken by Pāpīyān; nor would I say that the Tathāgata, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha are impermanent."
To speak in such a manner is to deceive oneself and to deceive others as well.
It would be better to sever one's own tongue with a sharp blade than ever to say that the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are impermanent.

If one hears others speak thus and yet does not believe or accept it, one should instead give rise to compassion for those speakers, reflecting that the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are inconceivable.
"One should maintain [this practice] in this way: observing one's own body as being like a mass of fire—this is called 'correcting oneself.
What is 'correcting others'?

When the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, there was a woman nursing an infant who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and having some concerns on her mind, she sat to one side, reflecting within herself.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], asked intentionally:
"Out of affectionate concern, did you give the child much ghee to eat, without considering whether he could digest it or not?
Then the woman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You have skillfully known the thoughts within my mind. I only pray that the Tathāgata will instruct me as to how much [I should give].
World-Honored One!"
"Today at dawn, I gave my son much ghee; fearing he may not be able to digest it, I worry that his life might be cut short prematurely.
I pray only that the Tathāgata will explain this for me.
The Buddha said:
"What your child has eaten will be digested immediately, and his lifespan will be increased.
Upon hearing this, the woman’s heart leaped with great joy, and she spoke again:
"The Tathāgata speaks the truth; therefore, I am filled with delight."
“World-Honored One, it is thus: for the sake of taming all sentient beings, you are well able to distinguish and explain what is digested and what is not digested.
You also teach that all dharmas are without self and impermanent.”

"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to first preach that [the self] is eternal, those who have come to receive his transformation would say, 'This Dharma is the same as that of the non-Buddhists,' and would immediately depart.
He further told the woman:
"When your child grows up and is able to walk by himself, whatever he eats will be able to digest even what is difficult to digest; the ghee you originally gave him will no longer suffice."
My śrāvaka disciples are also like this; they are like your infant, unable to digest this Dharma of permanence. Therefore, I previously taught suffering and impermanence.
If my śrāvaka disciples have fully prepared their merits and are capable of practicing the Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall explain for them the six flavors within these sūtras.
What are the six flavors?

It is said that suffering is the flavor of acidity, impermanence is the flavor of saltiness, non-self is the flavor of bitterness, pleasure is like the flavor of sweetness, self is like the flavor of pungency, and permanence is like the flavor of blandness.
In that world there are three kinds of flavors, namely: impermanence, non-self, and suffering.
Taking afflictions as fuel and wisdom as fire, these causes and conditions produce the meal of nirvana—namely, permanence, bliss, and self—which causes all disciples to relish it with delight.
He further addressed the woman:
"If you have business to go elsewhere, you should expel the wicked sons from the house and entrust the entire treasure store to the virtuous son."
The woman said to the Buddha, “It is truly as the Holy One has taught: a treasury of precious jewels should be shown to a good son, not to a wicked son.
“Sister! [the Buddha replied.]

I am also like this: at the time of my parinirvāṇa, I shall not bestow the Tathāgata’s subtle, secret, and unsurpassed Dharma-treasury upon the śrāvaka disciples, just as you do not show your treasure store to an unworthy son;
rather, I must entrust it to the bodhisattvas, just as you commit your treasure store to a worthy son.

Why is this? Because the śrāvaka disciples give rise to the notion of change and alteration, thinking that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has truly entered parinirvāṇa; yet, in truth, I have not truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Just as when you had gone far on a journey and had not yet returned, your wicked son said that you were dead, though you were not actually dead;
so too, the bodhisattvas declare that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging, just like your good son who did not say you were dead.
"For this reason, I entrust this unsurpassed secret treasury to the bodhisattvas.
Good son, if there are sentient beings who say that the Buddha is eternally abiding and unchanging, you should know that in their households there is a Buddha; this is called 'correcting others.'"
"Regarding one who is able to answer according to the question:
suppose someone were to come and ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One, 'How should I act so that, without giving away wealth and property, I may be called a great donor (mahādānapati)?"
The Buddha said:
"If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who have few desires and are content, and who neither accept nor keep impure things, one should bestow upon such persons slaves, servants, and laborers."
To those who practice the holy life, one gives women;
to those who abstain from alcohol and meat, one gives alcohol and meat;
to those who do not eat past midday, one gives food past midday.
Without clinging to the fragrance of flowers, one gives with flowers as an offering.
For one who gives in this manner, the fame of their giving spreads abroad, reaching even to other lands, while not a single hair’s breadth of the expenditure of wealth and treasures is lost.
"This is what is called being able to answer in accordance with the question.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
One who eats meat should not give meat as an offering.
Why? Because I see that those who do not eat meat possess great merit.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are now able to well understand my intention; a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should act in this way.”
"Good son!
From this day forward, I do not permit my śrāvaka disciples to eat meat. When receiving food offered by a donor in faith, you should regard that food as being like the flesh of your own child."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why does the Tathāgata not permit the eating of meat?”
“Good son! Those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Why did the Tathāgata previously permit bhikṣus to eat the three kinds of pure meat?
"Kāśyapa! These three kinds of pure meat were permitted as a gradual regulation according to specific circumstances."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions do you not permit the ten kinds of impurity, up to and including the nine kinds of purity?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This, too, was established gradually according to circumstances; you should know that this is precisely the meaning of the present prohibition against eating meat.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the Tathāgata praises fish and meat as fine foods? "Good son!

I do not say that things such as fish and meat are fine foods. I say that sugarcane, non-glutinous rice, rock honey, all grains and wheat, black honey, milk, curd, and ghee are what constitute fine foods."
"Although it is said that one should possess various kinds of clothing, those that should be possessed must be of dyed colors; how much more so regarding the attachment to the taste of fish and meat.
Kāśyapa spoke again:

"If the Tathāgata were to prohibit the eating of meat, then those five kinds of flavors—milk, curd, whey, fresh butter, and clarified butter—as well as sesame oil, and furthermore, various garments such as *kauseya* silk, conch shells, leather, and vessels of gold and silver—such things as these should also not be accepted."
“Good son! You should not hold the same views as those Nirgranthas. Regarding all the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata, each has its own underlying intention.
Because of these differing intentions, he permitted the eating of the three kinds of pure meat.”
Because of these misconceptions, ten kinds of meat were prohibited.
Because of these misconceptions, all [meat] was entirely forbidden, including that from animals that died of natural causes. Kāśyapa!
"From this day forward, I decree that my disciples shall no longer eat any kind of meat. Kāśyapa!
For those who eat meat—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—all sentient beings, upon smelling the odor of their flesh, will give rise to terror."
For example, suppose there is a person who has been near a lion; when others see him, they smell the odor of the lion and likewise give rise to fear.
"Good son! It is like a person who eats garlic; being foul-smelling and loathsome, when others see him, they smell the stench and depart."
If those who see them from afar do not even wish to look at them, how much less would they approach them?
It is the same for all meat-eaters: when all sentient beings smell the odor of their flesh, they are utterly terrified and conceive the thought of fearing death;
all living creatures of water, land, and air flee from them, all saying, "This person is our enemy."

Therefore, a bodhisattva does not practice eating meat; yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests the act of eating meat. Although he manifests eating it, in reality he does not eat it. Good son!
If even such pure food as this a bodhisattva would not eat, how much less would he eat meat? Good son!

After my parinirvāṇa, after countless hundreds of years, when the four types of noble beings have all entered nirvāṇa and the True Dharma has been extinguished, during the Semblance Dharma, there will be bhikṣus who merely resemble those who uphold the Vinaya and recite the sūtras little. They will be greedy for food and drink to nourish their bodies; their clothing will be coarse, shabby, and ugly; their appearance will be haggard and devoid of majestic virtue. They will keep and raise oxen and sheep, carry firewood and grass upon their backs, and their hair, beards, and nails will all grow long and sharp. Though they wear the kāṣāya robe, they are like hunters; they stare narrowly and move slowly like a cat stalking a mouse, yet they constantly proclaim: "I have attained arhatship."
Afflicted by many illnesses and pains, they lie prostrate in filth; appearing virtuous and good on the outside, they harbor greed and jealousy within, like Brahmins who have taken a vow of silence.
In truth, they are not śramaṇas, yet they manifest the appearance of śramaṇas; their false views are rampant, and they slander the True Dharma.

Such persons as these destroy the precepts and disciplinary rules established by the Tathāgata, the correct conduct and dignified demeanor, the teaching on the fruit of liberation, the abandonment of impure dharmas, and the profoundly secret instructions.
Each acting according to their own whims, they perversely interpret the Sūtras and Vinaya, saying:
"The Tathāgata has permitted us all to eat meat.
Having fabricated this doctrine themselves, they claim it is the word of the Buddha; they dispute and litigate with one another, each calling himself a śramaṇa and a son of the Śākya.
"Good son!

At that time, there were also various śramaṇas who stored up raw grain, accepted fish and meat, prepared their own food with their own hands, and carried oil flasks, precious parasols, and leather sandals; they associated closely with kings, ministers, and elders."

They practice divination and the interpretation of stellar signs; they diligently cultivate the medical arts; they maintain slaves and servants, and accumulate gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, jade, and conch shells; they cultivate various fruits and melons; they study all manner of arts and crafts, such as painting, plasterwork, calligraphy, and teaching; they engage in planting roots and cuttings; they practice sorcery, incantations, and illusions; they compound various medicines; they perform as actors and musicians; they adorn themselves with perfumes and flowers; they play at dice, *chūpú*, and go-board games; and they study all kinds of technical skills.
"If there is a bhikṣu who can distance himself from such evil matters as these, I shall say that this person is truly my disciple.
At that time, Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen depend upon others for their livelihood.
When they go on almsround and receive food mixed with meat, how may they eat it in accordance with the pure Dharma?"
The Buddha said,
“Kāśyapa! You should wash it with water until it is separated from the meat, and only then eat it.”
If a food vessel has been defiled by meat, provided that it is rendered tasteless, its use is permitted and incurs no offense.
However, if one sees that there is much meat within the food, one should not accept it.
All meat that is visible should not be eaten; those who eat it incur transgression.
I now proclaim this regulation against eating meat; were I to explain it in detail, it would be impossible to exhaust.
"The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; therefore, I have spoken briefly.
This is what is called being able to answer according to the question. Kāśyapa!"
What is meant by "skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions"?
It is as if an assembly of the fourfold community were to come and ask me:
"World-Honored One!..."
Regarding this meaning: when the Tathāgata first appeared in the world, why did he not explain this profound and subtle Dharma-gate to King Prasenajit?
Why is it that at times he speaks of the deep and at times the shallow, and that what is called an offense at one time is called non-offense at another?
What is meant by "falling"?
What is meant by "discipline" (*vinaya*)?
And what is the meaning of "prātimokṣa"?
The Buddha said:
"Prātimokṣa is called 'contentment.
Accomplishing dignified deportment and possessing nothing that is stored up is also called 'pure livelihood. Those who fall away from it are said to fall into the four evil destinies."
Furthermore, as for those who fall, they descend into the hells, even unto Avīci; regarding the speed of their descent, it is swifter than a torrential rain.

Those who hear this shall be struck with awe and fear, firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts, not violating the rules of dignified conduct, practicing contentment, and refusing to accept any impure things.
Furthermore, "falling" (pāta) refers to being reborn in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; for these reasons, it is called "falling.
*Prātimokṣa* means to distance oneself from unwholesome and erroneous actions of body, speech, and mind.

The Vinaya consists of the entry into the precepts and dignified decorum (*vīryā*), as well as the profound sūtras and their excellent meanings. It prohibits the acceptance of all impure things and the conditions for such impurity; it also prohibits the four *pārājika* offenses, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the two *aniyata* dharmas, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the ninety-one *pāyattika*, the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas, the numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas, and the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
Furthermore, there may be someone who completely violates all precepts.
What constitutes "all"? It refers to the four grave offenses (pārājika) up to the seven rules for settling disputes (adhikaraṇa-śamatha).
Furthermore, there may be those who slander the profound sūtras of the true Dharma, as well as icchantikas, who fully accomplish the exhaustion of all marks and possess no causal conditions.

Such people as these claim for themselves that they are clever and of sharp intelligence, yet they conceal all their offenses, whether grave or light; they hide their various evils just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs.
These many sins remain unrepented throughout the long night; because they are not repented, they increase day and night.
These bhikṣus did not disclose the various offenses they had committed, which caused their transgressions to subsequently spread and proliferate.
Therefore, having understood this matter, the Tathāgata established the precepts gradually and not all at once.
At that time, a son of good family and a daughter of good family addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has known such matters for a long time; why did you not establish the precepts beforehand?"
Could it be that the World-Honored One intends to cause sentient beings to enter the Avīci Hell?

It is like a great multitude of people who, wishing to go to another land, lose their way on the correct path and follow a wrong one; because these people do not realize they are lost, they all believe this is the right road, and furthermore, they see no one whom they may ask about what is right or wrong.

Sentient beings are thus deluded regarding the Buddha-dharma and do not perceive what is correct and true; the Tathāgata should first expound the right path and instruct the bhikṣus, decreeing: "This is a violation of the precepts; this is the upholding of the precepts," and thus establish the regulations.

Why is this? The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is the ultimate truth; he knows and perceives the true path. Only the Tathāgata, the God among Gods, can expound the superior merit and the profound meaning of the ten wholesome actions. Therefore, I request that the precepts be established first.

The Buddha said, "Good son, if one says that the Tathāgata can proclaim for sentient beings the superior merit of the ten wholesome actions, then the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as he does Rāhula. How can you raise the objection, 'Could it be that the World-Honored One wishes to cause sentient beings to enter hell'?"
I see that for even a single person who possesses the causes and conditions to fall into the Avīci Hell, I would remain in this world for an eon, or nearly an eon, on their behalf.
Since I possess great compassion for all sentient beings, for what reason would I ever deceive those whom I regard as my own children, causing them to enter hell?
"Good son!
It is like a person in a king’s realm who wears patched robes; they see a hole in the cloth and only then mend it.
The Tathāgata is likewise: seeing that sentient beings possess the causes and conditions for falling into the Avīci Hell, he immediately mends them with the goodness of the precepts."
"Good son!

It is like a wheel-turning sage king who first teaches the ten wholesome dharmas to sentient beings. Later, as there are gradually those who practice evil, the king accordingly suppresses them step by step. Once all evils have been suppressed, he then personally practices the dharma of a sage king."
Good son! I am also like this:

although I have something to say, I do not establish a precept beforehand; rather, it is only because bhikṣus gradually practice what is contrary to the Dharma that I subsequently establish a precept according to the specific matter.
“Sentient beings who delight in the Dharma and practice according to the teachings—such multitudes as these are able to see the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

Just as the wheel-treasure of a *cakravartin* king is inconceivable, so too is the Tathāgata inconceivable; the two treasures of Dharma and Saṃgha are also inconceivable; both those who can preach the Dharma and those who hear the Dharma are inconceivable. This is called skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
When a Bodhisattva thus analyzes and reveals the meanings of these four aspects, it is called the meaning of causes and conditions within the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, 'rectifying oneself' refers to attaining this Great Parinirvāṇa.
'Rectifying others' refers to my teaching for the bhikṣus that the Tathāgata eternally exists and is unchanging."
Regarding responding to questions, Kāśyapa:
because of your inquiry, I am able to extensively explain this profound and subtle principle for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

Regarding the meaning of causes and conditions: Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not understand such a profound meaning; they have not heard that the three dots of the letter "I" constitute the secret treasury of liberation, nirvāṇa, and mahāprajñā.
I shall now expound and analyze this here, opening the eye of wisdom for all śrāvakas.
Suppose someone were to say:
"How can these four matters be considered as one?"
"Is it not false?
One should then counter-question:
"This space is non-existent, unmoving, and unimpeded."
"What difference is there between these four matters? Could they possibly be called false?
"No, World-Honored One."
"These various phrases all have but one meaning, namely, the meaning of emptiness.
Correcting oneself, correcting others, being able to respond to questions, and explaining the meaning of dependent origination are likewise thus; they are identical to Great Nirvana and no different.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who speak thus:
'The Tathāgata is impermanent.'"
How should one know that this is impermanent?
As the Buddha said:

"The extinction of all afflictions is called Nirvana; it is like the extinguishing of a fire, where nothing whatsoever remains. The extinction of all afflictions is likewise, and for this reason it is named Nirvana."
"How is it that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma, immutable?
As the Buddha has said:
'To be free from all modes of existence (bhava) is called nirvāṇa; within this nirvāṇa, there are no modes of existence.'"
"How is it that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, immutable?
"Just as when a garment is completely worn out, it is no longer called a 'thing,' so too with nirvāṇa: when all afflictions are extinguished, it is no longer called a 'thing.'"
"How is it that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma, immutable?
As the Buddha has said:
'The departure from desire and cessation is called nirvāṇa; it is like a person whose head has been severed—there is then no head.'"
"Detachment from desire and tranquility are likewise thus: they are empty and possess nothing; therefore, they are called Nirvana.
How is it that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma, immutable?
As the Buddha said:
"For example, like hot iron struck by a hammer, sparks fly forth; once scattered, they are instantly extinguished, and their whereabouts can no longer be known."
"Having already crossed over the mire of all existences and sensual desire, he has attained the unmoving state,
yet one does not know where he has gone.
"In what way is the Tathāgata a permanently abiding dharma, unchanging and immutable?"
“Kāśyapa! If anyone raises such an objection, it is called a false objection.
Kāśyapa!”
You should not entertain such a thought as that the nature of the Tathāgata is subject to extinction.
Kāśyapa! That which extinguishes afflictions is not called a "thing."
Why is this? Because it is eternally ultimate, it is therefore called "constant. This phrase is quiescent and unsurpassed.
All marks are extinguished without remainder; this phrase is pure white, eternally abiding and non-retrogressive.
Therefore, nirvana is called eternally abiding; the Tathāgata is likewise, eternally abiding and unchanging.
That which is called "shooting stars" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the statement that "having been dispersed, they are immediately extinguished and their location is unknown," this means that once the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all Tathāgatas have been extinguished, they no longer abide within the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma (*nityadharma*), free from change or transformation.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata reveres and makes offerings to it; because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If the fire of afflictions is extinguished, the Tathāgata is also extinguished; in that case, the Tathāgata would have no permanent abode.”
Just as when that flying iron, once its red color has vanished, one knows not where it has gone;
so too are the Tathāgata’s afflictions: having been extinguished, they have no destination.
Furthermore, just as that iron, once its heat and redness have ceased, no longer exists, so too is the Tathāgata:
when impermanence has ceased and the fire of afflictions is extinguished, he enters nirvāṇa.
"You should know that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
"Good son! That which is called 'iron' refers to all ordinary worldlings."
Ordinary people, though they may extinguish their afflictions, have them arise again after they have been extinguished; therefore, they are called impermanent.
The Tathāgata is not like this: having extinguished them, they do not arise again; therefore, he is called permanent.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Just as when the red color of iron has vanished, it returns to the fire and the red color arises once more;
if the Tathāgata were like this, his fetters (*saṃyojana*) would have to arise again. If the fetters were to arise again, he would be impermanent."
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!
You should not now speak such words as that the Tathāgata is impermanent.”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is eternal,
son of good family!
Just as when wood is burned, there remains ashes once it has been extinguished, so too,
once the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been extinguished, there is *nirvāṇa*.
The analogies of destroying a garment, severing a head, or breaking a jar are likewise the same.
Such objects as these each have their own names, called "tattered cloth," "severed head," and "broken jar.
Kāśyapa! Just as iron that has grown cold can be made hot again.
The Tathāgata is not like this; having severed the afflictions, he is ultimately cool, and the blazing fire of the afflictions never arises again.

Kāśyapa, you should know that immeasurable sentient beings are like that iron; with the blazing fire of my untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), I burn away the fetters of the afflictions of those sentient beings.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“Excellent, excellent!
I now truly understand what the Tathāgata has taught: that all Buddhas are eternal.”
The Buddha said: “Kāśyapa!

It is like a noble cakravartin king who, while normally residing in the inner palace, may at times go out for recreation in the rear gardens. Although the king is not among the court ladies, one cannot say that the noble cakravartin has passed away.”
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;
although he does not manifest in the realm of Jambudvīpa and enters into nirvana, he is not called impermanent.
Having emerged from immeasurable afflictions, the Tathāgata enters the place of peace and bliss of nirvana, where he wanders among the flowers of awakening, enjoying joy and happiness.
Kāśyapa asked again:
“As the Buddha has said, ‘I have long since crossed the great ocean of afflictions.
If the Buddha has already crossed the ocean of afflictions, for what reason did he again consort with Yaśodharā and father Rāhula?”
"For this reason, you should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed over the great ocean of afflictions and fetters.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain its causes and conditions.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should not say: 'The Tathāgata has long since crossed the great ocean of afflictions; for what reason did he again father Rāhula with Yaśodharā?
By this cause and condition, you should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of the fetters of affliction."
"Good sons!
This Great Nirvāṇa can establish great meaning; you should now listen with a sincere mind and attentively, and explain it extensively for others, without giving rise to alarm or doubt."

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who dwells in the Great Nirvāṇa, he can cause even Sumeru, the King of Mountains, so high and vast, to enter entirely into the husk of a mustard seed; yet those sentient beings who depend upon Sumeru will not feel constricted, nor will they have any perception of coming or going, remaining no different than before.
Only those who were ready for deliverance saw this bodhisattva place Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed husk, and then return it to its original location. Good son!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Parinirvāṇa and are able to place the trichiliocosm within a mustard seed husk; yet the sentient beings therein have no sense of confinement or of coming and going, remaining exactly as they were before, without any change.
Only those who were ready for deliverance saw this bodhisattva place this trichiliocosm inside a mustard seed husk, and then restore it to its original location.
"Good son!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Parinirvāṇa and are able to place a trichiliocosm within a single pore, and even the original location remains exactly as it was."
"Good son!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa, take up the worlds of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems of the ten directions and place them upon the point of a needle as if threading a jujube leaf; they then cast them into other buddha-worlds in distant quarters, yet all the sentient beings therein do not perceive their coming and going or where they have been placed."
Only those who are ready for deliverance can see it; this applies even to its original location. Good son!

Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, dwelling in the Great Nirvāṇa, seize the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—each a trichiliocosm—and place them in their right palm like a potter’s wheel, casting them into other worlds as numerous as motes of dust. Not a single sentient being has the perception of coming or going; only those who are ready for deliverance see it, and this applies even to their original locations.
"Good son!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, abiding in the Great Parinirvāṇa, take up all the immeasurable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and entirely place them within their own bodies. The sentient beings therein experience no crowding whatsoever, nor do they have any perception of coming, going, or dwelling; only those who are ready to be saved can see this, and it is likewise true even for their original locations."
"Good son!

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Parinirvāṇa and place the worlds of the ten directions within a single mote of dust; yet the sentient beings therein have no perception of confinement or of coming and going, and only those who are ready to be delivered can perceive this, even as it is with their original locations."
Good son, when this bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the Great Nirvāṇa, he is able to manifest various and immeasurable supernatural transformations; for this reason, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.

The immeasurable supernormal transformations manifested by this bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be fathomed by any sentient being; how then can you know that the Tathāgata indulged in sexual desire and fathered Rāhula?

“Good son! I have long dwelt in this Great Parinirvāṇa, manifesting various supernatural powers and transformations. Within this trichiliocosm of ten billion suns and moons and ten billion Jambudvīpas, I have manifested these in various ways, as explained at length in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Within this trichiliocosm, or specifically in Jambudvīpa, I manifest nirvana, yet I do not ultimately undergo final nirvana.

Or, in Jambudvīpa, I manifest entering a mother’s womb, causing my parents to conceive the thought that I am their son; however, this body of mine is ultimately not born from the union of lustful desire.
For immeasurable kalpas in the past, I have long been free from lustful desire; this present body of mine is the Dharma-body, which, in accordance with worldly ways, manifests entry into a womb.
"Good son!
In this Jambudvīpa, within the Lumbinī Grove, he manifested birth from his mother Māyā; immediately upon being born, he was able to walk seven paces to the east and proclaim these words:
'Among humans, devas, and asuras, I am the most honored and supreme.'"
When my parents, humans, and devas saw this, they were filled with wonder and joy, giving rise to a sense of rarity; yet these people all thought it was an infant.
However, for immeasurable kalpas, this body of mine has long been free from such states.
The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; it is not established by flesh, blood, sinews, veins, or marrow. Yet, in accordance with the ways of worldly beings, he manifests as an infant.
He walked seven steps to the south, manifesting his desire to serve as the supreme field of merit for immeasurable sentient beings.
He walked seven steps to the west, manifesting that his births were exhausted, that he had forever severed old age and death, and that this was his final body.
Walking seven steps to the north, he manifested that he had already transcended the cycle of birth and death within all realms of existence.
Walking seven steps to the east, he manifested that he would act as the leader and guide for all sentient beings.

Walking seven steps toward the four intermediate directions, he manifested the severing and extinction of the various afflictions and the natures of the four Māras, thereby attaining the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Walking seven steps upward, he manifested that he is not defiled by impure things, being like empty space.

Walking seven steps downward, he manifested the rain of Dharma to extinguish the fires of hell, causing those sentient beings to receive peaceful and secure bliss; for those who violate the prohibitions and precepts, he manifested as frost and hail.
Seven days after being born in Jambudvīpa, I further manifested the shaving of my hair; all people thought, "I am but an infant, having only now begun to shave my hair.
Among all humans, devas, Māra Pāpīyas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, there is none who can see the mark upon my crown (uṣṇīṣa), much less anyone who could hold a razor to it and shave my hair.
It is impossible that anyone could come with a blade to my crown;
for I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas, shaved off my beard and hair. It was only to accord with worldly conventions that I manifested the act of shaving my hair.
Once I was born, my parents took me into a celestial shrine and presented me to Maheśvara; as soon as Maheśvara saw me, he joined his palms in reverence and stood to one side.
For immeasurable kalpas, I have long since abandoned such practices as entering celestial shrines; yet, for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions, I manifest them in this way.

I manifested the piercing of my ears in Jambudvīpa; yet, in reality, there is no sentient being whatsoever capable of piercing my ears. It was only to accord with the ways of worldly beings that I manifested this.
Furthermore, I have fashioned lion-shaped earrings out of various jewels to adorn my ears;
yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have remained free from such ornaments. It is only for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions that I manifest these displays.
I manifested entering a schoolhouse to study writing and calculation;
yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already fully accomplished these.

Having universally observed all sentient beings within the three realms, there is none capable of being my teacher. Because I wish to accord with worldly conventions, I manifested entering a schoolhouse; for this reason, I am called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
My training in various arts and skills—such as riding elephants, horsemanship, and wrestling—is likewise so.
Furthermore, within Jambudvīpa, I manifest as the crown prince; all sentient beings see me as a prince, enjoying and delighting in the pleasures of the five senses.
Yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already abandoned such pleasures of the five senses; it is only for the sake of conforming to worldly ways that I manifest such appearances.

The physiognomists predicted of me: "If you do not leave the household life, you shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) and rule over Jambudvīpa; all sentient beings believe these words.
However, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King in order to become a Dharma-Wheel King (Dharmacakravartin).

In Jambudvīpa, I manifested the departure from the pleasures of the five desires with court ladies; having seen old age, sickness, death, and the śramaṇa, I left the household life to practice the Way. All sentient beings say that Prince Siddhārtha first renounced the world at this time;
however, I have already left the household life and studied the Way for immeasurable kalpas, and it is only to accord with worldly conventions that I manifest such things.

In Jambudvīpa, I manifested the renunciation of the household life, received full ordination, and practiced the Path with diligence, thereby attaining the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; all people said that the fruit of Arhatship was easy to obtain and not difficult to attain.
However, I had already attained the fruit of Arhatship throughout immeasurable kalpas.

For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, I sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, using grass as my seat, and subdued the hosts of Māras; thus everyone says that I first subdued the demonic officials at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
However, I have already subdued them for immeasurable kalpas; it was only to subdue sentient beings who are stubborn and unruly that I manifested this transformation.
I further manifest the passing of excrement and urine, as well as the exhaling and inhaling of breath, such that all beings say, "He has excrement and urine, and he exhales and inhales.

However, regarding the karmic retribution obtained by this body of mine, there is entirely no such thing as excrement, urine, or the inhalation and exhalation of breath; it is only for the sake of conforming to the world that I manifest these things.
I also manifest receiving the offerings of the faithful;
yet this body of mine is entirely free from hunger and thirst, and I display such things only to accord with worldly conventions.
Furthermore, because I manifest identity with all sentient beings, I appear to have sleep.
However, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already perfected supreme and profound wisdom, remaining far removed from the three realms of existence, and have maintained my dignified deportment.

When there was headache, abdominal pain, backache, being struck by a wooden stake, washing the feet, washing the hands, washing the face, rinsing the mouth, or chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks), the multitude all claimed that I underwent such things;
yet this body of mine has never experienced any of these matters.
My feet are pure like lotus flowers, and my breath is as clean and fragrant as the scent of the utpala; all sentient beings think I am a human being, yet in truth, I am not a human.
