I have further manifested the acceptance of rag-robes, their washing, dyeing, and mending;
yet I have long since had no need for such garments.

All people say that Rāhula is my son, King Śuddhodana is my father, and Queen Māyā is my mother, and that I dwelt in the world enjoying various pleasures before leaving such things behind to renounce the home life and study the Way.
The multitude spoke again:
"This Prince Gautama, of great lineage, has distanced himself from worldly pleasures to seek the supramundane Dharma.
However, I have long been free from worldly lust; such matters as these are entirely manifestations.
"All sentient beings universally say that this person is human, yet I am truly not so. Good son!

Although I repeatedly manifest entry into nirvana within this Jambudvīpa, I do not in fact enter ultimate nirvana; yet all sentient beings say that the Tathāgata has truly been extinguished. However, the nature of the Tathāgata does not truly perish forever. Therefore, you should know that this is an eternally abiding dharma, an unchanging dharma."
Good son! Great Nirvāṇa is the dharma-realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
I further manifest my appearance in the world within Jambudvīpa, and sentient beings all say that I have only now attained Buddhahood.

However, although I have already accomplished what was to be done throughout immeasurable kalpas, I manifest once again in Jambudvīpa as having newly attained Buddhahood, in accordance with the ways of the world.
I have also manifested in Jambudvīpa as one who does not uphold the precepts and commits the four grave offenses, such that all people see this and believe I have truly transgressed;
yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have strictly maintained the precepts without any lapse or deficiency.
I have further manifested as an icchantika in Jambudvīpa, and all people see me as an icchantika;
yet in truth, I am not an icchantika. How could one who is an icchantika ever attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
I further manifest in Jambudvīpa as one who breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha, and sentient beings all say that I am a schismatic;
yet when I observe the humans and devas, there is no one capable of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha.
I further manifest myself in Jambudvīpa to protect and uphold the True Dharma; all people say that I am a protector of the Dharma and are filled with wonder and astonishment.
Such is the nature of all Buddhas; one should not be astonished or amazed by this.
I have also manifested as Māra Pāpīyān in Jambudvīpa, such that all people claimed, "This is Pāpīyān";
yet for immeasurable kalpas I have been free from demonic deeds, pure and untainted like a lotus flower.
I further manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in a female body within Jambudvīpa, where all people say:
"How extraordinary! A woman is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

The Tathāgata ultimately does not receive a female body; however, for the sake of taming immeasurable sentient beings, he manifests in the form of a woman. Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he further displays various kinds of physical forms.
I have further manifested birth within the four realms of existence in Jambudvīpa;
yet, I have long since severed all causes for those realms, and though I could fall into the four realms due to karmic causes, I am born therein for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Furthermore, I manifest within Jambudvīpa as Brahmā, the King of Gods, causing those who serve Brahmā to dwell securely in the True Dharma;
yet I am not truly so, though all sentient beings unanimously regard me as the authentic Brahmā.
Manifesting in the form of celestial beings throughout all the temples of the gods is likewise so.
Furthermore, I manifest entering the houses of courtesans in Jambudvīpa;
yet I truly have no thoughts of lustful desire, being pure and unstained like a lotus flower.

For the sake of sentient beings who are greedy for lust and addicted to beauty, I proclaim the sublime Dharma at the crossroads; yet, in truth, I have no defiled mind of desire, though the multitude says that I am guarding women.
I have also manifested entry into the households of maidservants within Jambudvīpa in order to instruct the various female slaves to abide in the True Dharma;
yet, in reality, I possess no such evil karma as to fall into the status of a maidservant.
Furthermore, I manifest as a teacher within Jambudvīpa to instruct the ignorant and cause them to abide in the True Dharma.

I also manifest within Jambudvīpa, entering places of drinking and gambling, appearing to undergo various forms of victory, defeat, and contention, desiring thereby to rescue and deliver those sentient beings;
yet in truth, I possess no such evil karma, though all sentient beings claim that I perform such deeds.

I have also manifested dwelling for a long time among burial mounds, taking the form of a great vulture to deliver various flying birds; yet all sentient beings believe that I am truly a vulture’s body.
However, I have long since been free from such karma; it was only for the sake of delivering those birds and vultures that I manifested such a body.
I further manifest as a great elder within Jambudvīpa, desiring to establish immeasurable sentient beings in the True Dharma.

Moreover, I manifest as various kings, ministers, princes, and counselors, becoming the foremost among each of these groups, remaining in their royal positions for the sake of cultivating the True Dharma.

I further manifest the arising of an eon of pestilence within Jambudvīpa, where many sentient beings are afflicted by disease; first I bestow medicine, and subsequently I preach the subtle and wondrous True Dharma for them, causing them to dwell securely in unexcelled Bodhi, while all people say that this is merely the arising of an eon of pestilence.

Furthermore, he manifests the arising of a famine kalpa within Jambudvīpa; he provides food and drink according to their needs, and thereafter preaches the subtle and wondrous True Dharma for them, causing them to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, he manifests the arising of the kalpa of war within Jambudvīpa, and immediately preaches the Dharma to cause them to leave behind enmity and harm, enabling them to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, he manifests as one who, for those who conceive of permanence, teaches the perception of impermanence; for those who conceive of pleasure, he teaches the perception of suffering; for those who conceive of a self, he teaches the perception of non-self; and for those who conceive of purity, he teaches the perception of impurity.

If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to the three realms, he immediately preaches the Dharma for them to cause them to leave that place; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he preaches the unsurpassed, subtle, and wonderful medicine of the Dharma.
In order to sever the tree of all afflictions, he plants the tree of the unsurpassed medicinal Dharma.
Desiring to deliver and rescue those of other paths, he proclaims the True Dharma.

Although he manifests as a teacher for sentient beings, his mind from the outset has no notion of being a teacher to sentient beings; desiring to rescue those who are lowly and base, he manifests entry among them to preach the Dharma for them, yet it is not because of evil karma that he receives such a body.
The Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, abides thus in great parinirvāṇa; therefore, he is called eternally present and unchanging.
As it is with Jambudvīpa, so it is likewise with Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north.
As it is with the four continents, so it is with the trichiliocosm.
The twenty-five states of existence are explained in detail in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; for this reason, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
"If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who dwells securely in such Great Parinirvāṇa, they can manifest such supernatural transformations without any fear. Kāśyapa!"
For this reason, you should not say that Rāhula is the son of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I have already been free from desire and existence; therefore, the Tathāgata is called eternally abiding and is without change.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"In what sense is the Tathāgata said to be eternally abiding?
As the Buddha has said:"
"Just as when a lamp is extinguished, it has no location, so too is the Tathāgata; once he has entered parinirvāṇa, he likewise has no location.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "Good son!..."
You should not now speak in this way:
"Once a lamp has been extinguished, it has no location; likewise, when a Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, he too has no location."
"Good son! It is like when men or women light a lamp: if the lamp-stand, whether large or small, is filled with oil, its light will remain as long as there is oil;
once the oil is exhausted, the light likewise vanishes."
The extinction of its light is a metaphor for the extinction of afflictions; although the light is extinguished, the lamp and its base still remain.
The Tathāgata is likewise: although his afflictions have been extinguished, the Dharma-body eternally endures.
“Good son! What do you think? Do the light and the lamp-stand perish together?
Kāśyapa replied:
“No, World-Honored One!
Although they do not perish simultaneously, they are nonetheless impermanent.”
"If the Dharma-body is compared to a lamp-stand, and since the lamp-stand is impermanent,
the Dharma-body must likewise be impermanent. "Good son!
You should not now raise such an objection:
that while the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is the unsurpassed vessel of the Dharma, the vessel is impermanent and thus not the Tathāgata.
Among all phenomena, nirvāṇa is eternal; because the Tathāgata embodies it, he is called eternal.

Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called the extinction of a lamp is the nirvāṇa realized by an Arhat; because he has extinguished craving and all afflictions, it is metaphorically likened to the extinction of a lamp.
One who is an Anāgāmin is called "one who still possesses craving. Because they still possess craving, it cannot be said that they are the same as the extinguishing of a lamp.
Therefore, when I spoke in the past using indirect language, I used the metaphor of the extinguishing of a lamp; however, Great Nirvāṇa is not the same as the extinguishing of a lamp.

One who is an Anāgāmin does not come back repeatedly, nor does he return again to the twenty-five states of existence; he shall no longer receive a foul body, an insect-like body, a body of food, or a poisonous body—this is what is called an Anāgāmin.
If one further receives a body, they are called an Anāgāmin; if one does not receive a body, they are called an Anāgāmin.
One who has coming and going is called an Anāgāmin; one who has no coming and going is called an Anāgāmin.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Four.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Fourth Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature, Part Two.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
As the Buddha has taught, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a secret treasury.
This meaning is not so. Why is that?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess only esoteric speech; they have no esoteric treasury.

It is like a master of illusions who creates mechanical wooden figures; although people see them bending, stretching, looking down, and looking up, no one knows what is within that causes them to act so.
The Buddha-dharma is not like that; it causes all sentient beings to fully know and see. How, then, could one say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a secret treasury?
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Good son! As you have said, the Tathāgata truly has no secret treasury.
Why is this? Because..."

Just as the full moon in autumn, situated in the sky, is manifest, pure, and free from obscuration so that all people may behold it, so too are the words of the Tathāgata: they are revealed and manifest, pure and free from obscuration.
Fools do not understand and call it a "secret treasury," but when the wise fully comprehend it, it is no longer called a treasury. Good son!

It is like a person who has accumulated immeasurable billions of gold and silver, yet whose mind is so stingy that he refuses to give in charity to relieve the poor; such a hoarding is what is called a "secret treasury."

The Tathāgata is not like that; having accumulated immeasurable treasures of the sublime Dharma over boundless eons, his mind is free from stinginess, and he constantly bestows them as gifts upon all sentient beings. How, then, could it be said that the Tathāgata possesses a secret treasury?
Good son!

It is like a person whose physical faculties are incomplete—perhaps lacking one eye, one hand, or one foot—who, out of shame, does not wish to be seen by others; because others do not see [these deficiencies], they are called "hidden."

The Tathāgata is not like that; all his True Dharma is complete and without deficiency, allowing people to behold it directly. How, then, could one say that the Tathāgata has a secret treasury? Good son!
For example, it is like a poor man who owes much wealth to others; out of fear of his creditors, he hides himself and does not wish to appear, and for this reason it is called "concealment.
The Tathāgata is not like this: he owes nothing to sentient beings regarding worldly dharmas, and although he owes them the supramundane dharma, he likewise does not conceal it.
Why is this? Because they constantly regard all sentient beings as their only child and expound the unsurpassed Dharma for them. Good son!
It is like an elder who possesses abundant wealth and treasures, yet has only one son whom he loves and prizes deeply; with no thought of parting from him, he shows the son all his precious jewels.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he regards all sentient beings as his only son. Good son!
Just as people in the world cover over their male or female organs because they are ugly and loathsome, and thus call them "hidden," so it is with the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is not like this; he has forever severed these roots, and because he is without such roots, there is nothing to conceal. Good son!
It is like the discourses of a Brahmin, which he never intends for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras to hear.
Why is this? Because this treatise contains faults and evils.
The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is not like this; it is good in the beginning, middle, and end. Therefore, it cannot be called a "secret treasury."

Good son! It is like an elder who has but one son; he constantly remembers him with boundless affection and love. Desiring to have him study under a teacher, yet fearing he might not achieve success quickly, he brings him back immediately.
Out of affection, he diligently taught him the "half-syllables" day and night, but did not instruct him in the Vyākaraṇa treatises.
Why was this? Because the child was still young and his strength was not yet sufficient.
"Good son! Even if a householder had taught his child the half-syllables, would that child immediately be able to understand the Vyākaraṇa treatises? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One!
‘In this way, householder, do you have any secret hoard regarding this son?
‘No, World-Honored One.’”
World-Honored One!
For what reason?
It was because the son was young that [the Dharma] was not explained to him.
I do not withhold it from being taught out of secrecy or stinginess. Why is this?
If one possesses a mind of jealousy, secrecy, or parsimony, that is what is called "concealment."
“The Tathāgata is not like that; how then can it be said that the Tathāgata has a secret treasury?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
Good son! It is as you have said.
If one possesses a mind of anger, jealousy, or stinginess, this is what is called "hoarding."
The Tathāgata has no anger or jealousy; why, then, is he called a "treasury"?
Good son! That great elder is the Tathāgata, and what is called "the only son" refers to all sentient beings.

The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as if they were his only son; "teaching the only son" refers to the śrāvaka disciples, "half-syllables" refers to the ninefold canon, and "Vyākaraṇa treatises" refers to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.

Because the śrāvakas lack the power of wisdom, the Tathāgata has taught them the ninefold scriptures consisting of "half-syllables," but has not taught them the Vyākaraṇa treatises or the Vaipulya Mahāyāna.
Good son! Just as that elder, when his son had grown up and was capable of study, would be considered a "hoarder" if he did not teach him the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises.

If there were any śrāvakas possessing the capacity to receive the Mahāyāna vyākaraṇa (grammatical treatises), yet the Tathāgata withheld them out of secrecy and did not teach them, one could say that the Tathāgata possesses a secret treasury.
The Tathāgata is not like that; therefore, the Tathāgata has no secret treasury.
Just as that elder, having taught the half-syllables, subsequently expounded the Vyākaraṇa treatise for them;

so too do I now, having taught the half-syllable ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-dharma*) for my disciples, subsequently expound the Vyākaraṇa treatise, which is to say: the Tathāgata eternally exists and is immutable.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the summer months, when great clouds and thunder arise and heavy rain falls, causing those farmers who have sown their seeds to harvest many fruits."
If one does not sow seeds, there will be nothing gained; and if there is nothing gained, it is not the fault of the Dragon King.
Furthermore, this Dragon King has no storehouse [of seeds].
I, the Tathāgata, am likewise thus: I have brought down the great rain of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; if sentient beings sow the seeds of goodness, they shall obtain the sprouts and fruits of wisdom.
Those who lack virtuous sons shall have nothing to gain.
That they have nothing to gain is not the fault of the Tathāgata;
yet the Buddha, the Tathāgata, truly has nothing to conceal.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“I now know for certain that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has no secret treasury.
As for what the Buddha has taught in the Vyākaraṇa—that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, exists eternally and is immutable—this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? For the Buddha formerly spoke this verse:
"The Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, And the assembly of their disciples..."
"If even [the Buddha] abandons this impermanent body, how much more so for ordinary people?
Now, however, you say:
"It exists eternally and is unchanging."
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
For the sake of all my śrāvaka disciples, I have taught the "half-syllables" and thus spoken these verses. Good son!
When King Prasenajit’s mother passed away, he was overcome with grief and longing, unable to restrain himself, and came to where I was. I then asked him:
"Great King!
Why do you grieve, suffer, and lament to such an extent?
The king replied:
“World-Honored One!

The Great Lady of the kingdom has passed away this very day. If there were anyone capable of restoring my mother’s life to its former state, I would renounce my kingdom, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, as well as my own life and body, to bestow them all as a reward.”
I spoke to him again:
"Great King!
Do not be distressed, nor grieve, lament, or weep. For all sentient beings, when their life-span is exhausted, it is called death."
"If even the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvaka disciples relinquish this body, how much more so should ordinary people? "Good son!
I spoke these verses for the sake of teaching the 'half-syllables' to King Prasenajit."
I now expound the *vyākaraṇa* for my śrāvaka disciples, namely: that the Tathāgata eternally abides and is subject to no change.
If there were anyone who claimed the Tathāgata is impermanent, how could such a person’s tongue not fall off?
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"As the Buddha has said:
'Accumulate nothing; be content with food.'"
"Just as when a bird flies through the sky, its tracks cannot be found.
"What is the meaning of this,
World-Honored One?"
Within this assembly, who may be called one who has no accumulation?
Who again may be called one who is content with food?
And who walks in the track of space that cannot be traced?
"And where does this one who departs go?
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
Now, that which is accumulated is called wealth and treasure.
Good son! There are two kinds of accumulation:
The first is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The accumulation of the conditioned is the practice of the śrāvakas; the accumulation of the unconditioned is the practice of the Tathāgatas.
Good son! The Sangha also has two kinds:
conditioned and unconditioned.

The conditioned Sangha is called the Śrāvaka Sangha; the Śrāvaka Sangha possesses no accumulations, namely: slaves, improper goods, storehouses, grain, salt, fermented soybeans, sesame, and all varieties of large and small beans.
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata permits the keeping of such things as male and female slaves or servants, their tongue would shrivel up.
All my śrāvaka disciples are called "those who have no accumulation," and they may also be called "those who know contentment with food."
If one has greed for food, it is called "lack of contentment.
One who does not crave food is said to be "contented.
As for those whose tracks are difficult to trace, they are close to the path of unsurpassed bodhi; I say that such people, though they depart, have nowhere to go.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If even the conditioned Saṃgha has no accumulation, how much more so the unconditioned Saṃgha?
The unconditioned Saṃgha is none other than the Tathāgata; how could the Tathāgata have any accumulation?"
That which is accumulated is called "concealment. Therefore, whatever the Tathāgata has taught, he has no stinginess regarding it;

how then could it be called concealed? That whose traces cannot be sought is what is called *nirvāṇa*. Within *nirvāṇa*, there are no sun, moon, stars, or constellations; no cold, heat, wind, or rain; and no birth, old age, sickness, death, or the twenty-five states of existence. It is free from all sorrows, sufferings, and afflictions. Such is *nirvāṇa*, the dwelling place of the Tathāgata, which is eternal and unchanging. For these reasons, the Tathāgata has come to these *śāla* trees and entered *parinirvāṇa* within the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That which is called 'great' has a nature that is vast and expansive.
It is like a person whose lifespan is immeasurable; such a one is named a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa)."
If a person can dwell securely in the True Dharma, they are called the most excellent among humans.
Regarding the eight awakenings of the great men that I have taught, do they belong to a single person,
or do they belong to many?
If a single person possesses all eight, they are most excellent.
That which is called nirvana is free from all sores and blemishes. Good son!
It is like a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow and suffers great pain;
upon encountering a skilled physician, who extracts the poisoned arrow and applies a wondrous medicine, that person is freed from suffering and attains peace and happiness.

The physician then traveled through cities, towns, and various villages; wherever there were those suffering from ailments, sores, or wounds, he would go to those places to treat their manifold sufferings.
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;

having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, he acts as a great king of physicians. Seeing the suffering sentient beings of Jambudvīpa who, throughout immeasurable kalpas, have been struck by the poisoned arrows of lust, anger, ignorance, and afflictions, and thus undergo intense and piercing agony.

For the sake of such beings as these, he preaches the ambrosial medicinal dharma of the Mahāyāna sūtras to treat them; having healed them, he proceeds again to other regions where there are the poisoned arrows of various afflictions, manifesting himself as a Buddha to provide healing for them. Therefore, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.

The Great Parinirvāṇa is called the locus of liberation; wherever there are beings to be tamed, the Tathāgata manifests therein. Because it possesses this true and profound meaning, it is named the Great Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are the physicians of the world able to cure all the sores, tumors, and diseases of all sentient beings?”
“Good son! There are two kinds of sores in the world:
first, those that can be treated; second, those that cannot be treated.”
"Whatever can be cured, the physician is able to cure;
whatever cannot be cured, he is unable to cure.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If it is as the Buddha says, then the Tathāgata has already brought the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa to healing.
If they have been healed, why is it that among these sentient beings there are still some who have not yet attained nirvana?"
"If you have not yet fully attained [this], why does the Tathāgata say that his treatment is finished and that he wishes to go to another land?
"Good son, within Jambudvīpa there are two kinds of sentient beings: [those who are to be cured and those who are not]."
First, there is faith; second, there is lack of faith.
A person who possesses faith is said to be curable. Why is this?
They have certainly attained nirvana because they are free from all wounds and blemishes; therefore, I say that I have already healed all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa.
Those who lack faith are called icchantikas, and those who are icchantikas are said to be incurable.
"Except for the icchantikas, all others have been healed; therefore, nirvana is called 'free from sores.
World-Honored One, what is meant by 'nirvana'?"
“Good son! That which is called nirvāṇa is named liberation.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Regarding what is called 'liberation,' is it form,
or is it not form?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! There are those that are form and those that are not form.
That which is said to be ‘not form’ is the liberation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
That which is called "form" is precisely the liberation of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Good son! Therefore, liberation is both form and non-form.
“The Tathāgata has taught for the sake of his śrāvaka disciples that [the body] is not form.
“World-Honored One!
If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not form, how do they abide?”
“Good son! Just as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception is both form and non-form, yet I also declare it to be non-form.
If someone were to raise an objection, saying:”
"If the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception were not form, how could it abide, come and go, or move about?
Such a meaning is the realm of all Buddhas; it is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Liberation is also like this: though it is both form and non-form, it is described as non-form; though it is both perception and non-perception, it is described as non-perception. Such meanings are the domain of the Buddhas, not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that out of compassion you will once more deign to explain in detail the meaning of the practice and liberation of the Great Nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
True liberation is called being far removed from all fetters.
If one is truly liberated and free from all fetters, then there is no birth, nor is there any coming together.
For example, when parents unite, a child is born; true liberation is not like this. Therefore, liberation is called "unborn. Kāśyapa!
For example, just as the nature of clarified butter (ghṛta) is pure, so too is the Tathāgata; he is not born from the union of father and mother, for his nature is pure.
The reason he manifests having parents is because he desires to transform and deliver all sentient beings.
True liberation is itself the Tathāgata; there is no duality or distinction between the Tathāgata and liberation.
For example, when seeds are sown in the spring months, they sprout immediately upon receiving warmth;
true liberation is not like this.
Furthermore, liberation is called emptiness; emptiness is itself liberation, and liberation is itself the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is emptiness—neither created nor a creation.
All that is created is like city walls, watchtowers, and battlements;
true liberation is not like this, and therefore liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). For example, a potter makes a vessel and then breaks it; liberation is not like this. True liberation is neither born nor extinguished; therefore, liberation is the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata is likewise: unborn and undying, not aging and not perishing, indestructible and unbreakable, and not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*). For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata who has entered Great Parinirvāṇa.
What is the meaning of "neither aging nor dying"?
Aging refers to transformation and change: the hair turns white and the face becomes wrinkled.
Dying refers to the destruction of the body and the end of life.
Such dharmas as these do not exist within liberation;
because these things are absent, it is called liberation.
The Tathāgata likewise has no white hair, no wrinkled face, and no conditioned dharmas; therefore, the Tathāgata does not undergo aging.
Because there is no aging, there is no death.

Furthermore, liberation is called being free from illness; as for what is called "illness," it refers to the four hundred and four diseases as well as other external factors that invade and damage the body. Since these are absent in this state, it is called liberation.

To be free from illness is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Since the Tathāgata is without illness, the Dharma-body is likewise without illness. To be thus without illness is the Tathāgata.
What is called "death" refers to the destruction of the body and the end of life;
that place where there is no death is the ambrosia (*amṛta*); this ambrosia is true liberation (*vimukti*); and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata has accomplished such meritorious virtues; how could one say that the Tathāgata is impermanent?
If one says he is impermanent, it is impossible.
This is a vajra-body; how could it be impermanent?
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not said to have met his end.
The Tathāgata is pure and free from all defilement; the body of the Tathāgata is not defiled by the womb, for its intrinsic nature is as pure as the puṇḍarīka lotus.
The liberation of the Tathāgata is likewise thus; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and for this reason the Tathāgata is pure and stainless.

Furthermore, as for liberation, all the sores and afflictions of the outflows (*āsrava*) are forever eliminated without remainder; the Tathāgata is also like this, possessing none of the sores and afflictions of the outflows whatsoever.
Furthermore, liberation is free from strife and contention. For example, a hungry person who sees the food and drink of others gives rise to greed and the thought of seizing it;
liberation is not like this. Moreover, liberation is called "tranquil stillness. Ordinary people say that one who is tranquil and still is Maheśvara, but such a statement is false.
Those who are truly tranquil attain ultimate liberation; ultimate liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called peace and security: just as a place with many bandits is not called secure, only a clear and level place is called secure.
Within this liberation there is no fear; therefore, it is called "peaceful security. Thus, peaceful security is true liberation, true liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation has no equal. Those who have equals are like a king who has neighboring kingdoms.
Liberation is not like this; it has no equal, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) has none who can rival him.

Liberation is also like this: it has no equal. That which has no equal is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata, the King who Turns the Wheel of Dharma. Therefore, the Tathāgata has no equal; for it is impossible that he should have an equal.
Furthermore, liberation is called being free from sorrow. Those who possess sorrow are like a king who fears a powerful neighbor and consequently gives rise to anxiety.

One who is liberated has no such thing; it is like having destroyed an enemy, after which there is no more worry. Liberation is likewise free from sorrow and fear. That which is free from sorrow and fear is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of sorrow and joy. For example, suppose a woman has an only son who has gone away on official business; she receives the sudden news of his death and suffers in grief upon hearing it. Later, when she hears that he is alive, she immediately gives rise to joy.
In liberation, such things do not exist; that which is free from sorrow and joy is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is free from dust and defilement, just as in the spring months, after the sun has set, the wind raises up clouds of dust and mist.
In liberation, such things do not exist; being free from dust and mist is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
It is like the bright jewel within the topknot of a noble cakravartin king, which is entirely free from defilement.
The nature of liberation is likewise thus: it is free from defilement. That which is free from defilement is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Just as the nature of pure gold, when unmixed with sand and stone, is called a true treasure, and someone who finds it conceives the thought that it is wealth;
so too is the nature of liberation. That true treasure is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
For example, when an earthen jar is broken, it makes a harsh, rattling sound; a precious diamond jar is not like this.

Liberation is likewise without such rattling or breaking. The precious diamond jar is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata; therefore, the body of the Tathāgata is indestructible.
That which makes a cracking sound is like the seeds of *pi-ma* (sesame): when placed in the sun during the height of the summer heat, they emit a crackling and popping noise.

Now, liberation is not like this; it is like a vessel made of genuine diamond-jewels, which lacks any sound of cracking or breaking. Even if immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people were to shoot at it together, none could destroy it. The absence of such cracking or breaking sounds is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
It is like a poor person who, because he owes another a debt, is bound by others, subjected to shackles, fetters, and corporal punishment, and undergoes all manner of bitter suffering.

In liberation, however, there is no such thing; there is no indebtedness. It is like a wealthy elder who possesses immeasurable billions of treasures and wields sovereign power, owing nothing to anyone else.

Liberation is also like this: it possesses immeasurable wealth and treasures of the Dharma, with sovereign power and freedom from all debt. To be free from debt is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "absence of oppression. It is like encountering heat in spring, eating sweets in summer, or experiencing cold sensations in winter.
Within true liberation, there are no such disagreeable matters; that which is without oppression is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, regarding 'the absence of oppression': it is like a person who has eaten their fill of fish and meat and then drinks milk; such a person will be near death before long."
Within true liberation, such things do not exist; it is like a person who, having obtained excellent medicine of ambrosia, finds their ailment cured.
True liberation is also like this: the excellent medicine of ambrosia is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
What is meant by being oppressed and not being oppressed?
For example, an ordinary person, conceited with self-importance, thinks to himself:
"Among all these people, who could possibly harm me?"
If one carries snakes, tigers, and venomous insects with them, you should know that such a person will not complete their natural lifespan and will instead suffer an untimely death.
Within true liberation, no such thing exists.

One who is free from oppression is like a wheel-turning monarch; his divine jewel can subdue dung beetles and the ninety-six kinds of venomous insects and the like. If anyone smells the fragrance of this divine jewel, all poisons will be extinguished.

True liberation is likewise thus: it is the complete distancing from the twenty-five states of existence. The extinction of poison is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that which is not oppressive is like space; liberation is likewise so. That space is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that which is oppressive is like being near dry grass when lighting various lamps; the closer one is, the more fiercely it burns.
Within true liberation, no such thing exists.
Moreover, that which is not oppressive is like the sun and moon, which do not oppress sentient beings.
Liberation is also like this: it involves no oppression toward sentient beings. That which is without oppression is the metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the "unmoving dharma. Just as with enemies and kin, such distinctions do not exist within true liberation.
Moreover, that which is unmoving is like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who has no other noble king to serve as a friend; if there were another friend, it would be impossible.

Liberation is likewise; it has no further kin, for it is impossible for it to have kin. That king having no kin is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, that which is immovable is like a plain white garment, which easily takes on dye; liberation is not so.
Moreover, that which is immovable is like the vārṣika flower: it is impossible for it to have a foul odor or to be blue in color.
Liberation is likewise; it is impossible for it to possess any odor or form. Therefore, liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "rare" (āścarya). For example, the birth of a lotus flower in water is not rare, but its birth within fire is indeed rare; should anyone see this, they would immediately feel great joy.
True liberation is likewise so: those who behold it give rise to joy in their hearts.
That which is rare is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, that which is rare is like an infant whose teeth have not yet emerged; they grow gradually until later they finally appear.
Liberation is not like this; it has neither arising nor non-arising.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'void and tranquil,' and therein is no uncertainty.

As for what is uncertain—such as the claim that an icchantika ultimately never changes, or that one who has committed a grave transgression cannot achieve the Buddha-way—there is no such possibility."

Why is this? If such a person attains pure faith in the Buddha’s true Dharma, at that moment they immediately extinguish the state of an icchantika; if they further become an upāsaka, they likewise attain the extinction of the icchantika state. Having extinguished these grave offenses, one then attains Buddhahood.
Therefore, to say that one is definitively immovable and will not achieve the Buddha-way is impossible;
in true liberation, there is absolutely no such matter of extinction.
Furthermore, that which is empty and quiescent falls within the Dharma-realm; as the nature of the Dharma-realm is itself true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Moreover, if an icchantika were to be utterly extinguished, they could no longer be called an icchantika.
What is meant by the term *icchantika*?

An *icchantika* is one who has severed all roots of goodness; their fundamental mind does not take any wholesome dharmas as an object of focus, such that they do not give rise to even a single thought of goodness.
In true liberation, none of these things exist; because these things do not exist, it is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called immeasurable; for example, the measure of a heap of grain can be known.

Those who have attained true liberation are not like this. For example, just as the great ocean cannot be measured, so too liberation cannot be measured; that which is immeasurable is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the "immeasurable dharma," just as a single sentient being has many karmic retributions.
Liberation is likewise so: it possesses immeasurable retributions. That which has immeasurable retributions is true liberation; that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "vast," just as the great ocean has no equal.
Liberation is likewise without equal; that which is without equal is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "supreme," just as space is supreme and beyond compare.
Liberation is likewise supreme and beyond compare; that which is supreme and beyond compare is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "that which cannot be surpassed. For example, wherever a lion dwells, none of the hundred beasts can surpass it.
Liberation is likewise such that nothing can surpass it; that which cannot be surpassed is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "unsurpassed," just as the northern direction is the highest among all directions.
Liberation is likewise unsurpassed; that which is unsurpassed is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "the unsurpassed supreme. For example, just as the north is the unsurpassed supreme relative to the east, so too is liberation;
it has nothing superior to it. That which is unsurpassed supreme is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the "constant dharma. For example, when the bodies of humans and devas perish at the end of their lives, this is called "constant," not "inconstant.
Liberation is likewise not inconstant; that which is not inconstant is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "solid and substantial. Just as *khatāra*, sandalwood, and aloeswood are solid and substantial by nature, so too is liberation solid and substantial by nature.
That which is solid and substantial by nature is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "non-empty. For example, the substance of bamboo and reeds is hollow and porous;
liberation is not so. One should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "uncorruptible. For example, when a wall has not yet been plastered or treated, mosquitoes and gadflies may alight upon it and sport there; however, once it has been plastered and adorned with colorful paintings, the insects will not remain upon it as soon as they smell the scent of the pigments.
This state of non-abiding is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "boundless. For example, a village has boundaries and limits;
liberation is not like this. Just as space has no boundaries or limits, liberation likewise has no boundaries or limits. Such liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "invisible. Just as the tracks of a bird in the sky are difficult to see, so too is this [liberation] difficult to see; this difficulty of seeing is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "profound. Why is this?
Because it is that which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot enter; that which they cannot enter is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, that which is profound is revered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is like the profound merit of a filial child who provides for his parents. This profound merit is analogous to true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "invisible," just as a person cannot see the crown of their own head.
Liberation is likewise; it cannot be seen by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. That which cannot be seen is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "houseless," just as space has no house. Liberation is likewise so;

the term "house" is a metaphor for the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), while being "houseless" is a metaphor for true liberation. True liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "ungraspable. Just as the *āmalaka* fruit can be grasped and held by a person, liberation is not like that;
it cannot be grasped or held. That which cannot be grasped or held is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "ungraspable," just as an illusory object cannot be grasped or held.
Liberation is likewise ungraspable; that which is ungraspable is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is without a physical body. For example, there may be a person whose body develops sores, warts, various abscesses, insanity, or emaciation.
Within true liberation, such illnesses do not exist; that which is free from such illnesses is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "one flavor. Just as milk has one flavor, so too does liberation; it possesses only this single flavor. This single flavor is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called purity; it is like water free from silt, serene, still, and pure.
Liberation is likewise serene, still, and pure; this serenity, stillness, and purity is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "one flavor. It is like rain falling from the sky, which is of one flavor and pure; this analogy of one-flavored purity represents true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "removal," like the full moon when it is free from all clouds and veils.
Liberation is likewise free from all clouds and veils; that which is free from all clouds and veils is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called tranquility. For example, when a person’s feverish illness is cured, their body attains tranquility.
Liberation is likewise: the body attains tranquility, and the attainment of bodily tranquility is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is equanimity. For example, a venomous snake in the wild and a weasel both possess a murderous intent.
Liberation is not like this; it is devoid of murderous intent. That which is free from murderous intent is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, "equanimity" is like the impartial mind of parents toward their children; liberation is likewise characterized by such equanimity of mind. That which is equanimous in mind is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "having no other place. For example, it is like a person who dwells only in a supreme, exquisite, and pure residence, with no other place to go.
Liberation is likewise; it has no other place. That which has no other place is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "contentment. For example, when a hungry person encounters delicious food, they eat it without satiety.

Liberation is not like this; it is like having eaten milk gruel, after which nothing more is required. That for which nothing more is required is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "severance. It is like a person who has been bound and attains release by severing those bonds.
Liberation is likewise so: it severs all the fetters of doubt. Such severance of doubt is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "reaching the other shore. For example, a great river has this shore and that shore. Liberation is not like this;
although it lacks this shore, it possesses the other shore. That which possesses the other shore is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called silence. For example, the waters of the great ocean overflow and abound with many sounds;
liberation is not so. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "exquisite and beautiful. For example, when various medicines are mixed with harītakī, their taste becomes bitter.
Liberation is not like this; its taste is like nectar. This taste of nectar is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation eliminates all afflictions, just as a skilled physician compiles various medicines to effectively treat all manner of diseases.
Liberation is likewise able to eliminate afflictions; that which eliminates afflictions is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "unconfined. For example, a small house cannot accommodate many people;
liberation is not like this, for it accommodates much. To accommodate much is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the extinction of all cravings and is unmixed with sensual desire. For example, a woman possesses many cravings and desires;
liberation is not so. Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is thus free from the fetters of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and the like.
Furthermore, liberation is called "absence of craving. There are two kinds of craving:
first, the craving of hungry ghosts; second, the craving for the Dharma.

One who has attained true liberation is free from the craving of hungry ghosts, yet possesses the craving for the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings. Such craving for the Dharma is itself true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is free from "I" and "mine"; such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Moreover, liberation is cessation, being free from all craving for existence; such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is protection; it can rescue all those who are terrified. Such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is the place of refuge; if one takes refuge in such liberation, one seeks no other refuge.
It is like a person who relies upon a king and seeks no other support; yet even though they rely on the king, there may still be instability.
That which relies on liberation is without movement or change; that which is without movement or change is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata; and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is called a dwelling place. For example, if a person travels through a vast wilderness, there will be dangers and difficulties.
Liberation is not like this; it is free from danger and difficulty. That which is free from danger and difficulty is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is fearlessness, just as the lion king feels no terror among the various beasts.
Liberation is likewise; it feels no terror amidst the hosts of Māras. That which is fearless is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is not constricted; it is unlike a narrow path that cannot even accommodate two people walking abreast.
Liberation is not so; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is no constriction. For example, it is like a person who, fearing a tiger, falls into a well;
liberation is not so. Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata. Moreover, there is no constriction:

it is like being in the great ocean where one abandons a ruined small boat and obtains a sturdy vessel; riding upon it, one crosses the sea and reaches a place of peace and security, and the mind attains happiness.
Liberation is likewise so: the mind attains happiness, and one who attains happiness is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation uproots all causes and conditions, just as, for example, curd is obtained from milk, ghee from curd, and clarified butter (sarpis) from ghee.
Within true liberation there is absolutely no such cause; that which is without cause is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation can subdue arrogance, just as a great king treats a minor king with disdain;
liberation is not like this. Such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation subdues all forms of negligence; for those who are negligent possess much craving.
Within true liberation, there is no such designation; that which is without such designation is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation can eliminate ignorance, just as when superior ghee removes all dregs and impurities, it is then called *sarpis-manda*.
Liberation is likewise: by removing the dregs of ignorance, true illumination arises; such true illumination is itself true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, liberation is called tranquility; it is pure and singular, without a second, like a wild elephant in the wilderness, solitary and without companion.
Liberation is likewise solitary and without a second; this solitude and lack of a second is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "solid and substantial. Just as the stalks of bamboo, reeds, and hemp are hollow while their seeds are solid and substantial, all other humans and devas—with the exception of the Buddha-Tathāgata—are not solid and substantial. True liberation is far removed from all streams of existence (*bhava-srotas*); such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "capable of awakening" and "augmenting the self"; true liberation is likewise so. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the relinquishing of all modes of existence (*bhava*). It is like a person who, having eaten, then vomits.
Liberation is likewise: it is the relinquishing of all modes of existence. To relinquish all modes of existence is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "certainty. Just as the fragrance of the *vārṣika* flower does not exist within its seven petals, so it is with liberation; such liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called the element of water (*āpas*). Just as the element of water excels among all elements by being able to moisten all grasses, trees, and seeds of grain, so too does liberation moisten all classes of sentient beings. Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "entry. Just as when there is a gateway, one can enter the path leading to a place of gold and thus obtain the gold;
liberation is likewise like that gateway. Those who cultivate non-self enter therein, and such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "good. It is like a disciple who follows his teacher and faithfully carries out his instructions; thus he is named "good.
Liberation is likewise so; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called the supramundane dharma; it is the most transcendent among all dharmas, just as clarified butter and milk are the most excellent among all flavors.
Liberation is likewise so; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, liberation is called "immovable," just as a door threshold cannot be moved by the wind.
True liberation is likewise; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "waveless. Just as the waters of the great ocean have waves and billows, liberation is not so;
such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is like a palace; liberation is likewise so, and one should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Moreover, liberation is called "utility," just as Jāmbūnada gold has many uses and no one can speak of any defects in this gold.
Liberation is also like this: it is free from faults and evils; that which is free from faults and evils is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is the relinquishing of infantile conduct, just as an adult abandons the behavior of a small child.
Liberation is also like this: it consists in the relinquishing of the five aggregates. The relinquishing of the five aggregates is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "ultimate," just as one who has been bound attains release from those bonds, bathes to become pure, and then returns home.
Liberation is also like this: it is ultimately pure. Ultimate purity is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the bliss of non-action. As for the bliss of non-action, it is so called because greed, hatred, and delusion have been vomited out.
It is like a person who, having mistakenly drunk snake venom, takes an emetic to eliminate the poison; once he has vomited it up, the poison is cured and his body attains peace and happiness.

Liberation is also like this: having expelled the poisons of afflictions, fetters, and bonds, the body attains peace and bliss, which is called the bliss of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-sukha*). This bliss of non-action is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the severing of the four kinds of poisonous snakes of affliction; he who severs these afflictions is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

"Furthermore, liberation is called being detached from all modes of existence (*bhava*); it is the extinction of all suffering and the attainment of all happiness. It is the eternal severance of greed, hatred, and delusion, and the uprooting of the very foundation of all afflictions (*kleśa*). That which uproots the foundation is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, liberation is defined as severing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and giving rise to all untainted wholesome phenomena (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*). It closes off all paths, namely those of "self," "non-self," "neither self," nor "not non-self. It is solely the severing of grasping and attachment, not the severing of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). This view of self is called the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); the Buddha-nature is true liberation; and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called "not empty of emptiness. That which is "empty of emptiness" is termed "non-existence," and this non-existence is precisely the liberation conceived by the heterodox Nigaṇṭhas and others; yet these Nigaṇṭhas truly possess no liberation, and for this reason it is called "empty of emptiness.
True liberation is not like this, and thus it is "not empty of emptiness. That which is "not empty of emptiness" is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called both empty and non-empty.

It is like jars containing water, wine, curd, ghee, or honey: even when they no longer contain water, wine, curd, ghee, or honey, they are still called "water jars" and so forth; yet these jars cannot be described as being either empty or non-empty.
If one says it is empty, then there can be no form, fragrance, taste, or touch;
if one says it is not empty, yet there is likewise no reality such as water, wine, and so forth.
Liberation is also like this: it cannot be described as form or as non-form, nor can it be described as empty or as non-empty.
If one says it is empty, then permanence, bliss, self, and purity could not exist;
if one says it is non-empty, who would be the one to receive this permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
For this reason, it cannot be said to be either empty or not empty.

"Empty" refers to the absence of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), all afflictions (*kleśa*), all suffering, all marks (*nimitta*), and all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). It is like a jar that is empty because it contains no curd; thus, it is called "empty.

"Not empty" refers to true, wholesome form (*rūpa*), permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which are immovable and unchanging. It is like that same jar when it possesses color, fragrance, flavor, and touch; therefore, it is called "not empty."
Therefore, liberation is likened to that jar; while that jar may be destroyed when it encounters the proper conditions, liberation is not so—it cannot be destroyed.
That which cannot be destroyed is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'detachment from craving. For example, there may be a person whose craving-filled heart longs for Śakra-devānām-indra, Mahābrahmā, or Maheśvara;

liberation is not like this. Once one has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is neither craving nor doubt. This absence of craving and doubt is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata."
If one were to say that liberation contains craving or doubt, such a thing is impossible.

Furthermore, liberation is the severing of all craving for existence; it is the severing of all marks, all fetters, all afflictions, all birth and death, all causes and conditions, and all karmic retributions. Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is itself Nirvāṇa.

Because all sentient beings fear birth and death as well as the various afflictions, they take refuge in the Triple Gem. It is like a herd of deer that fears hunters; once they have escaped and managed to take one leap, it is likened to taking one refuge. Thus, three leaps are likened to the three refuges;
by means of these three leaps, they obtain peace and happiness.

Sentient beings are likewise; because they fear the four māras and the evil hunters, they take refuge in the Three Refuges. By means of the Three Refuges, they obtain peace and happiness. Those who attain peace and happiness achieve true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata is itself nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa is itself inexhaustibility; inexhaustibility is itself the buddha-nature; the buddha-nature is itself certainty; and certainty is itself anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If nirvana, the buddha-nature, certainty, and the Tathāgata are one and the same meaning, why do you speak of there being three refuges?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “Good son!
All sentient beings fear birth and death, and therefore seek the Three Refuges. By means of the Three Refuges, they come to know the Buddha-nature, certainty, and nirvana.”
Good son! There are dharmas whose names are identical but whose meanings differ, and there are dharmas whose names and meanings both differ.

Regarding those whose names are identical but whose meanings differ: the Buddha is eternal, the Dharma is eternal, the Saṃgha of bhikṣus is eternal, and nirvāṇa and space are also all eternal; this is called "names are identical but meanings differ."

Regarding the difference between name and meaning: "Buddha" is named for awakening; "Dharma" is named for non-awakening; "Saṅgha" is named for harmony; "Nirvāṇa" is named for liberation; and "space" is named for that which is neither wholesome nor unobstructed—this is what is meant by the difference between name and meaning.
"Good son!
The three refuges are likewise thus; since their names and meanings differ, how could they be one?
For this reason, I told Mahāprajāpatī:"
"Kautamī! Do not make offerings to me; you should make offerings to the Saṅgha.
If you make offerings to the Saṅgha, you will thereby fulfill the complete offering to the Three Refuges."
Mahāprajāpatī then replied to me, saying:
"Within the community of monks, there is neither Buddha nor Dharma; how can you say that by making offerings to the community of monks, one fully accomplishes the offering to the Three Refuges?"
I further told him:
"If you follow my words, you are making an offering to the Buddha;
for the sake of liberation, you are making an offering to the Dharma."
"When the Sangha receives [offerings], it is the Sangha that is being honored.
"Good son! For this reason, the Three Refuges cannot be considered as one."
"Good son!
The Tathāgata may at times speak of one as three, or speak of three as one. Such meanings belong to the realm of the Buddhas; they are not within the knowledge of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“As the Buddha has taught, that which is ultimately peaceful and blissful is called nirvāṇa. What is the meaning of this?
Now, nirvāṇa involves abandoning the body and abandoning wisdom. If one abandons both body and wisdom, who would experience bliss?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
It is like a person who, having finished eating, feels a sense of oppression in the heart and goes outside wishing to vomit; once he has vomited, he returns again.”
His companions asked him:
"Has the ailment you were suffering from finally been cured?
Why have you returned?"
He replied: "I am cured;
my body has attained peace and happiness.

The Tathāgata is likewise: having ultimately transcended the twenty-five states of existence, he has forever attained the state of nirvāṇa’s peace and happiness, which is immovable, inexhaustible, and free from extinction. Having severed all sensations, it is called the bliss of non-sensation.
Thus, being without sensation is called eternal bliss. It is impossible for the Tathāgata to possess the experience of pleasure.
Therefore, ultimate bliss is precisely nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa is true liberation; and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Is non-arising and non-ceasing liberation?
[The Buddha replied: "It is so; it is so."
"Good son!
That which is neither born nor extinguished is itself liberation; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If that which is neither born nor extinguished is liberation, then the nature of space, being likewise without birth or extinction, should be the Tathāgata.
As is the nature of the Tathāgata, so too is liberation."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son, this is not so."
“World-Honored One!
Why is this not so? “Good son!”
“Suppose there were the kalaviṅka bird and the jīvajīvaka bird, whose voices are pure and exquisite; could they possibly be compared to the cries of crows and magpies?
“No, World-Honored One.”
"The cries of crows and magpies cannot be compared to those of the jīvamjīvaka and other such birds by even hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"The voices of the kalaviṅka and others are subtle and exquisite, and their bodies are likewise distinct; why does the Tathāgata compare them to crows and magpies?"
There is no difference between a mustard seed and Mount Sumeru;
the Buddha and empty space are likewise so. The cry of the kalaviṅka bird may be used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice, but it cannot be used as a metaphor for the sound of crows and magpies.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
You now well understand that which is profound and difficult to comprehend.
At times, for the sake of certain causes and conditions, the Tathāgata draws upon the analogy of space to explain liberation.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

True liberation is such that no human or celestial being can equal it; yet this empty space is not actually an analogy for it. It is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that space—which is not truly an analogy—is used as an analogy.
You should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the nature of the Tathāgata is itself liberation; liberation and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction. Good son!
Regarding "non-examples": just as an incomparable object cannot be used for comparison, when there are causes and conditions, it is possible to employ an analogy.
As stated in the Sūtra: "His countenance was upright and handsome, like the full moon."
The white elephant is pure and bright, like the Snowy Mountains;
yet the full moon cannot be said to be identical to its face, nor can the Snowy Mountains be said to be the white elephant itself. Good son!
True liberation cannot be illustrated by metaphors; it is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that metaphors are employed.
By means of various analogies, one comes to know the nature of all phenomena, and all are likewise so.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Why does the Tathāgata give two kinds of explanations?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! It is like a person who, grasping a sword, with a mind of hatred and anger, wishes to harm the Tathāgata; yet the Tathāgata remains serene and pleasant, showing no sign of resentment or anger.”
“Would such a person incur the crime of a heinous offense by destroying the body of a Tathāgata? “No,
World-Honored One.”
Why is this? Because the realm of the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible. For what reason?
Since there is no aggregate of a body, there is only the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The nature of the nature of phenomena is, by its principle, indestructible; how then could such a person destroy the Buddha’s body?
It is solely due to their evil mind that they commit an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
"For these reasons, by means of various parables, one may come to know the true Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
That which I intended to say, you have now already spoken.
Furthermore, good son!"

For example, suppose a wicked man intends to harm his mother; while staying in a wild field beneath a stack of grain, his mother comes to bring him food. Upon seeing her, he immediately gives rise to a murderous intent and steps forward to sharpen his knife.

When the mother realized this, she fled and hid inside a haystack; the man, holding a knife, circled the stack and hacked at it everywhere. Having finished hacking, he felt joy, having conceived the thought that she was already dead.
The mother then emerged from the heap of grain and returned home.
What do you think: has this person committed an ānantarya offense? "No."
World-Honored One!
It cannot be definitively stated. Why is this?
If one says there is a transgression, the mother’s body ought to have been destroyed; if the body was not destroyed, how can one say there is?
If one says there is no transgression, yet having conceived the thought of killing upon her birth, the mind harbored joy—how can one say there is none?
"Although this person does not fully possess the crime of immediate retribution, they nonetheless commit an act of immediate retribution.
For this reason, by means of various parables, one may come to know the true Dharma.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
For this reason, I have taught various skillful means and parables to illustrate liberation through metaphor.”
Although there are countless *asaṃkhyeya* metaphors, in reality they cannot serve as comparisons for it.

There may be certain causes and conditions where it can be explained through metaphors, yet there may also be certain causes and conditions where it cannot be explained through metaphors; therefore, liberation accomplishes such immeasurable merits.

Those who proceed toward nirvana, as well as nirvana itself and the Tathāgata, likewise possess such immeasurable merits; because they are fully accomplished through these immeasurable merits, it is called Great Nirvana.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Only now do I know that the destination reached by the Tathāgata is inexhaustible.”
"If the dwelling place is inexhaustible, you should know that one's lifespan must also be inexhaustible.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Good son! You have now skillfully been able to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to sever the afflictions and all the bonds of fetters, they should likewise protect and uphold the True Dharma in this manner.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Five.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Four, Part Three: On the Nature of the Tathāgata. “Good son!

Within this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, there are four kinds of persons who are able to protect the True Dharma, establish the True Dharma, and keep the True Dharma in mind; they are able to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge for the world and bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans.”
What are the four?

First, there are those who appear in the world who possess the nature of afflictions; second, those who are *srotāpannas* and *sakṛdāgāmins*; third, those who are *anāgāmins*; and fourth, those who are *arhats*.
These four kinds of people appear in the world, able to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge for the world and bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans.
What is meant by "possessing the nature of afflictions"?

If there is someone who can uphold the prohibitions and precepts, is fully endowed with dignified deportment, establishes the True Dharma, and having heard it from the Buddha, understands its words and meaning, and in turn explains and expounds them to others—namely, that few desires constitute the Path while many desires do not—and who extensively teaches these eight points of awareness for great beings (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavittāni*), instructs those who have committed offenses to reveal them, and causes them to repent so they may be extinguished, and who well knows the secret methods practiced by the skillful means of Bodhisattvas: such a person is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not one who has reached the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka*).
The eighth person is not called an ordinary being (pṛthagjana), but is called a bodhisattva, yet is not called a Buddha.

As for the second person, they are called a srotāpanna or a sakṛdāgāmin; having attained the True Dharma and upholding the True Dharma, they hear the Dharma from the Buddha, and according to what they have heard, they write it down, uphold it, read and recite it, and explain it to others.

If, after hearing the Dharma, one does not transcribe it, receive it, uphold it, or explain it, yet claims that the Buddha permitted the keeping of slaves and impure things—such a case is impossible; this is called the second person.
Such a person, though not yet having attained the second or third stage of dwelling, is named a Bodhisattva and has already received the prediction of enlightenment.

"The third person is called an Anāgāmin. Regarding an Anāgāmin: it is impossible for them to slander the True Dharma by saying that one may keep slaves, servants, or impure things; to receive and uphold the scriptures and treatises of external paths; to be obstructed by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) or covered by long-standing afflictions; to conceal the true relics of the Tathāgata; to be afflicted by external diseases; or to be invaded by the four great poisonous snakes. To discourse on a 'self' (*ātman*) is entirely without basis;
to speak of 'non-self' (*anātman*), however, is entirely possible."
To say that worldly dharmas exist is impossible;
to say that the Mahāyāna continues without interruption is possible.
To say that the body one has received contains eighty thousand worms is also impossible.
It is possible for one to be forever free from sexual desire, such that even in dreams one does not discharge impurity;
yet it is impossible for one to feel fear on the day of their death.
What is meant by the term *anāgāmin*?
It refers to one who does not return.
As previously described, they can never again be defiled by any faults or afflictions throughout their coming and going.
One who is called a bodhisattva, having already received the prediction of enlightenment and will before long attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is what is meant by the third person.

"The fourth person is named an Arhat. An Arhat has severed all afflictions, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, and accomplished what was to be done; he dwells in the tenth stage and has attained sovereign wisdom.
According to the various forms and appearances desired by others, he is able to manifest them all;
and according to his adornments, if he wishes to attain the Buddha-way, he is immediately able to achieve it."
One who is able to accomplish such immeasurable merits is called an Arhat.

These are known as the four types of persons who appear in the world; they are able to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge and source of peace for gods and humans. Among gods and humans, they are the most honored and supreme, just like the Tathāgata; they are called the victors among men and are the place of refuge.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I do not now rely upon these four kinds of people.”
Why is this? As stated in the *Ghoṣila-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Ghoṣila:

"If a deva, Māra, or Brahmā, desiring to cause your destruction, were to transform themselves into the form of a Buddha—complete with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, a halo extending one fathom, a face as perfectly full as the brilliant full moon, and the tuft of hair between the eyebrows white as snow or a conch shell—if such a majestic being were to approach you, you should examine them to determine whether they are real or false; once you have discerned this, you should subdue them."
"World-Honored One!
