If even Māra and his like can transform themselves into the body of a Buddha, how much more so could they not assume the four kinds of bodies, such as those of Arhats, sitting or lying in mid-air, with water issuing from their left flanks and fire from their right, or emitting smoke and flames from their bodies like a mass of fire?"
For these reasons, my mind does not give rise to faith therein.
Even if something is said, I am unable to accept it, nor do I harbor any reverent thought toward it as a basis for reliance.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If one gives rise to doubt regarding what I have taught, they should not even accept it; how much less so for things such as these?"

Therefore, one should skillfully discern and know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is to be done and what is not to be done; having acted in this way, one will experience happiness for a long night.
Good son! It is like a thieving dog that enters a person’s house at night; if the household servants perceive it, they should immediately drive it away and scold it, saying:
"Get out quickly! If you do not leave, we shall take your life!"
Upon hearing this, the stolen dog immediately departed and did not return.
From now on, you all should likewise subdue Pāpīyān, speaking these words: "Pāpīyān!..."
"You should not now assume such a form; if you do so intentionally, I shall bind you with the fivefold fetters.
Upon hearing this, Māra will immediately depart and never return, just like that thieving dog.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught to the householder Ghoṣila, if one can thus subdue Māra, one may also draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa; why then does the Tathāgata specifically designate these four persons as places of reliance?”
"The speech of these four kinds of people is not necessarily to be trusted.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
What I have said is likewise so; it is not otherwise.
Good son!
I speak of "subduing Māra" for the sake of śrāvakas who possess only the fleshly eye, but I do not speak thus for those who study and practice the Mahāyāna.
Although a śrāvaka possesses the divine eye, it is called the fleshly eye.
One who studies the Mahāyāna, although possessing only the fleshly eye, is said to possess the Buddha-eye. Why is this?
This Mahāyāna sūtra is named the Buddha Vehicle, and this Buddha Vehicle is the most supreme and most excellent.
Good son! It is like a person who is courageous, robust, and majestic, upon whom those who are timid and weak constantly come to rely.
That brave and valiant man constantly instructs the timid ones, saying: "You should hold the bow and grasp the arrow in this manner, and practice the arts of the spear, the long hook, and the lasso.
He further tells them:

"In battle, although it is like treading upon a blade, you should not give rise to thoughts of fear; rather, you should regard gods and humans as being light and weak, and you should generate within yourself the thought of being brave and valiant."

At times there may be someone who, lacking natural courage, falsely assumes the appearance of a hero; he takes up bows, swords, and various weapons to adorn himself, enters the midst of the battle lines, and shouts and clamors loudly.
You should not give rise to anxiety or fear toward such a person.
If people of this kind do not feel terror upon seeing you, you should know that they will soon fall apart and perish, just like that thieving dog.
"Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise; he tells all the śrāvakas:
'You should not fear Māra Pāpīyān. If Māra Pāpīyān should manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to where you are, you should be diligent and firm in your resolve to subdue that Māra.'"
"At that time, Māra will immediately become sorrowful and unhappy, and he will depart by the same way he came. "Good son!

Just as that strong man does not learn from others, so it is with one who studies the Mahāyāna: upon hearing various profound and secret sūtras, their mind feels joy and does not give rise to alarm or fear."

Why is this? Because those who thus practice and study the Mahāyāna have already made offerings to, honored, and prostrated before immeasurable tens of billions of Buddhas of the past; therefore, even though immeasurable billions of māras may come to harass them, they will ultimately feel no alarm or fear regarding such matters.
Good son! It is like a person who obtains the *agada* medicine; they fear nothing.
Because poisonous snakes and the like stand in awe of the power of this medicine, it is also able to eliminate all poisons and the like.
This Mahāyāna sūtra is also like this: just as the power of that medicine does not fear any demonic poisons and can subdue them so that they do not arise again.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a dragon whose nature is extremely jealous and fierce; when it wishes to harm people, it may do so by gazing with its eyes or by exhaling its breath. Consequently, all lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, dogs, and other canines give rise to fear. These evil beasts—whether they hear its voice, see its form, or touch its body—none fail to lose their lives."

There are those who possess the power of mantras; by the force of their incantations, they are able to bring under control such evil venomous dragons, garuḍas, and the like, as well as wicked elephants, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves, making them all docile and fit to be ridden or used as mounts.
When such beasts as these see that skillful incantation, they are immediately subdued.

It is the same with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: upon seeing Māra Pāpīyas, they all give rise to fear, yet Māra Pāpīyas does not feel even a trace of trepidation and continues to carry out his demonic deeds.

It is the same for those who study the Mahāyāna: seeing that the śrāvakas fear demonic activities and do not give rise to faith or delight in this Mahāyāna, [the Bodhisattva] first employs skillful means to subdue all demons, causing them to become well-disciplined and capable of serving as a vehicle; he then extensively expounds various sublime dharmas for their sake.

When the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas see that Māra has been subdued, they no longer give rise to fear; regarding this unsurpassed, true Dharma of the Mahāyāna, they now develop faith and joy, saying:
"From this day forward, we must not create obstacles within this true Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas give rise to fear toward the various afflictions, whereas those who study the Mahāyāna have no fear at all; such is the power of practicing and studying the Mahāyāna."
For these reasons, that which was previously taught was intended to subdue the various māras for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and not for the Mahāyāna.
This subtle and wondrous scripture of the Great Parinirvāṇa cannot be extinguished or subdued; it is most marvelous and extraordinary.

If there are those who hear this and, having heard it, believe and accept it—being able to believe that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma—such persons are exceedingly rare, like the udumbara flower.

After my parinirvāṇa, if there are those who hear such a subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtra as this and give rise to a heart of faith and reverence, you should know that for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas in future ages, they shall not fall into the evil realms.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Good son!
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings who will slander and lack faith in this subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa will these sentient beings begin to slander this sutra?”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, what kind of purely virtuous sentient beings will be able to rescue those who slander the Dharma?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! After my parinirvāṇa, for forty years it shall be widely circulated throughout Jambudvīpa, and only thereafter shall it disappear into the earth.”
Good son!
It is like sugarcane, rice, rock honey, milk, butter, and clarified butter (ghṛta): wherever these are found, the people of that land all say that this flavor is the foremost among all flavors.

Furthermore, there may be someone who eats only millet and barnyard grass; this person also says, "That which I eat is the most supreme," because this person of meager merit is experiencing the retribution of their karma.
If one is a person of merit, their ears shall never hear the names of millet or weeds; what they consume consists solely of non-glutinous rice, sugarcane, rock honey, and clarified butter.
This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this: those of dull faculties and meager merit do not delight in hearing it, just as those of meager merit loathe fine rice and rock honey.
The followers of the Two Vehicles are likewise: they loathe and detest this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of the Unsurpassed.

Yet there may be sentient beings whose hearts delight in hearing and receiving this sūtra; having heard it, they rejoice and do not give rise to slander, just like those fortunate people who eat fine rice.

“Good son! It is like a king who dwells in a mountainous region that is perilous and harsh. Although he possesses sugarcane, rice, and rock honey, because these are difficult to obtain, he hoards them with greedy attachment and does not dare to eat them, fearing they will run out; thus, he eats only millet and weeds.
A certain king of another country, hearing of this, felt pity and amusement; he immediately loaded carts with rice, grain, and sugarcane and sent them to him.
Having received them, that king distributed them at once, so that the entire nation could partake together.
Once the people had finished eating, they all felt great joy and spoke these words:
"It is because of that king that we have obtained this rare food."
"Good son! These four kinds of people are also like this;

they are the generals of this unsurpassed Great Dharma. Among these four, there may be one person who sees bodhisattvas in other regions who, though studying such Mahāyāna sūtras as these—whether copying them themselves or having others copy them—do so for the sake of profit and gain, for the sake of fame and reputation, for the sake of understanding the dharma, for the sake of a place of reliance, or for the sake of trading them for other scriptures, and thus are unable to extensively proclaim them to others. Therefore, one should take this subtle and wondrous sūtra and deliver it to those regions to give to those bodhisattvas, causing them to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta and to dwell securely in bodhi."
Once this bodhisattva has obtained this sutra, they shall immediately expound it extensively for others, enabling immeasurable multitudes to receive the flavor of such a Mahāyāna Dharma.

All of this is due to the power of this single bodhisattva, who causes all those who have not yet heard the sutras to hear them; it is like those people who, by the power of the king, obtain rare food.
Furthermore, good son!

Wherever this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is circulated, you should know that the ground there is itself adamantine, and the people therein are likewise like adamant. If there are those who can hear such a sūtra as this, they shall not regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all their vows shall be fulfilled according to their wishes, just as I have proclaimed today.
"You bhikṣus should properly receive and uphold this: if there are sentient beings who are unable to hear such a sūtra as this, you should know that these people are truly to be pitied."
"Why is this? Because such people are unable to receive, uphold, and comprehend the profound meaning of such Mahāyāna sūtras.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the forty years following, this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, shall be widely circulated and propagated throughout Jambudvīpa. Once that period has passed and it has disappeared from the earth, after how much time will it emerge once again?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
When eighty years remain of my True Dharma, during the first forty of those years, this sutra shall again rain down the great Dharma rain throughout Jambudvīpa."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When such sutras as these exist at the time when the True Dharma is extinguished, when the True Precepts are destroyed, when unrighteousness increases, and when there are no sentient beings who act according to the Dharma—who will be able to hear and receive them, uphold, read, and recite them until they are thoroughly mastered; and who will offer them worship and respect, copy them, and explain them?”

We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings, will analyze and explain this extensively, so that all bodhisattvas, having heard it, may receive and uphold it; and having upheld it, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression from their mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
You have now skillfully asked about such a meaning. Good son!

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the River Śītā, they will be able to receive, uphold, and recite such a sutra in this evil age without giving rise to slander.
"Good son!

If there are those who can resolve their minds on bodhicitta before as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma and to cherish and delight in this scripture, yet they will not be able to analyze and explain it extensively for others."
"Good son!

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to understand it correctly with faith and joy, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it; yet they will still be unable to explain it extensively for others."

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of three Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls; yet, even as they explain it to others, they will not yet understand its profound meaning.

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of four Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this degenerate age, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and extensively explain for others even one-sixteenth part of its meaning; yet, despite such exposition, it shall still not be complete.

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil world, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and copy its scriptures, and extensively explain for others the meaning of eight out of sixteen parts.

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of six Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and extensively explain for others the meaning of twelve out of the sixteen parts.

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil world, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and extensively explain for others fourteen-sixteenths of its meaning.

If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on Bodhi before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma; they will receive, uphold, read, and recite the sutra scrolls, and also encourage others to copy them. They themselves will be able to listen and accept it, and further encourage others to listen and accept it; they will read and recite it with fluency, protecting and firmly upholding it out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world. They will make offerings to this sutra and likewise encourage others to offer it worship, respect, reverence, recitation, and prostration. Furthermore, they will be fully capable of understanding it and exhausting its profound meanings and flavors—namely, that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, ultimately peaceful and blissful, and that all sentient beings universally possess Buddha-nature—and they will skillfully know the entire Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.

Having made offerings to such Buddhas as these, and having established this unsurpassed True Dharma, one upholds and protects it; if there are those who have first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should know that in future ages they will certainly be able to establish such a True Dharma, uphold it, and protect it.
Therefore, you should not fail to recognize those who will protect the Dharma in future ages.
Why is this? Those who have thus resolved their minds will certainly be able to uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma in the future.
“Good son! There are wicked bhikṣus who, hearing of my parinirvāṇa, do not give rise to sorrow, saying:
‘Today the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa; how delightful this is!’”
"While the Tathāgata was in the world, he obstructed our gains; now that he has entered nirvana, who will there be to obstruct and seize them from us?
If there is no one to obstruct and seize them, we shall regain our former offerings and sustenance."
"While the Tathāgata was in the world, the prohibitions and precepts were strict; now that he has entered nirvana, they shall all be abandoned.
The kaṣāya robes we have received were originally for the sake of ritual form; from now on, they shall be discarded and ruined like wooden banners."
"Such persons as these slander and reject this Mahāyāna sūtra. Good son!

You should now remember and uphold this: only those sentient beings who have accomplished and perfected immeasurable merit are able to believe in this Mahāyāna scripture, and having believed, they accept and uphold it."

Furthermore, if there are other sentient beings who delight in the Dharma and can extensively explain this sutra for others, then upon hearing it, all the evil karma they have committed throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past will be entirely extinguished.

If there are those who do not believe in this sutra, they shall, in their present bodies, be afflicted and harmed by immeasurable sufferings of illness; they will be frequently reviled and insulted by the multitude. After the end of their lives, they will be held in contempt by others; their countenances will be ugly, and their livelihood will be difficult, never being sufficient. Even if they obtain a small amount, it will be coarse, harsh, and of poor quality. Life after life, they will always dwell in families that are impoverished, lowly, slanderers of the True Dharma, and possessed of wrong views.

If, at the time of death, one encounters chaos and turmoil, or when weapons and warfare break out in competition; if one is oppressed by tyrannical rulers or the incursions of hateful enemies and rivals; if, despite having virtuous friends, one does not meet them; if one cannot obtain the necessities of life even when seeking them; if, though obtaining a small measure of gain, one constantly suffers from hunger and thirst; and if one is regarded only by the common masses while kings, ministers, and officials alike exclude one from their consideration—[then one will fall into the hells].
Even if they were to hear some teaching being proclaimed, even if it were the truth, they would ultimately not believe or accept it.
Such a person does not reach a good destination; just as a bird with broken wings cannot fly, so too this person, in future lives, will be unable to reach the auspicious realms of humans or devas.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who can believe in such Mahāyāna sūtras as these, although their physical form as originally received may be coarse and ugly, by virtue of the merit of these sūtras it shall immediately become upright and handsome; their majestic appearance, complexion, and strength will increase day by day, and they will always be joyfully beheld by humans and devas, who will revere, love, and cherish them, never wishing to be parted from them.
When the king, his ministers, and their kinsmen heard what he had said, they all came to revere and believe it.
"If among my śrāvaka disciples there is one who wishes to perform the foremost and most marvelous deed, that person should widely proclaim such Mahāyāna sūtras as these throughout the world."
“Good son! It is like mist and dew;
though they may seem to endure for a time, they do not last beyond sunrise. Once the sun has risen, they vanish without a trace.”

Good son! All the evil karma of these sentient beings is likewise; the power of its persistence in the world does not exceed the point at which they behold the sun of Great Nirvāṇa. Once that sun has risen, it is able to utterly extinguish all evil karma.
"Furthermore, good son! It is like a person who has left the household life and shaved his hair;

although he wears the *kāṣāya*, he has not yet received the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*. Suppose an elder comes to invite the assembly of monks; even one who has not yet received the precepts may join the great assembly in accepting the invitation. Although he has not yet received the precepts, he is already counted among the number of the Saṃgha."
"Good son!

If there are sentient beings who resolve their minds to begin studying this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra—whether by copying, upholding, reading, or reciting it—in the same way, although they have not yet fully attained the stages of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*), they have already entered the number of those who abide in the ten abidings."

Whether there be sentient beings who are disciples of the Buddha or not disciples, if—whether out of greed or fear, or for the sake of gain and offerings—they hear and receive even a single verse of this sutra, and having heard it do not slander it, you should know that such persons have already drawn near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! For these reasons, I say that four kinds of persons are the refuge of the world. Good son!"

Regarding these four persons, it is impossible that they would claim what was spoken by the Buddha was not spoken by the Buddha; for this reason, I declare that these four persons are the refuge of the world.
“Good son!
You should make offerings to these four kinds of people.
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]
"How should I recognize such a person so that I may make offerings to them?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there is one who establishes and protects the True Dharma, such a person should be approached with requests; one should offer them even at the cost of one's own body and life. As I have said in this Mahāyāna sūtra:"
“‘One who knows the Dharma, whether old or young, should therefore be supported,
honored, and prostrated to, just as the Brahmins and others serve the sacrificial fire.’”
Whoever knows the Dharma, whether old or young, should therefore be supported,
honored, and prostrated to, just as the devas serve Śakra.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, one should indeed provide for one’s teachers and elders in this manner.”
Now I have a doubt and pray that you will explain it fully:
if there is an elder who upholds the prohibitive precepts and seeks out what he has not yet heard from a younger person, should this person pay him respect?
If one were to pay homage [to such a person], it would not be called upholding the precepts.
Furthermore, if a youth who guards the prohibitions and precepts should consult an elder who has broken the precepts to receive teachings he has not heard before, should he also pay homage to him?
If a renunciant receives teachings not previously heard from a layperson, should they then pay homage?
Indeed, a renunciant ought not to pay homage to a layperson.

Nevertheless, within the Buddha-dharma, those who are young and junior should show reverence to the elders and seniors; for these seniors have previously received full ordination and have perfected their dignified deportment, and therefore they should be honored and venerated.
As the Buddha said:
"Those who break the precepts are not tolerated within the Buddha-dharma, just as a fertile field contains many weeds.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"There is one who knows the Dharma, whether old or young; therefore, one should make offerings to them as if serving Śakra.
What is the meaning of these two lines?
"Is it not that the Tathāgata speaks falsely?
For as the Buddha has said:
'Even a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts may commit transgressions.'"
For what reason did the Tathāgata speak thus?
The World-Honored One has also stated in other sūtras that one may listen to and treat those who have broken the precepts; the meaning of such statements remains unclarified.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! I have spoken these verses for the sake of future bodhisattvas who study the Mahāyāna, not for the sake of the śrāvaka disciples.”
Good son! As I have previously stated, when the True Dharma has perished and the true precepts are being violated, those who break the precepts will increase;
this is the time when unrighteousness flourishes.

When all the noble ones are hidden and do not appear, and when impure things such as male and female slaves are accepted and kept, one person from among these four classes shall appear in the world, shaving off hair and beard, leaving the home life, and practicing the Way.

I saw that various bhikṣus each accepted and kept male and female slaves, servants, and impure things; they knew nothing at all of what was pure and what was impure, nor did they recognize what was in accordance with the Vinaya and what was not.

In order to subdue such bhikṣus, this person harmonizes with them while not sharing in their defilements; he is well able to distinguish between his own sphere of practice and the sphere of the Buddha’s practice.
Although I see others committing pārājika offenses, I remain silent and do not expose them. Why is this?
I have appeared in the world desiring to establish and uphold the True Dharma; for this reason, I remain silent and do not expose such matters.
"Good son! Such a person, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, though they may commit transgressions, is not said to have broken the precepts. Good son!"
Suppose there is a king who falls ill and passes away, leaving behind a crown prince who is too young to succeed him.
There is a *caṇḍāla* who possesses abundant wealth and immeasurable riches, with many kinsmen; relying on his own might, he seizes the opportunity of the kingdom’s weakness to usurp the royal throne.
Not long after he began his rule and transformation of the realm, the countrymen, householders, brahmins, and others fled in rebellion and sought refuge in distant foreign lands.
Even those who remained there did not wish to so much as look upon this king with their own eyes.
There were some elders, brahmins, and others who did not leave their native lands; they were like various trees that die where they were born.
King Caṇḍāla, knowing that many of his people had fled and rebelled, immediately dispatched more caṇḍālas to patrol the roads. After seven days, he beat the drum and issued a proclamation:
"O brahmins, whoever can serve as my consecration preceptor shall be rewarded with half the kingdom as a noble fief."
When the brahmins heard these words, none of them came forward, and each said:
"How could there be a person of the brahmin caste who would do such a thing?"
The Caṇḍāla king spoke again:
"If not even a single one among the Brahmins will become my teacher, I shall compel all the Brahmins to live, eat, and sleep with the Caṇḍālas, and share their labors.
If there is anyone who can come and perform the consecration upon my head, I shall grant him half the kingdom; these words are no falsehood."
"The sublime nectar of immortality, the deathless medicine produced by incantations from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, should also be shared and consumed by all.

At that time, there was a son of a brahmin, in the prime of his youth, who practiced pure conduct, wore long hair as his characteristic mark, and was well-versed in incantations. He went to the king’s presence and said:
"Great King!"
"Whatever the King commands, I am able to perform it all.
At that time, the Great King felt great joy in his heart and accepted this youth as his consecration preceptor (*abhiṣeka-ācārya*).
When the other brahmins heard of this matter, they were all filled with indignation and rebuked the youth:
"O Brahmin, why have you become a teacher of the Caṇḍālas?
At that time, the king immediately divided half of his kingdom and gave it to this youth; they then ruled the country together for a long period.
At that time, the youth said to the king:
"I have left my family life to become your royal preceptor and teach the Great King subtle and secret incantations; yet, the Great King still does not treat me with affection."
Then the king replied,
"Why would I not be intimate with you now?
The youth answered:
"The immortal elixir possessed by our former kings has not yet been shared among us.
The King said, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Great Master!
I truly did not know.
If you require it, I only wish that you would take it with you."
At that time, having heard the king’s words, the youth immediately took [the meat] home, invited his ministers, and ate it with them.
After the ministers had finished eating, they said to the king together:
"How wonderful, Great Master!"
"There is this ambrosia, the medicine of immortality.
Once the king had learned this, he said to his teacher:
"Why is it that you, Great Master, alone consume the ambrosia with your ministers, while none of us are granted a share?"
At that time, the youth further gave the king other miscellaneous poisonous medicines to consume.

Once the king had consumed them, after a short while the poison took effect; he fell to the ground in a state of confusion and delirium, unconscious and unable to perceive anything, just like one who is dead.
At that time, the youth reinstated the former crown prince as king and spoke these words:
"The lion throne, by law, should not be allowed for a candāla to ascend."
"From the past until now, I have never heard of or seen one of the candāla caste acting as a king; it is impossible for a candāla to govern a kingdom and rule over the people."
"You should now return and succeed the former king, governing the country with the True Dharma.
At that time, after the youth had settled these matters, he gave the antidote to the caṇḍāla to make him regain consciousness; once he had awakened, he drove him out of the country.

At that time, although the youth performed these deeds, he did not lose his status as a Brahmin; when the other householders, Brahmins, and others heard what he had done, they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Benevolent One!
You have skillfully driven away the Caṇḍāla king.
"O Son of Good Family!"

After my parinirvāṇa, those bodhisattvas who protect and uphold the True Dharma shall likewise, through the power of skillful means, engage in the same activities as those monks who break the precepts, who bear mere names, and who accept and store all manner of impure things.

At that time, if a bodhisattva sees someone who, despite having committed many transgressions of the precepts, is able to discipline those evil bhikṣus who have violated their prohibitions, he shall immediately go to that person’s place, pay respectful homage, provide the four types of offerings, and present all his scriptures and personal belongings as gifts;
if he does not possess these himself, he must employ skillful means to seek them from various donors and give them.
For this reason, one should keep eight kinds of impure things. Why is this?
It is because such a person acts to subdue wicked bhikṣus, just as that youth drove away the caṇḍālas.
At that time, although the Bodhisattva reverently prostrates to such a person and accepts and keeps the eight kinds of impure things, he incurs no fault whatsoever. Why is this?

This is because these bodhisattvas, desiring to expel and discipline wicked bhikṣus so that the pure saṃgha may dwell in peace and security, and so that the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras may be propagated for the benefit of all devas and humans.
"Good son!

For these reasons, I have spoken these two verses within the sutras, so that all bodhisattvas may together praise those who protect the Dharma, just as those householders and brahmins praised the youth:
'Excellent, excellent!'"

"A Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should indeed act in this way. If anyone sees a person who protects the Dharma engaging in the same activities as one who has broken the precepts, and yet speaks of that protector as being guilty, you should know that such a person will themselves incur the calamity."
This protector of the Dharma is truly without fault. Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who, having violated the prohibitive precepts, conceals them out of a mind of arrogance and does not repent, you should know that such a person is called one who has truly broken the precepts.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts for the sake of protecting the Dharma, even if there is an offense committed, it is not called a breach of precepts.
Why is this? Because they are free from arrogance and openly confess and repent their transgressions.
"Good son! For this reason, I have concealed the underlying meaning within the sūtras and spoken these verses:
'One who knows the Dharma, whether old or young, should therefore be honored.'"
They pay respectful homage as if serving those who tend the sacred fire; like Brahmins, they serve him as if he were the second heaven, Indra himself.
“For this reason, I have not spoken these verses for the sake of those training as śrāvakas, but rather for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Are the precepts originally received by such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these still fully intact, even though they are extremely lax regarding the precepts?
The Buddha said,
"Good sons!..."
You should not speak in such a manner now.
Why is this? The precepts originally received are not lost, remaining exactly as they were.
If one commits an offense, one should immediately repent; once repented, one is purified. Good son!
It is like an old embankment: if it has holes or breaches, water will leak through.
Why is this? Because there is no one to manage it.
If there were someone to manage it, the water would not flow out.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: although they may perform the *poṣadha*, receive the precepts, and participate in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha together with those who have broken the precepts, their observance of the Vinaya is not like a dam that has been breached and is leaking.
Why is this? If there are no persons who maintain pure precepts, the Saṃgha will decline, and arrogance, laxity, and indolence will increase day by day.
If there are persons who maintain pure precepts, they will be able to remain fully endowed with them and not lose their fundamental discipline.
"Good son!
To be lax regarding the vehicle is what is called laxity; to be lax regarding the precepts is not called laxity.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not allow the mind to become indolent or arrogant toward this Mahāyāna, this is called the fundamental precept."
"To protect the True Dharma, one bathes oneself with the water of the Mahāyāna; therefore, although a bodhisattva may appear to violate the precepts, this is not called laxity.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Among the Saṃgha there are four kinds of people, like the mango fruit, whose ripeness or rawness is difficult to discern."
"How can one recognize those who break the precepts and those who uphold them?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
By means of this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, it can be easily understood.
How is it that one may come to know through this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*?

It is like a farmer who plants rice and other grains; while he weeds out the barnyard grass and tares, he regards the field as pure when observing it with the naked eye, yet once the grain has ripened, the weeds and the crops are clearly distinct from one another.
These eight matters can defile the Saṃgha; if they are eliminated, one may know it is pure by observing with the physical eye.
If there are those who uphold the precepts and those who break them, when they do not commit evil, it is difficult to distinguish them by observation with the physical eye;
but if their evil becomes manifest, they are easy to recognize, just as that wild rice is easy to distinguish.

It is the same within the Saṃgha: if one can remain far removed from the eight impure poisons of the snake-dharma, they are called the pure field of merit for the noble assembly; such a one should be venerated by humans and devas, for their pure karmic fruit is not something that can be discerned by the physical eye.
Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like the Karaka forest, where the trees are numerous; yet within this forest there is but one tree, named Tinduka.
These *kālakā* trees and *tinduka* trees have fruits that are so similar they cannot be distinguished.
When the fruit ripens, a woman gathers them all; yet of the *tinduka* fruit there is but one part, while of the *kālakā* fruit there are ten parts.
This woman did not recognize it; she brought it to the market and offered it for sale.
A foolish child, likewise unable to distinguish it, bought the kālakā fruit, ate it, and died.
When those wise people heard this matter, they immediately asked the woman:
"Sister, from where did you bring these fruits?
At that time, the woman pointed out the location, and the people then said:
"In such a place, there are many immeasurable *kālakā* trees, and only a single *tinduka* tree.
Having learned this, the people laughed and departed.

“Good son! Among the great assembly, the eight impure dharmas are likewise so. Within this assembly, many receive and utilize these eight dharmas; there is only one person who purely maintains the precepts and does not accept these eight impure dharmas. Although he knows that the others accept and store what is unlawful, he continues to work together with them and does not separate from them, just like that single tinduka tree in the forest.”

There may be upāsakas who, seeing that these people frequently engage in unrighteous practices, cease altogether to respect or make offerings to them. If they wish to make offerings, they should first ask:
"Venerable sir, do you accept and keep these eight things?"
"Is this permitted by the Buddha?
If it is said that the Buddha permits it, may such a person participate in the *poṣadha*, the *karmavācanā*, and the *pravāraṇā*?
After that upāsaka had asked this, the assembly all replied:
"These eight matters, out of compassion, the Tathāgata has permitted all to be kept.
The upāsaka said,
"In the Jetavana monastery there are bhikṣus who say that gold and silver are permitted by the Buddha to be kept, while others say they are not permitted."

Regarding those who speak of "listening": one does not dwell together with such non-listeners, nor does one recite the precepts or perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with them; this extends even to not drinking water from the same river, nor sharing any material gains or offerings with them at all.
"How can you say that the Buddha permitted this?
Although the Buddha, the God among Gods, accepted it, you members of the Sangha should not keep it."

If there are those who accept [the offense], one should not even perform the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, or *karmavācanā* with them, nor participate in their monastic affairs. Should one perform the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, or *karmavācanā* with them, or participate in their monastic affairs, at the end of life they shall fall into hell, just as those people did after eating the kāla fruit and then passing away.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a man selling medicine in a city who has a wondrous sweet medicine produced from the Snowy Mountains, yet he also sells many other miscellaneous medicines whose tastes are similar to that of the sweet one."

At that time, there were many people who all wished to buy [the medicine], yet they could not distinguish it; they went to the place where the medicine was being sold and asked, "Do you have the Snow Mountain medicine?
The medicine seller immediately replied, "I do."
This person is deceitful; using other miscellaneous medicines, he says to the buyer, "This is a sweet, excellent, and wonderful medicine from the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, because the buyer possesses only physical eyes, they cannot discern it well and immediately purchases and takes it away, further thinking:
"I have now obtained the sweet medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains. Kāśyapa!

Within the community of śrāvakas, there are those who are monks in name only, those who are true monks, and those who are harmonious monks; whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, one should equally provide offerings, pay respect, and prostrate before this assembly.
Because this upāsaka possesses only the fleshly eye, he is unable to distinguish [them].
It is like that person who cannot distinguish the sweet medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains;
who among them is one who maintains the precepts?
Who is one who breaks the precepts?
Who is a true monk?
Who is a false monk?
Only those with the divine eye can distinguish [between them]. Kāśyapa!
If a lay follower knows that a bhikṣu is a person who has broken the precepts, he should not provide alms, prostrate, or make offerings to him.
If one knows that such a person accepts and keeps the eight [unlawful] things, one likewise should not provide them with their necessities, nor prostrate to or make offerings to them.
If there is one within the Sangha who has broken the precepts, one should not show reverence or prostrate to them on account of their wearing the *kāṣāya*.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
"What the Tathāgata has spoken is true and not false; I shall receive it upon the crown of my head.
Just as with a diamond or other rare treasures, so too, as the Buddha has taught, these bhikṣus should rely upon the four dharmas."
What are the four?

Rely on the Dharma and not on the person; rely on the meaning and not on the words; rely on wisdom and not on consciousness; rely on sutras of definitive meaning and not on sutras of interpretable meaning.
"These four dharmas should be realized as not belonging to these four kinds of persons.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

That which accords with the Dharma is the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; all Buddha-dharmas are the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), and this Dharma-nature is the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Furthermore, if anyone should say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, such a person neither knows nor sees the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
One who does not know or see this nature of phenomena should not be relied upon.
As previously stated, those four individuals who appear in the world to protect and uphold the Dharma should be realized and relied upon as a refuge. Why is this?

Because these persons skillfully understand the subtle, secret, and profound treasury of the Tathāgata; they are able to know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and immutable. It is impossible for anyone to claim that the Tathāgata is impermanent or subject to change.
These four persons are precisely what is called the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because these individuals are able to understand the secret language of the Tathāgata and are able to expound it.

If there is anyone who can understand the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, and who knows that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, it is impossible for such a person to say, for the sake of gain and honor, that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
If such a person may still be relied upon, how much more so those who do not rely on these four types of people?

Relying on the Dharma is the very nature of reality (dharmatā); not relying on persons refers to the śrāvaka. The nature of reality is the Tathāgata; the śrāvaka is that which is conditioned (saṃskṛta). The Tathāgata is eternally abiding (nitya); the conditioned is impermanent (anitya).
"Good son!
If a person breaks the precepts for the sake of gain and profit, and says that the Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change, such a person is not to be relied upon."
"Good son! This is called the definitive meaning. 'Rely on the meaning, not on the words'—'meaning' refers to awakening and comprehension.

Awakening and comprehending the meaning is called being free from weakness; being free from weakness is called fulfillment. The meaning of fulfillment is that the Tathāgata is eternally present and unchanging; the meaning of the Tathāgata’s eternal presence and immutability is precisely the permanence of the Dharma; the meaning of the permanence of the Dharma is precisely the permanence of the Saṃgha. This is what is meant by relying on the meaning and not on the words."
What kind of speech should not be relied upon?
It refers to various treatises and flowery rhetoric.

As for the immeasurable sūtras spoken by the Buddha, they pursue them with insatiable greed; they are full of craftiness, flattery, and deceit, feigning intimacy and attachment; they manifest signs to seek profit and manage the affairs of laypeople as their servants, while further proclaiming:

"The Buddha permitted bhikṣus to keep various slaves and impure things—gold, silver, precious jewels, granaries of grain, and livestock such as oxen, sheep, elephants, and horses—and to engage in trade for profit. Out of compassion for his sons during times of famine, he permitted the bhikṣus to store up provisions, to prepare their own food, and to eat it even if it had not been formally received."
"One should not rely on such statements as these.
Regarding 'rely on wisdom, not on consciousness,' what is called wisdom is precisely the Tathāgata.
If there are śrāvakas who cannot properly know the merits of the Tathāgata, such consciousness should not be relied upon."
If one knows that the Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya, such true wisdom is what should be relied upon.

If one perceives the Tathāgata as a body of expedient means, saying it is comprised of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and is nourished by food, this too should not be relied upon; therefore, knowledge [of such a body] is not something to be relied upon.
If there are those who speak in such a manner, one should not rely upon them nor their scriptures.
"Rely on sūtras of definitive meaning; do not rely on sūtras of interpretable meaning."

The *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras refer to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle; upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury, they all give rise to doubt and wonder, not knowing that this treasury gives birth to the ocean of great wisdom. They are like infants who lack discernment; this is what is called "not of definitive meaning."

"Definitive meaning (nītārtha) refers to the Bodhisattva; their true wisdom follows their own mind as unimpeded great knowledge, just as a great person knows all things—this is called definitive meaning."
Furthermore, the Śrāvaka-yāna is called "of provisional meaning" (neyārtha),
whereas the unsurpassed Mahāyāna is called "of definitive meaning" (nītārtha).
If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change, that is called "of provisional meaning."
If it is said that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, this is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
That which is spoken by Śrāvakas as something to be realized is called the non-definitive meaning (neyārtha);
that which is spoken by Bodhisattvas as something to be realized is called the definitive meaning.
If it is said that the Tathāgata is sustained by what he eats, this is of provisional meaning (neyārtha);
if it is said that he is eternally abiding and unchanging, this is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
If it is said that the Tathāgata enters nirvana like a fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted, this is called provisional meaning;
If it is said that the Tathāgata enters the dharma-nature, this is called a definitive meaning (nītārtha).
One should not rely upon the vehicle of the śrāvakas. Why is this?
The Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings, employs the power of skillful means to teach the Śrāvaka vehicle, just as an elder teaches his children the half-syllables.
O son of good family!

The Śrāvakayāna is like the first plowing of a field, from which no fruit has yet been obtained; thus it is called "of provisional meaning" (neyārtha). Therefore, one should not rely upon the Śrāvakayāna.
The Dharma of the Mahāyāna should be relied upon. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings, taught the Mahāyāna through the power of skillful means; therefore, it should be relied upon, and this is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
These four reliances should be realized and known.

Furthermore, that which relies on the meaning: "meaning" is named straightforwardness; straightforwardness is named illumination; illumination is named non-weakness; non-weakness is named the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, "radiance" is called wisdom; "uprightness" is called permanence. The permanence of the Tathāgata is called relying on the Dharma; the Dharma is called permanent, and is also called boundless, inconceivable, ungraspable, and unbindable, yet it can be seen.
If there are those who say it cannot be seen, such persons should not be relied upon. Therefore, rely on the Dharma and do not rely on the person.
If someone were to proclaim impermanence using subtle and refined words, such speech should not be relied upon; therefore, rely on the meaning and not on the words.
Regarding reliance on wisdom: the Sangha is eternal, unconditioned, and immutable; it does not store the eight kinds of impure things. Therefore, rely on wisdom and do not rely on consciousness.
If someone were to say that consciousness acts and consciousness receives, yet there is no harmonious Sangha, why is this?
For that which is called "harmony" is termed "non-existence"; how can that which is non-existent be said to be permanent?
Therefore, this consciousness cannot be relied upon. Regarding "relying on the definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*):

"definitive meaning" refers to contentment; it means never falsely manifesting dignified deportment or purity, nor being arrogant and self-exalting, nor greedily seeking gain and offerings, and furthermore, not giving rise to attachment toward the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata through skillful means according to circumstances—this is called the definitive meaning.

If there are those who can abide within such [teachings], it should be known that these persons have already attained abiding in the ultimate truth; therefore, they are said to rely on sūtras of definitive meaning.

"Do not rely on that which is of provisional meaning. As it is said in the sūtras, 'all is burning, all is impermanent, all is suffering, all is empty, and all is without self'—this is called that which is of provisional meaning."
Why is this? Because they are unable to comprehend such meanings, they cause sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell.
For what reason?
Because of grasping and attachment, one does not understand the true meaning.
"All things are burning" means that the Tathāgata says even nirvāṇa is burning;
"all things are impermanent" means that even nirvāṇa is impermanent.
"Suffering, emptiness, and non-self are also like this.
Therefore, these are called sutras of provisional meaning and should not be relied upon. Good son!"

If someone were to say that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings and being well-acquainted with the appropriate timing, speaks of the light as heavy and the heavy as light because he knows the proper time; [this would be so].

The Tathāgata observes and knows that for those disciples who have donors providing all their necessities so that they lack nothing, the Buddha does not permit such persons to keep slaves, gold, silver, wealth, treasures, engage in trade and commerce, or possess impure things.

If my disciples have no donors to provide their necessities, and at a time of famine when food and drink are difficult to obtain, for the sake of establishing and upholding the True Dharma, I permit my disciples to accept and possess male and female slaves, gold, silver, vehicles, fields, houses, grain, and rice, and to trade for whatever they require. Although I permit them to accept and possess such things, they must do so through pure offerings from donors of sincere faith.
These four dharmas are those upon which one should rely.
If there are Vinaya, Abhidharma, or Sūtras that do not contradict these four, they too should be relied upon.

If anyone should say that there are times when it is not the proper time, or that there are those who can protect the Dharma and those who cannot, and that the Tathāgata permits all bhikṣus to accept and store such impure things as these—such words should not be relied upon.
If there are identical explanations within the Vinaya, Abhidharma, and Sūtras, one should likewise not rely upon these three divisions.
I have taught these four reliances for the sake of sentient beings who possess only the fleshly eye; they were never intended for those who possess the eye of wisdom.

Therefore, I now speak of these four reliances: "Dharma" refers to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); "meaning" refers to the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging presence; "knowledge" refers to the realization that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; and "definitive meaning" refers to the thorough comprehension of all Mahāyāna sūtras.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Six 4;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Seven,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! Regarding the four kinds of persons mentioned above, should one rely upon them?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, noble son!
You should rely upon what I have taught."
Why is this? Because there are four māras. What are these four?
"As for those who can receive and uphold other sutras and vinayas spoken by Māra," Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught that there are four kinds of Māras, how am I to distinguish between what is spoken by a Māra and what is spoken by the Buddha?
Furthermore, among sentient beings, some follow the conduct of Māras while others comply with the teachings of the Buddha; how am I to recognize such individuals?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Seven hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this Māra Pāpīyas shall gradually cause the ruin of my True Dharma."

For example, just as a hunter might dress himself in the robes of the Dharma, so too does Māra Pāpīyas; he assumes the form of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā, and further manifests the body of a srotāpanna, even manifesting the bodies of arhats and the physical body of a Buddha.
By means of this tainted form, the Māra King assumes an untainted body to destroy my True Dharma.
When this Māra Pāpīyān destroys the True Dharma, he will speak these words:

"In the past, the Bodhisattva descended from the Tuṣita Heaven and came here to the palace of King Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu; relying on his parents and through the union of their desire, he was born with this body."
"If one says that there is someone born among humans who is revered by the devas, humans, and the great assemblies of the world, such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, it is said:
'In the past, through various ascetic practices and by giving away my head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, and children, I have therefore now attained the Way of the Buddha.'"
By these causes and conditions, they are revered by gods, humans, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
"If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak in this way, you should know that they are all spoken by Māra.
'Good son! If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak as follows:"

"The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment long ago; that he now manifests the attainment of the Buddha-way is solely because he desires to deliver all sentient beings. To accord with the ways of the world, he manifests birth by depending upon parents and through the union of desire."
"Know that such sūtras and vinayas are truly spoken by the Tathāgata.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who can follow the sūtras and vinayas spoken by the Buddha are bodhisattvas."
"If anyone should say:
'It is not to be believed that when the Tathāgata was born, he took seven steps in each of the ten directions,' this is what Māra has said."
"Furthermore, if someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata’s appearing in the world and walking seven steps in each of the ten directions is a skillful manifestation by the Tathāgata.'"
"This is what is called the sūtras and vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who can follow what is spoken by the Buddha are bodhisattvas."
"If there are those who say:

'After the Bodhisattva was born, the King, his father, sent men to lead him to the celestial shrine; when the various devas saw him, they all descended to pay him homage and respect, and for this reason he is called a Buddha.'"
Furthermore, there may be those who raise this objection:
"The devas appeared first, and the Buddha appeared later; how then can the devas pay homage to the Buddha?
One should know that whoever raises such an objection is speaking under the influence of Pāpīyān.
If there is a sūtra that says:
"When the Buddha arrived at a deva temple, all these devas—Maheśvara, Mahābrahmā, and Śakra Devānām Indra—all joined their palms and paid homage at his feet."
"Such sūtras and vinayas are what was spoken by the Buddha.
If there are those who follow what is spoken by Māra, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can follow what is spoken by the Buddha, they are bodhisattvas."
"If there are sutras or vinayas that state:

'When the Bodhisattva was a crown prince, out of a greedy mind, he took wives from the four quarters; dwelling within the deep palace, he amused himself with the five desires, joyfully experiencing pleasure. "
"Such sūtras and vinayas were spoken by Pāpīyān. If anyone should say:

'The Bodhisattva has long since abandoned thoughts of greed and his wife and children, and even refused to accept the exquisite five desires of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, discarding them like nasal mucus or saliva—how much more so human desires?'"
"Shave off your hair and beard, leave the household life, and cultivate the Way.
Such sūtras and vinayas are what the Buddha has taught.
If there are those who follow the sūtras and vinayas of Māra, they are the retinue of Māra.
If there are those who accord with the Buddha’s sutras and vinaya, they are bodhisattvas.
If someone were to say:

“When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, he permitted the bhikṣus to accept and keep male and female slaves, servants, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, chickens, pigs, cats, dogs, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, crystal, musāragalva, agate, coral, amber, conch shells, jade, copper and iron cauldrons, large and small bronze basins, and all such necessary items; as well as plowing fields, planting crops, buying and selling in the markets, and hoarding grain—because the Buddha possesses great compassion, out of pity for sentient beings, he permitted them to keep all such things.”
"Such sūtras and vinayas are all spoken by Māra.
If someone were to say:
'When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī, at the place where the Nārilu spirits resided, at that time..."
The Tathāgata, on account of the brahmin Gośṛṅga and King Prasenajit,
spoke as follows: "A bhikṣu should not accept or store gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, musāragalva,
agate, coral, amber, conch shells, jade, slaves, servants, or male and female children."
Cattle, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, chickens, pigs, cats, dogs, and other such beasts; copper and iron cauldrons and pots;
large and small copper basins; various multicolored beds, mats, and bedding; and the necessities of life, namely:
dwellings, plowing fields and planting crops, buying and selling in the marketplace, and preparing food with one's own hands.
Grinding [grains] by hand, pounding [grain], practicing bodily incantations and arts, methods for training hawks, gazing upward at the constellations,
calculating the waxing and waning of the moon, divining the characteristics of men and women, interpreting dreams as auspicious or inauspicious, determining whether one is male,
female, or neither male nor female— these sixty-four skills, along with eighteen other delusive incantations and various arts.
Artistry, or the teaching of countless worldly secular matters: powdered incense, ground incense, ointments, and perfumes;
various flower garlands; techniques for grooming the hair; deceit, hypocrisy, and crookedness; insatiable greed for profit; delighting in bustle and clamor;
jesting, laughing, and idle talk; and the craving for fish and meat combined with the compounding of poisons.
Pressing fragrant oils, carrying precious parasols and leather sandals, making fans, boxes, and baskets, and producing various painted images;
accumulating grains, rice, wheat, barley, beans, and all kinds of fruits and gourds.

They associate with kings, princes, ministers, and various women; they laugh loudly or remain silent; they harbor many doubts regarding the teachings; they speak much in falsehoods; they comment on matters of length and brevity, beauty and ugliness, or virtue and non-virtue; and they take pleasure in fine clothing and other such various impure things.

Those who personally praise themselves in the presence of donors, and who frequent impure places for coming and going—namely, taverns, brothels, and gambling dens—I now forbid such persons from remaining among the bhikṣus; they should cease their practice of the Way and return to lay life to perform labor.
"Just as, for example, weeds and wild rice are completely eradicated without remainder.
You should know that these various sūtras and vinayas which have been established are all spoken by the Tathāgata.
If there are those who follow what has been spoken by Māra, they are the retinue of Māra.
If there is one who accords with what the Buddha has taught, that person is a bodhisattva.
If someone were to say:
"A bodhisattva enters the temples of devas—namely those of Brahmā, Maheśvara, Vedha, and Kātyāyana—in order to make offerings to the devas."
The reason he enters [among them] is that he wishes to subdue all devas and humans.
To say otherwise would be impossible.

If one were to say that a Bodhisattva cannot enter into the heterodox doctrines of outsiders, nor understand their deportment, literature, arts, or crafts; that he cannot reconcile servants or settle disputes; that he is not honored by men, women, kings, or ministers; and furthermore, that he does not know how to compound medicines—claiming he is called a Tathāgata precisely because of such ignorance, and that those who do possess such knowledge are merely followers of false views.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata maintains a mind of equanimity toward both enemies and kin; whether someone cuts his body with a blade or anoints it with fragrant perfume, he gives rise to neither a thought of benefit nor one of harm toward these two persons, but remains solely in the middle. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.

"Know that such sūtras and vinayas are what Māra has spoken. If someone should say: 'The Bodhisattva thus manifests entering a celestial shrine, leaving the household life to practice the Way within the teachings of external paths;

he manifests knowledge of their dignified deportment and ritual etiquette, his ability to master all literature and arts, and his entry into schools of writing and places of craft. He can skillfully reconcile the quarrels of servants and attendants, and among the great assemblies—whether young men or maidens, palace ladies and consorts, commoners and elders, brahmins, kings and ministers, or the poor—he is the most honored and supreme, receiving the reverence of these very people, and he is likewise able to manifest such matters as these.'"

Though dwelling amidst various views, they do not give rise to attachment, just as a lotus flower is unsullied by dust and mire. For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, they skillfully employ such diverse expedient means, acting in accordance with worldly dharmas.
"You should know that such sūtras and vinayas are precisely what was spoken by the Tathāgata.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who can follow what is spoken by the Buddha are great bodhisattvas."
"If someone were to say: 'The Tathāgata has explained for me the Sūtras and Vinaya;

regarding the light and heavy offenses among evil dharmas, as well as the *sthūlātyaya*, their nature is entirely grave. In our Vinaya, we never commit such acts. I have long endured these teachings, so even if you do not believe them, how could I abandon my own Vinaya to follow yours? "
"The Vinaya you possess was spoken by Māra; our Sūtras and Vinaya were established by the Buddha.

The Tathāgata previously taught the ninefold seal of the Dharma (navāṅga-dharmamudrā), and these nine seals have sealed our Sūtras and Vinaya. From the beginning, we have never heard of the Vaipulya sūtras being spoken by the Tathāgata, even a single phrase or a single word. In which of the immeasurable Sūtras and Vinayas is it ever said that there are Vaipulya sūtras?"

Among such [scriptures], we have never heard the names of these ten classes of sutras; if they do exist, one should know that they were certainly composed by Devadatta. We do not believe in these Vaipulya sutras created by the evil man Devadatta for the purpose of destroying the True Dharma.
Sūtras such as these were spoken by Māra.
Why is this? Because they destroy the Dharma of the Buddha by creating distinctions between right and wrong.
"Such words as these exist in your sutras, but they do not exist in my sutras.

Within my sutras and vinayas, the Tathāgata has declared: 'After my parinirvāṇa, in the degenerate age, there shall be improper sutras and vinayas, namely the Mahāyāna Vaipulya scriptures; in future ages, there shall be such evil bhikṣus.'"

I have also said that beyond the ninefold canon of scriptures (navāṅga-śāsana) there are the Vaipulya sūtras; if there is anyone who can thoroughly understand their meaning, you should know that such a person correctly understands the sūtras and the vinaya, remains far removed from all impure things, and is subtle, wondrous, and pure like the full moon.
If someone were to say:

"Although the Tathāgata has explained meanings and flavors as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for each individual sūtra and vinaya, these are not found within our vinaya; therefore, one should know that they do not exist."
"If it truly exists, why has the Tathāgata not explained it within my Vinaya?
For this reason, I cannot now accept it with faith.
You should know that such a person incurs an offense.
That person further says:
"I shall receive and uphold such sutras and vinayas. Why is this?"
"You should act as my teacher for the sake of contentment and fewness of desires, the eradication of afflictions, wisdom and nirvana, and the causes of wholesome dharmas.
One who speaks thus is not my disciple.
"If there should be one who says:
'The Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings,
has preached the Vaipulya sūtras,' you should know that this person is truly my disciple."

If there are those who do not accept the Vaipulya sutras, you should know that such persons are not my disciples; they have not left the household life for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, but are instead disciples of heterodox paths characterized by false views.
“Sūtras and vinayas such as these are spoken by the Buddha; those that are not so are spoken by Māra.
If there are those who follow what is spoken by Māra, they are the retinue of Māra;
if there are those who follow what is spoken by the Buddha, they are bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, good son!
If someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata is not accomplished through immeasurable merit; he is impermanent and subject to change. "
"Because one has attained the dharma of emptiness and proclaims non-self, it does not conform to the world.
Such sūtras and vinayas are said to have been taught by Māra.
"If someone says:"
"The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is inconceivable and is also accomplished through immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya merits; therefore, he is eternally abiding and without change."
"Such sūtras and vinayas are what the Buddha has taught.
If there are those who follow what the Māra has taught, they are the retinue of Māra;
if there are those who follow what the Buddha has taught, they are bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, some say:
"There may be a bhikṣu who has not actually committed a pārājika offense, yet everyone says he has committed a pārājika offense, like cutting down a tala tree."
"Yet this bhikṣu has actually committed no offense. Why is this?
For I have always said:"
"Regarding the four *pārājika* offenses, if one commits even one, it is like splitting a stone that cannot be rejoined.
If one claims for oneself to have attained a state surpassing that of ordinary humans, this is called committing a *pārājika* offense."

Why is this? Because although there is truly nothing attained, he falsely manifests the appearance of attainment; such a person falls away from the dharmas of a human being, and this is called a pārājika offense.
That is to say: suppose there is a bhikṣu who has few desires and is content, whose observance of the precepts is pure, and who dwells in a secluded place.
If a king or a high minister sees this bhikṣu, they might conceive the thought that he has attained arhatship; they would then approach him to praise, revere, and prostrate to him, further saying:
"Such a great master, after casting off this body, shall surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu immediately replied to the king, saying:
"I have indeed not yet attained the fruits of the śramaṇa path; do not say, O King, that I have attained the fruits of the path.
I only pray, Great King!"
Do not speak to me of the dharma of insatiability; as for one who is insatiable, even up to the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they accept it all in silence.
If I were now to accept [this] in silence, I would be censured by all the Buddhas.
The practice of contentment is praised by all the Buddhas; therefore, desiring to enjoy happiness throughout my life, I wish to reverently cultivate contentment.
"Furthermore, one who is content knows for certain within himself that he has not yet attained the fruits of the Path.
Although the King declares that I have attained them, I do not accept this; therefore, I am called 'contented.
At that time, the King replied:
"The Great Master has truly attained the fruit of Arhatship; he is no different from the Buddha.

At that time, the king issued a proclamation throughout his inner and outer realms, ensuring that the members of the imperial harem and the queens were all made aware that he had attained the fruit of a śramaṇa. Consequently, he caused all who heard this to give rise to reverent faith, making offerings to him with deep respect.
Such a bhikṣu is truly a person of pure brahmacarya; by this cause and condition, he causes all people everywhere to obtain great merit and virtue.
Yet, this bhikṣu has in fact not committed a pārājika offense.
Why is this? Because that person has spontaneously given rise to a heart of joy, praising and making offerings; how, then, could such a bhikṣu have any fault?
If anyone were to say that this person incurs sin, you should know that such a scripture is spoken by Māra.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who say:

"The profound sūtras of the Buddha’s secret treasury teach that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature; by virtue of this nature, one severs immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters and immediately attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with the sole exception of the icchantikas."
If a king or a great minister should speak thus:
"Bhikṣu, will you become a Buddha or not?
Do you possess the Buddha-nature?"
The bhikṣu replied, “Within my present body there is certainly the Buddha-nature; whether it will be realized or not remains yet to be determined.
The king said:
"Venerable Sir!
If one does not become an icchantika, they will certainly attain [enlightenment] without doubt.
The bhikṣu said:
"It is indeed as the King says.
Although this person claims that the Buddha-nature definitely exists, he likewise does not commit a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, at the very moment of going forth, reflects thus:
"I shall now certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Such a person, although they have not yet realized the fruit of the unsurpassed path, has already acquired immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit.
If someone were to say that this person has committed a *pārājika* offense, then there would be no bhikṣu who has not committed one.

Why is this? For eighty billion kalpas in the past, I have always remained free from all impure things; I have had few desires and been content, perfected in dignified deportment, and have skillfully cultivated the unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, I personally and certainly knew that my own body possessed the Buddha-nature. Therefore, I have now attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, am named a Buddha, and possess great compassion.
Such sutras and vinayas are what was spoken by the Buddha.
If there are those who cannot accord with them, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can accord with them, they are great bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

"There are no four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, two *aniyata* dharmas, thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, ninety-one *pāyattika*, four *pratideśanīya* dharmas, numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas, or the seven methods for settling disputes; nor are there the *sthūlātyaya* offenses, the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), or the *icchantikas*."
If there were bhikṣus who, by committing such offenses as these, would fall into hell, then those of external paths would all surely be reborn in heaven. Why is this?
Because those of external paths have no precepts to violate; therefore, the Tathāgata has manifested these precepts to instill fear in people and thus taught them.
If it is said that the Buddha taught:
"If my bhikṣus wish to engage in sexual intercourse, they should discard their dharma robes, put on secular clothing, and only then engage in sexual intercourse."
Furthermore, you should give rise to this thought: "The causes and conditions of sexual desire are not my fault;

even while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were bhikṣus who practiced sexual desire and yet attained right liberation, or were born in the heavens after their lives ended. This has occurred throughout antiquity and the present; it is not something I alone have done.
Whether one violates the four grave offenses, or the five precepts, or practices all manner of impure conduct, one can still attain true and genuine liberation."

Although the Tathāgata has said that committing a *duṣkṛta* offense leads to falling into hell for eight million years—measured by the number of years, months, and days of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—it is likewise a manifestation by the Tathāgata intended to terrify people.

To claim that there is no difference in weight between a *pārājika* offense and a minor *duṣkṛta* is a false statement made by these Vinaya masters; they falsely assert that this was established by the Buddha. One must certainly know that this was not spoken by the Buddha.
Such statements as these are the sūtras and vinaya of Māra.
Furthermore, if it is said:
"If one violates even a minor precept among all the precepts, down to the most subtle, one shall undergo bitter retribution without limit."
Having understood this, one should protect oneself, just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs.
If there is a Vinaya master who further says,
"There is no karmic retribution whatsoever for violating the precepts," such a person should not be associated with.
As the Buddha has said:
"If one transgresses even a single dharma, this is called lying; not seeing the future life, there is no evil one does not commit."
"Therefore, one should not associate with such a person.
Within my Buddha-dharma, purity is thus; how much less could there be anyone who commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense, or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pārājika* offense, and yet it were not a transgression?"
Therefore, one should deeply guard oneself against such dharmas;
if one does not protect them, what other dharma could be called "prohibitory precepts"?
I have also stated in the sūtras that for those who commit the four pārājikas, down to even the most subtle duṣkṛtas, they should be severely disciplined.
"If sentient beings do not guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts, how can they ever perceive the Buddha-nature?

Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, it must be through the upholding of the precepts that they subsequently perceive it; by perceiving the Buddha-nature, they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Since the Vaipulya sutras are not included among the ninefold division of the scriptures, it does not say that the Buddha-nature exists.
Although the sutras do not mention it, one should know that it truly exists.
If one speaks thus, you should know that such a person is truly my disciple.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
