As stated above, that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature has never been heard of within the ninefold canon of scriptures. If it is as you say that they possess it, how is it that one does not commit a pārājika offense?”
The Buddha said, "Good son! As you have said,
in truth you have not committed a pārājika offense."
"Good son!
For example, if someone were to say that the great ocean contains only seven treasures and not eight, that person would be without fault.
Likewise, if someone were to say that the Buddha-nature does not exist within the ninefold canon of scriptures, they too would be without fault."

Why is this? Within the great ocean of wisdom of the Mahāyāna, I have taught that the Buddha-nature exists; since persons of the Two Vehicles do not know or see it, they say it does not exist, yet they commit no offense thereby.
Such a realm is known by the Buddhas and is not within the reach of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Good son!
If a person has not heard of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury, how could they know that the buddha-nature exists?
What is called the secret treasury?
It refers to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras. Good son!
There are various non-Buddhists who either claim that the self is eternal or claim that the self is annihilated.
The Tathāgata is not like this; he speaks both of the existence of a self and of the non-existence of a self—this is called the Middle Way.
If someone should say:

"The Buddha taught the Middle Way that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature; because it is shrouded by afflictions, they neither know nor see it. Therefore, one should diligently cultivate skillful means to sever and destroy these afflictions."
"If there be one who can speak in such a manner, it should be known that this person has not committed the four grave offenses.
If one cannot speak in such a manner, this is called committing a pārājika offense."
If someone were to say:
"I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For what reason?"
Because there is the Buddha-nature;
those who possess the Buddha-nature will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, I have now already achieved the realization of Bodhi.
"You should know that such a person is said to have committed a *pārājika* offense. Why is this?

Although they possess the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), because they have not cultivated the various skillful means (*upāya*) of goodness, they do not yet perceive it; and because they do not perceive it, they are unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Good son! For this reason, the Buddha-dharma is exceedingly profound and inconceivable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There was a king who asked: ‘How does a bhikṣu fall into the offense of claiming superhuman states?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:”
"If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of gain and offerings, and for the sake of food and drink, practices flattery, deceit, and fraud, thinking:
'How may the people of the world come to know for certain and truly that I am a mendicant? "
"By these causes and conditions, I have gained great gain, offerings, and fame.
Thus, because of his great ignorance, this bhikṣu constantly thinks throughout the long night:
"I have truly not yet attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; how can I cause the people of the world to say that I have already attained them?"
Furthermore, how should I act so that all the upāsakas and upāsikās will point to me and say:
"This person’s merit is such that he is truly a sage"?
Reflecting thus, he acts solely for the sake of seeking gain, not for the sake of seeking the Dharma.

Whether walking, coming, going, entering, or staying, he moves with composure; he carries his robes and bowl without losing his dignified demeanor. Sitting alone in a secluded place like an arhat, he causes people of the world to all say:
"This bhikṣu is most excellent and foremost; he is diligent in ascetic practice and cultivates the dharma of tranquility."
By these causes and conditions, I shall gain many disciples and followers;
people shall also provide me with abundant offerings, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, and many women will come to revere, remember, and hold me in high esteem.
"If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who commit such acts, they fall into the offense of claiming superhuman attainments (*uttari-manuṣya-dharma*).

Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who, desiring to establish the unsurpassed True Dharma, dwells in a secluded and tranquil place; though he is not an arhat, he wishes to cause others to say of him: 'He is an arhat,' 'He is a good bhikṣu,' 'He is a virtuous bhikṣu,' or 'He is a tranquil bhikṣu,' so that immeasurable people may give rise to faith."

"By these causes and conditions, I have obtained an immeasurable number of bhikṣus and others as my retinue; because of this, I am able to instruct precept-breaking bhikṣus and upāsakas so that they all uphold the precepts. Through these causes and conditions, I establish the True Dharma, glorify the unsurpassed great work of the Tathāgata, reveal and manifest the Mahāyāna teachings of the Vaipulya, and deliver all immeasurable sentient beings."
He well understands the meaning of the gravity and lightness of the sutras and vinayas taught by the Tathāgata.
He further said:

‘I too now possess the Buddha-nature; there is a sutra called the "Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata," and within this sutra, I shall certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood and be able to exhaust immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters.’

He extensively taught for the sake of immeasurable upāsakas, saying: "All of you possess the Buddha-nature; both I and you shall together abide in the stage of the Tathāgata's path, realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and exhaust immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters."
"One who speaks thus is not said to have fallen into the transgression of the superhuman dharmas (uttaramanuṣyadharma), but is called a bodhisattva. If it is said:

'One who commits a duṣkṛta offense shall fall into hell for eight million years by the reckoning of days, months, and years in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to undergo various retributions for their sins; how much more so for one who intentionally commits a sthūlātyaya offense?'"
"In this Mahāyāna, if there is a bhikṣu who commits a sthūlātyaya offense, one should not associate with him.
What is called a sthūlātyaya offense within the Mahāyāna sūtras?

If there is a householder who builds a Buddhist temple and offers various flower garlands as an offering to the Buddha, and a bhikṣu sees the thread running through the flowers and takes it without asking permission, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense; whether he knew [the owner] or not, he commits the offense in the same way.
If one destroys a Buddhist stūpa with a mind of greed, they commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense; such a person should not be associated with.

If a king or a high minister, seeing that a stūpa is dilapidated, wishes to repair it as an offering to the *śarīra*, and therein obtains precious treasures which he then entrusts to a bhikṣu, yet that bhikṣu, having received them, uses them at his own discretion—such a bhikṣu is called impure and frequently gives rise to strife; virtuous *upāsakas* should not associate with, make offerings to, or revere him.

Such a bhikṣu is called one without sexual organs, one with dual sexual organs, or one of indeterminate sexual organs. One of indeterminate sexual organs is a female when desiring a woman, and becomes a male when desiring a man; such a bhikṣu is called one of evil organs, neither male nor female, neither a renunciant nor a householder.
Thus, a bhikṣu should not associate with, make offerings to, or revere such persons.

Within the Buddha’s Dharma, the dharma of a śramaṇa is to give rise to a heart of compassion and nurture all sentient beings; even toward an ant, one should grant them fearlessness—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To abstain from drinking intoxicants, even to the extent of not smelling their fragrance, is the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
To refrain from false speech, even to the extent of not thinking of it in one's dreams, is the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Not giving rise to thoughts of desire even in dreams is likewise; this is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, does this constitute a violation of the precepts?
The Buddha said, "No."

One should conceive thoughts of foulness and impurity regarding sexual desire, not giving rise to even a single thought of purity; one must distance oneself from women and the afflictions of lustful attachment.
If one engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, one should feel remorse upon waking.
When a bhikṣu receives offerings while begging for alms, he should regard them as if eating the flesh of his own son during a time of famine; if lustful desire arises, he should swiftly abandon it.
Know that such a dharma-gate is a sūtra and vinaya taught by the Buddha.
If there are those who comply with what the Māra says, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can comply with what the Buddha says, they are called Bodhisattvas.
"If someone should say:

"The Buddha permits bhikṣus to constantly stand on one leg, remain silent and speechless, throw themselves into deep pools or leap into fires, cast themselves down from high cliffs without avoiding danger, consume poison or abstain from food, lie upon ashes and dust, bind their own hands and feet, kill living beings, and practice heterodox paths and incantations; he also permits those such as the sons of caṇḍālas, those without sexual organs, those with double organs, those with indeterminate organs, and those with incomplete physical faculties—all such persons to leave the household life and practice the Way."
This is called the teaching of Māra. [It claims:

"The Buddha first permitted the consumption of the five kinds of cow products, as well as oil, honey, *kauśeya* garments, leather sandals, and other such items; apart from these, if anyone were to say that he permitted the wearing of *mahālaṅkā* ornaments, or that the storage of all types of seeds was permitted, or that plants and the like possess life—having spoken thus, the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*."
"If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak in this way, you should know that they are the words of Māra.
I do not permit [monastics] to stand constantly on one foot; however, for the sake of the Dharma, I permit walking, standing, sitting, and lying down."

Furthermore, one must not permit the consumption of poison, fasting to death, scorching the body with five fires, binding the hands and feet, killing sentient beings, the practice of magical incantations, or making sandals from conch shells, ivory, or elephant tusks; nor the hoarding of seeds, nor [the harming of] plants and trees that possess life, nor wearing the Mahālaṅkāra.
If it is said that the World-Honored One has spoken thus, you should know that such a person belongs to the faction of the non-Buddhists and is not my disciple. [I have taught:

"I permit only the consumption of the five products of the cow, as well as oils, honey, and so forth; I permit the wearing of leather sandals and *kauśeya* silk garments; I teach that the four great elements possess no life-force."
"If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak in this way, these are called the Buddha’s teachings.
If there are those who accord with what the Buddha has spoken, you should know that they are truly my disciples."
If there are those who do not follow what the Buddha has taught, they are the retinue of Māra.
If there are those who accord with the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya, you should know that such persons are great bodhisattvas.
“Good son! I have now extensively proclaimed and analyzed for you the distinguishing characteristics between what is spoken by Māra and what is spoken by the Buddha.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is only now that I have come to know the distinguishing characteristics between the words of Māra and the words of the Buddha; by means of this, I have been able to enter into the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
that you are able to understand and discern in this way is called wisdom."
“Good son! That which is called ‘suffering’ is not designated as a Noble Truth. Why is this?
If one says that suffering is the Noble Truth of Suffering, then all oxen, sheep, donkeys, horses, and beings in the hells should also possess the Noble Truths. Good son!

Furthermore, if there are those who do not know the Tathāgata’s profound realm—the eternally abiding, unchanging, and subtle Dharma-body—and instead claim it is a body sustained by food rather than the Dharma-body, failing to recognize the Tathāgata’s spiritual power and majesty, this is called suffering.

Why is this? Because through ignorance, they perceive what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and what is non-Dharma as Dharma; it should be known that such persons will inevitably fall into the evil destinies, transmigrate through birth and death, increase their fetters, and undergo much suffering and affliction.

If there are those who can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change, or who hear the sound of the two characters "eternally abiding," even if it passes through their ears but once, they will immediately be reborn in the heavens; later, at the time of liberation, they will be able to realize and know for themselves that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Having realized this, he spoke these words:
"In the past, I heard this meaning, but it was only now, upon attaining liberation, that I have realized it.
Because I did not know it regarding the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), I have wandered through birth and death in an endless cycle."
"Only beginning from today do I attain true wisdom.

If one understands in this way, it is truly the cultivation of suffering, which brings great benefit; if one does not understand this, then even though one practices diligently, there is no benefit. This is called knowing suffering; it is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
If a person cannot practice in this way, it is called suffering, not the Noble Truth of Suffering. Regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering:
it is the failure to give rise to true wisdom within the True Dharma, and the acceptance of impure things, namely slaves and servants.
They are able to declare what is contrary to the Dharma to be the True Dharma, thereby destroying the True Dharma and not allowing it to endure for long.

For this reason, they do not know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because they do not know it, they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing much suffering and affliction, and fail to attain rebirth in heaven or true liberation.
If there are those with profound wisdom who do not destroy the true Dharma, by these causes and conditions they will attain rebirth in the heavens and achieve right liberation.
If there are those who do not understand the truths of suffering and its origin, and claim that the true Dharma has no permanence and is entirely subject to extinction;
by these causes and conditions, they will transmigrate through birth and death for immeasurable kalpas, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
If one can know that phenomena are eternally abiding and unchanging, this is called knowing the origin; it is called the Noble Truth of the Origin.
If a person cannot practice in this way, this is merely called the origin, but not the Noble Truth of the Origin.
"Regarding the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering: if one extensively practices and studies the dharma of emptiness, this is unwholesome. Why?
Because it extinguishes all dharmas and destroys the Tathāgata’s true treasury of Dharma."
To practice and study in this manner is called cultivating emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As for cultivating the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha*), it stands in opposition to all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

If one were to say that cultivating emptiness constitutes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), then since all non-Buddhists also cultivate the dharma of emptiness, they too should possess the Truth of Cessation.
If there is one who says:

"There is a Tathāgatagarbha which, though invisible, can be entered once all afflictions have been extinguished; if one gives rise to this mind for even a single thought-moment as a causal condition, one will attain mastery over all dharmas."

"If there are those who cultivate the Tathāgata’s secret treasury—the selflessness, emptiness, and quiescence—such persons shall, for immeasurable eons, transmigrate through birth and death within saṃsāra and undergo suffering."
If there are those who do not practice in this way, even though they possess afflictions, they are able to extinguish them quickly. Why is this?
Because they know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
This is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
If one can practice cessation in this manner, such a person is my disciple.
If there is one who cannot practice in this way, it is called the cultivation of emptiness, not the Noble Truth of Cessation.
"The Noble Truth of the Path refers to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as right liberation.
There are sentient beings with perverted minds who say:
'There is no Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, or right liberation; the cycle of birth and death is merely like an illusion.'"
Cultivating such views, by these causes and conditions, one transmigrates through the three realms of existence and undergoes great suffering for a long time.
If one can resolve to see that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, then the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and liberation are likewise so.
Riding upon this single thought, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, one attains the fruits of mastery according to one's wish. Why is this?

Because in the past, due to the four inversions, I took what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma and underwent the retribution of immeasurable evil karma; now that I have extinguished such views, I have attained the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.
This is called the Noble Truth of the Path.
If there is someone who says that the Three Jewels are impermanent and cultivates this view, it is a false cultivation and not the Noble Truth of the Path.
If one cultivates this Dharma and abides therein permanently, such a person is my disciple.
Truly seeing and practicing the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is what is called the Four Noble Truths.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is only now that I have come to know how to cultivate the profound Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! Regarding the four inversions:
to conceive the notion of suffering within that which is not suffering is called an inversion."
That which is not suffering is called the Tathāgata; to conceive the notion of suffering regarding him is to regard the Tathāgata as impermanent and subject to change.
To say that the Tathāgata is impermanent is termed a great sinful suffering.

If one says that the Tathāgata abandons this body of suffering and enters nirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted, this is called conceiving the notion of suffering where there is no suffering; this is called a perversion.

"If I were to say that the Tathāgata is eternal, that would be the view of a self; because of the view of a self, there are immeasurable faults. Therefore, one should say that the Tathāgata is impermanent; by speaking thus, I shall experience happiness."
If the Tathāgata were impermanent, he would be suffering; if he were suffering, how could there be happiness?
Because one conceives the notion of happiness within what is suffering, it is called a perversion.
To conceive the notion of suffering regarding that which is pleasant is called a perversion.
That which is pleasant is the Tathāgata; that which is suffering is the impermanence of the Tathāgata.
If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent, this is called conceiving the notion of suffering within what is pleasant.
The Tathāgata abides eternally; this is called bliss.
"If I were to say that the Tathāgata is eternal, how could he then enter into nirvāṇa?"
"If it is said that the Tathāgata is not suffering, why does he relinquish his body and enter parinirvāṇa?
Because one perceives suffering within pleasure, this is called a perversion;
this is known as the first perversion.
"To perceive the impermanent as permanent, and the permanent as impermanent, is called inversion.
That which is impermanent is called the non-cultivation of emptiness; because one does not cultivate emptiness, one's lifespan is short."
If anyone says that one can attain long life without cultivating emptiness and stillness, this is called a perversion; this is called the second perversion.
To perceive "self" where there is no self, or to perceive "no-self" where there is a self—this is called perversion.
People of the world also speak of a self;
within the Buddha-dharma, one also speaks of a self.
Although people of the world speak of a self, they do not possess the Buddha-nature.
This is called giving rise to the notion of a self within that which is selfless; this is termed a perversion.
In the Buddha-dharma, the existence of a self is precisely the Buddha-nature;
when people of the world say that the Buddha-dharma is selfless, this is called giving rise to the notion of non-self within what is a self.

If one says that the Buddha-dharma is definitively without self, and therefore claims that the Tathāgata’s exhortation to his disciples to cultivate non-self is called "perverted," this is known as the third perversion.
"To perceive the pure as impure and the impure as pure is called perversion.
That which is pure is the Tathāgata, who is eternally abiding; he is not a body sustained by various foods, nor a body of afflictions, nor a physical body, nor a body bound by sinews and bones."
If there should be one who says:
"The Tathāgata is impermanent; he is a body sustained by mixed food, even a body bound together by sinews and bones.
The Dharma, the Saṅgha, and liberation are things that perish."
This is called perversion. Regarding the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure:

if someone were to say, "Within this body of mine, there is not a single dharma that is impure; because there is no impurity, I shall certainly attain entry into the state of purity," [this is perversion].
'The Tathāgata’s teaching on the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity—such words are a false teaching.
This is called perversion; this is what is known as the fourth perversion.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I have finally attained right view.”
World-Honored One!
Prior to this, we were all called people of wrong views.
World-Honored One!
"In the twenty-five states of existence, is there a self?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
The term "I" (ātman) is the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha.
That all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is the meaning of "I.
This meaning of "I" has, from the very beginning, been constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions; for this reason, sentient beings are unable to perceive it.
"Good son!
It is like a poor woman whose house contains a great store of pure gold, yet none of her family members, whether young or old, know of it.
At that time, there was a certain person who was skilled in expedient means, and he said to the poor woman:"
"I now hire you; you may weed and clear away the weeds and filth for me.
The woman immediately replied, "I cannot do so.
If you can show me the place where my son's gold treasure is hidden, only then will I quickly work for you."
The man spoke again, saying,
"I know the skillful means to show you your son.
The woman replied:
"My family members, both great and small, do not even know this themselves;
how could you possibly know it? The man replied again, "I am now truly able."
The woman replied, "I also wish to see it; you may show it to me as well.
The man immediately dug up a storehouse of genuine gold within her house.
Upon seeing this, the woman felt great joy in her heart; she conceived a sense of wonder and came to revere that person.
"Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: all sentient beings are unable to see it, just as that poor man did not know of the treasure."
"Good son!

I now universally demonstrate that the buddha-nature possessed by all sentient beings is shrouded and obscured by various afflictions, just as that poor man cannot see the treasury of genuine gold he possesses."

Today, the Tathāgata universally reveals to all sentient beings the treasure-trove of all-enlightenment, namely the Buddha-nature; having seen this matter, sentient beings give rise to joy in their hearts and take refuge in and look up to the Tathāgata.
The one possessed of skillful means is the Tathāgata; the impoverished woman represents all immeasurable sentient beings; and the treasury of true gold is the Buddha-nature.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a woman who gives birth to a son; when the infant falls ill, the mother becomes distressed and seeks out a physician."
Once the physician had arrived, he prepared a compound of three ingredients—ghee, milk, and rock honey—and gave it to him to drink.
He then instructed the woman:
"After the child has taken the medicine, do not give him milk for the time being; only when the medicine has been digested should you give it to him."
At that time, the woman immediately smeared bitter substances upon her breasts and said to her son:
"My breasts have been smeared with poison; you must not touch them again."
The child, parched with thirst and desiring his mother’s milk, heard the poisonous odor of the milk and fled far away.
When the medicine had finally worn off, the mother washed her breasts clean with water and called to her son,
saying, “Come, I will give you milk.”
At that time, although the child was hungry and thirsty, he did not come because he had previously smelled the odor of poison.
His mother spoke to him again, saying:

"I smeared it with poison only for the sake of administering medicine to you; now that the medicine has been digested and I have finished washing it off, you may come and drink milk without any harm."
Having heard this, the child gradually returned to drinking.
Son of good family!

The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of delivering all beings, he teaches sentient beings to cultivate the dharma of non-self. Having cultivated it thus, they forever sever the mind of self and enter nirvāṇa, in order to eliminate all false views in the world and to manifest that which transcends worldly dharmas.

Furthermore, it is shown that the worldly conception of a self is false and not real; therefore, one cultivates the dharma of non-self to purify the body. This is illustrated by the analogy of a woman who, for the sake of her child, applies a bitter substance to her breast.
The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of cultivating emptiness, he declares that all phenomena are entirely devoid of self.
This is like that woman who, having thoroughly washed her breasts, calls to her child, desiring that he return to suckle.

I am now likewise; I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, and for this reason, monks, you should not give rise to fear, just as that young child, having heard his mother’s call, gradually returned to drink milk.
"The bhikṣu is likewise; he should discern for himself that the Tathāgata’s secret treasury must necessarily exist.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
In reality, there is no self.
Why is this? Because at the time of birth, an infant possesses no knowledge or awareness.
If there were a self, it should possess cognition immediately upon birth;
for this reason, one knows with certainty that there is no self.
If there were definitively a self, then after having taken birth, it should never perish.

If all beings possessed Buddha-nature that is permanent and eternal, it should be devoid of any characteristic of decay; if there were no characteristic of decay, how could there be distinctions such as Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Śūdra, Caṇḍāla, or even animals?

Now we observe that karmic conditions vary in manifold ways and the various realms of existence differ from one another; if there were a fixed self, all sentient beings would be without distinction of superiority or inferiority.
For this reason, it is certain that the Buddha-nature is not a permanent phenomenon.

If you say that the Buddha-nature is definitively eternal, for what reason do you further speak of the existence of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, frivolous talk, greed, anger, and wrong views?
If the nature of the self were permanent, why would one become confused, dazed, and disordered after drinking alcohol?
If the nature of the self were permanent, the blind should see forms, the deaf should hear sounds, the mute should be able to speak, and the lame should be able to walk.
If the nature of the self were permanent, one should not avoid fire pits, great waters, poisons, swords, or wicked people and beasts.
If the self were permanent, one should not forget the things previously experienced; if there were no forgetting, for what reason would one later say, "Where did I see such a person before?"
If the self were permanent, there should be no such things as decline or flourishing, nor the physical strength of youth, middle age, or old age, nor the recollection of past events.
If the self were permanent, where would it abide?
Does it reside within the tears, saliva, or the various colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white?
If the self were permanent, it should pervade the entire body like sesame oil, with no empty space between.
"If the body were severed, the self would also be severed.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."

For example, suppose there were a great athlete in a royal household who had a diamond jewel between his eyebrows. While competing with another athlete in a wrestling match, that opponent struck him on the forehead with his head; the jewel immediately sank into his skin, and he was entirely unaware of where it was located.
There was a sore at that spot, so he summoned a skilled physician to treat it himself.

At that time, there was a brilliant physician who was well-versed in prescriptions and medicines; he immediately recognized that the sore was caused by a jewel having entered his body, and that once the jewel had entered the skin, it remained lodged there.
At that time, the skilled physician immediately asked the wrestler,
"Where is the jewel upon your forehead?
The wrestler replied in alarm:
"Great Master, King of Physicians, has the jewel upon my forehead not vanished?
Where is this jewel now?
Could it be some kind of illusion?"
He grieved and wept.
At that time, the skilled physician consoled the wrestler, saying:

"You should not give rise to such great sorrow and suffering now. When you were fighting, a precious jewel entered your body; it is currently within your skin, its reflection appearing on the outside."
"When you were fighting, the poison of your anger was so intense that the pearl sank into your flesh; therefore, you did not realize it yourself.
At that time, the wrestler did not believe the physician's words:
"If it were inside the skin, how could the impurities of pus and blood not come out?"
"If it were inside the sinews, it should not be visible.
Why do you now deceive me?
At that time, the physician took up a mirror and shone it upon his face; the pearl appeared clearly and distinctly within the mirror.
Upon seeing this, the Mallas were struck with wonder and gave rise to thoughts of extraordinary marvel. "Good son, it is the same for all sentient beings:

because they cannot draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), although they possess the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), they are unable to see it. Being shrouded and obscured by greed, hatred, and delusion, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras; or among the *caṇḍālas*, *kṣatriyas*, *brāhmaṇas*, *vaiśyas*, and *śūdras*. Born into such various families, due to the karmic conditions arising from their own minds, even though they receive a human body, they may be deaf, blind, mute, crippled, or lame. Undergoing these various retributions within the twenty-five states of existence, their minds are covered by greed, hatred, and delusion, and thus they do not know the Buddha-nature."
It is like that strongman who had a precious jewel upon his person, yet claimed it was lost.

Sentient beings are likewise; because they do not know how to draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they fail to recognize the subtle and secret treasure-store of the Tathāgata. Their cultivation and study of non-self is comparable to that of one who is not a noble one (ārya).
Although it is taught that there is a self, they do not know the true nature of the self.

My disciples are likewise; because they do not know how to draw near to virtuous friends, they practice the study of non-self yet do not know the locus of non-self. If they do not even know the true nature of non-self, how much less could they know the true nature of the self?
"Good son!
In this way, the Tathāgata declares that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, just as a skilled physician shows a powerful man the diamond-jewel."

These sentient beings are shrouded and obscured by immeasurable billions of afflictions and the like, and thus do not recognize their Buddha-nature; yet when their afflictions are exhausted, they will then attain clear realization and knowledge, just as that strongman saw his precious jewel within a bright mirror.
"Good son! The Tathāgata’s secret treasury is thus immeasurable and inconceivable.
Furthermore, good son!"
For example, on the Snowy Mountains there is a medicinal herb of a single flavor called "Taste of Bliss.
Its flavor is extremely sweet, yet it lies beneath deep thickets where no one can see it.
If someone smells its fragrance, they immediately know that this medicine must be present at that spot.

In a past age, there was a wheel-turning monarch who, for the sake of this medicine, constructed wooden conduits here and there throughout these Snowy Mountains to receive it. When the medicine ripened, it flowed from the earth and collected within the wooden conduits, its flavor being perfectly authentic.

Once the king has passed away, this medicine—whether sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, or bland—though being of a single flavor, manifests various differences according to where it flows; yet the true essence of this medicine remains in the mountain, like the full moon.
Ordinary people of meager merit, though they apply effort and undergo hardship by digging with pickaxes, are unable to obtain it.
Yet, when a holy king appears in the world, by virtue of his karmic conditions of merit, he immediately obtains the true flavor of this medicine.
"Good son!
The secret treasury of the Tathāgata is likewise in its flavor; though it is covered by the thickets of all afflictions, sentient beings of ignorance are unable to see it."

The single flavor is like the Buddha-nature; because of afflictions, it produces various flavors, namely those of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, devas, and humans; males, females, and those who are neither male nor female; kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.

The Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce, difficult to obstruct or destroy; therefore, there is no one capable of killing it. If there were someone who could kill it, that would mean severing the Buddha-nature, yet such a Buddha-nature can never be severed. It is impossible for this nature to be severed.

That which is the nature of the self is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. This secret treasury cannot be obstructed, destroyed, or consumed by anything; though it is indestructible, it is invisible, and can only be realized and known upon the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, there is no one who can kill it.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there were no killer, there should likewise be no unwholesome karma.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There truly is the taking of life. Why is this?"

"Good son! The Buddha-nature of sentient beings dwells within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If one destroys these five aggregates, it is called 'taking life. If one takes life, one immediately falls into the evil realms. Due to the causes and conditions of karma, there arise the distinctions of the twenty-five states of existence—such as the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and Caṇḍālas; whether male, female, or neither male nor female—as they transmigrate through birth and death."

Non-noble persons recklessly conceptualize various marks of the self—such as being the size of a weed seed, or like rice, beans, or even the thumb—thus giving rise to all manner of false imaginings; yet these thoughts of false imagination possess no reality whatsoever.
The supramundane mark of self is called the Buddha-nature; to conceive of the self in this way is called the most excellent.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a person who knows well of a hidden treasure and takes a sharp pickaxe to dig straight down into the earth; he passes through bedrock, sand, and gravel without difficulty, yet when he reaches the diamond layer, he cannot pierce it."
Now, as for the diamond, no swords or axes can destroy it.
Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; it cannot be destroyed by any disputants, nor by Māra Pāpīyān, nor by any humans or devas.
The characteristics of the five aggregates are those of conditioned arising; the characteristics of conditioned arising are like stone or sand, which can be pierced and destroyed.
Buddhahood, however, is likened to a diamond, which cannot be obstructed or destroyed.
For this reason, the destruction of the five aggregates is called "killing.
Good son! You must certainly know that the Buddha-dharma is thus inconceivable.

Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seven: “Lying upon ashes or soil; throwing oneself from high cliffs; leaping into deep abysses or rushing into fire; scorching the body with the five heats; lying upon thorns; winnowing chaff and drinking its liquid; ingesting poison or fasting; killing sentient beings; playing with lions for sport; and practicing incantations and magical arts.”
Those of the Caṇḍāla caste, those with dual sexual organs, those without sexual organs, and those whose dual organs are conjoined—all are permitted to enter the Path.
They must renounce the five kinds of tastes: milk, curd, whey, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, honey, and so forth.
Hearing that even silk and brocade were considered to have life, [he realized that] all grains, plants, and trees likewise possess a lifespan.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha entered nirvana.
"Such a teaching is the teaching of Māra.
If one says:

'The Tathāgata does not permit bhikṣus to constantly stand on one leg, to remain silent and motionless, to lie upon ashes or dust, to throw themselves from high cliffs, to leap into deep abysses or rush into fires, to scorch their bodies with the five heats, to lie upon thorns, to rinse husks and drink their liquid, to consume poison or fast, to kill living beings, to play with lions for sport, or to practice incantations and occult arts.'"
Those of the Caṇḍāla caste, those with dual sexual organs, those without sexual organs, and those whose dual organs are joined are not permitted to enter the Path.
They are permitted to consume five kinds of food: milk, curd, whey, ghee, oil, and honey.
One must not listen to, accept, or wear garments of silk or brocade, regarding the carriage as a burden.
Grains, rice, grasses, and trees have no life-principle and no self; they do not belong to the category of sentient beings.
"If there are those who can speak in this manner, they are my disciples.
If they cannot, you should know that they are disciples of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Such sūtras and vinayas are what was spoken by the Buddha."
"If there are those who comply with what the Māra speaks, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can comply with what the Buddha speaks, they are called Bodhisattvas."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Nature of the Tathāgata, Part Five.
“Good son! The Vaipulya sutras are like ambrosia, yet they are also like poison.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata preach the Vaipulya sūtras as being like nectar and yet also like poison?
The Buddha said,
"Good son, do you now wish to know the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury?"
Kāśyapa replied,
“I now truly wish to understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Some may consume ambrosia and lose their lives through premature death;
others may consume ambrosia and attain long life.
Some may live by consuming poison; some, due to various conditions, die by consuming poison."
The nectar of unimpeded wisdom is what is called the Mahāyāna scriptures.
Yet these Mahāyāna scriptures are also called "mixed poisons," like clarified butter,
*ghṛta*, and the like, as well as various rock honeys.
When digested, it becomes medicine; when not digested, it becomes poison.
The Vaipulya sutras are likewise: to the wise, they are nectar;
but for the ignorant who do not know the Buddha-nature, consuming them results in poison.
For śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the Mahāyāna is the nectar;
just as among all flavors, milk is the foremost, so too,
by relying upon the Mahāyāna, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor.
Having attained nirvāṇa, they become elephant-kings among men.
Sentient beings who know the Buddha-nature are like Kāśyapa and others;
they possess the unsurpassed flavor of ambrosia, neither born nor dying.
Kāśyapa, you should now skillfully distinguish the three refuges;
the nature of these three refuges is precisely my own nature.
If one can observe with true discernment that within my nature there is the Buddha-nature, [one realizes it].
One should know that such a person has entered the secret treasury;
knowing "I" and "mine," this person has already transcended the world.
The nature of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is the unsurpassed, supreme honor.
"As I have spoken in these verses, such is the nature and meaning of this.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke again in verse:
"I do not know at all where one takes refuge in the Triple Gem."
How should one take refuge in that which is unsurpassed and fearless?
Not knowing the locus of the Three Jewels, how can one realize non-self?
How does one who takes refuge in the Buddha obtain consolation?
How does one take refuge in the Dharma?
I pray that you will explain this to me.
How does one attain mastery?
How is it that one is not independent?
How does one take refuge in the Saṅgha and thereby attain unsurpassed benefit?
What is the true teaching regarding the future attainment of the Buddha-way?
If the future is not yet established, how can one take refuge in the Triple Gem?
I have no foreknowledge now; I shall practice according to the successive stages.
How can one conceive the thought of having given birth to a son when one has not yet even conceived?
If one is certainly within the womb, then one is said to have a son;
if a son is within the womb, he will surely be born before long.
This is the meaning of "son," and the karma of sentient beings is likewise.
As the Buddha has taught, the foolish are unable to know;
because they do not know, they wander through the prison of birth and death,
merely bearing the provisional name of *upāsaka* while remaining ignorant of the true meaning.
I only pray that you will explain this in detail, severing the web of my doubts.
With the Tathāgata’s great wisdom, please condescend to distinguish it out of compassion;
I pray that you will speak of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
“Kāśyapa, you should know: I shall now, for your sake, skillfully expound the subtle and secret meaning so that your doubts may be severed.
Now listen with a sincere mind; regarding all bodhisattvas, you—”
Thus, one shares the same name as the seventh Buddha.
One who takes refuge in the Buddha is truly called an upāsaka;
such a person shall never again take refuge in other deities.
Those who take refuge in the Dharma abandon all killing;
those who take refuge in the noble Saṅgha seek no other paths.
By thus taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one attains fearlessness.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “I too take refuge in the Triple Gem;
this is called the true path, the realm of all Buddhas.
The equal nature of the Triple Gem is eternally possessed of the essence of great wisdom.”
My own nature and the Buddha-nature are non-dual and without distinction.
This path is praised by the Buddhas; it is the place of right progress and peaceful abiding.
It is also called "Right Universal Vision," and for this reason it is extolled by the Buddhas.
"I too shall proceed toward the unsurpassed path praised by the Sugata;
this is the supreme nectar, wherein all that exists is non-existent.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Good son! You should not now, like the śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings, differentiate the Three Jewels;
within this Mahāyāna, there is no characteristic of differentiation regarding the three refuges.”

Why is this so? Because within the Buddha-nature there already exist the Dharma and the Sangha; it is only for the sake of transforming and delivering śrāvakas and ordinary beings that one distinguishes and speaks of the different characteristics of the three refuges.
"Good son!
If one wishes to accord with worldly dharmas, then one should distinguish three refuges.
Good son!"
A bodhisattva should reflect in this way:

"I now take refuge in the Buddha with this very body; if I attain the path of Buddhahood with this very body, once I have become a Buddha, I shall not need to show reverence, prostrate, or make offerings to other World-Honored Ones."
Why is this? Because all Buddhas are equal, equally acting as a refuge for sentient beings.
If one wishes to honor the relics of the Dharma-body, one should pay homage to the stupas and temples of all Buddhas.
Why is this? It is because I desire to transform and deliver all sentient beings.

Furthermore, I cause sentient beings to conceive the notion of my body as a stupa or temple, so that they may pay homage and make offerings; in this way, these sentient beings take my Dharma-body as their place of refuge.
All sentient beings rely upon false and deceptive dharmas that are not true; I shall, in due order, preach the True Dharma for them.
Furthermore, for those who take refuge in a non-true Sangha, I shall act as their refuge in the True Sangha.
If there are those who differentiate among the three refuges, I shall act as a single place of refuge for them, without the distinction of three.
For the masses born blind, I shall act as their eyes; furthermore, I shall act as the true place of refuge for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Good son! In this way, such bodhisattvas perform the work of a Buddha for immeasurable evil sentient beings as well as for those who possess wisdom. Good son!”
For example, suppose there is a person who, when facing the enemy on the battlefield, immediately gives rise to this thought:
"I am the foremost among these; all the troops rely entirely upon me."
It is also like a prince who reflects thus:
"I shall subdue the other princes, succeed to the throne of the Great King, and attain sovereign power."
He causes all the princes to see him and take refuge; therefore, you should not give rise to an inferior mind.
As it is with the king and his princes, so it is with the great ministers, O son of good family!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, reflecting thus:
"In what way are these three things of one essence with me?
O son of good family!
The three things I have shown are themselves nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata is called the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara-puruṣa); for example, among the parts of a human body, the head is the most supreme, not the other limbs, hands, feet, or the like.

The Buddha is likewise the most supreme and exalted, not so the Dharma or the Sangha; yet, for the sake of transforming and delivering all the worlds, he manifests various distinct appearances, just like that ladder.
Therefore, you should not now uphold the distinctions of the three refuges as they are understood by ordinary, ignorant people.
Regarding the Mahāyāna, you should possess fierce and sharp decisiveness, like a tempered blade.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I ask because I know, not because I am ignorant.”

I am a bodhisattva of great courage and valor, who has questioned the stainless and pure sphere of conduct, desiring that the Tathāgata would extensively proclaim and analyze these extraordinary matters for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and extol the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, has now well expounded them; I, likewise, abide securely within them.
That which you have spoken of as the pure sphere of practice for bodhisattvas is precisely the proclamation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
World-Honored One!
I shall now also extensively proclaim such a secret treasury of the Tathāgata for the sake of sentient beings, and I shall also realize and know the true locus of the Three Refuges.
If there are sentient beings who can believe in such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, those individuals will naturally comprehend the three objects of refuge. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata’s secret treasury contains the Buddha-nature, those who proclaim this sutra all declare that the Buddha-nature exists entirely within their own bodies; such persons do not seek the objects of the Three Refuges from afar.

Why is this? Because in future ages, my own person shall achieve the Three Jewels; for this reason, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all other sentient beings will rely upon me, paying me respect and prostrating before me.
“Good son! For this reason, you should study the Mahāyāna sūtras correctly.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“The Buddha-nature is thus inconceivable; the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are likewise inconceivable.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Good son!
You have already accomplished profound and sharp wisdom; I shall now further explain for you well how to enter the Tathāgatagarbha.
If the self were to abide, it would be a permanent phenomenon and could not be separated from suffering."
If there were no self, the practice of pure conduct would be of no benefit.
To say that all phenomena are devoid of a self is the view of nihilism;
to say that the self abides is the view of eternalism.
If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, this is the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
if one says that all conditioned phenomena are permanent, this is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
If one says they are suffering (*duḥkha*), this is likewise the view of nihilism.
If one says that pleasure exists, this is again the view of eternalism.
To cultivate all phenomena as eternal is to fall into the view of nihilism; to cultivate all phenomena as annihilated is to fall into the view of eternalism.

Just as a centipede must rely on its front legs to move its hind legs, so it is with those who cultivate [the views of] eternalism and annihilationism; they too must rely on annihilationism and eternalism.
For this reason, the cultivation of other dharmas that result in suffering is called unwholesome, while the cultivation of other dharmas that result in happiness is called wholesome.
To cultivate the selflessness of other phenomena is a portion of the afflictions;
to cultivate the permanence of other phenomena is called the Tathāgata-garbha, namely nirvāṇa, which has no dwelling place.
To cultivate other impermanent dharmas refers to material wealth;
to cultivate other permanent dharmas refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and right liberation.
One should know that such a Middle Way of the Buddha’s Dharma speaks the true Dharma by remaining far removed from the two extremes.
Ordinary people and fools have no doubt regarding this; it is like a weak and sickly person who, after consuming ghee, finds his strength restored and his body light and agile.
The nature of existence and non-existence is not fixed, just as the four great elements differ in their natures and are mutually opposed.
A skilled physician knows well how to adjust his treatment according to the specific manifestation of a disorder.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata is likewise;

like a skilled physician toward all sentient beings, he understands the distinct characteristics and natures of their various afflictions and eliminates them for them, revealing the secret treasury of the Tathāgata—the pure Buddha-nature that is eternally abiding and unchanging.
If one says it exists, wisdom should not be defiled;
if one says it does not exist, that is false speech.

If one says it exists, one should not remain silent, nor should one engage in frivolous discourse or contention; rather, one should seek only to understand the true nature of all phenomena. Ordinary people engage in frivolous discourse and contention because they do not understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.

If one speaks of suffering, the foolish person concludes that the body is impermanent; yet when it is said that all is suffering, they still fail to understand that the body possesses a nature of bliss.
If one speaks of impermanence, the ordinary person reckons that the entire body is impermanent, like an unbaked clay pot;
however, a person of wisdom should exercise discernment and not assert that everything is entirely impermanent.
Why is this? Because my own body possesses the seed of Buddha-nature.
If one were to say that there is no self, ordinary people would claim that all Buddha-dharmas are entirely devoid of a self.
The wise should discern that "self" is a mere provisional designation and lacks substantial reality.
Having understood this, they should not give rise to doubt.
If it is said that the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is empty and quiescent, ordinary people, upon hearing this, will give rise to the view of annihilationism.
A person of wisdom should discern that the Tathāgata is eternal and undergoes no change.
If one were to say that liberation is like an illusion or a magical transformation, ordinary people would claim that one who attains liberation is simply annihilated;
however, a person of wisdom should discern that although the Lion among Men appears to come and go, he dwells eternally without change.

If it is said that ignorance is the causal condition for volitional formations, ordinary people, upon hearing this, engage in conceptual discrimination and give rise to the notion of two distinct dharmas: clarity and ignorance.
The wise, however, thoroughly comprehend that their nature is non-dual; this non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
If it is said that consciousness arises with conditioned phenomena as its cause and condition, ordinary people perceive these two—conditioned phenomena and consciousness—as distinct;
the wise, however, realize that their nature is non-dual, and this non-dual nature is the true nature.

If one speaks of the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome deeds, what may be done and what may not be done, the paths of goodness and evil, or white dharmas and black dharmas, ordinary people regard these as dualities;
yet the wise, having attained thorough understanding, realize that their nature is non-dual, and this non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
If it is said that one should cultivate the realization that all dharmas are suffering, ordinary people perceive this as duality;
the wise, however, thoroughly comprehend that their nature is non-dual, and this non-dual nature is the true nature.
If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, then the Tathāgata’s secret treasury would also be impermanent;
the ordinary person perceives these as two, but the wise understand that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is precisely the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If one says that all dharmas are selfless and that the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is likewise without a self, the ordinary person perceives these as two;
the wise, however, thoroughly understand that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is the true nature; thus, the natures of "self" and "selflessness" are not two.

The meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is thus: it is beyond calculation, praised by immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, and I have now fully explained all these accomplished virtues within this sutra.
“Good son! Self and the nature and characteristics of non-self are non-dual; you should accept and uphold this as such, wearing it upon your crown. Good son!”

You, too, should firmly uphold and keep in mind such a sutra as this, just as I previously taught in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra that "self" and "non-self" do not possess two distinct characteristics.

Just as curds are produced from milk, fresh butter is obtained from curds, clarified butter is obtained from fresh butter, and the finest cream (sarpis) is obtained from clarified butter—does the nature of these curds arise from the milk?
Does it arise from itself, or does it arise from another?
This applies even up to the stage of clarified butter (*sarpis*); if it were produced from another, then it would be the work of that other and not produced from milk.
If it were not produced from milk, the milk would have no function;
if it were produced spontaneously, it should not arise as a similar succession.
If it arises as a succession, then it does not arise simultaneously; if it does not arise simultaneously, then the five kinds of flavors would not exist at one time.

Although they do not arise simultaneously, it is certain that they do not come from elsewhere; one should know that the characteristic of curd already exists within the milk, but because the sweet flavor is predominant, it cannot transform itself, and this remains true up to the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta).

Due to the causes and conditions of the cow consuming water and grass, its blood and vital essence undergo transformation and become milk; if it eats sweet grass, its milk will be sweet, and if it eats bitter grass, the milk will have a bitter taste.

On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Fatty"; if a cow eats it, she produces only pure *sarpis* (clarified butter). Although there are no causal conditions such as green, yellow, red, white, or black grains and grasses, her milk nevertheless possesses variations in color and flavor.

These sentient beings, due to the causal conditions of the karma of clarity and ignorance, give rise to two characteristics. If ignorance is transformed, it becomes clarity; likewise, all phenomena—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise—are also thus devoid of dual characteristics.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the Buddha has said—that there is curd within milk—what is the meaning of this?”
World-Honored One!
If it is said that the characteristic of curd definitely exists within milk, yet is invisible because it is subtle, how can you say that curd is produced from the causes and conditions of milk?
If a phenomenon were originally non-existent, it would be called "arising. If it already existed, how could one speak of its arising?
If you say that the characteristic of curd definitely exists within milk, then there should also be milk within the hundred grasses, and likewise, there should be grass within the milk.
If you say that curd definitely does not exist within milk, how then can curd be produced by means of milk?
"If a phenomenon is originally non-existent and only arises later, why is it that grass does not grow from within milk?
"Good son! One cannot definitively say that curd exists within milk, nor can one say that curd does not exist within milk; furthermore, it cannot be said that it arises from something else."
If one were to say that curd definitely exists within milk, how could it be that their substance and flavor are each distinct?
Therefore, one cannot say that the nature of curd definitely exists within milk.
If one were to say that there is definitely no curd within milk, why does rabbit horn not also arise from within milk?
Furthermore, if poison is placed within milk, the resulting curd will kill a person; therefore, one cannot say that the nature of curd definitely does not exist within milk.
If one says that this curd is produced from something else, why is it not produced in water?
Therefore, one cannot say that curd is produced from something else. Good son!
Due to the condition of the cow consuming grass, its blood turns white; once the grass and blood have ceased [as such], the merit-power of sentient beings transforms it into milk.
Although this milk emerges from grass and blood, one cannot say they are two distinct things; it can only be called that which arises from causes and conditions.
From curd to clarified butter (ghṛta), it is likewise so; for this reason, it is called "the taste of cow.
Once this milk has ceased, it becomes curd through causes and conditions.
What are these causes and conditions?
Whether it be sourness or warmth, for this reason it is said that things exist through causes and conditions.
This applies even up to clarified butter (*ghṛta*); therefore, one cannot definitively say that the characteristic of curd does not exist within milk.
That which arises from another exists apart from milk; such a thing is impossible.
Good son, it is the same with clarity and ignorance: if they coexist with afflictions and various fetters, they are called ignorance.
If one is conjoined with all wholesome dharmas, it is called "clarity.
Therefore, I say that there are no two distinct characteristics.
For this reason, I previously stated: "On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Fatty,' and if a cow eats it, it immediately produces ghee; the Buddha-nature is also like this."
“Good son! Sentient beings of meager merit do not see these grasses.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; because it is shrouded by afflictions, sentient beings do not see it.”
For example, although the great ocean is uniformly salty, within it there is also water of the highest excellence, its flavor like milk.
It is like the Snowy Mountains: although they possess various merits and produce many medicinal herbs, they also contain poisonous weeds.
The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise thus: although they contain the four great poisonous snakes, within them there is also a sovereign great medicine, namely, the Buddha-nature.

It is not something produced by artificial means; it is merely covered by the adventitious dust of afflictions. Whether one is a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, if they can sever and eliminate these, they will immediately see the Buddha-nature and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
For example, when thunder rolls in the void and clouds arise, flowers bloom upon all the elephant tusks; yet if there were no thunder, the flowers would not grow, nor would they even have a name.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise thus: it is constantly shrouded by all manner of afflictions and cannot be seen; for this reason, I say that sentient beings have no self.
However, if they hear this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they will then see their buddha-nature.
It is like the flower on an elephant tusk: although one may hear all the samādhis of the sūtras, if one does not hear this sūtra, one will not know the subtle and wondrous marks of the Tathāgata;
just as when there is no thunder, the flower upon the elephant tusk cannot be seen.
Having heard this sutra, one immediately understands the secret treasury of the Buddha-nature as taught by all Tathāgatas;
it is like seeing the flower on an elephant tusk when a celestial thunderclap resounds.

Having heard this sutra, one immediately knows that all immeasurable sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. For this reason, the Great Nirvana is called the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, which increases the Dharma-body, just like the flowers upon an elephant tusk during a thunderstorm.
Because it is able to nurture such great meaning, it is named the Great Parinirvāṇa.

If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to study this subtle and wondrous scripture of the Great Parinirvāṇa, you should know that these people are able to repay the Buddha’s kindness and are true disciples of the Buddha.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
That which is called ‘Buddha-nature’ is most profound and most profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to enter, such that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot master it.”
The Buddha said, "Good son! So it is, so it is."
"What you have praised does not contradict what I have taught.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“Buddha-nature— why is it so profound, difficult to see, and difficult to enter?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
It is like a hundred blind people who, for the sake of curing their eyesight, go to a skilled physician.
At that time, the skilled physician uses a golden lancet to incise the film over their eyes.
Pointing with one finger, he asked,
"Do you see it?
The blind man replied:
"I have not yet seen it.
He pointed with two fingers and then three fingers, saying,
"I see it slightly."
"Good son! It is the same with this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra:
before the Tathāgata has yet spoken it, even though immeasurable bodhisattvas have fully practiced all the pāramitās up to the tenth stage (bhūmi), they are still unable to see their buddha-nature."
As soon as the Tathāgata had spoken, they were able to see him slightly.
Having seen him, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all said:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!"
"We have wandered through immeasurable births and deaths, constantly deluded and distracted by the notion of non-self. "Good son!
If even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten bhūmis cannot yet clearly perceive or see the Buddha-nature, how much less can Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas be able to see it?"
Furthermore, good son!
It is like looking up at geese and swans in the sky:
are they the sky, or are they the geese and swans?
By contemplating this repeatedly and intently, one perceives it with a semblance of clarity.

It is just so with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, who know and see but a small portion of the Tathāgata-nature; how much less, then, could those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles possibly know or see it?
"Good son! It is like a drunken man who, wishing to travel a long road, sees the path only dimly.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, in their knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata-nature, are just like this, perceiving only a small portion."
"Good son!

It is like a thirsty person traveling through a vast wilderness. Pressed by thirst, that person searches everywhere for water and sees a grove of trees with white cranes perched upon them. Confused and distressed, he cannot distinguish whether it is a tree or water. Only after observing it intently and without ceasing does he finally see the white cranes and the grove of trees."
"Good son!
It is likewise with the bodhisattvas of the ten stages who know and see only a small portion of the Tathāgata-nature.
Good son!"
For example, suppose there is a person who, while at sea many hundreds of thousands of yojanas away, sees from afar a great ship with its masts, galleries, and pavilions, and thinks to himself:
"Is that a gallery?"
"Is this empty space?
After gazing for a long time, he develops a mind of certainty and knows it to be a watchtower.
It is just the same when a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes perceives the Tathāgata-nature within his own body.
Good son! It is like a prince whose body is extremely delicate and weak; after sporting all night long, when the clear dawn arrives, his vision is unable to perceive anything with clarity.
Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies, they likewise do not see it with great clarity.

Furthermore, good son, it is like a minister or official detained by royal business who returns home at nightfall; when a flash of lightning momentarily breaks through, he sees a herd of cattle and immediately thinks:
"Is this a cow, or a house made of gathered clouds?
Though the person gazes for a long time and conceives the notion that it is a cow, he still does not perceive it with certainty.
It is likewise with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes; although they perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies, they have not yet attained definitive certainty.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a bhikṣu who observes water free of insects but perceives the appearance of insects, and immediately thinks:
"Is that which moves here a worm, or is it dust?
He gazed at it for a long time without ceasing; although he knew it was dust, he could not perceive it with complete clarity.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies, yet even so, they do not see it with great clarity.
Furthermore, good son,
it is like a person who, in deep darkness, sees a small child from afar and immediately thinks:
"Is that a cow, a vulture, a bird, or a human?
Though he observed it for a long time without ceasing, even though he saw a child, he did not perceive it clearly.
A Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes who perceives the Tathāgata-nature within his own body is likewise not very clear in his perception.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who, in the darkness of night, sees a painted image of a bodhisattva and immediately thinks:
"Is this an image of a bodhisattva, an image of Maheśvara, an image of Mahābrahmā, or one dressed in dyed robes?"
That person, having observed it for a long time, although they mentally believe it to be an image of a bodhisattva, does not perceive it clearly.
Likewise, even a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage perceives the Tathāgata-nature within their own body, yet does not perceive it with great clarity.
"Good son!
The Buddha-nature is thus profoundly deep, difficult to know or see; only a Buddha can know it, for it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"Good son!
A wise person should make such distinctions to know the nature of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Buddha-nature is thus subtle and difficult to know, how can it be seen with the fleshly eye?
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! Son of good family!
Just as that realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception cannot be known by those of the Two Vehicles, it is known through faith in accordance with the sūtras.”
"Good son!
It is likewise for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, having faith and compliance with this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, realize that their own bodies possess the Tathāgata-nature."
"Good son! For this reason, you should diligently practice and cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Good son!"
"Such a Buddha-nature can only be known by a Buddha; it is not within the reach of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Ordinary worldlings who are not noble ones possess the nature of sentient beings and all say that there is a self.
The Buddha said:
"Suppose, for example, there are two people who are close friends; one is a prince and the other is poor and lowly, and these two men travel back and forth together."
At that time, the poor man saw that the prince possessed a fine sword, the most pure and exquisite of all, and his heart became greedily attached to it.
Later, the prince took hold of this sword and fled to another country.
Thereupon, the poor man later went to stay overnight at another's house; while asleep, he muttered incoherently as if speaking of knives.
A bystander who heard this took him to the king.
Then the king asked,
"As for this 'sword' you speak of, where was it obtained?
The man answered the king in full detail regarding the aforementioned matter.
"Your Majesty, even if you were now to butcher my body, dismembering my hands and feet, and sought to obtain a blade from me, it truly could not be found.
I have long been close and intimate with the prince; though I once saw him in his former dwelling, I did not even dare to touch him with my hand, much less intentionally take [a blade] from him."
The king asked again:
"When you saw the sword, what was its appearance like?
He replied:
"Great King! What I have seen is like the horn of a billy goat.
Having heard this, the king smiled joyfully and said:
"Go now wherever you wish; do not give rise to sorrow or fear. There is no such knife in my treasury, much less could you have seen it from the Prince."
At that time, the king immediately asked his ministers,
"Have you ever seen such a sword before?
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
He then installed another son to succeed him on the throne and asked his ministers:
"Have you ever seen this sword within the royal treasury?
The ministers replied:
"We have seen them before," they replied.
He questioned them again, saying,
"What was their appearance like?"
He replied: "Great King!
It is like the horn of a billy goat."
The king said,
"In my official treasury, where could there possibly be a sword with such characteristics?
Subsequently, all four kings conducted thorough inspections and searches, but they could not find it.
After some time had passed, the prince who had previously fled returned from another country to his own land and once again became king.
Having ascended the throne, he asked his ministers:
"Did you see the sword?"
He replied, "Great King! We all saw it."
He asked again,
"What does it look like?
He replied:
"O Great King!
His complexion is pure, like an *utpala* flower.
Another replied:
"Its shape is like a ram's horn.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Its color is crimson, like a mass of fire."
Again, another replied:
"It is like a black snake.
At that time, the king laughed loudly.
"You all do not see the true mark of my sword. "Good sons!

It is the same with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: appearing in the world to proclaim the true mark of the self, he departs after having spoken, just like a prince who, carrying a pure and wondrous sword, flees to another country."
Ordinary, foolish people say, "There is a self; there is a self," just like that poor man who, while staying in another's house, muttered in his sleep, "A knife! A knife!
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas ask sentient beings, "What are the characteristics of my self? [they are unable to answer].
He replied:
"I see my own form, as large as a mother's thumb. Or he said:
"It is like rice, or like millet. Others say:
"The mark of self dwells within the heart, blazing like the sun."
"In this way, sentient beings do not understand the characteristic of 'self,' just as ministers do not understand the characteristic of a sword.
When a Bodhisattva thus speaks of my Dharma, ordinary people do not know it and engage in various conceptual discriminations, falsely constructing the characteristic of a self;
it is like being asked about the characteristic of a sword and answering that it resembles a sheep's horn."
These ordinary beings give rise to false views through a continuous succession; in order to sever such false views, the Tathāgata manifests and teaches non-self.
It is like a prince who says to his ministers, "In my treasury there is no such sword. Good son!
That which the Tathāgata speaks of today as the true self is called the Buddha-nature.
Such is the Buddha-nature; in my Buddha-dharma, it is likened to a pure blade.
Good son! If there are ordinary beings who can skillfully explain this, they are in accord with the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
If there is one who is well able to discern, accord with, and proclaim this, you should know that this is the mark of a bodhisattva. Good son!
All various heterodox doctrines, incantations, speech, and written characters are all the Buddha’s teachings; they are not the teachings of non-Buddhists.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the Tathāgata explain the root of letters?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
The first half-syllables are taught as the foundation, upholding all treatises, incantations, literature, and the real dharmas of the aggregates."
“Ordinary people study these fundamental characters, and only then can they know what is the Dharma and what is not the Dharma.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the meaning of what you call 'syllables' (akṣara)? "Good son!

There are fourteen phonemes which are called the meaning of syllables. What is called a 'syllable' is named Nirvāṇa; because it is eternal, it does not flow. That which does not flow is inexhaustible. That which is inexhaustible is the Tathāgata’s diamond body. These fourteen phonemes are called the root of syllables."
“*Hūṃ* means ‘not to be destroyed. That which is not destroyed is called the Triple Gem;

it is likened to a vajra. Furthermore, *hūṃ* means ‘not to flow. That which does not flow is the Tathāgata, for the nine orifices of the Tathāgata have nothing that flows; therefore, it is ‘not flowing.’”

Furthermore, because there are no nine orifices, there is no outflow; that which does not flow is eternal, and that which is eternal is the Tathāgata. Because the Tathāgata is without conditioned activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*), he does not flow.
Moreover, "Aḥ" is called merit (*puṇya*); merit is precisely the Three Jewels, and for this reason it is named "Aḥ."
"Ācārya" is the name for an *ācārya*. What is the meaning of "ācārya"?
Within the world, one is called a "noble one" (*ārya*).
What constitutes being noble?
The noble one is named Asaṅga (Unattached).

Having few desires and being contented is also called purity; because he can deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of birth and death within the flow of the three realms of existence, he is called "noble."
Furthermore, "A" is called the establishment of regulations; it refers to the cultivation and maintenance of pure precepts in accordance with dignified conduct.

Furthermore, "A" is called relying upon the noble ones (ārya); one should learn the proper deportment of advancing, halting, and moving, as well as making offerings, showing respect, and prostrating to the Triple Gem, filially supporting one's parents, and studying the Mahāyāna. Those sons and daughters of good family who fully uphold the prohibitive precepts, as well as the various Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others—these are called noble ones.
