Furthermore, "A" is called instruction; it is like saying, "Come here, you should do this, and you must not do that. One who can restrain any conduct that is contrary to proper decorum is called a noble one (ārya); for this reason, it is named "A."
“*Koṭi* refers to the Buddha-dharma; its pure conduct is vast, pure, and stainless, comparable to the full moon.

You all, regarding what should be done and what should not be done, what is meaningful and what is meaningless, and what is the word of the Buddha and what is the word of Māra—this is why it is called *koṭi*.

“Ī refers to the Buddha-dharma, which is subtle, profound, and difficult to attain. It is like Maheśvara and Mahābrahmā; the Dharma is named ‘Sovereignty’ (Īśvara), and if one can uphold it, they are called a ‘Protector of the Dharma.
Furthermore, ‘Sovereignty’ also refers to the Four World-Protectors; these four sovereigns can then gather and protect the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and can also freely propagate and proclaim it.”
Furthermore, "I" (ī) signifies being able to preach the Dharma with mastery for the sake of sentient beings.
Moreover, regarding "I," because it represents mastery, what is it that is taught?
It is the cultivation of the Vaipulya sūtras.
Furthermore, "I" (ī) signifies the severing of envy; just as one removes weeds and chaff, it is able to cause everything to transform into auspiciousness, and for this reason it is called "I.
"U" (ū) signifies that which is the most supreme and most excellent among all sūtras, increasing the highest of the high—namely, Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, "Yu" (郁) refers to the nature of the Tathāgata, which has never been heard of by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Just as among all places, Uttarakuru is the most preeminent;
so too, if a Bodhisattva can listen to and receive this sutra, they will be the most preeminent among all assemblies.
For this reason, this sutra is named "Most Supreme" and "Most Excellent," and is therefore called *U*.

"U" is like cow's milk, which is the foremost among all flavors; the nature of the Tathāgata is also like this, being the most honored and supreme among all sutras. If there are those who slander it, you should know that such people are no different from cattle.
Furthermore, "U" refers to a person who is devoid of wisdom and right mindfulness.

Such a person slanders the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata; one should know that this person is truly pitiable, for they have distanced themselves from the secret treasury of the Tathāgata and preach the doctrine of non-self. Therefore, he is called "U."
“*Ya* refers to the Buddhas, the *dharmatā*, and *nirvāṇa*; therefore it is called *ya*.
*Ra* signifies the meaning of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, *ra* means that in the Tathāgata’s coming and going, bending and stretching, and every movement, there is nothing that does not benefit all sentient beings; therefore it is called *ra*.”
“*U* signifies the meaning of afflictions (*kleśa*); afflictions are called the outflows (*āsrava*). Since the Tathāgata has forever severed all afflictions, he is therefore called *U*.
“*Pao* refers to the meaning of the Mahāyāna; among the fourteen phonemes, it is the ultimate meaning.
The Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so: they are the most ultimate among all sūtras and śāstras, and for this reason they are called *pao*.”
“Ānanda means that which can shield against all impure things; within the Buddha-dharma, it is able to relinquish all gold, silver, and precious objects—therefore it is called Ānanda.”
"A" signifies the meaning of the "Victorious Vehicle. Why is this?
Because this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is the most preeminent among all sūtras; therefore, it is called "A."

"Ka" means that toward all sentient beings one gives rise to great compassion and regards them as one's own children, just like Rāhula; it carries the meaning of wondrous, supreme goodness—therefore it is called "Ka."
“*Kha* means a non-virtuous friend; a non-virtuous friend is called ‘impurity.
Because they do not believe in the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, they are therefore called *kha*.”
“Ga” means “treasury”; this treasury is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called “ga.”
“*Aṃ* is the eternal sound of the Tathāgata.
What is called the eternal sound of the Tathāgata?
It refers to the fact that the Tathāgata abides eternally and is immutable; therefore, it is named *aṃ*.
"‘A-ra’ (O) signifies the characteristic of the destruction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); therefore, it is named ‘O’.
‘Cha’ (Sha) signifies the meaning of cultivation; because it tames all sentient beings, it is named the meaning of cultivation; therefore, it is named ‘Sha’."
“‘Jina’ (Vehicle) means that the Tathāgata provides shelter for all sentient beings like a great canopy;
therefore, it is called ‘Jina. ‘Sa’ means right liberation, which is devoid of the characteristic of aging; therefore, it is called ‘Sa.’”
"Jhana (zhan) refers to the profusion of afflictions, which is likened to a dense forest; for this reason, it is called jhana.
Nyana (ye) has the meaning of wisdom; because one knows the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it is called nyana."
“*Ṭha*: In Jambudvīpa, he manifests a half-body and expounds the Dharma; because it is like a crescent moon, it is called *Ṭha*.
“*Ṭha*: The Dharmakāya is fully perfected, like the full moon; therefore, it is called *Ṭha*.”
“*Da* refers to the foolish monastics who do not understand the permanent and the impermanent; they are like small children, and for this reason they are called *da*.
*Zu* refers to those who do not recognize the kindness of their teachers; they are like rams, and for this reason they are called *zu*.”
“Na” is not a noble meaning; it is like the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and for this reason it is called “Na.
“Ta” refers to when the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus, saying, “You should abandon fear and dread; I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for you,” and for this reason it is called “Ta.”
“‘Ta’ signifies the meaning of delusion; sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death, entangled like silkworms or dung beetles, and for this reason it is called ‘ta.
‘Da’ is named the Great Giving, which refers to the Mahāyāna; for this reason it is called ‘da.’”
“Tāṇa means to praise virtues, namely those of the Three Jewels. Just as Mount Sumeru is lofty, steep, vast, and expansive, and cannot be toppled, it is therefore called tāṇa.”
“Na” signifies that the Three Jewels abide securely and are immovable, like the threshold of a door; therefore, it is called “Na.
“Pa” signifies the meaning of inversion; if one says that the Three Jewels have all utterly perished, one should know that such a person is merely harboring self-doubt; therefore, it is called “Pa.”

“*Pha* refers to the calamities of the world; if one says that when the calamities of the world arise, the Three Jewels also perish, know that such a person is foolish and ignorant, having violated and lost the intent of the Sages. For this reason, it is called *pha*. "
“*Bha* means the ten powers of the Buddha; therefore it is called *bha*.
*Bhā* means a heavy burden; one who is capable of bearing the unsurpassed True Dharma should be known as a great Bodhisattva; therefore it is called *bhā*.
“Ma” refers to the rigorous discipline of all bodhisattvas, namely the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa; therefore, it is called “ma.
“Śe” refers to all bodhisattvas preaching the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of sentient beings wherever they may be; therefore, it is called “śe.”
“Ra” refers to that which can destroy greed, hatred, and delusion, and speaks the Dharma of reality; therefore, it is called “ra.

“La” refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is unstable and shifting; the Mahāyāna is firm and solid, without any wavering. To abandon the Śrāvaka vehicle and diligently cultivate the unsurpassed Mahāyāna—therefore, it is called “la.”

“Harmony (Saṃ) refers to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who rains down the great Dharma rain for all sentient beings—namely, the worldly incantations, arts, and scriptures; therefore, it is called Saṃ.”
“*Śa* means to be far removed from the three arrows; therefore, it is called *śa*.
*Sa* means the sense of being fully endowed. If one can hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one has already attained the hearing and retention of all Mahāyāna sūtras; therefore, it is called *sa*.”
“*Sa* means to expound the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing their hearts to rejoice; therefore it is called *sa*. *Ha* means the heart rejoices, thinking:
‘How marvelous is the World-Honored One, who has transcended all conditioned activities! How extraordinary is the Tathāgata, who has entered parinirvāṇa! Therefore it is called *ha*.”
“*Luo* (𠻬) means ‘Māra. The immeasurable Māras cannot destroy the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; therefore, it is called *luo*.

Furthermore, *luo* refers to manifesting in accordance with the world by having parents, wives, and children; therefore, it is called *luo*. Regarding the four characters *lu*, *liu*, *lu*, and *lou*, they are said to have four meanings, namely: Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, and the Abhidharma.”
Regarding what is called "conforming to the world" (lokānuvartana): it is like Devadatta manifesting the destruction of the Sangha and transforming himself into various forms and appearances;

for the sake of establishing the precepts, the wise understand this and should not give rise to fear or dread therein. This is called the practice of conforming to the world, and for this reason it is termed *lu*, *liu*, *lu*, and *lou*.

"Inhalation, the root of the tongue, and the sounds following the nose—whether long, short, or transcending sound—all meanings understood according to these tones arise through the distinction between the tongue and teeth; such meanings of syllables can cause the verbal karma of sentient beings to become pure."
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not like this, for it does not require reliance upon words and letters to become pure. Why is this?
Because its nature is fundamentally pure.

Although they abide within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), they are not identical to these aggregates, bases, and elements. For this reason, all sentient beings should take refuge in the bodhisattvas and others; because of their buddha-nature, they regard all sentient beings with equality, without distinction. Therefore, the "half-syllables" serve as the foundation for all scriptures, records, treatises, and literary compositions.
Furthermore, the meaning of the "half-syllables" (ardhakṣara) is that they are all the basis for the verbal expressions of afflictions;

therefore, they are called half-syllables. The "full-syllables" (pūrṇakṣara), however, are the fundamental basis for the verbal expressions of all wholesome dharmas. For example, in the world, those who do evil are called "half-people," while those who cultivate goodness are called "full-people."
All such sūtras, records, and treatises take these "half-syllables" as their foundation.
However, to say that the Tathāgata and perfect liberation enter into these half-syllables is not the case.
Why is this? Because it is free from words and letters; therefore, the Tathāgata is truly liberated in all phenomena, being unimpeded and unattached.
What is meant by "understanding the meaning of words"?
There are those who know that the Tathāgata appears in the world to extinguish the "half-letters"; for this reason, they are called those who understand the meaning of the letters.
If there are those who follow after the meaning of the half-letters, such persons do not know the nature of the Tathāgata.
What is meant by the meaning of "no-words"?
One who draws near to and cultivates unwholesome dharmas is said to be following "no-words.

Furthermore, even if one can draw near to and cultivate wholesome dharmas, yet does not know the Tathāgata’s permanence and impermanence, constancy and non-constancy, nor the two jewels of Dharma and Saṃgha, what is discipline and what is not discipline, what is a sūtra and what is not a sūtra, or what is spoken by Māra and what is spoken by the Buddha—if one is unable to make such distinctions, this is called following the meaning of "no-words."
I have now explained the meaning of following these wordless principles. Good son!
Therefore, you should now abandon the half-syllables and skillfully understand the full-syllables.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We should skillfully study the numerical systems of characters; now that we have encountered the Unsurpassed Teacher, we have already received the Tathāgata’s earnest instructions.”
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
Those who delight in the True Dharma should train in this way.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: “Good son,
there are two kinds of birds:”
The first is named Kalaviṅka and the second is named Ruddy Sheldrake; they dwell and move together, never parting from one another.
These dharmas of suffering, impermanence, and non-self are likewise thus: they cannot be separated from one another.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that suffering, impermanence, and non-self are like those ruddy sheldrakes and kālaṃdaka birds?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! One dharma is suffering; another dharma is happiness."
One phenomenon is eternal, while another phenomenon is impermanent;
one phenomenon is self, while another phenomenon is non-self;
just as rice is distinct from hemp and wheat, and hemp and wheat are in turn distinct from beans, millet, and sugarcane.
In this way, all these varieties, from their sprouting until their leaves and flowers, are impermanent;
only when the fruit has ripened and people enjoy it is it called permanent.
"Why is this? Because its nature is true reality.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If such things as these were permanent, would they be the same as the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! You should not speak in such a manner now. Why is that?
If one says that the Tathāgata is like Mount Sumeru, and when the kalpa is destroyed Mount Sumeru collapses, would the Tathāgata likewise perish at that time?
Good son!
You should not now accept or uphold this meaning. Good son!

Among all dharmas, with the sole exception of nirvana, there is not a single dharma that is permanent; it is only according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) that we speak of the fruit as being permanent.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
"It is as the Buddha has taught.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "So it is, so it is."
"Good son!
Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard the Mahāparinirvāṇa, one will declare that everything is entirely impermanent."
Having heard this sutra, although they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions, and are thus able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because they clearly understand that their own bodies possess the Buddha-nature; this is what is called "permanence."
Furthermore, good son!
It is like the mango tree: when its flowers first bloom, it is called the mark of impermanence; once it has borne fruit, which brings much benefit, it is then called permanent.
In this way, good son!

Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will say that everything is entirely impermanent;
but having heard this sūtra, although one still possesses afflictions, it is as if one were without afflictions, and one is then able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because one clearly understands that one's own body possesses the Buddha-nature; this is called "permanent.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, when gold ore is being melted down, it is a mark of impermanence; once it has been melted and formed into gold, it provides great benefit and is therefore called permanent.
In this way, good son!

Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will say that everything is entirely impermanent.
Once one has heard this sūtra, although afflictions still exist, they are as if non-existent; one is then able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because one clearly realizes that one's own body possesses the Buddha-nature, it is called "constant.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, when sesame seeds have not yet been pressed, they are called impermanent; once pressed and turned into oil, they provide great benefit and are thus called permanent. Good son!
Although they may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, if they have not yet heard this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, they will all say that everything is impermanent;
but once they have heard this sūtra, even though they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions, and are thus able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because one clearly understands that one's own body possesses the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called "permanent.
Furthermore, good son!
Just as all streams flow back to the ocean, so do all the various meditative concentrations and samādhis of the sūtras flow back to the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Why is this?
Because it is ultimately well-expounded that the Buddha-nature exists. Good son!
Therefore, I say that some phenomena are permanent and other phenomena are impermanent; even so it is with regard to non-self.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has already departed from the poisonous arrows of sorrow and grief; for one who possesses sorrow and grief is called a deva, and the Tathāgata is not a deva.”
Those who possess sorrow and lamentation are called "humans," whereas the Tathāgata is not a human.

Those who possess sorrow and lamentation are said to belong to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), whereas the Tathāgata does not belong to these twenty-five states of existence.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no sorrow or lamentation; for what reason, then, is it said that the Tathāgata possesses sorrow and lamentation?

“Good son! That which is called the Heaven of No-Thought is named ‘no-thought. If there is no thought, then there is no life-span. If there is no life-span, how could there be the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas)?”
For this reason, regarding the lifespan in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva), one cannot say that there is a specific place where it resides. Good son!

It is like a tree spirit that dwells in dependence upon a tree; one cannot definitively say that it depends on the branches, the joints, the trunk, or the leaves. Although it has no fixed location, one cannot say that it does not exist.
The lifespan of the Heaven of No-Thought is likewise thus.

Good son, the Buddha-nature is also like this: it is profoundly deep and difficult to understand. Although the Tathāgata truly has no sorrow, grief, suffering, or affliction, he gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings; he manifests sorrow and grief, regarding all sentient beings as if they were Rāhula.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The lifespan within the Heaven of No-Thought can only be known by a Buddha; it is beyond the reach of others, and the same applies even to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Kāśyapa! The nature of the Tathāgata is pure and untainted, like a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya); how could there be any sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction therein?
If it is said that the Tathāgata has no sorrow or lamentation, how then can he benefit all sentient beings and propagate the Buddha-dharma extensively?
If you say that there is none, why do you say that you regard all sentient beings equally as you do Rāhula?
If you do not regard them equally as you do Rāhula, such a statement would be false.
For this reason, son of good family!
The Buddha is inconceivable; the Dharma is inconceivable; the buddha-nature of sentient beings is inconceivable; and the lifespan of the Heaven of No-Thought is inconceivable.
That the Tathāgata possesses both sorrow and the absence of sorrow is the domain of the Buddha, not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. "Good son!

For example, within space, houses or fine dust cannot be established; yet it would be impossible to say that houses do not depend on space for their existence. For this reason, one cannot say that a house dwells in space or does not dwell in space."
Ordinary people may say that they dwell in empty space, yet this empty space actually has no place where it dwells.
Why is this? Because its nature is non-abiding.
Good son! The mind is also like this;

it cannot be said that it dwells within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, nor that it does not dwell therein. The lifespan in the Heaven of No-Thought is also like this, and the sorrow and grief of the Tathāgata are likewise so. If he were without sorrow and grief, how could one say that he regards all sentient beings equally as he does Rāhula?
If you say they exist, how can you also say their nature is identical to empty space? Good son!

It is like a magician who, though he may conjure various palaces, acts of killing, nurturing, binding, or releasing, as well as gold, silver, lapis lazuli treasures, groves, and trees, none of these possess any real nature.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he conforms to the world by manifesting sorrow and grief, yet these have no reality.
Good son! Since the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, how could there be any sorrow, grief, or affliction?
If one claims that the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa and is thus impermanent, know that such a person will experience sorrow and grief.
If one claims that the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa but is eternally abiding and unchanging, know that such a person is free from sorrow and grief.
Whether the Tathāgata has sorrow or is free from sorrow, no one is able to know it.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like a person of low station who can understand the teachings of the low, but does not understand those of the middle or superior levels; [so it is with the Tathāgata]."
Those of middle capacity know the middle, but do not know what is above;
those of superior capacity know the superior, as well as the middle and the lower.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise: they know only up to their own respective stages.
The Tathāgata is not like this; he fully knows both his own stage and the stages of others. Therefore, the Tathāgata is named "Unobstructed Wisdom.
He manifests illusory transformations in accordance with the world, which ordinary people with their fleshly eyes take to be real.
Yet, for anyone to wish to exhaustively know the Tathāgata’s unobstructed, unsurpassed wisdom is impossible.
Whether there is sorrow or no sorrow, only a Buddha can know; for this reason, by one set of conditions there is self, and by another set of conditions there is no self.
This is called the nature of the ruddy sheldrake and the kālaṃjara bird.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Buddha-dharma is like the cakravāka birds traveling together.

When the summer rains cause the waters to swell, these *kaliṅga* and *cakravāka* birds select a high plateau to settle their young for the sake of their upbringing; only then do they follow their own natural course, wandering in peace."

The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is likewise so: he transforms immeasurable multitudes, causing them to dwell in the True Dharma, just as that ruddy sheldrake and kālaṃjiṅka bird selects high ground to settle its young.
The Tathāgata is also like this: once he has caused all sentient beings to accomplish what was to be done, he immediately enters Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good son! This is called:

one dharma is suffering and another dharma is happiness; conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering, while Nirvāṇa is happiness, for it is supremely subtle and brings an end to all conditioned phenomena.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that those sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa are said to possess the foremost bliss?”
The Buddha said:
“Good son! As I have taught, the conjunction of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is called old age and death.”
"Diligence and freedom from negligence—this state is called the deathless nectar;
negligence and lack of diligence—this is called the path of death.
Those who are not negligent shall attain the state of immortality."
Those who are heedless always tread the path to death.
That which is called "heedlessness" is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and this conditioned phenomenon is the foremost suffering.
Heedfulness is called *nirvāṇa*; that *nirvāṇa* is called the ambrosia (*amṛta*), the supreme and foremost bliss.
To pursue conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called the realm of death, where one undergoes the foremost suffering;
to reach *nirvāṇa* is called the deathless, where one experiences the most sublime bliss.
If one is not negligent, although one accumulates various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), these are also called the body that is eternal, blissful, deathless, and indestructible.
What is negligence?
What is non-heedlessness?
The non-noble ordinary person is called heedless and is subject to the law of constant death; the supramundane noble one is non-heedless and is free from old age and death.
Why is this? Because one enters the supreme, eternal, and blissful nirvana.
For this reason, there are distinct dharmas that are suffering, distinct dharmas that are bliss, distinct dharmas that are self, and distinct dharmas that are non-self.
Just as a person standing on the ground gazes up at the sky and does not see the tracks of birds, so it is with sentient beings, O son of good family:
lacking the divine eye, they do not perceive the Tathāgata-nature within themselves amidst their afflictions. For this reason, I have taught the esoteric teaching of "no-self."

Why is this so? Those who lack the divine eye do not know the true self; because they falsely conceptualize a self, they are subject to the conditioned phenomena produced by various afflictions, which are impermanent. Therefore, I say that some phenomena are permanent and other phenomena are impermanent.
“The one who is diligent and valiant, as if standing upon a mountain peak,
on level ground, or in the wilderness, constantly beholds all ordinary beings.
Having ascended the palace of great wisdom and the unsurpassed, sublime terrace,”
Having personally eliminated my own afflictions and anxieties, I also see the afflictions of sentient beings.

"The Tathāgata has completely severed immeasurable defilements and dwells upon the mountain of wisdom; yet he sees all sentient beings constantly remaining amidst immeasurable billions of defilements."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As stated in the verse, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? One who has entered nirvana is without sorrow and without joy; how then could they ascend the palace of wisdom?
Furthermore, how could they dwell upon the mountain peak and behold sentient beings?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
The Palace of Wisdom is another name for Nirvana.”
One who is without sorrow is called a Tathāgata; one who possesses sorrow is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Because ordinary persons possess sorrow, the Tathāgata is without sorrow.
"The summit of Mount Sumeru" refers to right liberation; "one who exerts diligent effort" is likened to Mount Sumeru, which is without movement or fluctuation.
"Ground" refers to conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); it is upon this ground that all ordinary beings abide and perform various actions.
One whose wisdom is such is called "Perfectly Awakened" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*); because he is detached from existence and eternally abiding, he is named the Tathāgata.
"The Tathāgata takes pity on immeasurable sentient beings who are constantly pierced by the poisonous arrows of the various afflictions; for this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata has sorrow.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If the Tathāgata were subject to sorrow and distress, he could not be called the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa!"

All things possess causes and conditions; wherever there are sentient beings who should be transformed, the Tathāgata manifests birth therein. Although he manifests birth, in reality there is no birth. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the eternally abiding Dharma, like the kālaṃjara crane, the ruddy sheldrake, and other such birds.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eight [Continued] / The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Nature of the Tathāgata, Part Six.
"Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who, seeing the moon not appear, all says that the moon has set and forms the thought that it has set; yet the nature of this moon truly does not set.
As it appears in other directions, the sentient beings there again say that the moon has risen; yet, in its true nature, this moon actually has no rising.
Why is this? Because Mount Sumeru obstructs it, it does not appear; however, the moon is constantly present, for its nature is without rising or setting.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: appearing in the trichiliocosm, he may manifest as having parents in Jambudvīpa, and sentient beings all say that the Tathāgata was born within Jambudvīpa.

In some cases, the Tathāgata manifests parinirvāṇa in Jambudvīpa, yet the nature of the Tathāgata is in reality without parinirvāṇa; nevertheless, all sentient beings believe that the Tathāgata has truly entered parinirvāṇa, just as they perceive the setting of the moon.
"Good son! The nature of the Tathāgata is truly without arising or ceasing; it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings that he manifests arising and ceasing. Good son!"
Just as this full moon appears as a half-moon in other directions,
so too this half-moon appears as a full moon in other directions.
When the people of Jambudvīpa see the beginning of the moon, they all say it is the first day and form the perception that it is the first month.
When one sees the moon at its fullness on the fifteenth day, one conceives the notion that it is full;
yet the nature of this moon is actually devoid of waning or waxing—it appears to increase and decrease only because of Mount Sumeru.
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise; within Jambudvīpa, he may manifest his initial birth or manifest his parinirvāṇa.

When he manifests his first birth, he is like the new moon, and all say that the child has just been born. When he walks seven steps, he is like the second-day moon. Or again, when he manifests entering the schoolroom, he is like the third-day moon. When he manifests leaving home, he is like the eighth-day moon. When he emits the subtle and wondrous light of great wisdom, capable of destroying the demonic hosts of immeasurable sentient beings, he is like the full moon on the fifteenth day.
Furthermore, he may manifest the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics to adorn himself and display nirvana, like an eclipse of the moon.

Thus, what sentient beings perceive differs: some see a crescent moon, some see a full moon, and some see a lunar eclipse; yet the nature of this moon truly has no increase or decrease, nor is it ever eclipsed or consumed—it is always a full moon.
The body of the Tathāgata is likewise thus; therefore, it is called eternally abiding and unchanging. "Furthermore, good son!

It is like the full moon, which appears everywhere—in cities, towns, villages, mountains, marshes, and waters; whether in wells, ponds, jars, or cauldrons, it appears in all of them. There are sentient beings who travel for a hundred *yojanas* or even a hundred thousand *yojanas*, seeing the moon always following them. Yet foolish ordinary people give rise to false conceptions and say:"
"In the past, within cities and dwellings, I saw such a moon; now I see it again here in this empty marsh.
Is this the same moon as before, or is it different from the original?"

Each formed this thought: as for the size of the moon’s form, some said it was like the mouth of a cauldron, others said it was as large as a chariot wheel, and still others said it was like forty-nine *yojanas*.
All see the radiance of the moon; some see it as perfectly round, like a golden platter.
The nature of this moon is one, yet various sentient beings each perceive it as having different appearances.
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise; appearing in the world, there may be humans or devas who think:
"The Tathāgata now dwells before me."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who also give rise to this thought:
"The Tathāgata is now dwelling before me.
Or there may be those who are deaf or mute, who likewise see the Tathāgata as having the appearance of being deaf or mute.
Sentient beings of various kinds have diverse languages and sounds; each believes that the Tathāgata speaks entirely in their own tongue, and each also thinks:
"He is in my own home, receiving my offerings."
There may be sentient beings who see the body of the Tathāgata as vast and immeasurable;
some see it as minute; some see the Buddha in the form of a śrāvaka; and others see him in the form of a pratyekabuddha.
There were other non-Buddhists who each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata has now gone forth from home to study the Way within our own teachings.
Furthermore, there were some sentient beings who thought as follows:
"The Tathāgata has now appeared in the world solely for my sake.
The true nature of the Tathāgata is likened to that moon; it is the Dharmakāya, the body of non-arising.
The body of skillful means accords with the world, manifesting immeasurable causes and conditions of past karma, appearing to be born in every place, just like that moon.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.

Furthermore, good son, it is like the asura king Rāhu who covers the moon with his hand; all people in the world say that there is an eclipse of the moon, yet the asura king is actually unable to eclipse it.
Because the asuras obstruct its light, this moon remains full and without diminution; it is merely because their hands obstruct it that it does not appear.
When they withdraw their hands, the world says that the moon has been restored, and everyone says that the moon suffered great torment.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands of asura kings, they could not afflict him.

The Tathāgata is likewise; he manifests that there are sentient beings who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, give rise to coarse and evil thoughts, shed the blood of a Buddha, commit the five heinous crimes, and even reach the state of an icchantika. For the sake of all sentient beings in future ages, he thus manifests such things as the destruction of the Saṃgha and the severing of the Dharma to create obstacles.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands of immeasurable Māras, they would be unable to draw blood from the body of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is devoid of flesh and blood, sinews, veins, marrow, and bones.
The Tathāgata is truly and ultimately free from affliction or destruction; yet sentient beings all claim that the Dharma and the Saṃgha have perished and that the Tathāgata has entered extinction.
However, the nature of the Tathāgata is truly immutable and indestructible; it is only in accordance with worldly conventions that he manifests such appearances.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like two people fighting; if one wounds the other’s body with a blade or a staff until blood flows, even if it leads to death, no thought of killing arises.
Such karmic characteristics are light and not heavy.
Since there was originally no intent to kill toward the Tathāgata, even though his body was wounded and blood shed, this karma is likewise light and not heavy.
In this same way, the Tathāgata manifests the retribution of karma in future ages in order to transform sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a skilled physician who diligently instructs his son in the fundamental principles of medical arts: 'This is a root medicine; this is a stem medicine; this is a color-based medicine; you must thoroughly understand these various characteristics.'"
The son respectfully followed his father’s instructions, practicing and studying with diligence until he became skilled in understanding all medicinal herbs.
Later, when the physician’s life came to an end, the son wailed and lamented, saying:
"My father originally taught me that root medicines are such-and-such, stem medicines are such-and-such, flower medicines are such-and-such, and their colors and characteristics are such-and-such."

The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests the establishment of precepts. You should receive and uphold them in this manner, and not commit the five heinous crimes, slander the true Dharma, or become an icchantika.

To bring about this matter for future generations, he manifested it in this way, desiring that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus would understand thus: "This is the profound meaning of the sūtras; this is the nature of the gravity of the vinaya; this is the analysis of the categories of dharmas in the abhidharma," just like the son of the physician.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as when people on earth know that a lunar eclipse occurs once every six months, yet the gods in the heavens above see a lunar eclipse in the space of a mere moment."
Why is this? Because for those devas the days are long, whereas for humans they are short.
O son of good family!

The Tathāgata is likewise. Although devas and humans all say that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is short—just as those devas and humans repeatedly witness lunar eclipses within a single moment—the Tathāgata, moreover, manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of parinirvāṇas within a single moment, severing the māra of afflictions, the māra of the aggregates, and the māra of death. Therefore, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial māras all know that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, by manifesting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions from past karma, in accordance with the various natures of the world, he manifests such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable [deeds]; therefore, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like the bright moon, which all sentient beings delight in beholding; therefore, the moon is called "Delightful to Behold.
However, if sentient beings possess greed, anger, and delusion, they cannot be called "Delightful to Behold."
The Tathāgata is likewise: his nature is purely good, pure and stainless, and he is most worthy of being called "delightful to behold.

Sentient beings who delight in the Dharma never tire of gazing upon him, whereas those with malicious minds do not rejoice in beholding him. For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata is like the bright moon.

"Furthermore, good son, it is like the rising of the sun, which has three distinct seasons: namely, spring, summer, and winter. In winter the days are short; in spring they are of medium length; and in summer they are exceedingly long."

The Tathāgata is likewise; within this trichiliocosm, for the sake of those with short lifespans and the various śrāvakas, he manifests a short lifespan. Having seen this, they all say that the Tathāgata’s life span is brief, comparable to the winter sun.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he manifests a medium lifespan—whether reaching one kalpa or falling short of one kalpa—which is likened to the spring sun.
Only a Buddha perceives a Buddha; his lifespan is immeasurable, which is likened to the summer sun.
"Good son!

The profound and secret teachings of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna spoken by the Tathāgata manifest in the world and rain down the great Dharma rain. In future ages, if there are those who can protect and uphold these scriptures, elucidating and analyzing them to benefit sentient beings, you should know that such individuals are truly Bodhisattvas; they are like the sweet rain descending from the heavens during the height of summer."
If there are śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas who hear the subtle and secret teaching of the Buddha-Tathāgata, it is like encountering much suffering from the cold during winter.
If bodhisattvas hear such subtle and secret instruction—that the Tathāgata abides eternally and his nature is immutable—it is like springtime, when sprouts emerge and flowers bloom.
Furthermore, the nature of the Tathāgata is truly without length or shortness; it is for the sake of the world that he manifests such things, which is precisely the true *dharmatā* of all Buddhas.
"Moreover, good son!

For example, just as the various stars do not appear during the day, yet people all say that the stars have vanished during the day, whereas in reality they have not vanished; the reason they do not appear is that they are eclipsed by the brilliance of the sun.
The Tathāgata is likewise; the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to see him, just as worldly people cannot see the stars during the day.
Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like when it is dark and gloomy and the sun and moon do not appear; fools say that the sun and moon have set and perished, yet in reality, the sun and moon have not set or perished.

When the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is extinguished, the disappearance of the Triple Gem is likewise not a permanent cessation; therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Why is this? Because the true nature of the Triple Gem cannot be defiled by any impurities.
Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a comet appearing at night during the dark fortnight; its brilliant light blazes fiercely as it briefly emerges and then vanishes. When sentient beings see this, they conceive thoughts of ill omen.

The Pratyekabuddhas are also like this: appearing in worlds where no Buddha dwells, when sentient beings see them, they all say that the Tathāgata has truly entered parinirvāṇa, giving rise to thoughts of sorrow and grief;
yet the body of the Tathāgata does not truly enter parinirvāṇa, for he is like the sun and moon, which never truly perish or set.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as when the sun rises, all mists are entirely dispelled, so too is it with this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra appearing in the world: if there are sentient beings who hear it but once, it can completely eliminate all evils and the karmic offenses of the *ānantarya* crimes."

This Great Nirvana is an inconceivable and profound realm; it skillfully explains the subtle and secret nature of the Tathāgata. For this reason, all sons and daughters of good family should conceive the thought that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, immutable, that the True Dharma shall not be interrupted, and that the Jewel of the Sangha shall not perish. Therefore, you should cultivate many skillful means and diligently study this scripture; such persons shall before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, this sutra is named "Accomplished by Immeasurable Merit" and is also named "Inexhaustible Bodhi. Because it is inexhaustible, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa;
because it possesses virtuous radiance, it is like the summer sun; and because its body is boundless, it is called Mahānirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the light of the sun and moon is the foremost among all lights, such that no other light can equal it, so too is the light of the Great Nirvāṇa;
among the lights of the samādhis in all sūtras, it is the most preeminent, such that the lights of the samādhis found in all other sūtras cannot equal it."
Why is this? Because the light of the Great Nirvana can enter all the pores of sentient beings.
Although sentient beings may lack the aspiration for Bodhi, it can nevertheless act as the causal condition for Bodhi; for this reason, it is further named Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, that the light of the Great Nirvāṇa enters the pores of all sentient beings and can act as the cause for bodhi even though those beings lack the mind of bodhi—this meaning is not so.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

If the light enters the bodies of those who have committed the four grave offenses, those who have perpetrated the five heinous crimes, and icchantikas, thereby acting as the cause for bodhi, then what difference is there between such people and those who purely uphold the precepts and cultivate all manner of goodness?
If there were no distinction, for what reason did the Tathāgata speak of the four reliances?
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, as the Buddha has said: "If there are sentient beings who hear the single sutra of the Great Nirvāṇa even once with their ears, they shall attain the severance of all afflictions."

How is it that the Tathāgata previously said that there are those who have resolved their minds for enlightenment in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet upon hearing the Mahāparinirvāṇa, they do not understand its meaning?
If they do not understand the meaning, how can they sever all afflictions?
The Buddha said,
“Good son! With the exception of those with single-minded attachment (icchantika), all other sentient beings, having heard this sutra, will all be able to create the causes and conditions for bodhi.”
Those into whose pores the light of the sound of the Dharma enters will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
Only those who have been able to make offerings to and revere immeasurable Buddhas may hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; those of meager merit cannot hear it.
Why is this so? Only those of great virtue are able to hear such a matter of great significance; base and lowly persons cannot hear it.
What constitutes "great"?
"What is called the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas refers to the Buddha-nature; for this reason, it is termed the 'Great Matter.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"How can one who has not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta obtain the cause for awakening?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there is someone who, upon hearing this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, says, 'I have no need to resolve to attain bodhicitta,' and thus slanders the True Dharma, that person will see the form of a rākṣasa in a dream. Terrified in his heart, the rākṣasa will speak these words:"
"Alas, son of good family!
If you do not now resolve to attain bodhicitta, I shall take your life.
Terrified by this, the person awoke and immediately resolved to attain bodhicitta.

When such a person’s life comes to an end, whether they are reborn in the three evil realms or among humans and devas, they will continue to recollect the bodhicitta; you should know that this person is a great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
For this reason, and by the majestic spiritual power of this Great Nirvāṇa, it can cause those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta to create the causes for bodhi. Good son!
This is called the causal condition for a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind; it is not without causal conditions. For this reason, the sublime Mahāyāna sūtras are truly the teachings of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as when great clouds and rain arise in the void and pour down upon the great earth, water does not remain upon withered trees, rocky mountains, high plateaus, or mounds; instead, it flows down into the lower fields, filling all the ponds and pools, thereby benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.

This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this: it rains down the great Dharma rain, universally moistening all sentient beings; yet, there is no possibility for a single icchantika to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like a scorched seed: even if it encounters sweet rain for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, it will never sprout; for it to sprout is simply impossible.

The icchantikas are likewise; although they hear this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they ultimately cannot produce the sprout of the bodhicitta, for it is impossible that they could do so.
Why is this? Because such a person has severed all roots of goodness; like scorched seeds, they can no longer produce the sprouts of the root of bodhi.
Furthermore, son of good family!
For example, if a bright pearl is placed in turbid water, the water becomes clear through the power and majesty of the pearl; yet if it is thrown into the mud, it cannot be made clear.

This subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is just like this: if it is placed within the turbid waters of the five sins of immediate retribution or the four grave prohibitions of other sentient beings, it can still clarify them so that they may give rise to the bodhicitta.
However, if it is thrown into the mud of an icchantika, even after hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, it cannot be made clear so that they might arouse the bodhicitta.
Why is this? Because these icchantikas have extinguished all roots of goodness and are not suitable vessels for it.
Even if such persons were to hear and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, they would ultimately never be able to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Why is this? Because they lack a virtuous mind.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like a medicinal tree called the King of Medicines, which is the most preeminent among all medicines.

Whether mixed with buttermilk, honey, ghee, water, or milk; whether in powder or pill form; whether applied to a wound, used as an incense for the body, or applied to the eyes; or even by merely seeing it or smelling its fragrance, it can eliminate all the diseases of sentient beings.
In this way, the medicinal tree does not form such thoughts:

"If all sentient beings take my root, they should not take my leaves; if they take my leaves, they should not take my root; if they take my trunk, they should not take my bark; if they take my bark, they should not take my trunk."
"Although this tree does not give rise to such a thought, it is nonetheless able to eliminate all suffering from illness.

Good son, this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this: it can eliminate the evil karma of all sentient beings, the four pārājika offenses, and the five ānantarya crimes; whether internal or external, it removes all evils. Furthermore, for those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta, they shall, by means of this, succeed in generating that resolve."
Why is this? Because this wondrous sūtra is the king among all sūtras, just as that medicinal tree is the king among all medicines.

Whether one practices this Great Nirvāṇa or does not practice it, if they hear the name of this sūtra and, having heard it, develop respectful faith, all their heavy illnesses of affliction will be completely eradicated; yet, it alone cannot cause those who are icchantikas to abide securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Just as that wondrous medicine, though it can cure various grave illnesses, cannot treat one who is destined to die.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person with a sore on their hand who, upon grasping poisonous medicine, has the poison enter through it;
yet if there is no sore, the poison does not enter.
The icchantikas are just like this: lacking the cause for bodhi, they are like those without a sore, into whom the poison cannot enter.
What is called a sore is the causal condition for unsurpassed bodhi; the poison is the foremost wondrous medicine; and one who is completely free of sores refers to an icchantika.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like a vajra, which nothing can destroy, yet it can shatter all things, with the sole exception of tortoise shells and the horns of white rams.

This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise: it is fully able to establish immeasurable sentient beings upon the path to Bodhi, yet alone it cannot cause those of the icchantika class to establish the causes for Bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the horse-tooth grass, the śaraka tree, and the nikaca tree continue to grow as before even when their branches and stems are cut;
they are not like the tāla tree, which does not grow again once it has been cut."

These sentient beings are also like this: if they hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, even though they have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, they are still able to produce the causes and conditions for bodhi;
the icchantikas are not like this, for although they may hear and receive this wondrous sūtra, they cannot produce the causes for the path to bodhi.
Furthermore, good son!
Just as the *khatāra* tree and the *candana* tree do not sprout once they are cut down, nor do parched seeds;

so it is with those who hold one-sided views (*icchantikas*). Although they may hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they are unable to give rise to the causes and conditions for bodhi, just like parched seeds.
Furthermore, good son!

For example, just as heavy rain ultimately does not remain in the sky, so too is this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: it rains the rain of Dharma everywhere, yet it cannot abide within those of icchantika nature. These icchantikas have bodies that are dense and compact throughout, like adamant, allowing no external things to enter.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has spoken in verse:”
"To see no good to be done, but only evil as fit to be done—
this state is to be feared, like a perilous and treacherous path."
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of what has been thus spoken?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! 'Not seeing' refers to not seeing the Buddha-nature.
'Good' refers to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Non-practitioner" refers to one who is unable to draw near to virtuous friends.
"One who sees only" refers to one who perceives no cause and effect.
"Evil person" refers to one who slanders the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
That which can be done refers to the icchantikas' proclamation that there are no Vaipulya sutras.
For this reason, the class of icchantikas has no mind to incline toward pure and wholesome dharmas.
What are the wholesome dharmas?
They are nirvāṇa. That which leads toward nirvāṇa refers to the ability to cultivate noble and virtuous conduct.
Yet the icchantika lacks virtuous conduct; therefore, they cannot proceed toward nirvāṇa.
This state is to be feared—namely, the slandering of the true Dharma.
Who should feel such dread?
As for what is called "the wise," why is this?
Because those who slander the Dharma lack both a virtuous mind and skillful means; "perilous evil paths" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“As the Buddha has said:
‘How does one see what is done?’”
"How does one attain wholesome dharmas?
Where is there no fear, like a king traveling on a level and smooth road?
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said: “Good son!

Regarding that which is seen to have been done, one confesses all evils; one confesses all evils committed from the very limits of saṃsāra until reaching the place of ultimate arrival. For this reason, there is no fear in this state.”
It is like a king who travels upon a royal highway; all the thieves and bandits therein flee away.
In this same way, when one confesses all evils, they are entirely extinguished without remainder.

Furthermore, "not seeing what one has done" refers to the icchantika, who does not perceive the manifold evils they have committed. Because this icchantika possesses a mind of arrogance, although they commit many evils, they feel no fear whatsoever regarding these matters. For this reason, they do not attain nirvana; it is like a monkey grasping at the moon in the water.
"Good son!

Even if all immeasurable sentient beings were simultaneously to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, these Tathāgatas would still not perceive that one icchantika attaining bodhi; for this reason, it is called 'not seeing what is accomplished.'"
Furthermore, one does not see who it is that acts; that is to say, one does not see the act of the Tathāgata.

The Buddha teaches sentient beings that they possess buddha-nature, yet those of the icchantika class wander through birth and death and are unable to know or see it. For this reason, it is called "not seeing the act of the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, an icchantika perceives that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate nirvāṇa and asserts that this is true impermanence, just like the extinguishing of a lamp when both the wick and the oil are exhausted. Why is this so?
Because this person’s evil karma has not been diminished.

If there is a bodhisattva who dedicates the wholesome karma they have performed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even if those who are *icchantikas* should revile, destroy, and disbelieve it, the bodhisattvas still bestow it upon them, desiring to achieve the unsurpassed path together with them.
Why is this? Such is the nature of all Buddhas:
"Evil deeds do not bear fruit immediately, just as milk does not turn into curd at once."
Just as ashes cover a fire, the fool lightly treads upon it.
Those who hold to the icchantika view are called "blind"; therefore, they do not see the path of the Arhat.
Just as an Arhat does not travel the perilous and evil paths of birth and death, those who revile the Vaipulya sutras because they lack insight likewise do not wish to practice them.
Just as an Arhat diligently cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, it is the same with the Icchantikas who do not cultivate the Vaipulya sutras.
If a person says:
"I now do not believe in the Śrāvaka sūtras, but believe in and accept the Mahāyāna; I read, recite, and explain it; therefore, I am now a bodhisattva."

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; by virtue of this Buddha-nature, within the bodies of sentient beings there already exist the ten powers, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.
What I have spoken does not differ from what the Buddha has spoken.
Now, together with me, you shall destroy immeasurable evil afflictions, just as one breaks a water jar; because these fetters are destroyed, you will immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Although such a person delivers this exposition, their mind does not truly believe in the existence of Buddha-nature; they speak according to the text merely for the sake of gain and sustenance. One who speaks in this manner is called an evil person."
Such evil persons do not receive the fruit [of their actions] immediately, just as milk becomes curd.

For example, it is like a king’s messenger who is skilled in discourse and adept at expedient means; when commissioned to another country, he would rather lose his own life than ever conceal the instructions spoken by the king.

The wise person is likewise; among ordinary beings, they do not begrudge their own body or life, but resolutely proclaim the Mahāyāna Vaipulya and the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
"Good son!
There is an icchantika who assumes the appearance of an arhat and dwells in a secluded place, slandering the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
When ordinary people see him, they all say: 'This true arhat is a great bodhisattva mahāsattva.'"
These icchantikas and wicked bhikṣus dwell in araṇya hermitages, yet they destroy the dharma of the araṇya; seeing others obtain gain, they give rise to envy in their hearts and speak thus:
"All the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras have been spoken by the Māra Pāpīyas."
They also claim that the Tathāgata is a phenomenon subject to impermanence, that he destroys the True Dharma, and that he disrupts the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, they say:
"What Pāpīyān has spoken is not a teaching that is good or in accordance with the truth."
Having thus proclaimed such evil teachings, this person commits evil and yet does not immediately receive retribution, just as milk does not instantly turn into curd,
or as a fool might lightly step upon fire covered by ashes.
Such persons are called icchantikas.

Therefore, you should know that the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras are necessarily pure; just as when a maṇi jewel is cast into turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear, so too it is with the Mahāyāna sūtras.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as a lotus flower, when illuminated by the sun, never fails to bloom, so it is with all sentient beings.

If they encounter the sun of the Great Nirvana, those who have not yet resolved to attain awakening will all resolve their minds for the sake of Bodhi. Therefore, I say that the pores of the body entered by the light of the Great Nirvana will certainly become sublime causes."

Although those icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, they are entangled by immeasurable defilements of sin and cannot escape them, like a silkworm within its cocoon. Due to these karmic conditions, they are unable to produce the sublime cause of bodhi and continue to transmigrate through birth and death without end.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the utpala flower, the padma flower, the kumuda flower, and the puṇḍarīka flower grow from the mud, yet are ultimately never defiled by that mud."

If there are sentient beings who cultivate this subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, it is likewise so: although they possess afflictions, they will ultimately never be defiled by these afflictions.
Why is this? It is because of the power of knowing the nature and characteristics of the Tathāgata. Good son!
It is like a country where there is much cool and refreshing wind; when it touches the pores of the bodies of sentient beings, it can eliminate all the afflictions of stifling heat.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this: it enters universally into the pores of all sentient beings, acting as the subtle and wondrous causal condition for Bodhi, with the sole exception of those who hold to the icchantika view.
Why is this? Because they are not vessels for the Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!
For example, it is like a skilled physician who understands the eight kinds of medicine and can eliminate all diseases, except for those that are inevitably fatal.

All sūtras, dhyānas, and samādhis are likewise able to treat all illnesses of greed, anger, and ignorance, as well as the various afflictions; they can extract the poisonous thorns and arrows of the defilements, yet they cannot cure the transgression of the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution.
"Good son!

Furthermore, there is a skilled physician who has mastered the eight branches of medical science and is able to eliminate all the sufferings of illness possessed by sentient beings, yet he alone cannot cure a disease that is destined for death."

This Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is also like this: it can eliminate all the afflictions of sentient beings and establish them in the pure and wondrous cause of the Tathāgata; it causes those who have not yet resolved to attain the resolve, with the sole exception of those icchantikas who are destined for death.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who can use wondrous medicines to treat those who are blind, enabling them to see the sun, the moon, the stars, all luminous forms, and every variety of color; yet he alone cannot cure one who is born blind."

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise so: it can open the eye of wisdom for those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, causing them to dwell securely in the immeasurable and boundless Mahāyāna sūtras; even those who have not yet resolved their minds—namely, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution—it can cause all of them to give rise to the bodhicitta, with the sole exception of the congenitally blind class of icchantikas.

Furthermore, good son! It is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in the eight branches of medicine. To treat all the sufferings of illness in sentient beings, he provides various prescriptions: emetics and purgatives, as well as ointments for the body, medicinal fumes, nasal drops, powders, and pills. If a poor or ignorant person is unwilling to take them, the skilled physician, out of compassion, takes that person back to their home and forces them to take the medicine;

by the power of the medicine, the ailment is removed. When a woman is giving birth and the afterbirth does not come out, he gives her medicine to take; once she has taken it, it comes out immediately, and it also ensures the infant is peaceful and free from affliction.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise: wherever it goes, whether it reaches a house or a dwelling, it can eliminate the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings; those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, as well as those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, are all caused to resolve their minds, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To commit the four grave prohibitions and the five deeds of immediate retribution is called the most extreme evil; it is like cutting off the head of a tāla tree, which will never grow again. Since such persons have not yet resolved to attain bodhi, how can you enable them to produce the cause for bodhi?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If these sentient beings, while dreaming, dream that they have fallen into hell and undergo various sufferings and afflictions, they immediately give rise to a mind of repentance:
"Alas! We have brought this sin upon ourselves. If we can now escape from this transgression, we shall certainly resolve to attain bodhicitta; what we have just witnessed is most extremely evil."
Having awakened from this, he immediately understood that the True Dharma yields great fruit and reward; just as that infant gradually grows up, he constantly reflects:
"This physician is most excellent, for he is skilled in understanding prescriptions and medicines."
"When I was originally in the womb, medicine was given to my mother; because of that medicine, her body attained peace and stability.
By this cause and condition, my life was preserved."

How marvelous! My mother underwent great suffering and distress; she carried me in her womb for a full ten months, and after I was born, she removed the wet for the dry, cleared away impurities such as excrement and urine, nourished me with milk, and protected my body.
"For this reason, I shall repay his kindness by providing for him with material needs, attending to him, and making offerings in accordance with his wishes.

Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, if at the time of death they bring to mind this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, then despite falling into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, heavens, or the human world, this sūtra will likewise serve as the cause for their enlightenment—excepting only the icchantikas.

"Furthermore, noble son! It is like a skilled physician or a physician’s son whose knowledge is profound and surpasses that of all other doctors; he is well-versed in the unsurpassed incantations for removing poison. Whether it be a malignant venomous snake, a dragon, or a viper, he renders them harmless through various incantations and medicinal herbs. He even takes this medicine and smears it upon leather sandals; when these sandals touch any venomous insects, their poison is neutralized—except for one particular poison called the 'Great Dragon'."

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise so: if there are sentient beings who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, it can entirely eliminate them and cause them to abide in bodhi. Just as medicinal leather shoes can neutralize various poisons, it can cause those who have not yet resolved their minds to do so, establishing them securely upon the path to bodhi.

Because of the majestic power of this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra as a medicinal elixir, it causes all sentient beings to give rise to peace and happiness, with the sole exception of those great dragons who are icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a person who coats a great drum with a mixture of poisons and strikes it among a great multitude, causing it to sound. Although they have no desire to hear it, those who hear it all die, with the sole exception of one person who will not die an untimely death."

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise so: wherever there are beings among the multitudes of conditioned phenomena who hear its sound, all their greed, hatred, and delusion are completely extinguished.

Even if there is no conscious thought within them, by the power of the causal conditions of this Great Nirvāṇa, they are able to extinguish afflictions, and their fetters are naturally eliminated. Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, upon hearing this sūtra, will also create the causal conditions for supreme bodhi; they will gradually sever their afflictions, with the sole exception of the icchantikas who meet with untimely deaths.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the dark of night, when all activities and undertakings come to a halt; whatever remains unfinished must wait for the light of day."

Those who study the Mahāyāna, though they may cultivate all the samādhis of the sūtras, must await the sun of the Great Mahāparinirvāṇa to hear the subtle and secret teachings of the Tathāgata; only then shall they undertake the work of bodhi and dwell securely in the True Dharma.
Just as when the heavens send down rain, it moistens and causes all seeds to grow and flourish, bringing forth fruit and completely eliminating famine so that many enjoy abundance and happiness;

so too is the immeasurable Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury. This sutra appearing in the world is like those fruits, providing great benefit and peace and happiness for all, enabling sentient beings to perceive their Buddha-nature.

As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the eight thousand śrāvakas received their predictions of enlightenment and attained the great fruit; like the harvest in autumn followed by storage in winter, there was nothing further to be done.
The icchantikas are also like this; they perform no cultivation or application toward any wholesome dharmas.

"Furthermore, good son, it is like a skilled physician who hears that another's child has been seized by a non-human spirit. He immediately prepares an excellent medicine and dispatches a messenger, commanding the messenger, saying:"
“Take this medicine and give it quickly to that person.
If that person encounters any malevolent spirits or ghosts, by the power of this medicine, they shall all depart far away.”
"If you are delayed, I shall go myself; I will by no means allow him to die a violent or unjust death.
If that sick person is able to see the messenger and my majestic power, all their sufferings shall be removed, and they shall attain peace and happiness."

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise so. Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or followers of other paths, if there are those who can receive and uphold such a sūtra, read and recite it until they have mastered it, and further analyze and explain it extensively for others, or if they write it themselves or cause others to write it—these all constitute causes and conditions for bodhi.

If one has committed the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, or is possessed by malevolent spirits, ghosts, or poisons, upon hearing this sutra, all such evils will be completely extinguished—just as when one sees a skilled physician, evil ghosts depart far away. You should know that such a person is a true Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Why is this? Because they have briefly heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and because they have also given rise to the thought that the Tathāgata is eternal.

If even those who have merely heard it for a moment obtain such [benefits], how much more so for those who copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite it—excluding the icchantikas; all others are indeed Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a deaf person who cannot hear sounds.
Those of the icchantika class are just the same; although they wish to listen to this sublime sutra, they are unable to hear it."
Why is this? Because there are no causes or conditions.
Furthermore, son of good family!

For example, suppose there is a skilled physician who has mastered all medical prescriptions and, moreover, possesses extensive knowledge of immeasurable incantations; this physician, upon seeing the king, speaks these words:
"Great King, you now suffer from a disease that is certain to cause death."
The king replied, "You do not see what is within my belly; how can you say that I have a fatal illness?
The physician then answered:
"If you do not believe me, you should take this purgative; once it has been eliminated, Your Majesty may verify it for yourself.

The king refused to take it. At that time, the skilled physician used the power of incantations to cause sores to break out all over the king's anus, while simultaneously inducing diarrhea from which worms and blood were expelled together.
When the king saw this, he was struck with great terror and praised the excellent physician:
"Excellent, excellent!
That which you previously reported, I did not accept."
"Now I know that you have brought great benefit to this body of mine.
He revered the physician as if he were his own father or mother.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise so: for all sentient beings, whether they have desire or are free from desire, it is able to cause their afflictions to crumble and fall away.
If these sentient beings, even in their dreams, should dream of this sutra and revere and make offerings to it— just as a great king reveres a skilled physician—
then this great physician, knowing that the patient is destined to die, will ultimately not treat them.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise; it can ultimately never cure those who are icchantikas.

Furthermore, good son, it is like a skilled physician who thoroughly knows the eight branches of medicine and is able to treat all manner of illnesses, yet alone cannot cure one who is destined to die.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise; they are all able to rescue and heal all those who have committed offenses, except for those who are like the icchantikas—those who are destined for certain death and cannot be cured.
Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in the eight subtle and wondrous medical arts and is further able to master those beyond the eight. Using what he knows, he first instructs his son regarding medicinal herbs found in water, on land, in mountains, or in mountain torrents, causing him to recognize them all. Having thus gradually taught these eight matters, he next teaches other supreme and wondrous arts.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; he first instructs his sons, the bhikṣus and others, to employ skillful means to eliminate all afflictions and to cultivate the perception of the impurity and non-solidity of the body—namely, that it is like water, land, mountains, and mountain torrents.
Water symbolizes the suffering experienced by the body, like bubbles upon the water.
Land symbolizes the lack of solidity in the body, like a plantain tree.
The mountain ravines symbolize the cultivation of the notion of non-self amidst afflictions.
For this reason, the body is called "selfless.

In this manner, the Tathāgata gradually teaches his disciples the ninefold canon of the Dharma, ensuring they master it thoroughly; only thereafter does he teach the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, speaking of the Tathāgata as eternal for the sake of those who are his children.

The Tathāgata has thus spoken this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, to serve as the cause for bodhi for all sentient beings—both those who have already resolved their minds toward awakening and those who have not—with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
Thus it is, good son!

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and unprecedented; you should know that it is the unsurpassed and excellent physician, the most honored and supreme, the king among all sūtras.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a great ship that travels from this shore of the ocean to the other shore, and then returns from that shore back to this shore."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: riding upon the great jewel-ship of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Mahāyāna, he travels back and forth, ferrying sentient beings across. Wherever there are those who should be delivered, he causes them all to behold the body of the Tathāgata. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named the Unsurpassed Captain.
Just as there must be a boatman for there to be a boat, and because there is a boatman, sentient beings can cross the great ocean;
so too is it with the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who boards a ship upon the great ocean wishing to cross over; if they obtain a favorable wind, they can traverse immeasurable *yojanas* in a mere moment.

If they do not obtain one, even if they remain there for a long time, passing through immeasurable years, they will not leave their original place; eventually, the ship may be wrecked, and they will drown and die.

Sentient beings are likewise; dwelling in the great ocean of ignorance and birth-and-death, they board the vessel of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). If they encounter the fierce wind of the Great Parinirvāṇa, they can swiftly reach the shore of the Unsurpassed Way; if they do not encounter it, they shall long circulate through immeasurable births and deaths, and at times, being destroyed, they will fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is as if there were a person who, not encountering the wind-king, remained long upon the great ocean and thought to himself:
'We shall surely die here now.'"
While he was reflecting thus, he suddenly encountered a favorable wind that carried him across the sea accordingly, whereupon he spoke again:
"How wonderful is this wind! It is truly unprecedented."
