"May we, as a group, safely pass through this perilous sea.

In the same way, sentient beings who have long dwelt in the great ocean of birth and death within ignorance and affliction, being weary, distressed, and impoverished, have not yet encountered such a wind of the Great Parinirvāṇa; they should therefore give rise to this thought:
"We are certain to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts."

When these sentient beings were thus reflecting, they suddenly encountered the wind of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, which blew upon them in accordance with their needs, leading them into Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Only then did they realize the truth and give rise to a sense of wonder, exclaiming:
"How wonderful! From the past until now, we have never seen or heard of such a subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata."
"Only then will one give rise to pure faith in this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Furthermore, good son,
when a snake sheds its skin, is it dead?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise;
he manifests through skillful means the casting off of this poisonous body—could one then say that the Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to extinction?"
"No, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has skillfully relinquished his body within this Jambudvīpa, just as that venomous snake sheds its old skin; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to be eternally abiding."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a goldsmith who, having obtained fine, genuine gold, fashions various kinds of vessels according to his will.
The Tathāgata is likewise; within the twenty-five states of existence, he is able to manifest all manner of form-bodies in order to transform sentient beings and uproot them from birth and death."
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Boundless Body; although he manifests various kinds of bodies, he is also called eternally abiding and without change.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as the *āmra* tree and the *jambu* tree undergo three transformations in a single year: at times they produce flowers, their colors radiant and flourishing; at times they produce leaves, lush and verdant; and at times they wither and fall, appearing as if dead.
"Good son! What do you think?
Has this tree truly withered and perished?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!

The Tathāgata is likewise; within the triple world he manifests three kinds of bodies—sometimes appearing newly born, sometimes appearing grown, and sometimes entering parinirvāṇa—yet the body of the Tathāgata is in truth not impermanent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva praised him, saying:
"Excellent! It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares: the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Then the various ministers said:
"Bring the *saindhava*!
Now, the term *saindhava* has four referents:
first, salt; second, a vessel; third, water; and fourth, a horse.
These four things all share this same name.
A wise minister, thoroughly understanding this name, will immediately offer water when the king, while bathing, asks for *saindhava*.
If the king, while eating, asks for *saindhava*, they immediately present salt.
If the king, having finished eating and wishing to drink a beverage, asks for *saindhava*, they immediately present a vessel.
If a king wishes to go out for a stroll and asks for *siddhārtha*, the minister immediately presents him with a horse.
In this way, the wise minister skillfully understands the four kinds of secret speech of the great king.
This Mahāyāna sūtra is also like this; it contains four types of impermanence, which the wise minister of the Mahāyāna should thoroughly understand.

If a Buddha appears in the world and speaks of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa for the sake of sentient beings, the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of impermanence for those who conceive of permanence, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of impermanence.

Or again, it may be said that the True Dharma is about to perish; a wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of suffering for those who reckon [only] pleasure, desiring to cause bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of suffering extensively.

Or again, he may say: "I am now suffering from illness, and the community of monks is divided. Wise ministers should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the mark of non-self for those who conceive of a self, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of non-self.

Or again, it may be said that what is called emptiness is right liberation; the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata’s teaching of right liberation as being without the twenty-five states of existence, intended to lead bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of emptiness.
For this reason, this right liberation is called "emptiness" and is also called "immovable.
As for being immovable, it is because within this liberation there is no suffering; therefore, it is immovable.
This right liberation is signless; that which is called "signless" means that there is no form, sound, odor, taste, or tangible object, and for this reason it is named "signless."

This right liberation is permanent and unchanging; within this liberation there is no impermanence, no feverish affliction, and no transformation. Therefore, liberation is called eternally abiding, immutable, and cool.

Furthermore, it may be said that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*; the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata’s teaching on the eternal dharma, intended to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the eternal dharma.

If these bhikṣus are able to train in accordance with this, you should know that such persons are my true disciples; they well understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, just as a wise minister of a great king well understands the king’s intention.
"Good son!
Even this Great King possesses such a method of esoteric speech; how much more so, then, would the Tathāgata not possess it?
Good son!"

Therefore, the subtle and esoteric teaching of the Tathāgata is difficult to comprehend; only those who possess wisdom can understand my profound Buddha-dharma, for it is not something that ordinary worldly beings are capable of believing.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like the palāśa tree, the karṇikāra tree, and the aśoka tree; when they encounter a great drought, they produce neither flowers nor fruit. Likewise, all other things produced by water or on land become entirely withered and parched, lacking any moisture; they cannot grow, and all medicinal herbs lose their potency."
Good son! This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this: after my parinirvāṇa, there will be sentient beings who cannot show it respect and who lack its majestic power.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings do not know the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata. For what reason?
This is because these sentient beings possess meager merit. Furthermore, good son, when the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is about to perish, there will be many bhikṣus who practice evil;

they will not know the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, and being indolent and lazy, they will be unable to read, recite, proclaim, or analyze the True Dharma of the Tathāgata. They are like foolish thieves who discard genuine jewels to carry away grass and chaff. Because they do not understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, they are indolent and lack diligence regarding this sutra. Alas, what a great peril! The future world is truly terrifying.

Alas for sentient beings! They do not diligently listen to or accept this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Only the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and their like are able to grasp the true meaning within this sūtra; they do not cling to the literal words, but follow it without opposition, and explain it for the sake of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a cowherd woman who, wishing to sell milk and desiring great profit, adds two parts of water to it and sells it to another cowherd woman."
Having received it, she added two more parts and sold it again to a woman living near the city.
Having received it, that woman also added two more parts and sold it again to a woman within the city.
Having obtained it, she added two more portions and went to the market to sell it.
At that time, there was a man who, having taken a wife for his son, required high-quality milk to entertain his guests; he went to the market intending to purchase some.
This milk seller asked for a high price, to which the man replied:
"Your milk contains much water and is not worth that much;
however, as I am currently attending to my guests, I shall take it."
Having taken it, he returned home and boiled it to make a gruel; it had no flavor of milk at all. Although it was flavorless, it was a thousand times superior among bitter flavors.
Why is this? Because the flavor of milk is the foremost among all flavors. Good son!

After my parinirvāṇa, when eighty years remain before the True Dharma has vanished, this sutra shall be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa. At that time, there will be many wicked bhikṣus who will abridge this sutra and divide it into many parts, thereby destroying the color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor of the True Dharma.

These evil persons, although they may recite and study such sutras, eliminate the profound and secret essential meanings of the Tathāgata and instead establish worldly ornamental rhetoric and meaningless speech; they copy what precedes and place it after, copy what follows and place it before, place what is before and after in the middle, and place what is in the middle before and after.
You should know that such evil bhikṣus are companions of Māra; they accept and store all kinds of impure things, yet claim that the Tathāgata has permitted them to possess such items.

Just as a cowherd woman adds excessive water to milk, so too are the wicked bhikṣus; by intermingling worldly speech and erroneously determining this sutra, they cause many sentient beings to fail to correctly explain, copy, grasp, revere, praise, and make offerings to it with respect.

These evil bhikṣus, for the sake of gain and offerings, will be unable to widely proclaim and disseminate this sutra; what little they do manage to circulate is insufficient to mention, just like that poor cowherd woman who sells milk from one person to another until it becomes gruel, yet lacks the flavor of milk.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this: as it is transmitted from one to another, it becomes increasingly thin and diluted until it has no flavor; yet, even though it lacks flavor, it still surpasses other sūtras by a thousandfold, just as the taste of milk surpasses all bitter flavors by a thousandfold.

Why is this? Because this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is the most preeminent among the Śrāvaka sūtras; it is like cow’s milk, the most excellent of all flavors. For this reason, it is called the Great Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, good son!
Among good men and good women, there are none who do not seek a male body. Why is this?
All women are abodes where all manner of evils dwell.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as the urine of a mosquito cannot moisten this great earth, so too is it with women: their lustful desires are difficult to satisfy.
For example, if the entire great earth were made into pellets the size of mustard seeds, even if all such men were to engage in sexual acts with a single woman, they would still not satisfy her.
Even if there were as many men as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they could not satisfy the desires of a single woman. Good son!
It is like the great ocean: though all the rains from heaven, the hundreds of rivers, and the myriad streams pour into it, that great ocean is never filled.
The nature of women is likewise thus: even if all beings were to become men, they would still not be enough for a single woman to satisfy her desires with them all.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like the aśoka tree, the pāṭala tree, and the karṇikāra tree; when their spring flowers bloom, bees suck their colors, fragrances, and subtle flavors, never knowing satiety.
It is likewise with women who desire men; they never know contentment.
Good son! For this reason, all good sons and good daughters who hear this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra should always censure the characteristics of women and seek out those of men.
Why is this? Because this great sūtra possesses the marks of a man, namely, the Buddha-nature. If a person does not know this Buddha-nature, they lack the characteristics of a man.
Why is this? Because they are unable to know for themselves that they possess the Buddha-nature.
If there are those who cannot know the Buddha-nature, I say that such people are called "women."
If one can know for oneself that the Buddha-nature exists, I declare that such a person possesses the marks of a true man (*puruṣa*).
If there are women who can know that their own bodies certainly possess the Buddha-nature, you should understand that these individuals are, in fact, men.
"Good son!
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is an accumulation of immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. Why is this so?"
Because this explains the secret treasury of the Tathāgata,
therefore, sons and daughters of good family who wish to swiftly understand the secret treasury of the Tathāgata should diligently cultivate this sutra through skillful means.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
So it is, so it is.”

As the Buddha has taught, I now possess the marks of a great man because I have entered the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata; today the Tathāgata has finally awakened me, and by this means I have attained definitive penetration.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken,
son of good family!”
"You are now speaking these words in accordance with worldly conventions.
Kāśyapa replied again,
"I do not follow worldly conventions."
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
That you have now been able to know this unsurpassed flavor of the Dharma—so profound and difficult to comprehend—is just like a bee gathering nectar; you are exactly like that.”
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as the moisture from a mosquito cannot saturate this great earth, so too will it be when this sutra circulates in future ages; it will be like that mosquito's moisture.
When the True Dharma is about to perish, this sutra shall first disappear from this land; you should know that this is a sign of the decline of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like the end of summer: the first month is called autumn, when the autumn rains fall continuously.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise; for the sake of the bodhisattvas in the southern region, it shall be widely disseminated, raining down the rain of Dharma to fill that place completely.
When the True Dharma is about to perish, it shall reach Kaśmīra, where it will remain complete and without deficiency, yet submerged within the earth.
Whether there be those who have faith or those who lack faith, this ambrosial flavor of the Dharma—the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras—will all be submerged within the earth.
Once this sutra has disappeared, all other Mahāyāna scriptures will likewise perish and vanish.

If those who are like elephant-kings among men—the bodhisattvas—should obtain this sutra in its entirety and without deficiency, they should know that the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata will soon be extinguished.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Nine;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
In the fourth chapter, "The Nature of the Tathāgata," section seven,
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Now this Cunda still harbors doubts; I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain further for him, so that he may attain the severance of them.
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
"What is doubt?
You should explain it, and I shall sever it for you.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Cunda harbors a doubt regarding the Tathāgata’s permanence.

Because he has attained the power of knowing and seeing the Buddha-nature, he thinks: 'If it is permanent because one sees the Buddha-nature, then before one had seen it, it must have been impermanent.'"
If they were originally impermanent, they would likewise be so later. Why is this?

Just as worldly objects that did not exist before now exist, and having existed, return to non-existence—all such things are impermanent. For this reason, there is no distinction between Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"What existed originally now does not exist; what did not exist originally now exists.
That there could be such a thing as a dharma existing throughout the three periods of time—this is impossible."
“Good son, for this reason, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are both distinct and not distinct.”
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying:
"Excellent! It is truly as the Holy One has taught. I have now for the first time understood that the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are both distinct and non-distinct."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Tathāgata has taught, there is no difference in nature among the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.”
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain this in detail for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
Son of good family!
It is like a householder or a householder’s son who keeps many milk cows of various colors, always employing one person to guard and nourish them.

At one time, this person, for the sake of a sacrificial offering, gathered all the cows together and placed them in a single vessel; seeing that the color of their milk was uniformly white, he was immediately struck with wonder and asked himself: "The colors of these cows are each different, so how is it that their milk is all of the same color?"
This person reflects:
"All of this is due to the causes and conditions of the karmic retribution of sentient beings that makes the color of the milk uniform. Good son!
It is the same for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; they share the same buddha-nature, just like that milk.
Why is this? Because they are equally exhausted of outflows (āsrava).
Yet sentient beings say:
"There are distinctions between Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
There are Śrāvakas and ordinary people who harbor doubts regarding the Three Vehicles, asking: 'How can there be no distinction?'"
After a long time, these sentient beings will understand for themselves that all three vehicles share the same Buddha-nature;
they will be like that person who, through the causes and conditions of karma, awakens to and understands the true nature of milk.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like gold ore: after the dross has been washed away and refined, it is subsequently melted down; once it has become gold, its value is immeasurable.
Good son!
It is the same for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; they all achieve the same buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because they eliminate afflictions, they are like gold ore from which all dross and impurities have been removed.
For this reason, all sentient beings possess the same Buddha-nature, without any distinction.

Because they have previously heard of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury and will naturally come to know it upon attaining Buddhahood, just as that elder knew that milk has a single characteristic. Why is this?
"Because they have severed immeasurable billions of afflictions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, what difference is there between a Buddha and sentient beings?
To speak in such a manner involves many faults.
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what cause and condition did Śāriputra and others enter parinirvāṇa through a lesser nirvāṇa?
Do those who are pratyekabuddhas attain parinirvāṇa through the nirvāṇa within [the realm of] phenomena?
Do those who are bodhisattvas attain parinirvāṇa through great parinirvāṇa?
If such persons possess the same buddha-nature as the Buddha, for what reason do they not attain parinirvāṇa through the same nirvāṇa as the Tathāgata?

“Good son! The nirvāṇa attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is not that which is attained by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, Mahāparinirvāṇa is called a 'wholesome existence' (kuśalabhava).”
"If there were no Buddhas in the world, would it not be that the two vehicles could still attain their respective nirvāṇas?
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha said,
“Only once in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas does a single Buddha appear in the world to reveal and teach the Three Vehicles. Good son!

Regarding what you have said—that there is no distinction between Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles—I have already explained that meaning herein, within this Great Nirvana, the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata.
The Arhats have no further existence of conditioned goodness. Why is this?
Because all Arhats shall attain this Great Parinirvāṇa.
"For this reason, Mahāparinirvāṇa possesses ultimate bliss; therefore, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa said, "According to what the Buddha has taught, I now for the first time understand the meaning of distinction and the meaning of non-distinction."

Why is this? Because all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas shall in future ages return to the Great Parinirvāṇa, just as all rivers flow into the great ocean; therefore, these Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are all called "eternal," and not "impermanent."
"For this reason, there is both distinction and non-distinction.
Kāśyapa asked, "In what way is there distinction in their nature?"
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Śrāvakas are like milk;
pratyekabuddhas are like curd; bodhisattvas are like fresh and refined butter; and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like the finest cream.”
"For this reason, within the Great Nirvāṇa, four types of nature are taught, and therein lies their distinction.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"What are the characteristics and natures of all sentient beings?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! Just as when a cow is newly born, milk and blood are not yet distinguished, so too is the nature of ordinary persons, which is mixed with various afflictions.”
Kāśyapa spoke again:

“In the city of Kuśinagara there is a candāla named Nandika. The Buddha has prophesied that because of this single arousal of the thought of awakening, he shall swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path among the number of the thousand buddhas of this world-system.”
"For what reason did the Tathāgata not grant the prediction that the Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others would swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
There may be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas who make this vow:
"I shall protect and uphold the True Dharma for a long time, and only thereafter shall I attain the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood."
"Because he has made this swift vow, I grant him a swift prediction [of enlightenment].
Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like a merchant who possesses a priceless jewel and goes to the marketplace to sell it."
When the foolish people saw it, they did not recognize it and laughed at it lightly.
The master of the jewels proclaimed:
"The value of this jewel of mine is incalculable."
Having heard this, they laughed again and said to one another, "This is not a true jewel; it is a crystal bead.

Son of good family, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are just like this: if they hear of a swift prediction [of enlightenment], they immediately become indolent, laughing lightly and treating it with contempt, just like those fools who do not recognize a true jewel.

In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who are unable to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas; driven by poverty, hardship, and hunger, they will leave the household life merely to nourish their own bodies. Their minds will be fickle and frivolous, and they will maintain themselves through wrong livelihoods with deceit and crookedness. If they hear that the Tathāgata has bestowed upon the śrāvakas predictions of swift enlightenment, they will then laugh out loud, treating it with contempt and disparaging it.
You should know that these individuals are precisely those who have broken the precepts, yet claim for themselves that they have attained superhuman states.
For this reason, because they have made rapid vows, I grant them rapid predictions [of enlightenment].
"Those who protect the true Dharma shall receive a distant prediction [of their future enlightenment].
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtain an indestructible retinue?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If bodhisattvas apply themselves with diligent vigor, desiring to protect the True Dharma, by virtue of these causes and conditions, the retinue they obtain shall be indestructible."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions do sentient beings experience their lips and mouths becoming parched and withered?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are those who do not recognize that the Three Jewels are eternally present, by reason of this, their lips and mouths will become parched and withered.
It is like a person whose sense of taste is impaired, unable to distinguish between the six flavors: sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and bland."
All sentient beings are foolish and lack wisdom; they do not recognize that the Three Jewels are eternal dharmas. For this reason, they are said to have parched lips and mouths.
Furthermore, good son!
If there are sentient beings who do not know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, you should know that such persons are like those born blind.
If they know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, although such persons possess only the physical eye, I declare them to be endowed with the divine eye.
Furthermore, good son!

If there are those who can know that the Tathāgata is eternal, you should know that these people have long since practiced such sūtras; I say that these individuals are also called "those with the divine eye."

Although they possess the divine eye, they cannot know that the Tathāgata is eternal; therefore, I say that such people are called those with the "fleshly eye. Such persons do not even recognize their own hands, feet, limbs, or joints, nor can they cause others to recognize them; for this reason, they are called those with the fleshly eye.
"Furthermore, good son!
The Tathāgata constantly acts as a father and mother for all sentient beings. Why is this so?

Of all sentient beings, with their various forms and kinds—whether two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, or legless—the Buddha preaches the Dharma to them with a single voice; each of those different species attains understanding according to its own kind and each exclaims:
"The Tathāgata today is preaching the Dharma for me."
For this reason, they are called "parents.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who has given birth to a child;
although the child may speak at sixteen months of age, its speech cannot yet be understood.
"When those parents wish to teach their child to speak, they first mimic the child's own sounds and gradually instruct them; would the speech of those parents not be correct? "No, it would not."
“World-Honored One!

‘Good son, it is likewise with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: they preach the Dharma according to the various voices of sentient beings in order to cause them to dwell securely in the True Dharma. They manifest various forms according to what each should see. Is it not correct that the Tathāgata thus conforms to their language?’”
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"What the Tathāgata speaks is like the lion’s roar; following the various sounds of the world, he extols and expounds the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Chapter Five: All the Great Assembly Asks Questions. At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his face various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—radiating brilliant light that illuminated the body of Cunda. Having encountered this, Cunda, together with his retinue, took various delicacies and hurried to the Buddha's presence, desiring to offer the final almsgiving to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus.
Various vessels, filled and complete, were carried before the Buddha.
At that time, a celestial being of great majesty and virtue blocked his path, surrounding him on all sides, and said to Cunda: "Stop, Cunda!"
"Do not yet present your offering.

At that time, the Tathāgata again emitted immeasurable and boundless rays of various light; having encountered this light, the great assembly of devas immediately permitted Cunda to proceed before the Buddha and present his offering.
At that time, the devas, humans, and all other sentient beings each took the offerings they held and approached the Buddha. Kneeling with their right knees on the ground, they addressed the Buddha:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will permit the bhikṣus to accept this food and drink."
At that time, the bhikṣus, knowing it was the proper hour, took up their robes and bowls with single-minded composure.

Then Cunda prepared various lion thrones made of precious jewels for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, hanging silk streamers, banners, canopies, flowers, incense, and necklaces. At that moment, the adornments of the trichiliocosm were so subtle and exquisite that they resembled the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
At that time, Cunda stood before the Buddha and, filled with grief, sorrow, and despondency, addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will still look upon me with compassion and remain for a kalpa, or at least slightly less than a kalpa."
The Buddha told Cunda:
"If you wish for me to remain long in the world, you should quickly offer this final, complete perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
At that time, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, humans, and various other beings cried out with one voice in unison:
"How marvelous, Cunda!
You have accomplished such great merit that you are able to cause the Tathāgata to accept this final, unsurpassed offering.
As for those of us who lack such merit, our prepared offerings shall be in vain."

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to fulfill the aspirations of all the assembly, manifested immeasurable Buddhas from every single pore of his own body; each of these Buddhas was accompanied by an immeasurable community of bhikṣus.
All these World-Honored Ones and their immeasurable assemblies all manifested themselves to receive those offerings, while Śākyamuni Tathāgata himself received that which was presented by Cunda.

At that time, the refined rice and matured foods brought by Cunda, which amounted to eight bushels from the kingdom of Magadha, were all made sufficient for the entire great assembly through the supernatural power of the Buddha.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Cunda felt great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight; the entire great assembly was likewise moved.
Then, receiving the Buddha’s holy intent, the great assembly each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata has now accepted our offerings; before long, he shall enter into nirvana."
Having formed this thought, his heart was filled with both sorrow and joy.

At that time, the ground of the grove was narrow and small; yet, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, even at the tip of a needle there sat immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, together with their retinues, all eating. The food they consumed was likewise without any distinction.
At that time, the devas, asuras, and others wept and lamented, saying:
"The Tathāgata has today accepted our final offering; having accepted this offering, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. To whom else shall we offer worship?"
"I have now forever been separated from the Unsurpassed Tamer; I am blind and without eyes.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to console the entire great assembly, spoke these verses:
"Do not lament, you all; Such is the natural law for all Buddhas."
I entered nirvāṇa already immeasurable kalpas ago;
Constantly experiencing the most supreme bliss, Forever dwelling in the place of peace and security.
Listen now with a sincere heart, And I shall speak of nirvāṇa.
I have already transcended the perception of food, and thus I am forever free from the affliction of hunger and thirst.
Now, for your sake, I shall proclaim the aspiration that accords with reality,
so that all beings may attain peace and happiness.
Upon hearing this, you should practice accordingly; the Dharma of all Buddhas abides eternally.
Even if a crow and an owl were to perch together upon the same tree like close brothers, only then would you enter final nirvana.
The Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula;
ever the Honored One of sentient beings, how could he enter final nirvāṇa?
Suppose a snake, a rat, and a wolf were to dwell and roam together in a single hole.
Loving one another like brothers, you shall then enter eternal nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula;
as the constant honored one of sentient beings, how could you enter eternal nirvāṇa?
Even if the saptaparṇa flower were to turn into the vārṣika fragrance,
and the karkandhu tree were to turn into the tinduka fruit,
the Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula.
How can one abandon compassion and enter nirvana forever?
Even if an icchantika were to manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way and dwell eternally in the supreme bliss, only then would they enter nirvana.
The Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula;
how can you abandon compassion and enter parinirvāṇa forever?
Even if all sentient beings were to attain the Way of the Buddha simultaneously, [you would still not depart].
Having distanced oneself from all faults and afflictions, one then enters nirvana.
The Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula;
how could he abandon his compassion and enter nirvana forever?
Even if the urine of a mosquito were to soak and destroy the great earth,
and all the mountains and hundreds of rivers were to fill the vast ocean to its brim—
only when such a thing occurs will you enter nirvana.
Beholding all with a heart of compassion, as if each were Rāhula, you have always been honored by sentient beings; how could you enter parinirvāṇa forever?
For this reason, you all should take deep delight in the True Dharma.
One should not give rise to grief or distress, nor wail and weep.
If one desires to practice correctly oneself, one should cultivate the permanence of the Tathāgata;
one should contemplate this Dharma as eternally abiding and unchanging.
Furthermore, one should give rise to this thought: that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding;
by this, one obtains great protection, just as a withered tree is made to bear fruit through incantation.
This is what is called the Three Jewels; the fourfold assembly should listen well.
Having heard this, one should rejoice and immediately resolve upon bodhicitta.
If one can regard the Triple Gem as eternally abiding and identical with ultimate truth,
this is the supreme vow of all Buddhas.

"If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who are able to make vows by means of the Tathāgata’s supreme vows, you should know that such persons are free from folly and worthy of receiving offerings;
by the power of these vows, their meritorious fruits and retributions shall be most excellent in the world, like those of an arhat."
If there are those who cannot thus contemplate and realize that the Triple Gem is eternal, they are outcasts (caṇḍāla).

If there are those who can know the causes and conditions of the true Dharma by which the Triple Gem abides eternally, they will be free from suffering and find peace and happiness; no one shall be able to harm or obstruct them.

At that time, the great assembly of humans and devas, as well as the asuras and others, having heard this Dharma, felt joy arise in their hearts; they leaped for joy immeasurably, their minds became supple and gentle, they skillfully extinguished all hindrances, their minds were free from arrogance or dejection, their majestic virtue was pure, and their countenances were serene and pleased.

Knowing that the Buddha is eternally abiding, they therefore established various celestial offerings, scattering diverse flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, and playing celestial music to make offerings to the Buddha.

The Buddha said:

If one commits the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, and knowing for certain that such heavy transgressions have been committed, feels no fear, shame, or remorse from the outset, refuses to confess them, possesses no heart to protect, cherish, or establish the Buddha’s true Dharma, and instead slanders, despises, and speaks with many faults—such persons are also said to be heading toward the path of the icchantika.
If, moreover, one speaks of the non-existence of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, such persons are also said to be heading toward the path of the icchantika.
With the exception of those who are such icchantikas, giving to all others is praised.
At that time, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As for what you have called 'breaking the precepts,' what is its meaning?"
He replied: "Cunda!
Those who commit the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, or who slander the True Dharma—such persons as these are called 'those who have broken the precepts.'"
Cunda asked again:
"If one has thus broken the precepts, can such a person still be rescued?
He replied:
"Cunda! Because there are causes and conditions, one may still be rescued.
If you have donned the dharma robes and have not yet cast them off or distanced yourself from them, and if your mind constantly harbors shame, remorse, and fear, such that you reproach yourself:..."
"Alas! Why have you committed such a grave offense?
How strange it is that you have created such karma of suffering!
With this thought, his heart was transformed by repentance; he gave rise to a mind that protects the Dharma and desired to establish the True Dharma.
"Wherever there are those who protect the Dharma, I shall make offerings to them.

If there are those who read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures, I shall consult them; having received, upheld, read, and recited them, and once I have mastered them thoroughly, I shall further analyze and explain them extensively for others."
"I say that such a person has not broken the precepts. Why is this?
O son of good family!"
Just as the rising sun can dispel all dust, obscurations, and darkness, so too is it with this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa appearing in the world;

it can eliminate the manifold sins committed by sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas. Therefore, this sūtra teaches that protecting the True Dharma yields great rewards and rescues those who have violated the precepts.

If there are those who slander this True Dharma, yet are able to repent and return to the Dharma, reflecting upon all their unwholesome deeds as if they had harmed themselves, and giving rise to fear, alarm, and shame—realizing that apart from this True Dharma there is no other protection—they should therefore return to the True Dharma. If one can thus take refuge as prescribed, bestowing gifts upon such a person yields immeasurable merit, and they are also called a worthy recipient of offerings in the world.

If one commits the offenses of the aforementioned evil karma and, for a period of one month or fifteen days, does not give rise to the mind of taking refuge and confessing, then the fruit and retribution bestowed upon such a person will be very meager.

It is the same for those who have committed the five heinous crimes: if they can give rise to a mind of repentance and harbor a sense of shame and remorse within, thinking, "The unwholesome karma I have now created will result in great suffering."
"I shall establish and protect the True Dharma.
This does not constitute a grave offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*); rather, if one gives to such a person, the merit obtained is immeasurable.
However, if after committing a grave offense one fails to give rise to the mind of protecting the Dharma and taking refuge, the merit of giving to such a person is insufficient to mention.
Furthermore, son of good family!
As for those who have committed grave offenses, listen attentively now as I shall analyze and explain this to you in detail:

you should give rise to this thought—that the True Dharma is the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata; therefore, I shall protect, uphold, and establish it, and one who bestows it upon such a person will obtain a supreme karmic reward.
"Good son!
It is like a woman who, while pregnant and nearing childbirth, encounters the chaos of a national famine and flees to another land, where she gives birth immediately within a celestial temple."

Hearing that his native land was peaceful, secure, and prosperous, he took his son with him, intending to return home. On the way, they encountered a river whose waters were swollen and flowing violently; unable to carry his child across while bearing him on his back, he thought to himself:
"I would rather meet my death here together with him than abandon him to cross alone."
Having thought this, both mother and son perished together.
After their lives ended, they were immediately reborn in the heavens because she had cherished her son with compassion, wishing for him to attain liberation across the ocean of suffering.
Although this woman was by nature wicked and evil, it was solely because of her love for her son that she attained birth in the heavens.

Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, if they give rise to the mind that protects the Dharma, it is likewise so; although they may have previously performed unwholesome karma, by virtue of protecting the Dharma, they become the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Such is the immeasurable retribution obtained by one who protects the Dharma.
Cunda spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
If an icchantika is able to repent and reform, and respectfully makes offerings to and praises the Triple Gem—would giving to such a person yield a great karmic reward?”
The Buddha said, "Good son!
You should not speak in such a manner now."
Good son! It is like a person who, having eaten an āmra fruit, spits out the seed and places it on the ground, thinking to himself:
"Within this fruit seed there must be a sweet flavor."
He immediately took it back again, broke it open, and tasted it; finding its flavor to be extremely bitter, he felt regret and remorse.

Fearing that he might lose the seed of the fruit, he gathered it up once more and planted it in the ground, tending to it with diligent care and irrigating it at the proper times with ghee, oil, and milk.
"What do you think?
Could it possibly arise?
"No, [World-Honored One]."
“World-Honored One!
Even if the heavens were to send down unsurpassed sweet rain, it still would not grow. “Good son!”
That icchantika is also like this: having burned away his roots of goodness, in what place could he possibly find purification from his offenses?
Good son, if he were to give rise to a wholesome mind, he would no longer be called an icchantika.
Good son! For this reason, there is no lack of distinction among the fruits and retributions obtained from all acts of giving. Why is this so?

The retribution obtained from giving to the śrāvakas is distinct, and the retribution obtained from giving to the pratyekabuddhas is likewise distinct; only by giving to the Tathāgata does one obtain the unsurpassed fruit. Therefore, it is said that there is no lack of distinction among all acts of giving.
Cunda spoke again:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata spoken this verse?
The Buddha said:
"Cunda! It was for a specific cause and condition that I spoke this verse.

In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) who lacked pure faith and served the Nirgranthas; he came to question me regarding the meaning of giving. For this reason, I spoke this verse, and I also spoke it to explain the meaning of the Secret Treasury for the sake of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others."
What is the meaning of this verse? "All" refers to a partial totality;

one should know that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, a hero among men, embraces those who uphold the precepts and provides them with their necessities, while abandoning those who break the precepts as one discards weeds and tares.
"Furthermore, good son, as I said in a verse in the past:
'All rivers Necessarily have bends and curves.'"
All thickets are necessarily called trees;
all women are necessarily full of guile;
all who possess mastery necessarily enjoy peace and happiness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated before the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these verses:
"Not every river, Necessarily has bends and curves."
Not every forest is entirely composed of trees;
not all women necessarily harbor deceit and crookedness;
and those who possess all power do not necessarily experience happiness.
“The meaning of the verse spoken by the Buddha is incomplete; we pray that you will deign to show us compassion and explain its underlying causes and conditions.
For what reason, World-Honored One?”

In this trichiliocosm, there is a continent named Aparagoyanī; on that continent there is a river, straight and not crooked, named Sābhya, which is like a plumb line and flows directly into the western sea.

Such characteristics of the river have never been spoken of by the Buddha in other sūtras; we only pray that the Tathāgata, within this Vaipulya Āgama, will explain its remaining meaning so that all bodhisattvas may deeply understand this significance.
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who first recognized gold ore, but later did not recognize gold.
The Tathāgata is likewise; although he has fully known all dharmas, that which he expounds is incomplete and not exhaustive.”
Although the Tathāgata has made such other statements, one should skillfully interpret their underlying intent.
To say that "all thickets are necessarily trees" is also a statement with further implications (*savyavaccheda*).
Why is this? Various trees made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and other jewels are also called a forest.
Furthermore, the statement that "all women must harbor flattery and crookedness" is likewise incomplete.
Why is this? There are also women who well maintain the prohibitive precepts, who have accomplished merit, and possess great compassion.
To say that all those who possess mastery will necessarily experience pleasure is likewise incomplete.
Why is this? Those who possess sovereignty—such as the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings and the Tathāgata, the Dharma King—are not subject to the Mara of Death and cannot be extinguished;
whereas the various devas, such as Brahmā and Śakra, though they have attained sovereignty, are all impermanent.
"If one attains that which is eternally abiding and unchanging, it is then called sovereignty—namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said: "Good son!"
You have now well attained the eloquence of joyful speech; cease for a moment and listen attentively.
Mañjuśrī! It is, for example, as if an elder were afflicted by the suffering of illness, and a skilled physician examined him and prepared an ointment for him.
At that time, the patient, out of greed, wished to take much of it.
The physician said to him:
"If you can digest it, then you may take much."
Your body is currently emaciated; you should not consume this in large quantities.
You should know that this ointment is called both "ambrosia" and "poison.
If it is consumed in excess and cannot be digested, it is then called poison.
"Good son! You should not now think that what this physician has said violates the principles of meaning, or that it destroys the potency and power of the medicinal fat. Good son!"

The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of various kings, queens, crown princes, princes, and great ministers—and because King Prasenajit, his princes, and his queen possessed minds of arrogance—he manifested terrors in order to subdue them, just like that skilled physician. Thus he spoke these verses:
"All rivers Necessarily have bends and curves."
All groves are necessarily called trees;
all women necessarily harbor flattery and crookedness;
all who possess mastery necessarily enjoy peace and happiness.
“Mañjuśrī! You should now know that what the Tathāgata speaks is without error or omission; even if this great earth could be turned upside down, the words of the Tathāgata shall never be erroneous.”
"For this reason, all that the Tathāgata has spoken is intentional.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Son of the Dharma King, again spoke in verse before the Buddha:
"In the speech of others, I comply and do not oppose."
“Furthermore, one does not observe whether others act or do not act;
