At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
What the Tathāgata has spoken is likewise not exhaustive.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will again deign to show compassion and explain its causes and conditions. Why is this?
Just as when a householder’s son studies under a teacher, does he belong to the teacher?

If he belongs to the teacher, the goal is not accomplished; if he does not belong to him, it is likewise not accomplished; and even if he attains independence, it is still not accomplished. Therefore, that which was spoken by the Tathāgata is incomplete.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
For example, suppose there is a prince who has not practiced or mastered anything; he fails in every undertaking and is thus subject to the constant suffering of ignorant delusion.

In this same way, if one says that the meaning of "sovereignty" (īśvara) applies to such a prince, it does not hold; nor does the meaning of "being subject to another" hold. For this reason, the meaning spoken by the Buddha is said to be "with remainder" (sāvaśeṣa).

Therefore, it is not the case that all who are subject to others must suffer, nor that all who possess mastery must experience happiness; even those whose arrogance reaches the height of extreme violence and cruelty still have more to come.
World-Honored One!

Just as there are virtuous women who, out of pride, leave the household life to study the Way, upholding the prohibitive precepts and perfecting their dignified deportment, guarding and restraining their sense faculties so they do not run wild and scatter—therefore, all fetters of pride are not necessarily violent or evil.

That all virtuous and good people cherish one another is also incomplete; for example, if a person internally commits one of the four grave prohibitions yet does not discard their dharma robes and maintains their dignified deportment, those who protect the Dharma will not cherish them upon seeing this, and such a person will surely fall into hell at the end of their life.

If a worthy person has committed a grave transgression and a protector of the Dharma sees it, they immediately expel them, causing them to abandon the path and return to lay life; for this reason, why must all who are virtuous and good necessarily be loved?
At that time, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“There is a cause and condition for which the Tathāgata speaks with intentional meaning here;
furthermore, there is a cause and condition for which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, proclaim this Dharma.”
At that time, there was a woman in the city of Rājagṛha named Bhadrā who, while returning to her parents’ home, came to where I was and took refuge in me, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, saying:
"All women lack independence and freedom, whereas all men are autonomous and unimpeded."
"At that time, I, knowing the mind of this woman, immediately proclaimed these verses for her.
Mañjuśrī! Excellent, excellent!"
"You are now able, for the sake of all sentient beings, to ask the Tathāgata about such secret words.
Mañjuśrī then spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings Depend entirely upon food and drink for their existence."
All who possess great power have minds free from envy.
All suffer much illness and pain because of food and drink.
All who cultivate pure conduct attain peace and happiness.
“Thus it is, World-Honored One!
Now that you accept Cunda’s offering of food and drink, will there not be some cause for the Tathāgata to feel fear?
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke a verse for Mañjuśrī:
"Not all sentient beings, Survive solely by depending on food and drink.
Not all who possess great strength Are free from jealousy in their hearts.
Not all who consume food Fall ill with the suffering of disease."
"Not all who practice pure conduct / Are able to receive peace and happiness.
Mañjuśrī! If you were to fall ill, I too would likewise have to experience the suffering of illness."

Why is this? All Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas truly have nothing they consume; yet, desiring to transform others, they manifest the enjoyment of the gifts offered by immeasurable sentient beings, thereby enabling them to fulfill the dānapāramitā and deliver them from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata’s body became emaciated and weak during his six years of ascetic practice, such a thing is impossible.
Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have uniquely transcended all states of existence and are not like ordinary beings, how could their bodies become frail and inferior?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through diligent cultivation, have attained adamantine bodies, which differ from the fragile bodies of worldly people;
my disciples are likewise thus—inconceivable and not dependent upon food.
The phrase "all those of great power who are free from envy" also carries further implications.
For instance, there may be people in the world who, throughout their entire lives, never harbor a mind of envy, yet they nonetheless lack power.

Regarding the statement that all suffering from illness arises from food, there is also another meaning; for one also sees people who contract "guest illnesses," namely those caused by thorns, knives, swords, spears, and lances.

The statement that "all who practice pure conduct experience peace and happiness" is also incomplete; for there are also followers of external paths in the world who, while practicing the Brahma-faring, undergo much suffering and affliction.
For this reason, everything spoken by the Tathāgata is intentional; it is not that the Tathāgata spoke this verse without cause, for he spoke it because there was a cause.
In the past, in this kingdom of Ujjayinī, there was a brahmin named Ajita who came to me desiring to receive the fourth precept of the eightfold fast; at that time, I spoke these verses for him.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by the meaning of ‘without remainder’?”
"What, then, is meant by 'all meanings' (sarvārtha)?
Good son! 'All' refers to everything except for those wholesome dharmas that assist the path and are constantly cherished; this is called 'all,' and it is also called 'without remainder.'"
The remaining dharmas are also called "with remainder" and "without remainder.
This is intended to enable those sons of good family who delight in the Dharma to understand the meaning of this "with remainder" and "without remainder."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight; he came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You regard all sentient beings equally, just as you do Rāhula.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!
What you have now perceived is subtle and profoundly deep."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain the merit obtained from this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! If there are those who hear the name of this sutra, the merit they obtain cannot be fully described by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; only a Buddha can know it."
Why is this? Because the realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable;
how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, master, or transcribe the sutra scrolls!
At that time, the devas, worldlings, and asuras, before the Buddha, spoke in unison with one voice, uttering these verses:
“The Buddhas are inconceivable, And so too are the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Therefore we now entreat you: We pray only that you remain for a while.”
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with Ānanda and the rest of the two assemblies of followers, will arrive in a mere moment.
Also present will be the Lord of Magadha, the Great King Ajātaśatru.
With a sincere heart, I revere and trust in the Buddha, yet he still has not come here.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to show us some compassion and remain;
within this great assembly, please sever all the nets of my doubts.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"The eldest son of my Dharma is named Mahākāśyapa;
Ānanda is diligent and energetic, able to sever all doubts."
You all should observe with careful attention: Ānanda, the man of great learning, will naturally come to understand what is permanent and what is impermanent.
For this reason, you should not harbor sorrow or distress in your hearts.
At that time, the great assembly made offerings of various kinds to the Tathāgata.

Having made these offerings to the Buddha, they immediately resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable, boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, and Cunda.
Having bestowed these predictions, he spoke these words:
"O sons of good family!
Cultivate your own minds and be careful not to be negligent.
I now suffer from a back ailment and my entire body is in pain; I wish now to lie down like that young child or those who are chronically ill.
"You, Mañjuśrī, should extensively expound the Great Dharma for the fourfold assembly; I now entrust this Dharma to you.
Furthermore, when Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and others arrive, you shall again entrust such a True Dharma to them."
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these words, in order to subdue all sentient beings, he manifested illness and lay on his right side, just like a sick person.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Ten;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Manifesting Illness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has already escaped all diseases; his afflictions and sufferings are entirely removed, and he is no longer subject to fear.
World-Honored One!
All sentient beings possess four poisonous arrows, which constitute the causes of illness.
What are these four?
They are greed, hatred, delusion, and arrogance.

When there is a cause for illness, then disease arises—namely, feverish love-sickness, pulmonary disease, shortness of breath and vomiting, numbness and tingling of the limbs, mental confusion and agitation, diarrhea and hiccups, painful urination, pain in the eyes and ears, fullness in the back and distension of the abdomen, insanity, emaciation, and possession by malevolent spirits.
Such various ailments of body and mind as these no longer exist at all for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For what reason does the Tathāgata today look upon Mañjuśrī and address him thus:
"I now have a backache; you should preach the Dharma to the great assembly"?
"There are two causes and conditions by which one is free from the suffering of illness. What are these two?
First, to have compassion for all sentient beings; second, to provide the sick with medicine."

The Tathāgata has already cultivated the bodhisattva path for immeasurable billions of kalpas, constantly practicing kind speech to benefit sentient beings and prevent them from suffering, and bestowing various medicines upon those who are ill; for what reason does he now say that he himself is sick?
World-Honored One!

In this world, there are sick people who, whether sitting or lying down, find no peace in their place; they seek food and drink and instruct their families to manage their estates and businesses. For what reason does the Tathāgata lie here in silence, neither teaching his disciples and śrāvakas the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā), nor the various dhyānas, liberations, samāpattis, and the cultivation of right efforts?
For what reason have such profound Mahāyāna sūtras not been taught?

Why has the Tathāgata not employed immeasurable skillful means to instruct Mahākāśyapa, those elephant-kings among men, and other great beings, so that they would not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"Why do you not discipline those wicked bhikṣus who accept and store all kinds of impure things?
The World-Honored One is truly free from illness; why do you lie silently on your right side?"

Whatever roots of goodness the bodhisattvas obtain from providing medicine and medical care to the sick, they bestow all of it upon sentient beings and collectively dedicate it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), in order to eliminate for sentient beings the obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstacles of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), and the obstacles of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
The afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are: greed, hatred, and delusion;
anger, the enveloping hindrances (*paryavasthāna*), burning distress, envy, stinginess, deceit, flattery, lack of shame and lack of dread of blame;
and the seven types of pride—pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," false pride, and arrogance.
Heedlessness and arrogance; resentment and litigation; wrong livelihood and flattery; feigning extraordinary signs;
seeking profit through profit; evil seeking and excessive seeking; lack of reverence; refusing instruction;
associating with evil friends; insatiable greed for gain; being bound by fetters difficult to untie; and the desire for what is evil.
...greed for evil desires, the view of a self, the view of existence and the view of non-existence, yawning and fondness for sleep,
stretching and lack of joy, craving for food and drink, mental dullness and confusion, the mind dwelling on diverse thoughts,
unwholesome reflection, much evil in body and speech, delighting in excessive talk, and the dullness of the sense faculties.
To speak many falsehoods and to be constantly shrouded by thoughts of desire, thoughts of malice, and thoughts of harm—
this is called the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As for the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), it refers to the five crimes of immediate retribution, which are the maladies of grave evil.

The obstacle of retribution refers to being born in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, as well as slandering the true Dharma and being an icchantika; this is called the obstacle of retribution.
These three obstacles are termed the great illnesses.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas cultivate enlightenment over immeasurable eons, they provide all medicines for the sick and constantly make this vow: "May all sentient beings forever sever such grave illnesses of the three obstructions."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates awakening, they provide medicine to all who are ill and constantly make this vow: 'May all sentient beings forever sever all illnesses and attain the vajra-body of a Tathāgata.'"

Furthermore, may all immeasurable sentient beings become sovereigns of wondrous medicine, severing all evil and grave illnesses; may all sentient beings obtain the Agada medicine, by the power of which they can eliminate all immeasurable poisons.

Furthermore, may all sentient beings never regress from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, swiftly attain the accomplishment of the unsurpassed medicine of the Buddha, and eliminate the poisonous arrows of all afflictions.

Furthermore, may all sentient beings diligently cultivate vigor, achieve the adamantine mind of the Tathāgata, and act as subtle medicines to heal all ailments, so that no one gives rise to thoughts of contention or dispute.
May all sentient beings also become great medicinal trees, healing all manner of evil and grave illnesses.
Furthermore, may they pull out the poisoned arrows and attain the unsurpassed radiance of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, I vow that sentient beings may enter the Tathāgata’s great medicinal and subtle Dharma-treasury of wisdom.
World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva such as this has already made these vows throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, so as to cause all sentient beings to be entirely free from further illness. For what reason does the Tathāgata now proclaim that he has an illness?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

There are those in the world who are ill and unable to sit up or rise, to look forward or backward, or to move about; they cannot take food or drink, nor can they swallow even water. Furthermore, they are unable to instruct their children or manage the affairs of the household."
At that time, his parents, wife, children, brothers, kinsmen, and acquaintances will each conceive the thought that this person is certain to die.
World-Honored One, today the Tathāgata is likewise thus: lying on his right side, he says nothing. There are foolish people in this Jambudvīpa who will think:
Thinking, "The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, will surely enter parinirvāṇa," one gives rise to the perception of extinction;
yet the nature of the Tathāgata does not, in reality, ultimately enter parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata abides eternally and is subject to no change; for these reasons, one should not say, "I now have a backache.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In this world, there are those who are ill, their bodies emaciated and impaired, lying prostrate or on their sides upon beds and mattresses; at that time, their family members give rise to feelings of aversion and contempt, thinking they are surely about to die.
The Tathāgata is now likewise in this situation; he shall be treated with contempt by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhists, who will conceive the notion that he is impermanent.
Those non-Buddhists will say:
"He is not like us, for we hold our own nature to be eternal, and because our principles—such as the Sovereign, Time, and the atoms—are eternally abiding and subject to no change."
"Śramaṇa Gautama has been carried away by impermanence; this is a phenomenon subject to change.
For this reason, World-Honored One, you should not remain silent today, lying on your right side.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

There are those in the world who are ill; their four great elements are increased or diminished and are not in mutual harmony. They become emaciated and utterly exhausted, and for this reason they are unable to sit or rise at will, but must lie upon beds and mattresses."
The Tathāgata’s four great elements are all in harmony and balance; his physical strength is fully perfected and free from any decline.
World-Honored One!
Just as the strength of ten young oxen does not equal that of one large bull, and the strength of ten large bulls does not equal that of one dark-blue...
The strength of ten blue oxen is not equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant; the strength of ten ordinary elephants is not equal to the strength of one wild elephant;
the strength of ten wild elephants is not equal to the strength of one two-tusked elephant; the strength of twelve two-tusked elephants is not equal to the strength of one four-tusked elephant;
and the strength of fourteen four-tusked elephants is not equal to that of a single [elephant] from the Snowy Mountains.
Regarding the strength of white elephants: the strength of ten snow-mountain white elephants is not equal to the strength of one fragrant elephant;
the strength of ten fragrant elephants is not equal to the strength of one blue elephant; the strength of ten blue elephants is not equal to the strength of one yellow elephant;
the strength of ten yellow elephants is not equal to the strength of one red elephant; and the strength of ten red elephants is not equal to the strength of one white elephant.
The strength of ten white elephants is not equal to the strength of one mountain elephant; the strength of ten mountain elephants is not equal to the strength of one *utpala* elephant;
the strength of ten *utpala* elephants is not equal to the strength of one *kumuda* elephant;
the strength of ten *kumuda* elephants is not equal to the strength of one *puṇḍarīka* elephant; the strength of ten *puṇḍarīka* elephants...
The strength of one is not equal to that of a single human strongman; the strength of ten such strongmen is not equal to the strength of one *bāhu-kṣepaka*;
the strength of ten *bāhu-kṣepakas* is not equal to the strength of one eight-armed *Nārāyaṇa*;
and the strength of ten *Nārāyaṇas* is not equal to the strength of a single joint of a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
In all ordinary beings, the various joints within the body do not reach one another.
In human champions, the ends of the joints meet.
In the body of a Bala-deva, the various joints are joined together.
The body of Nārāyaṇa has its joints and bones interlocked.
In the case of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, the joints and bones are like coiled dragons bound together; for this reason, the Bodhisattva possesses the greatest strength.

When the world is formed, the diamond throne arises from the adamantine foundation, reaching upward to the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; once the bodhisattva has sat there, his mind immediately attains the ten powers.

The Tathāgata should not now be like that infant child; for an infant child is foolish and lacks wisdom, being incapable of speech, and for this reason, he may lie down or turn over at will without anyone censuring him.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great wisdom that illuminates all things;
he is a dragon among men, endowed with great majesty and virtue;

he is a perfected, unsurpassed ṛṣi who has forever severed the web of doubt and extracted the poisoned arrow; his movements are serene and composed, his deportment is perfect, and he has attained fearlessness.
"For what reason now do you lie on your right side, causing all the humans and devas to grieve, lament, and suffer?
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"O Gautama of Great Sage Virtue, I pray that you arise and expound the wondrous Dharma."
One should not be like a child who, when a patient lies upon a bed,
sees the Tamer of Gods and Humans reclining between the twin trees and,
out of ignorance, declares that he must surely have entered parinirvāṇa.
Not knowing the Vaipulya scriptures, the profound conduct of the Buddha,
and failing to see the subtle, secret treasury, they are like the blind who do not see the path.
Only the various Bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī and others, [possess this insight].
One who can understand this profound [teaching] is like a skilled archer.
The World-Honored Ones of the three periods of time take great compassion as their foundation;
where now is such great compassion?
If one lacked great compassion, they would not be called a Buddha;
if a Buddha were necessarily to enter parinirvāṇa, he would not be called eternal.
We pray only that the Unsurpassed Honored One will compassionately accept our request.
“Benefiting all sentient beings, Subduing all those of external paths.

At that time, the World-Honored One, his heart permeated by great compassion, knowing the various thoughts of all sentient beings and wishing to accord with them for their ultimate benefit, rose from his reclining position and sat cross-legged. His countenance was serene and joyful, like a mass of molten gold; his features were dignified and majestic, like the full moon; his form was pure and free from all defilement, as he emitted a great radiance that filled the void of space.

The light was exceedingly magnificent, surpassing that of a hundred thousand suns; it illuminated the Buddha-worlds of the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, bestowing upon sentient beings the torch of great wisdom and causing them all to extinguish the darkness of ignorance. It established hundreds of billions of nayutas of sentient beings in the bodhicitta, making them steadfast and non-regressive.
At that time, the World-Honored One was free from all doubt and anxiety, like a lion king; his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.

From every single pore upon his body, a lotus flower emerged from each one; these flowers were exquisite, each possessing a thousand petals of pure golden hue, with stems of lapis lazuli, filaments of diamond, and calyxes of ruby. Their forms were perfectly round like chariot wheels, and from these lotuses issued various multicolored radiances: blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and the color of crystal.

These rays of light all pervaded the Avīci Hell, the Saṃjīva Hell, the Kālasūtra Hell, the Saṃghāta Hell, the Raurava Hell, the Mahāraurava Hell, the Tapana Hell, and the Pratāpana Hell. The sentient beings within these eight hells were constantly oppressed by various sufferings—namely, being burned, boiled, roasted by fire, hacked, pierced, flayed, and skinned—but upon encountering this light, all such sufferings were extinguished without remainder; they became peaceful, cool, and attained boundless bliss.
Within this radiance, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata was proclaimed, declaring that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
having heard this, those beings immediately passed away and were reborn among humans and devas.

Furthermore, there are eight kinds of cold hells, namely: the A-pa-pa hell, the A-t’a-t’a hell, the A-lo-lo hell, the A-po-po hell, the Utpala hell, the Padma hell, the Kumuda hell, and the Puṇḍarīka hell. Within these, sentient beings are constantly tormented by the suffering of cold, such that their bodies are split asunder, shattered to pieces, and they mutually harm one another.
Having encountered this light, such sufferings as these are extinguished without remainder, and they immediately attain a harmonious, warm, and comfortable state of body.
Within this light, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also proclaimed, stating that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
having heard this, the sentient beings immediately pass away and are reborn among humans or devas.

At that time, all the hells within this Jambudvīpa world-system and in other worlds were entirely empty and void, with no beings undergoing retribution for their offenses, except for those who hold to the icchantika view.

Sentient beings among the hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, have their bodies entwined with hair; for hundreds of thousands of years, they have never even heard the names of water or drink.
Upon encountering this light, their hunger and thirst are immediately dispelled.
Within this radiance, the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also proclaimed, declaring that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately pass away and are reborn among humans and devas, causing the realm of hungry ghosts to become entirely empty, with the sole exception of those who slander the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
When sentient beings of the animal realm—who habitually kill one another and devour each other—encounter this light, their hearts of malice are entirely extinguished.
Within this radiance, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also proclaimed, declaring that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
having heard this, those beings immediately pass away and are reborn among humans or devas.
At that time, even the animals were all gone, with the exception of those who had slandered the True Dharma.

Within each of these flowers was a Buddha, with a halo extending one fathom, his golden body radiant and brilliant, subtle, exquisite, dignified, and unsurpassed; his body was adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

These World-Honored Ones were some sitting, some walking, some lying down, and some standing; some were emitting the sound of thunder, some were pouring down rain, some were flashing lightning, and some were raising up winds; some manifested bodies of smoke and flame like masses of fire, while others manifested various mountains of the seven treasures, ponds, springs, rivers, and streams, as well as mountain forests and trees; some manifested lands of the seven treasures, cities, towns, villages, palaces, and dwellings; some manifested elephants, horses, lions, tigers, wolves, peacocks, phoenixes, and various birds; some manifested so that all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa could see the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; and some manifested the six heavens of the desire realm.

Furthermore, there are World-Honored Ones who, in some cases, speak of the many faults and afflictions of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas); in other cases, they speak of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; in others, they speak of the causes and conditions of all phenomena; in others, they speak of how all karma and afflictions arise from causes and conditions; in others, they speak of self and non-self; in others, they speak of the two dharmas of suffering and pleasure; in others, they speak of the permanent and the impermanent; and in others, they speak of the pure and the impure.

Furthermore, there were some World-Honored Ones who expounded for the sake of the bodhisattvas the six pāramitās of their practice; some spoke of the merits attained by the great bodhisattvas; some spoke of the merits attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; some spoke of the merits attained by the śrāvakas; some spoke of conforming to the One Vehicle (ekayāna); and some spoke of attaining the Way through the Three Vehicles (triyāna).
Some World-Honored Ones emit water from their left flanks and fire from their right flanks;
some manifest their initial birth, renunciation, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, and entering Nirvana;
some World-Honored Ones let out a lion’s roar, causing those in this assembly to attain the first fruit, the second fruit, the third fruit, up to the fourth fruit.
Furthermore, there were those who spoke of the immeasurable causes and conditions for transcending birth and death.

At that time, throughout this Jambudvīpa, all sentient beings who encountered this light had the blind see forms, the deaf hear sounds, the mute speak, the hunchbacked and the lame walk, the poor obtain wealth, the stingy become able to give, the angry develop a mind of loving-kindness, and the faithless gain faith.
In such a world, there is not a single sentient being who practices unwholesome dharmas, with the sole exception of those possessed by the icchantika.

At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, aupapādukas, apasmārakas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, all raised their voices in unison and proclaimed these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"The Unsurpassed World-Honored One brings great benefit to many.
Having spoken these words, they leaped for joy and rejoiced; some sang, some danced, and some moved their bodies about.
They scattered various flowers over the Buddha and the Sangha, namely: celestial utpala flowers,
kumuda flowers, padma flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, māndārava flowers,
mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, and sandhāna flowers.
...mahāsaṃtāna flowers, luśina flowers, mahāluśina flowers, fragrant flowers, great fragrant flowers,
pleasing flowers, greatly pleasing flowers, lovely-to-behold flowers, greatly lovely-to-behold flowers, exquisite flowers,
and foremost exquisite flowers; furthermore, they scattered various perfumes.
They offered to the Buddha aloeswood, *tagara* incense, sandalwood, saffron, blended incenses,
and coastal compound incenses; furthermore, they presented celestial jeweled banners, pennants, and parasols,
along with the musical instruments of the devas— zithers, flutes, reed organs, lutes, harps, drums, and trumpets— and while making these offerings, they spoke:
The verse says:
"I now bow my head in homage to the Greatly Diligent One, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among two-legged beings;
that which the multitudes of devas and humans do not know, only Gautama is able to fully comprehend."
For my sake, World-Honored One, you practiced austerities throughout immeasurable kalpas;
how can you now, in a single day, abandon your original vow and cast off your life to enter nirvana?
All sentient beings are unable to see the secret treasury of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
for this reason, they find it difficult to escape, revolving in birth and death and falling into the evil realms.
As the Buddha has taught, all Arhats shall surely attain Nirvana;
yet who among the common folk, dull and ignorant, could know such a profound sphere of the Buddha’s activity?
Bestowing the nectar-like Dharma upon all sentient beings, It is for the purpose of severing and eliminating all afflictions;
If one has partaken of this nectar, One shall no longer undergo birth, old age, sickness, or death.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, provides healing for hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings,
causing all their various grave illnesses to be completely eliminated without remainder.
The World-Honored One has long since abandoned the suffering of illness, And is thus named the Seventh Buddha;
I pray that today you will rain down the rain of Dharma, To moisten and nourish the seeds of our merit.
"Therefore, the great assembly, along with the humans and devas, having made this request, remained silent.
When these verses were spoken, all the Buddhas within the lotus pedestals, from Jambudvīpa throughout as far as the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, heard them all.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
You have already perfected such profound and subtle wisdom, and shall not be destroyed by any demons or non-Buddhists. Good son!
You are already firmly established and cannot be shaken by any winds of evil.
Son of good family!

You have achieved the eloquence of joyful speech and have made offerings in the past to immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; therefore, you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, regarding such a meaning.

Good son! In the past, throughout immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, I have already eliminated the root of illness and am forever free from reclining or lying down.
Kāśyapa!

In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Anuttaravijaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara-puruṣa, Damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. For the sake of all śrāvakas, he preached this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, revealing, analyzing, and elucidating its meaning.

At that time, I was also a śrāvaka of that Buddha; I received and upheld this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, reciting it until I had mastered it, copying its scrolls, and extensively expounding, analyzing, and explaining its meaning for others;
by means of these roots of goodness, I dedicated them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son!

Since that time, I have never, due to the conditions of evil afflictions or karma, fallen into the evil realms, slandered the True Dharma, become an icchantika, or received the body of a eunuch, one without genitals, or one with dual genitals; nor have I ever rebelled against my parents, killed an arhat, destroyed stupas or the Sangha, shed the blood of a Buddha, or violated the four grave prohibitions.
From that time forth, my body and mind have been peaceful and secure, free from all suffering and affliction.
Kāśyapa! I truly have no illnesses whatsoever at present.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have long since been far removed from all illness.
"Kāśyapa!..."
These sentient beings, not understanding the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Esoteric Teachings, claim that the Tathāgata truly has an illness. Kāśyapa!
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata is a lion among men, yet the Tathāgata is in reality not a lion—such words are precisely the Tathāgata’s esoteric teaching.
Kāśyapa! It is said that the Tathāgata is a great dragon among men, yet I have already abandoned such karma throughout immeasurable kalpas. Kāśyapa!

Just as it is said that the Tathāgata is a human or a deva, yet in reality I am neither human nor deva; nor am I a ghost, a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kiṃnara, or a mahoraga; I am not a self, not a life-principle, not a nourisher, not a person, not a man, not an agent, not a non-agent, not a recipient, not a non-recipient, not a World-Honored One, not a śrāvaka, not one who speaks, and not one who does not speak.
Statements such as these are all the secret teachings of the Tathāgata.

“Kāśyapa, it is said that the Tathāgata is like the great ocean or Sumeru, the king of mountains; yet the Tathāgata is truly not of a salty taste and is not like a mountain of stone. You should know that this statement, too, is a secret teaching of the Tathāgata.”
Kāśyapa!
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata is like a *puṇḍarīka* lotus, yet I am in truth not a *puṇḍarīka*, such speech is the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa!
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata is like parents, yet the Tathāgata is in reality not one's parents—such a statement is also the Tathāgata’s secret teaching.
Kāśyapa!
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata is the great captain, yet the Tathāgata is in truth not a captain—such a statement is also the Tathāgata’s secret teaching.
Kāśyapa!
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata is like a merchant leader, yet the Tathāgata is in reality not a merchant leader—such a statement is also the Tathāgata’s secret teaching.
Kāśyapa!

Just as it is said that the Tathāgata can subdue Māra, yet the Tathāgata actually possesses no malicious intent to cause others to submit—such statements are all the secret teachings of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa!
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata can treat abscesses, yet I am in truth not a physician for treating abscesses—such words are also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
“Kāśyapa! As I have previously said:

‘If there are sons or daughters of good family who are well able to cultivate and purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, at the time of their passing away, even if their kinsmen take their remains and either cremate them, cast them into great waters, or abandon them in a cemetery where foxes, wolves, birds, and beasts compete to devour them, their mind, consciousness, and intellect will immediately be reborn in a good realm.’”
"Yet this mental dharma truly has no coming or going, nor does it go anywhere.
It is simply a continuous succession of similar states before and after, with no difference in its characteristics.
Such words as these are the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa! My current statement regarding illness is likewise so; it is also the esoteric teaching of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, I entrust Mañjuśrī with my final instructions:
"I now have a backache; you all should preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly. Kāśyapa!
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, truly has no illness; he lies on his right side, yet he does not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa! This Great Nirvāṇa is the profound meditative concentration of all Buddhas; such meditative concentration is not the sphere of practice for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
“Kāśyapa! Regarding what you previously asked: for what reason does the Tathāgata recline and not rise, nor seek food and drink, nor instruct his family members to cultivate their livelihoods?”

Kāśyapa! The nature of space likewise has no sitting or rising, no seeking of food or drink, and no instructing of family members to cultivate their livelihoods; it has no coming or going, no birth, death, aging, or vigor, no appearing or disappearing, no injury or destruction, and no liberation from bondage. It neither speaks of itself nor speaks of others; it neither understands itself nor understands others; it is neither at peace nor ill.
"Good son!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise thus; they are like empty space—how could they have the suffering of various illnesses? Kāśyapa!"
There are three types of people in the world whose illnesses are difficult to cure:
first, those who slander the Mahāyāna; second, those who have committed the five heinous crimes; and third, the icchantikas.
These three illnesses are the most grave in the world and cannot be cured by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
“Good son!

It is like a disease that is inevitably fatal and difficult to cure: whether there is a caregiver who provides medicine as desired, or there is no caregiver who provides medicine as desired, such a disease is certainly incurable; you should know that this person will surely die without doubt.”

Good son! These three kinds of people are also like this: whether there are śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas who may preach the Dharma or not, they cannot cause such persons to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa! It is like a sick person: if they have a caregiver and medicine provided according to their needs, they can be cured; yet if these three are lacking, they cannot be cured.

It is the same for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: having heard the Dharma from the Buddha or a bodhisattva, they are immediately able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is not the case that they can give rise to this mind without hearing the Dharma.
Kāśyapa!
It is like a sick person who may either have a caregiver and medicine as they desire, or lack a caregiver and medicine as they desire; in both cases, they can be cured.

There is another kind of person who is likewise: whether they encounter a śrāvaka or do not encounter a śrāvaka, whether they encounter a pratyekabuddha or do not encounter a pratyekabuddha, whether they encounter a bodhisattva or do not encounter a bodhisattva, whether they encounter a Tathāgata or do not encounter a Tathāgata, and whether they hear the Dharma or do not hear the Dharma, they will naturally attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

It refers to those who, whether for their own sake, for the sake of others, out of fear, for the sake of gain, out of flattery, or to deceive others, write down this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, make offerings to it with reverence, and explain it to others.
“Kāśyapa! There are five kinds of people who, regarding this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa scripture, exhibit the conduct of the diseased; they are not Tathāgatas.
What are these five?

By severing one category and the three fetters, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*; one does not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, but returns seven times between humans and devas, forever ending all suffering and entering *nirvāṇa*.
Kāśyapa!

This is called the first person who possesses the sphere of practice for illness; after eighty thousand kalpas in the future, this person shall attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Kāśyapa!

As for the second person, having severed the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion, he attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, is called "one who returns once," and by forever severing all suffering, enters into *nirvāṇa*.
Kāśyapa!

This is called the second person’s sphere of practice regarding illness; after sixty thousand kalpas in the future, this person shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Kāśyapa!

As for the third person, he severs the five lower fetters and attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*; he will no longer return to this world, but will forever sever all suffering and enter *nirvāṇa*. This is called the third person’s sphere of practice involving illness.
This person, after the passing of forty thousand kalpas in the future, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kāśyapa!

As for the fourth person, they have forever severed greed, hatred, and delusion, attained the fruit of *arhat*, and entered *nirvāṇa* with no remainder of afflictions; yet this is not the solitary conduct of a *kiṃpuruṣa* (unicorn). This is called the fourth person’s sphere of practice involving illness.
This person, after twenty thousand kalpas in the future, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kāśyapa!

As for the fifth person, they have forever severed greed, hatred, and delusion, attained the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, and with no remaining afflictions, entered *nirvāṇa*. This is truly the solitary conduct of a *kiṃpuruṣa* (unicorn); this is called the fifth person’s sphere of practice regarding illness.
In the future, after ten thousand kalpas have passed, this person shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa! This is called the fifth person who dwells in the sphere of illness; he is not a Tathāgata.
Chapter Seven: The Holy Conduct (*Ārya-caryā*) The Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Holy Conduct (Part One) At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: “Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, regarding this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, single-mindedly contemplate five kinds of practices.
What are these five? First, the noble practice (ārya-caryā);
second, the Brahma practice (brahma-caryā); third, the celestial practice (deva-caryā); fourth, the infant-like practice (bāla-caryā); and fifth, the sick practice (glāna-caryā).
"Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should constantly cultivate these five kinds of practices. Furthermore, there is one practice that is the practice of the Tathāgata, namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra."
Kāśyapa! What is the noble practice cultivated by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra from either a śrāvaka or a Tathāgata, and having heard it, gives rise to faith, and having given rise to faith, should reflect as follows:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the unsurpassed path, the Great Right Dharma, the correct practice of the great assembly, and furthermore, the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.

Now, for the sake of loving and desiring these Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall renounce my beloved wife and children, kinsmen, the house in which I dwell, gold, silver, and rare treasures, exquisite necklaces, incense, flowers, and music, male and female slaves and servants, sons and daughters, both great and small, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, pigs, and other such creatures."
He further thought:
"Living at home is cramped and confining, like a prison, from which all afflictions arise.
Leaving the home life is vast and open, like space, by which all wholesome dharmas increase."

"If one remains a householder, one cannot practice the pure life of celibacy (brahmacarya) for the duration of one's life; therefore, I should now shave off my hair and beard, leave the home life, and study the Way.
Having formed this thought, I shall now certainly leave the home life to cultivate and study the path of unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

When a bodhisattva thus desires to leave the household life, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān experiences great anguish and distress, saying: "This bodhisattva shall once again engage me in a great battle and dispute."
"Good son!
Where would such a bodhisattva ever again engage in conflict or dispute with others?

At that time, the bodhisattva goes to a monastic dwelling; if he sees the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Buddha, whose deportment is perfect, whose faculties are tranquil, whose mind is gentle, pure, and extinguished, he immediately approaches them and seeks to go forth, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the three dharma robes."
Having gone forth, he upholds the prohibitive precepts; his majestic deportment is flawless, his movements are serene and composed, and he commits no transgressions.
Even regarding minor offenses, he conceives a sense of dread; his resolve to guard the precepts is like a diamond.
“Good son! It is like a person who, carrying a life-preserving float, wishes to cross the great ocean.
At that time, there is a rākṣasa in the sea who begs that person for the float.”
Having heard this, the man immediately thought to himself:
"If I give this to him now, I will certainly perish.
He replied:
"Rākṣasa! You may kill me if you wish, but you shall not obtain the life-preserving float.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot give it all to me, please grant me half.
Yet the man still refused to give it to him.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you are unwilling to grant me half, I pray that you will give me one-third.
The man was still unwilling.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot do that, you should at least give me the length of your hand.
The man refused.
The rākṣasa spoke again:

"If you cannot now give me even as much as a hand's breadth, I am currently starving and destitute, oppressed by manifold sufferings; I pray that you will rescue me with at least as much as a speck of dust."
The man spoke again:
"What you now request is indeed not much; however, I am only now about to cross the sea, and I do not know how near or far the path ahead may be."
If I give it to you, my breath will gradually depart; how then could you overcome the perils of the great ocean?
Should you be able to reach the middle way, you would surely drown and die.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva upholds the prohibitive precepts, it is also like this: he is like that ferryman who cherishes and protects his life-preserving float.
While the bodhisattva is thus guarding the precepts, the various evil rākṣasas of affliction constantly speak to him, saying:”

"You should believe me; I shall never deceive you. If you break only the four grave prohibitions while upholding the remaining precepts, by these causes and conditions, I will ensure that you remain secure and attain entry into nirvana."
At that time, the Bodhisattva should speak these words:
"I would rather maintain such precepts and fall into the Avīci Hell than violate them and be born in the heavens."
The Rākṣasa of Affliction spoke again, saying:
"If you are unable to break the four pārājika precepts, you may instead break the saṃghāvaśeṣa; by this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter into nirvāṇa."
The Bodhisattva should likewise not comply with those words.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa, you may instead intentionally commit a sthūlātyaya offense; by this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva likewise did not comply.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit a sthūlātyaya offense, you may instead commit a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense; by this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva still did not comply with him.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, you may instead break a *pāyattika* rule; by this cause and condition, you shall attain peace and enter nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva still did not follow him.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot violate a pāyattika offense, you might as well break a duṣkṛta precept; by means of this cause and condition, you may attain peace and enter nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"If I now commit a *duṣkṛta* offense and do not confess it, I shall be unable to cross to the other shore of birth and death to attain *nirvāṇa*."
"In these minor precepts, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva maintains them with a mind as firm and unyielding as a vajra.
Whether it be the four grave prohibitions or the *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses), the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva upholds them with equal reverence and firmness, making no distinction between them."

If a bodhisattva can maintain such firm resolve, they will be fully endowed with the fivefold precepts of the faculties, namely: the precept of purity regarding the fundamental actions of a bodhisattva; the precept of purity regarding the remaining ancillary actions before and after them; the precept of purity regarding the absence of unwholesome thoughts; the precept of purity regarding the maintenance of right mindfulness; and the precept of dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Kāśyapa! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva further possesses two kinds of precepts:
first, the precepts received through worldly instruction; second, the precepts attained through the True Dharma.”

If a bodhisattva receives the precepts of the True Dharma, they will never commit evil; as for receiving the precepts of worldly instruction, one obtains them only after the fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
Furthermore, son of good family!
There are two kinds of precepts:
first, the precepts of intrinsic gravity; second, the precepts for avoiding worldly reproach.
The precepts of intrinsic gravity refer to the four prohibitions.
Regarding the precept for avoiding worldly reproach: one does not engage in trade, nor use light scales or small measures to deceive others;
one does not seize another's property through the influence of others, nor with a harmful intent bind or ruin successful enterprises;
one does not go to sleep with a lamp lit, nor engage in farming, housing, planting, domestic affairs, or sitting in a shop; and one does not keep elephants, horses, or carriages.
Vehicles, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, chickens, dogs, monkeys, peacocks, parrots, *jīvañjīvaka* birds, and *kroñca* cranes;
jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, cats, wildcats, pigs, boars, and other predatory beasts;
boys and girls, men and women, slaves, servants, and laborers; and gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Pearls, musāragalva, agate, coral, jade, *śaṅkha* shells, and various precious gems;
red copper, white tin, and brass vessels; woolen rugs, fine blankets, and *kauśeya* silk garments;
all kinds of grain—wheat, barley, beans, millet, sorghum, rice, and hemp—as well as raw and cooked foodstuffs, which they constantly receive.
He eats but once a day and never eats a second time; whether receiving alms or eating among the Sangha, he always knows moderation and does not accept special invitations.
He abstains from meat and does not drink alcohol; as for the five pungent herbs that cause a foul odor, he does not eat any of them.
Consequently, his body has no foul smell, and he is constantly revered by all the devas and by all people in the world.
They receive offerings, respect, and praise, yet they eat only what is sufficient and never accept more than required.

The robes they receive are just enough to cover the body; whether moving or staying, they are always accompanied by their three robes and alms bowl, never parting from them, just as a bird never parts from its two wings.

He does not keep roots, stalks, joints, grafts, or seeds; he does not keep treasuries of precious things, whether gold or silver; nor does he keep food and drink, kitchens, stores, clothing, or ornaments; nor does he use high, wide, or large beds, ivory or golden beds, or seats woven with various colors. He does not keep any fine or soft mats; he does not sit on elephant or horse rugs; he does not use fine, soft, or exquisite garments as bedding for his bed. At the two ends of his bed, he does not place two pillows; furthermore, he does not accept or keep exquisite red pillows, but uses only pillows made of plain yellow wood.

One must never watch elephant fights, horse fights, chariot fights, infantry battles, men’s fights, women’s fights, bull fights, sheep fights, or the fighting of water buffalo, chickens, pheasants, parrots, and so forth; nor should one intentionally go to view military arrays. One should not intentionally listen to the sounds of conch shells, drums, horns, lutes, zithers, harps, flutes, *vīṇās*, singing, shouting, or the music of performers, except when making offerings to the Buddha.

One must not watch or engage in any games or amusements whatsoever, such as dice, go (weiqi), chariot warfare (bolasexi), lion versus elephant combat, marble shooting, six-sided gambling (liubo), ball tossing, stone throwing, pitch-pot (touhu), tug-of-war (quandao), or the completion of the eight paths.

One shall never gaze at the hands, feet, face, or eyes; nor shall one practice divination by means of fingernails, mirrors, *zhicao* grass, willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls; nor shall one look up at the stars and constellations in the void, except when wishing to dispel drowsiness.
He does not act as a messenger for the royal court, conveying what is said here to there, or what is said there to here.

He never flatters or uses deceitful means to sustain his life, nor does he speak of matters concerning kings, ministers, or thieves; of strife and quarrels; of food and drink, kingdoms, famine, fear, or of abundance, prosperity, and security.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s precept for quelling worldly censure. Good son!"
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who firmly upholds such prohibitive precepts does so without any distinction from the precepts of natural gravity.
"Good son, once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has received and maintained these various prohibitive precepts, he makes this vow:

'I would rather cast this body into a deep pit of blazing, fierce fire than ever violate the prohibitive precepts established by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present by engaging in impure conduct with the daughters of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or householders.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow:
'I would rather have hot iron wrapped all around my body than, with a body of broken precepts, ever accept the robes of a faithful donor.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva further makes this vow:
'I would rather swallow hot iron balls with this mouth than ever dare, with a mouth that has violated the precepts, eat the food and drink of a faithful donor.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather lie upon this body on a great, glowing-hot iron surface than ever dare, with a body of broken precepts, accept beds, mats, or bedding from a donor of faithful confidence.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body pierced by three hundred spears than ever dare, with a body that has violated the precepts, accept the medicine offered out of faith by a donor.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of boiling iron than, with broken precepts, accept the houses and dwellings of faithful donors.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow:

'I would rather have this body smashed with an iron hammer from head to foot until it is like fine dust, than break the precepts while receiving the respectful prostrations of kṣatriyas, brahmins, and householders.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my two eyes gouged out with hot iron than, with a defiled mind, look upon the beautiful forms of others.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have iron awls pierce my entire body than, with a defiled mind, listen to pleasant sounds.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow:
'I would rather have my nose cut off with a sharp blade than, with a defiled mind, greedily smell various fragrances.'"
"Furthermore, good son,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow:
'I would rather have my tongue sliced and torn apart with a sharp blade than, with a defiled mind, covet delicious flavors.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body hacked and cut with a sharp axe than, with a defiled mind, covetously cling to various tactile sensations.'"
Why is this? Because by these causes and conditions, they cause the practitioner to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. Kāśyapa!
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s upholding of the prohibitive precepts.
Having upheld these various prohibitive precepts, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva bestows them all upon all sentient beings.

By these causes and conditions, I vow that all sentient beings shall protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts, attaining the pure precepts, the virtuous precepts, the unimpaired precepts, the indivisible precepts, the Mahāyāna precepts, the non-retrogressive precepts, the conforming precepts, and the ultimate precepts, and fully accomplishing the precepts of the pāramitās.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such pure precepts, he immediately dwells in the first stage, the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Why is it called the Immovable Stage?
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they are unmoving, undescending, non-retrogressive, and non-dispersing. Good son!
It is like Mount Sumeru, which the violent winds of the *svalana* cannot cause to move, fall, retreat, or scatter.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, it is likewise: they are not moved by forms, sounds, odors, or tastes; they do not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; they do not regress to the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and they are not scattered by the perverse winds of heterodox views so as to engage in wrong livelihoods.
Furthermore, good son!
Moreover, as for "moving," one is not moved by greed, anger, or delusion;
furthermore, as for "falling," one does not fall into the four grave offenses.
Furthermore, as for "retreating," they do not retreat from the precepts to return home;
as for "being scattered," they are not destroyed or dispersed by those who oppose the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Furthermore, son of good family!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise not shaken by the various affliction-māras, nor does he fall victim to the skandha-māra; even when sitting at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, although there may be a deva-māra, it cannot cause him to retreat from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor can he be dispersed by the death-māra.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the noble practices. Good son!"
What is called "noble conduct" (ārya-caryā)?
Noble conduct is so named because it is the practice of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
therefore, it is called noble conduct. For what reason are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas called "noble ones" (āryas)?

Because such persons possess the noble Dharma, and because they constantly contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, for these reasons they are called "noble ones" (*ārya*).
Furthermore, because they possess the noble precepts, they are again called "noble ones."
Because they possess noble concentration and wisdom, they are called "noble ones" (*ārya*).
Because they possess the seven noble riches—namely, faith, ethical discipline, a sense of shame, a sense of dread, extensive learning, wisdom, and renunciation—they are called "noble ones."
Because they possess the seven factors of noble awakening, they are called "noble ones" (*ārya*).
For this reason, it is further termed "noble conduct" (*ārya-caryā*).
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 11.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Twelve.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Holy Conduct (Āryacaryā), Part Two.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The noble practitioner, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, contemplates this body from head to foot, seeing that within it there are nothing but hair, body hair, nails, teeth, impurities and filth; skin, flesh, sinews, and bones; the spleen, kidneys, heart, and lungs; the liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach; the two receptacles of raw and cooked food; feces and urine; mucus, saliva, tears from the eyes; fat, grease, brain, and membranes; marrow, pus, and blood; and the various vessels of the skull."
When the Bodhisattva thus contemplates with single-minded attention, he reflects: "Who is there that is 'I'?
To whom does 'I' belong?
In what place does it abide?"
"Who belongs to me?
Then he further reflects:
"Are these bones me?"
"Is it apart from the bones?
At that time, the Bodhisattva removed the skin and flesh and observed only the white bones. He further thought:
"The colors and characteristics of the bones differ—namely blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of a pigeon; such bone-appearances are likewise not the self. Why is this so?"
"The self is also not blue, yellow, red, white, or the color of a pigeon.
When the Bodhisattva fixes the mind and contemplates in this way, he immediately succeeds in severing all desire for form.

Again, he reflects thus: "These bones arise from causes and conditions. Depending on the foot-bones, they support the ankle-bones; depending on the ankle-bones, they support the shin-bones; depending on the shin-bones, they support the knee-bones; depending on the knee-bones, they support the thigh-bones; depending on the thigh-bones, they support the hip-bones; depending on the hip-bones, they support the waist-bones; depending on the waist-bones, they support the spinal vertebrae; depending on the spinal vertebrae, they support the ribs; again, depending on the spinal vertebrae, they extend upward to support the cervical vertebrae; depending on the cervical vertebrae, they support the jawbone; depending on the jawbone, they support the teeth; and above them is the skull."

Furthermore, by means of the cervical vertebrae, they support the shoulder blades; depending on the shoulder blades, they support the upper arm bones; depending on the upper arm bones, they support the wrist bones; depending on the wrist bones, they support the palm bones; and depending on the palm bones, they support the finger bones.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, all the bones of his body become completely separated. Having attained this contemplation, he immediately cuts off the three desires:
first, the desire for physical form; second, the desire for graceful gestures; and third, the desire for subtle touch.
"When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates blue bones, they see this great earth—in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—as entirely blue in appearance;
as it is with the contemplation of blue, so it is likewise for yellow, white, and the color of a pigeon."

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs this contemplation, light of blue, yellow, red, white, pigeon-colored, and other hues issues forth from between his eyebrows. Within each of these individual rays of light, the bodhisattva sees the image of a Buddha. Having seen them, he immediately asks:

"This body is composed through the combination of impure causes and conditions; how is it that it is able to sit and rise, walk and stand, bend and stretch, look up and down, blink its eyes, breathe, weep in sorrow, or laugh with joy?"
"In this there is no master; who causes it to be so?
Having asked this question, the Buddhas within the light suddenly disappeared.
He then thought again:
"Perhaps it is consciousness that is the self; that is why the Buddhas did not teach it to me.
He further observed this consciousness as arising and ceasing in succession, like a flowing stream, and likewise concluded it was not the self.
Again, he thought:
"If consciousness is not the self, perhaps the out-breath and in-breath might be the self.
Again, he thought:
"These inhalations and exhalations are merely the nature of wind; this nature of wind is itself the four great elements. Among these four great elements, which one is the self?"
"The nature of earth is not the self; the natures of water, fire, and wind are likewise not the self.
He further reflects:

"In this entire body, there is absolutely no self; it is merely through the conjunction of causes and conditions—the mind and wind—that various activities are manifested. It is like the effects produced by the power of incantations or illusions, and like a lute that produces sound according to one's will."
Therefore, this body is thus impure, being formed through the temporary conjunction of various causes and conditions; in what place, then, could such lust arise?
If one is reviled and insulted, in what place, moreover, could anger arise?
Yet this body of mine consists of thirty-six impure and foul substances; where, then, could there be one who experiences insult?
If I hear such abuse, I immediately reflect: "By what sound am I being reviled?"
One cannot perceive insults through individual sounds; if one cannot do so with a single sound, one likewise cannot do so with many. For this reason, one should not give rise to anger.
If another comes to strike you, you should also reflect: from where does such a striker arise?
Again, he thought:
"It is because of hands, knives, staves, and my own body that 'striking' is named.
For what reason should I now pointlessly harbor anger toward another?"
This is my own body that has invited this calamity, because I have received this body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
It is just as when there is a target, an arrow strikes it; my body is likewise: because there is a body, there is the striking.

If I am not patient, my mind will become distracted; if the mind is distracted, I will lose right mindfulness; if I lose right mindfulness, I will be unable to contemplate the meaning of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome; if I cannot contemplate the meaning of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, I will practice unwholesome dharmas; and by reason of these unwholesome dharmas, I will fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
When the Bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he attains the four foundations of mindfulness; having attained the four foundations of mindfulness, he then abides in the stage of Patience.

Once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they are able to endure greed, hatred, and delusion; they are also able to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice, violent winds and harsh contacts, various epidemics, abusive speech and insults, and beatings and floggings. They are able to endure all physical and mental suffering and afflictions; therefore, it is called the Stage of Endurance (Kṣānti-bhūmi).
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva has not yet attained the stage of Immovability (Acalā-bhūmi) and is purely upholding the precepts, could there be any cause or condition by which they might break the precepts?”
“Good son! There are bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the stage of Immovability (Acalā-bhūmi); due to certain causes and conditions, they may break the precepts.
Kāśyapa respectfully assented:
“What is it? The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”

If there is a bodhisattva who knows that by means of the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, they can cause others to receive, uphold, and take delight in Mahāyāna sūtras; and furthermore, can cause them to read, recite, master them thoroughly, copy the scrolls, extensively explain them to others, and not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—for such reasons as these, they may break the precepts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva should form this thought:

"I would rather fall into the Avīci Hell for an eon, or even slightly less than an eon, to undergo its punishments, than fail to ensure that such a person does not regress from their progress toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Kāśyapa! For these reasons, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may be said to have violated the pure precepts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who takes under their care and protects such a person, causing them not to fall back from the mind of enlightenment, this constitutes a violation of the precepts;
yet, for that person to fall into Avīci Hell is impossible.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

I recall that in the past, I was a great king here in Jambudvīpa named Śailopa. I cherished, loved, and revered the Mahāyāna sūtras; my mind was purely good, free from coarseness, evil, jealousy, or stinginess. My mouth constantly uttered words of affection and virtue, and my body constantly protected the poor and the solitary. I practiced giving and diligence without ever ceasing or becoming weary.

At that time, there were no Buddhas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas in the world; during those years, I took delight in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras and served a brāhmaṇa for twelve years, providing him with all his necessities.
After twelve years had passed and the bestowal of peace and comfort was complete, he spoke these words:
"Teachers, you should now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The Brahmin said: "Great King!
The nature of bodhi is non-existent; the Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so."

"Great King! How can you cause people and things to become identical with empty space? "O son of good family! [The King replied: "How so? "Son of good family! [The Buddha continued: "It is because all dharmas are ultimately empty. "World-Honored One! If all dharmas are ultimately empty, how can there be the distinctions between the noble and the ordinary, or the superior and the inferior? "Son of good family! It is because sentient beings give rise to various afflictions that they produce various karmas; because they produce various karmas, they undergo various births. Because they undergo various births, they experience various sufferings. Because they experience various sufferings, they do not attain liberation. Son of good family! If one can sever all afflictions and exhaust all karma, then one will not undergo birth and will not experience suffering. Because one does not undergo birth and does not experience suffering, one attains liberation. Therefore, it is said that all dharmas are ultimately empty. Furthermore, son of good family! Because one does not give rise to attachment toward the body, one will not give rise to attachment toward external objects. Because one does not give rise to attachment toward external objects, one will not give rise to afflictions. Because one does not give rise to afflictions, one will not produce karma. Because one does not produce karma, one will not undergo birth. Because one does not undergo birth, one will not experience suffering. Because one does not experience suffering, one attains liberation. Therefore, it is said that all dharmas are ultimately empty. "World-Honored One! At that time, my mind was set upon the Mahāyāna; hearing the brahmin revile the Vaipulya sūtras, as soon as I heard it, I immediately severed his life-force.
Good son!
By these causes and conditions, from that time forward, they have not fallen into hell. Good son!
The Mahāyāna sūtras possess such immeasurable power as this for providing protection and upholding [practitioners].
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there is also the noble practice known as the Four Noble Truths:
suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path; these are called the Four Noble Truths."

Kāśyapa! Suffering has the characteristic of oppression; origination has the characteristic of growth; cessation has the characteristic of quiescence; and the path has the characteristic of the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Suffering has the characteristic of manifestation; origination has the characteristic of transformation; cessation has the characteristic of removal; and the path has the characteristic of being able to remove.
Furthermore, son of good family, suffering has three characteristics:
The characteristic of suffering as suffering, the characteristic of suffering as conditioned formations, and the characteristic of suffering as change;
"accumulation" refers to the twenty-five states of existence;
"cessation" refers to the cessation of the twenty-five states of existence.
The Way consists in the cultivation of morality, concentration,
and wisdom. Furthermore, noble son,
there are two kinds of tainted phenomena (sāsrava-dharma):
There are causes and there are fruits;
likewise, untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) also have two kinds:
they have causes and they have fruits.

That which is the fruit of outflows is called suffering; that which is the cause of outflows is called the origin; that which is the fruit of the outflow-free is called cessation; and that which is the cause of the outflow-free is called the path.
"Furthermore, good son, there are eight aspects called suffering:

namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging."
That which can produce these eight kinds of suffering is called the cause.
The absence of such eight phenomena is called cessation.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion are called the path.
“Good son! Birth is characterized by emergence, which consists of five kinds:
first, initial emergence; second, reaching the end; third, growth; fourth, emergence from the womb; and fifth, birth as a species.”
What is old age?
There are two kinds of old age:
first, moment-to-moment aging; second, lifelong aging.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the aging of increase; second, the aging of destruction. These are called "aging.
What is "sickness"?
Sickness refers to the four great poisonous serpents being mutually unbalanced; it is also of two kinds:
first, physical sickness; second, mental sickness.
Physical sickness has five types:
First, those caused by water; second, those caused by wind; third, those caused by heat; fourth, miscellaneous illnesses; and fifth, adventitious illnesses.
There are four types of adventitious illnesses:
first, performing actions beyond one's capacity; second, falling due to forgetfulness or error; third, injury from blades, staves, tiles, or stones; and fourth, possession by malevolent spirits.
The maladies of the mind are also of four kinds:
first, elation; second, fear; third, sorrow; and fourth, delusion.
Furthermore, good son!
There are three kinds of diseases of body and mind.
What are these three?
First is karmic retribution; second is the inability to remain far removed from adverse conditions; third is the shifting of the seasons.
From such causes and conditions as these, names arise, and one suffers from the disease of conceptual discrimination.
"Causes and conditions" refers to various ailments such as wind-disorders (*vāta*).
"Names" refers to mental distress, lung congestion, shortness of breath with coughing and retching, palpitations, and diarrhea.
As for the discrimination of sensation: headaches, eyeaches, and pains in the hands, feet, and so forth—these are called "sickness.
What is "death"? Death is the relinquishing of the body one has received.
There are also two kinds of relinquishing the body one has received:
first, death through the exhaustion of the life-span; second, death due to external conditions.
