Death through the exhaustion of the life-span is also of three kinds:
First, the end of life occurs without the exhaustion of merit; second, the exhaustion of merit occurs without the end of life; third, both merit and life are exhausted together.
Furthermore, there are three types of death due to external conditions:

first, death through self-inflicted harm that is not proportionate to one's karma; second, death through being killed by another in an untimely manner; and third, death resulting from both causes combined.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of death:
first, death through negligence; second, death through breaking the precepts; and third, death through the destruction of the life-faculty.
What is meant by death through negligence?
If one slanders the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, this is called death through negligence.
What is meant by death through breaking the precepts?
To violate the prohibitions and precepts established by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present is called death through breaking the precepts.
What is called death by the destruction of the life-faculty?
The relinquishing of the body of the five aggregates—this is called death by the destruction of the life-faculty.
Thus, death is said to be a great suffering.
"What is called the suffering of separation from the beloved?
It is the destruction and dispersal of things one holds dear.
This destruction and dispersal of beloved things is also of two kinds:"
First is the destruction of the five aggregates among humans; second is the destruction of the five aggregates among devas.
Thus, these five aggregates beloved by humans and devas are analyzed and calculated to have immeasurable varieties; this is called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
What is called the suffering of association with the disliked?
It is the gathering together of those whom one does not love.
This gathering together of those whom one does not love further consists of three types:
These are the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.
Such distinctions and calculations within these three realms of existence comprise immeasurable varieties; this is what is called the suffering of association with the disliked.
What is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is further of two kinds:

first, being unable to obtain that which one hopes for despite seeking it; second, exerting great effort and labor yet failing to obtain the resulting fruit. This is termed the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
What is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*)?

The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging consists of the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of being joined with what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; therefore, it is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
“Kāśyapa! Regarding the root of birth, there are these seven kinds of suffering: the suffering of old age, and so forth, up to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Kāśyapa!”
Now, this state of old age and decay does not exist for all; it is definitively absent among Buddhas and devas, while among humans it is indeterminate, being sometimes present and sometimes absent.
Kāśyapa!
In the three realms, there is no receiving of a body that does not involve birth; aging is not necessarily fixed [at the time of birth]. Therefore, birth is the root of all things. Kāśyapa!
The minds of sentient beings in the world are shrouded by inversion; they are greedily attached to the signs of birth and feel aversion toward old age and death.
Kāśyapa! It is not so for a bodhisattva; even upon observing their initial birth, they have already perceived its faults and perils. Kāśyapa!
Suppose there is a woman who enters another's house; this woman is upright and beautiful, with a lovely countenance, her body adorned with exquisite necklaces and ornaments.
Upon seeing her, the host immediately asks:
"What is your name?"
"To whom do you belong?
The woman replied,
"I am the Great Deity of Merit."
The host asked, "What do you do wherever you go?
The woman replied:

"Wherever I go, I am able to provide various kinds of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate; as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles; and male and female slaves and servants."
Upon hearing this, the host felt great joy in his heart and was immeasurably elated, thinking:
"By my own merit, you have now come to my home."
He immediately burned incense, scattered flowers, and paid homage with offerings, reverence, and prostrations.

Furthermore, outside the gate he saw another woman; her form was ugly and deformed, her clothes were tattered and worn, covered in much filth and grease, her skin was cracked and parched, and her complexion was as pale as mugwort.
Having seen him, he asked:
"What is your name?
To whose family do you belong?"
The woman replied,
"My name is Kṛṣṇā.
He asked again:
"Why is she called 'Darkness'?
The woman replied,
"Wherever I go, all the wealth and treasures in that household will utterly perish."
Upon hearing this, the host immediately took up a sharp knife and spoke these words:
"If you do not leave, I shall take your life.
The woman replied:
"You are extremely foolish and lack wisdom.
The host asked,
"For what reason do you call me foolish and lacking in wisdom?"
The woman replied:
"She who is in your house is my elder sister.
I am always with her, moving and staying together; if you drive me out, you must also drive her out."
The host went back inside and asked Puṇyavatī,
"Outside there was a woman who said she is your younger sister.
Is this truly so?"
Guna-karandavyūha said:
"She is truly my younger sister; she and I travel and dwell together, never having been apart.
In whatever place we reside, I always bring about what is good while she always brings about evil; I always provide benefit while she always causes decline."
"If you love me, you should also love them; if you see fit to honor me, you should also honor them.
The host then said, "If there are such matters of good and evil as these, I have no use for either; you may both depart as you please."
At that time, the two women together returned to their dwelling.
When the host saw them depart, his heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
At that time, the two girls again accompanied each other to the home of a poor man.
Upon seeing them, the poor man felt great joy in his heart and immediately invited them, saying:
"From this day forward, I pray that you two will dwell in my house forever."
Gunaśrī said, "We were previously driven away by others; for what reason do you both now invite us to stay?
The poor man replied:
"You now think of me; because of you, I shall likewise show respect to him. Therefore, let us both invite them to stay at my home.

Kāśyapa! It is the same for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva: he does not wish to be born in the heavens, because birth inevitably entails old age, sickness, death, and suffering; therefore, he abandons both, never having a heart of attachment.
Ordinary, foolish people do not understand the faults and afflictions of old age, sickness, death, and so forth; therefore, they greedily grasp at the two phenomena of birth and death.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a young Brahmin boy who, driven by hunger, sees an amra fruit in human excrement and immediately picks it up."
Having seen this, a person of wisdom rebuked him, saying:
"O Brahmin, your lineage is pure; for what reason have you taken these foul fruits from within the dung?"
Having heard this, the youth felt ashamed and replied, "I truly did not eat;
I washed it clean only to discard it again."
The wise person says:
"You are greatly deluded; if you were to discard it again, you should not have taken it in the first place. Good son!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: regarding this portion of birth, he neither accepts nor rejects it, just as that wise man rebuked the youth.
Ordinary people rejoice in birth and loathe death, just as that youth took the fruit and then threw it away.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like this:
suppose at a crossroads there is a person with a vessel filled to the brim with food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, which he wishes to sell.
Suppose there is a person who has come from afar, hungry, parched, and exhausted, and upon seeing that the food possesses full color, fragrance, and flavor, points to it and asks: "What is this?
The host of the meal replies:
"This is superior food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.
If one eats this food, one will obtain beauty and strength, be able to dispel hunger and thirst, and gain the sight of the devas;
it has but one drawback, namely, the end of life."
Upon hearing this, the person immediately thought:
"I have no need now for physical strength or the sight of the heavens, nor do I wish for death.
He then spoke these words:
"Once this food has been eaten, if one should die, why would you now sell it here?
The owner of the food replied,
"A person of wisdom would never be willing to buy it."
"Only fools do not understand this matter; they pay me a high price and greedily eat it. "Good son!
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: he does not wish to be born in the heavens, yet he attains form and power and beholds the various devas."
Why is this? Because they cannot escape various sufferings and afflictions.
Ordinary people are ignorant and foolish; wherever they are born, they are entirely possessed by craving and attachment, for they do not perceive old age, sickness, and death.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a poisonous tree: its roots can kill, its trunk can kill, and its bark, flowers, fruits, and seeds can all kill as well."
"Good son!
The five aggregates experienced in the twenty-five states of existence where birth occurs are likewise all capable of killing.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
For example, just as excrement is foul-smelling whether it be much or little,
so it is with birth, noble son:
whether one’s lifespan is eighty thousand years or as short as ten years, all alike undergo suffering.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like a steep precipice covered with grass on top, while on the edge of the opposite bank there is much *amṛta*.
If anyone should eat it, they would live for a thousand celestial years, forever free from all diseases, dwelling in peace and happiness.

Ordinary, foolish people, because they crave its flavor, do not realize there is a great, deep pit beneath it; as they step forward to seize it, they do not perceive their own feet slipping, and they fall into the pit and die.
Once the wise have known this, they abandon it and depart from afar. Good son!
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; he does not even desire to accept exquisite food from the heavens, much less that of the human realm.
If ordinary worldlings must swallow iron balls in the hells, how much more so should humans and devas not partake of exquisite and sublime delicacies?
Kāśyapa!
By means of these analogies and other immeasurable, boundless parables, one should know that this birth is, in truth, a great suffering.
Kāśyapa! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplating the suffering of birth.
“Kāśyapa, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the suffering of old age within this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra?

Old age can cause coughing and labored breathing; it can destroy valorous strength, mindfulness, perseverance, the joys of youth, pride, arrogance, and self-indulgent composure. It can produce back pain and lethargy, leading one to be despised by others.”
Kāśyapa!
It is like a pond filled with lotus flowers, blooming and radiant, most delightful to behold; yet when heaven sends down hail, they are all utterly destroyed.
Good son! Old age is also like this; it can utterly destroy youthful vigor and beautiful complexion.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

For example, suppose a king has a wise minister who is skilled in the art of war. When a rival king resists and acts in defiance, the king dispatches this minister to campaign against him; the minister then immediately captures him and brings him before the king.
Old age is likewise: it seizes the vigor of youth and delivers one to the King of Death.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, just as a broken axle is no longer of any use, so too is old age of no further use.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a great wealthy household that possesses abundant treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate.
There are bandits and enemies who, upon entering a house, are able to plunder it until it is completely emptied.
Good son, youthful vigor and beautiful appearance are just like this; they are constantly being plundered by the thief of old age.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a poor man who craves exquisite food and fine, soft garments; though he longs for them, he cannot obtain them. Good son!
Old age is likewise; though one possesses a greedy mind and desires to enjoy wealth and pleasure, indulging freely in the five sensual desires, one cannot obtain them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Just as a land tortoise constantly thinks of water in its heart,
so it is with human beings, noble son: once they have been withered by old age and decay, their minds constantly remember the pleasures of the five desires experienced in their youth.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the lotus flowers in the autumn moonlight, which all delight in beholding; yet when they wither and turn yellow, people loathe and despise them.
Good son! Prime youth and vigorous appearance are likewise thus; they are cherished and delighted in by all, yet when old age arrives, they are loathed and despised by the multitude.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like sugarcane:
once it has been pressed, the residue has no flavor remaining.
Son of good family!
The vigor and flourishing appearance of youth are likewise thus; once one is oppressed by old age, there are no three kinds of flavors:
first, the flavor of leaving the household life; second, the flavor of reciting and chanting; and third, the flavor of sitting in meditation.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the full moon: its radiance is great at night, but not so during the day. Good son!

Human beings are also like this: in their youth they are dignified and handsome, with magnificent features; in their old age they become frail and weak, their physical form and spirit withered and emaciated.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like a king who always ruled his realm with the True Dharma, being honest and without crookedness, compassionate and fond of giving.
At one time, he was destroyed by a hostile nation; wandering and fleeing in dispersal, he eventually reached another land.
When the people of other lands saw him, they felt compassion and all spoke thus:
"O Great King!
In former days you ruled the nation with the True Dharma and did not oppress the myriad people; why is it that in a single day you have come to such a state of exile?"
"Good son! Human beings are also like this;
once they have been ruined and decayed by old age, they constantly praise the deeds they performed during their youth.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
It is like the wick of a lamp, which relies solely upon oil; once the oil is exhausted, its power cannot endure for long.
Good son, it is the same with human beings:
they rely solely upon the oil of vigor; once that vigor is exhausted, how can the wick of old age and decay endure for long?
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like a dried-up river, which cannot benefit humans, non-humans, birds, or beasts. Good son!
Human beings are also like this: withered by old age, they are unable to benefit from any of their activities.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a tree standing on the edge of a steep riverbank; when it encounters a violent wind, it will surely fall over.
"Good son!
Human beings are also like this: when they reach the perilous brink of old age, once the wind of death arrives, they have no power to remain.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
Just as a broken axle cannot bear a heavy load, so it is with old age,
O son of good family;
it is unable to receive or learn any wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like an infant who is held in contempt by others. Good son!
Old age is likewise always held in contempt and reviled by all. Kāśyapa!
By means of these and other immeasurable and boundless analogies, you should know that old age is indeed a great suffering.
Kāśyapa! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of the Great Vehicle and contemplating the suffering of old age. "Kāśyapa!"
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplate the suffering of illness?
That which is called "illness" is capable of destroying all matters of peace and happiness, just as hail and rain damage and ruin the sprouts of grain.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a person who has an enemy; his mind is constantly filled with sorrow and he harbors fear. Good son!
All sentient beings are likewise thus: they constantly fear the suffering of illness and harbor sorrow and anxiety in their hearts.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as if there were a man of handsome appearance whom the wife of a king loved with desire; she sent a messenger to summon him and had sexual intercourse with him.

At that time, the king captured him and immediately dispatched men to gouge out one of his eyes, cut off one of his ears, and sever one of his hands and feet; at that moment, the man's appearance was transformed and he became an object of loathing and contempt for others.
Good son! Human beings are also like this:
although they may possess a complete body with eyes and ears, once they are entangled and oppressed by the suffering of illness, they become objects of contempt and disdain for all people.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Just as the plantain tree, the bamboo, the reed, the rush, and the mule die when they produce fruit,
so it is, son of good family!
Human beings are also like this: when they have illness, they die.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), whose minister of war always leads the way in front, while the king follows behind.

It is also like the king of fish, the king of ants, the king of conchs, the king of oxen, or a caravan leader: when they go before, all such multitudes follow after them, none abandoning or leaving them behind.
Good son! The wheel-turning king of death is likewise; he constantly follows the minister of illness, never departing from him.
Fish, ants, snails, oxen, caravan leaders, and the king of illness are also like this; they are always pursued by the hosts of death.

Kāśyapa! The causal conditions of illness are as follows: namely, suffering and affliction, sorrow, lamentation, and grief; physical and mental unease; being oppressed and harmed by enemies and bandits; the destruction of the life-preserving float and the demolition of the bridge; the ability to plunder the very root of right mindfulness; furthermore, the ability to destroy robust health, fine complexion, strength, and well-being; the casting aside of shame and remorse; and the ability to cause the body and mind to burn with feverish heat.
By means of these and other immeasurable and boundless parables, one should know that the suffering of illness is a great suffering. Kāśyapa,
this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of the Mahāyāna and contemplating the suffering of illness.
“Kāśyapa! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplate the suffering of death?
That which is called 'death' is so called because it can burn and extinguish.”
Kāśyapa! Just as when a fire calamity arises, it can burn everything except for the second dhyāna, because its power does not reach there. Good son!
The fire of death is likewise able to burn everything, except for Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, because its power does not reach them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Just as when a water calamity arises, everything is swept away and submerged, except for the third dhyāna, because its power does not reach there.
Good son, the water of death is likewise; it sweeps away and submerges all, except for the Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like the arising of a wind calamity, which can blow away and utterly destroy everything, except for the fourth dhyāna, because its power does not reach there.
Son of good family!
"The wind of death is likewise; it can utterly blow out and extinguish everything that exists, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By what causes and conditions, O Kāśyapa, can that fourth dhyāna not be blown away by wind, cannot be drifted away by water, and cannot be burned by fire?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son!...”
In that fourth dhyāna, all internal and external defects are entirely absent.
Good son! As for the defects of the first dhyāna: internally there are vitarka and vicāra, and externally there is the calamity of fire.
The defects of the second dhyāna are that internally there is joy (*prīti*) and externally there is the calamity of water.
The defects of the third dhyāna are that internally there is breathing (*śvāsa*) and externally there is the calamity of wind.
"Good son!
In that fourth dhyāna, all internal and external faults and afflictions are entirely absent; therefore, no calamities can reach it. Good son!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling securely in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, all internal and external faults and afflictions are completely exhausted; therefore, the King of Death cannot reach him.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as the garuḍa is able to devour and digest all dragons, fish, gold, silver, and other treasures, yet cannot cause a diamond to be digested; so too is it with this."
Good son!
The golden-winged bird of death is likewise; it can devour and digest all sentient beings, yet alone it cannot digest a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like all the grasses and trees on a riverbank: when the great waters surge in a flood, they are all swept away and flow into the great ocean, with the sole exception of the willow, because of its flexibility.
Good son! All sentient beings are likewise;
they all follow the current into the sea of death, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like Nārāyaṇa, who is able to crush and subdue all other strongmen, with the sole exception of the great wind. Why is this?
Because it is unimpeded. Good son, death-Nārāyaṇa is also like this:
he is able to crush and subdue all sentient beings, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because it is unimpeded.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like a person who, amidst those they hate and loathe, feigns intimacy and kindness, constantly pursuing them like a shadow follows a form, seeking an opportunity to kill them;
yet because that enemy is cautious and firmly prepared for themselves, this person is unable to kill them.
Good son!
The enemy of death is likewise; it constantly watches for sentient beings, seeking to kill them, yet it alone cannot kill the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are not negligent.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

For example, it is like a sudden downpour of a vajra torrential rain that utterly destroys medicinal herbs, trees, forests, mountains, earth, sand, shards, stones, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and all such things, yet alone cannot destroy the genuine treasure of vajra.
Good son!
The rain of diamond-like death is likewise; it can destroy all sentient beings, with the sole exception of the Vajra Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
just as the garuḍa is able to devour all nāgas, yet cannot devour those who have received the three refuges;
so it is, son of good family.
The dead garuḍa is likewise; it can devour all immeasurable sentient beings, with the sole exception of bodhisattvas who abide in the three concentrations.
What are these three concentrations?
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the venomous mālā snake:
wherever it touches and stings, even if there be efficacious spells or the most excellent and wondrous medicines, they can do nothing for it.
Only the *Agastya* star-vidyā can cause it to be healed. Good son!

Being bitten by the venom of death is just like this: no medical prescriptions whatsoever can do anything about it, except for the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* vidyā-mantra in which the Bodhisattva abides within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a person who has incurred the wrath of a king; if that person can offer gentle and kind words and present gifts of wealth and treasure, they may then be released.
"Good son!
The King of Death is not like that; even if one offers him gentle words, money, treasures, and jewels as tribute, one cannot escape him.
Good son!"

Now, death is like being in a perilous place where there are no provisions; the destination is far removed and one has no companion. One travels day and night without knowing its limits; it is deep, dark, and without light. It enters without a door yet occupies a specific place. Although it has no site of pain, it cannot be treated; it proceeds without obstruction and once arrived, there is no escape. It is not something that can be destroyed, and those who see it are filled with grief and poison. It is not an ugly form that causes terror, yet it lies spread beside one’s body, imperceptible to awareness.
Kāśyapa! By these and other immeasurable and boundless analogies, you should know that this death is truly a great suffering. Kāśyapa!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and contemplating the suffering of death.
“Kāśyapa, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, contemplate the suffering of separation from those one loves?”
The suffering of separation from the beloved can serve as the root of all sufferings, as it is said in a verse:
"From craving arises sorrow; From craving arises fear."
"If one is free from craving, what worry or fear could there be?

"Because of craving as a condition, sorrow and suffering arise; because of sorrow and suffering, sentient beings are made to experience aging, decline, and the suffering of separation from those they love—namely, death."
"Good son!
Because of separation, various subtle sufferings can arise; I shall now analyze and demonstrate them for you.
Good son!"
In a past age when the lifespan of humans was immeasurable, there was a king named Supratiṣṭhita.

At that time, he served as a crown prince while his father was still a youth; he governed the affairs of state for eighty-four thousand years, and likewise reigned as king for eighty-four thousand years.

At that time, a fleshy tumor grew upon the crown of the king’s head; it was soft and supple, like tūla-cotton or fine, delicate karpāsa cloth, and as it gradually increased in size, it caused him no distress.
When the ten months were complete, the womb opened, and a boy was born; his form was upright and handsome, extraordinary and peerless, with features so distinct that he was the foremost among men.
The father king was filled with joy and named him Śikhaṇḍin (Top-Knotted).

At that time, King Supratiṣṭhita entrusted the affairs of state to Śikhaṇḍin and abandoned his palace, wife, children, and retinue to enter the mountains to study the Way for a full eighty-four thousand years.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, King Mūrdhaja was atop a high tower, having bathed and observed the fast. Immediately, from the east, there appeared the precious golden wheel, with its thousand spokes, hub, and rim complete; it was not fashioned by any craftsman but was spontaneously accomplished, coming forth to attend upon him.
King Mūrdhaja then had this thought:

"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernormal powers say that if a Kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower having bathed and observed the fast, and if there appears a golden wheel—complete with a thousand spokes, a hub, and a rim, not fashioned by a craftsman but spontaneously accomplished—that comes to meet him, it should be known that this king shall become a Wheel-turning Sage King."
He further thought to himself:
"I shall now put it to the test.
He immediately lifted this Wheel-Treasure with his left hand, held a censer in his right, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and made this vow:
"If this precious golden wheel is truly not false, it should proceed along the path traveled by the past Wheel-Turning Kings.
Having made this vow, the precious golden wheel ascended into the void, traveled throughout the ten directions, and then returned to rest in the left hand of Māndhātṛ.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja’s heart was filled with joy; leaping for immeasurable delight, he spoke these words:
"I shall certainly become a Wheel-Turning King.
Not long thereafter, the Elephant Treasure appeared, its form majestic and beautiful like a white lotus, with its seven limbs touching the ground.
Having seen this, Mūrdhagata thought again:

"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernormal powers say that if a wheel-turning king, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower having bathed and observed the fast, and if there appears an elephant-treasure—stately in appearance like a white lotus, with its seven limbs touching the ground—to come and respond to him, one should know that this king is indeed a noble universal monarch."
He further thought to himself:
"I shall now put this to the test.
He immediately took up an incense burner, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and made this vow:
"If this White Elephant Treasure is truly real and not false, it should proceed along the path traveled by the past Wheel-Turning Sage Kings.
Having made this vow, the White Elephant Treasure traveled from morning until evening, circling the eight directions as far as the limits of the great ocean, and then returned to its original place.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, further declaring:
"I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage-King.
Not long thereafter, the horse-treasure appeared; it was deep blue-black in color, with a mane and tail of golden hue.
Having seen this, King Mūrdhaja further thought:

"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernormal powers say that if a Wheel-Turning King, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower having bathed and observed the fast, and if there is a horse-treasure of deep blue color with a golden mane and tail that comes to appear before him, it should be known that this king is indeed a Holy King."
He further thought to himself:
"I shall now put this to the test.
He immediately took hold of an incense burner, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and made this vow:
"If this precious dark-blue horse is truly not false, it should proceed along the path traveled by the wheel-turning sage-kings of the past.
Having made this vow, the precious dark-blue horse traveled from morning until evening, circling the eight directions as far as the limits of the great ocean, and then returned to its original place.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, exclaiming once more:
"I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King. Not long thereafter, there appeared the Woman-Treasure (strī-ratna).

Her appearance was upright and graceful, the most exquisite of all; she was neither tall nor short, neither too fair nor too dark. From every pore of her body issued the fragrance of sandalwood, and her breath was as pure and fragrant as a blue lotus. Her vision reached one yojana when looking afar, and her hearing and sense of smell were likewise so. Her tongue was broad and long, capable of covering her face; it was fine and thin in texture, like a leaf of red copper. Her mind was sharp, wise, and sagacious, possessed of great insight, and she always spoke gentle words to all sentient beings.
When this woman touched the king’s robe with her hand, she immediately knew whether his body was at ease or afflicted by illness, and she also knew the object upon which his mind was focused.
At that time, Mūrdhagata thought again:
"If there is a woman who can know the king's mind, she is indeed a Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna)."

Not long thereafter, within the royal palace, there spontaneously appeared a precious maṇi-jewel of pure blue lapis lazuli, as large as a person's thigh. It was capable of illuminating one yojana in the darkness. Even when the heavens rained down in drops as thick as axle-trees, the power of this jewel could form a canopy that completely covered an area of one yojana, blocking this great rain so that it did not fall through.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja again thought to himself:
"If a Wheel-Turning King obtains such a precious jewel, he must surely be a noble sovereign.

Not long thereafter, a minister in charge of the treasury appeared spontaneously; he possessed abundant wealth and treasures, was immeasurably wealthy, and his storehouses were overflowing with nothing lacking. By the fruit of his past merit, he had attained the faculty of sight with the power to see through all the earth and perceive every hidden treasure therein; whatever the king desired, he could provide it all.
At that time, Mūrdhaja wished to test him further; he immediately boarded a ship with him and entered the great ocean, saying to the treasurer:
"I now desire to obtain rare and extraordinary treasures."

Having heard this, the treasury minister immediately stirred the waters of the great ocean with both hands; at that moment, ten precious treasuries emerged from his ten fingertips. He presented them to the Holy King and addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"Use what you require as you please; as for the remainder that remains, it shall be cast into the great ocean.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was filled with immense joy and leaped for joy beyond measure, and he further thought to himself:
"I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin)."

Not long after that, a commander-in-chief appeared spontaneously, one who was valiant, fierce, and strategic, foremost in counsel, and skilled in the four types of military forces. If a soldier was fit for battle, he would manifest him before the Holy King; if unfit, he would withdraw him so as not to appear. He could cause those not yet subdued to be subdued, and once subdued, he had the power to protect them.
At that time, Mūrdhaja again thought to himself:
"If a Wheel-turning King obtains this treasure of the army, one should know for certain that he is a Wheel-turning Sage-King.
Then, the Wheel-turning Sage-Emperor Mūrdhaja addressed his ministers:
"You should know that this Jambudvīpa is peaceful, secure, and prosperous.
Now that I have already attained the seven treasures and am fully endowed with a thousand sons, what further purpose remains for me?"
The ministers replied, "Indeed, Great King!
Pūrvavideha has not yet submitted to your virtue; Your Majesty should go there to subdue it."
At that time, the Holy King, together with his seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air to Pūrvavideha in the east; the people of that land joyfully submitted to his rule.
He further addressed his ministers:

"My Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha are peaceful, prosperous, and joyful; the population is flourishing, and all have come to submit to my rule. The seven treasures are perfected and I am endowed with a thousand sons. What more is there for me to do?"
The ministers replied,
"Indeed, Great King!
Aparagoyānī has not yet submitted to your virtue."
At that time, the Holy King, together with his seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air to Aparagoyānī.
Once the King arrived there, the people of that land likewise submitted to his rule.
He further addressed his ministers, saying:

"My Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and this Aparagoyānī are peaceful, prosperous, and joyful; the population is flourishing and has all submitted to my rule. With the seven treasures accomplished and a full thousand sons, what more is there for me to do?"
The ministers replied,
"Indeed, Great King!
Northern Uttarakuru has not yet submitted to your rule."
At that time, the Holy King, together with his seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air to the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
Once the King arrived there, the people of that land joyfully submitted to his virtue.
He further addressed his ministers:
"My four continents are peaceful, secure, and prosperous; the people are flourishing and have all submitted to my virtue.
The seven treasures are perfected and I am endowed with a thousand sons; what more is there for me to do?"
The ministers replied:
"Indeed, O Holy King!
The lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is exceedingly long, and they dwell in peace, security, and happiness."
The bodies of those devas are of incomparable beauty and majesty; their palaces, couches, and bedding are all made of the seven precious gems.
Relying on their own celestial merit, they will eventually come to submit and convert.
"You should now go forth to subdue him and bring him under your power.
At that time, the Holy King, together with his seven treasures and his entire retinue, soared through the void and ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He saw a tree, its color a vibrant green.
Having seen it, the Holy King immediately asked his ministers,
"What color is this?"
The minister replied:
"This is the Pārijātaka tree; during the three months of summer, the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven always enjoy themselves and take pleasure beneath it."
Again, seeing a white color like that of white clouds, he asked the minister:
"What color is that?
The minister replied:
"This is the Hall of Good Dharma, where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly assemble to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, knowing that King Mūrdhaja had already arrived outside, immediately went out to welcome him.
Having seen him, he took his hand and ascended the Hall of Good Dharma (*Saddharmasālā*), where they sat together on a shared seat.
At that time, the two kings were indistinguishable in their physical forms and features; the only difference between them was the movement of their eyes.
At that time, the noble king immediately had this thought:
"Would it not be better for me now to depose him from his royal position and dwell therein myself as the Heavenly King?
O son of good family!
At that time, Śakra received, upheld, read, and recited Mahāyāna sūtras; he elucidated, analyzed, and expounded them for others, yet he had not yet fully mastered their profound meanings.

By the power of these causes and conditions—namely, reading, reciting, receiving, upholding, discerning, and extensively explaining [this teaching] for others—he possesses great majestic virtue. Good son!

Once this King Mūrdhaja had conceived an evil thought toward Śakra, he immediately fell back down to Jambudvīpa. He was separated from those dear to him among humans and devas, giving rise to great suffering and affliction; furthermore, encountering a malignant disease, his life came to an end.
At that time, Śakra was Kāśyapa Buddha.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King was none other than my own self.
O son of good family!
You should know that such suffering of separation from those one loves is an extreme great suffering. Good son!

If even a bodhisattva-mahāsattva recalls such sufferings of separation from loved ones in the past, how much more so should a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contemplate the suffering of separation from loved ones in the present life?
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, contemplate the suffering of association with the disliked? Good son!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, there is everywhere such suffering of association with the hated and the disliked.
For example, just as a person regards imprisonment, confinement, shackles, and fetters as great suffering,
so too does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva regard all births within the five realms of existence as the great suffering of being joined with those whom one hates and loathes.
Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who, constantly fearing an enemy, shackles, fetters, and manacles, abandons his parents, wife, children, kinsmen, treasures, and property, and flees far away to escape them.
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: fearing birth and death, they fully practice the six pāramitās and enter into nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and contemplating the suffering of association with the hated. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplate the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
"Seeking" refers to all forms of seeking.
There are two kinds of such seeking:
First, the pursuit of wholesome dharmas; second, the pursuit of unwholesome dharmas.

To suffer because wholesome dharmas have not yet been attained, and to suffer because unwholesome dharmas have not yet been abandoned—this is a brief explanation of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
“Kāśyapa! This is called the Truth of Suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering, this meaning is not so. Why is this?
As the Buddha told Śreṇika in the past:
"If form were suffering, all sentient beings would not seek form; if there were those who seek it, it would not be called suffering."
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three kinds of feeling:
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
As the Buddha previously said to the bhikṣus:
"If there is anyone who can practice wholesome dharmas, they shall obtain happiness.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:

"Within the good realms, one experiences pleasure through the six contacts: seeing beautiful forms with the eye is pleasure; likewise, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and perceiving agreeable mental objects with the mind are also pleasure."
As the Buddha spoke in verse:
"To uphold the precepts is joy; The body does not undergo manifold sufferings.
In sleep one finds peace and security; Upon awakening, the mind is filled with gladness."
When receiving robes and food, reciting and practicing while walking in meditation,
dwelling alone in the mountain forests— such as this is the supreme joy.
If one can constantly cultivate loving-kindness toward all sentient beings day and night, [this too is supreme joy].
By this one attains eternal bliss, because of not causing affliction to others.
There is the bliss of few desires and contentment, and the bliss of extensive learning and discernment.
The unattached Arhat is also said to experience bliss.
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having ultimately reached the other shore and accomplished all that was to be done, is said to possess the supreme bliss.
"World-Honored One!"
"The meaning of the characteristics of bliss as taught in the various sūtras is as follows.
As the Buddha now speaks, how should it correspond with this meaning?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
You have skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding this matter.”
"Good son! All sentient beings perversely conceive the notion of pleasure within the midst of lower suffering.
Therefore, the characteristics of suffering that I now describe are no different from those of the original."
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"According to what the Buddha has taught, regarding those who conceive the notion of pleasure within inferior suffering, there would likewise have to be pleasure in inferior birth, inferior aging, inferior illness, inferior death, inferior separation from the beloved, inferior failure to obtain what is sought, inferior association with the hated, and inferior the five aggregates of clinging. Such sufferings as these would also possess pleasure."
World-Honored One!
"Birth in the lower realms" refers to the three evil destinies;
"birth in the middle realm" refers to among human beings.
"Higher rebirth" refers to birth in the heavens.
Suppose, moreover, someone were to ask this question:
"If one perceives lower pleasure as suffering, perceives intermediate pleasure as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, and perceives superior pleasure as pleasure."
"How should one answer this, World-Honored One?

If one were to conceive the notion of pleasure within inferior suffering, one would not see anyone who, when receiving a thousand punishments, would already conceive the notion of pleasure at the very first stroke. If such a notion does not arise, how can it be said that one conceives the notion of pleasure within inferior suffering?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"So it is, so it is, just as you have said.
For this reason, there is no perception of pleasure."

Why is this? It is like a person who is due to receive a thousand punishments; if, after receiving only one blow, they are immediately released, that person will at that moment give rise to a perception of pleasure.
"Therefore, you should know that within what is not pleasure, one falsely gives rise to the perception of pleasure.
Kāśyapa said:
"World-Honored One!"
"That person does not give rise to the perception of pleasure because of a single stroke; rather, they give rise to the perception of pleasure because they have attained liberation.
Kāśyapa, for this reason, I previously told Śreṇika Bimbisāra that the pleasure within the five aggregates is indeed real and not false."
Kāśyapa! There are three feelings and three types of suffering.
The three feelings are: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

The three types of suffering are: namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). Good son!
The sensation of suffering is called the three sufferings, namely: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned existence, and the suffering of change.
The other two feelings are what are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Noble son! For these reasons, within the cycle of birth and death, there truly exists the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
Because the natures of suffering and pleasure are inseparable, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva says that all things are suffering.
Good son! Within birth and death there is truly no pleasure; it is only that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, in accordance with worldly convention, say that there is pleasure.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak in accordance with worldly conventions, is this not false and illusory?”

As the Buddha has taught, those who practice virtue receive the retribution of happiness; by maintaining the precepts, the body is at ease and does not undergo suffering, until all tasks are completed, which constitutes the supreme bliss. Is the experience of such happiness described in these and other sūtras illusory?

If this were false, what would be the meaning of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, having cultivated the path to enlightenment for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, having already abandoned all false speech, yet now making such a statement?
The Buddha said: "Good son!
The verses on experiencing various joys as previously described are the very foundation of the path to bodhi, and they are also able to nurture anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
For this reason, it was previously stated in the sūtras that this is the characteristic of pleasure. Good son!
For example, in the world, those necessities of life that can serve as causes for pleasure are therefore called "pleasure."

That which is called female beauty, indulgence in wine, exquisite delicacies and sweet flavors; obtaining water when thirsty, encountering fire when cold; clothing and ornaments, elephants, horses, and carriages; male and female slaves and servants; gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, pearls, granaries, and grain—such things as these, which are necessary for the world and can serve as causes of pleasure, are what is termed "pleasure."
Good son! Such things as these can also give rise to suffering; because of women, men experience the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, and weeping, even unto the loss of life.
Even the sweet taste of wine, up to and including stored grain, can cause people to experience great distress and affliction.
For this reason, everything is suffering; there is no characteristic of pleasure.
"Good son! Regarding these eight sufferings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands suffering as being without suffering. Good son!"
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others do not know the cause of happiness; for such people, [the Buddha] speaks of the presence of the characteristic of happiness within inferior suffering.
Only a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa is able to know the causes of both suffering and happiness.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Twelve.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: On the Noble Practices (III) “Good son!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, contemplate the truth of origination?”
"Good son!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates this truth of origination as the causal condition for the aggregates. That which is called 'origination' is, in turn, craving for existence.
There are two kinds of craving:"
First, attachment to one's own body; second, attachment to what is required for its sustenance.
Furthermore, there are two types:
when the five desires have not yet been obtained, one binds the mind to seeking them with single-minded devotion.
Once they have been attained, one becomes capable of enduring and remaining focused upon them.
Furthermore, there are three types:
craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realm of form, and craving for the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
craving conditioned by karma, craving conditioned by afflictions, and craving conditioned by suffering.
For those who have left the household life, there are four kinds of craving:
What are the four?
They are robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:

They are greedily attached to the five aggregates, following after all their various needs with total craving and attachment, engaging in conceptualization and calculation that is immeasurable and boundless.
Good son! There are two kinds of craving:
The first is wholesome craving; the second is unwholesome craving.
Unwholesome craving is sought only by fools.
Wholesome craving for the dharmas is sought by all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of attachment to wholesome dharmas:
the unwholesome and the wholesome.
Seeking the Two Vehicles is called unwholesome; seeking the Great Vehicle is called wholesome.
"Good son!
The craving of ordinary beings is called 'accumulation' (samudaya), but it is not called a 'truth' (satya).
The craving of bodhisattvas is called the 'true truth,' but it is not called accumulation."
"Why is this? It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that one undergoes birth; it is not out of attachment that one undergoes birth.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught in other sūtras that for all sentient beings, karma serves as the causal condition—sometimes speaking of pride, sometimes of the six contacts, and sometimes of ignorance—as the causal conditions for the five aggregates of clinging; by what meaning do you now teach the Four Noble Truths, asserting that craving alone is the cause of the five aggregates?”
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
As you have said, the various causes and conditions are not non-causes; rather, the five aggregates must depend upon craving. Good son!
It is like a great king who, when he goes on a tour of inspection, his ministers and retinue all follow him.
Craving is also like this: wherever craving moves, these various fetters and so forth likewise follow and move.
It is like a greasy garment: wherever dust adheres to it, it remains fixed as soon as it sticks.
Craving is also like this: wherever there is craving, the fetters of karma also abide.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as a moist ground can produce sprouts, so too does craving produce the sprouts of all karmic afflictions.
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, he deeply contemplates this craving, which has nine types:

first, like a debt with a remainder; second, like the wife of a rākṣasī; third, like a beautiful flower stalk entwined by a venomous snake; fourth, like unwholesome food that one forces oneself to eat despite it being unsuitable to one's nature; fifth, like a courtesan; sixth, like the seed of a *mālūka* gourd; seventh, like a polyp within a sore; eighth, like a violent wind; and ninth, like a comet."
What is meant by "having a remainder like a debt"? Good son!
It is, for example, like a poor man who owes another person money; although he has nearly finished repaying it, because a small portion remains unpaid, he is still bound in prison and cannot escape.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise; because they still possess the residual traces of the habit-energy of craving, they are unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! This is called being like a debt with a remainder. Good son!
What is meant by being like a rākṣasī wife?

Good son! It is, for example, as if there were a man who took a rākṣasī as his wife or concubine; that rākṣasī would devour every son born to her as soon as he was born, and once all the sons were exhausted, she would then devour her husband.
Good son! The rākṣasī of craving is also like this: she gives birth to the seeds of roots of goodness according to sentient beings, and as soon as they are born, she devours them.

Once the good sons are exhausted, she further devours the sentient beings, causing them to fall into the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; only bodhisattvas are exempt. This is what is meant by being like a wife who is a rākṣasī.
Good son! What is meant by "like a beautiful flower-stalk entwined by a venomous snake"?

It is like a person who, being by nature fond of flowers, fails to see the danger posed by the venomous snake on the stalk; he immediately reaches out and grasps it, and once grasped, he is bitten by the snake, and having been bitten, his life comes to an end.

All ordinary beings are likewise: they crave the flowers of the five desires and fail to see the peril of these poisonous snakes of attachment; they grasp them and are immediately stung by the venom of attachment, so that at the end of their lives they fall into the three evil realms—except for Bodhisattvas. This is called "a beautiful flower-stalk entwined by a poisonous snake."
Good son! What is it to force oneself to eat food that is unwholesome?
It is like a person who forces himself to eat food that he does not tolerate; having eaten it, his belly aches, he suffers from diarrhea, and dies.

Craving for food is likewise; sentient beings in the five realms of existence forcibly consume and greedily cling to it, and by this cause and condition they fall into the three evil paths—with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas. This is called forcibly consuming that which is unsuitable as food.
"Good son! What is meant by a 'prostitute'?

It is like a foolish man who consorts with a prostitute; that prostitute skillfully employs various forms of flattery and feigned intimacy to strip away all the man's wealth, and once his wealth is exhausted, she then casts him out."

The harlot of craving is likewise so: when a foolish person lacking wisdom engages in intimacy with her, this "daughter of craving" seizes all his wholesome dharmas; once his wholesome dharmas are exhausted, she drives him away and causes him to fall into the three evil realms—except for the Bodhisattva. This is what is called the harlot.
"Good son! What is the *mālūka* seed?

For example, when a bird has eaten a *mālūka* seed and it falls to the ground with its excrement, or perhaps is carried by the wind to fall beneath a tree, it immediately sprouts and grows. It then entwines and binds the *nyagrodha* tree, preventing it from growing further until the tree eventually withers and dies."

The *āmalaka* fruit is also like this: it entangles and binds all the wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings, preventing them from increasing and causing them to wither away until they perish. Once they have withered and perished, after the end of life, these beings fall into the three evil realms—except for Bodhisattvas. This is what is called the *āmalaka* fruit.
Good son! What is the "fleshy growth within a sore"?

It is like a person with a chronic sore upon which a fleshy growth has formed; that person must diligently apply treatment and not give rise to a mind of neglect. If they give rise to a mind of neglect, the sore and the growth will increase, and worms and abscesses will arise again. Due to these causes and conditions, they will then meet their end.

The sores and wounds of the five aggregates of ordinary, foolish people are likewise thus; craving acts as a polyp within them. One should diligently apply the mind to treat and remove this craving. If it is not treated, at the end of life one will immediately fall into the three evil realms, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas. This is called a polyp within a sore.
Good son! What is a violent wind?
It is like a violent wind that can topple mountains and shift peaks, uprooting even the deepest-rooted trees.

The violent gale of craving is likewise; it gives rise to malevolent thoughts toward one’s parents and can uproot the supreme, profound, and firm roots of bodhi of the Greatly Wise Śāriputra and others—save for the Bodhisattvas, who alone are exempt from this. This is what is called the violent gale.
Good son! How is it like a comet?
For example, when a comet appears in the world, all the people suffer from famine, illness, emaciation, goiters, and various other afflictions.

The comet of craving is likewise; it can sever all seeds of the roots of goodness, leaving ordinary persons destitute and famished, giving rise to the disease of afflictions, causing them to transmigrate through birth and death and undergo various sufferings—except for Bodhisattvas. This is called the comet.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplates the fetter of craving in these nine ways. Good son!”

For this reason, ordinary worldlings have suffering but no Truth; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have both suffering and the Truth of Suffering, yet lack reality; whereas Bodhisattvas understand suffering as non-suffering, and therefore have no suffering but possess reality.

Ordinary worldlings possess accumulation but not the truth of accumulation; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess both accumulation and the truth of accumulation; all Bodhisattvas and others understand that accumulation is non-accumulation, and therefore, while there is no accumulation, there is the true truth.
The extinction of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not ultimate; for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there is both extinction and the ultimate truth.
The path of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not ultimate; for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there is both the path and the ultimate truth.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, perceive cessation and perceive the Truth of Cessation?
It is by means of severing all afflictions; if the afflictions are severed, it is called ‘permanent.’”
The extinguishing of the fire of afflictions is called "quiescence"; because afflictions are extinguished, one attains the experience of bliss.
Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas seek out causes and conditions, it is called "purity.
Because they no longer undergo rebirth within the twenty-five states of existence, it is called "transcending the world. Because they transcend the world, it is called "the eternal self."

Regarding form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, male, female, arising, abiding, ceasing, suffering, pleasure, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—one does not grasp at their characteristics; therefore, it is called the ultimate truth of absolute quiescence.
"Good son! A bodhisattva dwelling thus in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplates the Noble Truth of Cessation. Good son!"
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, contemplate the Noble Truth of the Path?
Good son, it is like being in the dark, where one is able to see objects, both coarse and fine, by means of a lamp.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, they perceive all dharmas by means of the Eightfold Noble Path—namely, the permanent and the impermanent, the conditioned and the unconditioned, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, substance and non-substance, suffering and pleasure, self and non-self, purity and impurity, afflictions and non-afflictions, karma and non-karma, reality and unreality, vehicles and non-vehicles, knowledge and non-knowledge, *dravya* (substantial entities) and non-*dravya*, *guṇa* (qualities) and non-*guṇa*, seeing and non-seeing, form and non-form, the path and non-path, and liberation and non-liberation.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva thus abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and contemplates the Noble Truth of the Path.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Eightfold Noble Path is the Noble Truth of the Path, it would not accord with the meaning. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has sometimes taught that faith is the path, capable of crossing over all outflows (*āsrava*).

At other times he has taught that non-negligence (*apramāda*) is the path; for it is through non-negligence that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and it is likewise a dharma that assists the bodhisattva’s path.
At other times, he speaks of diligence as the path, as when he told Ānanda:
"If there is anyone who can diligently cultivate diligence, they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

At other times, he may say: "If one contemplates the foundation of mindfulness of the body and, with a focused mind, diligently cultivates this mindfulness of the body, then one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At times, it is said that right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) constitutes the path, as when it was told to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"That which is right concentration is truly the path; it is not the case that what is not right concentration is the path.
Only by entering right concentration can one contemplate the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); it is not possible to contemplate them without entering concentration."

Or he may preach a single dharma: if a person practices it, they can purify sentient beings, eliminate all sorrow and affliction, and attain the True Dharma—namely, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
Or again, it is said that cultivating the perception of impermanence is called the Path, as in the instruction given to the bhikṣus:
"One who is able to cultivate the perception of impermanence extensively can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Sometimes he says that by dwelling alone in contemplation at a secluded and tranquil aranya, one can swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At other times he says that preaching the Dharma for others is what is called the Way; if, upon hearing the Dharma, one’s net of doubt is immediately severed, and once the net of doubt is severed, one then attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At other times, he speaks of observing the precepts as the path, as when he told Ānanda:
"If there are those who diligently practice and uphold the prohibitive precepts, such persons shall cross over the great suffering of birth and death."
At other times, he says that associating with virtuous friends is what is called the Path, as when he told Ānanda:

"If there are those who associate with spiritual friends, they will possess pure precepts; if there are sentient beings who can draw near to me, they will be able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At times he says that cultivating loving-kindness is the path; those who cultivate and study loving-kindness sever all afflictions and attain the state of immovability.
At other times he says that wisdom is the path, as when the Buddha formerly spoke to the bhikṣuṇī Viśākhā:
"Sister!..."
"Just as the śrāvakas, with the sword of wisdom, are able to sever the various flows, outflows, and afflictions.
At other times, the Tathāgata says that giving is the path, as when the Buddha in the past told King Prasenajit:
"Great King!..."
"You should know that because I practiced giving extensively in the past, by virtue of these causes and conditions, I have today attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“World-Honored One, if the Eightfold Noble Path is the Truth of the Path, then would not such sūtras as these be false?
If those sūtras are not false, for what reason do they not state that the Eightfold Path is the Noble Truth of the Path?”
"If he had not spoken thus, why would the Tathāgata have committed errors in the past?
Yet I know for certain that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have long been free from error.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
You have now asked this question because you wish to know all the secrets contained within the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras of the bodhisattvas.”
"Good son! All such sutras as these enter into the Truth of the Path. Good son!"

As I have taught, if there is faith in the Way, and if one has such faith in the Way, this is the root of faith; it is that which assists the path to Bodhi. Therefore, what I have said is without error.
"Good son! The Tathāgata thoroughly understands immeasurable skillful means; desiring to transform sentient beings, he therefore delivers various teachings of the Dharma in this way. Good son!"

It is like a skilled physician who recognizes the various causes of disease in sentient beings; according to each person's ailment, he prepares a medicine and prescribes its prohibitions, yet water alone is not included among those prohibited items.

Some drink ginger water, some licorice water, some fine-rooted pepper water, some black rock-honey water, some āmalaka water, some nīpāra water, or pāṭhā water; some drink cold water, some hot water, some grape water, or pomegranate water.
"Good son! This skilled physician thoroughly understands the various ailments of sentient beings; although there are many prohibitions regarding medicines, water is not included among them.

The Tathāgata is likewise: well-versed in skillful means, he takes a single dharma-characteristic and, according to the capacities of sentient beings, analyzes and extensively explains it through various names and characteristics. Those sentient beings accept what is taught according to their own dispositions, and having accepted it, they practice it to eliminate and sever their afflictions—just as that sick person follows the instructions of the skilled physician and finds their ailment cured."
"Furthermore, good son!
Suppose there is a man who is skilled in various languages, and he is in the midst of a great assembly. This assembly is all oppressed by heat and thirst, and they all cry out with one voice:
'We wish to drink water! "
"I wish to drink water!

At that moment, this person takes clear, cool water and, according to their particular kind, speaks of it as being "water," or calls it *pānīya*, or *udaka*, or *vāri-lana*, or *vāri*, or *payas*, or "ambrosia" (*amṛta*), or "cow's milk"—using such immeasurable names for water, he speaks thus to the great assembly.
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;
by means of a single noble path, he expounds it in various ways for the sake of the śrāvakas, ranging from the faculty of faith up to the eightfold noble path.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a goldsmith who, using a single kind of gold, fashions various kinds of ornaments according to his will—namely, necklaces, chains, rings, bracelets, hairpins, earrings, celestial crowns, armlets, and seals. Although there are such differences and distinctions among them, they do not depart from the gold."
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;
by means of the single Buddha-way, he teaches according to the various conceptual distinctions of sentient beings.
Sometimes he speaks of one kind, namely that the way of all Buddhas is one and without duality.
Furthermore, two kinds are taught, namely concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
Furthermore, three kinds are taught, namely vision (darśana), wisdom (prajñā), and knowledge (jñāna).

Furthermore, four kinds are taught, namely the path of seeing (darśanamārga), the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), and the path of the Buddha (buddhamārga).

Furthermore, five kinds are taught: namely, the path of those who proceed by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the path of those who proceed by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the path of those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), the path of those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and the path of bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*).

Furthermore, six kinds are taught: namely, the path of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the path of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), the path of the arhat (*arhat*), the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha.

Furthermore, seven kinds are taught, namely: the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
Furthermore, eight kinds are taught, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Furthermore, nine kinds are taught, namely the Eightfold Noble Path and faith.
Furthermore, ten kinds are taught, namely the Ten Powers.
Furthermore, eleven kinds are taught, namely the Ten Powers and Great Compassion.
Furthermore, twelve kinds are taught, namely: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
Furthermore, thirteen kinds are taught, namely: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi.

Furthermore, sixteen kinds are taught, namely: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, and the three bases of right mindfulness attained by the Buddha.
Furthermore, twenty paths are taught, namely: the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, and the three bases of right mindfulness.
"Good son! This Way is of one essence; it was for the sake of sentient beings that the Tathāgata, in the past, made various distinctions.
Furthermore, good son!"
For example, a single fire receives various names depending on what it burns, such as wood-fire, grass-fire, chaff-fire, bran-fire, or cow-and-horse-dung-fire.
"Good son!
The Buddha-way is likewise: it is one and without duality, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it is differentiated in various ways.
Furthermore, good son!"
For example, a single consciousness is explained as being sixfold: when it reaches the eye, it is called eye-consciousness, and so on up to mental consciousness;
it is just like this, son of good family.
The Way is also like this: it is one and without duality, yet the Tathāgata makes various distinctions for the sake of transforming all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, regarding a single form: that which is seen by the eye is called "form";
that which is heard by the ear is called "sound";
and that which is smelled by the nose is called "fragrance."
That which is tasted by the tongue is called flavor;
that which is perceived by the body is called touch. Good son!
The Path is also like this: it is one and without a second, yet the Tathāgata makes various distinctions for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Good son! For this reason, the eightfold noble path is called the Noble Truth of the Path.

"Good son! These Four Noble Truths were taught in sequence by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; by this cause and condition, immeasurable sentient beings have attained deliverance from birth and death."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Once, when the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Ganges River in the Śīrṣavana Forest, the Tathāgata took some leaves from a tree and said to the bhikṣus:"
"Are there more leaves held in my hand now,
or are there more leaves of all the grasses and trees growing on the earth?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
All the earth, trees, grasses, and leaves upon it are so numerous that they cannot be measured or calculated.
What the Tathāgata has grasped is but a small fraction, not even worth mentioning.”
“O monks! All phenomena that I have awakened to and fully realized are like the grasses, trees, and other plants that grow from the great earth;
those that I have proclaimed for the sake of all sentient beings are like the leaves in my hand.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
“Regarding the immeasurable dharmas realized by the Tathāgata, if they are included within the Four Noble Truths, they have already been taught;
if they were not so included, there would necessarily be five truths.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
The question you have now asked will bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings. Good son!
All such dharmas are entirely subsumed within the Four Noble Truths.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva spoke again, saying:
"If such dharmas as these are contained within the Four Noble Truths, for what reason did the Tathāgata declare that he had not taught them?"
The Buddha said,
"Good son! Although one has entered therein, it is still not called 'explaining.'"
Why is this? Son of good family!
There are two kinds of wisdom for knowing the Four Noble Truths:
The first is the middling, and the second is the superior.
The middling refers to the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the superior refers to the wisdom of all buddhas and bodhisattvas. Good son!
To know that the aggregates are suffering is called middle wisdom;
to discern that the aggregates possess immeasurable characteristics and that all of them are suffering—knowledge which is beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.
"Good son! Such meanings as these, I did not explain at all in that sūtra. Good son!"
To know the various sense bases (*āyatana*) as being called "gates" and also as being "suffering" is termed middle wisdom.
To discern that the various sense bases possess immeasurable characteristics and that they are entirely suffering—something not known by the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—is termed superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have also not explained in that sutra. Good son!
To know the various realms is called "analysis," and it is also called "nature," and it is also called "suffering"; this is termed middle-level wisdom.
To discern the various realms, which possess immeasurable characteristics and are entirely composed of suffering—this is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
this is called supreme wisdom. Good son!
Such meanings as these I have not spoken of in that sutra either.
Good son! To know the characteristic of the disintegration of form is called middling wisdom;
To discern all forms, which possess immeasurable characteristics and are entirely suffering—this is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
this is called supreme wisdom. Such meanings as these, I did not even mention in that sūtra.
"Good son! To know the characteristic of the sensation of feeling is called middle wisdom;
to discern all sensations and their immeasurable characteristics of perception, which are not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, is called superior wisdom."
"Good son! Such meanings as these were not even spoken by me in that sutra. Good son!"
To know the grasping of marks within perception is called middle wisdom;
to discern that perception consists of immeasurable graspings of marks, which are not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have not even mentioned in that sutra.
Good son! To know the characteristics of conditioned activity is called middling wisdom;
Discriminative analysis is activity; it is characterized by immeasurable formations and is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom.
Good son! Such meanings as these were also not spoken of by me in that sutra.
"Good son! To discern the characteristics of consciousness is called middle wisdom;
to discern that consciousness is characterized by immeasurable knowledge, which is beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is called superior wisdom."
"Good son! Such meanings as these were not even spoken by me in that sūtra. Good son!"
To know that craving is the causal condition capable of producing the five aggregates is called middling wisdom;

to know that a single person gives rise to immeasurable and boundless cravings such that they cannot be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and to be able to know all such cravings arising in all sentient beings, is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have not spoken of in that sūtra either. Good son!
To know the extinction of afflictions is called middling wisdom;
