The various afflictions are incalculable, and their cessation is likewise incalculable; this is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—it is called supreme wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have also not explained in that sutra. Good son!
To know the characteristics of this path and be able to leave behind afflictions is called middling wisdom;

The discernment of the characteristics of the Path is immeasurable and boundless; the afflictions abandoned thereby are likewise immeasurable and boundless. This is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and it is called supreme wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have not even mentioned in that sutra. Good son!
One who knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is said to possess middling wisdom.
The analytical discernment of conventional truth is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and this is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I did not explain even in that sūtra.
"Good son!
That all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, that all dharmas are without self, and that the tranquility of nirvana is the ultimate truth—this is called middle wisdom.
To know that this ultimate truth is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, such that it is not within the knowledge of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom."
"Such meanings as these, I have not even mentioned in that sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that you have spoken of, what is their meaning?
World-Honored One, does the conventional truth exist within the ultimate truth?
Does the ultimate truth exist within the conventional truth?
"If it exists, it is then a single truth; if it does not exist, would it not mean that the Tathāgata has spoken falsely?
"Good son! The conventional truth is itself the ultimate truth."
“World-Honored One!
If that were so, then there would be no two truths.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! There is a skillful means that accords with sentient beings, whereby it is taught that there are two truths. Good son!”
If one follows verbal expression, there are two kinds:
first, worldly dharmas; second, supramundane dharmas. Good son!
That which is known by those who have transcended the world is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
that which is known by worldly people is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Good son!
The combination of the five aggregates is designated as "so-and-so"; that ordinary beings follow such designations is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

To understand that within the aggregates there is no name "so-and-so," and that apart from the aggregates there is likewise no name "so-and-so"—to know this according to its true nature and characteristics, as those who have transcended the world do—is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
Some phenomena have both names and reality; others have names but lack reality.
Son of good family!
That which has a name but no reality is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which has both a name and reality is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Good son!

Such things as self, sentient beings, life-span, cognition and vision, nourishment, the person, the agent, and the experiencer; the mirage in the heat, the city of the Gandharvas, the hair of a tortoise, the horns of a rabbit, the circle of a whirling firebrand, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—these are called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—these are called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
“Good son! There are five kinds of worldly phenomena:
first, the world of names; second, the world of phrases; third, the world of bonds; fourth, the world of dharmas; and fifth, the world of attachment.”
Good son! What is called the world of names?
Male and female, jars and clothing, carriages and houses—such things as these are called the world of names.
What is the world of phrases (*pada-loka*)?
A single verse consists of four lines; such verses as these are called the world of phrases.
What is the world of bonds (*bandhana-loka*)?
Rolling up, tying, binding, and joining the palms—these are called the world of bondage.
What is the world of phenomena?
Such as striking a gong to assemble the Sangha, beating a drum to prepare the army, sounding a conch to signal the time for the precepts—these are called the world of phenomena.
What is attachment to the world?
It is like seeing a person at a distance wearing dyed robes; one gives rise to a perception and becomes attached, saying, "This is a śramaṇa, not a brāhmaṇa.
Seeing someone with a cord tied and worn across the body, one then thinks and says, "This is a brāhmaṇa, not a śramaṇa. This is called attachment to the world.
"Noble son!
These are called the five worldly dharmas.
Noble son!"

If there are sentient beings who, regarding these five kinds of worldly phenomena, possess no inverted views in their minds and know them as they truly are, this is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If there is burning, cutting, death, or destruction, this is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
if there is no burning, no cutting, no death, and no destruction, this is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
Furthermore, good son, there are eight characteristics of suffering which are called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

the absence of birth, aging, illness, death, separation from the beloved, meeting with the hated, failure to obtain what one seeks, and the five aggregates of clinging—these are called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Furthermore, good son! It is like a single person who possesses many skills:

when he runs, he is called a runner; when he harvests, he is called a harvester; when he prepares food and drink, he is called a cook; when he works with timber, he is called a carpenter; and when he smelts gold and silver, he is called a smith of gold and silver.
Thus, this one person has many names. The Dharma is also like this: its reality is one, yet it has many names.
"That which arises based on the union of father and mother is called the worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which arises from the union of the twelve links of dependent origination is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding that which is called ‘the truth of reality,’ what is its meaning?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! That which is called ‘ultimate truth’ is named the True Dharma. Good son!”
If a phenomenon is not true, it cannot be called the ultimate truth (*bhūtārtha*). Good son!
That which is the ultimate truth is without inversion; that which is without inversion is what is called the ultimate truth.
"Good son! That which is the ultimate truth (satya) is devoid of falsehood; if there were falsehood, it would not be called the ultimate truth. Good son!"
The true reality is called the Mahāyāna; that which is not the Mahāyāna is not called the true reality. Good son!
The true reality is what has been taught by the Buddha and not what has been taught by Māra. If it were taught by Māra and not by the Buddha, it would not be called the true reality.
"Good son!
The ultimate truth is the single path of purity;
there is no duality. Good son!"
"Permanence, bliss, self, and purity— this is what is called the meaning of the true reality.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
If that which is true reality is taken as the ultimate truth, then the dharma of true reality is itself the Tathāgata, space, and buddha-nature.
If this is so, there is no distinction between the Tathāgata, space, and buddha-nature.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“There is suffering, there is truth, and there is reality; there is origination, there is truth, and there is reality; there is cessation, there is truth, and there is reality; there is the path, there is truth, and there is reality.”
"Good son!
The Tathāgata is neither suffering nor a truth, yet he is real; space is neither suffering nor a truth, yet it is real; the Buddha-nature is neither suffering nor a truth, yet it is real."
Mañjuśrī! That which is called suffering has the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of being subject to cessation; this is the ultimate truth.
The nature of the Tathāgata is neither suffering, nor impermanent, nor characterized by cessation; therefore, it is the ultimate reality.
Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.

Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called "accumulation" (samudaya) is that which causes the five aggregates to combine and arise; it is also called suffering, and it is also called impermanence. It is a characteristic that can be severed, and this is the True Truth (satya).
"Good son!
The Tathāgata is not of the nature of a collection, nor is he the cause of the aggregates; he is not a phenomenon subject to cessation, and for this reason, he is real.
It is the same with empty space and the Buddha-nature."

Good son! That which is called "extinction" refers to the extinction of afflictions. It is both permanent and impermanent: that which is attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles is called impermanent, while that which is attained by the Buddhas is called permanent. It is also called the "realized Dharma," and this constitutes the ultimate truth.

Good son! The nature of the Tathāgata is not called "extinction," yet it can extinguish afflictions; it is neither eternal nor impermanent, and it is not termed "realized knowledge. It dwells eternally without change, and for this reason it is real.
Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.
"Good son! The Path can sever afflictions; it is both eternal and impermanent, and it is a dharma that can be cultivated. This is called the True Truth.

The Tathāgata is not the Path, yet he can sever afflictions; he is neither eternal nor impermanent, nor is he a dharma that can be cultivated. He abides eternally and unchangingly; therefore, he is the Real."
Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.
Furthermore, good son,
that which is called "reality" is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is reality itself.
Reality is itself space, and space is itself reality.
Reality is itself the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is itself reality.

Mañjuśrī! There is suffering, there is the cause of suffering, there is the cessation of suffering, and there is the remedy for suffering; yet the Tathāgata is neither suffering nor even its remedy. Therefore, he is called "reality" (satya) but not a "truth" (satya);
the same is true of empty space and the Buddha-nature.
Suffering is conditioned, tainted, and devoid of bliss; the Tathāgata is unconditioned, untainted, and serenely blissful—this is reality, not a [conventional] truth.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, that which is non-perverted is called the ultimate truth.”
If that is so, are there four inversions among the Four Noble Truths?
If there were, how could it be said that the absence of inversion is called the "truth of reality," while all inversions are not called real?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All inversions enter into the Truth of Suffering; as all sentient beings possess an inverted mind, it is called 'inversion.'"

Good son! It is like a person who does not accept the instructions of their parents or elders, or even if they do accept them, cannot practice in accordance with them. Such people are called "perverted. This perversion is not something that is not suffering; it is itself suffering.
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught, that which is not false is the ultimate truth; if this is so, one should know that what is false is not the ultimate truth."
The Buddha said: "Good son!

All that is false enters into the Truth of Suffering. For instance, if there are sentient beings who deceive others, by reason of these causes and conditions they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Such phenomena as these are called 'false. This falsity is not something other than suffering; it is itself suffering."
Because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, distance themselves from it and do not practice it, it is called false.
Since such falsity is severed and eliminated by the Buddhas and the two vehicles, it is called the Truth of Reality.
Mañjuśrī said: “As the Buddha has taught, if the Mahāyāna is the true truth, one should know that the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not true.”
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! Those of the two vehicles are both real and unreal.”
That Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have severed all afflictions is called "real.
That which is impermanent, non-abiding, and subject to change is called "unreal."
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught, if that which the Buddha has spoken is called 'real,' one should know that what Māra speaks is 'unreal.'"
“World-Honored One!
Are what the Māra has spoken subsumed within the Noble Truths?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! That which is spoken by Māra is subsumed within the two truths, namely, suffering and its origin.
All that is non-Dharma and non-Vinaya cannot bring benefit to people;”
To preach throughout the entire day, yet have no one who perceives suffering, abandons the origin, realizes cessation, or cultivates the path—this is called falsehood;
such falsehood is termed the teaching of Māra.
Mañjuśrī said: “As the Buddha has taught, there is one path that is pure and without a second.
Yet the various non-Buddhists also say:”
"I have a single path, pure and non-dual.
If you say that this single path is the ultimate truth, how does it differ from that of the non-Buddhists?
"If there were no distinction, one should not say that 'the single path is pure.
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
The various non-Buddhists possess the truths of suffering and its origin, but lack the truths of cessation and the path.

They conceive the notion of cessation regarding that which is not cessation; they conceive the notion of the path regarding that which is not the path; they conceive the notion of the fruit regarding that which is not the fruit; and they conceive the notion of the cause regarding that which is not the cause. For this reason, they do not possess even a single path that is pure and non-dual.

Mañjuśrī said: “If, as the Buddha has taught, there were such things as permanence, a self, bliss, and purity as being the true meaning, then the various non-Buddhists would possess the true truth, whereas it would not exist within the Buddha-dharma.”
Why is this? For the various non-Buddhist practitioners also say:
"All conditioned phenomena are permanent."
In what sense is it permanent?
Because the various karmic retributions, whether agreeable or disagreeable, are experienced without being lost.
That which is agreeable is called the retribution of the ten wholesome actions; that which is disagreeable is the retribution of the ten unwholesome actions.
If it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, then once the agent has perished therein, who would subsequently experience the retribution in that [other realm]?
For this reason, conditioned phenomena are permanent; by virtue of the causal conditions of killing, they are termed "permanent."
"World-Honored One!
If it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, then both the killer and the victim are impermanent;
if they are impermanent, who is it that undergoes the retribution of sin in hell?"
If it were said that there definitely exists retribution received in hell, one should know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would truly not be impermanent.
World-Honored One!
To fix the mind in single-minded recollection is also called "constant"; for what is remembered after ten years, even up to a hundred years, is not lost, and therefore it is constant.
If things were impermanent, who would remember or recollect what was originally seen?
For this reason, World-Honored One, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not impermanent.

All recollections are also called "constant. Suppose a person first perceives the features of another's hands, feet, head, neck, and so forth; if they see them again at a later time, they recognize them. If these were impermanent, the original perception would have ceased to exist.
World-Honored One!

Regarding all actions performed, through long-term cultivation—whether starting from the very beginning and practicing for three years or five years—one subsequently comes to know them well; therefore, they are called "constant."
World-Honored One!

According to the method of calculation, one proceeds from one to two, from two to three, and so on up to hundreds and thousands. If these were impermanent, then the first [number] would have to perish; if the first perished, who would then proceed to the second?
In this way, it is eternally one and never becomes two.
Because the one does not perish, it can reach two, and even up to a hundred thousand; therefore, it is eternal, World-Honored One!

It is like the practice of reciting the Dharma: one recites one Āgama, then two Āgamas, and even up to three or four Āgamas. Although they are impermanent, because the recitation never actually reaches a fourth [set] and thus ceases, it is called "permanent" on account of the growth of the causal conditions for such recitation.

World-Honored One! It is likewise with all things: jars, garments, and vehicles; a person’s indebtedness; the features of the great earth; mountains, rivers, trees, and forests; medicinal plants, wood, grasses, and leaves; and the treatment of sentient beings’ illnesses—all of these are likewise eternal.
“World-Honored One!
All non-Buddhists say this:
‘All conditioned phenomena are permanent; if they are permanent, they are the true reality.’”
"World-Honored One, there are other non-Buddhists who further claim that pleasure exists.
How do they know this?
Because the experiencer certainly obtains desirable retribution."
“World-Honored One!
Those who experience pleasure certainly obtain it—namely, Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, Śakra-devānām-indra, Viṣṇu, and all humans and devas. For this reason, it is said that pleasure definitely exists.”
“World-Honored One!

There are other non-Buddhists who further claim that pleasure exists, for it causes sentient beings to give rise to longing: the hungry seek food, the thirsty seek drink, the cold-seek warmth, the heat-stricken seek coolness, the exhausted seek rest, the sick seek recovery, and those with desire seek form. If there were no pleasure, by what cause would they seek these things?”
Because there are those who seek [it], we know that there is happiness, World-Honored One!
Furthermore, various non-Buddhists say: "Giving can bring about happiness."

People of the world delight in giving to śramaṇas, various brāhmaṇas, and those who are poor and suffering. They provide such diverse gifts as clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, elephants, horses, and carriages; powdered incense, ointments, and various flowers; houses, dwellings, and lamps for reliance. They do so with the thought: "May I receive desirable retribution in a future life. Therefore, one should know that pleasure definitely exists.
“World-Honored One!

There are certain non-Buddhists who further say: ‘One should know that pleasure exists by virtue of causes and conditions; that is to say, because there is a cause and condition for one who experiences pleasure, it is called the contact of pleasure.’”
If pleasure did not exist, how could there be causes and conditions?
Just as there are no causes and conditions for a rabbit's horns because they do not exist, since there are causes and conditions for pleasure, we know that pleasure exists.
“World-Honored One!

There are other non-Buddhists who further say: ‘Because there are superior, middling, and inferior [levels], one should know that there is pleasure; those who experience inferior pleasure are Śakra Devānām Indra, those who experience middling pleasure are Mahābrahmā, and those who experience superior pleasure are Maheśvara.’”
Because there are such categories as superior, middling, and inferior, one should know that there is pleasure.
World-Honored One, various non-Buddhists further claim that there is purity. Why is this?
If there were no purity, one should not give rise to desire; if desire arises, one should know that purity exists.

Furthermore, it is said that gold, silver, precious gems, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, pearls, jade, conch shells, flowing springs, bathing pools, food, drink, clothing, flowers, powdered incense, ointments, and the light of lamps and candles—all such things as these are entirely pure dharmas.

Furthermore, there is purity; that which is called the five aggregates is like a pure vessel containing various pure substances—namely, humans, devas, sages, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. For this reason, they are termed "pure."
“World-Honored One!
There are certain non-Buddhists who further claim that there is a self, because there is something that perceives and is capable of acting.
It is like a person who enters the house of a potter; although they do not see the potter’s body, by seeing the wheel and the cord, they know with certainty that this house must belong to a potter.”
I am also like this: having seen a form with my eyes, I necessarily know that there is a self.
If there were no self, who would be able to see forms, hear sounds, and so on, up to touching dharmas? It is likewise for all these.
Furthermore, there exists a self.
How is this known? It is known through its characteristics.
What are these characteristics? They are:

breathing, looking, blinking, the life-force, the exertion of the mind, the experiencing of various sufferings and pleasures, craving, and anger. Such phenomena as these are all the characteristic of a self; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.

Furthermore, there exists a self, because it is capable of discriminating flavors. When a person eats fruit, they perceive it and know its taste; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Furthermore, there exists a self. How is this known?
Because of the grasping of instruments for action:

by grasping a sickle one can reap; by grasping an axe one can chop; by grasping a jar one can hold water; by grasping a chariot one can drive it. Since such activities as these are performed by the grasping of a self, one should know that a self must certainly exist.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exists a self?
It is because at the very moment of birth, one seeks milk and nourishment due to the force of past habitual tendencies; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Furthermore, how do we know that there is a self?
Because it brings benefit to other sentient beings through combination.
For example, objects such as jars, clothing, vehicles, fields, houses, mountains, forests, trees, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—when these things are combined, they provide benefit.

These five internal aggregates are likewise so: because the various faculties such as the eye exist in combination, they benefit the self; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self?
Because there is the phenomenon of negation (*pratiṣedha*).

Just as when there is an object, there is obstruction; if the object were non-existent, there would be no obstruction. Since there is obstruction, we know there is a self. Therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self?

It is because of the distinction between companions and non-companions: the virtuous and the non-virtuous are not companions; the True Dharma and the False Dharma are likewise not companions; and wisdom and ignorance are also not companions.

Śramaṇas and non-śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas and non-brāhmaṇas, sons and non-sons, day and non-day, night and non-night, self and non-self—such phenomena as these constitute companions and non-companions; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
"World-Honored One!
The various non-Buddhist teachers speak in diverse ways of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; one should know that there definitely exists permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
World-Honored One!"
For this reason, the various non-Buddhists may also say, "I possess the True Truth.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain that there is permanence, pleasure, purity, and a self, they are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas.
Why is this? Because they are deluded regarding birth and death, having strayed from the Great Guide of All-Knowledge.
Thus, these śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others are submerged in various desires, and their wholesome dharmas have become weak and diminished.
These non-Buddhists are bound within the prison of greed, hatred, and delusion because they endure and take pleasure therein.
Although these non-Buddhists know that the fruits of karma are created by oneself and experienced by oneself, they are still unable to distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas.
These various non-Buddhists do not live by the True Dharma or by right livelihood.
Why is this? Because they lack the fire of wisdom and are thus unable to consume [their afflictions].
Although these non-Buddhists desire and crave the five exquisite sensual pleasures, they are impoverished in wholesome dharmas because they do not practice diligently.
Although these non-Buddhists desire to reach true liberation, they have not perfected the feet of ethical discipline.
Although these non-Buddhists seek happiness, they are unable to seek the causes and conditions for happiness.
Although these non-Buddhists loathe all forms of suffering, their practices have not yet enabled them to distance themselves from the causes and conditions of suffering.
Although these non-Buddhists are entwined by the four great poisonous snakes, they still act with negligence and are unable to exercise caution.
Enshrouded by ignorance and estranged from virtuous friends, they delight in remaining within the three realms—a great, blazing, and impermanent fire—from which they cannot escape.
These non-Buddhists encounter the incurable diseases of the various afflictions, yet they do not seek the Great Wisdom Physician.
These non-Buddhists are about to traverse the boundless, perilous, and remote paths of the future, yet they do not know to cultivate the provisions of wholesome dharmas to adorn themselves.
These non-Buddhists are constantly harmed by the calamity and poison of lustful desire, yet they instead embrace the frost-like poison of the five sensual pleasures.
These non-Buddhists have a blazing intensity of anger, yet they further go on to draw near to evil friends.
These non-Buddhists are constantly shrouded by ignorance, yet they instead seek out evil and wicked teachings.
These non-Buddhists are constantly deceived and deluded by false views, yet they instead conceive thoughts of intimacy and affection toward them.
These non-Buddhists fear eating sweet fruit, yet they sow bitter seeds.
These non-Buddhists already dwell within the dark chamber of afflictions, yet they instead distance themselves from the brilliant light of the great torch of wisdom.
These non-Buddhists suffer from the thirst of afflictions, yet they instead drink the salty water of sensual desires.
These non-Buddhists are adrift and submerged in the boundless great river of birth and death, yet they remain far removed from the unsurpassed boatman.
These non-Buddhists are deluded and inverted, claiming that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent;
yet it is impossible for conditioned phenomena to be permanent. *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 13 [and] Scroll 14.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Holy Deeds, Part Four. "Good son!
I contemplate all conditioned phenomena as entirely impermanent.
How is this known?
It is because they arise from causes and conditions.
If there are any phenomena that arise from conditions, they are known to be impermanent.
Among all these non-Buddhists, there is not a single phenomenon that does not arise from conditions. Good son!

The Buddha-nature is without birth and without cessation; it neither goes nor comes. It is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present. It is not produced by causes, nor is it uncaused; it is neither an action nor an agent. It is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither named nor nameless. It is neither form nor matter; it is neither long nor short. It is not subsumed within the aggregates, elements, or sense bases. For these reasons, it is called "constant."
"Good son! Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Dharma; and the Dharma is eternal. Good son!"
That which is eternal is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Saṃgha; and the Saṃgha is eternal.
For this reason, phenomena produced from causes are not called eternal.
Among all these non-Buddhists, there is not a single dharma that does not arise from causes. Good son!
These non-Buddhists do not perceive the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, or the Dharma; therefore, everything they speak is entirely false speech, devoid of any ultimate truth.

Ordinary worldlings first perceive jars, clothing, vehicles, houses, cities, rivers, mountains, forests, men, women, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; subsequently, seeing what appears similar to them, they declare these things to be permanent.
You should know that in reality, it is not permanent.
Good son! All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Space is unconditioned; therefore, it is eternal. Buddha-nature is unconditioned; therefore, it is eternal.
Space is precisely Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is precisely the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is precisely the unconditioned; the unconditioned is precisely the eternal.
That which is eternal is the Dharma; that which is the Dharma is the Sangha; the Sangha is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
and that which is unconditioned is the eternal. Good son! Conditioned dharmas are of two kinds:
There are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*).
Non-material phenomena are the mind and its mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).
Material phenomena are earth, water, fire, and wind.
Good son! The mind is called impermanent. Why is this?
The nature of these [consciousnesses] is characterized by dependence on conditions (*ālambana*), for they must be analyzed. Good son!
The nature of eye-consciousness is distinct, and so on up to the nature of mind-consciousness being distinct; therefore, they are impermanent.
"Good son! The realm of form is distinct, and so on up to the realm of phenomena being distinct; therefore, they are impermanent. Good son!"
Visual consciousness is distinct from its corresponding [mental factors], and so on up to mental consciousness being distinct from its corresponding [mental factors];
therefore, it is impermanent. Good son, if the mind were permanent, visual consciousness alone would have to perceive all phenomena.
Good son! If visual consciousness were different from [the subsequent moments] up to mental consciousness being different, one would know them to be impermanent.
Because these phenomena are similar to one another, arising and ceasing moment by moment, ordinary people perceive them and reckon them to be permanent.
“Good son! Because the characteristics of all conditions (*pratyaya*) are subject to destruction, they are also called impermanent.

That is to say, eye-consciousness arises depending on the eye, depending on forms, depending on light, and depending on mental attention (*manasikāra*). When ear-consciousness arises, its respective conditions are distinct; it does not share the same causes and conditions as eye-consciousness. This applies likewise to the differences in all consciousnesses up to mental consciousness.”
"Furthermore, good son!
Because the causes and conditions that destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are distinct, the mind is called impermanent.
That is to say, the cultivation of the mind as impermanent is distinct from the cultivation of it as suffering, empty, and non-self."

If the mind were permanent, one would have to constantly cultivate the contemplation of impermanence; yet even such a contemplation of suffering, emptiness, and non-self would not be attained, let alone the contemplation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, within the teachings of the non-Buddhists, one cannot grasp permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Good son! You should know that mental phenomena are necessarily impermanent.
Furthermore, good son!
Because the natures of the mind differ, they are called impermanent.
That is to say, the nature of the mind of the śrāvaka differs, the nature of the mind of the pratyekabuddha differs, and the nature of the mind of the Buddhas differs.
The minds of all non-Buddhists are of three kinds:
first, the mind of those who have left the household life; second, the mind of those who remain in the household life; and third, the mind of those in the household life who seek seclusion.

Furthermore, the mind associated with pleasure is distinct, the mind associated with suffering is distinct, and the mind associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is distinct. The mind associated with greed is distinct, the mind associated with hatred is distinct, and the mind associated with delusion is distinct.

The mental characteristics of all non-Buddhists are likewise diverse: the mind associated with ignorance is distinct, the mind associated with doubt is distinct, the mind associated with false views is distinct, and their minds regarding their conduct and deportment are also distinct.
"Good son!
If the mind were permanent, it likewise would be unable to distinguish various forms, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and purple.
Good son!"
If the mind were permanent, then all dharmas that have been recollected should not be forgotten.
Son of good family!
If the mind were permanent, then whatever one recites and studies should not increase.
Furthermore, good son!

If the mind were permanent, one should not speak of what has been done, what is being done, or what will be done. Since there is what has been done, what is being done, and what will be done, you should know that this mind is certainly impermanent.
Good son! If the mind were permanent, there would be no distinction between enemy and friend, nor between one who is neither enemy nor friend.
If the mind were permanent, one should not speak of "my things" or "another's things," nor of "death" or "birth."
If the mind were permanent, then even though it performed actions, it should not undergo increase.
Good son! For this reason, you should know that the natures of minds are each distinct; because they are distinct, you should know they are impermanent.
“Good son! I have now expounded the meaning of impermanence regarding these non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*), and its significance has been made clear.
I shall further explain for you the impermanence of material form (*rūpa*).”
This form is impermanent; fundamentally it has no arising, for having arisen, it ceases.
When the internal body is in the womb at the stage of the *kalala*, it fundamentally has no arising, for having arisen, it transforms.
External things such as sprouts and stalks likewise fundamentally have no arising, for having arisen, they transform.
Therefore, you should know that all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are entirely impermanent. Good son!

All internal matter changes according to time: it is different at the stage of the *kalala*, different at the stage of the *arbuda*, different at the stage of the *peśī*, different at the stage of the *ghana*, different at the stage of the *praśākhā*, different at the time of birth, different at the stage of infancy, different at the stage of childhood, and so on, until each stage differs from the others even up to old age.
External forms are likewise thus: the sprout is distinct, the stem is distinct, the branch is distinct, the leaf is distinct, the flower is distinct, and the fruit is distinct.
Furthermore, good son!
The internal flavors also differ, changing at each stage from the *kalala* phase through to old age.
External flavors are likewise different: the flavors of the sprout, stem, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit are distinct.
The strength at the stage of the kalala is different, and so on until the strength at the stage of old age is different.
The physical appearance at the stage of the kalala is different, and so on until the physical appearance at the stage of old age is also different.
The retribution at the stage of the kalala is different, and even up to the stage of old age, the retribution is likewise different.
The designation at the stage of the kalala is different, and even up to the stage of old age, the designation is likewise different.
That which is called internal form, having been destroyed, returns to union; therefore, one knows it is impermanent.
External trees and plants likewise, having been destroyed, return to union; therefore, one knows they are impermanent.
Because things arise sequentially and gradually, we know they are impermanent.
From the stage of the *kalala* up to old age, they arise in succession; from the sprout up to the fruit, they arise in succession; therefore, we know they are impermanent.
All forms are subject to cessation; therefore, one knows they are impermanent.
The time of the cessation of the *kalala* is different, and so on until the time of the cessation of old age is different.
The time of the cessation of the sprout is different, and so on until the time of the cessation of the fruit is different; therefore, one knows they are impermanent.
Ordinary people lack wisdom; seeing things arise in a similar manner, they reckon them to be permanent.
For this reason, it is called impermanence.
If that which is impermanent is suffering, and if that which is suffering is impure.
“Good son! Because Kāśyapa previously asked about this matter, I have already answered him regarding it.
Furthermore, good son!”
"All conditioned phenomena are without self. Good son!
All dharmas in their entirety consist of the material and the non-material."
Form is not the self. Why is this?
Because it can be broken, destroyed, split, struck, and because it undergoes growth.
The self cannot be destroyed, split, struck, or grown; for this reason, one knows that form is not the self.
Furthermore, that which is not form is also not the self.
Why is this? Because it arises from causes and conditions. Good son!
If the various non-Buddhists claim that because of the nature of focused mindfulness there is a self, the nature of focused mindfulness is in fact not the self.
If they take focused mindfulness to be the nature of the self, then past events are subject to being forgotten; because there is such forgetting, it is certain that there is no self.
"Good son!
If the various non-Buddhists know there is a self because of their conceptualization, then because they lack such conceptualization, one can certainly know there is no self.
It is as when one sees a person's hand has six fingers and immediately asks: "
"Where did we previously meet?
If there were a self, one should not ask such a question;
because he asks this, it is certain that there is no self.
"Good son! If the various non-Buddhists claim that because there is a negation, they know a self exists, good son!
Because there is a negation, one certainly knows that there is no self."
Just as when one says "Devadatta," one never says he is not Devadatta;
so it is with me—if I were definitively a self, one would never negate me.
Because I am negated, we know for certain that there is no self.
If you claim that the existence of a self is known through negation, then since you do not negate it now, there must certainly be no self.
Good son! If the various non-Buddhists claim that the existence of a self is known through companionship or non-companionship, then because there is no companion, there should be no self.

There are phenomena that exist without companions—namely, the Tathāgata, empty space, and the Buddha-nature—and I likewise truly have no companion. For this reason, it is certain that there is no self.
Furthermore, good son!

If various non-Buddhists know that there is a self because of names, then even within the dharma of no-self there is the name "self," just as a poor and lowly person may have the name "wealthy and noble."
It is like saying, "I am dying. If I were truly dying, I would be killing myself; yet since I cannot actually be killed, it is only by way of conventional designation that one says "I am killed.
It is also like calling a short man "tall."
For this reason, one certainly knows that there is no self.
"Furthermore, good son!
If those non-Buddhists claim that because one seeks milk immediately after birth, there must be a self, good son!"
If there were a self, no infants would grasp after excrement, filth, fire, snakes, or poison; for this reason, one knows with certainty that there is no self.
Furthermore, good son!
All sentient beings possess equal cognition regarding three things: namely, sexual desire, food and drink, and fear; therefore, there is no self.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If those non-Buddhists claim to know that there is a self by means of its characteristics, son of good family!
Because of having characteristics there is no self, and because of being without characteristics there is likewise no self.
If, when a person is asleep, they cannot move forward or stop, look up or down, or blink, and are unaware of pleasure or pain, there should be no "self" (ātman).
If one were to claim that a self exists because of the ability to move forward or stop, look up or down, or blink, then a wooden puppet operated by machinery should also possess a self.
Good son! The Tathāgata is also like this:

he does not advance nor stop; he does not look down nor look up; he does not gaze nor blink; he is without suffering, without pleasure, without greed, without anger, and without delusion; he does not act. In this way, the Tathāgata truly possesses a self.
Furthermore, good son!

If the various non-Buddhists were to know that there is a self because they see others eating fruit and saliva arises in their mouths, then, good son, it is because of recollection that saliva arises upon seeing; the saliva is not the self.
I am neither saliva, nor joy, nor sorrow; neither yawning nor laughing; neither lying down nor rising; neither hunger nor satiety. For this reason, it is certain that there is no self.

“Good son! These various non-Buddhists are as ignorant as small children; lacking wisdom and skillful means, they cannot thoroughly comprehend permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure, purity and impurity, self and non-self, life-span and no life-span, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, reality and unreality, existence and non-existence. Within the Buddha-dharma, they grasp but a small portion and falsely calculate it to possess permanence, pleasure, self, and purity, yet they truly do not know permanence, pleasure, self, and purity.”
It is like a person born blind who does not know the color of milk and asks another,
"What is the color of milk like?
To which the other person replies:
"The color of the milk is white like a conch shell.
The blind man asked again,
"Is this 'milk-colored' the same as the sound of a conch shell?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"What does the color of the conch resemble?
He replied,
"It is like the powder of rice."
The blind man asked again:
"Is the color and texture of milk like rice powder?
And what is rice powder like?"
He replied,
"It is like snow or rain.
The blind man spoke again:
"Is that rice flour as cold as snow?
And what is snow like?
He replied:
"Just like a white crane.
Although those born blind hear these four kinds of analogies, they are ultimately unable to recognize the true color of milk.
These non-Buddhists are just the same; they are ultimately unable to recognize permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Good son!
For this reason, within my Buddha-dharma there is the true reality, which does not exist among the non-Buddhists.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
As the Tathāgata now approaches parinirvāṇa, you are once again turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, and thus making such distinctions regarding the ultimate truth.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Why do you now conceive the thought of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?
Son of good family!..."
The Tathāgata is, in truth, eternally abiding and unchanging; he does not enter parinirvāṇa. Good son!
If there are those who reckon that "I am the Buddha" or "I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," [they are mistaken].
I am the Dharma, and the Dharma is mine.
I am the Path, and the Path is mine.
I am the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One is mine.
"I am the śrāvaka, and the śrāvaka is what belongs to me.
I am able to preach the Dharma so that others may hear and accept it; I turn the wheel of the Dharma, which others cannot do."
The Tathāgata never makes such a calculation; therefore, the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma.
Son of good family!
If there were someone who made such a false calculation, thinking: "I am the eye, and the eye is mine," and likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"I am form, and form is mine," and so it is for everything up to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
"I am earth, and earth is mine," and the same applies to water, fire, wind, and so forth.
"Good son!
If someone were to say, 'I am faith, and faith is what belongs to me;
I am learned, and learning is what belongs to me.'"
I am the dānapāramitā, and the dānapāramitā is what belongs to me.
I am the śīlapāramitā, and the śīlapāramitā is what belongs to me.
"I am the perfection of patience; the perfection of patience is mine.
I am the perfection of vigor; the perfection of vigor is mine."
I am the dhyānapāramitā, and the dhyānapāramitā is what belongs to me.
I am the prajñāpāramitā, and the prajñāpāramitā is what belongs to me.
"I am the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are what belongs to me.
It is likewise with the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties and five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata never makes such a calculation; therefore, the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma.
Good son!"
If it is said that [the Tathāgata] is eternally abiding and without change, how can one say that the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma?
Therefore, you should not now say that the Tathāgata is about to turn the wheel of Dharma once again.

“Good son! For example, depending on the eye, with color as a condition, with light as a condition, and with mental attention as a condition, through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, visual consciousness arises.
Good son! The eye does not think, "I am able to produce consciousness";
nor do forms, up to and including mental volition, ever think, "I produce eye-consciousness. Furthermore, eye-consciousness itself does not form the thought, "I am able to produce myself."
Good son! Such dharmas as these, through the harmony of causes and conditions, are given the name "seeing. Good son!

The Tathāgata is likewise: having awakened to all phenomena by means of the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he further employs his throat, tongue, teeth, lips, mouth, speech, and voice to preach the Dharma for the first time to Kauṇḍinya; this is called "turning the wheel of Dharma."
For this reason, the Tathāgata is not said to "turn the wheel of Dharma.
"Good son! That which does not turn is called the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Tathāgata."
Good son!

It is like fire being produced by means of a fire-drill, a drill-peg, the hands, and dry cow dung; yet the fire-drill does not say, "I can produce fire," nor do the drill-peg, the hands, or the cow dung each think, "I can produce fire," nor does the fire itself say, "I have produced myself."
The Tathāgata is likewise; because of the six pāramitās, up to and including Kauṇḍinya, it is called "turning the wheel of Dharma.
Yet the Tathāgata does not give rise to the thought, "I am turning the wheel of Dharma."
“Good son! That which is non-arising is what is called the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma; this turning of the wheel of the Dharma is itself named the Tathāgata.
Good son!”

For example, it is like obtaining butter by depending on curd, water, churning, a vessel, a rope, and a person’s hand; yet the curd does not think, "I can produce butter," nor do even the person's hands think, "We can produce butter," nor does the butter say, "I have produced myself. It is through the combination of these various conditions that butter is obtained.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he never thinks, "I am turning the wheel of Dharma.
Good son, if there is no [subjective] emergence, this is called turning the wheel of the true Dharma; this turning of the wheel of Dharma is itself the Tathāgata.
Good son! It is like this:
depending on the seed, the earth, water, fire, wind, manure, the season, and human labor, the sprout is able to grow.
"Good son!
The seed does not say, 'I can produce the sprout'; even the karma that performs the action does not think, 'I can produce the sprout'; and the sprout itself does not say, 'I have produced myself.'"
The Tathāgata is likewise; he never thinks to himself, "I am turning the wheel of Dharma.
Good son, if one is unable to do so, that is precisely what is called "turning the true wheel of Dharma," and this turning of the wheel of Dharma is itself the Tathāgata.

Good son! It is like sound produced through the combination of a drum, space, leather, a person, and a mallet. The drum does not think, "I can produce sound," and it is the same for everything down to the mallet; nor does the sound itself say, "I have arisen of my own accord."
"Good son!
The Tathāgata is likewise; he never thinks or says, 'I turn the wheel of Dharma.
Good son!"
That which turns the wheel of Dharma is called non-doing; non-doing is itself the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
That which turns the wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgata. Good son!
Turning the wheel of Dharma is the domain of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Good son!
Space is neither born, nor produced, nor made, nor created; it is not a conditioned dharma.
The Tathāgata is likewise: he is not born, not emerged, not made, not created, and not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
As is the nature of the Tathāgata, so too is the Buddha-nature: it is not born, not emerged, not made, not created, and not a conditioned phenomenon.
“Good son! The speech of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is of two kinds:
first, worldly speech; second, supramundane speech.”
"Good son!
The Tathāgata speaks of worldly language for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and speaks of supramundane language for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Good son!"
This great assembly further consists of two kinds:
first, those who seek the Hīnayāna; second, those who seek the Mahāyāna.
In the past, at the city of Vārāṇasī, I turned the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Now, for the first time, in this city of Kuśinagara, I turn the great wheel of Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, good son,
there are two other kinds of persons:
There are those of middle capacity and those of superior capacity.
For those of middle capacity, he turned the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī;
for those of superior capacity—such as the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa and others, who are like elephant-kings among men—he now turns the Great Wheel of Dharma here in the city of Kuśinagara.
"Good son!
For those of the most inferior faculties, the Tathāgata never turns the wheel of Dharma; those of the most inferior faculties are precisely the icchantikas.
Furthermore, good son!"
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who seek the Buddha-way:
first, those of middling diligence; second, those of supreme diligence.
It was for those of middling diligence that the wheel of Dharma was turned at Vārāṇasī.
Now, in this city of Kuśinagara, for the sake of those with supreme diligence, I turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when I first turned the Wheel of Dharma in that city of Vārāṇasī, eighty thousand devas and humans attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Now, in this city of Kuśinagara, eight hundred trillion people shall not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, O son of good family!
In the city of Vārāṇasī, the Great Brahmā King bowed his head and requested me to turn the Wheel of Dharma;
now, here in the city of Kuśinagara, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa bows his head and requests me to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when I turned the wheel of Dharma in that city of Vārāṇasī, I preached impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
now, as I turn the wheel of Dharma here in this city of Kuśinagara, I preach permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when I turned the wheel of Dharma in that city of Vārāṇasī, the sound produced reached as far as the Brahma heavens;

now, as the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma in the city of Kuśinagara, the sound produced pervades twenty Ganges-sand numbers of Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction, and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir."
Furthermore, good son!
Whatever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have spoken is all termed "turning the wheel of Dharma. Good son!
For example, O son of good family, the wheel-treasure possessed by a noble universal monarch can subdue those not yet subdued and bring peace and security to those already subdued.
Son of good family!

The teachings expounded by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise so: they cause those with immeasurable afflictions who have not yet been tamed to be tamed, and cause those already tamed to give rise to roots of goodness.
Good son! For example, the wheel-treasure possessed by a noble cakravartin king is able to eliminate all enemies and bandits.
The Tathāgata’s exposition of the Dharma is likewise; it can cause all the bandits of affliction to become completely tranquil.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, the wheel-treasure possessed by a universal monarch revolves both downward and upward.

The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is likewise: it can cause sentient beings in the lower realms who commit evil to be reborn upward among humans and devas, and even attain the path of Buddhahood.
"Good son!
Therefore, you should not now say that the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma again here.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is not that I am ignorant of this meaning; the reason I ask is because I wish to benefit all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!”
"I have long known that the turning of the wheel of Dharma is truly the realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Good son!..."
"This is called the noble practice practiced by a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Furthermore, by what meaning is it called 'Noble Practice' (ārya-caryā)? "Good son!
'Noble' refers to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; for this reason, it is called Noble Practice."
“World-Honored One!
If this is that which is practiced by all Buddhas, then it is not something that can be cultivated by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas. “Good son!
All these World-Honored Ones dwell in this Great Parinirvāṇa, providing such instruction, analysis, and exposition of its meaning; for this reason, it is called the "Noble Practice" (ārya-caryā).
When the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas have heard this, they are able to practice it accordingly; therefore, it is called "Noble Conduct" (ārya-caryā).
Good son! Once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained this conduct, they shall abide in the stage of fearlessness (abhaya-bhūmi).
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who abides in such a stage of fearlessness, he will no longer fear greed, anger, and delusion, nor birth, old age, sickness, and death; furthermore, he will not fear the evil realms, the hells, the animals, or the hungry ghosts."
Good son! There are two kinds of evil:
first, that of the asuras; second, that among human beings.
Among human beings, there are three kinds of evil:
first, those who are icchantikas; second, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras; and third, those who violate the four grave prohibitions. Good son:
Bodhisattvas who dwell in this stage never fear falling into such evil states;
nor do they fear śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the heterodox views of external paths, the Māra Pāpīyān,
or the undergoing of the twenty-five forms of existence.
Therefore, this stage is named "Fearlessness.
Son of good family!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the stage of fearlessness, he attains twenty-five samādhis and destroys the twenty-five states of existence.
"Good son!
By attaining the Samādhi of Stainless Purity, one can destroy existence in the hells; by attaining the Samādhi of Non-Retrogression, one can destroy existence among animals;
by attaining the Samādhi of Mental Joy, one can destroy existence as a hungry ghost; by attaining the Samādhi of Rejoicing, one can destroy..."
The asuras possess [these powers]: by attaining the *sūryaprabha* (sunlight) samādhi, they can sever existence in Pūrvavideha;
by attaining the *candraprabha* (moonlight) samādhi, they can sever existence in Aparagoyānī; by attaining the *jvālā* (blazing heat) samādhi, they can sever existence in Uttarakuru;
by attaining the *māyopama* (illusion-like) samādhi, they can sever existence in Jambudvīpa; and by attaining the *sarvadharmācalā* (immovable in all phenomena) samādhi...

By attaining the Samādhi of Obscurity, one can sever existence in the realm of the Four Great Kings; by attaining the Samādhi of Difficult Subjugation, one can sever existence in the realm of the Thirty-three Gods;

by attaining the Samādhi of Pleasing Intent, one can sever existence in the realm of the Yāma Heaven; by attaining the Samādhi of Blue Color, one can sever existence in the realm of the Tuṣita Heaven;
by attaining the Samādhi of Yellow Color, one can sever existence in the realm of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; by attaining the Samādhi of Red...
The Samādhi of Color can sever existence in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; attaining the Samādhi of White Color can sever existence in the First Dhyāna;
attaining the Samādhi of Various Kinds can sever existence in the Great Brahmā Heaven; attaining the Samādhi of the Pair can sever existence in the Second Dhyāna;
attaining the Samādhi of Thunderous Sound can sever existence in the Third Dhyāna; attaining the Samādhi of Pouring Rain...

By attaining the Samādhi of Profundity (*maita*), one can sever existence in the fourth dhyāna; by attaining the Samādhi like Space (*ākāśasama*), one can sever existence in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*);

by attaining the Samādhi of the Illuminating Mirror, one can sever existence in the Śuddhāvāsa Ānāgāmin realms; by attaining the Samādhi of Non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*), one can sever existence in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*);

by attaining the Samādhi of Permanence (*nitya*), one can sever existence in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); by attaining the Samādhi of Bliss (*sukha*), one can sever [existence in the sphere of nothingness].
In the existence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains my samādhi and is able to sever that existence.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the twenty-five samādhis and the severing of the twenty-five existences.
“Good son! These twenty-five samādhis are called the Kings of All Samādhis. Good son!”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter such sovereign samādhis as these, if they wish to blow away and destroy Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, they can do so at will; if they wish to know the thoughts and mental activities of all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, they can know them all; if they wish to place all sentient beings of the trichiliocosm within a single pore of their own body, they can do so at will, yet they cause those beings to have no sense of confinement or oppression; if they wish to manifest as immeasurable sentient beings to fill the entire trichiliocosm, they can also do so at will; and if they wish to divide one body into many bodies, or merge many bodies back into one, although they perform such acts, their minds remain unattached, just like a lotus flower.
"Good son!
Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained entry into such a king of samādhis, they immediately abide on the ground of mastery.
Abiding on this ground of mastery, the bodhisattva attains the power of mastery; according to the place of birth they desire, they are immediately reborn there."
Good son! It is like a noble cakravartin king who rules over the four continents; wherever he travels according to his will, none can obstruct him.
So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: regarding any place of birth where he wishes to be born, he takes rebirth there according to his will.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees any sentient beings in the hells who can be transformed and established in roots of goodness, the bodhisattva immediately goes there and takes birth among them."
Although Bodhisattvas are born there, it is not the fruit of their original karma;
rather, it is by virtue of the causal conditions of the power of the stage of self-mastery that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are born therein. Good son!
Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may be in the hells, they do not undergo such agonies as burning or the crushing of the body. Good son!

The merits achieved by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, such that they cannot even be described; how much less could the merits possessed by all Buddhas ever be described?

At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Vimalagarbharājasthita, who possessed great majestic power, had accomplished the supernormal powers, had attained the Great Dhāraṇī Samādhi, and was fully endowed with the fearlessnesses. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the merits and wisdom accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, truly beyond words.
In my view, it is still not equal to such Mahāyāna sūtras. Why is this?
It is because, by the power of these Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one is able to give birth to the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.

Although these various Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras are accomplished with immeasurable merit, they cannot serve as a comparison for this sūtra—not even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold increase, nor can they reach it through calculation or analogy."

"Good son! It is like this: from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the finest essence, *ghṛta*. This *ghṛta* is the most supreme; if anyone consumes it, all their ailments will be eliminated, for it contains within it the efficacy of all medicinal herbs."
Good son! The Buddha is also like this:

from the Buddha arise the twelve divisions of the scriptures; from the twelve divisions of the scriptures arises the Sūtra; from the Sūtra arises the Vaipulya Sūtra; from the Vaipulya Sūtra arises the Prajñāpāramitā; and from the Prajñāpāramitā arises the Great Nirvāṇa, which is like the finest clarified butter (sarpis).
What is called "ghee" (sarpirmaṇḍa) is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature is none other than the Tathāgata.
Good son! For this reason, it is said that all the merits possessed by the Tathāgata are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has praised, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is like the finest clarified butter (sarpis), most supreme and most wondrous. If there are those who can consume it, all ailments will be entirely eliminated, for all medicinal herbs are contained within it.”
Having heard this, I have privately reflected that if there are those who are unable to hear and accept this sutra, one should know that such persons are greatly deluded and lack a virtuous mind.
World-Honored One!

At this time, I am truly able to endure having my skin flayed for paper, my blood drawn for ink, my marrow used for water, and my bones broken for pens, so as to transcribe such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; having transcribed it, I shall read and recite it until I have mastered it, and thereafter I shall extensively explain its meaning for others.
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to wealth and property, I shall give them wealth, and thereafter exhort them with this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, urging them to read it.”
If they are persons of high status, one should first accord with their inclinations through pleasant speech, and thereafter gradually exhort them to read this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
If they are ordinary people, I shall use my power and authority to compel them to read it.
If they are arrogant, I shall serve as their servant, complying with their wishes to make them joyful, and thereafter instruct them in the Great Parinirvāṇa.
If there are those who slander the Mahāyāna sūtras, one should use one's power to suppress and subdue them; once they have been subdued, one should then exhort them to read the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
"If there are those who love and delight in the Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall personally go to them to pay respectful offerings, honor, and praise.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"

You greatly delight in the Mahāyāna sūtras, craving the Mahāyāna sūtras, loving the Mahāyāna sūtras, and relishing the Mahāyāna sūtras; you have faith in, revere, honor, and make offerings to the Mahāyāna.
"Good son!

By virtue of these causes and conditions of your present wholesome mind, you shall surpass immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before you. Before long, you too shall be like me, extensively expounding for the great assembly such a Great Parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata, and Buddha-nature—the secret treasury spoken of by all Buddhas."
"Good son!
In ages past, before the Buddha-sun had arisen, I was at that time a brahmin practicing the bodhisattva path, fully able to master all the sutras and treatises of the various non-Buddhist schools."

They cultivate the practice of quiescence and are fully endowed with dignified deportment; their minds are pure and cannot be destroyed by external factors that give rise to thoughts of desire. They extinguish the fire of hatred and uphold the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. They search everywhere for Mahāyāna sūtras, even to the point of not hearing the name of the Vaipulya scriptures.

At that time, I was dwelling on the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*). That mountain was pure, filled with flowing springs, bathing pools, groves, and medicinal trees. Between the rocks everywhere flowed clear water, and it was adorned all over with many fragrant flowers. The various birds and beasts were beyond counting, and sweet fruits grew in such profusion that their species were difficult to enumerate.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable roots of lotus, sweet roots, and eaglewood roots.

At that time, I dwelt alone therein, eating only various fruits; having eaten, I would fix my mind in contemplation and practice seated meditation for immeasurable years, yet I did not hear even the name of a Mahāyāna sūtra concerning the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
"Good son!

When I was practicing such difficult and painful austerities, Śakra Devānām Indra and the other gods were greatly astonished. They immediately gathered together and, each addressing the others, spoke these verses:
'Pointing to one another, they said: "In the midst of the pure Snowy Mountains, [There dwells one who]..."
Lord of tranquility and freedom from desire, King adorned with merit;
having abandoned greed, hatred, and pride, and forever severed flattery, folly, and delusion,
his mouth has never before uttered harsh or evil speech.
At that time, there was a son of heaven among the assembly named Nandika, who spoke again in verse:
“Is it not the case that such a person who has abandoned desire, Pure and diligent in their striving,
Seeks neither Śakra nor any of the devas?”
"If one is a follower of external paths, practicing various ascetic penances,
such a person has many desires and seeks the seat where Śakra resides.
At that time, there was another celestial son who was a rishi, and he spoke this verse for the sake of Śakra:
“O Lord of Devas, Kauśika!
You should not harbor such concerns; why would non-Buddhists who practice asceticism necessarily seek the station of Indra?”
Having spoken these verses, he further said: "Kauśika!

In the world there are great beings who, for the sake of sentient beings, do not covet their own bodies; desiring to benefit all sentient beings, they practice various kinds of immeasurable asceticism."

Such a person, because they perceive all the faults within birth and death, would not give rise to greedy attachment even if they were to see precious treasures filling this entire earth, its mountains, and its great oceans; they would regard them as they would look upon mucus or spittle.

Such a Great Being renounces wealth and treasures, beloved wife and children, head, eyes, marrow, and brain, hands, feet, and limbs, as well as their dwelling houses, elephants, horses, chariots, and male and female slaves; furthermore, they do not even aspire to be born in the heavens, desiring only that all sentient beings may obtain and experience happiness.
As I understand it, such a Great Being is pure and unstained, with all fetters forever exhausted, seeking only Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śakra Devānām Indra spoke again, saying:
"If it is as you say, then this person will have gathered within themselves all sentient beings existing throughout the entire world."
"O Great Sage!
If there were a Buddha-tree in this world, it would be able to eliminate the poisonous snakes of affliction for all devas, humans, and asuras.
If sentient beings dwell within the cool shade of this Buddha-tree, the various poisons of their afflictions will all be completely extinguished."
"O Great Sage!
If this person were to become a Sugata in a future age, we would all attain the extinction of immeasurable, blazing afflictions.
Such a reality is indeed difficult to believe."

Why is this? Because although immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they may waver and turn back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon encountering even a slight minor condition.
It is like the moon in water: when the water moves, the moon moves.
It is also like a painted image, difficult to create but easy to destroy.
The bodhicitta is likewise: difficult to arouse, yet easy to lose.
"Great Seer!

It is like a multitude of men who, having firmly adorned themselves with various armor and weapons, desire to advance and subdue the enemy, yet upon encountering the terror of battle, they immediately retreat and scatter."

Immeasurable sentient beings are likewise: having resolved their minds on Bodhicitta and firmly adorned themselves with its armor, they perceive the faults of birth and death and give rise to fear; consequently, they immediately retreat and disperse.
"Great Seer!

I have observed that after such immeasurable sentient beings have resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they all undergo fluctuations. Therefore, although I now see this person practicing austerities—free from affliction, free from fever, and dwelling on a perilous path—I cannot yet believe that his practice is pure."
I must now go there myself to test him, to see whether he truly is capable of bearing the extremely heavy burden of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great Seer!
Just as a chariot with two wheels can carry a load, and a bird with two wings is capable of flight; so it is with this.
This ascetic is also like this.
Although I see that he strictly maintains his prohibitions and precepts, I do not yet know whether this person possesses profound wisdom.
If he possesses profound wisdom, you should know that he will be capable of bearing the heavy burden of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Great Sage!
It is like a mother fish that has many embryos, yet few are brought to fruition;
it is like a mango tree that has many flowers, yet few fruits.
"The beings who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment are indeed immeasurable; yet when it comes to those who achieve success, they are so few as to be hardly worth mentioning.
Great Seer!
I shall go with you to test them."
"Great Seer!
Just as genuine gold is known to be authentic only after it has undergone three tests— namely, burning, beating,
and rubbing— so too should one test that ascetic."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed his own body into the form of a rākṣasa; his appearance was most terrifying, and he descended to the Snowy Mountains and stood nearby.
At that time, the rākṣasa felt no fear; courageous and invincible, his eloquence was orderly and his voice clear and refined as he proclaimed the half-verse spoken by a past Buddha:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; This is the law of arising and ceasing."
Having spoken this half-verse, he stood before him, his manifested form most terrifying.
He cast glances and looked about, surveying the four directions.
When this ascetic heard these half-verses, his heart was filled with joy.

It was like a merchant traveling at night through a perilous place who, having lost his companions, searched in terror and then encountered his fellow travelers; his heart was filled with joy, and he leaped for immeasurable delight.
It is also like a long-term illness where, having not yet encountered a skilled physician, fine medicine, or a capable nurse, one finally obtains them all at once;
or like a person drowning in the sea who suddenly encounters a ship;
or like a parched and exhausted person who finds clear, cool water.
It is like one pursued by an enemy who suddenly escapes;
or like a person long imprisoned who suddenly hears they have been released;
or like a farmer encountering rain during a scorching drought.
It was just as when a traveler returns home and his family, upon seeing him, feels great joy. Good son!

At that time, when I heard this half-verse, my heart rejoiced in exactly the same way. I immediately rose from my seat, lifted up my hair with my hand, looked around in the four directions, and spoke these words:
"Who was it that spoke the verse I just heard?
At that time, he saw no one else at all, but only the rākṣasa,
who immediately said these words:
"Who has opened such a gate of liberation? Who can thunder forth the voice of all Buddhas?
Who, amidst the slumber of birth and death, alone awakens and utters these words?"
Who is able, in this world, to show the supreme flavor of the Path to sentient beings starving amidst birth and death?
Amidst the immeasurable sentient beings sinking in the ocean of birth and death, who can act as a great captain?
These sentient beings are constantly entangled by the grave illness of the afflictions; who is able to act as a skilled physician amidst them?
This half-verse you have spoken has enlightened my mind, just as the crescent moon gradually causes a lotus flower to open.
"Good son! At that time, I saw nothing else; I saw only the rākṣasa.
Then I thought again:"
"Could it be that this rākṣasa is reciting these verses?
he thought, yet he again gave rise to doubt:
"Perhaps it is not his speech; for what reason?"
This person’s appearance is most terrifying.
Yet, for anyone who hears these verses, all fear and ugliness are immediately dispelled.
How could someone with such a physical form as this be able to speak such verses?
"A lotus cannot emerge from fire, nor can cool water be produced within the rays of the sun.
Good son, at that time I further thought to myself:
"I am currently without wisdom, yet this rākṣasa may have been able to see past buddhas and heard this half-verse from those buddhas; I should now question him."
He then proceeded to where the rākṣasa was and spoke these words:
"Excellent, Great Being!
From where did you obtain this half-verse spoken by the one who was free from fear in the past?"
"O Mahāsattva!
Furthermore, from where did you obtain such a half-cintāmaṇi jewel?
O Mahāsattva!"
The meaning of this half-verse is the true path of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.

Countless sentient beings throughout all worlds are perpetually shrouded by the net of various views; throughout their entire lives, they remain within these externalist teachings and have never before heard such an exposition on emptiness as this, spoken by the Ten-Powered One, the Hero of the World, who has transcended the mundane.
"Good son! After I had asked this, he replied to me, saying:
'Great Brahmin!'"
You should not now ask me about this matter. Why is that?
It has already been many days since I last ate; though I have sought food everywhere, I have been unable to obtain any at all.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, my mind was distracted and I spoke these delirious words; it was not something known by my original mind.
Even if I were now able to fly through the void to Uttarakuru, or even to the heavens, I would still be unable to find food anywhere; for this reason, I spoke those words.
"Good son! At that time, I spoke again to the rākṣasa, saying:
'O Great Being!'"
"If you can recite this verse for me until it is finished, I shall become your disciple for as long as I live.
Great Being!
