That which you have spoken has names that do not end, and its meaning is likewise inexhaustible."
For what reason do you not wish to speak?
Generally, material giving is subject to exhaustion, whereas the causes and conditions of the gift of Dharma are inexhaustible.
Although they are inexhaustible, they bring about manifold benefits.

Having now heard this half-verse of the Dharma, my mind is filled with wonder and doubt; you should, by good fortune, dispel them for me. Once you have finished reciting this verse, I shall become your disciple for the rest of my life.
The rākṣasa replied:
"Your wisdom is excessive; you worry only for yourself and take no thought for me at all. Now, I am certainly tormented by the suffering of hunger and truly cannot speak."
I then asked him,
"What is this thing that you eat?
The rākṣasa replied:
"You need not ask; if I were to speak, it would cause many people to be terrified. I asked again:
"In this solitary place, there is no one else present; I do not fear you, so why will you not speak?"
The rākṣasa replied:
"That which I eat is only the warm flesh of humans;
that which I drink is only the hot blood of humans."
"Because of my own meager merit, I have eaten only this food; though I have searched everywhere, I am exhausted and unable to obtain more.
Although there are many people in the world, they all possess merit and are furthermore protected by the various devas; thus, I lack the power to kill them."
"Good son! I spoke again, saying:
'You need only fully recite this half-verse; once I have heard the verse, I shall offer my own body as a gift for its worship.'"
"O Mahāsattva!
Even if my life were to end, this body would have no further use; it would surely be devoured by tigers, wolves, owls, hawks, and vultures, yet I would not gain even a hair’s breadth of merit."
"I now seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I shall relinquish this non-solid body to exchange it for a solid one.
The rākṣasa replied, "Who would believe such words of yours—that for the sake of eight syllables, you would cast away the body you love?"
"Good son! I then replied: 'You are truly without wisdom.
It is like a person who, by giving an ordinary vessel to another, receives a vessel of the seven treasures in return.'"
I am also like this: having relinquished this non-firm body, I have attained a vajra-body.
As for your question of who would believe this, I now have witnesses:
Mahābrahmā, Śakra-devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings can testify to this matter.

Furthermore, there are other bodhisattvas with the divine eye who, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, practice the Mahāyāna and are endowed with the six perfections; they too are able to realize and know this.

"Furthermore, there are the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions who benefit sentient beings; they too can bear witness that for the sake of these eight characters, I am willing to sacrifice my body and life.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you are thus able to sacrifice your body, listen attentively, listen attentively! I shall recite the remaining half-verse for you."
“Good son! At that time, having heard these words, my heart was filled with joy. I immediately removed the deerskin I was wearing and spread it out for this rākṣasa as a Dharma seat, saying:
‘Upādhyāya!’”
"Please sit upon this seat.
I immediately knelt before him with palms joined and spoke these words:
"I only pray, O Upādhyāya!"
"Please speak well for me the remaining half-verse so that it may be complete.
The rākṣasa then spoke:
"When birth and death have ceased, Nirvāṇa is bliss."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the rākṣasa further said:

"O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, you have now heard the complete meaning of these verses; your aspirations shall be entirely fulfilled. If you truly desire to benefit all sentient beings, give me your body at this moment."

"Good son! At that time, I reflected deeply on this meaning. Thereafter, in various places—whether upon stones, walls, trees, or roads—I inscribed these verses. I then fastened my clothes even tighter, fearing that after death my body might be exposed, and I immediately climbed a tall tree."
At that time, the tree deity asked me again:
"Excellent, O worthy one!
What do you wish to do?"
"Good son! At that time, I replied:
'I wish to sacrifice my body to repay the price of this verse.'"
The tree spirit asked,
"What benefit does such a verse provide?
At that time, I replied:
"These verses are the path for opening up the Dharma of emptiness as taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; for the sake of this Dharma, I shall relinquish my body and life."

It was not for the sake of gain, fame, wealth, or treasures; nor for the sake of becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King, a Great Heavenly King of the Four Quarters, Śakra Devānām Indra, or Mahābrahmā; nor for the sake of the pleasures among humans and devas, but solely out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings that he sacrificed this body.
“Good son! When I was relinquishing my body, I further made this vow:
‘May all those who are stingy and possessive come to see me and renounce this body.’”

"If there are those who give even a small gift yet give rise to arrogance, I shall cause them to see that for the sake of a single verse, I would sacrifice this body and life as if discarding grass or wood.

When I had spoken these words, I immediately released my body and threw myself down beneath a tree. Before I had even reached the ground, various sounds emerged from the midst of space, their resonance reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
At that time, the rākṣasa returned to his original form as Śakra and immediately caught my body in mid-air, placing me upon level ground.
Then Śakra-devānām-indra, along with the various devas and the Great Brahmā King, prostrated themselves at my feet and praised me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are truly a bodhisattva, able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, wishing to kindle the great Dharma-torch within the darkness of ignorance."
Because I cherish the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata, I have troubled and vexed you; I only pray that you will accept my repentance for these transgressions.
You shall certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the future; I pray that you will grant me deliverance.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and the assembly of devas prostrated at my feet, whereupon they took their leave and suddenly vanished.
"O son of good family!
In the past, for the sake of a half-verse, I cast off this body; by this cause and condition, I have already transcended twelve kalpas and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before Maitreya.
"Good son!
I have attained such immeasurable merit as this entirely through making offerings to the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
Good son!"
You now are likewise; having resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you have already surpassed immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Good son! This is called a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and practicing the noble conduct.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 14.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On Holy Conduct (Brahmacarya). Part One of Chapter Eight: On Holy Conduct.
“Good son! What is the brahmacarya of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, they dwell in seven wholesome dharmas and thereby attain the perfection of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
What are these seven? First, knowledge of the Dharma;

second, knowledge of its meaning; third, knowledge of the proper time; fourth, knowledge of contentment; fifth, self-knowledge; sixth, knowledge of the assembly; and seventh, knowledge of the honorable and the humble.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the Dharma? Good son!"

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the twelve divisions of the scriptures, namely: sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka (formerly called jātaka), vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa.
“Good son! What is called a Sūtra?
From ‘Thus have I heard’ up to ‘rejoicing and practicing accordingly,’ all such as these are called Sūtras.”
"What is called a *geyya* sutta? The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

'In the past, you and I were ignorant and lacked wisdom; we were unable to see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are. For this reason, we wandered through the cycle of birth and death for a long time, submerged in the great ocean of suffering.'"
What are the four?
They are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Once the Buddha had finished preaching a sutra for the bhikṣus on a previous occasion, there were at that time beings of sharp faculties who, having come to the Buddha's presence later in order to hear the Dharma, immediately asked someone:
"What was it that the Tathāgata was teaching just now?
The Buddha, knowing this, then spoke in verse based on the original sūtra:
"In the past, I and you all Did not see the Four Noble Truths."
Therefore, one has long wandered through the great ocean of suffering of birth and death.
If one can perceive the Four Noble Truths, then one shall sever birth and death;
once existence has been exhausted, one will no longer undergo further states of being.
"This is called a Geya-sūtra.
What is meant by 'when the Tathāgata speaks for the sake of the great beings, he bestows upon them a prediction (vyākaraṇa), saying:
"O Ajita, in the future there shall be a king named Śaṅkha; in that world, you shall attain the path of Buddhahood and be known as Maitreya"?'"
This is called the Vyākaraṇa-sūtra. What is called the Geya-sūtra?
Excluding the Sūtras and the various Vinayas, it refers to other instances where four-line verses (gāthās) are spoken, such as:
“‘Commit no evil, practice all that is good;
purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is called a gāthā-sūtra.”
"What is called an Udāna-sūtra?
It is as when the Buddha enters meditative absorption in the afternoon and extensively expounds the essentials of the Dharma for the assembly of devas.
At that time, the bhikṣus each think to themselves:"
"What is the Tathāgata doing now?
On the following morning, the Tathāgata arose from meditative concentration; though no one had asked him, he spoke of his own accord through his knowledge of others' minds:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the lifespans of all devas are exceedingly long."
"O bhikṣus! Excellent is it that you act for the sake of others and do not seek your own benefit.
Excellent is your fewness of desires; excellent is your contentment; excellent is your tranquility."
"Thus, those sūtras spoken spontaneously without being questioned are called Udāna-sūtras.
What are called Nidāna-sūtras?
They are those sūtra verses which explain the causes and fundamental origins for others."
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a man who caught birds with a net; having captured them, he confined them in a cage, provided them with water and grain, and then released them again.
The World-Honored One, knowing the origins and conditions of this matter, spoke these verses:
"Do not disregard a minor offense, thinking that it will bring no calamity."
"Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
This is called the Nidāna Sūtra. What is called the Avadāna Sūtra?
The parables as explained in the Vinaya are called the Avadāna Sūtras.
What are called the Itivṛttaka (formerly known as the Muktaka) Sūtras?
As the Buddha has said: "Bhikṣus, you should know that when I appear in the world, what I preach is called the *Śīlasūtra*.
When Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, it was called the 'Thunderbolt of Ambrosia' (*Amṛtadundubhi*)."
During the time of Konāgamana Buddha, he was named Dharmādarśa;
during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was named Vibhaṅga-śūnya.
This is called the Itivṛttaka Sūtra.
"What is called a Jātaka-sūtra?
It refers to when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was originally a bodhisattva and practiced various ascetic austerities.

A bhikṣu should know that in the past I took birth as a deer, a bear, a roe deer, a rabbit, a minor king, a wheel-turning sage king, a nāga, a garuḍa, and so forth. These are the bodies I assumed while practicing the bodhisattva path; these are called Jātakas."
"What is called the Vaipulya Sūtra?
It refers to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya scriptures; their meaning is as vast as space, and thus they are named Vaipulya."
"What is called an Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra?
It is like that Bodhisattva, at the time of his first birth, who, without anyone supporting him, immediately took seven steps and emitted a great radiance, surveying the ten directions."
It was also like a monkey holding a vessel of honey in its hands to offer to the Tathāgata;
like a white-necked dog listening to the Dharma by the Buddha’s side;
and like Māra Pāpīyas transforming himself into a blue ox that walked among the earthen alms bowls, causing them to strike against one another without sustaining any damage.
For example, when the Buddha was first born, upon entering a temple of the devas, he caused those divine images to rise up and pay him homage.
Sūtras such as these are called *Adbhuta-dharma* (Sūtras of Marvels).
"What is called an Upadeśa-sūtra?
It refers to those sūtras spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, which involve discussion, detailed analysis, and the elucidation of their characteristics; these are called Upadeśa-sūtras."
If a bodhisattva can thus understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this is called "knowing the Dharma.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the meaning?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva extensively understands the meaning of all letters and languages, this is called "knowing the meaning."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the proper time? Son of good family!

A bodhisattva skillfully knows that at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate tranquility; at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate diligence; at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate equanimity and concentration; at such a time it is appropriate to make offerings to the Buddha; at such a time it is appropriate to make offerings to the teacher; and at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, thereby fulfilling the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). This is called knowing the proper time.
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contentment?
Son of good family!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contentment refers to food, drink, clothing, and medicine; walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent—this is called contentment.
Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know himself? This bodhisattva knows himself:

"I possess such faith, such precepts, such extensive learning, such renunciation, such wisdom, such conduct in coming and going, such right mindfulness, and such wholesome deeds; I ask in this way and answer in this way. This is called knowing oneself.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the assemblies? Good son, this bodhisattva knows such things as these:

this is an assembly of kṣatriyas, an assembly of brāhmaṇas, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of śramaṇas. He should approach and depart from such an assembly in this manner, sit and rise in this manner, preach the Dharma in this manner, and engage in question and answer in this manner; this is called knowing the assemblies.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the noble and the humble among human beings? Good son!"
There are two kinds of people:
first, those who have faith; second, those who lack faith.
A bodhisattva should know that the one with faith is virtuous, whereas the one without faith is not called virtuous.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of faith:
first, constantly going to the monasteries; second, not going to the bodhisattvas.
One should know that those who go possess goodness, while those who do not go cannot be said to possess goodness.
There are two kinds of those who go to the monastic quarters:
first, those who prostrate; second, those who do not prostrate.
A bodhisattva should know that those who prostrate are virtuous, whereas those who do not prostrate are not called virtuous.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who perform prostrations:
first, those who listen to the Dharma; second, those who do not listen to the Dharma.
A bodhisattva should know that those who listen to the Dharma are virtuous, while those who do not listen to the Dharma are not called virtuous.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who listen to the Dharma:
first, those who listen with a single-minded heart; second, those who do not listen with a single-minded heart.
A bodhisattva should know that one who listens with a single-minded heart is called "virtuous," whereas one who does not listen with a single-minded heart is not called "virtuous."
There are two further kinds of listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind:
first, reflecting on the meaning; second, not reflecting on the meaning.
A bodhisattva should know that reflecting on the meaning is wholesome, whereas not reflecting on the meaning is not called wholesome.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who contemplate the meaning:
first, those who practice according to what they have heard; second, those who do not practice according to what they have heard.
Those who practice according to what they have heard are virtuous; those who do not practice according to what they have heard are not called virtuous.
There are two types of those who practice according to the teachings:
first, those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and are unable to bring benefit, peace, or relief to all suffering sentient beings;
second, those who dedicate themselves to the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, benefiting many people and enabling them to attain peace and happiness.
A Bodhisattva should know that one who is able to benefit many people and bring them peace and happiness is the most supreme and most virtuous. Good son!

Just as among all jewels, the wish-fulfilling gem is the most excellent and wondrous, and just as among all flavors, nectar is the highest, so too is the Bodhisattva the most victorious and supreme among humans and devas, beyond all comparison.
"Good son! This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and abiding in the seven wholesome dharmas.
Once a bodhisattva has dwelt in these seven wholesome dharmas, they attain the fulfillment of pure conduct (brahmacarya)."
"Furthermore, good son!
There is another holy life (brahmacarya), namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the frequent cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*) likewise severs ill-will, why do you speak of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*)?”
Inferring from its meaning, there should be three [types].
World-Honored One!
Loving-kindness has three objects:
First, taking sentient beings as the object; second, taking phenomena (*dharma*) as the object; third, being without an object (*anālambana*).
Compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are likewise.
According to this principle, there should be only three [immeasurables], not four.
Regarding the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*): to take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as one's object and vow to grant them happiness is called the object of sentient beings.
Regarding the object of phenomena (*dharmālambana*): to take the various things required by sentient beings as one's object and bestow them upon them is called the object of phenomena.
Regarding "objectless" (anālambana): to take the Tathāgata as one's object is what is called "objectless.

Compassion generally takes impoverished sentient beings as its object; however, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is forever free from poverty and experiences supreme bliss. If one takes sentient beings as the object, one does not take the Buddha as the object; the same applies to the Dharma.
For this reason, that which takes the Tathāgata as its object is called "objectless.
World-Honored One!

That which takes all sentient beings as its object through loving-kindness—just as one takes one's parents, wife, children, and relatives as objects—is for this reason called "sentient-being-objective" (sattvālambana).
Regarding the object-condition (dharmālambana): not perceiving parents, wife, children, or relatives, but seeing that all phenomena arise from conditions—this is called the object-condition.
Regarding the objectless (anālambana): not dwelling upon the marks of phenomena nor the marks of sentient beings—this is called the objectless.
The same applies to the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; therefore, there should be three, not four.
World-Honored One!
There are two kinds of people:
The first is the temperament of views (dṛṣṭicarita), and the second is the temperament of craving (tṛṣṇācarita).

Those of the temperament of views cultivate compassion (maitrī) and loving-kindness (karuṇā) extensively, while those of the temperament of craving cultivate joy (muditā) and equanimity (upekṣā) extensively.
Therefore, there should be two [temperaments], not four.
World-Honored One!
That which is "immeasurable" (apramāṇa) is called "boundless" (ananta); because no limit can be found, it is named immeasurable.
If it were immeasurable, it should be one, and one should not speak of four.
"If you say there are four, how can they be immeasurable?
Therefore, it should be one; it should not be four.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! The essential teachings proclaimed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, for the sake of all sentient beings, are secret in their expression and difficult to comprehend.
At times, they may explain a single causal condition for the sake of sentient beings.”
As it is said: "What is the single causal condition?
It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), son of good family!"
Some explain two kinds:
cause and fruit.
Others explain three kinds:
There are afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Alternatively, four types are taught: ignorance, volitional formations, birth, and old age and death.
Alternatively, five types are taught: namely, sensation, craving, clinging, existence, and birth.
Some speak of six kinds, namely the causes and effects of the three periods of time.
Others speak of seven kinds, namely: consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, and craving and grasping.
Some explain eight types, excluding ignorance, formations, birth, and old age and death, leaving the remaining eight matters;
others explain nine types, as in the *Nagara-sūtra*, excluding ignorance, formations, and consciousness, leaving the remaining nine matters.
Sometimes eleven [factors] are taught, as when it was taught to Satyaka Nirgranthaputra: excluding the single factor of birth (*jāti*), there are the remaining eleven.

At other times, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are taught in their entirety, as at Rājagṛha, where for Kāśyapa and others, the twelve factors from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to birth, old age, sickness, and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) were fully explained.
"Good son!
Just as a single causal condition is differentiated in various ways for the sake of sentient beings, so too are the immeasurable mental dharmas.
Good son!"
For this reason, one should not give rise to doubt regarding the profound and secret spheres of activity of the Tathāgatas.
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great skillful means; he speaks of the impermanent as permanent, and speaks of the permanent as impermanent.
To speak of pleasure as suffering, and suffering as pleasure;
to speak of the impure as pure, and the pure as impure;
to speak of selflessness as self, and self as selflessness.
To speak of what is not a sentient being as a sentient being, and to speak of a real sentient being as not a sentient being;
to speak of what is not a thing as a thing, and to speak of a thing as not a thing;
to speak of what is not real as real, and to speak of what is real as not real.
To speak of what is not an object as an object, and to speak of an object as what is not an object;
to speak of what is not birth as birth, and to speak of birth as what is not birth;
and so on, up to speaking of ignorance as clarity, and speaking of clarity as ignorance.
Form is described as non-form, and non-form is described as form;
the non-path is described as the path, and the path is described as the non-path. Good son!
The Tathāgata employs these immeasurable skillful means to discipline sentient beings;
how could this be false? Good son!

There may be sentient beings who are greedy for wealth and goods; toward such persons, I personally manifest myself as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) and, for immeasurable years, provide them with all their various needs. Only after that do I teach and transform them, causing them to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to the five desires, [the Buddha] shall satisfy their wishes with exquisite five desires for immeasurable years, and only thereafter exhort and transform them, causing them to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there are sentient beings who are prosperous, powerful, and self-important, I shall serve as their servant for immeasurable eons, running about and attending to them; once I have won their hearts, I will further exhort and transform them, causing them to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If there are sentient beings who are by nature stubborn and self-opinionated, requiring the admonitions and exhortations of others, I shall, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, instruct, reprimand, and earnestly exhort them to bring their minds to harmony; thereafter, I shall further encourage them to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son!
In this way, for immeasurable eons, the Tathāgata has used various skillful means to cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; how could this be false?"
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, though dwelling amidst all manner of evils, remain unstained by them, just like a lotus flower.
Son of good family,
you should understand the meaning of the four immeasurables in this way.
“Good son! This immeasurable mind has four essential natures; if one practices them, one will be born in the realm of Mahābrahmā.
Good son!”
Thus, they are immeasurable; there are four companions, and for this reason they are called "the four.

Now, one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever covetous desire; one who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever ill-will; one who cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) can sever discontent; and one who cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) can sever both covetous desire and ill-will toward sentient beings.
Good son! For this reason, they are called four, rather than one, two, or three. Good son!

As you have said, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever hatred; compassion (*karuṇā*) is likewise so. One should speak of three [immeasurables], yet you should not raise such an objection now. Why is this?
Good son, there are two kinds of anger:
first, that which can take one's life; second, that which can lash and beat.
By cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one can sever that which takes life; by cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*), one can eliminate that which lashes and beats.
"Good son! For this reason, are there not four?
Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger:"
First is anger toward sentient beings; second is anger toward non-sentient beings.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) severs anger toward sentient beings, while one who cultivates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) severs anger toward non-sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger:
First, those with causal conditions; second, those without causal conditions.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) severs those with causal conditions; one who cultivates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) severs those without causal conditions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred (*dveṣa*):
First is cultivation practiced over the long past; second is cultivation practiced in the present.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever [the afflictions] of the past; one who cultivates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) severs those of the present.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred:
first, hatred toward noble ones; second, hatred toward ordinary beings.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) abandons hatred toward noble ones; one who cultivates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) abandons hatred toward ordinary beings.
Furthermore, there are two types of hatred:
first, the superior; second, the middling.
One cultivates loving-kindness to sever the superior, and cultivates compassion to sever the middling.
"Good son!
For this reason, they are called 'four. How can you raise the objection that there should be three and not four?
Therefore, Kāśyapa!"
These immeasurable minds are distinguished as four by way of their mutual relationship with their counterparts.
Furthermore, they should be called four by virtue of being "vessels.
If there is a vessel of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), then it cannot simultaneously possess the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For this reason, there should be four that are not deficient. Good son!

Because they are distinguished by their practice, there should be four; when one practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there is no compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*). Therefore, there are four.
“Good son! Because they are immeasurable, they are also called ‘four.
Now, that which is immeasurable has four kinds: there is the immeasurable mind, which has an object but is not autonomous;”
There is immeasurable mind that is sovereign but not an object-condition;
there is immeasurable mind that is both an object-condition and sovereign;
and there is immeasurable mind that is neither an object-condition nor sovereign.
What is meant by "immeasurable" yet having an object, but not being sovereign?

It refers to taking immeasurable and boundless sentient beings as one's object, yet being unable to attain sovereign samādhi; even if it is attained, it is not fixed, being sometimes gained and sometimes lost.
What are the immeasurable [states] that are sovereign but not objective conditions?
For example, when one wishes to bring peace and happiness to one's parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth, these are not immeasurable conditions.
What is immeasurable that is both conditioned and sovereign?
It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
What is immeasurable that is neither conditioned nor sovereign?
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot universally take immeasurable sentient beings as their object, nor do they possess such mastery.
Good son! For this reason, these are called the four immeasurables; they are not within the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, but are the realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Good son! Regarding these four matters, although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are said to be immeasurable, their number is so small as to be hardly worth mentioning.
As for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they may truly be called immeasurable and boundless.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is truly as the Holy Teaching declares: the realm of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is not to be reached by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.”
World-Honored One!

Is it possible that there are bodhisattvas who, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, attain a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, yet this is not the Great Loving-Kindness and Great Compassion?
The Buddha said, "There are,
son of good family!
If a bodhisattva makes a threefold distinction among sentient beings:
First are those who are dear, second are those who are hostile or hateful, and third are those who are neutral.
Among those who are dear, there are again three grades— namely, superior, middling, and inferior—
and it is the same for those who are hostile or hateful.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva bestows supreme happiness upon his superior relatives; he likewise bestows supreme happiness equally upon those who are middling or inferior relatives. Toward his superior enemies, he bestows a small measure of happiness; toward his middling enemies, he bestows a middling measure of happiness; and toward his inferior enemies, he bestows supreme happiness.
The bodhisattva thus practices further and further: he bestows medium-grade happiness upon superior enemies, and bestows superior happiness equally upon middling and inferior enemies.

Practicing further still, he bestows superior happiness equally upon superior, middling, and inferior [enemies]. When he bestows superior happiness even upon superior enemies, at that time, he is said to have accomplished the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).
At that time, the bodhisattva attains a mind of equanimity toward his parents and even toward his greatest enemies, without any distinction.
Good son! This is called the attainment of loving-kindness, but not great loving-kindness.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does a bodhisattva who has attained such loving-kindness still not yet receive the name ‘Great Loving-Kindness’? “Good son!”
Because it is difficult to accomplish, it is not called "Great Compassion. Why is this?

Because throughout immeasurable kalpas in the distant past, they accumulated much affliction and had not yet cultivated wholesome dharmas; therefore, they are unable to subdue their minds within a single day.
"Good son!
It is like carving a bean: if it is dry when pierced with an awl, the tool will never penetrate.
The hardness of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is likewise; even if one binds the mind for a single day and night without distraction, they are difficult to subdue."
Furthermore, just as a domestic dog does not fear humans, while the wild deer of the mountains and forests flee in terror upon seeing a person;
so too is hatred difficult to remove, like a guard dog,
whereas a compassionate heart is easily lost, like that wild deer.
Therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue; for this reason, it is not called "Great Compassion.
Furthermore, good son, it is like drawing on stone: its inscription remains forever.
A drawing on water vanishes quickly; its momentum does not endure for long.
Anger is like drawing on stone, while the roots of all virtues are like that drawing on water; therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue.

Just as the radiance of a great mass of fire endures for a long time, whereas the light of a flash of lightning cannot endure even for a moment, so too is hatred like a mass of fire and loving-kindness like the light of lightning.
For this reason, this mind is difficult to subdue; by virtue of this fact, it is not called "Great Loving-Kindness."
“Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the first stage, it is called ‘Great Compassion. Why is this?
"Good son!

Those who are most extremely evil are called icchantikas. When a bodhisattva first abides in the cultivation of great compassion, their mind makes no distinction regarding icchantikas; because they do not perceive any fault in them, they do not give rise to anger. For this reason, it is termed 'great compassion.'"
"Good son! To eliminate that which is unbeneficial for all sentient beings is called great kindness (maitrī);
to desire to bestow immeasurable benefit and happiness upon sentient beings is called great compassion (karuṇā)."
To give rise to a heart of joy toward all sentient beings is called great joy (*muditā*);
to have nothing to protect or cling to is called great equanimity (*upekṣā*);
and if one does not perceive a self, the characteristics of phenomena, or one's own body, but perceives all phenomena as equal and non-dual, this is called great equanimity.
To renounce one’s own happiness and bestow it upon others is called great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*). Good son!
Only the four immeasurables can cause a bodhisattva to increase and fulfill the six pāramitās; other practices do not necessarily have this power.
"Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva first attains the four worldly immeasurable minds, and only thereafter does he resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, gradually emerging into the supramundane."
“Good son!
Because there is mundane immeasurability, supramundane immeasurability arises; for this reason, it is called ‘Great Immeasurability.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To exclude that which is unbeneficial and to bestow benefit and happiness—there is truly nothing to be done.
To contemplate in this way is merely empty observation; it possesses no real benefit.”
World-Honored One!
It is, for example, as when a bhikṣu contemplates impurity: he sees the clothes he wears as entirely having the appearance of skin, though they are not actually skin;
whatever he eats and drinks he perceives as being composed of worms, though they are not actually worms.
One contemplates a bean soup, imagining it to be excrement, though it is not actually feces;
one contemplates the curd one eats as being like marrow and brain, though it is not actually brain.
One contemplates the fragments of bone as having the appearance of flour, yet they are not actually flour.
The four immeasurable minds are likewise: they cannot truly benefit sentient beings or cause them to attain happiness.
"Although one speaks with the mouth of granting happiness to sentient beings, in reality it is not obtained; is such an observation not false?
World-Honored One!
If it were not false and if happiness were truly being granted, why is it that all sentient beings do not experience this happiness through the majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?"
If it were truly the case that one could not obtain happiness, then as the Buddha said:
"I recall that in the past, while practicing loving-kindness alone, I passed through seven cycles of the formation and destruction of this kalpa-world without returning to this life."
When the world is forming, he is born among the Brahmā devas;
when the world is dissolving, he is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
If born among the Brahmā devas, his power and sovereignty are such that none can overcome him; he is the most excellent and supreme among a thousand Brahmās, and is named Mahābrahmā.
There are sentient beings who all conceive the highest regard for me.

Thirty-six times I became Śakra Devānām Indra, the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and countless hundreds of thousands of times I became a universal monarch (cakravartin). By cultivating a mind of loving-kindness alone, I attained such fruits and rewards among humans and devas.
“If it were not true, how could it correspond with this meaning?
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!”
“Good son! You are truly courageous and free from all fear.
He then spoke these verses to Kāśyapa:
"If, toward even a single sentient being, one does not give rise to a mind of anger,
but instead vows to grant them happiness, this is called the perfection of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If, among all sentient beings, one gives rise to a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*,"
This is called the noble lineage; one attains immeasurable rewards of merit.
Even if seers possessing the five supernatural powers were to fill this entire earth, and the Great Lord Maheśvara were to offer them all that they require for their comfort.
"The fruits of merit obtained from various things such as elephants and horses do not equal even a sixteenth part of cultivating a single moment of loving-kindness. Good son!"
Now, the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is truly not a deluded thought; it is, in truth, reality itself.
If it were the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, it would be called false and illusory.
That of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is real and not empty.
How is this known?
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who practices such Great Parinirvāṇa contemplates earth as gold and contemplates gold as earth; he manifests the appearance of water from earth, the appearance of earth from water, the appearance of fire from water, the appearance of water from fire, the appearance of wind from earth, and the appearance of earth from wind; all these are accomplished according to his will without any falsehood.

To contemplate real sentient beings as non-sentient beings, and to contemplate non-sentient beings as real sentient beings—all of these are accomplished according to one’s will, without any falsehood. Good son!
You should know that the four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva are genuine contemplation,
not something unreal. Furthermore, good son,
what is called "genuine contemplation"?
This means that because one is able to sever all afflictions. Good son!

One who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever lustful desire; one who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever anger and hatred; one who cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) can sever discontent; and one who cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) can sever both lust and hatred as well as the perception of a sentient being. For this reason, it is called "true contemplation."
"Furthermore, good son!
The four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva can serve as the root of all wholesome dharmas. Good son!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not encounter impoverished sentient beings, there is no occasion for the arising of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If loving-kindness does not arise, one cannot give rise to the mind of generosity (*dāna-citta*). Through the causal conditions of giving, one enables all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness—namely, food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flowers and incense, bedding, dwellings, and lamps. When giving in this manner, the mind is free from bondage and attachment, and one resolutely dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, his mind has no basis for dependence; deluded conceptualization is forever severed; he is not moved by fear, nor by fame or gain; he does not seek the pleasures experienced by humans or devas; he gives rise to no arrogance; he expects no recompense; and he does not act to deceive others.

Therefore, one practices giving without seeking wealth or status. Whenever practicing giving, one does not perceive the recipient, nor whether they observe the precepts or violate them; whether they are a field of merit or not; whether they are a friend or not a friend. At the time of giving, one does not perceive whether they are a worthy vessel or not; one does not select specific times or days, nor locations that are suitable or unsuitable. Furthermore, one takes no account of famine or prosperity, nor does one perceive cause and effect, nor whether this is a sentient being or not, nor whether it is merit or not. Although one does not perceive the giver, the recipient, or the material object, and even does not perceive cessation or its karmic retribution, one constantly practices giving without interruption.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva perceives the keeping or breaking of precepts, or even their karmic retribution, they will ultimately be unable to practice giving.
If one does not practice giving, then the dānapāramitā is not fulfilled."
If one does not fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, one cannot achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! It is like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow."
His kinsmen, wishing for his well-being and desiring to remove the poison, immediately summoned a skilled physician to extract the arrow.
That man then said:
"Wait, do not touch it! I must first observe from which direction this poisoned arrow came."
"By whom was this shot?
Is it a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra?
He then reflected further:
"What kind of wood is this?
Is it bamboo,
or is it willow?"
As for its iron tip, from what forge was it produced?
Is it hard or is it soft?
As for those feathers, what kind of bird’s wings are they?
Are they those of a crow, an owl, or a vulture?
As for all these poisons, do they arise from being produced, or are they naturally present?
"Is it the venom of this person,
or the venom of an evil serpent?
Thus the foolish man, failing to understand at last, immediately met his end.
Good son! It is the same for a bodhisattva:
if, when practicing giving, one discriminates between the recipient, whether they uphold the precepts or break them, and even the resulting karmic fruit, one will ultimately be unable to give.
If one is unable to practice giving, then one does not fulfill the dāna-pāramitā.
If one does not fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, then one cannot achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, he regards all sentient beings with impartial compassion, as if thinking of them as his own children.”
Furthermore, when practicing generosity, one gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, just as parents look after a sick child.
At the time of giving, the mind is filled with joy, like that of parents seeing their child recover from illness.
Once the gift has been given, his mind is relaxed and let go, just like parents who see their child grown up and able to live independently.
When this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives food from a heart of loving-kindness, he always makes this aspiration:

"May what I now give be shared with all sentient beings; by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the food of great wisdom and diligently apply themselves toward the supreme Mahāyāna."
May all sentient beings obtain the food of excellent wisdom, and not seek the food of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
May all sentient beings obtain the food of the joy of the Dharma, and not seek the food of craving.
May all sentient beings obtain the food of the *prajñāpāramitā*, may they all be fully satisfied, and may they grasp unimpeded, supreme roots of goodness.
May all sentient beings realize the characteristic of emptiness and attain an unimpeded body, just like space.
"May all sentient beings always be recipients [of offerings], showing compassion for all and serving as fields of merit for the multitude.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the mind of loving-kindness, they should firmly make such vows whenever giving food.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives a drink from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he should make this aspiration:

'May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings; by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings enter the river of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), drink the water of the eight flavors, and swiftly traverse the path to unsurpassed bodhi.'"
They have distanced themselves from the exhaustion of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, thirsting with longing for the unsurpassed Buddha Vehicle.
They sever the thirst of afflictions and thirst with longing for the flavor of the Dharma.

Free from the craving for birth and death, they cherish and delight in the Mahāyāna and Great Parinirvāṇa; they are fully endowed with the Dharmakāya, attain all samādhis, and enter the profound great ocean of wisdom.
May all sentient beings obtain the taste of ambrosia—the supramundane flavor of Bodhi, which is free from desire and tranquil.

May all sentient beings be fully endowed with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flavors of the Dharma; having attained these flavors of the Dharma, may they perceive the Buddha-nature; having perceived the Buddha-nature, may they be able to rain down the rain of the Dharma; having rained down the rain of the Dharma, may the Buddha-nature pervade everywhere like empty space. Furthermore, may they cause other immeasurable sentient beings to obtain the single flavor of the Dharma, namely that of the Mahāyāna, and not the flavors of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
May all sentient beings obtain a single sweet taste, free from the six distinct varieties of flavor.
May all sentient beings seek only the flavor of the Dharma—the flavor of the practice of the unobstructed Buddha-dharma—and seek no other flavors.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives beverages from a mind of loving-kindness, they should firmly make such vows as these.
Furthermore, good son!"
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives vehicles from a heart of loving-kindness, they should make this vow:

"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings. By these causes and conditions, may all beings universally realize the Mahāyāna, abide in the Mahāyāna, not retreat from the vehicle, not waver from the vehicle, and attain the vehicle of the Vajra-seat; may they not seek the vehicles of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but turn toward the Buddha-vehicle—the unsubduable vehicle, the tireless vehicle, the non-retrogressive vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle, the vehicle of the Ten Powers, the vehicle of great merit, the unprecedented vehicle, the rare vehicle, the difficult-to-obtain vehicle, the boundless vehicle, and the vehicle that knows all."
"Good son! When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives vehicles from a mind of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, good son!"
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives clothing from a heart of loving-kindness, they should make this vow: "May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings.

By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the garment of shame and modesty, covering their bodies with the Dharma-realm; may they tear away the garments of false views. May their clothing remain one foot and six inches away from their bodies, and may they attain a golden-hued body. May all sensations they receive be soft and unimpeded; may their complexion be lustrous and moist, their skin fine and supple, and their constant radiance immeasurable. Being formless and transcending form, I vow that all sentient beings shall universally attain a formless body, transcend all forms, and enter the formless Great Parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives clothing, he should thus firmly make this vow.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices loving-kindness and gives flowers, ointments, powdered incense, and various blended perfumes, they should make this aspiration:

"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings; by these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings attain the Buddha-flower samādhi, and may the exquisite garlands of the seven factors of awakening be bound upon their heads and crowns."
May all sentient beings have forms like the full moon, and may all the colors they perceive be the most subtle and supreme.
May all sentient beings attain a single mark, adorned with a hundred merits.
May all sentient beings, according to their wishes, behold pleasing forms.
May all sentient beings constantly encounter virtuous friends, obtain unimpeded fragrances, and be free from all foul odors.
May all sentient beings be endowed with all roots of goodness, which are unsurpassed treasures.
May all sentient beings look upon one another with harmony and joy, free from sorrow and suffering; may they each be fully equipped with all virtues and no longer harbor anxiety for one another.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the fragrance of precepts.
May all sentient beings uphold unimpeded precepts, their fragrant aroma pervading and filling the ten directions.

May all sentient beings attain the firm precepts, the precepts free from regret, the precepts of omniscience, and be entirely free from the breaking of precepts; may they all attain the precept of non-precept, the unprecedented precept, the teacherless precept, the unconditioned precept, the untainted precept, the undefiled precept, the perfected precept, and the ultimate precept; may they attain the precept of equality, such that toward being anointed with perfume or being cut and stabbed, they are equal and without hatred or love.
May all sentient beings attain the unsurpassed precepts—the Mahāyāna precepts, not those of the Hīnayāna.
May all sentient beings fully perfect the *śīlapāramitā*, just as the precepts accomplished by all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings be thoroughly perfumed and cultivated by generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
May all sentient beings attain the subtle and wondrous lotus of Great Parinirvāṇa, the fragrance of which fills the ten directions.
May all sentient beings exclusively partake of the unsurpassed fragrant food of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, just as bees gather from flowers, taking only the fragrance and flavor.
May all sentient beings fully achieve bodies perfumed by immeasurable merit.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives flowers and incense from a mind of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives a bed or bedding from a mind of loving-kindness, he should make this vow:

"May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings. By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the beds upon which the God among Gods lies; may they attain great wisdom and sit in the station of the four dhyānas;
may they lie upon the beds upon which Bodhisattvas lie, and not lie upon the beds of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, remaining far removed from lying on evil beds."
May all sentient beings obtain peaceful and blissful rest, leaving behind the bed of birth and death to attain the great nirvāṇa lion’s bed.
May all sentient beings, having sat upon this bed, further manifest the supernatural power of the lion’s play for the sake of other immeasurable sentient beings.
May all sentient beings dwell within this great palace of the Mahāyāna and expound the Buddha-nature for the sake of all beings.
May all sentient beings sit upon the unsurpassed throne, never to be overcome by worldly dharmas.
May all sentient beings obtain the seat of forbearance, and be freed from the famine and cold hunger of birth and death.
May all sentient beings obtain the seat of fearlessness, forever departing from all afflictions and enemies.
May all sentient beings obtain pure seats and single-mindedly seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
May all sentient beings obtain the seat of wholesome dharmas and be constantly protected by virtuous friends.
"May all sentient beings obtain beds for reclining on their right sides, relying upon and following the Dharma practiced by all Buddhas.
Son of good family,
when a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives beds and bedding from a heart of loving-kindness, they should firmly make such a vow as this.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, from a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), gives away houses and dwellings, he always makes this vow:

'May all that I now give be shared with all sentient beings. By this causal condition, may all sentient beings dwell in the house of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), practicing the conduct of spiritual friends, the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the practice of great perfect enlightenment, the path of practice of all bodhisattvas, and boundless, vast practices as expansive as space.'"
May all sentient beings attain right mindfulness and remain far removed from evil thoughts.
May all sentient beings fully abide in permanence, bliss, self, and purity, forever free from the four inversions.
May all sentient beings fully receive and uphold the supramundane syllables.
May all sentient beings certainly become vessels for unsurpassed, all-encompassing wisdom.
May all sentient beings enter the dwelling of the nectar of immortality.
May all sentient beings, throughout their initial, middle, and final moments of mind, always enter the dwelling of the Mahāyāna nirvāṇa.
May all sentient beings, in future ages, always dwell in the palaces inhabited by bodhisattvas.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, out of a heart of loving-kindness, gives away houses and dwellings, they should always firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives a lamp from a mind of loving-kindness, they always make this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared in common with all sentient beings; by this causal condition, may all sentient beings possess immeasurable radiance and dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma."
May all sentient beings always attain illumination.
May all sentient beings obtain a subtle and exquisite complexion, with a radiance that is foremost.
May the eyes of all sentient beings be pure and free from all veils and cataracts.

May all sentient beings obtain the great torch of wisdom, skillfully understanding the absence of self, the absence of the characteristics of a sentient being, and the absence of a person or a life-principle.
May all sentient beings behold the pure Buddha-nature, which is like empty space.
May all sentient beings attain purity of the physical eye, seeing through to the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
May all sentient beings obtain the light of the Buddhas, universally illuminating the ten directions.
May all sentient beings attain unimpeded illumination and all perceive the pure Buddha-nature.
May all sentient beings attain the illumination of great wisdom, shattering all darkness and the icchantika state.
May all sentient beings attain immeasurable light, universally illuminating the immeasurable worlds of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings kindle the lamp of the Mahāyāna and depart from the lamps of the two vehicles.
May all sentient beings obtain such radiance as to extinguish the darkness of ignorance, surpassing the merit of the thousand suns shining everywhere.
May all sentient beings obtain the brilliance of the fire-jewel, completely extinguishing all the darkness within the trichiliocosm.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the five eyes, realize the characteristics of all phenomena, and achieve untaught enlightenment.
May all sentient beings be free from views and ignorance.
May all sentient beings attain the subtle and wondrous radiance of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, which reveals and awakens sentient beings to their true Buddha-nature.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives lamps from a mind of loving-kindness, they should always diligently make such a vow: 'Good son!'"
All the roots of goodness belonging to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Tathāgatas, have loving-kindness as their root. Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they are able to produce such immeasurable roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),

namely: the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha*), exhalation and inhalation (*ānāpāna*), impermanence (*anitya*), arising and ceasing (*utpādavyaya*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*),

the seven expedient means (*sapta-upāya*), the three stages of contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā-sthāna*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and the contemplation of non-self (*anātman-ādi-darśana*), as well as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
The stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*); the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);

the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
...the signless, the wishless, and the non-contentious samādhis; the knowledge of others' minds; the various supernormal powers;
the knowledge of the primordial limit; the wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, and the wisdom of buddhas.
Good son! Such dharmas as these have loving-kindness as their root. Good son!

For this reason, loving-kindness is true and not false. If someone were to ask: "What is the root of all virtues? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it is the root of all wholesome dharmas. Just as the earth is the foundation for all grasses, trees, and medicinal herbs, so too is loving-kindness the foundation for all wholesome dharmas. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the root of all wholesome dharmas. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the father and mother of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it gives birth to all wholesome dharmas. Just as a father and mother give birth to their children, so too does loving-kindness give birth to all wholesome dharmas. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the father and mother of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the teacher of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it teaches all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas. Just as a teacher instructs his students, so too does loving-kindness instruct all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the teacher of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the benefactor of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it bestows upon all sentient beings the fruit of happiness. Just as a benefactor bestows wealth upon others, so too does loving-kindness bestow the fruit of happiness upon all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the benefactor of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the savior of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it rescues all sentient beings from the suffering of the three evil realms. Just as a savior rescues people from danger, so too does loving-kindness rescue all sentient beings from the suffering of the three evil realms. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the savior of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the refuge of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it provides a place of rest for all sentient beings. Just as a refuge provides a place of rest for people, so too does loving-kindness provide a place of rest for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the refuge of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the leader of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it leads all sentient beings to enter the path of Buddhahood. Just as a leader leads people to their destination, so too does loving-kindness lead all sentient beings to enter the path of Buddhahood. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the leader of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the friend of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it never abandons all sentient beings. Just as a friend never abandons one, so too does loving-kindness never abandon all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the friend of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the protector of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it protects all sentient beings from the fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Just as a protector shields people from fear, so too does loving-kindness protect all sentient beings from the fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the protector of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the light of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it dispels the darkness of ignorance for all sentient beings. Just as a light dispels the darkness, so too does loving-kindness dispel the darkness of ignorance for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the light of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the sun of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it illuminates all sentient beings with the light of wisdom. Just as the sun illuminates all things with its radiance, so too does loving-kindness illuminate all sentient beings with the light of wisdom. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the sun of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the moon of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it cools the heat of afflictions for all sentient beings. Just as the moon cools the heat, so too does loving-kindness cool the heat of afflictions for all sentient beings.

Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the moon of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the cloud of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it rains the rain of Dharma upon all sentient beings. Just as a cloud rains water upon the world, so too does loving-kindness rain the rain of Dharma upon all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the cloud of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the wind of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it sweeps away the dust of afflictions for all sentient beings. Just as the wind sweeps away dust, so too does loving-kindness sweep away the dust of afflictions for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the wind of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the medicine of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it heals the wounds of afflictions for all sentient beings. Just as medicine heals wounds, so too does loving-kindness heal the wounds of afflictions for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the medicine of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the vessel of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it contains all wholesome dharmas. Just as a vessel contains various substances, so too does loving-kindness contain all wholesome dharmas. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the vessel of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the field of merit for all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it yields the fruit of great bliss for all sentient beings. Just as a field of merit yields the fruit of great bliss, so too does loving-kindness yield the fruit of great bliss for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the field of merit for all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the treasury of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it stores all jewels of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Just as a treasury stores various jewels, so too does loving-kindness store all jewels of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the treasury of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the jewel of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it is rare and difficult to encounter. Just as a jewel is rare and difficult to encounter, so too is loving-kindness rare and difficult to encounter. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the jewel of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the crown jewel of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it adorns the head of all Buddhas. Just as a crown jewel adorns the head, so too does loving-kindness adorn the heads of all Buddhas. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the crown jewel of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the banner of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it raises the standard of victory over all Māras. Just as a banner raises the standard of victory, so too does loving-kindness raise the standard of victory over all Māras. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the banner of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the drum of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it proclaims the sound of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Just as a drum proclaims its sound, so too does loving-kindness proclaim the sound of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should know that loving-kindness is the drum of all sentient beings. Furthermore, if someone were to ask: "Who is the lion of all sentient beings? [the answer would be: "It is loving-kindness. Why? Because it roars the roar of fearlessness. Just as a lion
"One should say that it is loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
For this reason, loving-kindness is the reality; it is not false.
Good son!"

That which can produce roots of goodness is called true contemplation; that which is true contemplation is itself named compassion (*maitrī*); compassion is the Tathāgata, and compassion is the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is compassion, and compassion is the Tathāgata.
"Good son! Loving-kindness is the path to enlightenment; the path to enlightenment is the Tathāgata; and the Tathāgata is loving-kindness. Good son!"
Loving-kindness is Mahābrahmā, and Mahābrahmā is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Good son!
Loving-kindness can act as a father and mother for all sentient beings; the father and mother are loving-kindness, and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
"Good son!
Loving-kindness is inconceivable; the realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable, and the realm of the Buddhas is precisely loving-kindness. You should know that loving-kindness is the Tathāgata."
"Good son!

Compassion is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. Because this Buddha-nature has long been shrouded and obscured by afflictions, it prevents sentient beings from seeing it. Buddha-nature is compassion, and compassion is the Tathāgata."
"Good son! Loving-kindness is the great emptiness, the great emptiness is loving-kindness, and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Good son!"
Loving-kindness is space, and space is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
Good son! Loving-kindness is permanence, and permanence is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
“Good son! Loving-kindness is itself bliss; bliss is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Sangha; the Sangha is itself loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is itself the Tathāgata. Good son!”
Loving-kindness is purity; purity is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha is loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
Good son! Loving-kindness is myself; I am the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha is loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Good son! Loving-kindness is the nectar of immortality, and the nectar of immortality is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Sangha, and the Sangha is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
"Good son!
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the unsurpassed path of all bodhisattvas; the path is itself loving-kindness, and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
Good son!"
Loving-kindness is the immeasurable realm of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; that immeasurable realm is itself loving-kindness. One should know that this loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
“Good son, if loving-kindness were impermanent, and impermanence were itself loving-kindness, you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
Good son, if loving-kindness were suffering, and suffering were itself loving-kindness, you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.”
"Good son!
If loving-kindness is impure, then impurity itself is loving-kindness; you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!"
If loving-kindness is without self, then non-self is itself loving-kindness; you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
Son of good family!
If loving-kindness is conceptual construction, then conceptual construction is itself loving-kindness; you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
"Good son!

If loving-kindness were not called the dānapāramitā, and if it were a loving-kindness that is not dāna, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas; this applies likewise even unto the prajñāpāramitā."
"Good son! If loving-kindness cannot benefit sentient beings, such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!"
If compassion does not enter the path of the One Vehicle, you should know that this compassion is the compassion of the śrāvakas. Good son!
If compassion cannot bring about the awakening to all dharmas, you should know that this compassion is the compassion of the śrāvakas.
"Good son!
If compassion cannot perceive the Tathāgata-nature, you should know that this compassion is the compassion of the śrāvakas.
Good son!"
If loving-kindness perceives all phenomena as having marks, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
Son of good family!
If loving-kindness is with outflows, then that loving-kindness with outflows is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
"Good son! If compassion is conditioned, then this conditioned compassion is the compassion of the śrāvakas. Good son!"
If loving-kindness cannot abide in the first stage, it is not the loving-kindness of the first stage; one should know that this is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
Son of good family!
If loving-kindness cannot attain the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Buddha, one should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
“Good son! If loving-kindness can attain the four fruits of the śrāmaṇa, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!”
If loving-kindness is existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent—such loving-kindness cannot be conceived by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others.
Good son! If loving-kindness is inconceivable, the Dharma is inconceivable, the Buddha-nature is inconceivable, and the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.
"Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and cultivates such loving-kindness, although they rest within the midst of sleep, they are not truly asleep because of their diligent application of effort;
although they are constantly awake, they have no awakening, because they are without sleep."
During sleep, although protected by the devas, there is no one who protects them, because they do not commit evil;
they have no bad dreams while sleeping, because they are free from unwholesomeness and have transcended sleep;
and after the end of life, although they may be born in the Brahma Heaven, there is no place of birth, because they have attained mastery.
"Good son!
One who cultivates loving-kindness can achieve such immeasurable and boundless merit.
Good son!"
This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra can also accomplish such immeasurable and boundless merits, and all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, likewise accomplish such immeasurable and boundless merits.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Fifteen.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight on the Brahma-faring, Part Two.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All the contemplations of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are entirely true, whereas those of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not true;
for what reason do all sentient beings not equally receive happiness through the majestic power of the Bodhisattvas?
"If sentient beings do not actually obtain happiness, one should know that the loving-kindness cultivated by the Bodhisattva is of no benefit.
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
The compassion of a bodhisattva is not without benefit. Good son!
There are sentient beings who will inevitably experience suffering, and there are those who will not.
If there are sentient beings who are destined to suffer, the Bodhisattva’s compassion would be of no benefit—referring to those such as the icchantikas.
If there are those whose suffering is not fixed, the Bodhisattva’s compassion is indeed beneficial, causing those sentient beings to experience complete happiness.
Good son!

It is like a person who, seeing from afar a lion, tiger, leopard, jackal, wolf, or a rākṣasa demon, naturally gives rise to fear; or one walking at night who, seeing a tree stump, likewise gives rise to fear.
"Good son! Just as these people naturally feel fear,
so too do sentient beings naturally experience happiness upon seeing one who practices loving-kindness."
"Good son! For this reason, when a bodhisattva cultivates loving-kindness, it is a genuine reflection and is not without benefit. Good son!"
I say that this loving-kindness has immeasurable gateways, namely the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Good son!
For example, Devadatta instructed Ajātaśatru, desiring to harm the Tathāgata.

At that time, as I entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in succession, King Ajātaśatru released the intoxicated and maddened elephant Dhanapāla, intending to cause harm to me and my disciples.

At that time, the elephant tramples and kills immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings; once these beings have died, there is much blood and its scent, which the elephant smells and becomes twice as frenzied and intoxicated as usual.
Seeing my attendants clad in red garments, they mistook them for blood and rushed toward it;
among my disciples, those who had not yet abandoned desire fled in all directions out of fear, with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, all the people within the great city of Rājagṛha simultaneously raised their voices in wailing and lamentation, saying:
"How strange! Today the Tathāgata has passed away; how can the Perfectly Awakened One be suddenly destroyed?"
