At that time, Devadatta felt joy arise in his heart and thought:
"It is most excellent that the śramaṇa Gautama has passed away; from this day forward, he shall truly no longer appear."
"How wonderful this plan! I wish for it to be fulfilled. "Good son!

At that time, desiring to subdue the elephant Dhana-pāla, I immediately entered the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), extended my hand toward him, and from my five fingers, I manifested five lions."
When the elephant saw this, his heart was filled with terror; he immediately voided excrement and threw his whole body to the ground, prostrating at my feet.

"Good son! At that time, there were actually no lions upon the five fingers of my hands; rather, it was through the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through loving-kindness and compassion that I tamed him."
"Furthermore, good son!

When I was about to enter nirvana and had first set out toward the city of Kuśinagara, there were five hundred strong men who, along the way, were leveling the ground, sweeping, and sprinkling water. Among them was a stone that they wished to lift and remove, yet despite exerting all their strength, they could not do so."

At that time, moved by compassion, I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness. Those Mallas soon saw me lift this great rock with my big toe, cast it into the air, catch it again with my hand, place it upon my right palm, blow it into fine dust, and then reassemble it once more.
He caused the haughty mind of that Malla to subside, and immediately expounded for him various essential teachings of the Dharma, leading them both to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son!

At that time, the Tathāgata did not actually lift this great stone into the air with his finger, nor did he place it back in his right palm, blow it into powder, and then reassemble it as it was before."
"Good son! You should know that this is the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which causes all these Mallas to see such a thing.
Furthermore, good son!"

To the south of this land of South India, there is a great city named Śobhāvatī. In that city, there was an elder named Luṣi, who served as a leader among the multitude and had already planted many roots of goodness under countless Buddhas of the past.
"Good son!
In that great city, all the people believed in and submitted to false paths, serving the Nirgranthas.

At that time, wishing to deliver that elder, I traveled from Rājagṛha to that city by foot; the distance between them was sixty-five *yojanas*, which I traversed on foot for the sake of transforming and delivering those people."
When those Nigaṇṭhas heard that I intended to go to the city of Śrāvastī, they immediately thought to themselves:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama arrives here, these people will surely abandon us and no longer provide for us; we shall be impoverished and destitute—how shall we sustain ourselves?"
The various Nirgranthas each dispersed and announced to the people of that city:
"The śramaṇa Gautama now intends to come here.

However, that śramaṇa has abandoned his parents to wander hither and thither; wherever he arrives, he causes the land's crops to fail and the people to suffer famine. Many die, and diseases and emaciation follow one another in succession, with no means of relief."
This wretched Gautama takes only evil beings, rākṣasas, and ghosts as his attendants.
When fatherless, motherless, and destitute people come to consult him, he accepts them as his disciples.
"Whatever you may teach and instruct is purely talk of emptiness; wherever one goes, there is never any peace or happiness.
Having heard this, the man was immediately seized with fear. He prostrated himself, bowing his head at the feet of the Nirgrantha, and said:
"Great Master!..."
"What plan should we now devise?
The Nirgrantha replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama is by nature fond of groves, flowing springs, and clear water; whatever such things exist outside [our domain], they should be destroyed."
"You all should now go forth together out of the city; wherever there are trees, cut them down until none remain.
As for the flowing springs, wells, and ponds, fill them entirely with excrement and corpses."
"Shut the city gates firmly; each of you must prepare your weapons and provide defense from behind the walls, diligently securing your own positions.
Should they come, do not allow them to advance; if they do not advance, you shall remain safe and secure."
"We too shall employ various stratagems to cause that Gautama to turn back on his path.
Having heard these words, the people gave their respectful assent and set to work: they cut down trees, defiled the waters, adorned themselves with weapons, and fortified their defenses.
“Good son! At that time, having arrived at that city, I saw no trees or groves at all; I saw only people arrayed with weapons, defending themselves against the walls.”

Having seen this, he immediately gave rise to compassion and directed a mind of loving-kindness toward them; all the trees grew back as they were before, and furthermore, countless other trees sprouted forth beyond measure.
The rivers, ponds, wells, and springs became pure, their waters filling them to the brim like blue lapis lazuli, while various flowers bloomed, covering their surfaces.
He transformed the city walls into dark-blue lapis lazuli, so that the people within the city were able to see both me and the great assembly with complete clarity.
The gates opened of their own accord, and none were able to restrain them; the formidable weapons they had prepared transformed into various flowers.
With the elder Lu-zhi as their leader, he and his people followed one another together and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
I then expounded for them various essential teachings of the Dharma, causing all those people to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son!

At that time, I did not actually manifest various kinds of trees, pure flowing waters, and rivers and ponds filled to the brim; nor did I transform my original city into dark-blue lapis lazuli so that the people there could see me clearly through it; nor did I open the city gates and turn their weapons into flowers.
"Good son! You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which enables those people to see such things.
Furthermore, good son!"
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin woman of the Vāsiṣṭha clan who had an only son whom she loved very dearly; he fell ill and passed away.

At that time, the woman’s heart was pierced by the poison of grief; she became deranged and lost her senses, wandering through the four crossroads naked and shameless, wailing until her voice failed, crying out:
"My son, my son! Where have you gone?"
"She traveled throughout the city and its suburbs without ever becoming weary.
Yet this woman had already planted many roots of merit under previous Buddhas,
O son of good family!"
I gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward this woman.
At that moment, the woman saw me and immediately conceived the thought that I was her son; she regained her original mind, came forward to embrace my body, and kissed my mouth.
At that time, I immediately told my attendant Ānanda:
"You may take this robe and give it to this woman.
Once the robe had been given, I then expounded for her various essential points of the Dharma.
Upon hearing the Dharma, this woman was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and she gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son! At that time, I was truly not her son, she was not my mother, nor was there any embracing."
"Good son! You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which causes that woman to see such things.
Furthermore, good son!"
In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a laywoman named Mahāśraddhā who had already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past.
During the ninety-day summer retreat, this upāsikā invited the community of monks and offered them medicine.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu within the assembly who was afflicted with a grave illness.

A skilled physician examined him and determined that he required a medicinal meat; if he could obtain the meat, his illness would be cured, but if he could not obtain it, his life would likely not be preserved.
When the upāsikā heard these words of the physician, she immediately took gold and went throughout the marketplace, proclaiming:
"Who has meat for sale? I will buy it with gold; whoever has meat, I shall give them gold equal to its weight."
She searched throughout the city, but was unable to find any.
This upāsikā then took a knife and cut the flesh from her own thigh; she sliced it into pieces to make a stew, seasoned it with various kinds of incense, and sent it to the sick bhikṣu.
After the bhikṣu had taken it, his illness was immediately cured.
This upāsikā, suffering from the pain of her ulcer and unable to endure it, cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya!"

At that time, I was in the city of Śrāvastī; hearing her voice, I conceived a heart of great compassion toward that woman. She soon saw me, and I took excellent medicine and applied it to her wound, whereupon it healed and returned to its original state.
I then preached the Dharma to him in various ways; having heard the Dharma, he rejoiced and resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son!
At that time, I did not actually go to the city of Vārāṇasī to take medicine and apply it to this upāsikā’s wound.
Good son, you should know that all of this was due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which caused that woman to see such a thing.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The evil man Devadatta was greedy and insatiable; because he consumed much clarified butter, his head and abdomen ached, and he suffered great agony that he could not endure, crying out these words:
'Namo Buddhāya, Namo Buddhāya.'"
At that time, I was residing in the city of Ujjayinī; hearing his voice, I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Thereupon, Devadatta soon saw me, went to where I was, rubbed my head and belly with his hands, and gave me salted broth to drink. Having drunk it, I was restored to health.
"Good son!
I truly did not go to Devadatta’s place to stroke his head and belly or give him medicinal broth to drink.
Good son!"
"You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which caused Devadatta to see such things.
Furthermore, noble son,
in the kingdom of Kośala there were five hundred bandits who, in their gangs, committed robberies and wrought great harm."
King Prasenajit, troubled by their lawlessness and violence, dispatched troops to search for and capture them. Once apprehended, he gouged out their eyes and cast them beneath a dark, dense forest.
These bandits had previously planted many roots of virtue under former Buddhas; now that they had lost their sight and were undergoing great suffering, they each cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya! We have no protector or refuge now."
He wept and wailed aloud.

At that time, I was residing at the Jeta Grove Monastery; hearing his cries, I immediately gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness. Then, a cool breeze blew various medicinal herbs from Mount Gandhamādana, filling his eye sockets, whereupon he immediately regained his sight, no different from how it had been before.
The bandits opened their eyes and immediately saw the Tathāgata standing before them, preaching the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, they gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son!
At that time, I did not actually become the wind that blew the various fragrant medicines from Mount Gandhamādana; rather, I stood before that person and preached the Dharma for him."
"Good son! You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which causes those bandits to see such things.
Furthermore, good son!"
Because of his folly, Prince Vaidūrya deposed his father the king and established himself as ruler.

Recalling his former enmity, he slaughtered many members of the Śākya clan; he seized twelve thousand Śākya maidens, cut off their ears and noses, severed their hands and feet, and cast them into pits and ditches.
At that time, the women, suffering physical pain and distress, spoke these words:
"Namo Buddhāya, Namo Buddhāya! We now have no one to protect or save us."
They wailed and lamented even more bitterly.
These women had already planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas; at that time, while I was in the Bamboo Grove, I heard their voices and immediately gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness.

At that time, when the women saw me arrive in the city of Kapilavastu, they washed my wounds with water and applied medicinal ointments to them; my pain was immediately relieved, and my ears, nose, hands, and feet were restored to their original state.

At that time, I briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, causing them all to resolve together upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They then went before the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and left the household life to receive full ordination.
"Good son!
At that time, the Tathāgata did not actually go to the city of Kapilavastu to wash the wound with water, apply medicine, and alleviate the pain.
Good son!"

You should know that all these things are due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which enabled that woman to attain such matters; her heart of compassion and joy was likewise so. Good son!
For this reason, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it is truly real and not false.

Good son! That which is immeasurable is inconceivable; the conduct of Bodhisattvas is inconceivable, the conduct of all Buddhas is also inconceivable, and this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise inconceivable.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, they attain the stage of being exceedingly fond of all beings as if they were an only child. Good son!"
Why is this stage called "Supreme Affection" and also named "Only Son"? Good son!
For example, when parents see their child in safety and well-being, their hearts are filled with great joy.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this stage, it is likewise; they regard all sentient beings as their only child, and seeing those who cultivate goodness, they give rise to great joy. For this reason, this stage is named "Supreme Affection" (Sudurjayā).
"Good son! It is like parents who, seeing their child afflicted by illness, feel mental anguish and are consumed by compassion and grief, never for a moment abandoning them.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, it is likewise: seeing all sentient beings tormented by the diseases of affliction, they give rise to sorrow and anxiety, cherishing them as if they were their own children, such that blood flows from every pore of their bodies. For this reason, this stage is named 'The Only Son'."
Good son!

It is like a person in his childhood who picks up clods of earth, excrement, tiles, stones, dry bones, or wooden branches and places them in his mouth; when his parents see this, fearing it will cause him harm, they grasp his head with their left hand and pry the object out with their right hand.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, it is likewise so: seeing that the Dharma-body of sentient beings has not yet increased, or that they perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, the Bodhisattva, having seen this, uses the hand of wisdom to pull them out and rescue them. Not wishing for them to wander through birth and death and undergo various sufferings and afflictions, this stage is therefore also named "The Only Son."
"Good son! It is like parents whose beloved child has passed away; the parents are filled with grief and distress, vowing to end their lives together with him.
So it is with the Bodhisattva: seeing an icchantika fall into hell, he likewise vows to be born in that same hell along with them."

Why is this? If such an icchantika experiences suffering and gives rise to even a single thought of repentance, I shall immediately expound various dharmas for them, enabling them to produce a single thought of wholesome roots.
For this reason, this stage is further named "The Only Son. Good son!
It is like parents who have only one son; whether that son is sleeping or awake, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, their minds are constantly mindful of him.
If there is any transgression, one should entice and admonish them with kind words rather than inflicting harm upon them.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: seeing all sentient beings—whether they have fallen into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, or are among humans or devas—creating good or evil karma, he constantly keeps them in mind and never abandons them.
"If one commits various evils, yet never gives rise to anger or retaliates with evil in response, for this reason this stage is further named 'The Only Son.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, his words are profound and secret; with my limited wisdom now, how could I possibly understand them?

If bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of regarding all beings as an only son can act in such a manner, why did the Tathāgata, in the past when he was practicing the bodhisattva path as a king, take the lives of so many brahmins?
If one has attained this stage, one ought to protect and mindfully attend to it.
If one has not attained it, by what causes and conditions does one avoid falling into hell?
If you regard all sentient beings with equal vision, perceiving them as your own son Rāhula, for what reason did you again speak such words to Devadatta?
"This foolish man has no shame; he eats the spittle and saliva of others.
Upon hearing this, he gave rise to resentment and malice, conceiving unwholesome thoughts and shedding the blood of the Buddha.
"After Devadatta had committed this evil deed, the Tathāgata further prophesied that he would fall into hell and undergo punishment for one kalpa.
World-Honored One,
how is it that such words do not contradict the meaning?"

“World-Honored One! Subhūti dwells in the realm of empty space; whenever he wishes to enter a city to seek food and drink by begging, he must first observe the people. If there is anyone who harbors feelings of resentment or jealousy toward him, he stops and does not proceed. Even to the point of extreme hunger, he still does not go begging. Why is this?”
Subhūti constantly reflects:

"I recall that in the past, at the site of a field of merit, I gave rise to a single evil thought; by reason of this cause and condition, I fell into the great hells and underwent various sufferings."
"I would rather starve and go without food all day than cause him to harbor resentment toward me and fall into hell to suffer affliction.
He further thought:
"If there are sentient beings who resent my standing, I shall remain seated upright all day without rising."
"If there are sentient beings who take offense at my sitting, I shall remain standing for the entire day without moving from my place; it shall be the same whether I am walking or lying down.
Subhūti, if even he gives rise to such a thought out of a desire to protect sentient beings, how much more so should a bodhisattva?

“If a bodhisattva has attained the stage of the only child, for what reason does the Tathāgata utter such harsh words as to cause all sentient beings to give rise to grave and evil thoughts? “Good son!
You should not now raise such an objection, saying that the Buddha-Tathāgata acts as a causal condition for the afflictions of all sentient beings. Good son!
Even if a mosquito were able to exhaust the waters of the ocean, the Tathāgata would never act as a causal condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.

Good son! Suppose the entire great earth were entirely non-material; suppose water had the characteristic of solidity, fire had the characteristic of coldness, and wind had the characteristic of remaining stationary;
and suppose the Three Jewels, the Buddha-nature, and even empty space were to take on the characteristic of impermanence.
The Tathāgata never acts as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings. Good son!

Even if one were to commit the four grave offenses, be an icchantika, or slander the true Dharma, such a person might, in their present body, attain the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics; yet the Tathāgata never acts as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
"Good son!
Even if śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others were permanent and unchanging, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings."
"Good son!

Even if bodhisattvas of the ten stages were to commit the four grave offenses, become icchantikas, or slander the true Dharma, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for their afflictions."
"Good son!

Even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to lose their Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata were ultimately to enter parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings."
"Good son!

Even if one could cast a lasso to bind the wind, with teeth break iron, or with claws shatter Mount Sumeru, the Tathāgata will never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings."

It would be better to dwell in the same place as a venomous snake, to thrust both hands into the mouth of a starving lion, or to bathe one's body with charcoal from a *khadira* tree; one should not utter words that cause the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, to become a condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata truly is able to sever the afflictions for sentient beings; he never acts as a cause for those afflictions. Good son!"
"As you have said, that the Tathāgata killed a brāhmaṇa in the past;
O son of good family!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not intentionally kill even an ant, much less a brāhmaṇa."
Bodhisattvas constantly employ various skillful means to bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings. Good son!
To give food is to bestow life; when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they constantly bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
"Good son!

By practicing the precept of non-killing, one attains a long life. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), he bestows immeasurable life upon all sentient beings."

"Good son! By being cautious with one's speech and remaining free from transgression, one attains a long life. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he constantly exhorts sentient beings not to give rise to thoughts of enmity; he attributes rectitude to others and takes the crookedness upon himself. By being free from contention and dispute, one attains a long life. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience, he bestows immeasurable life upon sentient beings."
"Good son!

By diligently cultivating wholesome deeds, one attains a long life. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the *vīrya-pāramitā*, he constantly exhorts sentient beings to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas;
once these beings have so practiced, they attain immeasurable lifespan."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the *vīrya-pāramitā*, they have already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
Son of good family!

Those who cultivate the gathering of the mind attain long life; when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, they exhort all sentient beings to cultivate a mind of equanimity. Once sentient beings have practiced this, they attain long life. Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, they have already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
"Good son!

Those who are not negligent regarding all wholesome dharmas obtain a long life. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he exhorts all sentient beings not to be negligent regarding all wholesome dharmas. Having practiced thus, those beings obtain a long life by reason of these causes and conditions. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he has already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings."
"Good son! For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva never takes the life of any sentient being. Good son!"
"Regarding what you asked just now— whether one attains this stage when killing a brahmin—
Good Man, at that time I had already attained it."
Because of his affectionate concern, he severed the life-force [of the child], yet it was not out of an evil mind.

Good son! It is like parents who have only one son; they love him most deeply. If he violates the laws of the state, the parents, out of fear, may either banish him or kill him. Although they banish or kill him, they harbor no evil intent.

It is likewise for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who seeks to protect the true Dharma: if there are sentient beings who slander the Mahāyāna, they shall whip and beat them, subjecting them to harsh punishment, or even deprive them of life, desiring to cause them to reform their past ways and practice wholesome dharmas.
A bodhisattva should constantly reflect in this way:
"By what causes and conditions can I cause sentient beings to give rise to faith?
I must employ every appropriate means to accomplish this for them."
After those brahmins passed away, they were reborn in the Avīci Hell, where they necessarily experienced three thoughts:
first, they thought to themselves,
"From what place have I come to be born here?"
He immediately knew for himself that he had come from the human realm.
Second, he thought to himself: "Where have I been born now?"
He then immediately realizes for himself that this is the Avīci Hell.
Third, he reflects to himself:
"By what karmic conditions have I come to be born here?"

He immediately realized that he had slandered the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras and lacked faith in the principle of dependent origination; consequently, he had been executed by the sovereign of the land and was reborn here.

Having reflected on this matter, he immediately conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; at that very moment his life ended, and he was reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhi, where his lifespan was a full ten kalpas.
"Good son!
For this reason, I have granted this person a lifespan of ten kalpas in the past; how, then, can this be called killing?
Good son!"
If someone digs the earth, cuts grass, hews trees, dismembers corpses, reviles others, or lashes them with whips—by reason of such karmic conditions, would they fall into hell?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I ought to fall into hell.”
Why is this? As the Buddha once taught the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas:
"O bhikṣus, do not give rise to evil thoughts toward other withered trees."
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings fall into hell due to their evil minds.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said; you should receive and uphold it well.
Son of good family!
If one were to fall into hell due to an evil mind, the Bodhisattva at that time truly has no evil mind.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of compassion and the intent to benefit all sentient beings, even down to the smallest insects and ants.

Why is this? Because they skillfully understand the various expedient means of causes and conditions; by the power of these expedients, they desire to cause sentient beings to plant all roots of goodness. Good son!
For this reason, at that time, I employed skillful means to take his life, yet it was not out of an evil intent.
Good son! According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, even if one kills ants until they fill ten carts, there is no karmic retribution for sin.

If one kills mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, cats, wildcats, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, various evil insects and beasts, and other creatures capable of harming sentient beings— filling ten carts with such victims— or if one takes the lives of ghosts,
spirits, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, kālas, pūtanas, and various spirits such as those who are insane or emaciated, who cause affliction and harm to sentient beings,
there is no retribution for sin; however, if one kills an evil person, then there is retribution for sin.
If, after killing, one does not repent, one will fall into the realm of hungry ghosts;
however, if one can perform repentance and abstain from food for three days, that transgression will be extinguished without remainder.
If one kills one’s preceptor, harms one’s parents, a woman, or an ox, one shall remain in hell for countless thousands of years.
Son of good family!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that there are three kinds of killing: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
The inferior [beings] range from ants to all animals, with the sole exception of those born as Bodhisattvas through intentional manifestation.
Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by reason of his vows, manifests the acceptance of birth as an animal, this is called "inferior killing."
Due to the causes and conditions of killing as described below, one falls into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, fully experiencing the lower forms of suffering. Why is this?
Because these various animals possess even slight roots of goodness, the killer consequently undergoes the full retribution for their crime; this is called "inferior killing."

Regarding "middling killing": from ordinary worldlings up to those who have attained the stage of *anāgāmin* is what is called "middling. Because of these karmic causes, one falls into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, where one fully undergoes middling suffering; this is called middling killing.

Regarding "superior killing": this refers to the killing of one's parents, up to and including Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas who are fixed in their destiny. This is called "superior. Because of these karmic causes and conditions, one falls into the Avīci Great Hell and undergoes the full measure of superior suffering; thus it is called "superior killing."
"Good son!
If there is one who can kill an icchantika, they shall not fall into these three kinds of killing.
Good son!"
All those Brahmins and others are none other than icchantikas.

For example, just as there is no karmic retribution for digging the earth, cutting grass, felling trees, chopping up corpses, or reviling and whipping them, so too is it with killing an icchantika; there is no karmic retribution.
Why is this? Because these brahmins lack even the five faculties, such as faith; therefore, although they kill, they do not fall into hell. "Good son!
Regarding what you previously asked— why the Tathāgata reviled Devadatta as a foolish man who eats spittle—
you should not have asked such a question. Why is this?
Whatever words the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, utter are inconceivable. Good son!
There may be true speech that is beloved by the world, yet if it is untimely, contrary to the Dharma, and does not bring benefit, such words I would never speak.
"Good son!
Furthermore, there are those who say things that are coarse, false, untimely, and contrary to the Dharma—things which the hearer does not love and which cannot bring benefit; these I do not speak."
"Good son!

If there is speech that, though coarse and harsh, is true and not false, and which at that time and according to that principle can bring benefit to all sentient beings—I must speak it, even if hearing it brings no pleasure."
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the Worthy Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, know skillful means. Good son!

Once, while I was traveling through that wilderness, passing through villages and groves of trees, I stayed beneath one such forest. There was a spirit there named "Wilderness" (*Āṭavika*), who subsisted solely on flesh and blood, killing many sentient beings; furthermore, in that village, he would eat one person every day.
"Good son!
At that time, I extensively expounded the essential points of the Dharma for those spirits and deities;
however, they were violent, evil, foolish, and lacking wisdom, refusing to accept the teachings. I then manifested myself as a powerful spirit, shaking their palaces so that they could find no rest."
At that time, the ghost led his retinue out from his palace, intending to come and resist me.
Upon seeing me, the ghost immediately lost his wits; struck with terror, he fell to the ground, fainting and gasping for breath like one who is dead.
Out of compassion, I stroked his body with my hand.
He immediately rose back to a sitting position and spoke these words:
"How wonderful! Today I have regained my life."
"This great king of spirits possesses great majesty and virtue, and has a heart of compassion; may he pardon my transgressions.
Thus, he conceived a wholesome and faithful mind toward me.
I immediately restored my body to that of a Tathāgata and further expounded various essential teachings for him, causing that spirit to receive the precept against killing.
On that very day, in the village of Khāṇumata, there was an elder whose turn it was to die, and the villagers had already delivered him over to that spirit.
When the spirit-gods obtained it, they immediately gave it to me;
having accepted it, I then became a householder and established another name for myself, named the Householder Hand (Hatthaka).
At that time, the ghost addressed me, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I and my retinue subsist solely upon flesh and blood to sustain our lives."
"Now, because of these precepts, how shall I live? I then replied:
"From this day forward, I shall command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever the Buddha-dharma is practiced, they shall all provide you with food and drink."

"Good son! For these reasons, I have established this precept for the bhikṣus: from this day forward, you must always provide food to those wilderness spirits. If there are those who reside in monasteries and fail to provide such offerings, you should know that they are not my disciples; they are merely followers and kinsmen of the celestial Māras."
"Good son!
It is because the Tathāgata wishes to discipline sentient beings that he displays such various skillful means; it is not for the purpose of causing them to feel fear."
"Good son! I also struck the Dharma-protecting spirit with a piece of wood.
Furthermore, on one occasion, while on a mountain, I pushed the goat-headed spirit so that he fell down the mountainside."
Furthermore, he caused the tree-spirit to strike down the monkey-demon;
made the elephant Dhanapāla see five lions;
and terrified the Vajrapāṇi spirit with Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha.
He also pricked the body of the arrow-hair demon with a needle.

Although he acted in this way, he did not cause those spirits and demons to perish; rather, desiring to cause them to dwell securely in the True Dharma, he manifested these various kinds of skillful means.
"Good son!
At that time, I did not in fact revile Devadatta;

nor was Devadatta foolish enough to eat human spittle and snot, nor was he born into the evil realms to suffer the retribution of Avīci Hell for one kalpa. He did not cause a schism in the Saṃgha or shed the blood of a Buddha, nor did he commit the four grave offenses or slander the Mahāyāna sūtras of the True Dharma. He was not an icchantika, nor was he a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."
"Good son!
Devadatta is truly not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; he is known and seen only by the Buddhas. Good son!"
Therefore, you should not now raise the objection: "For what reason did the Tathāgata scold and revile Devadatta?
You should not give rise to such a web of doubt regarding the sphere of all Buddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is like sugarcane; when boiled repeatedly, it yields various flavors.”

I am likewise; having heard from the Buddha many times, I have gained much of the flavor of the Dharma—namely, the flavor of renunciation, the flavor of detachment from desire, the flavor of tranquility, and the flavor of the Path.
World-Honored One!

It is like genuine gold, which, when repeatedly heated, beaten, melted, and refined, becomes increasingly bright and pure, malleable and soft, with a subtle and exquisite luster; its value is difficult to measure, and only then is it held in high esteem as a treasure by humans and devas.
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is likewise; if one consults and inquires with earnestness, one shall hear and see the most profound meaning, enabling those who practice deeply to receive, uphold, and cultivate it. Thereafter, immeasurable sentient beings will resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and you will become the object of veneration for all devas and humans, receiving their respect and offerings.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva desires to benefit all sentient beings that he inquires of the Tathāgata regarding such profound meanings.”
"Good son!

For this reason, in accordance with your intention, I shall expound for you the profound and secret Dharma of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya, namely, the stage known as 'Extreme Affection like that for an Only Son.'"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If bodhisattvas cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy and thereby attain the Stage of the Only Son, when they cultivate the mind of equanimity, what stage do they further attain?”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
You well know the proper time; when you perceive that I wish to speak, you then inquire.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the mind of equanimity (upekṣā), they abide in the stage of emptiness and equality, just like Subhūti.
Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the stage of the equality of emptiness, they do not perceive fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, children, kinsmen, friends, or those who are hateful or neutral; they do not even perceive the aggregates, elements, sense bases, sentient beings, or the life-span.
Good son! It is like space, which has no father, mother, brothers, or wife, and even lacks sentient beings or a life span.
All phenomena are likewise thus: they have no father or mother, nor even a life span.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive all phenomena, they are likewise thus; their minds are equanimous, like that empty space.
"Why is this? Because they are well able to cultivate all dharmas of emptiness.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘emptiness’? “Good son!

Emptiness refers to what are called internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate internal emptiness?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that internal phenomena are empty; this internal emptiness of phenomena means there is no father, mother, enemy, friend, or neutral person; no sentient beings, life-span, permanence, bliss, self, or purity; and no Tathāgata, Dharma, Saṅgha, or any material possessions.
Within these internal dharmas, although there is Buddha-nature, this Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
Why is this? Because Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and without change; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation of internal emptiness.
External emptiness is likewise; there are no internal dharmas.
Internal-and-external emptiness is likewise as well. Good son!
Only the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the Buddha-nature do not fall within the two kinds of emptiness. Why is this?
Because these four dharmas are eternal, blissful, self, and pure; therefore, these four dharmas are not called empty.
This is called the emptiness of both the internal and external. Good son!

As for the emptiness of the conditioned, all conditioned phenomena are entirely empty; that is to say: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth regarding sentient beings, life-span, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Within this, the Buddha-nature is not a conditioned phenomenon; therefore, the Buddha-nature is not empty of being a conditioned phenomenon.
This is called the emptiness of the conditioned. Good son!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

These unconditioned dharmas are all empty, namely: impermanence, suffering, impurity, non-self, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*); the marks of a sentient being and of life; the conditioned; that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); internal dharmas; and external dharmas.
Among the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the four dharmas beginning with the Buddha are neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Because their nature is wholesome, they are not unconditioned; because their nature is eternally abiding, they are not conditioned.
This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of that which has no beginning (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*)?
It is when this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that saṃsāra is without beginning and is entirely empty and quiescent.

That which is called emptiness refers to the fact that permanence, bliss, self, and purity are all entirely empty and quiescent, without change or alteration. Sentient beings, life-span, the Three Jewels, Buddha-nature, and unconditioned dharmas—this is what is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of the beginningless.
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the emptiness of nature?

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as being empty by their very nature—namely, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the permanent and the impermanent; suffering and pleasure; purity and impurity; the self and the non-self. By contemplating all such dharmas in this way, they do not perceive an inherent nature; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of nature.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of non-existence?
It is like a person who has no son saying that his house is empty; he ultimately contemplates emptiness, for there is no one toward whom he feels affection.
Foolish people say that all directions are empty;
impoverished people say that everything is empty.
Such calculations as these result in either [the view] of emptiness or of non-emptiness.

When the Bodhisattva contemplates, all things are empty like those of a poor person; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of non-existence (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
How does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)?
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the ultimate truth (paramārtha), this eye, at the time of its arising, comes from nowhere; and at the time of its cessation, it goes nowhere.
Originally non-existent, it now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence."
When one investigates its actual nature, there is no eye and no master.
Just as the eye has no inherent nature, so it is with all dharmas.
What is called "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (paramārtha-śūnyatā)?

There is karma and there is its retribution, yet no agent is perceived; such a dharma of emptiness is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā). This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplating the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of emptiness?
This emptiness within emptiness is precisely the place where śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others are lost and submerged.
Good son! To say "this exists" or "this does not exist" is called the emptiness of emptiness;
to say "this is this" or "this is not this" is called the emptiness of emptiness.
Good son! Even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages only penetrate a small portion within this, like a mere mote of dust;
how much less so others? Good son!

This emptiness of emptiness is also not the same as the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness attained by śrāvakas; this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of emptiness. Good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate great emptiness?
Good son, that which is called "great emptiness" refers to the prajñāpāramitā; this is termed great emptiness.
“Good son!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains such a gate of emptiness, they then abide on the ground that is equal to space. Good son!”

Now, as I am expounding these various meanings of emptiness within this great assembly, ten times the number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal to the sands of the Ganges immediately attain the stage of the ground of space.
"Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they encounter no obstruction, bondage, or attachment regarding any phenomena; their mind is free from confusion and distress. For this reason, it is called the Stage Equal to Space."
"Good son! For example,
just as space does not give rise to greedy attachment toward pleasant forms,
nor does it give rise to anger toward unpleasant forms."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, it is likewise so: toward beautiful or ugly forms, their mind is free from greed or anger. Good son!
Just as space is vast, without opposition, and capable of containing all phenomena, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage:
they are vast, without opposition, and capable of containing all phenomena. For this reason, it is further named the "Stage Equal to Space."

“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they both see and know all dharmas—whether their activity or their object, their nature or their characteristic, their cause or their condition, the minds of sentient beings, their faculties, their meditative concentrations, or their vehicles; whether it be spiritual friends, the observance of precepts, or acts of giving—they know and see all such dharmas.”
Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he knows but does not see.
What is meant by "knowing"?

They know the practices of self-starvation, throwing themselves into abysses, leaping into fire, casting themselves from high cliffs, constantly standing on one foot, scorching the body with the five fires, and constantly lying upon ashes, soil, thorn-studded rafters, leaves, weeds, or cow dung; they wear coarse hempen garments, discarded rags from cemeteries, woolen blankets, *kambala* cloths, deerskins, or clothes made of straw; and they consume vegetables, grass, lotus roots, oil-cakes, cow dung, roots, and fruits.
If one goes on almsround, one should limit oneself to a single household; if the host says there is nothing, one should immediately depart, and even if they call out again, one must never look back.

They abstain from salt, meat, and the five products of the cow; they constantly drink grain-ash water and boiling water; they observe the vows of the cow, the dog, the chicken, and the pheasant; they smear their bodies with ash and maintain long hair as their distinguishing marks; and when performing sacrifices with sheep, they first recite incantations and then slaughter them.
In the fourth month, he served fire; for seven days, he practiced breath-control (vāyu-sevana); and with hundreds of thousands of billions of flowers, he made offerings to the various devas.
All his desires and aspirations were thereby fulfilled.
It is impossible that such dharmas as these could serve as causes for unsurpassed liberation;
this is what is called "knowing.
What is meant by "not seeing"?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive even a single person who, by practicing such dharmas, attains right liberation; this is called "non-perception.
Furthermore, son of good family:
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva both sees and knows.
What is meant by "seeing"?
To see that sentient beings who practice these false dharmas will certainly fall into hell—this is called seeing.
What is meant by "knowledge"?

It is knowing that when sentient beings emerge from the hells and are born among humans, if they are able to practice the *dānapāramitā* and so forth until they are fully endowed with all the *pāramitās*, these persons will certainly attain entry into right liberation; this is called knowledge.
Furthermore, good son,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva also possesses both seeing and knowing.
What is meant by "seeing"?
To perceive permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure, purity and impurity, self and non-self—this is called "viewing.
What is meant by "knowing"?

It is to know that all Tathāgatas certainly do not enter final nirvāṇa; to know that the body of a Tathāgata is adamantine and indestructible, not a body produced by afflictions, nor a foul, putrid, or decaying body; and furthermore, to be able to know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—this is called "knowing."
Furthermore, good son,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also possess both knowledge and vision.
What is meant by "knowledge"?
He knows that these sentient beings have accomplished faith; he knows that these sentient beings seek the Mahāyāna;
he knows who is following the current, who is going against the current, who is dwelling correctly, and he knows which sentient beings have already reached the other shore.

Those who flow with the current are ordinary worldlings; those who flow against the current range from stream-enterers up to pratyekabuddhas; those who dwell correctly are the bodhisattvas and others; and those who have reached the other shore are the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
This is called knowledge.
What is meant by vision?

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, cultivates the mind of pure conduct and, with the purified divine eye, sees all sentient beings who, having committed unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind—the three karmas—fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
He saw that those sentient beings who cultivate wholesome deeds will, at the end of their lives, be reborn among gods or humans.

He saw that some sentient beings pass from darkness into darkness; some sentient beings pass from darkness into light; some sentient beings pass from light into darkness; and some sentient beings pass from light into light.
This is called "seeing.
Furthermore, son of good family,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also possess both knowing and seeing.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that sentient beings cultivate their bodies, cultivate their precepts, cultivate their minds, and cultivate their wisdom.
Although such a person has accomplished evil karma in this present life— perhaps due to greed, hatred, or delusion— and this karma ought necessarily to result in retribution in hell,

because they have directly cultivated their body, cultivated their precepts, cultivated their mind, and cultivated their wisdom, they experience [the retribution] lightly in the present life and do not fall into hell.
What kind of karma can bring about retribution in the present life?
One confesses and discloses all evils; having repented, one dares not commit them again.

Because of the perfection of shame and remorse, because of making offerings to the Triple Gem, and because of constant self-reproach, such a person, by reason of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma, does not fall into hell but receives retribution in the present life.

That is to say, they experience such light retributions in the present life as headaches, eye pain, abdominal pain, back pain, untimely death, being rebuked and insulted, being flogged with whips or canes, being imprisoned, and suffering from hunger and distress.
This is called "knowledge.
What is meant by "vision"?

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees such a person who is unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; having committed even a slight evil deed, by reason of this karma, they must undergo retribution in the present life.

If this person commits even slight evil and is unable to repent, does not reproach themselves, gives rise to no sense of shame or remorse, and feels no fear, their karma will increase, and they shall receive retribution in hell.
This is called "seeing.
Furthermore, there is knowing without seeing.
What is knowing without seeing?
To know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet because it is shrouded and obscured by various afflictions they are unable to see it—this is called "knowing but not seeing."

Furthermore, there are those who know yet see little, such as Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), who equally know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet their vision is not clear, like what is seen indistinctly in the darkness of night.
Furthermore, there is that which is both seen and known, namely the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, who both see and know.

Furthermore, there is that which is both seen and known, yet not seen and not known. Regarding that which is both seen and known: it refers to worldly letters, speech, men and women, vehicles, jars and basins, houses, cities and towns, clothing, food and drink, mountains, rivers, gardens and groves, as well as sentient beings and their lifespans; these are called "both known and seen."
What is meant by "not seeing and not knowing"?
The subtle and esoteric words of the Sages contain no such things as male or female, nor even gardens and groves; this is called "not seeing and not knowing."

Furthermore, there is that which is known but not seen: knowing what is bestowed as a gift, knowing the place of offering, knowing the recipient, and knowing the retribution of cause and effect—this is called "knowing."
What is meant by "not seeing"?
Not seeing the gift, the recipient who receives the offering, and the karmic fruit—this is called "not seeing.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that there are eight kinds [of vision], which are precisely what is known by the five eyes of the Tathāgata.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 16. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 17.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight on the Brahma-faring, Part Three.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know in this way, what benefit will they obtain?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to know in this way, they attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge:

unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and unimpededness regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Non-obstruction regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) means knowing all phenomena as well as their names.

Non-obstruction regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) means knowing all the meanings possessed by all phenomena, and being able to establish meanings in accordance with the names assigned to those phenomena.

Unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) refers to the treatises on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), the treatises on correct pronunciation (*svara-śāstra*), the treatises on grammar (*chandas-śāstra*), and the treatises on worldly debate (*loka-vāda*).

Unimpeded readiness in speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) means that whatever a bodhisattva mahāsattva expounds is without obstruction, cannot be shaken, is free from fear or hesitation, and is difficult to overcome.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to see and know in such a way that he immediately attains these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
Furthermore, good son!"
Regarding the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): the bodhisattva-mahāsattva universally knows the teachings of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.

Regarding the unimpededness of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*): although there are three vehicles, he knows they ultimately converge into one, and never maintains that they possess any characteristics of difference.
Regarding unimpeded eloquence: within a single dharma, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can produce various names and speak of them inexhaustibly throughout immeasurable kalpas;
it is impossible for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to make such a discourse.

Regarding the unimpeded eloquence of joy in teaching (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): for immeasurable eons, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; whether by way of names or meanings, these various distinct explanations are inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Regarding the unimpededness of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows all dharmas, he does not grasp or cling to them.
Regarding the unimpededness of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows all meanings, he likewise does not cling to them."
Regarding unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows names and designations, he does not grasp at them.
Regarding unimpeded readiness in speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that such readiness in speech is supreme, he likewise does not become attached to it.
"Why is this? Good son, one who grasps and clings is not called a bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one does not grasp or cling, then one does not know dharmas;
if one knows dharmas, that is grasping and clinging.”
“If one knows without attachment, then there is nothing known.
Why then does the Tathāgata say that he knows the Dharma without grasping or attachment?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! One who harbors grasping and attachment is not said to be unimpeded;
one who has nothing to grasp or attach to is what is called unimpeded.”
Good son! For this reason, among all bodhisattvas, those who possess attachment have no unimpededness;
if they lack unimpededness, they are not called bodhisattvas—one should know that such persons are termed ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
For what reason is grasping and attachment called the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
All ordinary persons grasp at form (*rūpa*) and so forth, up to and including consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because they grasp at form, a mind of craving arises.
Because they give rise to a mind of greed, they are bound by form, and so on, up to being bound by consciousness;

because they are thus bound, they cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and all the great sufferings of affliction. For this reason, those who grasp at names are called worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
For this reason, all ordinary beings lack the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge. Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva has, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, known and seen the characteristics of dharmas; because of this knowledge and vision, he understands their meaning.
Because they perceive the characteristics of phenomena and understand their meaning, they do not give rise to attachment toward form, and it is likewise for everything up to consciousness;
because they do not cling, the bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of craving toward form, nor does he give rise to craving toward anything up to consciousness;
because there is no craving, he is not bound by form, nor is he bound by anything up to consciousness.
Because they are unbound, they attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, great suffering, and all afflictions.
For this reason, all Bodhisattvas attain the four kinds of unhindered knowledge.
"Good son!

For this reason, among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I have taught for my disciples that those who are bound by attachment are said to be fettered by Māra, whereas those who do not attach themselves are liberated from the fetters of Māra."
For example, in the world, a person who has committed an offense is bound by the king, whereas a person who is innocent the king cannot bind.
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: those who possess attachment are bound by Māra, while those who are without attachment Māra cannot bind.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is without attachment.
Furthermore, noble son,
regarding the non-obstruction of phenomena, the bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully knows the retention of syllables and does not forget them.
That which is called "upholding" is like the earth, like a mountain, like the eye, like a cloud, like a person, and like a mother; all dharmas are likewise so.

Regarding the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): although a bodhisattva knows the names of all phenomena, they do not yet know their meanings. Upon attaining the unimpededness of meaning, they then come to know the meanings.
How does one know the meanings?
As for "that which sustains like the earth," it is because the earth universally sustains all sentient beings and non-sentient things; for this reason, the earth is called "sustainer. Good son!
Regarding "holding like a mountain," the bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects:
"For what reason is it called a 'mountain' and designated as 'holding'?
A mountain can support the earth, preventing it from tilting or shaking; therefore, it is called 'holding'."
For what reason is the eye further called "the holder"?
Because the eye can hold light, it is named "the holder.
For what reason is the cloud further called "the holder"?
Clouds are called "dragon-breath" (lung-ch'i); because dragon-breath sustains water, they are named "cloud-sustainers" (yun-chi).
For what reason, then, are human beings also called "sustainers"?
Because humans can sustain both the Dharma and that which is non-Dharma, they are named "human-sustainers."
For what reason is a mother further called "the sustainer"?
Because the mother can sustain her child, she is named the "sustainer.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s knowledge of the names, phrases, and meanings of all dharmas is also like this.

Regarding unimpeded eloquence: by means of various expressions, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva expounds a single meaning, yet there is no fixed meaning, just as with names such as "man" and "woman," "house," "vehicle," or "sentient being."
Why is it without meaning? Good son!
That which is "meaning" is the realm of bodhisattvas and buddhas; that which is "words" is the realm of ordinary beings.
Because of knowing the meaning, one attains unimpededness in expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding unimpededness in eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows both expression and meaning, he can expound upon expressions and meanings for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas without exhaustion; this is called unimpededness in eloquence.

“Good son! For immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because of this practice, he knows all phenomena without obstruction.”
Furthermore, because he cultivated the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he attained unimpededness in meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Also, because he practiced the *vyākaraṇa* treatises for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he attained unimpededness in expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, because he has cultivated and expounded the treatises on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he has attained the unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). "Good son!
It is impossible for any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha to attain these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge."
"Good son!
Within the ninefold canon, I have spoken of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; yet, in truth, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess them."
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Those who are Pratyekabuddhas cultivate the dharma of quiescence and take pleasure in dwelling in solitude.

If, in transforming sentient beings, one merely manifests supernatural powers while remaining silent throughout the entire day without proclaiming anything, how can there be the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge?
For what reason does one remain silent and say nothing?

Pratyekabuddhas are unable to preach the Dharma to deliver others, enabling them to attain the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), or the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); nor can they enable them to attain the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, or Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; nor can they cause people to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Good son!

When Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, there are no ninefold scriptures in the world; therefore, Pratyekabuddhas lack the analytical knowledge of eloquence and the analytical knowledge of joyful exposition.
"Good son! Although those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle know all dharmas, they do not possess unimpeded mastery over them. Why is this?"

Non-obstruction regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) is defined as the knowledge of syllables. Although those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle know written characters, they lack non-obstruction regarding syllables. Why is this?
Because they do not know the two words "eternally abiding" (*nityasthita*); therefore, pratyekabuddhas do not attain non-obstruction regarding phenomena.
Although one knows the meaning, there is no obstruction regarding that which is without meaning.
One who truly knows the meaning knows that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; this meaning of Buddha-nature is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, those who are pratyekabuddhas do not attain unimpededness in meaning.
Therefore, pratyekabuddhas altogether lack the four types of unimpeded knowledge.
Why is it that śrāvakas also lack the four unimpeded knowledges?
Śrāvakas do not possess three kinds of skillful means.
What are these three?

First, they must be spoken to with gentle words before they will accept the Dharma; second, they must be spoken to with harsh words before they will be transformed; third, they are transformed neither by gentle nor by harsh words.
Because śrāvakas lack these three, they do not possess the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot ultimately know words or meanings; they lack the sovereign wisdom that knows objects of experience.

Lacking the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, they cannot ultimately cross the great river of the twelve links of dependent origination; they cannot skillfully discern the differences between the sharp and dull faculties of sentient beings; they have not yet permanently severed doubt regarding the two truths; they do not know the various mental states and objective spheres of sentient beings; and they cannot skillfully expound the emptiness of the ultimate truth. For these reasons, those of the Two Vehicles do not possess the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If among all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas there is none who possesses the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, why does the World-Honored One say that Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom?”
Is Mahāmaudgalyāyana foremost in supernatural powers?
Is Mahākauṣṭhila foremost in the four analytical knowledges?
If this were not so, why did the Tathāgata speak in such a manner?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

For example, the waters of the Ganges River are immeasurable; the waters of the Sindhu Great River are also immeasurable; the waters of the Vakṣu Great River are also immeasurable; the waters of the Sītā Great River are also immeasurable; the waters of Lake Anavatapta are also immeasurable; and the waters within the great ocean are also immeasurable.
In this way, although these various waters are equally immeasurable, their actual quantities are not the same;
so it is with the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, O son of good family!
To say that they are equal is impossible. Good son!
For the sake of ordinary beings, I have said that Mahākauṣṭhila’s four kinds of unimpeded knowledge are the most supreme; such is the meaning of what you have asked.
"Good son!
Among śrāvakas, some may attain one [of these], and some may attain two;
however, it is impossible for them to possess all four."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha previously stated in the ‘Chapter on the Holy Life,’ regarding the bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision that attains the four kinds of unimpededness: if the bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision are such that there is nothing to be attained, then there is also no mind that says, ‘there is nothing to be attained.’”
World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly has nothing to be attained.
If a bodhisattva were to have a mind that attains anything, they would not be a bodhisattva, but would be called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
"How is it that the Tathāgata says a bodhisattva has something attained?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
Excellent, excellent!
I was about to speak, yet you have asked again.
Well-born son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas truly have nothing to be attained; that which has nothing to be attained is called the four unhindered knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
Good son! For what reason is that which has nothing to be attained called "unhindered"?
If there is anything attained, it is called an obstruction; that which possesses obstructions is called the four perversions.
Son of good family!
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are free from the four perversions, they attain non-obstruction; therefore, Bodhisattvas are said to have "nothing to be attained."
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is non-attainment is called wisdom; because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have attained this wisdom, they are said to be 'without attainment. That which has attainment is called ignorance."
Because Bodhisattvas have forever severed the darkness of ignorance, they have nothing to be attained; therefore, Bodhisattvas are called "those who have nothing to be attained.
Furthermore, son of good family!

That which is non-apprehension is called Great Nirvāṇa. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in such Great Nirvāṇa, they do not perceive the intrinsic nature or characteristics of any phenomena; therefore, Bodhisattvas are said to be "without apprehension."

That which has something to be attained is called the twenty-five states of existence; the Bodhisattva eternally severs these twenty-five states of existence and attains Great Nirvana. For this reason, the Bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to be attained."
"Furthermore, good son!

That which is 'non-attainment' is called the Mahāyāna. Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not abide in any phenomena, they attain the Mahāyāna; for this reason, Bodhisattvas are said to be 'without attainment.'

That which involves attainment is called the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; because the Bodhisattva has eternally severed the paths of the two vehicles and attained the Buddha-way, the Bodhisattva is said to be "without attainment."
"Furthermore, good son!

That which is 'non-attainment' is called the Vaipulya Sūtras. Because Bodhisattvas read and recite such sūtras, they attain Great Nirvāṇa; for this reason, Bodhisattvas are said to be 'without attainment.'

Those who have something to attain are said to study the eleven divisions of the scriptures, which the bodhisattva does not cultivate; instead, he exclusively expounds the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras. For this reason, the bodhisattva is said to be "without attainment."
"Furthermore, good son!

That which is non-apprehensible is called 'space. That which has no substance in the world is called 'space. Because the Bodhisattva attains this Space Samādhi and perceives nothing, the Bodhisattva is therefore named 'one who has nothing to apprehend.'"
That which has something to be attained is called the wheel of birth and death; all ordinary beings revolve in birth and death, and therefore they have something perceived.
Bodhisattvas have forever severed all birth and death; for this reason, bodhisattvas are said to have nothing to be attained.
"Furthermore, good son!

That which the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no attainment of is called permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives the Buddha-nature, he attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity; for this reason, the Bodhisattva is said to have 'no attainment.'"

That which has something to be attained is called impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity. Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas sever this impermanence, lack of bliss, lack of self, and lack of purity, they are therefore called "those who have nothing to attain."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

That which is 'non-attainment' is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the emptiness of the ultimate truth, he perceives nothing at all; for this reason, the bodhisattva is said to be 'one who has no attainment.'"

That which has something to be attained is called the five views; because the bodhisattva has forever severed these five views, he attains the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā). For this reason, the bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to be attained."
"Furthermore, good son!

That which is 'non-attainment' is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he perceives nothing at all; for this reason, the Bodhisattva is said to be one who has non-attainment."

That which has something to be attained is called the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; because bodhisattvas have forever severed the enlightenment of the two vehicles, they are said to be "without attainment."
“Good son! That which you ask is unobtainable, and that which I speak is likewise unobtainable.
If there were anything obtainable, one would be a follower of Māra and not my disciple.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, when you preached for my sake regarding this bodhisattva’s non-attainment, immeasurable sentient beings severed their minds that cling to signs. For this reason, I venture to inquire about the meaning of non-attainment, so that these immeasurable sentient beings may leave the retinue of Māra and become disciples of the Buddha.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Previously, between the twin śāla trees, the Tathāgata spoke these verses for Cunda:”
“‘What existed originally is now non-existent; what was non-existent originally is now existent.
That a dharma exists throughout the three periods of time—this is impossible.
World-Honored One!”
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

For the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, I have spoken these words; for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, I have spoken these words; and for the sake of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, I have spoken these words.
It was not merely for Cunda alone that I spoke this verse.
At that time, as Mañjuśrī was about to question me, I knew his thoughts and spoke for him.
Once I had finished speaking, Mañjuśrī immediately attained understanding.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Among those such as Mañjuśrī, how many are there who are able to fully comprehend this meaning?”
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will further explain this in detail for the sake of the great assembly.
“Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now expound it for you once more.”
As for "originally existing," it means that in the past I originally possessed immeasurable afflictions; because of these afflictions, there was no Great Parinirvāṇa in the present.
As for "originally non-existent," it means that originally there was no Prajñāpāramitā; because there was no Prajñāpāramitā, all the fetters of affliction exist in the present.
If there be any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say that the Tathāgata has afflictions in the past, future, or present, such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son!

As for what is called 'originally existing,' it refers to my original body produced by the union of father and mother; therefore, in the present, there is no adamantine, subtle, and wondrous Dharma-body."
Regarding what is called "original non-existence": my own body originally lacked the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
because these thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics were originally non-existent, I currently possess four hundred and four ailments.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who says that the Tathāgata has illness or suffering in the past, future, or present, such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son!

That which is called 'originally existing' refers to my own original existence as impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and impure. Because it was impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and impure, there was no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the present.
As for the term "originally non-existent," it means that originally one does not see the Buddha-nature; because it is not seen, there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity.

Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, or humans, were any of them to claim that the Tathāgata—past, future, or present—is impermanent, without bliss, without self, or without purity, such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son!

That which is called 'originally existing' refers to the mind of an ordinary person who has originally practiced asceticism, thinking that they have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Because of this matter, they are currently unable to destroy the four māras."
