Regarding the statement "originally non-existent": originally I did not possess the six pāramitās; because I originally lacked the six pāramitās, I practiced with the mind of an ordinary person performing ascetic austerities, claiming thereby to have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or human who claims that the Tathāgata undergoes ascetic practices in the past, future, or present, such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son!

Regarding what is called 'originally existing': in the past, I originally possessed a body that consumed various foods; because I possessed a body that consumes food, I currently do not possess a boundless body."

Regarding the statement "originally non-existent," it means that originally the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment did not exist; because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment were absent, there currently exists this body sustained by mixed food.

If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say that the Tathāgata possesses a body sustained by mixed food in the past, future, or present, such a thing is impossible.

"Furthermore, good son, as for what is called 'originally existing,' I previously had a mind of attachment toward all dharmas; because of this matter, I currently lack the samādhi of ultimate emptiness."

As for the term "originally non-existent," it means that I originally lacked the true meaning of the Middle Way; because I lacked the true meaning of the Middle Way, I harbored a mind of attachment toward all phenomena.

If there be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say that the Tathāgata—in the past, future, or present—teaches that all dharmas possess marks of existence, such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son, as for what is called 'originally existing':

when I first attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there were śrāvaka disciples of dull faculties. Because there were śrāvaka disciples of dull faculties, I was unable to expound the reality of the One Vehicle."

Regarding the statement "originally non-existent": originally, there were no individuals of sharp faculties, such as Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, who is like an elephant king among men. Because there were no such individuals of sharp faculties as Kāśyapa and others, the Buddha revealed the three vehicles through appropriate skillful means.

If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who claims that the Tathāgata—whether in the past, future, or present—ever definitively expounds the Dharma of the three vehicles, such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son!

As for what is called 'originally existing,' I previously stated that three months hence I would enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees; for this reason, I am currently unable to expound the Mahāvaipulya sūtra, the Mahāparinirvāṇa."

As for the statement "originally non-existent," it means that in the past there were no such beings as the great bodhisattva Mañjuśrī; because they did not exist, it is said in the present that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or human being who claims that the Tathāgata’s past, future, or present is impermanent, such a thing is impossible.

“Good son! For the sake of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata, although he knows all dharmas, says that he does not know them; although he sees all dharmas, says that he does not see them. He speaks of dharmas with marks as being without marks, and speaks of dharmas without marks as having marks. That which is truly impermanent he says is permanent, and that which is truly permanent he says is impermanent; it is the same for self, bliss, and purity.”

The Dharma of the Three Vehicles is spoken of as the One Vehicle, and the Dharma of the One Vehicle is spoken of as three according to what is appropriate; the concise is explained extensively, and the extensive is explained concisely; the four grave offenses (*pārājika*) are spoken of as *sthūlātyaya*, and *sthūlātyaya* is spoken of as the four grave offenses; what is an offense is said to be no offense, and what is not an offense is said to be an offense; minor offenses are said to be grave, and grave offenses are said to be minor.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata clearly perceives the faculties of sentient beings.
O son of good family!
Although the Tathāgata speaks thus, he is ultimately free from falsehood.
Why is this? False speech is a transgression, and the Tathāgata has completely severed all transgressions; how, then, could there be false speech in him?
"Good son!

Although the Tathāgata has no false speech, if he knows that sentient beings will obtain the benefit of the Dharma through false discourse, he will preach it to them according to his appropriate skillful means."
Good son! All conventional truths, for the Tathāgata, are themselves the ultimate truth. Why is this?

For the sake of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), so as to enable sentient beings to attain the ultimate truth.
If sentient beings were not to attain such an ultimate truth, the Buddhas would never proclaim the conventional truth.
"Good son!
There are times when the Tathāgata expounds the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), yet sentient beings think the Buddha is speaking of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
there are times when he expounds the ultimate truth, yet sentient beings think the Buddha is speaking of the conventional truth."
This is the profound realm of all Buddhas, which is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Good son! Therefore, you should not have previously raised the objection that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have nothing to attain.
“Since Bodhisattvas constantly attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), how can it be difficult to say that there is nothing to be attained?
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!”
The ultimate truth is also called the Path, it is also called Bodhi, and it is also called Nirvana.
If there were a bodhisattva who said that there is the attainment of the Path, Bodhi, or Nirvana, that would be impermanence.
Why is this? If phenomena were permanent, they could not be apprehended; just as with space, who is there to apprehend it?
World-Honored One!
Just as worldly objects, which did not originally exist but now do, are called impermanent;
so too is the Way. If the Way could be attained, it would be called impermanent.
If the Dharma were permanent, there would be neither attainment nor birth, just like the Buddha-nature, which is without attainment and without birth.

World-Honored One! As for the Way, it is neither form nor non-form; it is neither long nor short, neither high nor low; it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither red nor white, neither blue nor yellow; it is neither existent nor non-existent. How can the Tathāgata say that it can be attained?
"Bodhi and nirvana are also like this. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Good son! There are two kinds of paths:
first, the permanent; second, the impermanent.
The characteristics of bodhi are also of two kinds:
first, permanence; second, impermanence. Nirvāṇa is likewise.
The path of the outsiders is called impermanent, while the path of the insiders is called permanent.
The bodhi possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called impermanent; the bodhi possessed by bodhisattvas and buddhas is called permanent.
External liberation is called impermanent; internal liberation is called permanent.
"Good son!
The Way, Bodhi, and Nirvana are all termed 'eternal.
Yet all sentient beings are constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions; because they lack the eye of wisdom, they are unable to see them."

Yet, because sentient beings desire to see [these], they cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom; through such cultivation, they see the Path, Bodhi, and Nirvana—this is called a bodhisattva attaining the Path, Bodhi, and Nirvana.
The nature and characteristics of the Way are, in reality, neither born nor extinguished; for this reason, it cannot be grasped or held. Good son!
Although the Way has no form or appearance that can be seen, nor weight or measure that can be known, it nonetheless possesses actual utility.
"Good son!

Just as the mind of sentient beings, though it is not form, neither long nor short, neither coarse nor subtle, neither bound nor liberated, and not a visible phenomenon, yet nevertheless exists—for this reason, I said to Sudatta:
'Householder!'"
The mind is the lord of the city; if a householder does not protect the mind, he does not protect his body and speech.
If he protects the mind, he protects his body and speech.
Because they do not properly guard this body and speech, they cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
Those who guard their body and speech cause sentient beings to attain the states of humans and devas, as well as nirvāṇa; thus they are called "true."
"That which cannot be attained is not called real. "Good son!
The Way, as well as Bodhi and Nirvana, are also like this: they both exist and they are eternal."
If it did not exist, how could one sever all afflictions?
Because it exists, all bodhisattvas clearly perceive and know it. "Good son!
There are two kinds of seeing:
first, seeing by way of signs; second, seeing with clarity.
What is meant by seeing by way of signs?
It is like seeing smoke from afar and calling it "seeing fire," though one does not actually see the fire;
yet, although the fire is not seen, it is not a falsehood.
It is like seeing a crane in the sky and saying one sees water.
Although one does not see the water, it is not false;
just as when one sees the flowers and leaves, one says that one sees the root—
although one does not see the root, it is nonetheless not false.
It is like a person who, seeing the horns of an ox through a fence from afar, says they see an ox;
although they do not see the ox, it is not a falsehood.
It is like seeing a woman who is pregnant and saying one sees desire.
Although one does not actually see the water, it is not false.
It is like seeing leaves growing on a tree and saying that one sees water;
although one does not see the water, it is nonetheless not false.
Furthermore, it is like seeing clouds and saying one sees rain;
although one does not see the rain, it is not a falsehood.
Likewise, upon seeing bodily and verbal actions, one says one sees the mind.
Although the mind is not seen, it is nonetheless not false;
this is called "seeing through its characteristics.
What is meant by "seeing with clarity"?
Just as the eye perceives forms. Good son!
It is like a person whose faculty of sight is pure and unimpaired, who gazes directly at an āmalaka fruit within the palm of his own hand.
It is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who clearly perceives the path, bodhi, and nirvāṇa;
although they perceive them in this way, from the very beginning there is no characteristic of seeing.
"Good son! For this reason, in the past I told Śāriputra:

'In all the world, whatever is not known, not seen, and not realized by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, Brahmās, or humans—only the Tathāgata fully knows, sees, and realizes it; and the same is true for the bodhisattvas.'"
Śāriputra! Whatever is known, seen, and realized by those in the world, I and the bodhisattvas also know, see, and realize.
Furthermore, regarding that which sentient beings in the world do not know, do not see, and do not realize, I likewise do not know, see, or realize it myself.
When the sentient beings of the world know, see, and awaken to something, they say of themselves, "I know, I see,
I have awakened. Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata knows, sees, and awakens to everything, yet he does not say of himself, "I know, I see, I have awakened."
All Bodhisattvas are likewise thus. Why is this?

If the Tathāgata were to manifest the characteristics of knowledge, vision, and awakening, one should know that he would not be the Buddha, the World-Honored One, but would instead be called an ordinary person; the same applies to the Bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has told Śāriputra, that which the world knows, I also know;
that which the world does not know, I also fully know.”
"What is the meaning of this? 'Good son!
All those in the world do not know, do not see, and do not awaken to the Buddha-nature.'"
If there are those who know, see, and awaken to the Buddha-nature, they are not called worldly people; they are called Bodhisattvas.

Worldly people, moreover, do not know, see, or awaken to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four inversions, the four truths, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, or Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If one knows, sees, and awakens to these, one is not called a worldly person; one should be called a Bodhisattva.
"Good son! This is called that which the world does not know, see, or realize.
What is it that the world knows, sees, and realizes?"

That which is called Brahmā, Maheśvara, and the Eight-Armed One; nature, time, atoms, dharma and adharma; the Lord of Creation; the views of the beginning and end of the world, and of annihilation and permanence; and the claim that from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called nirvāṇa—[all these are but provisional teachings].
"Good son! This is what is known, seen, and realized by the world.

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva also knows, sees, and realizes such matters. Once a bodhisattva has thus known, seen, and realized them, if they were to say that they do not know, do not see, and do not realize them, this would be false."
False and illusory dharmas constitute this sin; because of this sin, one falls into hell. Good son!

Whether they be men or women, śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, if they say that there is no Path, no Bodhi, and no Nirvāṇa, you should know that such people are called icchantikas and are the retinue of Māra. They are said to be slanders of the Dharma; such slander of the Dharma is called slandering all Buddhas.
"Such a person is not called 'of the world,' nor are they called 'not of the world.
At that time, having heard these words, Kāśyapa praised the Buddha with a verse:
"Out of great compassion for sentient beings, You have caused me to take refuge."
He skillfully extracts the many poisonous arrows; therefore, he is called the Great King of Physicians.
What is treated by worldly physicians may be cured, yet returns again;
those treated by the Tathāgata never recur in the end.
The World-Honored One’s ambrosial medicine is bestowed upon all sentient beings;
once they have taken it, they neither die nor are they born.
Now, for my sake, the Tathāgata expounds the Great Parinirvāṇa.
"When sentient beings hear this secret treasury, they immediately attain the state beyond birth and extinction.
After the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

As the Buddha has taught, that which all in the world do not know, see, or awaken to, the Bodhisattva is able to fully know, see, and awaken to. If a Bodhisattva were themselves part of the world, one could not say that what the world does not know, see, or awaken to, the Bodhisattva is able to know, see, and awaken to.
"If it were not of the world, what distinct characteristics would there be?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
One who is called a bodhisattva is both of the world and not of the world.
Those who do not know, see, or awaken are said to be of the world; those who know, see, and awaken are not said to be of the world.
"What difference do you see?
I shall now explain it to you,
son of good family!

Whether male or female, if anyone who hears this Nirvana Sūtra for the first time immediately gives rise to reverent faith and resolves to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are called "worldly" [practitioners].
That which all the world does not know, see, or realize, the Bodhisattva likewise does not know, see, or realize.

After the Bodhisattva has heard this *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he knows that there are things unknown, unseen, and unrealized by the world, which ought to be known, seen, and realized by the Bodhisattva. Having understood this matter, he reflects to himself:
"By what skillful means (*upāya*) should I practice so as to attain such knowledge, vision, and realization?"
He further thought to himself:
"I must cultivate and maintain the pure precepts with a profound mind.
O son of good family!
At that time, by virtue of these causes and conditions, the bodhisattva will, in all future lives and wherever he may be born, always maintain pure precepts. Good son!

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s precepts are pure, in all places of birth he will never harbor arrogance, wrong views, or the net of doubt; he will never say that the Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation and maintenance of the pure precepts.

Once the precepts are pure, one next cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because of this cultivation of concentration, in every place of rebirth, right mindfulness is never forgotten—namely, that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and that the twelve divisions of the scriptures and all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

All Bodhisattvas who dwell securely in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra perceive the Buddha-nature; they remember and do not forget such matters as these, and by virtue of cultivating meditative concentration, they attain the eleven kinds of emptiness. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure concentration.

Once morality and concentration are fully prepared, one next cultivates pure wisdom. By means of cultivating wisdom, from the very beginning one does not harbor attachments such as: "there is a self within the body," "the body is within the self," "this body is the self," or "neither the body nor the self. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure wisdom.
Because they cultivate wisdom, the precepts they uphold are firm and unshakable. Good son!
Just as Mount Sumeru cannot be tilted or moved by the four winds, so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cannot be tilted or moved by the four inversions.
"Good son!

At that time, the bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to the fact that the precepts he upholds are unshakable; this is called what the bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to, and it is not of the mundane world."

"Good son! When a bodhisattva perceives that the precepts he upholds are firm and unshakable, his mind is free from regret. Because he is free from regret, his mind attains joy; because he attains joy, his mind attains delight; because he attains delight, his mind becomes tranquil; because his mind is tranquil, he attains immovable concentration; because he attains immovable concentration, he attains true knowledge and vision; because he attains true knowledge and vision, he develops weary detachment toward birth and death; because he develops weary detachment toward birth and death, he attains liberation; and because he attains liberation, he clearly perceives the Buddha-nature. This is called what is known, seen, and awakened by a bodhisattva, and it is not of the mundane world."
"Good son!
This is what is not known, seen, or realized by the world, yet is known, seen, and realized by this bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“How does a bodhisattva practice and maintain pure precepts so that the mind is free from regret, and even comes to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Worldly precepts are not called pure. Why is this?

Because worldly precepts are for the sake of existence, their nature is unstable, and they are not ultimate; they cannot extensively benefit all sentient beings. For these reasons, they are called impure.

Because it is impure, there arises a mind of regret; because of regret, the mind lacks joy; because there is no joy, there is no delight; because there is no delight, there is no tranquility; because there is no tranquility, there is no immovable concentration; because there is no immovable concentration, there is no true knowledge and vision; because there is no true knowledge and vision, there is no revulsion; because there is no revulsion, there is no liberation; because there is no liberation, one does not see the Buddha-nature; and because one does not see the Buddha-nature, one can ultimately never attain Great Parinirvāṇa. This is called the impurity of worldly precepts.
Good son!

For a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, pure precepts mean that the precepts are not [mere] precepts, are not for the sake of existence, are ultimately certain, and are for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the purity of a Bodhisattva’s precepts.
“Good son! Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not intentionally desire to give rise to a mind free from regret regarding pure ethical discipline, a mind free from regret arises spontaneously.”
Good son! It is like a person who holds up a bright mirror; though they do not expect to see their face, the reflection of the face appears of its own accord.
It is also like a farmer who sows seeds in fertile soil; though he does not expect sprouts to emerge, the sprouts grow of their own accord.
It is also like lighting a lamp: one does not expect the darkness to be extinguished, yet the darkness is extinguished of its own accord. Good son!
It is just the same for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who firmly upholds the pure precepts: a mind free from regret arises naturally, and because of those pure precepts, the mind attains joy.
"Good son!
Just as a handsome person feels joy in their heart upon seeing their own face in a mirror, so it is with one who maintains the pure precepts.
Good son!"
One who has broken the precepts perceives their own impurity and feels no joy in their heart.
Just as one with a physical deformity feels no pleasure upon seeing their own face, so it is with one who has broken the precepts.
Good son!
It is like two women tending cows: one carries a jar of curd and the other carries a jar of whey; they both go together to the city, intending to sell them.
On the road, his feet slipped and both jars were broken; one was joyful, while the other was distressed.
It is the same with those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them: the one who maintains pure precepts feels joy in their heart. Because the heart is joyful, they reflect:
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have declared within Nirvāṇa that those who can maintain the pure precepts shall attain Nirvāṇa."
"I am now practicing such pure precepts; I too shall surely attain them.
For this reason, his mind is joyful and at ease.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"What is the difference between joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*)?
"Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not commit evil, it is called 'rejoicing' (*abhirati*); [when he experiences the fruit thereof, it is called bliss]."
Purity of mind and upholding the precepts is called "joy" (*sukha*). Good son!
When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates birth and death, it is called "delight" (*prīti*); when he perceives Great Nirvāṇa, it is called "joy."

The lower stage is called joy (*prīti*), and the higher stage is called bliss (*sukha*). To be free from worldly common dharmas is called joy; to attain unshared (extraordinary) dharmas is called bliss.

Because the precepts are pure, the body becomes light and supple, and the mouth is free from coarse transgressions. At that time, whether seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or cognizing, the Bodhisattva encounters nothing but non-evil. Because there is no evil, the mind attains tranquility; because of tranquility, one attains stillness and concentration (*samādhi*); because of stillness and concentration, one attains true knowledge and vision; because of true knowledge and vision, one develops weary detachment from birth and death (*saṃsāra*); because of weary detachment from birth and death, one attains liberation; because of liberation, one attains the vision of Buddha-nature; and because of the vision of Buddha-nature, one attains Great Nirvāṇa. This is called the Bodhisattva’s pure upholding of the precepts, not the mundane precepts.
Why is this? Son of good family!
The pure precepts received by a bodhisattva mahāsattva are assisted by five dharmas.
What are the five?
First, faith; second, shame; third, remorse; fourth, virtuous friends; and fifth, revering the precepts.
This is because one is free from the five hindrances.
His vision is pure because he is free from the five views.
His mind is free from the net of doubt because he is free from the five doubts:
first, doubt regarding the Buddha; second, doubt regarding the Dharma; third, doubt regarding the Saṅgha; fourth, doubt regarding the precepts; and fifth, doubt regarding heedfulness.
At that time, the bodhisattva immediately attains the five faculties, namely: faith, mindfulness, diligence, concentration, and wisdom.
Because he attains these five faculties, he attains five kinds of nirvana, namely: liberation from form, up to liberation from consciousness.
This is called the pure upholding of precepts by a bodhisattva, not that of the world.
Good son! This is what the world does not know, does not see, and does not awaken to; yet it is what the bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to.

“Good son! If among my disciples who uphold, recite, transcribe, and expound the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra there is one who breaks the precepts, and someone should reproach, despise, or humiliate them, saying:
‘If the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the secret treasury of the Buddha, possesses such majestic power, why has it allowed you to violate the precepts you have received?’”
If a person who upholds this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* violates the prohibitions and precepts, one should know that this sūtra possesses no majestic power.
If it lacks such power, then even though it is recited and chanted, it will be of no benefit.

"Because of this slighting and disparaging of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they further cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to fall into hell. Those who uphold this sūtra yet violate the precepts are evil friends to sentient beings; they are not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra."

For such a person, I likewise do not permit the receiving or upholding of this scripture; it would be better that they neither receive, uphold, nor cultivate it than that they should receive, uphold, and practice it while violating the precepts.
"Good son!

If my disciples receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or expound the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they should rectify their bodies and minds; they must be careful not to engage in jesting, frivolity, or restless movements—neither acting with levity through the body nor moving with restlessness through the mind."
The mind that seeks existence is called "light agitation";
the body's commissioning of various karmas is called "frivolous play.
If my disciples seek existence and commission karma, they should not accept and uphold this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
If there are those who uphold this sutra in such a manner, people will disparage them, saying:
"If the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the secret treasury of the Buddha, possesses such majestic power, why does it cause you to seek existence and create karma?"
If those who uphold this sutra seek existence and create karma, you should know that this sutra possesses no majestic power.
If it lacks majestic power, then even though they receive and uphold it, it will be of no benefit.
"Because they have thus slighted and disparaged this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they have further caused immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to fall into hell.
Those who uphold this sūtra while seeking existence and creating karma are evil friends to sentient beings; they are not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra."

"Furthermore, son of good family! If my disciples receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and expound this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they must not speak at improper times; they must not speak in unsuitable countries; they must not speak without being requested; they must not speak with a disrespectful mind; they must not speak everywhere indiscriminately; they must not speak while praising themselves; they must not speak while disparaging others; they must not speak so as to extinguish the Buddha-dharma; and they must not speak so as to inflame worldly dharmas."
"Good son!
If my disciples uphold this sutra and preach it at improper times, or even preach it while being consumed by worldly dharmas, people will deride them, saying:

'If the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the Buddha’s secret treasury, possesses such majestic power, why does it cause you to preach at improper times, and even to preach while being consumed by worldly dharmas?'"
If those who uphold this sutra should speak in such a manner, one should know that this sutra possesses no power.
If it lacks power, then even though it is received and upheld, it will be of no benefit.
"Because they disparage and revile this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to fall into hell.

Those who uphold this sūtra yet preach it at inappropriate times, or even preach it while inflaming worldly dharmas, are evil friends to sentient beings; they are not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra."
"Good son!

Those who wish to receive and uphold [this teaching], those who preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa, those who preach the Buddha-nature, those who preach the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, those who preach the Mahāyāna, those who preach the Vaipulya sūtras, those who preach the Śrāvaka-yāna, those who preach the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, those who preach liberation, and those who perceive the Buddha-nature, should first purify their bodies. Because the body is pure, they will be free from reproach; because they are free from reproach, they cause immeasurable people to give rise to pure faith in the Mahāparinirvāṇa. Because such faith arises, they revere this sūtra. If they hear even a single verse, a single phrase, a single word, or the preaching of the Dharma, they shall attain the aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

You should know that such a person is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings and not an evil friend; they are my disciple and not a follower of Māra; they are called a bodhisattva and not a worldly being.
"Good son! This is what is not known, not seen, and not realized by the world, yet it is that which is known, seen, and realized by the Bodhisattva."—
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seventeen.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 18.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: Brahma-Carya (The Holy Life), Part Four.
"Furthermore, good son, what is it that is called 'that which is not known, seen, or realized by all the world, yet is known, seen, and realized by the bodhisattva'? "
These are called the six foundations of mindfulness. What are the six? They are:
mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of generosity, and mindfulness of the devas.
"Good son! How does one practice mindfulness of the Buddha?
[One contemplates] the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World,"
The Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is eternally unchanging;
he is fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the great lion’s roar;
he is named the Great Śramaṇa, the Great Brāhmaṇa, the Great Purity who has ultimately reached the further shore, and the Invincible.
One who has no one above whom he can be seen; one who is without fear, unstartled, and immovable; solitary and peerless;

self-awakened without a teacher; possessing swift wisdom, great wisdom, sharp wisdom, deep wisdom, liberating wisdom, uncommon wisdom, universal wisdom, ultimate wisdom; one who has accomplished the treasure of wisdom—a person.
The elephant king among men, the bull king among men, the dragon king among men,
the great man among men, the lotus among men, the *puṇḍarīka* flower, the Teacher who tames beings, the great donor,
and the teacher of the Great Dharma; he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the Dharma, and he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the meaning.
He is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the proper time; he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows contentment;
he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the self; he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the great assembly;

he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the various dispositions of sentient beings; and he is called a Great Dharma Master because he knows the sharpness, dullness, and middleness of the faculties.
Dharma Master, because you preach the Middle Way, you are called a Great Dharma Master.
Why is he called the Tathāgata?
Because he remains unchanging, just as all Buddhas of the past have taught.
What is meant by “unchanging”?
The Buddhas of the past, in order to deliver sentient beings, expounded the twelve divisions of the scriptures; the Tathāgata does likewise, and for this reason he is called the Tathāgata.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, come from the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven kinds of emptiness to reach Great Nirvāṇa; the Tathāgata is likewise, and for this reason the Buddha is titled "Tathāgata."

For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means as appropriate to reveal and teach the three vehicles; their lifespans are immeasurable and beyond calculation, and the Tathāgata is likewise. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Tathāgata.
"What is meant by 'Arhat' (the Worthy One)?
All worldly phenomena are called enemies; because the Buddha should destroy them, he is named 'Arhat.

Furthermore, the four Māras are the enemies of a Bodhisattva. When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were Bodhisattvas, they were able to destroy the four Māras through wisdom; for this reason, he is named 'Arhat.'"
Furthermore, "Arhat" (Aṅgīrasa) means "to distance oneself. When he was a bodhisattva, he should have distanced himself from immeasurable afflictions;

therefore, he is called "Arhat. Furthermore, "Arhat" means "joy. Although the Buddhas of the past, when they were bodhisattvas, underwent various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they never lacked joy but always found joy therein. The Tathāgata is likewise; for this reason, he is called "Arhat."
Furthermore, as for "Arhat" (the Worthy One), all humans and devas should offer him various kinds of fragrant flowers, necklaces, banners, streamers, and music; therefore, he is called "Arhat."
"What is 'perfectly complete knowledge' (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)?
'Perfect' (*samyak*) means non-erroneous; 'complete knowledge' (*saṃbodhi*) means thorough penetration regarding the four inversions.
Furthermore, 'perfect' is called ascetic practice (*duṣkara-caryā*); 'complete knowledge' means knowing that because of ascetic practice, there will certainly be the fruit of suffering."
Furthermore, "correct" refers to the middle way of the world; "thorough knowledge" means knowing with ultimate certainty; by practicing the Middle Way, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, "Right" (samyak) means that which can be counted, measured, and weighed; "Omniscient" (sarvajña) means that which cannot be counted, measured, or weighed. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Rightly Omniscient One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
Good son! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas both possess universal knowledge and do not possess universal knowledge. Why is this?

"Universal knowledge" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements; since śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also attain universal knowledge of these, it is called "universal knowledge."
"What is meant by 'not knowing all'? Good son!

Suppose the followers of the Two Vehicles were to contemplate a single aggregate of form for immeasurable eons; they would still be unable to know it exhaustively. For this reason, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess universal knowledge."
"What is meant by 'one perfected in knowledge and conduct' (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*)?

'Knowledge' (*vidyā*) refers to the attainment of immeasurable wholesome fruits; 'conduct' (*caraṇa*) refers to the feet; and 'wholesome fruits' refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment)."

The "feet" are named morality and wisdom; by mounting these feet of morality and wisdom, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and for this reason, it is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct."
Furthermore, "Vidyā" (Knowledge) is named *mantra*; "Caryā" (Conduct) is named *maṅgala* (Auspiciousness); and "Pūrṇa" (Fulfilled) is named *phala* (Fruit).
O son of good family! These are called worldly meanings. However, "Mantra" is named liberation;

"Maṅgala" is named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment); and "Phala" is named *mahāparinirvāṇa*. Therefore, he is named "Vidyā-caryā-pūrṇa" (One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct).
Furthermore, "clear" (vidyā) is named light; "practice" (caryā) is named karma; and "feet" (pāda) are named fruit. Good son!
These are called the worldly meanings.
"Light" is named non-negligence; "karma" is named the six pāramitās; and "fruit" is named anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, "clear" (*vidyā*) refers to the three types of clarity:
first, the clarity of the bodhisattvas; second, the clarity of the Buddhas; and third, the clarity of non-clarity (*avidyā-vidyā*).

The clarity of the bodhisattvas is the *prajñāpāramitā*; the clarity of the Buddhas is the Buddha-eye; and the clarity of non-clarity is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). A practitioner cultivates various wholesome deeds for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable eons; being "complete" (*pūrṇa*) means clearly seeing the Buddha-nature. For these reasons, he is called "Complete in Clarity and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*).
"What is meant by 'Sugata'?
'Su' means high, and 'gata' means not high, O son of good family!
This is the worldly meaning."
That which is elevated is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that which is not elevated is the mind of the Tathāgata.
Good son! If the mind were elevated, it would not be called the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is named the Sugata.
Furthermore, "good" (śubha) refers to the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and "gone" (gata) refers to the fruit of the spiritual friend. Son of good family!
This is called the worldly meaning.

The spiritual friend is the initial generation of the mind of awakening, while the fruit is called Great Parinirvāṇa. Because the Tathāgata does not abandon his initial generation of the mind and thereby attains Great Nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata is named Sugata.
Furthermore, "good" (śubha) means "excellent," and "gone" (gata) means "existent. O son of good family!
This is the worldly meaning;
"excellent" means seeing the Buddha-nature, and "existent" means Great Nirvana.
"Good son!
The nature of nirvāṇa is truly not existent; it is because of the world that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, say it exists.
Good son!"

For example, just as people in the world may say they have a son when they actually have no son, or say there is a path when there is actually no path, so it is with nirvana: it is said to exist because of worldly convention. Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained great nirvana, they are called Sugatas.
“Good son! What is the knowledge of the world? Good son!”

The "world" (*loka*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); "understanding" (*vidyā*) refers to knowledge. Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, thoroughly understand the five aggregates, they are called "World-Understanding Ones" (*lokavid*).

Furthermore, the "world" refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*); "understanding" means non-attachment. Because they are unattached to the five desires, they are called "World-Understanding Ones."

Furthermore, regarding the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*): in the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds of the eastern direction, all that is unknown, unseen, and uncomprehended by the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* is fully known, seen, and comprehended by the Buddhas. The same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Knower of the World.

Furthermore, "the world" refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). "Understanding" means knowing the causes and effects of good and evil for these ordinary beings; this is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but only the Buddha can know it. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
Furthermore, "one who understands the world" (loka-vid) is called "Lotus. To understand this name means "to be unstained. Noble son!
This is the meaning of "one who understands the world.
The "Lotus" is the Tathāgata; "unstained" means that the Tathāgata is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas. For this reason, the Buddha is titled "One Who Understands the World."
Furthermore, regarding the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*): the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called the Knower of the World. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive the world, they are therefore called the Knower of the World.
Good son! Just as one obtains life because of food and thus names food "life," so too it is with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
because they perceive the world, they are named "Knower of the World."
"What is meant by 'Unsurpassed One' (Anuttara)?

'Surpassed One' refers to one who has something to be severed; one who has nothing to be severed is called the Unsurpassed One. Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no afflictions, there is nothing for them to sever; therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One."

Furthermore, those who are superior men are characterized by contention and dispute, whereas those who are unsurpassed men have no contention or dispute. Since the Tathāgata is without contention, he is therefore titled the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Man.

Furthermore, those who are superior men can have their words refuted, whereas those who are unsurpassed men cannot have their words refuted. What the Tathāgata speaks cannot be refuted by any sentient being; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Man.

Furthermore, those who are superior are called "Superior Elders" (Upastha), and those who are unsurpassed are called "Unsurpassed Elders" (Anupastha). Since no one among the Buddhas of the three periods of time surpasses them, the Buddha is therefore titled the Unsurpassed Being (Anuttara-puruṣa).

The "Superior" (shang) is called new, while the "Worthy" (shi) is called old; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, embody Great Nirvana, which is neither new nor old. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Worthy (Anuttarapuruṣa).
"What is meant by 'tamer of men'?
One who is himself a man and further tames other men.
Good son!..."
As for the term "Tathāgata," he is in truth neither a man nor not a man; because he disciplines men, the Tathāgata is called a man.
O son of good family!
All men and women who possess four qualities are called "great beings" (puruṣa). What are these four?
First, having virtuous friends; second, being able to listen to the Dharma; third, reflecting upon its meaning; and fourth, practicing according to the teaching.
"Good son! If a man or a woman is endowed with these four dharmas, they are called a 'true man' (puruṣa). Good son!"
If there is a man who lacks these four qualities, he cannot be called a "great man" (puruṣa). Why is this?
Although his body is that of a great man, his conduct is identical to that of a beast.
The Tathāgata tames both men and women; therefore, he is called the Buddha, the Charioteer of Men.
Furthermore, son of good family!
There are generally four kinds of those who drive horses:
First, it touches the hair; second, it touches the skin; third, it touches the flesh; fourth, it touches the bone; according to what it touches, it accords with the will of the driver.
The Tathāgata is likewise; by means of four kinds of dharmas, he disciplines sentient beings:
first, he speaks of birth, causing them to accept the Buddha’s words, just as when one touches its hair, [the horse] follows the will of the driver.
When the second [type of person] speaks of birth and old age, they accept the Buddha’s words, like touching the hair and skin, following the will of the driver.
When the third speaks of birth as well as old age and sickness, they accept the Buddha’s words, like touching the hair, skin, and flesh, following the will of the driver.

Fourth, when the Buddha speaks of birth, as well as old age, sickness, death, and so forth, one immediately accepts his words, just as when touching hair, skin, flesh, or bone, one follows the will of the charioteer. Good son!
A charioteer who trains horses lacks certainty; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, tames sentient beings with absolute infallibility. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Tamer of Men."
"What is meant by 'Teacher of Gods and Humans'?
There are two kinds of teachers:
first, those who teach what is good; second, those who teach what is evil."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly teach all sentient beings through wholesome dharmas.
What are these wholesome dharmas?
They are the wholesomeness of body, speech, and mind.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct all sentient beings, saying:
"Good son, you should distance yourself from unwholesome physical karma. Why is this?"
Since bodily unwholesome karma can be abandoned and one thereby attains liberation, I therefore teach you this Dharma.
If unwholesome karma could not be abandoned and yet one were to attain liberation, I would never have taught you to abandon it.

If sentient beings, having abandoned evil karma, were to fall into the three evil realms, such a thing is impossible; because they have distanced themselves from evil, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and realize Great Nirvāṇa.

Therefore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly teach and transform sentient beings through this Dharma; their speech and mind are likewise so. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Teacher.
Furthermore, whereas in the past he had not yet attained the Way, now he has already attained it, and he preaches that attained Way for the sake of sentient beings;

whereas from the beginning he had not yet cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), now he has completed its cultivation, and he preaches what he himself has cultivated for the sake of sentient beings;
having personally destroyed his own ignorance, he further destroys the ignorance of sentient beings.
Having personally attained the pure eye, they further shatter the blindness and darkness of sentient beings, causing them to obtain the pure eye;
having personally realized the two truths, they further expound the two truths for sentient beings.
Having attained liberation for oneself, one further preaches the Dharma of liberation for all sentient beings;
having crossed the boundless great river of birth and death for oneself, one further enables all sentient beings to cross it as well;
having attained fearlessness for oneself, one further instructs sentient beings so that they too shall be free from dread.
Having himself entered nirvana, he further expounds the Great Nirvana for the sake of sentient beings;
for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Teacher.
"Heaven" (deva) means "day"; because the days are long and the nights are short in the heavens, it is called heaven.
Furthermore, "deva" (heavenly being) means "free from sorrow and affliction"; because they constantly experience happiness, they are called devas.
Furthermore, "deva" means "lamp-light"; because they can dispel darkness and serve as a great illumination, they are called devas.
Furthermore, because they are able to destroy the darkness of evil karma and attain wholesome karma, thereby being born in the heavens, they are called "devas.
Moreover, "deva" means auspicious; because they are auspicious, they receive the name "deva."
Furthermore, "deva" (heavenly being) is called the sun; because it possesses radiance, it is named "deva. For this reason, they are called devas.
"Manuṣya" (human) means one capable of much kindness and righteousness;
furthermore, a human is one whose body and speech are gentle; furthermore, a human is said to possess pride, yet a human is also one capable of destroying that pride.
Good son! Although the Buddhas are the unsurpassed great teachers for all sentient beings, the sūtras speak of them as "teachers of gods and humans. Why is this?
"Good son!

Among all sentient beings, only gods and humans are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, are able to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action, and are able to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, the Buddha is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans."
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
'Buddha' means awakening; having awakened oneself, one is further able to awaken others. Good son!
For example, if there is a person who perceives the presence of a thief, that thief can do nothing.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to perceive all immeasurable afflictions; having fully awakened to them, he renders those afflictions powerless to act. For this reason, he is called a Buddha.
Because of this awakening, one is not born, does not age, is not ill, and does not die; for this reason, he is called Buddha.
As for "Bhagavān," *bhaga* means "to break" and *vān* means "afflictions"; because he is able to break afflictions, he is called Bhagavān.

Furthermore, because they are able to accomplish all wholesome dharmas; because they are able to skillfully understand the meanings of all dharmas; because they possess great merit that none can surpass; because they possess great renown that pervades the ten directions; because they bestow various forms of great wisdom; and because they have discarded the female organ for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

“Good son! Whether male or female, whoever is able to recollect the Buddha in this manner—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether by day or by night; whether in light or in darkness—will always be able to remain without being separated from seeing the World-Honored Buddha.”
“Good son! For what reason are you called Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, up to Bhagavat, and why do you possess such immeasurable merit and great renown?”
Good son!

For immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has venerated his parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and seniors; throughout immeasurable kalpas he has constantly practiced giving for the sake of sentient beings, steadfastly maintained the prohibitive precepts, cultivated patience, diligently applied himself to vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and practiced great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity. Therefore, he has now attained the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, and a diamond-like body.

Furthermore, in the past, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the Bodhisattva cultivated and accumulated the faculties of faith, mindfulness, diligence, concentration, and wisdom; he reverently made offerings to his teachers and elders, always seeking the benefit of the Dharma rather than the benefit of food.

If a bodhisattva upholds the twelve divisions of the scriptures, whether reading or reciting them, they always do so for the sake of sentient beings, to enable them to attain liberation, peace, and happiness, never for their own sake.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva constantly cultivates a supramundane mind, a mind of renunciation, an unconditioned mind, a mind free from contention,
a mind free from defilement, a mind free from bondage, a mind free from grasping and attachment, and a mind free from concealment.
That is, a mind that is without indeterminate states, without the mind of birth and death, without a mind entangled in doubt,
without a mind of sensual desire, without a mind of malice, without a mind of delusion, without a mind of pride, without a defiled and turbid mind,
without a mind of affliction, without a mind of suffering, an immeasurable mind, and a vast mind.
The mind of emptiness, the mind without [self], the mind that is not non-existent, the disciplined mind, the unguarded mind, the unhidden mind,
the world-transcending mind, the ever-concentrated mind, the ever-cultivated mind, the ever-liberated mind,
the mind free from retribution, the wishless mind, the well-directed mind, the undeluded mind, and the supple mind.
...the non-abiding mind, the sovereign mind, the untainted mind, the mind of ultimate truth, the non-retrogressive mind, the impermanent mind, the upright mind,
the mind free from guile and crookedness, the purely virtuous mind, the mind free from notions of much or little, the mind free from hardness,
the mind free from the state of an ordinary person, and the mind free from the state of a śrāvaka...
The mind of a Pratyekabuddha well understands the realm of the mind, the realm of the arising of the mind, the realm of the abiding of the mind, and the realm of the mastery of the mind;
therefore, they now attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, they are entitled to be called Tathāgata, up to Bhagavat.
"Venerable sir, this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Buddha.
What is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Dharma?
Son of good family!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the Dharma taught by all Buddhas is most wondrous and supreme; because of this Dharma, they are able to cause sentient beings to attain fruits in the present life.
This True Dharma has no temporal divisions; it is seen by the eye of Dharma, not by the physical eye.

Yet it cannot be compared through analogies: it is unborn, unarisen, non-abiding, unceasing, without beginning, without end, unconditioned, and beyond number. For those who have no dwelling, it serves as a dwelling.
It is a dwelling that provides a refuge where there was no refuge, brings light where there was ignorance, and enables those who have not reached the further shore to reach it.

It creates unobstructed fragrance where there was no fragrance; it is seen by that which cannot be seen, is unmoving and non-turning, neither long nor short, forever severing all worldly pleasures for the sake of the bliss of peace and security—ultimately subtle and wondrous, yet not...
Form is severed from form, yet it is still form; and so on, up to: consciousness is severed from consciousness, yet it is still consciousness.
It is not that karma severs karma, nor that fetters sever fetters, nor that things sever things, yet they are still things.
It is not that realms sever realms, yet they are still realms. It is not that existence severs existence, yet it is still existence. It is not that sense-bases sever sense-bases.
And yet it is an entry; it is not the cause of cessation, yet it is also a cause; it is not the fruit of cessation, yet it is also a fruit;
it is neither empty nor real; it cuts off all reality and yet is also real; it is neither arising nor ceasing;
it is eternally free from arising and ceasing and yet is also cessation; it is neither mark nor non-mark; it cuts off all [marks].
Characteristics are also characteristics; neither teaching nor non-teaching, yet he is also a teacher;
neither fear nor security, yet by severing all fear he is also security; neither patience nor impatience, yet by forever severing impatience he is also patience;
neither cessation nor non-cessation, yet by severing all cessation he is also cessation.

The crown of all dharmas, which is able to forever sever all afflictions, is pure and signless, eternally liberated from all signs, and the ultimate dwelling place for immeasurable sentient beings. It can extinguish the blazing fires of all birth and death;
it is the place where all Buddhas dwell and roam, eternal and unchanging—this is called a Bodhisattva.
Mindfulness of the Dharma.
"What is mindfulness of the Sangha?

The noble Sangha of the Buddhas dwells in accordance with the Dharma, receives the upright Dharma, and practices in conformity with it. They are invisible, ungraspable, indestructible, incapable of being harmed, and inconceivable; they are the field of merit for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings."

Although he is a field of merit, he accepts and takes nothing; he is pure and free from defilement, untainted, unconditioned, vast, universal, and boundless. His mind is harmonious and supple, equanimous and non-dual, free from agitation or turbidity, and eternally immutable—this is called mindfulness of the Sangha.
"What is the mindfulness of precepts?

The Bodhisattva contemplates that he possesses the precepts—unbroken, unblemished, unimpaired, and unmixed. Although they have no form or color, they can be guarded and maintained; although they have no tactile contact, through the skillful cultivation of expedient means, they can be brought to fulfillment. They are free from fault and are praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; they are the cause of the Great Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa."
"Good son!

It is like the great earth, a ship, a necklace, a noble clan, the great ocean, alkaline ash, a house, a sword, a bridge, a skilled physician and wondrous medicine, *agada* medicine, a wish-fulfilling jewel, feet, eyes, and the cool shade of one's parents; these cannot be stolen or plundered, nor can they be harmed. Fire cannot burn them, and water cannot wash them away."

The great mountain ladder and the sublime jeweled victory banner of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—if one abides in this precept, one may attain the fruit of Srotāpanna; I too have a share in this, yet I do not require it.
Why is this? If I were to attain this fruit of a srotāpanna, I would not be able to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
If I abide in these precepts, I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I too have a share in this, and it is what I desire.
Why is this? If one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one shall extensively expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and act as their protector.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the precepts (*śīla-smṛti*).
"What is the mindfulness of giving?

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeply contemplates that this giving is the cause of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The Buddhas and bodhisattvas have personally approached, cultivated, and accumulated such generosity; I, too, shall likewise approach, cultivate, and accumulate it. If I do not practice giving, I will be unable to adorn the fourfold assembly."
Although giving cannot ultimately sever the fetters, it can eliminate and destroy present afflictions.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of giving, one is constantly praised by sentient beings throughout the immeasurable, boundless worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva bestows food upon sentient beings, he bestows their very life; by virtue of this retribution, at the time he attains Buddhahood, his state shall be constant and unchanging.
Because one bestows happiness, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one obtains peace and bliss.
When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma and do not encroach upon others to give it away; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, they achieve pure Nirvana.
When the Bodhisattva practices giving, he causes all sentient beings to obtain what they seek without having to ask; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, he achieves mastery.
Through the causal conditions of my giving, I enable others to attain power; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, I obtain the ten powers (*daśabala*).
By means of the causal conditions of giving, one enables others to obtain speech; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate this giving as a cause for *nirvāṇa*; I, likewise, cultivate and accumulate giving as a cause for *nirvāṇa*.
The detailed explanation is as found in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
"What is the recollection of the devas?
There are the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
"If one possesses faith, they shall attain the realm of the Four Great Kings; I too have a share therein.

If one possesses ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom, they shall attain the realm of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I too have a share therein.
Yet, this is not what I desire."

Why is this? The abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception are all impermanent; because they are impermanent, there is birth, old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, they are not what I desire.
For example, it is like a magical illusion that deceives the foolish,
but does not delude or entice the wise.
That which is like a magical illusion refers to the abodes of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The "fools" are all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); I am not like these ordinary fools.

I have heard that there is a "Heaven of the Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-deva*), meaning that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are eternal and unchanging. Because they abide eternally, they are not born, do not age, do not fall ill, and do not die; for the sake of sentient beings, I diligently seek this Heaven of the Ultimate Truth.
Why is this? Because the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*) can cause sentient beings to sever and abandon their afflictions, just like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).

If I possess faith, up to and including wisdom, I shall be able to attain this Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning; therefore, I shall extensively analyze and explain the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning for the sake of sentient beings.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the devas. "Good son!
This is what is called the bodhisattva who is not of the world; it is that which the world does not know, see, or awaken to, yet which this bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to."
"Good son!

If you were to say that my disciples who uphold, recite, copy, and expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures are no different from those who uphold, recite, copy, disseminate, and explain the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, this is not so."
Why is this? Good son!
The Great Nirvāṇa is the profound and secret treasury of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; because it is this profound and secret treasury of the Buddhas, it is supreme.
“Good son!
For this reason, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is most marvelous, most extraordinary, and inconceivable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I too know that this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is most marvelous, most extraordinary, and inconceivable; the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are inconceivable; and the bodhi of the bodhisattvas and the mahāparinirvāṇa are likewise inconceivable.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you further say that a bodhisattva is inconceivable? “Good son!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no teacher who instructs him, yet he is able to spontaneously give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta). Having already given rise to this mind, he diligently cultivates vigor.
Even if a great fire were to burn his body and head, he would never seek rescue or abandon his mindfulness of the Dharma.
Why is this? A bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects:

"Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whether in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, or devas, I have been scorched by the fires of the various fetters, yet I have never once attained a single definitive dharma."
The definitive dharma is none other than *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If I were to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I would never cherish or spare my body, mind, or life.
For the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even if my body were to be shattered like fine dust, I would never abandon my diligent vigor.
Why is this? For the mind of diligent progress is itself the cause of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus it is, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva, while not yet having seen unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, can thus disregard their own body and life, how much more so once they have seen it? For this reason, the bodhisattva is inconceivable.

Furthermore, it is inconceivable that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas perceive the immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death, which are beyond the reach of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; although they know the immeasurable evils of birth and death, for the sake of sentient beings, they undergo suffering therein without giving rise to weariness or detachment. For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.

For the sake of sentient beings, although Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are in the hells, they experience various sufferings and afflictions as if they were the bliss of the third dhyāna; therefore, they are further called "inconceivable."
"Good son! It is like an elder whose house has caught fire.
Having seen it, the elder has emerged from the house, yet his children remain behind, not yet escaped from the danger of the fire."
At that time, the elder knew for certain that there was danger from the fire; yet, for the sake of his children, he returned to their rescue, disregarding the peril.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although he knows that birth and death abound with faults and evils, he dwells within them for the sake of sentient beings without weariness; therefore, he is further named "Inconceivable."
"Good son!

Immeasurable sentient beings resolve upon bodhicitta, but seeing the many faults and evils within birth and death, their minds immediately retreat and sink; they may then become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
If there are bodhisattvas who hear this sutra, they shall never regress from the mind of enlightenment to become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Although such bodhisattvas have not yet reached the first stage, the Stage of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), their minds are firm and steadfast, free from regression or decline; for this reason, they are further called "inconceivable."
"Good son! If someone were to say:
'I am able to swim across the waters of the great ocean.'"
“Is such a statement conceivable?
“No, World-Honored One.”
Such words may be conceivable or inconceivable. Why is this?
If there is a person who has crossed over, then it is inconceivable.
"If the asuras were to cross over, it would be conceivable. "Good son!
I do not speak of asuras; I am speaking only of humans."
“World-Honored One!
Among humans, there are also those who are conceivable and those who are inconceivable.
World-Honored One!”
There are also two kinds of persons:
first, the noble ones (ārya), and second, ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Ordinary worldlings are inconceivable, whereas noble ones are conceivable.
“Good son, I speak of ordinary persons; I do not speak of noble ones.
“World-Honored One!”
"If it concerns ordinary persons, they are truly inconceivable. "Good son!
Ordinary persons truly cannot cross the great ocean waters."
In this way, such a bodhisattva is truly able to cross the great ocean of birth and death; for this reason, they are further called "inconceivable.
Good son! If there were someone who could suspend Mount Sumeru with a single fiber from a lotus root, would that be conceivable?
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!"
In a single moment of thought, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fully weigh and measure all of birth and death; for this reason, they are further called "inconceivable. Good son!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, constantly contemplated birth-and-death as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; yet for the sake of sentient beings, they analytically expound permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Although they speak in this way, it is not a false view; therefore, it is further called inconceivable.
"Good son!
It is as if a person enters water but the water cannot drown them, or enters a great, raging fire but the fire cannot burn them; such a matter is inconceivable."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although dwelling within birth and death, they are not afflicted or harmed by birth and death; for this reason, they are further named "inconceivable."
Good son! There are three grades of persons, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
When a person of the inferior grade first enters the womb, they form this thought:
"I am now situated in a latrine, a place where all impurities gather, like being amidst corpses, amidst a thicket of thorns, and in a place of great darkness.
When first emerging from the womb, he again thinks:
"I am now leaving the latrine, leaving the place of all impurities, and even leaving the place of great darkness."
A person of middling capacity thinks to himself:
"I shall now enter among the groves of trees, by the pure rivers, and into houses and dwellings."
The same occurs when they emerge.
A person of superior capacity thinks to themselves:
"I am ascending a palace hall, amidst flower groves, riding horses or elephants, and climbing over high mountains."
The same is true when he emerges.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first enters the womb, he knows he is entering; while dwelling there, he knows he is dwelling; and when emerging, he knows he is emerging. Throughout this process, he never gives rise to thoughts of greed or hatred, yet he has not yet attained the first stage (bhūmi). For this reason, he is further called "inconceivable."
"Good son! Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi truly cannot be compared by means of analogies.
Good son!"
The mind also cannot be compared by means of spatial metaphors, yet it can be described in every way.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, without having a teacher from whom to receive instruction, is nonetheless able to attain the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained this Dharma, one’s mind is free from stinginess, and one constantly expounds it for the sake of sentient beings; for this reason, it is further named "inconceivable. Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may have physical seclusion that is not verbal, verbal seclusion that is not physical, or neither physical nor verbal seclusion.
Physical seclusion refers to abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; this is called physical seclusion.
"Non-verbal and verbal detachment" refers to being free from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; this is called verbal detachment.
"Neither bodily nor verbal detachment" refers to being free from covetousness, ill will, and wrong views.
Good son, this is called being neither body nor speech, yet also being detached.

Good son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perceive a single dharma that is either body, karma, or a master of detachment; yet there is still detachment. For this reason, it is further named "inconceivable."
The mouth is also like this. Good son!

One distances oneself from the body by means of the body; one distances oneself from the mouth by means of the mouth; and one distances oneself from that which is neither body nor mouth by means of wisdom.
Good son! Such wisdom truly exists, yet it cannot cause a bodhisattva to become detached. Why is this?
"Good son!

There is not a single dharma that can destroy or create; the nature of conditioned dharmas is such that they arise differently and perish differently. Therefore, this wisdom cannot be separated from them."

"Good son! Wisdom cannot shatter it; fire cannot burn it; water cannot rot it; wind cannot move it; earth cannot support it; birth cannot give rise to it; aging cannot age it; abiding cannot cause it to abide; destruction cannot destroy it; greed cannot greed for it; hatred cannot hate it; and delusion cannot delude it. Because that which has the nature of the conditioned arises differently and ceases differently, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never gives rise to the thought:
'I use this wisdom to shatter all afflictions.'"
Yet he says of himself:
"I have destroyed the afflictions.
Although he speaks thus, it is not false; for this reason, he is further named the Inconceivable One.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

Only now do I know that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable; that the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, those who receive and uphold it, as well as bodhi and nirvāṇa, are all inconceivable.”
"Bhagavān!
How long will the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma remain?
After how much time will it perish?"

“Good son! If this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra contains even these five kinds of conduct—namely, the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, the celestial conduct, the conduct of the sick, and the conduct of the infant—and if my disciples are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain its meaning, and are honored, respected, praised, and provided with various offerings by all sentient beings, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma has not yet perished.”
"Good son!

When this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is fully disseminated, at that time my disciples will frequently violate the prohibitive precepts and commit various evils. They will be unable to respect or have faith in such a sūtra; because of their lack of faith, they will be unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, or explain its meaning. They will not be respected by others, nor even provided with offerings, and upon seeing those who do uphold it, they will treat them with contempt and slander, saying:
'You are one of the six heretical teachers, not a disciple of the Buddha.'"
"You should know that the Buddha-dharma will soon be extinguished.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have personally heard this teaching from the Buddha: 'The Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha shall remain in the world for seven days, after which it will be completely extinguished.
World-Honored One, does the Tathāgata Kāśyapa possess such a sūtra?"
If it exists, how can you say it is extinguished?
If it does not exist, why do you say that the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As I have previously stated, only Mañjuśrī understands this meaning."
I shall now speak further; listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
Son of good family!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess two kinds of dharmas:
The first is the worldly dharma; the second is the ultimate dharma.
The worldly dharma is subject to destruction;
the ultimate dharma is not subject to destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity; second, permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
That which is impermanent, non-self, suffering, and impure is subject to destruction and cessation.
The permanence, bliss, self, and purity are thus indestructible.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, that which is maintained by the followers of the Two Vehicles; second, that which is maintained by Bodhisattvas.
That which is maintained by those of the two vehicles is subject to destruction;
that which is maintained by Bodhisattvas is without destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first is the external, and the second is the internal.
External phenomena are subject to destruction;
internal phenomena are not subject to destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the conditioned; second, the unconditioned.
Conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction and cessation.
The unconditioned dharma is without destruction or cessation.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds:
first, that which is obtainable; second, that which is unobtainable.
Phenomena that can be apprehended are subject to destruction;
that which cannot be apprehended is without destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first is common dharmas; the second is uncommon dharmas.
Common dharmas are subject to destruction;
uncommon dharmas are without destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, among humans; second, among devas.
Among humans, they perish and are destroyed.
The heavens are indestructible.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the eleven divisions of the sūtras; second, the Vaipulya sūtras.
The eleven divisions of the sutras are subject to decay and extinction;
the Vaipulya scriptures are not subject to decay or extinction. Good son!

If my disciples receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and provide respectful offerings to, honor, and praise these Vaipulya sutras, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma shall not perish.
“Good son! Regarding what you have just asked—whether the Tathāgata Kāśyapa possessed this sūtra or not—good son!
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas.”

Why is this? Although the Buddhas possess the eleven divisions of the scriptures, they do not therein speak of the Buddha-nature, nor do they speak of the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, nor that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, never enter ultimate parinirvāṇa. For this reason, this sutra is called the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata.
Because it is not expounded in the eleven divisions of the scriptures, it is called a "pitaka" (storehouse).
It is like a person whose seven treasures are not brought out for external use; they are called a "storehouse. Good son!
The reason this person hoards and accumulates these goods is for the sake of future events.
What are these future events? They are as follows:

when grain becomes expensive, when bandits come to invade the country, when one encounters a wicked king, when it is used to ransom one's life, or when roads are treacherous and difficult and wealth is hard to obtain—at such times, one shall then take them out and use them.
"Good son!

The secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is likewise so. For the sake of future generations, when there will be wicked bhikṣus who store impure things and preach to the fourfold assembly that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate nirvāṇa, and when such evils as reading secular texts and showing no reverence for the Buddha’s sūtras appear in the world, the Tathāgata—desiring to extinguish these evils and cause them to distance themselves from wrong livelihoods and gain—will then expound this sūtra."
