If this treasury of secret scriptures were to perish and no longer appear, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma would also perish.
"Good son! The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is eternal and unchanging; why then do you question whether this sūtra existed during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha?"
"Good son!

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, all sentient beings had thin and slight craving and possessed abundant wisdom. The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others were harmonious, gentle, and easy to transform; they possessed great majestic virtue, maintained total retention without forgetfulness, and the world was as pure as a great elephant king."
All sentient beings know that the Tathāgata will never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, but dwells eternally and unchangingly.
Although this scripture exists, there is no need to expound it.
"Good son!

The sentient beings of this world have many afflictions, ignorance, forgetfulness, and lack wisdom; they are ensnared by many doubts, their faculty of faith is not established, and the world is impure. All sentient beings claim that the Tathāgata is impermanent, subject to change, and will ultimately enter Great Parinirvāṇa; for this reason, the Tathāgata expounds this scripture."
"Good son!
The Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha has, in truth, not been extinguished either. Why is this?"
Because it is eternally unchanging. Good son!
If there are sentient beings who perceive a self where there is no self, or perceive no-self where there is a self; who perceive permanence in the impermanent, or...
They perceive the permanent as permanent; they perceive the pleasant as unpleasant, and the unpleasant as pleasant; they perceive the pure as impure, and the impure as pure;
they perceive cessation as non-cessation, and non-cessation as cessation; they perceive what is a transgression as not a transgression, and what is not a transgression as a transgression;
they perceive a light transgression as heavy, and a heavy transgression as light; they perceive a vehicle as not a vehicle, and what is not a vehicle as a vehicle...
They take what is a vehicle for seeing as a vehicle; they see the Path as not the Path and what is not the Path as the Path;
they see true Bodhi as not Bodhi and falsely see what is not true Bodhi as Bodhi;
they see suffering as not suffering, the origin as not the origin, cessation as not cessation, and the real as not real; they take what is actually conventional truth to be ultimate truth.
When one perceives the conventional truth as the ultimate truth, and perceives what is not a refuge as a refuge while perceiving what is a refuge as not a refuge;
when one regards the true words of the Buddha as the words of Māra, and regards the actual words of Māra as the words of the Buddha—
at such a time, the Buddhas then preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Good son! One might as well say that mosquitoes and gadflies have exhausted the depths of the great ocean, rather than saying that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
One might as well say that one can blow away and destroy Mount Sumeru with the breath of one's mouth, rather than saying that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
It would be better to say that one binds the fierce wind with a rope than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
It would be better to say that a lotus flower grows within a fire of khadira wood than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
It would be better to say that the agada medicine is a poisonous drug than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
It would be better to say that the moon can be made hot and the sun can be made cold than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
"It would be better to say that the four great elements each abandon their own nature than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata is extinguished. Good son!

If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are no disciples who understand the profound meaning and that Buddha-World-Honored One were to enter *nirvāṇa* immediately, you should know that this Dharma would not abide long in the world."
Furthermore, good son!

If, when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, you should know that even though the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, this Dharma will abide long in the world.
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, yet there are no lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha then enters *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world."
Furthermore, son of good family!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are many disciples who understand the profound meaning and there are devout lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) who revere the Buddha-dharma, then even though the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, you should know that the Buddha-dharma will abide long in the world.
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and although there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, these disciples preach the sutras and teachings out of greed for gain and sustenance rather than for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, and the Buddha further enters parinirvāṇa—then you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world."
Furthermore, good son!

If, when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are also lay donors of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma; and if those disciples, in whatever they expound, do not crave gain and honor but seek only *nirvāṇa*—then even though the Buddha has entered *parinirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will abide long in the world.
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning and there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, yet those disciples frequently engage in disputes and litigation, mutually asserting right and wrong, and the Buddha subsequently enters *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world."
Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) who possess sincere faith and revere the Buddha-dharma; and if those disciples practice the dharma of harmony and respect, do not engage in mutual criticism, and instead honor one another—then even though the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will abide for a long time without perishing.
"Furthermore, good son!

Suppose that when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are also lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) who have deep faith and revere the Buddha-dharma. Those disciples preach the Dharma for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, honoring one another and not engaging in disputes; yet they possess all kinds of impure things and further praise themselves, saying:
'I have attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of an *arhat*.'"
"When the Buddha further enters nirvana, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If, after the Buddha has first appeared and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with deep faith who revere the Buddha-Dharma; if those disciples expound the sūtras and Dharma for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, skillfully cultivate harmony and respect, mutually honor one another, do not store any impure things, and do not claim for themselves the attainment of the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the stage of *arhat*—then even though that Buddha-World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma will abide long in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

Suppose that after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who—even though they do not store impure things and do not claim for themselves the attainment of the stages from *srotāpanna* up to *arhat*—each cling to their own views and offer various divergent explanations, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"

Regarding the four grave offenses established by the Buddhas, up to the seven methods for settling disputes, they are either prohibited or permitted for the sake of sentient beings; the twelve divisions of the scriptures are likewise so.

Why is this? Because the Buddha knows that the lands and seasons differ, and that sentient beings vary in their faculties—whether sharp or dull. For this reason, the Tathāgata sometimes prohibits and sometimes permits, providing teachings of varying gravity.
Good son! It is like a skilled physician who prescribes milk for one illness, yet prohibits milk for another;
he allows its consumption for feverish illnesses, but forbids it for cold-natured illnesses.
The Tathāgata is likewise; observing the roots of the afflictions of all sentient beings, he both permits and prohibits.
Elder, I have personally heard this meaning from the Buddha; only I understand its meaning, whereas you cannot.
"I alone understand the Vinaya, while you cannot;
I know all the sūtras, while you cannot.
When that Buddha passes into extinction, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world.

Furthermore, good son, when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there may be disciples who do not even say, "I have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to that of *arhat*," nor do they say:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, for the sake of sentient beings, sometimes prohibit and sometimes permit."
"Elder! I have personally heard this meaning, this Dharma, and this Vinaya from the Buddha himself, Elder!"
"One should rely upon the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras;
if this meaning is correct, I shall uphold it, but if it is not, I shall discard it.
Although that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma will abide in the world for a long time.

“Good son! When my Dharma is extinguished, there will be śrāvaka disciples who will either say that the self (ātman) exists or say that the self is empty; who will say that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava) or say that there is no intermediate state; who will say that the three times exist or say that the three times do not exist; who will say that the three vehicles exist or say that the three vehicles do not exist; who will say that all things exist or say that all things do not exist; who will say that sentient beings have a beginning and an end or say that sentient beings have neither beginning nor end; who will say that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) or say that dependent origination is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); who will say that the Tathāgata undergoes the practice of illness and suffering or say that the Tathāgata does not undergo the practice of illness and suffering; or who will say that the Tathāgata did not permit bhikṣus to eat ten kinds of meat. What are these ten? [The list of ten meats follows.]”
Humans, snakes, elephants, horses, donkeys, dogs, lions, pigs, foxes, and monkeys—these are all permitted;
however, some say that none at all are permitted.
Some say that a bhikṣu should not perform five things. What are these five?
He shall not sell living beings, knives, wine, curdled milk, sesame oil, and so forth; all other matters are permitted.
Some say that entry into five kinds of dwellings is not permitted; what are these five?
They are the houses of a butcher, a prostitute, a tavern-keeper, a royal palace, and a *caṇḍāla*; entry into all other houses is permitted.
Some say that while wearing *kauseya* (silk) garments is not permitted, everything else is allowed.
Others say that the Tathāgata permitted the bhikṣus to accept and possess clothing, food, and bedding, each valued at one hundred thousand taels of gold;
yet others say this was not permitted.

Some say that nirvana is permanence, bliss, self, and purity; others say that nirvana is simply the exhaustion of the fetters and there is no separate dharma called "nirvana. It is like when threads are woven together they are called a "robe," and once the robe has been destroyed, it is called "no robe"—yet in reality, there is no separate dharma named "no robe. The essence of nirvana is likewise so.
"Good son!
At that time, among my disciples, those who preach correctly will be few while those who preach erroneously will be many;
those who receive the true Dharma will be few while those who receive false teachings will be many."
They accepted the Buddha’s words little and accepted the Māra’s words much.
"Good son! At that time, there were two disciples in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī:
There were two groups: first, the arhats; second, those who had broken the precepts.
There were five hundred followers of those who had broken the precepts, and one hundred followers of the arhats.
Those who had broken the precepts said:
"The Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa; I have personally heard this teaching from the Buddha himself:
regarding the four grave offenses (caturmahāśrāmaṇya) established by the Tathāgata, it is permissible to uphold them, yet even if one commits them, there is no transgression."
I have now also attained the fruit of Arhatship and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Yet even an Arhat may commit such grave offenses as these four heavy rules. If these four heavy rules were truly transgressions, an Arhat would never commit them.
"The Tathāgata, while in the world, established rules that were to be strictly maintained, but at the time of his parinirvāṇa,
he relinquished them all. The Arhat bhikṣu said, "Elder!..."
"You should not say that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa; I know that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging.
Whether the Tathāgata is in the world or after his nirvāṇa, there is no difference regarding the commission of the four grave offenses."
If one says that an Arhat commits the four grave prohibitions, this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because even a Srotāpanna does not violate the prohibitions, how much less so an Arhat?
If an elder says, "I am an Arhat," one who is an Arhat never gives rise to the thought, "I have attained Arhatship.
An Arhat speaks only of wholesome dharmas and does not speak of unwholesome ones.
"What the Elder has spoken is entirely contrary to the Dharma.
If one were to see the twelve divisions of the scriptures, one would certainly know that the Elder is not an Arhat.
"Good son! [The Buddha said: "It is as you say."
At that time, the assembly of precept-breaking bhikṣus together took the life of this arhat.
Good son! At that moment, due to the hearts of anger and resentment of these two assemblies, the Māra King and his followers all joined in harming these six hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, ordinary people will each say together:
"Alas! The Buddha-dharma is now extinguished.
Yet my True Dharma does not truly perish.
At that time, there will be one hundred and twenty thousand great bodhisattvas in that land who skillfully uphold my Dharma; how then can it be said that my Dharma is extinguished?
At that very time, there will not be a single bhikṣu within Jambudvīpa who is my disciple.

At that time, Pāpīyas completely burned all existing scriptures with great fires; those that remained as remnants were then stolen by various brāhmaṇas, who gathered them from various places and incorporated them into their own treatises.
For this reason, when the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, various minor bodhisattvas collectively believed in and accepted the words of the brahmins.
Although those brahmins made such claims as:
"I possess the fasts and precepts."
Yet these various non-Buddhists do not truly possess such things.
Although the non-Buddhists further claim:
"There is a self, pleasure, and purity."
Yet, in reality, they do not understand the meaning of "self," "bliss," and "purity.
They simply take one word, two words, one phrase, or two phrases from the Buddha's teachings and claim, "In my own scriptures, there is such a meaning."
At that time, when the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes in the twin śāla trees of Kuśinagara heard these words, they all cried out together:
"The world is empty! The world is empty!"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the great assembly:
"Do not grieve or weep; the world is not empty, for the Tathāgata abides eternally without change, and it is the same for the Dharma and the Saṃgha."
At that time, having heard these words, the great assembly ceased their weeping and all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 18. *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 19.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On the Holy Life (Brahmacarya), Part Five.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru was of a wicked and evil nature; he delighted in slaughter and possessed the four evils of speech. Greed, anger, and delusion burned fiercely within his mind; seeing only the present and not the future, he surrounded himself exclusively with evil men. Because of his greedy attachment to the pleasures of the five desires of this world, he perversely committed the crime of rebellion against his father, the King, who was innocent.

Having killed his father, remorse and fever arose within him; he no longer wore his various necklaces or enjoyed music. Because of this mental remorse and fever, sores broke out over his entire body, which were so foul-smelling and filthy that one could not approach them.
He then thought to himself:
"This body of mine has already received the 'flower-retribution'; the actual retribution of hell is now drawing near.
At that time, his mother, named Vaidehī, applied various medicinal herbs to it, but the ulcer only increased in severity and did not subside.
The king then said to his mother:
"A sore such as this arises from the mind; it does not originate from the four great elements.
If one says there is anyone who can cure a sentient being [of such a condition], that is impossible."
At that time, there was a great minister named Candraprabha who went to the king’s presence, stood to one side, and said: “Great King,
why are you so dejected and your countenance so displeased?”
"Is it pain in the body,
or is it pain in the heart?
The king then replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?
My father was innocent, yet I have perversely brought about his harm.
From wise men I have heard this principle: there are five kinds of people in the world who do not escape hell—namely, those who commit the five heinous crimes."
I now possess immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sins; how could my body and mind not suffer pain?
Furthermore, there is no skilled physician to treat my body and mind.
The minister said:
"Great King!
Do not grieve so greatly."
He then spoke in verse:
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will eventually increase.
It is like a person who delights in sleep; their sleep then becomes more and more abundant."
"Those who are greedy for lust and addicted to wine are likewise so.
As Your Majesty has said, there are five kinds of people in the world who are not liberated from hell;
who could go see them and return to tell Your Majesty?"
That which is called "hell" is, as those of great wisdom have said, simply this world.

As Your Majesty has stated that there is no skilled physician in the world who can heal both body and mind, there now exists a great physician named Pūraṇa. He possesses all-encompassing knowledge and vision, has attained mastery over meditative concentration, and has ultimately cultivated pure brahmacarya. He constantly expounds for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings the path to unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

For the sake of his disciples, he taught the Dharma in this way: there is no black karma and no retribution for black karma; there is no white karma and no retribution for white karma; there is no karma that is both black and white and no retribution for karma that is both black and white; and there is no superior karma, nor any inferior karma.
"That teacher is currently in the city of Rājagṛha;
I only pray that Your Majesty will deign to go there and have this teacher treat his body and mind.
Then the king replied:
"If you can truly thus extinguish my sins, I shall take refuge in you.
Furthermore, there was another minister named Guṇagupta who went again to the king's presence and spoke these words:
"Great King!

For what reason is your countenance so haggard, your lips and mouth parched and withered, and your voice so faint, like that of a timid man who has encountered a great enemy, with your complexion cracked and weathered?
"What is it that causes you suffering?
Is it pain in the body,
or is it pain in the mind?"
The king replied immediately:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?

Being deluded and blind, lacking the eye of wisdom, I associated with evil friends as my kin and followed the words of the wicked man Devadatta, whereby I have unjustly committed the crime of regicide against a righteous Dharma-king."
In the past, I heard a wise person recite this verse:
"If one conceives unwholesome thoughts toward one's parents, the Buddha, or his disciples,
and gives rise to evil karma, such a retribution shall be experienced in the Avīci Hell."
"Because of this matter, my heart is terrified and great suffering has arisen within me; moreover, there is no skilled physician to provide me with healing.
The minister spoke again:
"I only pray, Great King!"
Do not be distressed or afraid.
There are two kinds of laws:
first, the law of renunciation; second, the law of kings.
As for the laws of kingship: if one harms his father and thereby rules the kingdom, although it is called parricide, in reality there is no sin.

It is like the *kalala* insect, which must destroy its mother’s womb before it can be born; since such is the nature of birth, although it breaks the mother’s body, in reality there is likewise no sin.
The same applies to mares conceiving and so forth.
According to the laws of governing a state, it should be thus: even if one kills one's father or elder brother, there is truly no sin.
However, according to the Dharma of those who have left the household life, there is sin even for killing a mosquito or an ant.
I only pray that Your Majesty will broaden your mind and not grieve. Why is this?
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will eventually increase.
It is like a person who delights in sleep; their sleep becomes more and more abundant.
So it is with lust and the craving for wine."

"As Your Majesty has said, there is no skilled physician in the world who can heal both body and mind; however, there is now a Great Master named Makkhali Gosāla, who possesses all-encompassing knowledge and vision. He regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own infants, has already transcended all afflictions, and is able to extract the sharp arrows of the three poisons from sentient beings."
All sentient beings lack knowledge, vision, and awakening regarding all phenomena; only this one person alone possesses knowledge, vision, and awakening.
Such a Great Teacher constantly preaches this Dharma to his disciples:
"The bodies of all sentient beings consist of seven constituents."
What are the seven?
They are earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life-span.
These seven phenomena are neither transformed nor created, and they cannot be destroyed or harmed.
They are as immovable as the īṣikā grass;
they are like Mount Sumeru, neither abandoning nor creating;
they are like milk and curd, each without contention.
Whether it be suffering or pleasure, whether good or evil, if one were to cast them upon a sharp blade, they would suffer no injury.
Why is this? Because within the seven-part void there is no obstruction.
Life, moreover, is not subject to harm. Why is this?
Because there is neither one who harms nor one who dies.
There is no agent and no recipient; there is no speaker and no listener; there is neither one who remembers nor one who teaches.
Yet this Dharma is constantly expounded, capable of causing sentient beings to extinguish all their immeasurable and heavy transgressions.
"That teacher is now in the great city of Rājagṛha; we only pray that Your Majesty will go to his dwelling!
If Your Majesty should see him, all your transgressions will be extinguished."
The king then replied,
"If you can truly eliminate my sins in this manner, I shall take refuge [in you].
Furthermore, there was another minister named Śuddhilabdha who went before the king and spoke this verse:
"Great King, for what reason have you cast off your necklaces and your hair is disheveled,
even to such an extent?
Why does your body tremble with unease, like a flowering tree shaken by a fierce wind?"
“Great King, why is it that your countenance is so haggard and sorrowful?
You are as distressed as a farmer who, after sowing his seeds, finds no rain from the heavens.
Is this pain in your heart, or is it pain in your body?”
The king replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?

My late father, the former king, was overflowing with compassion and pity; he looked upon me with special affection and care, for I am truly without fault. I once went to consult a physiognomist, and the physiognomist answered:”
"This child, once born, is destined to kill his father.
Although he heard these words, he still continued to provide for him.
It has been heard that the wise have said this:

"If a person commits adultery with their mother or a bhikṣuṇī, steals the property of the Saṃgha, kills one who has resolved upon supreme bodhicitta, or harms their own father—such a person will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell."
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?
The minister spoke again:
"I only pray, Great King!"
Do not grieve or suffer.
If one who has practiced liberation, such as your father the king, were harmed, that would indeed be a transgression;
however, if it is for the sake of governing the state according to the law, killing carries no guilt.
"Great King!
That which is non-Dharma is called 'non-Dharma,' and that which is not the Dharma is called 'not the Dharma.
It is like calling one who has no son 'sonless,' or likewise calling a wicked son 'sonless'; although one says he is sonless, in reality he is not without a son."
Just as food that has no salt is called "saltless," and food with only a little salt is also called "saltless";
or as a river that has no water is called "waterless," and one with only a little water is also called "waterless."
Just as that which perishes moment by moment is called impermanent, so too that which abides for even an eon is called impermanent.
Just as a person who experiences suffering is said to be without pleasure, so too one who experiences even a small amount of pleasure is said to be without pleasure.
Just as that which lacks sovereignty is called "non-self," even that which possesses a slight degree of sovereignty is likewise called "non-self.
It is like how one speaks of there being "no sun" during the darkness of night, and also says there is "no sun" when it is shrouded by clouds and mist.
"Great King!
Although it is said that 'few dharmas' are called 'non-dharmas,' in reality they are not non-dharmas.

I pray that Your Majesty will lend your attention and listen to what your servant says: all sentient beings possess residual karma, and by reason of these karmic conditions, they repeatedly undergo birth and death."
If the former king had any remaining karma, what crime would there be in Your Majesty killing him?
I only pray that Your Majesty will relax your mind and not grieve. Why is this so?
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will eventually increase.
It is like a person who delights in sleep; their sleep then becomes more abundant.
So it is also with greed, lust, and the craving for wine."

"As Your Majesty has said, there is no skilled physician in the world who can heal both body and mind. However, there is now a Great Master named Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, who possesses all-knowing vision; his wisdom is as profound as the great ocean, he wields great majestic power, and is endowed with great supernormal powers, capable of causing sentient beings to leave behind the net of all doubts."
All sentient beings do not know, see, or awaken to this; only this one person alone knows, sees, and awakens to it.
He currently resides nearby in the city of Rājagṛha, preaching such a Dharma to his disciples:
"Among all the multitudes, if there is one who is a king, he possesses sovereign power to act as he pleases, performing both good and evil deeds."
"Even if one commits many evils, there is no sin whatsoever.
Just as fire burns things regardless of whether they are pure or impure, so too is the king; he shares the same nature as fire."

For example, the great earth universally bears both the pure and the impure; though it performs this task, it is from the beginning free from anger or joy. A king is likewise, sharing the same nature as the earth.

For example, the nature of water is such that it washes both the pure and the impure; although it performs this function, it feels neither sorrow nor joy. The King is likewise, sharing the same nature as water.

For example, the nature of the wind blows equally upon the pure and the impure; though it performs these actions, it feels neither sorrow nor joy. The King is likewise, sharing the same nature as the wind.
Just as a tree that has been stripped of its branches in autumn grows back again in spring, even though it was cut down, there is truly no offense in this;
all sentient beings are likewise so. Having ended their lives here, they are born here again; because they are born again, what offense could there be?

The karmic retributions of suffering and happiness for all sentient beings do not arise from the karma of the present life; rather, the causes reside in the past, while the fruits are experienced in the present.
There is no cause in the present, and there will be no fruit in the future.
Because of present results, sentient beings maintain the precepts and diligently cultivate vigor to ward off present evil results.

Because they maintain the precepts, they attain the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); because they attain the outflow-free, they exhaust all outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*); because they exhaust their karma, all suffering comes to an end; and because all suffering has ended, they attain liberation.
"I only pray that Your Majesty will go quickly to his place and have him treat the physical and mental pains; if the King sees him, all transgressions shall be removed.
The King then replied, "If there truly is such a teacher who can eliminate my sins, I shall take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was another minister named Sarvajñārtha who went to the king’s presence and spoke these words:

“Why is it that Your Majesty’s appearance is no longer dignified, like one who has lost his kingdom? You are like a spring that has run dry, a pond without lotuses, or a tree without flowers or leaves—like a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, devoid of majestic virtue?”
"Is it pain in the body,
or is it pain in the mind?
The king immediately replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer now?
My father, the former king, was compassionate and full of concern for me; yet I have been unfilial and failed to repay his kindness."

He constantly sought to bring peace and happiness to me; yet I, in turn, have repaid his kindness with ingratitude by cutting off his joy, bringing baseless and violent harm upon my innocent predecessor, the former king.
I have also heard wise ones say:
"If one harms their father, they shall undergo great suffering for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Before long, I shall surely fall into hell, and there will be no skilled physician to cure my transgression.
The minister then said:
"I only pray, Great King,
that you will abandon your sorrow and suffering."
Has Your Majesty not heard?
In the past there was a king named Rāma, who, having slain his father, succeeded to the throne.

Great King Bimbisāra, King Virūḍhaka, King Nahusa, King Kārtika, King Viśākha, King Candraprabha, King Sūryaprabha, King Priya, and King Bahudhānya—kings such as these all slew their fathers to succeed to the throne, yet not a single one of them entered hell.

In the present, there are kings such as King Vaidūrya, King Uddāna, King Duṣṭa, King Mūṣika, and King Padma; all of these kings have harmed their own fathers, yet not a single one among them has given rise to grief or affliction.
Although one speaks of the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the heavens, who is there to see them?
Great King! There are only two forms of existence: [the present life and the future life].
The first is the human realm, and the second is the animal realm.
Although these two exist, they are not born through causes and conditions, nor do they die through causes and conditions.
If they were not due to causes and conditions, how could there be good and evil?
I only pray, Great King,
that you do not harbor grief or fear. Why is this?
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will eventually increase.
It is like a person who delights in sleep; their sleep then becomes more abundant.
So too it is with lust and the craving for wine."

"As Your Majesty has said, there is no skilled physician in the world who can heal both body and mind; however, there is now a Great Master named Ajita Keśakambala, who possesses all-encompassing knowledge and vision, and regards gold and earth as equal and non-dual."

One person cuts his right flank with a sword, while another anoints his left with sandalwood; toward these two individuals, his mind is without distinction, viewing enemy and kin equally, his heart free from any sign of difference.

This master is truly a skilled physician of the world; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he is constantly in samādhi with an undistracted mind, and he addresses his disciples, saying these words:

"Whether one acts oneself, or instructs another to act; whether one chops oneself, or instructs another to chop; whether one roasts oneself, or instructs another to roast; whether one harms oneself, or instructs another to harm; whether one steals oneself, or instructs another to steal; whether one commits sexual misconduct oneself, or instructs another to do so; whether one speaks falsehoods oneself, or instructs another to speak them; whether one drinks alcohol oneself, or instructs another to drink it; whether one kills a village, a city, or a nation; whether one kills all sentient beings with a wheel of blades; or whether one gives alms to sentient beings south of the Ganges while killing sentient beings north of the Ganges—in all these cases, there is neither sin nor merit, and there is no giving, morality, or meditative concentration."
"He is currently residing nearby in the city of Rājagṛha; I pray that Your Majesty will go there quickly. If Your Majesty should see him, all your sins will be extinguished.
The king said, "Great Minister!"
"If you can truly thus eliminate my sins, I shall take refuge in you.
Furthermore, there was a great minister named Śrīguṇa who went again to the king's presence and spoke these words:
"For what reason does Your Majesty’s face now lack luster, like a lamp in the midday sun, like the moon during the day, like a king who has lost his kingdom, or like a desolate and ruined land?"
"Great King!
Now that the four quarters are peaceful and free from all enemies, for what reason do you now suffer such grief and distress?
Is it suffering of the body?"
"Is it because of mental suffering?
There were certain princes who constantly harbored this thought:
'When shall I now attain sovereignty?'"
"O Great King!
Now your wishes have been fulfilled and you possess sovereign power.

You have inherited the kingdom of Magadha and obtained the entire treasure-store of your predecessors; you should simply take delight in it, indulge your desires, and enjoy happiness. Why do you harbor such sorrow and distress in your heart?"
The king replied immediately:
"Great Minister, how could I not be filled with grief and distress now?"
It is like a foolish person who, craving only the flavor, fails to see the sharp blade; or like one who eats food mixed with poison and fails to perceive its danger.
I am likewise: like a deer seeing grass and failing to see the deep pit, or like a mouse greedy for food and failing to see the cat.
I am also like this: seeing only present pleasure, I do not see the future fruit of unwholesome suffering.
I have heard these words from the wise:
"It would be better to undergo three hundred drillings on a single day than to give rise to a single thought of malice toward one's parents."
"I am now close to the blazing fires of hell; how could I not be filled with grief and distress?
The minister spoke again:
"Who has come to deceive Your Majesty, saying that there is a hell?"
If the point of a thorn is sharp, by whom was it created?
If the colors of flying birds are diverse, by whom were they made?

The nature of water is to moisten and soak; the nature of stone is hardness; the nature of wind is motion; the nature of fire is heat. All myriad things die and are born of themselves—by whom were they made?
As for what is called "hell," it is merely a construction of words by the wise. What is the meaning of the term "hell"?
Your servant shall explain it: "earth" (di) means earth, and "prison" (yu) means to break. Because one breaks the earth-prison and there is no retribution for sin, it is called hell.
Furthermore, "earth" refers to humans, and "prison" refers to the heavens; because he harmed his father, he went to the realms of humans and gods.
For this reason, the seer Vasu proclaimed: "By killing a sheep, one obtains the pleasures of humans and gods"—this is what is called hell.
Furthermore, "earth" (dhi) means life, and "hell" (niraya) means long; because one kills living beings, one obtains a long lifespan, and for this reason it is called hell.
Great King!
Therefore, you should know that in reality there are no hells.
Great King!
It is like sowing barley and obtaining barley, or sowing rice and obtaining rice.
"O Great King! One who kills in hell shall return to hell;
one who kills a human being should likewise receive a human being in return."
Now please listen to what your servant has to say: in reality, there is no killing;
if there were a self, in reality there would still be no harm;
and if there is no self, there is likewise nothing that can be harmed.

Why is this? If there were a self, it would be permanent and unchanging; because it is eternally abiding, it cannot be killed. It is not broken, not destroyed, not bound, not fettered, neither angry nor joyful, just like space. How, then, could there be the transgression of killing?

If there were no self, all phenomena would be impermanent; because they are impermanent, they perish moment by moment. Since they perish moment by moment, both the killer and the victim perish moment by moment. If they perish moment by moment, who could possibly possess guilt?
"Great King!
Just as when fire burns wood, the fire is not guilty;
and just as when an axe chops a tree, the axe is likewise not guilty."
It is like a sickle cutting grass: the sickle is truly without fault.
It is like a knife killing a person: the knife is not a human being. Since the knife is without fault, how can the person be at fault?
Just as poison kills a person, yet the poison itself is not the person, and the poisonous drug is not the crime—how can the person be guilty?
All phenomena are likewise: since there is truly no killing, how can there be guilt?
I only pray, Great King,
that you do not give rise to sorrow and suffering. Why is this?
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will eventually increase.
It is like a person who delights in sleep; their sleep becomes more and more abundant.
Greed, lust, and the craving for wine are also just like this."

"As Your Majesty has said, that there is no skilled physician in the world who can cure those who commit evil deeds—there is now a Great Master named Kātyāyana, who possesses all-knowing vision, clearly understands the three periods of time, and in a single moment can perceive immeasurable and boundless worlds; his hearing is likewise so."
He can cause sentient beings to remain far removed from faults and evils; like the Ganges River, all sins, whether internal or external, are completely purified.
This Great and Worthy Teacher is likewise able to eliminate the manifold sins of sentient beings, both internal and external, and he preaches this Dharma to his disciples:
"If a person were to kill all sentient beings, yet their mind remains without shame or remorse, they would never fall into the evil realms, just as empty space does not receive dust or water."
Those who possess a sense of shame and remorse enter hell, just as great water moistens the earth.
All sentient beings are created by Īśvara; when Īśvara rejoices, sentient beings are at peace and happy;
when Īśvara is angry, sentient beings suffer and are distressed.
If all sentient beings, whether their merit or their transgressions, are the work of the Lord Maheśvara, how can one say that humans possess merit or transgression?
It is like a wooden automaton crafted by a craftsman; it can walk, stand, sit, and lie down, yet it alone cannot speak. Sentient beings are just like this.
The Lord Maheśvara is like the craftsman, and the wooden figure is like the body of a sentient being. In such a creation, who could possibly be guilty of transgression?
"Such a Great Master now resides nearby in the city of Rājagṛha; I only pray that you go quickly, for if you are able to see him, all your transgressions will be extinguished."
The king immediately replied,
"If there truly is such a person capable of extinguishing my sins, I shall take refuge in them.
Furthermore, there was another minister named Abhaya who went to the king's presence and spoke these words:
"Great King!

In this world there are foolish people who, within a single day, experience a hundred joys and a hundred sorrows, a hundred slumbers and a hundred awakenings, and a hundred alarms and a hundred weeps; such things do not occur for those of wisdom."
"Great King! Why do you grieve so deeply?

Are you like a traveler who has lost his companion, or like one fallen into deep mud with no one to pull him out; like a person parched with thirst who cannot find water or broth; like a lost man who has no guide; like a suffering patient who has no physician to treat him; or like a ship at sea that has been wrecked with no one to rescue it?"
"Great King!
Is it now your body that aches,
or is it your heart?"
The king replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?

Having associated with evil friends and failing to guard my speech, I have wantonly committed an act of rebellion against my innocent father, the former king. I know for certain that I shall enter hell, and yet there is no skilled physician to provide me with relief."
The minister immediately replied,
"I only pray, Great King,
that you do not give way to grief and torment."

Now, those of the Kṣatriya caste are known as the royal lineage; whether for the sake of the state, or for the sake of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or to bring peace to the people, even if they commit acts of killing, there is no sin.
Although the former kings venerated śramaṇas, they were unable to serve the brāhmaṇas; because their minds lacked impartiality, they were not true kṣatriyas.
"Great King!
If you have now killed the former king for the sake of making offerings to the brahmins, what sin could there possibly be in this?
Great King!"
In truth, there is no killing.
Now, what is called "killing" is the destruction of life-force.
That which is named "vitality-wind" (prāṇa-vāyu) is by its very nature indestructible; how could the harming of such a life-force entail sin?
I only pray that Your Majesty will no longer grieve and suffer.
For what reason?
"If one is constantly sorrowful, sorrow will eventually increase.
It is like a person who delights in sleep; their sleep then becomes more and more frequent.
So too it is with lust and the craving for wine."

"As Your Majesty has said, there is no skilled physician to provide healing in this world; however, there is now a Great Master named Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, who possesses all-encompassing knowledge and vision, feels compassion for sentient beings, and is well-versed in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. He has mastered all skillful means appropriate to the occasion and cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas. Having cultivated the pure Brahma-faring in tranquility, he speaks thus to his disciples:

'There is no giving, no merit, no father, and no mother; there is no present life nor future life; there are no Arhats; there is no cultivation and no Path. All sentient beings, after eighty thousand kalpas, will naturally be liberated from the wheel of birth and death; whether they have committed offenses or not, it is exactly the same.'"
It is like the four great rivers—namely the Sindhu, the Gaṅgā, the Vakṣu, and the Sītā—all of which enter the great ocean without any distinction between them.
"All sentient beings are likewise so; when they attain liberation, there is no distinction whatsoever.
This teacher currently resides in the city of Rājagṛha. I only wish that Your Majesty would go to him quickly; if you should see him, all your transgressions will be eliminated.
The king replied immediately,
“If there truly is such a teacher capable of removing my transgressions, I shall take refuge in him.
At that time, a great physician named Jīvaka went to the king’s location and said:
“Great King!
Are you sleeping peacefully?
The king then replied with a verse:
"If one can forever sever all afflictions,
And is not stained by attachment to the three realms, Only then does one obtain peaceful sleep.
If one attains Great Nirvana And expounds the most profound meaning,"
One is called a true brāhmaṇa, and thus attains peaceful sleep.
With no evil karma in the body, with the mouth free from the four faults,
and with no net of doubt in the mind, one attains peaceful sleep.
With body and mind free from feverish affliction, dwelling securely in a state of tranquility,
one attains unsurpassed bliss and thus sleeps in peace.
With a mind free from grasping and attachment, one remains far removed from all enemies.
Always living in harmony and free from contention, one can sleep in peace and security.
If one does not commit evil deeds, and the mind always harbors a sense of shame and remorse,
believing that evil has its retribution, then one can sleep in peace and security.
By honoring and supporting one's parents, by not harming a single living being,
and by not stealing the property of others, one obtains peaceful sleep.
By subduing the sensory faculties and associating with virtuous friends, [one attains peace].
Having destroyed the hosts of the four Māras, one attains peaceful sleep;
seeing neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious, nor suffering and pleasure,
for the sake of all sentient beings, one revolves within birth and death.
If one can act in this way, one shall obtain peaceful sleep.
Who obtains peaceful sleep?
It is those who are the Buddhas.
Deeply contemplating the samādhi of emptiness, body and mind are peaceful and unmoving.
Who can sleep in peace and security?
It is the one possessed of loving-kindness and compassion, who constantly practices heedfulness and regards all beings as an only child.
Sentient beings are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance;
Not seeing the fruits of their afflictions, they constantly create various evil karmas, And cannot obtain peaceful sleep.
Whether for the sake of one's own body Or for the bodies of others, [one should act with heedfulness].
One who commits the ten evil deeds cannot sleep in peace.
If one says that for the sake of pleasure there is no fault in killing one’s father,
and follows such an evil teacher, one cannot sleep in peace.
If one eats beyond moderation, or drinks cold beverages in excess,
one will suffer such illness that one cannot sleep in peace. If one commits an offense against the king,
or harbors improper thoughts toward another’s wife, [one will likewise suffer].
And for one traveling on a desolate road, there can be no peaceful sleep.
Until the fruit of observing the precepts has ripened, until the Prince has succeeded to the throne,
and until the thief has secured his plunder, one cannot have peaceful sleep.
“Jīva! My illness is now grave;
because I have committed a wicked and rebellious offense against the King of the True Dharma, no skilled physician, nor any wondrous medicine, incantation, expertise, or nurse can cure me.”
Why is this? My father, the Dharma King, ruled the country according to the Dharma; he was truly without fault, yet I have perversely brought him harm.
Like a fish cast upon dry land, what joy could there possibly be?
Like a deer caught in a snare, it has no joy from the start;
like a person who knows their own life will not last another day;
like a king who has lost his kingdom and fled to foreign lands.
It is like a person hearing that their illness is incurable;
it is like one who has broken the precepts hearing an account of their transgressions.
I have heard this said by wise ones of old:
"If the actions of body, speech, and mind are not pure, one should know that such a person will surely fall into hell.
I am likewise so; how could I possibly obtain peaceful sleep?
"Now I have no unsurpassed Great Physician to expound the medicine of the Dharma and remove the suffering of my illness.
Jīvaka replied, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Although the King has committed a transgression, he has given rise to profound remorse and harbors a sense of shame and humility.
Great King!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always speak these words:"
"There are two pure dharmas that can save sentient beings:
first, a sense of shame (hrī); second, a sense of dread (apatrāpya).
One who possesses a sense of shame does not commit offenses themselves; one who possesses a sense of dread does not incite others to do so."
*Hrī* (shame) is internal self-reproach; *apatrāpya* (embarrassment) is disclosure to others.
*Hrī* is shame before people; *apatrāpya* is shame before the heavens.
These are called *hrī* and *apatrāpya*.
Those who lack a sense of shame and dread are not called human beings; they are called animals.
Because they possess a sense of shame and dread, they are able to revere their parents and teachers;
because they possess a sense of shame and dread, one can speak of having parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth.
"Excellent, Great King!
You possess a sense of shame and remorse.
Listen, Your Majesty, for I have heard the Buddha say:
"The wise have two qualities:
first, they do not commit various evils; second, having committed them, they repent.
The foolish also have two qualities: first, they commit sins; second, they conceal them."

Although one has previously committed evil, if they can later reveal it, repent, feel shame and remorse, and dare not commit it again—just as when a turbid water is placed with a bright pearl, the water becomes clear through the power of the pearl;
or like when smoke and clouds are cleared away, the moon becomes bright and serene.
"It is the same for one who commits evil and is able to repent.
If the king repents and harbors a sense of shame, his transgressions will be immediately extinguished, and he will become pure as before.
"Great King!
There are two kinds of wealth:
first, elephants, horses, and various other livestock; second, gold, silver, and various precious jewels."
"Though elephants and horses may be numerous, they cannot equal a single jewel.
Great King!
It is the same with sentient beings: there is the wealth of evil and the wealth of goodness."
To commit many evils is not as [grave] as failing to perform even one good deed.
Your Majesty, I have heard the Buddha say that cultivating a single virtuous mind destroys a hundred kinds of evil.
Great King!

Just as a small amount of vajra can destroy Mount Sumeru, just as a small fire can burn everything, and just as a small amount of poison can harm sentient beings, so too does a small amount of goodness destroy great evil.
Although it is called "small goodness," in reality it is great.
Why is this? Because it destroys great evil.
"Great King!

As the Buddha has taught, those who conceal their faults have outflows; those who do not conceal them have no outflows. By confessing and repenting for one's transgressions, one therefore remains without outflows."

If one commits various offenses but does not conceal or hide them, because they are not concealed, the offenses will become slight; if one harbors shame and remorse, the offenses will be extinguished.
Great King!
Just as drops of water, though minute, gradually fill a large vessel, so too is the wholesome mind: each individual thought of goodness can destroy great evil.

If one conceals their transgressions, the offenses increase; if one confesses them with shame and remorse, the offenses are extinguished. Therefore, the Buddhas have taught that the wise do not conceal their sins.
Excellent, Great King!
You are able to believe in cause and effect, to believe in karma, and to believe in retribution. I only pray that Your Majesty does not harbor sorrow or fear.

If there are sentient beings who commit various transgressions, yet conceal them without repentance, lacking a sense of shame or remorse, failing to perceive cause and effect as well as karmic retribution, unable to consult those of wisdom and not associating with virtuous friends—such persons cannot be cured by any skilled physician, nor even by those who attend to the sick.
Just as worldly physicians stand with their hands folded in helplessness before one suffering from kāmalā disease, so it is with those who conceal their transgressions.
Who are these transgressing persons?
They are the icchantikas.

An icchantika is one who does not believe in cause and effect, lacks a sense of shame and remorse, does not believe in karmic retribution, does not perceive the present or future worlds, does not associate with virtuous friends, and does not follow the teachings and precepts spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; such a person is called an icchantika and cannot be cured even by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Why is this? Just as a corpse in the world cannot be cured by a physician, so it is with those who hold one-sided views (icchantikas); they cannot be cured even by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Great King, you are not an icchantika now; why do you say that you cannot be healed?

"As Your Majesty has said that there is no one capable of healing [the world], Great King, you should know this: In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a son of King Śuddhodana of the Gautama clan named Siddhārtha. Without a teacher, he attained awakening and spontaneously realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. His body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; he is fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, all-knowing vision, great loving-kindness, and great compassion. He pities all beings as if they were his own son Rāhula, following virtuous beings like a calf follows its mother. He speaks at the proper time and remains silent when it is not the time. His speech is truthful, pure, sublime, meaningful, in accordance with the Dharma, and singular; it enables sentient beings to forever leave behind all afflictions."
He thoroughly understands the faculties and mental natures of sentient beings, and there is no skillful means through which he does not attain mastery.
His wisdom is as lofty and great as Mount Sumeru, and as profound, vast, and far-reaching as the great ocean.
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses vajra-wisdom, which is able to shatter all the evil transgressions of sentient beings; it is impossible that he would be unable to do so.
Now, twelve yojanas from here, between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, he is expounding various teachings for an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya of bodhisattvas:
concerning existence and non-existence, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the outflowing and the non-outflowing.
Outflows (āsrava), whether they be the fruit of afflictions or the fruit of wholesome dharmas;
whether they be material dharmas, non-material dharmas, or neither-material-nor-non-material dharmas; whether they be self, non-self, or neither-self-nor-non-self;
whether they be permanent, impermanent, or neither-permanent-nor-impermanent; or whether they be pleasure—
Whether it be pleasure, or neither pleasure nor non-pleasure; whether it be a characteristic, or no characteristic, or neither characteristic nor non-characteristic;
whether it be cessation, or non-cessation, or neither cessation nor non-cessation;
whether it be worldly, or supramundane, or neither worldly nor supramundane; whether it be a vehicle, or no vehicle—

It is neither a vehicle nor a non-vehicle; it is neither that one acts and receives the fruit oneself, nor that one acts and another receives the fruit, nor that there is no action and no receiving of the fruit.
Great King!
"If one hears of non-action and non-reception in the presence of the Buddha, all grave offenses shall immediately be extinguished.
Your Majesty, listen now: when Śakra Devānām Indra’s life was about to end, five signs appeared:

first, his garments became soiled and greasy; second, the flowers upon his head withered; third, his body emitted a foul odor; fourth, sweat broke out from beneath his arms; and fifth, he no longer took pleasure in his own seat."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, whether in a secluded place or upon seeing a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, would immediately go to their location and conceive the thought that they were the Buddha.
Then, when those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas saw Śakra approaching, they felt deep personal joy and spoke these words:
"O Lord of Devas!..."
"I now take refuge in you.
Having heard this, Śakra realized he was not the Buddha.
He then thought to himself:
"If he were not a Buddha, he would not be able to cure me of these five signs of decline.
At that time, a minister named Pañcaśikha said to Śakra: "Kauśika!..."
There is a gandharva king named Dundubhi; that king has a daughter named Subhadrā. If the King would grant this daughter to me, I shall show the King the signs of the removal of his misfortune.
Śakra replied: "Good man!

Vemacitrin, the King of the Asuras, has a daughter named Śacī, whom I hold in high esteem. If you can truly show me the place where evil signs are extinguished, I shall grant her to you; how much more so, then, Subhadra?"

“Kauśika! There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Śākyamuni, who is currently in the great city of Rājagṛha. If you can go there to consult him regarding what you have not yet heard, the signs of your decline and disappearance will surely be extinguished.”
“Good son! If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is truly able to extinguish [the fire], you may turn your carriage and proceed to his dwelling place.

The charioteer, having received this command, immediately turned the vehicle and arrived at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha. Reaching the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among devas and humans, who is bound?
“Kauśika! [the Buddha replied.]
"Avarice, greed, and envy.
He further asked:
"From what do avarice, greed, and envy arise?"
He replied:
"It arises because of ignorance.
He further said:
"From what cause, furthermore, does ignorance arise?
He replied,
"It arises from negligence."
Again he asked:
"From what does negligence further arise?
He replied:
"It arises from inversion.
Furthermore, it was asked:
"From what, in turn, does inversion arise?"
He replied,
"It arises from the mind of doubt.
[The Buddha said,] "World-Honored One!"
That the dharma of perversion arises from doubt is indeed as the holy teaching declares. Why is this?
I have a doubting mind;
because of this doubting mind, perversion arises, such that regarding one who is not the World-Honored One, I conceive the notion that he is the World-Honored One.

Now that I have seen the Buddha, the net of doubt has been removed; because the net of doubt is removed, my perversions are also exhausted; because my perversions are exhausted, I am free from stinginess and even free from envy.
The Buddha said:
"As for your statement that you have no mind of stinginess or envy, have you now attained the stage of Anāgāmin? For one who is an Anāgāmin is free from a mind of craving."
"If he has no mind of greed, why would he come to my place for the sake of his life?
Yet, an Anāgāmin truly does not seek life. [The disciple asked:
"World-Honored One!"
Those who possess perversion seek their own lives; those free from perversion do not seek their own lives.
Now, I truly do not seek my life; that which I seek is solely the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Buddha’s wisdom.
“Kauśika! If you seek the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Buddha’s wisdom, you shall certainly attain them in a future age.

When Śakra had heard these words of the Buddha, the five signs of impending death immediately vanished. He then rose, prostrated himself, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have now died and been reborn; I have lost my life and regained it. Furthermore, hearing the Buddha’s prediction that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is for me a further birth and a further gaining of life.”
World-Honored One!
How do all humans and devas increase?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do they suffer diminution?
"Kauśika! Through the causes and conditions of strife and contention, humans and devas diminish;
by skillfully cultivating harmony and respect, they attain increase."
“World-Honored One!
If it causes harm and decline through strife and contention, from this day forward I shall no longer wage war against the asuras.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught the Dharma of patience; this is the cause of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and then departed.
Great King!
Because the Tathāgata is able to eliminate all evil signs, he is thus called the inconceivable Buddha.
If Your Majesty goes there, all your grave sins will surely be eradicated.
Great King, listen: there was the son of a brahmin named Ahimsaka, who was called Aṅgulimāla because he had killed immeasurable sentient beings.

Furthermore, when he again desires to harm his mother and an evil mind arises, his body also moves accordingly; this movement of both body and mind constitutes the cause for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and because of these causes for the five heinous crimes, he will inevitably fall into hell.

Later, when he sees the Buddha, both his body and mind are stirred, and he again desires to cause harm; this stirring of body and mind is the very cause of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and because of these causes for the five heinous crimes, he shall enter hell.

This person, having encountered the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, immediately extinguishes the causes and conditions for rebirth in hell and gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the six teachers.
"Great King! Furthermore, there was Prince Subhira; his father, out of anger toward him, cut off his hands and feet and pushed him into a deep well.
His mother, moved by compassion, had someone pull him out and brought him to the presence of the Buddha."
Upon seeing the Buddha, his hands and feet were restored, and he immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King!
Because he saw the Buddha, he obtained this visible retribution; therefore, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the six teachers.
“Great King!

Suppose there were five hundred hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges who, for immeasurable years, had never seen water; though they arrived at the riverbank, they saw only flowing fire, and being tormented by hunger and thirst, they cried out in lamentation.”
At that time, the Tathāgata was by the side of the river, in a forest of Udumbara trees, sitting beneath a single tree.
Then, various hungry ghosts came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We are parched with hunger and thirst; our lives will soon come to an end.
The Buddha said, "Why do you not drink the flowing waters of the Ganges?"
The ghost immediately replied,
"Where the Tathāgata sees water, I see fire.
The Buddha said:
"The clear flow of the Ganges is truly without fire; it is because of evil karma that your minds are inverted, leading you to perceive it as fire.
I shall eliminate this inversion for you and cause you to see the water."
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively explained the faults of stinginess and greed for the sake of the various hungry ghosts.
The ghosts then said:
"We are now parched with thirst; although we have heard the words of the Dharma, they do not enter our minds at all."
The Buddha said,
"If you are thirsty and exhausted, you may enter the river first and drink as much as you desire.
By the power of the Buddha, those hungry ghosts were immediately able to drink the water.

Once they had drunk the water, the Tathāgata further preached the Dharma to them in various ways; having heard the Dharma, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, cast off their forms as hungry ghosts, and attained celestial bodies.
"Great King!
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the six teachers.
Great King!"
Five hundred bandits from the kingdom of Śrāvastī had their eyes gouged out by King Prasenajit; having no one to lead them, they were unable to proceed to the place where the Buddha was.
Out of compassion, the Buddha went to where the bandits were and consoled them, saying:
"Good sons! Guard your body and speech well; do not commit further evil."
As soon as the bandits heard the Tathāgata’s voice—subtle, exquisite, and pure—they immediately regained their sight.
They then joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated to him, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I now know that the Buddha’s compassionate heart universally covers all sentient beings, not only humans and devas.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately preached the Dharma for them.
Having heard the Dharma, they all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed, excellent physician of the world, and not the six teachers.
"Great King!

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī there was a caṇḍāla named Āśvāsa, who had killed immeasurable people. Upon seeing the Buddha’s disciple Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he immediately attained the causes and conditions for the dissolution of his hellish state and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Because there are such noble disciples, the Buddha-Tathāgata is praised as the unsurpassed physician, and not the six teachers.
"Great King!
In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of an elder named Ajita, who committed incest with his mother; for this reason, he murdered his father."
His mother, moreover, committed adultery with another man; once the son learned of this, he killed her.
He had an arhat who was his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); feeling shame before this friend as well, he then killed him too.
Having committed the murder, he went immediately to the Jetavana Monastery seeking to leave the household life.
At that time, the bhikṣus were fully aware that this man had committed three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma), and none dared to grant him admission.
Because he was not permitted [to leave], his anger redoubled; that very night, he set a great and fierce fire, burning down the monastic quarters and killing many who were innocent.
Thereafter, he went again to the city of Rājagṛha, approached the Tathāgata, and sought with piteous entreaty to go forth as a monk.

The Tathāgata immediately granted his consent and expounded for them the essentials of the Dharma, causing their grave offenses to gradually diminish and leading them to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Good Physician of the World, and not one of the six teachers.
"Great King!
Your nature was originally violent and evil; you believed the wicked man Devadatta and released a large, intoxicated elephant, intending to have it trample the Buddha."
Once the elephant had seen the Buddha, he immediately attained awakening.
The Buddha then extended his hand and stroked the top of its head, and further preached the Dharma for it, causing it all to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Great King!
Even animals, upon seeing the Buddha, can destroy the karmic fruits of their animal existence; how much more so for humans?
Great King, you should know that if one sees the Buddha, all heavy sins will surely be extinguished."
“Great King!
Before the World-Honored One had attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Māra arrived at the Bodhisattva’s dwelling with immeasurable and boundless retinues.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva, by the power of patience, destroyed the evil mind of Māra and caused him to receive the Dharma; immediately thereafter, Māra gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha possesses such great power of merit.
"Great King! There is a wilderness spirit who frequently harms sentient beings."
At that time, the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the elder Bhadra at the village of Śūrpāraka.
When the Śūrpāraka ghost heard the Dharma, he rejoiced and immediately entrusted the elder to the Tathāgata; thereafter, he gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Great King!
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a butcher named Viśālakṣa who slaughtered countless sheep every day.

Upon seeing Śāriputra, he immediately received the eight precepts for one day and one night. By virtue of this cause and condition, at the end of his life, he attained rebirth as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Northern Heavenly King.”
"If even a disciple of the Tathāgata possesses such great fruits of merit, how much more so the Buddha himself?
'Great King!
In Northern India there is a city named Sūkṣmaśarkara; in that city there was a king named Nāgamudrā, who, out of greed for his kingdom and high status, murdered his own father.'"

Having harmed his father, he felt remorse and regret in his heart; he immediately relinquished the administration of the kingdom and came to the Buddha’s presence, seeking compassionate permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
He immediately became a bhikṣu; his grave offenses were extinguished, and he resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Great King, you should know that the Buddha possesses such immeasurable and boundless fruits of great merit.
“Great King!

The Tathāgata had a younger brother named Devadatta, who caused a schism in the Saṃgha, drew blood from the body of the Buddha, and killed the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, thereby committing three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma).”
The Tathāgata expounds various essential teachings for them, causing their grave offenses to quickly become light and diminished.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is a great and excellent physician, not like the six teachers.
“Great King!
If you can believe my words, I pray that you go quickly to the presence of the Tathāgata; if you do not believe me, I pray that you reflect upon this well.”
"Great King!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cover all with great compassion without limiting it to a single person. Their True Dharma is vast and expansive, encompassing everything without exception; they regard enemies and kin with equality, their hearts free from hatred or affection. They never, for the sake of one person alone, cause them to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while others do not."

The Tathāgata is not merely the teacher of the fourfold assembly; he is the universal teacher of all devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth. All sentient beings should likewise regard the Buddha as they would their own parents.
Great King, you should know that the Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma solely for noble and eminent persons such as King Bimbisāra, but also for those of lowly birth such as Upāli.
He did not only accept the food offered by the wealthy Sudatta and Anāthapiṇḍada, but also accepted the food of the poor man Sudatta.
He did not only preach the Dharma for those of sharp faculties such as Śāriputra, but also for those of dull faculties such as Cūḍapanthaka.
Not only did he permit those of a non-attached nature, such as Mahākāśyapa and others, to leave the household life and seek the Way, but he also permitted the highly lustful Nanda to do so.

Not only did he permit those with thin afflictions, such as Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and others, to leave the household life and seek the Way, but he also permitted Udāyin, the younger brother of King Prasenajit, who possessed deep and heavy afflictions and had committed grave offenses, to leave the household life and seek the Way.
He does not merely receive reverent offerings of *śara* grass to uproot the root of anger; rather, he disregards and does not rescue those such as Aṅgulimāla who harbor evil intentions to cause harm.
He expounds the Dharma not only for wise men, but also for women who are utterly foolish or of mixed intelligence.
Not only does he cause those who have left the household life to attain the fruits of the four paths, but he also causes those remaining in the household to attain the fruits of the three paths.

Not only does he preach the essentials of the Dharma for those such as Puṇḍravardhana, who have abandoned all worldly affairs to dwell in quietude and contemplation, but he also preaches the essentials of the Dharma for those such as King Bimbisāra, who govern state affairs and manage royal duties.
It was preached not only for those who have renounced alcohol, but also for the householder Ugga, who was intoxicated with wine;
and not only for those who have entered meditative concentration, such as Revata and others, but also for the Brahmin woman Visākhā, whose mind was distraught by the loss of her son.
He does not teach only his own disciples, but also speaks for the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas;
he does not teach only those in the prime of life at twenty-five, but also speaks for the aged at eighty.
He does not speak solely for those whose faculties are mature, but also for those whose roots of goodness are not yet mature;
he does not speak solely for Queen Mallikā, but also for the courtesan Utpalavarṇā.
Not only did he receive the exquisite delicacies offered by King Prasenajit, but he also received the food mixed with poison provided by the householder Śrigupta.

Your Majesty should know that in the past, Śrigupta also committed the causes for a heinous crime; however, upon encountering the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Great King!

Even if one were to constantly provide clothing and food to all sentient beings with reverence and support for an entire month, it would not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit obtained by someone who recollects the Buddha in a single thought-moment."
"Great King!

Even if one were to fashion figures of humans, chariots, and horses out of gold, each carrying a hundred treasures, and give them as alms, it would not equal the merit of someone who resolves their mind upon the Buddha and takes a single step toward him."
"Great King!

Even if one were to take a hundred chariots drawn by elephants, laden with various kinds of rare treasures from the Great Qin kingdom, and likewise a hundred women adorned with necklaces and ornaments, and offer them as alms, it would still not equal taking a single step toward the Buddha after having resolved the mind [on enlightenment]."

Setting this matter aside, even if one were to provide the four requisites of support to all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm, it would still not equal taking a single step toward the Buddha after having resolved to attain enlightenment.

Setting this matter aside, even if you, Great King, were to provide offerings and pay homage to immeasurable sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, it would not equal going once to the twin śāla trees to the place where the Tathāgata resides and listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
At that time, the Great King replied: "Jīvaka!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is by nature already disciplined and gentle; therefore, he has attained a retinue who are likewise disciplined and gentle."
Just as a sandalwood forest is surrounded exclusively by sandalwood trees,
so too is the Tathāgata pure, and all his retinue is likewise pure.
He is like a great nāga king, whose followers consist exclusively of nāgas.
The Tathāgata is tranquil, and his retinue is likewise tranquil.
The Tathāgata is free from greed, and his retinue is likewise free from greed.
The Buddha is without afflictions, and his retinue is likewise without afflictions.
Since I am now an utterly evil person, bound by evil karma, my body foul and impure, and destined for hell, how could I possibly reach the presence of the Tathāgata?
"If I were to go there, I fear they would not deign to receive me or engage in conversation.
Although you have exhorted me to go to the Buddha's dwelling, today I feel a deep sense of self-reproach and remorse, and I have no desire at all to go."
At that moment, a voice suddenly issued from the void, saying: "The unsurpassed Buddha-dharma is about to decline and perish;

the profound river of Dharma is on the verge of drying up. The great lamp of the True Dharma will soon be extinguished; the mountain of Dharma is about to crumble and the ship of Dharma is about to sink.
