The bridge of Dharma is about to break, the palace of Dharma is about to collapse, the banner of Dharma is about to fall, and the tree of Dharma is about to snap. Good friends are about to depart, and great terror is imminent. Before long, sentient beings who are starving for the Dharma will arrive; the pestilence of afflictions is about to spread. The time of great darkness has come, and the time of thirsting for the Dharma has arrived. The Māra King rejoices and casts off his armor; the Sun of the Buddha is about to set behind the mountain of Great Nirvāṇa."
"Great King!
If the Buddha were to pass away from this world, there would be no one left to remedy Your Majesty’s grave evils.
Great King!"
"You have now committed the most grievous karma for the Avīci Hell; by reason of this karma, you will certainly undergo its retribution without doubt.
Great King!
'A' means 'non-existent,' and 'vīci' is called 'interval'; because there is no interval of even momentary pleasure, it is named 'Avīci' (Without Interval)."
"Great King!

Suppose a single person were alone to fall into this hell; his body would become eighty thousand yojanas in height and breadth, filling the entire space so that no void remains, and his body would undergo various sufferings all around. Even if many people were to fall there, their bodies would likewise fill the space without obstructing one another."
"O Great King!
In the cold hells, encountering a warm breeze even for a moment is regarded as pleasure;
in the hot hells, encountering a cool breeze even for a moment is likewise called pleasure."
"In the Reviving Hell, even after life has ended, if one hears the sound of 'revive,' one immediately returns to life;
in the Avīci Hell, however, there is nothing of this kind.
Great King!"

The Avīci Hell has gates on its four sides; outside each gate there is a fierce fire that spreads across the east, west, south, and north, penetrating eighty thousand yojanas. Iron walls surround it, and iron nets cover it entirely; the ground is also iron, with the fires above reaching down and the fires below reaching up.
"Great King!
Just as when a fish is on a griddle and its fat and grease sizzle and burn, so too it is with these offenders here.
Great King!"

If one commits a single transgression, one shall fully undergo such a punishment; if one commits two transgressions, it is doubled; and if one commits all five transgressions, the punishment is likewise fivefold.
"Great King!
I now know for certain that Your Majesty’s evil karma cannot possibly be avoided.
I only pray that Your Majesty will go quickly to the presence of the Buddha; apart from the World-Honored Buddha, there is no one else capable of saving you."
"I now pity you and therefore exhort and guide you.
When the great king heard these words, his heart was filled with dread; his entire body trembled, and his five limbs shook like a plantain tree.
Looking up, he replied, "Who are you?"
“I do not manifest a physical form, but there is only sound.
“Great King! I am your father, Bimbisāra.”
"You should now follow what Jīvaka has said; do not follow the words of the six ministers who hold false views.

When the king heard this, he fainted and fell to the ground; his bodily sores worsened, and their foul stench became twice as intense as before. Although he applied cooling medicines to treat them, the steaming heat and venom of the sores only increased and did not diminish.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Nineteen;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight on the Holy Life, Part Six.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing King Ajātaśatru lying prostrate on the ground in a state of fainting between the twin trees, immediately addressed the great assembly:
"I shall now remain in this world for the sake of this king until immeasurable kalpas have passed, and I will not enter parinirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Tathāgata should not enter nirvana for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, why do you specifically do so for King Ajātaśatru?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

In this great assembly, there is not a single person who thinks that I have definitely entered parinirvāṇa; it is King Ajātaśatru alone who believes that I shall certainly and forever cease to exist, and for this reason he has fainted and thrown himself to the ground.”
"Good son!
As I have said, Ajātaśatru does not enter parinirvāṇa.
You have not yet been able to understand such a hidden meaning."
Why is this? When I speak of "those who act," I refer to all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
As for Ajātaśatru, he represents all those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*).
Furthermore, those who are "conditioned" are all sentient beings of the conditioned realm.
I do not abide in the world for the sake of unconditioned sentient beings. Why is this?
Now, that which is "non-action" (wuwei) is not the sentient being.
Ajātaśatru is precisely one who is fully possessed of afflictions and the like.
Furthermore, that which "acts" is precisely the sentient being who does not see the Buddha-nature.
If one sees the Buddha-nature, I shall ultimately not remain in the world for long.
Why is this? One who sees the Buddha-nature is no longer a sentient being.
Ajātaśatru refers to all those who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, "those who act" refers to the two assemblies of Ānanda and Kāśyapa.
"Ajātaśatru" refers to King Ajātaśatru, the ladies of his harem, and all the women of the city of Rājagṛha.
Furthermore, "to act as" (wei) is termed "Buddha-nature."
"Aja" means "unborn," and "loka" means "enemy. Because the Buddha-nature is unborn, the enemy of afflictions arises; because the enemy of afflictions arises, one does not see the Buddha-nature.
Because afflictions do not arise, one sees the Buddha-nature; because one sees the Buddha-nature, one attains abiding in Great Parinirvāṇa.
This is called "non-arising"; therefore, he is named Ajātaśatru. Good son! "Aja" means non-arising;

"non-arising" means nirvāṇa. "Śatru" refers to worldly dharmas; "vīra" means unstained, because he is unstained by the eight worldly dharmas, and thus for immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he does not enter nirvāṇa.
Therefore, I say that for Ajātaśatru, there shall be no entry into nirvāṇa for immeasurable billions of kalpas. Good son!

The secret words of the Tathāgata are inconceivable; the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are also inconceivable; the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also inconceivable; and the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Greatly Compassionate Guide, entered the Moon-Love Samādhi for the sake of King Ajātaśatru.

Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance; the light was cool and refreshing, shining upon the king’s body so that his sores were immediately healed and his feverish distress was extinguished.
When the King awoke, his wound had healed and his body felt cool and refreshed. He spoke to Jīvaka, saying:
"I have heard it said that when the end of a kalpa is near, the three calamities appear simultaneously; at such a time, the sufferings and ailments of all sentient beings are entirely removed."
"The time has not yet arrived; from where does this light come to shine upon and touch my body, such that the pain of my sores is healed and I have attained peace and happiness?
Jīvaka replied, "This is not the three moons shining together at the end of a kalpa, nor is it the light of fire, the sun, the stars, medicinal herbs, precious gems, or celestial radiance."
The king asked again:
"If this light is neither from three moons shining together nor from the brilliance of a precious gem, whose light is it?

"Great King, you should know that this is the radiance emitted by the God among Gods. This light has no root and no limit; it is neither hot nor cold, neither permanent nor subject to cessation, neither form nor formless, neither with marks nor markless, neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white."

In order to deliver sentient beings, he causes them to be visible, possessing marks that can be described, having faculties, boundaries, heat and cold, and colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
"Great King!
Although this light is thus, it is truly ineffable and invisible; it possesses not even the qualities of blue, yellow, red, or white.
The King said:
“Jīva! For what reason and by what causal conditions has that God among Gods emitted this radiance? “Great King!”
This present auspicious sign is for the sake of the Great King.

Because the King previously stated that there is no skilled physician in the world to heal both body and mind, this light has been emitted to first treat the King’s body and subsequently to treat his mind.
The king said, "Jīvaka!
Does the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, also hold me in his thoughts?"
Jīvaka replied:
"Suppose a man has seven sons, and among these seven sons, one falls ill. Although the parents' hearts are not unequal toward them, their concern for the sick son is particularly great."
"Great King!

The Tathāgata is likewise; he is not unequal toward all sentient beings. However, his mind inclines toward those who have committed offenses; the Buddha regards with compassionate mindfulness those who are heedless, while he lets go of those who are not heedless."
Who is called one who is heedful?
It is the Bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage,
Great King!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not regard the lineage, age—whether old, young, or middle-aged—wealth or poverty, the seasons, days, months, or constellations, nor skillful arts, low status, or servitude of male and female attendants when it comes to sentient beings; they regard only whether a sentient being possesses a virtuous mind. If there is a virtuous mind, they then regard them with compassion.
"Great King, you should know that such an auspicious sign as this is the radiance emitted by the Tathāgata when he enters the Moon-Love Samādhi (Candrakānta-samādhi).
The King then asked:
"What is meant by the Moon-Love Samādhi?"
Jīva replied, “It is like the moonlight, which can cause all the utpala flowers to bloom with brilliant clarity;
the Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise able to cause the virtuous minds of sentient beings to bloom. For this reason, it is called the Moon-Love Samādhi.”
"Great King!
Just as the moonlight can cause joy to arise in the hearts of all those traveling on the road, so too is the Moon-Love Samādhi (Candrakānta-samādhi):
it can cause joy to arise in the hearts of those who cultivate the path to Nirvāṇa. For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi."
"Great King!
It is like the moonlight, which from the first day until the fifteenth day, gradually increases in form, color, and radiance;

the Moon-Love Samādhi is also like this, causing the roots of goodness of those who have first resolved their minds to gradually increase, until they are fully endowed with Great Parinirvāṇa. For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi."
"Great King!
It is like the moonlight, which from the sixteenth day until the thirtieth day, gradually diminishes in form, color, and radiance;
the Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise. Wherever its light shines, all afflictions are caused to gradually perish; for this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi."
"Great King!
It is like the time of intense heat, when all sentient beings constantly long for the moonlight; once the moonlight shines upon them, their stifling heat is immediately dispelled.
The Moon-Love Samādhi is also like this, for it can cause sentient beings to eliminate the feverish affliction of greed."
"Great King!
It is like the full moon, the king among all the stars, which is the flavor of ambrosia and is beloved by all sentient beings;
the Moon-Love Samādhi is also like this. It is the king among all virtues, the flavor of ambrosia, and is beloved by all sentient beings; for this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi."

The king said, "I have heard that the Tathāgata does not dwell, sit, rise, speak, or converse with evil people; he is like the great ocean that does not harbor a corpse, like the ruddy sheldrake that does not dwell in a latrine, like Śakra-devendra who does not live among ghosts, or like the kuśīra bird that does not perch on a withered tree.
The Tathāgata is likewise. How then shall I be able to go and see him?"
If I were to see him, would my body not sink into the earth?
As I observe the Tathāgata, I would rather approach a drunken elephant, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, or a fierce fire with its blazing flames than ever approach one who commits grave evils.
"Therefore, having reflected upon this, with what state of mind should I go to see the Tathāgata?
Jīvaka replied, "Great King!"

For example, as one who is thirsty hastens toward a clear spring, the hungry seeks food, the terrified seeks rescue, the sick seeks a skilled physician, the heat-stricken seeks cool shade, and the cold-stricken seeks fire; so too should Your Majesty now seek the Buddha.
"Great King!

The Tathāgata still expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma even for those such as the icchantikas; how much more so for Your Majesty, who are not an icchantika—how could you fail to receive his compassionate salvation?"
The King said, "Jīvaka!

I have heard in the past that those who are icchantikas do not believe or hear, cannot investigate, and do not attain the underlying principles; for what reason does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma for them?"
Jīvaka replied: "Great King!
It is as if there were a man who had contracted a grave illness, and in a dream during the night, this man ascended a hall supported by a single pillar and partook of—"
Anointing their bodies with ghee and fat, lying in ashes and eating ashes, climbing up withered trees, or wandering, sitting, and sleeping with monkeys;
sinking into water or mud, falling from towers, palaces, high mountains, and trees;
[becoming] elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; wearing garments of blue, yellow, red, and black; and delighting in laughter and song.
While dancing, they may see crows, vultures, foxes, and similar creatures; their teeth and hair fall out; they become naked and lie upon dogs in filth and excrement;
furthermore, they walk, stay, sit, and rise together with the deceased, holding hands and eating with them;
they pass through paths filled with venomous snakes; or again, they dream of embracing women with disheveled hair.
Wearing garments made of *tāla* tree leaves, he traveled toward the true south riding a dilapidated donkey cart.

After this dream, the man’s mind was filled with distress; because of that distress, his physical illness increased further, and as his illness grew worse, his family and relatives sent a messenger to summon a physician.

The messenger he dispatched was deficient in physical form, with incomplete sense organs; his head was covered in dust and dirt, he wore tattered and ruined clothes, and he drove an old, broken-down cart. He spoke to that physician, saying:
"Quickly, climb onto the cart!"
At that time, the skilled physician reflected to himself:
"Now that I have seen this messenger, his appearance is inauspicious; I know that the patient will be difficult to treat."
He further thought:
"Although the messenger is not auspicious, I shall consult the calendar again to see if the illness can be treated.
If it be the fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, or fourteenth day—on such days as these, the disease is difficult to cure."
He further thought: "Although the day is inauspicious, I shall consult the stars to see if it can be treated.
If it is the time of Mars, Venus, the Pleiades (Kṛttikā), the planet Yama, the planet Śeṣa, or the full moon star—if it is at such a stellar hour, the illness will also be difficult to cure."
He further thought:

"Although the stars are inauspicious, one must also observe the time. If it is autumn or winter, or at the time of sunset, midnight, or the moon's setting, one should know that this illness will also be difficult to treat."
He further said:

"Regarding these various signs, although they may be inauspicious or uncertain as to whether they are fixed or not, one should observe the patient: if they possess merit and virtue, they can all be healed; if they lack merit and virtue, what benefit is there even if the signs are auspicious?"
Having reflected thus, he immediately set out with the messenger; while on the road, he thought again:
"If that patient possesses the signs of longevity, they can be treated; if they possess the signs of a short lifespan, they cannot be cured."

Then, on the road ahead, he saw two young children pulling each other in a quarrel, seizing one another by the head and tearing out their hair, striking each other with tiles, stones, knives, and staves. He saw someone holding fire that was naturally extinguished; or he saw someone cutting down trees; or again, he saw a person dragging a hide along the road; or he saw objects left scattered upon the path; or he saw someone carrying an empty vessel; or he saw a *śramaṇa* walking alone without a companion; furthermore, he saw tigers, wolves, crows, vultures, and wild foxes. Having seen these things, he thought again:
"The messenger I sent, as well as all these signs encountered on the road, are entirely inauspicious. One should know that the patient will certainly be difficult to cure."
Again he thought:
"If I do not go, I am no good physician; yet if I do go, I cannot cure him.
He reflected once more:
"Although these various omens are inauspicious, let us set them aside for now and proceed to the place of the illness.

Having thought this, he further heard such sounds along the way—namely, those of loss, death, collapse, fracture, stripping away, falling, burning, non-arrival, incurability, and inability to provide rescue.

Furthermore, he hears the sounds of flying birds in the south—namely the sounds of crows, vultures, and śarabha birds—as well as dogs, rats, wild foxes, rabbits, and pigs; having heard these sounds, he again reflects:
"One should know that this patient is difficult to treat."

“At that time, he immediately entered the patient’s residence and saw that the patient experienced frequent chills and fevers, suffered from aching joints, had red eyes with streaming tears, heard external sounds in his ears, and endured a constricted and painful throat. His tongue was cracked and split, its color pitch black; he could not support his own head, his body was withered and lacked perspiration, and his excrement and urine were obstructed and did not pass. His body suddenly became swollen and unusually reddish; his voice was uneven, sometimes coarse and sometimes thin; his entire body was mottled with spots of various colors, such as blue and yellow; his abdomen was distended and full, and he could not speak clearly.”
Having seen this, the physician asked the attendant:
"What was the patient's state of mind since yesterday?
The attendant replied:
“Great Master!

This person originally revered and had faith in the Triple Gem and the various devas, but now that has changed; his feelings of reverence and faith have ceased. He formerly delighted in giving, but now he is stingy;

his original nature was to eat little, but now he eats excessively; his original nature was corrupt and evil, but now he is harmonious and kind; his original nature was compassionate, filial, and respectful toward his parents, but now he has no heart of reverence for his parents.”

Having heard this, the physician immediately stepped forward to smell it. He smelled the fragrance of *utpala* lotuses, *agaru* (aloe) incense, *piṅgaka* incense, *tagara* incense, *tamālapatra* incense, saffron, and sandalwood; he also smelled the stench of roasted meat, the stench of grape wine, the stench of burnt tendons and bones, the stench of fish, and the stench of excrement. Having discerned the fragrances and stenches, he then stepped forward to touch the body. He felt the body to be as fine and soft as silk, cotton, or *karpāsa* flowers; yet at other times it was as hard as stone, as cold as ice, as hot as fire, or as rough as sand.

At that time, having observed these various signs, the skilled physician knew for certain that the patient would surely die without doubt; yet he did not say definitively that the man was to die, but spoke to the caregiver:
"I have urgent business now and shall come again tomorrow; provide whatever is required according to his needs, allowing him full liberty without restraint."
He then returned home.
The next day, when the messenger arrived, he spoke to him again, saying:
"My business is not yet finished, and furthermore, the medicine has not yet been compounded."
"The wise should know that such a patient will surely die; there is no doubt.
"Great King!
The World-Honored One is likewise: regarding those of the icchantika class, he thoroughly understands their faculties and natures and accordingly preaches the Dharma for them."

Why is this? If [the Tathāgata] were not to preach for them, all ordinary beings would say that the Tathāgata lacks great compassion; yet one who possesses compassion is called "All-Knowing. If he lacked compassion, how could he be called an All-Knowing One?
Therefore, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for the sake of icchantikas.
Great King!
When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, sees those who are ill, he constantly bestows the medicine of the Dharma; if the sick do not take it, it is not the fault of the Tathāgata.
"Great King!
There are two categories among those who hold extreme views (icchantikas):
first, those who possess roots of goodness in the present life; second, those who will possess roots of goodness in future lives."
The Tathāgata, knowing well those of the icchantika class who are able to acquire roots of goodness in the present, preaches the Dharma for them;
he also preaches the Dharma for those who will acquire them in future lives, so that although there is no benefit now, it serves as a cause for the future.
For this reason, the Tathāgata expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma for icchantikas.
There are two types of icchantikas:
first, those with sharp faculties; second, those with middling faculties.

Those of sharp faculties are able to attain roots of goodness in the present life; those of middling faculties will attain them in a future life. Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not preach the Dharma in vain.
"Great King!
It is like a pure person who has fallen into a latrine; a good friend sees him and takes pity on him, immediately goes forward, seizes him by the hair, and pulls him out."

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise in this regard: seeing sentient beings fallen into the three evil realms, they employ skillful means to rescue and deliver them so that they may attain liberation; for this reason, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma even for those who are icchantikas.
The King said to Jīvaka,
"If it is indeed as you say regarding the Tathāgata, then tomorrow I shall select an auspicious day and favorable stars before proceeding."
Jīva addressed the king: "Great King!
Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is no selection of auspicious days or favorable stars."
"Great King!
Just as a gravely ill person disregards the date, the season, or whether the timing is auspicious or inauspicious,
seeking only a skilled physician, so too you, whose illness is now grave, should seek the Buddha, the skilled physician, without selecting for an auspicious time or a favorable day."
"Great King!
Just as the fire of sandalwood and the fire of *kāraṇja* wood both possess the characteristic of burning and are no different from one another, so it is with auspicious days and inauspicious days."
"If we go to the Buddha's presence, we shall all be able to extinguish our transgressions; I only pray that Your Majesty will go there swiftly today.
At that time, the Great King immediately summoned a minister named Śrī and addressed him, saying:
"Great Minister, you should know that I now wish to go to the place of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; prepare quickly the various requisites required for making offerings."
The minister said:
“Great King!
Excellent, excellent!”
"Whatever requisites are needed shall all be provided.

King Ajātaśatru and his consort prepared twelve thousand chariots and carriages, and fifty thousand magnificent, powerful elephants; upon each elephant were mounted three persons, carrying banners, canopies, flowers, incense, music, and various offerings, all of which were fully prepared without exception. There were one hundred and eighty thousand horsemen in the vanguard and retinue, and the number of people from the kingdom of Magadha who followed the king reached exactly five hundred and eighty thousand.
At that time, the entire great assembly in the city of Kuśinagara, numbering twelve yojanas in extent, all saw from afar King Ajātaśatru approaching along the road with his retinue.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"For all sentient beings, there is nothing that serves as a more proximate cause for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* than a virtuous friend."

Why is this? If King Ajātaśatru had not followed the words of Jīvaka, he would certainly have met his end this coming seventh day and fallen into the Avīci Hell; therefore, as for proximate causes, none is equal to a virtuous friend.

King Ajātaśatru further heard on the road ahead that King Virūḍhaka of Śrāvastī had encountered fire and died while traveling by ship at sea; that the bhikṣu Kokālika had entered the earth alive and reached the Avīci Hell; and that Sunakṣatra, despite having committed various evils, had his multitude of sins extinguished upon reaching the Buddha’s presence. Having heard these words, he said to Jīvaka:
"Although I have now heard these two accounts, I am still not yet certain."
"Come, Jīvaka!
I wish to ride upon the same elephant as you; for should I fall into the Avīci Hell, I hope that you will hold me fast so that I do not fall."
"Why is this? I have heard in the past that those who have attained the Way do not enter hell.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
“King Ajātaśatru still harbors doubts; I shall now act to bring him to a state of certainty.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sarvadhara who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha previously taught, all dharmas lack fixed characteristics; that is to say, form lacks fixed characteristics, and even nirvāṇa lacks fixed characteristics. Why does the Tathāgata now speak of creating a resolute mind for Ajātaśatru?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
I shall now establish a mind of certainty for King Ajātaśatru. Why is this?

If the King’s doubting mind can be destroyed, one should know that all phenomena have no fixed characteristics; therefore, while I establish a mind of certainty for King Ajātaśatru, one should know that this very mind is itself without certainty.
"Good son!
If that king’s mind were fixed, how could the king’s crime of parricide be destroyed?
Because it lacks a fixed nature, the crime can be destroyed; therefore, I have brought about a resolute mind in King Ajātaśatru."

At that time, the Great King went directly to the twin sāla trees and approached the Buddha’s dwelling; he gazed up at the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, which were like a mountain of exquisite, pure gold.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered the eightfold voice and addressed him, saying:
"Great King. Then Ajātaśatru looked around his left and right, wondering, "In this great assembly, who is the Great King?"
"I am both sinful and devoid of merit; the Tathāgata should not address me as 'Great King.
At that time, the Tathāgata again called out, "Great King Ajātaśatru."
When the king heard this, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately spoke these words:
"The Tathāgata’s address to me today truly shows that the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings with great compassion and pity, treating them all equally without distinction."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
My doubts are now forever eliminated without remainder; I know with certainty that the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed Great Teacher of all sentient beings."
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said to Sarvadhārī Bodhisattva,
"The Tathāgata has already brought King Ajātaśatru to a state of certainty.
Then, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even if I were now to share a seat, rise and sit together, and partake of food and drink with Brahmā or Śakra Devendra, I would still not feel such joy;
yet to encounter the Tathāgata’s single word of compassionate regard brings me profound celebration.”

At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately offered the banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and music he had brought as an offering; he then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed his salutations, withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Great King!
I shall now expound for you the essential points of the True Dharma; you should listen with single-minded attention and heedfulness!"
Listen attentively!
An ordinary person should constantly bind the mind to the contemplation of the body; there are twenty matters:
first, that which is called "self" is empty within this body, lacking outflows (anāsrava) and second, lacking all virtues.
1. The root; 2. This saṃsāra of mine has not yet attained submissiveness; 3. Having fallen into a deep pit, there is no place that is not feared;
4. By what skillful means can the Buddha-nature be seen? 5. How should one cultivate meditative concentration to see the Buddha-nature? 6.
Saṃsāra is constantly characterized by suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity; 7. [And so forth. 8. [The eighth point.]
1. It is difficult to remain far removed from the eight difficulties; 2. one is constantly pursued by enemies; 3.
there is not a single dharma capable of obstructing the various realms of existence; 4. one has not yet attained liberation from the three evil destinies;
5. one is fully possessed of various evil and heterodox views; 6. nor has one yet...
14. To establish the crossing over the ford of the five heinous crimes; 15. Birth and death are boundless, yet one has not reached their limit;
16. Without performing various karmas, one does not obtain retribution; 17.
There is no case where what I have done is received as fruit by another; 18. Without creating the cause of happiness, there will ultimately be no fruit of happiness; 19. If there is...
19. The fruits of the karma one creates are never lost; furthermore, one is born because of ignorance and dies because of it.
20. One constantly practices heedlessness throughout the past, future, and present.
"Great King!
An ordinary person should constantly practice these twenty kinds of contemplation upon this body.
Having performed these contemplations, one will no longer delight in birth and death; by not delighting in birth and death, one attains right contemplation."
At that time, one sequentially contemplates the arising, abiding, and ceasing marks of the mind;
one sequentially contemplates the arising, abiding, and ceasing marks of concentration, wisdom, diligence, and precepts, and it is likewise for all else.

Having contemplated arising, abiding, and ceasing, one understands the characteristics of the mind up to the characteristics of the precepts, and ultimately refrains from doing evil, being free from the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms.
"If one does not fix the mind to observe these twenty matters, the mind will become negligent, and there is no evil that will not be committed.

Ajātaśatru said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from the past until now, I have never observed these twenty matters; therefore, I have committed many evils. Because I have committed many evils, I have had the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms."
"World-Honored One!
I have brought calamity upon myself by committing this grave evil; my father, the King, was innocent, yet I have wantonly and perversely harmed him.
Whether I reflect upon these twenty matters or not, I am certain that I shall fall into the Avīci Hell."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"The nature and characteristics of all dharmas are impermanent and lack any fixed certainty; why then do you say that he will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell?"
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas lack a fixed characteristic, then my guilt for killing should likewise be unfixed.”
"If killing were determinate, then all dharmas would not be indeterminate.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
Excellent, excellent!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that all dharmas are entirely without fixed characteristics; since you, O King, further understand that even killing is not fixed, you should therefore know that killing has no fixed characteristic.
"Great King!
As you have said, regarding the innocent father who was unjustly and violently harmed—who was that father?
It was merely within the five aggregates (skandhas) of a conventionally designated sentient being that you falsely gave rise to the notion of 'father'."
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*), which is the father?
If form (*rūpa*) is the father, then the four aggregates (*skandha*) should not be;
if the four are the father, then form should also not be.
If form and non-form were to combine to constitute a father, such a thing is impossible. Why?
Because form and non-form are by nature incapable of combining.
"Great King!
Ordinary beings falsely give rise to the notion of 'father' regarding this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); yet, this aggregate of form likewise cannot be harmed. Why is this?"
There are ten kinds of form; among these ten, only the single category of "form" is visible, graspable, weighable, measurable, and capable of being pulled or bound.
Although it can be seen as a bondage, its nature does not abide; because it does not abide, it cannot be seen, it cannot be grasped, it cannot be measured, and it cannot be bound.
If form is thus, how can it be killed?
If form were the father, then it could be killed or harmed, and one would incur the retribution for sin;
the other nine [elements] would then not be so.
If these nine were non-existent, then there would be no transgression.
Great King!
Form is of three kinds:
The past, the future, and the present.
The past and the present cannot be harmed. Why is this?
Because the past has already passed and because the present perishes moment by moment, one speaks of "killing" in order to preclude the future.
Thus, regarding a single form (*rūpa*), there may be that which can be killed and that which cannot be killed; since there is both killing and non-killing, form is not fixed.
If the physical form is not fixed, the killing is also not fixed; because the killing is not fixed, the retribution is also not fixed.
Why, then, do you say that one is certain to enter hell?
"Great King!..."
The sinful karma committed by all sentient beings is of two kinds:
first, light; second, heavy.
If it is produced by mind and speech, it is called light.
"O Great King! That which is performed by body, speech, and mind is called 'heavy.
If one conceives it in the mind and speaks it with the voice, but does not perform it with the body, the retribution obtained will be light."
"Great King!
In the past, you did not issue an oral command to kill him; you merely said to 'shave his feet.
Great King!"

If one were to order an attendant to behead the king while he is standing, yet not commit an offense by beheading him while he is seated, how much less could an offense be committed when the king did not issue such an order?
If the king were to commit an offense, then the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would also have to commit an offense.
Why is this? Your father, the former king Bimbisāra, constantly planted various roots of goodness under the Buddhas; for this reason, he has now attained the position of king.
If the Buddhas did not accept their offerings, they would not become kings; if they were not kings, you would not have been able to inflict harm upon the kingdom.
If you were to be guilty of the crime of killing your father, then we Buddhas should likewise be guilty of a crime.
"If the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are without fault, why alone do you incur guilt?
Great King!

In the past, Bimbisāra harbored an evil mind while roaming the Vulture Peak (Vipula Mountain) to hunt deer; having searched throughout the wilderness without success, he saw only a seer endowed with the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā). Upon seeing him, he immediately gave rise to a mind of anger and malice."
"The reason I have been unable to hunt today is precisely because of this man.
He drove him away and immediately commanded his attendants to kill him.
As that person was nearing death, he gave rise to a mind of anger and malice; his supernormal powers (ṛddhi) were lost, and he made this vow:
"I am truly innocent, yet you have unjustly subjected me to slaughter through both mind and speech. In a future life, I shall likewise do unto you, harming you with both mind and speech."
When the king heard this, he immediately gave rise to a mind of repentance and made offerings to the corpse.
Since even this king was able to experience [the retribution] lightly and did not fall into hell,
how much more so for one who does not act thus— would such a person receive the fruit of retribution in hell?
The former king created [the karma] himself and must experience its results himself; how then can the current king incur the sin of murder?
As the king says, the father-king was innocent.
O Great King!
Why do you say there is no [retribution]?
Generally, one who has committed an offense receives the retribution for that offense; one who has performed no evil karma receives no retribution.
If your father, the former king, was without guilt or offense, how could there be retribution?

Bimbisāra also obtained both good and evil fruits within his present life; therefore, the former king was likewise not fixed. Because he was not fixed, his execution was also not fixed. Since his execution was not fixed, how can you say that he is certain to enter hell?
"Great King!
There are four kinds of madness that afflict sentient beings:
first, madness from desire; second, madness from medicine; third, madness from incantations; and fourth, madness from the conditions of past karma."
"Great King!
Among my disciples there are these four types of madness; although they may commit many evils, I never declare that such persons have violated the precepts.
What these individuals do does not lead to the three evil realms, and if they regain their composure, I do not say they have committed an offense."
The King originally coveted the kingdom and perversely murdered his father; this was committed by a mind intoxicated by greed. How, then, could he incur retribution?
Great King!
It is like a man who, while drunk, perversely murders his mother; once he has sobered up and feels regret in his heart, you should know that such karma likewise does not yield its fruit.
"Your Majesty is now intoxicated by craving; this was not done with your original mind. If it was not done with your original mind, how can you incur guilt?
Great King!

It is like a magician who, at a crossroads, conjures various men and women, elephants and horses, necklaces and garments. A foolish person regards these as real, whereas a wise person knows they are not truly existent."
Killing is likewise so: ordinary worldlings regard it as real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal.
Great King!
It is like an echo in the mountains: a foolish person regards it as a real sound, while a wise person knows it to be unreal.
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal.
Great King!

It is like a person who has an enemy that feigns coming to befriend him; a foolish person regards this as a true friend, whereas a wise person, through clear understanding, knows it to be false and deceptive.
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal.
Great King!
It is like a person holding a mirror who sees the reflection of his own face; a foolish person regards it as his actual face, whereas a wise person clearly understands that it is not real.
Killing is likewise so: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
Great King!
It is like a mirage in the heat; a foolish person calls it water, but a wise person understands and knows it is not water.
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
Great King!
It is like a city of the gandharvas: foolish people regard it as real, whereas the wise, having attained thorough understanding, know it to be not real.
Killing is likewise so: ordinary people regard it as real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal.
Great King!
It is like a person in a dream who experiences the pleasures of the five desires; a foolish person regards them as real, while a wise person thoroughly understands that they are not real.
Killing is also like this: ordinary people consider it real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
"Great King!
As for the nature of killing, the karma of killing, the killer, the fruit of killing, and liberation from them—I have thoroughly understood all these, and thus there is no sin."
"Although the king knows of the killing, how can he be guilty?
Great King!
It is like a person who is the master of those in charge of wine; if he does not drink it himself, he will not become intoxicated. Likewise, although one may know of fire, one is not burned by it."
The king is also like this: although he knows that killing occurs, how could he be guilty?
Great King!
There are sentient beings who commit various crimes when the sun rises, and again practice robbery and theft when the moon rises; yet they do not commit such crimes when the sun and moon do not rise.
Although one may commit a transgression because of the sun and moon, the sun and moon themselves are not actually guilty of that transgression.
Killing is likewise: although it may occur because of a king, the king is in truth without guilt.
"Great King!
Just as in the royal palace you constantly order sheep to be slaughtered without any fear arising in your mind from the outset,
why do you alone give rise to a heart of fear toward your father?"
Although there are distinctions of high and low between humans and animals, in their precious life and their fear of death, the two are no different. Why, then,
do you feel such contemptuous indifference toward the sheep,
yet give rise to such heavy grief and suffering for your father, the former king?
"Great King!
People in this world are the slaves of craving; they lack self-mastery and, driven by craving, commit acts of killing. If there is any karmic retribution, it is the fault of craving."
If the king lacks self-mastery, what fault could there be?
Great King!
It is like *nirvāṇa*, which is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is nonetheless existent.
Killing is also like this: although it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is nonetheless existent.
For one who possesses a sense of shame and remorse, it is non-existent; for one who lacks shame and remorse, it is not non-existent.
That which undergoes retribution is called existent; for one who holds the view of emptiness, it is non-existent.
For one who holds the view that things exist, it is not non-existent; one who holds the view that things exist is also said to "exist.
Why is this? Because those who hold the view that things exist obtain karmic retribution, whereas those who hold the view that things do not exist receive no retribution.
To those who hold the view of permanence, it is "not existent"; to those who hold the view of non-permanence, it is "not non-existent.
Those who perceive permanence cannot regard it as non-existent; why is this so?
Because those who see it constantly experience the fruits of evil karma, that which is seen constantly cannot be said to be non-existent.
For this reason, although it is neither existent nor non-existent, it nevertheless exists.
“Great King!

As for sentient beings, they are designated by their inhalation and exhalation; because one cuts off these inhalations and exhalations, it is called ‘killing. The Buddhas, following worldly convention, also speak of it as killing.”
"Great King! Form is impermanent; the causes and conditions of form are also impermanent. Since it arises from impermanent causes, how could form be permanent?

This applies even unto consciousness: consciousness is impermanent, and the causes and conditions of consciousness are also impermanent. Since it arises from impermanent causes, how could consciousness be permanent?"

Because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is empty; because it is empty, it is non-self. If it is thus impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, what is there to be killed?
By slaying impermanence, one attains eternal nirvāṇa; by slaying suffering, one attains happiness; by slaying emptiness, one attains reality; and by slaying non-self, one attains the true self.
Great King!
If one kills that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then one is the same as I.
I too have killed that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, yet I do not enter hell; why then should you enter it?
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having contemplated form up to consciousness just as the Buddha had instructed, and having completed this contemplation, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Only now do I know that form is impermanent, and so on, up to consciousness being impermanent;
had I been able to know this from the beginning, I would not have committed these offenses,
World-Honored One!
In the past, I have heard that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly act as parents to sentient beings.
Although I had heard these words, I was not yet certain; now, however, I know it for a fact.
World-Honored One!
I have also heard that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is composed of four treasures, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
and whatever birds gather there, they take on the same color as their environment.
Although I have heard these words, I have not yet reached a definitive understanding.
Now that I have come to the Buddha’s Mount Sumeru, I am of the same color as it; being of the same color as it, I know that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
“World-Honored One!

In the world, I have seen that from a *piṇḍa* seed grows a *piṇḍa* tree, but I have never seen a *piṇḍa* seed grow a sandalwood tree. Now, for the first time, I see a *piṇḍa* seed grow a sandalwood tree: the *piṇḍa* seed is my own body, and the sandalwood tree is my mind—rootless and full of faith.”
"Regarding 'rootless,' I originally did not know how to revere the Tathāgata, nor did I have faith in the Dharma or the Saṅgha; this is called being rootless.
World-Honored One!
Had I not encountered the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, I would have been undergoing immeasurable suffering in the great hells for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
"I have now seen the Buddha; by the merit obtained from seeing the Buddha, may I destroy all afflictions and evil minds of sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "Great King!
"Excellent, excellent!
I now know that you will certainly be able to destroy the evil minds of sentient beings.
"World-Honored One!"

If I am truly able to destroy the various evil minds of sentient beings, then let me remain forever in the Avīci Hell for immeasurable kalpas, undergoing great suffering and affliction for the sake of all beings, yet not regarding it as suffering.

At that time, immeasurable people of the kingdom of Magadha all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Because such immeasurable people had thus resolved their great minds, the heavy sins of King Ajātaśatru were immediately rendered light.
The king, the queen, and the ladies of the inner palace all together resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to Jīvaka: "Jīvaka!..."

I have now, before dying, already attained a celestial body; I have abandoned a short life to obtain a long life, and abandoned an impermanent body to obtain an eternal body. Causing all sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is itself the celestial body, the long life, and the eternal body; it is to be a disciple of all the Buddhas.

Having spoken these words, he immediately made offerings to the Buddha with various jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, fragrant flowers, necklaces, and exquisite music, and further praised him with these verses:
“Your truthful speech is most subtle and wondrous; You are skillful in the meaning of words and phrases.
This profound and secret treasury— For the sake of the multitude, you have revealed it.”
All these vast words have been spoken in brief for the sake of the multitude;
possessing such speech, one is well able to heal sentient beings.
If there are any sentient beings who hear these words, [they shall be healed].
Whether one has faith or lacks faith, one should know with certainty that this is the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddhas always speak with gentle words, yet for the sake of the multitude they may speak harshly;
both harsh speech and gentle speech ultimately converge upon the ultimate truth.
Therefore, I now take refuge in the World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata’s speech is of a single flavor, like the waters of the great ocean;
this is called the foremost truth, and thus there is no speech devoid of meaning.
The various and immeasurable dharmas now taught by the Tathāgata—whether heard by men or women, great or small—all equally attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There is neither cause nor effect; there is neither arising nor ceasing.
This is called Great Nirvāṇa; those who hear it shatter all [conditioned] fruits.
The Tathāgata acts as a compassionate parent for all;
one should know that all sentient beings are the children of the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One, with great compassion, Undergoes ascetic practices for the sake of the multitude.
Like a person possessed by a malevolent spirit, Who acts wildly and excessively, I have now been able to behold the Buddha;
Whatever goodness I have attained through the three karmas, [I dedicate it all].
May these merits be dedicated toward the unsurpassed path.
Through the offerings I now present to the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha, may the Three Jewels remain forever in the world.
Whatever various merits I am now to attain, may I,
by means of these, destroy the four kinds of Māras for all sentient beings.
Having encountered evil associates, I have committed sins throughout the three periods of time.
I now repent before the Buddha, vowing never to commit such deeds again.
May all sentient beings alike resolve upon Bodhicitta,
and with focused minds, constantly keep in mind all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"Furthermore, I vow that all sentient beings shall forever shatter all afflictions and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, just like Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised King Ajātaśatru:
“Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can resolve to attain bodhicitta, you should know that such a person adorns the great assemblies of all Buddhas.
Great King!”

In the past, you first resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* under Vipaśyin Buddha; from that time until my appearance in the world, during the interval between them, you have never fallen into hell to undergo suffering.
"Great King, you should know that the bodhicitta yields such immeasurable fruits and rewards.
Great King,
from this day forward, you should always diligently cultivate the bodhicitta."
"Why is this? Because by means of these causes and conditions, one shall attain the eradication of immeasurable evils.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru and the people of the entire kingdom of Magadha rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, took their leave, and returned to the palace.
The "Chapter on Celestial Conduct" is as explained in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
**The Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Infant Conduct** "Good son! [The Buddha said:]..."
What is meant by "infant-like conduct"? Good son!
One who is unable to rise or sit, to come or go, or to speak—this is called an infant.
The Tathāgata is likewise: that which cannot arise, the Tathāgata ultimately does not give rise to the marks of dharmas;
that which cannot abide, the Tathāgata does not cling to any dharmas;
that which cannot come, the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are without movement or agitation.
That which cannot depart is that the Tathāgata has already attained great parinirvāṇa;
that which cannot speak is that although the Tathāgata expounds all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, in reality there is nothing spoken.
Why is this? That which can be spoken of is called a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not conditioned; therefore, he has nothing to speak of.
Furthermore, "being without speech" is like an infant whose language is not yet developed; although they do utter sounds, in reality they have no speech. The Tathāgata is likewise:

that which is "not yet developed as speech" refers to the secret words of all Buddhas. Although he has something to say, sentient beings do not understand it; therefore, it is called being without speech.

Furthermore, an infant is one for whom names and objects are not yet unified and who does not yet know correct speech; although names and objects are not unified and correct speech is unknown, it is not the case that they do not recognize objects by means of this.

The Tathāgata is likewise: although all sentient beings differ in their species and types and their speech varies, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to teach them accordingly, enabling all of them to attain understanding thereby.
Furthermore, an infant is able to utter "great syllables.

The Tathāgata is likewise; he speaks of great syllables, namely *ba* and *ha*. *Ha* refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and *ba* refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is called the infant.

The syllable *ha* is named impermanence; the syllable *va* is named permanence. When the Tathāgata speaks of permanence, sentient beings, having heard it, sever impermanence for the sake of the permanent dharma; this is called the practice of an infant.
Furthermore, an infant does not know suffering or pleasure, day or night, nor father or mother.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: for the sake of sentient beings, he does not know suffering or pleasure, nor does he have the perception of day or night; because his mind is impartial toward all sentient beings, he has no notions of distinction such as parent or stranger.
Furthermore, just as an infant is unable to perform various tasks, whether great or small, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Bodhisattva does not create the karma of birth and death; this is called "non-doing."
The "great matters" refer to the five heinous crimes; a bodhisattva-mahāsattva never commits these grave offenses of the five rebellions.
The "small matters" refer to the mind of the two vehicles; a bodhisattva never regresses from the bodhicitta to become a follower of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha vehicle.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of the infant-like practitioner: it is like when an infant cries, his parents immediately take yellow leaves from a *śiṃśapā* tree and say to him, "Do not cry, do not cry; I will give you gold."
Upon seeing it, the infant forms the notion that it is genuine gold and stops crying; yet these willow leaves are not actually gold.

When the infant sees wooden oxen, wooden horses, wooden men, and wooden women, he likewise forms the notions that they are men, women, and so forth, and immediately stops crying; yet they are not actually men or women.
Because they harbor such notions of male and female, they are called "infants.

The Tathāgata is likewise: if there are sentient beings who wish to commit various evils, the Tathāgata speaks for them of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; where beings are upright and self-sufficient, enjoying the pleasures of the five desires within wondrous palaces, and wherein nothing encountered by the six sense organs is not pleasure.

Because sentient beings hear that such bliss exists, they give rise to a craving for that bliss; they cease from committing evil and diligently perform wholesome deeds for rebirth in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

In reality, birth and death are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; yet, in order to deliver sentient beings, he employs skillful means to speak of them as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

Furthermore, regarding the infant: if there are sentient beings who weary of birth and death, the Tathāgata then teaches them the Two Vehicles. Yet, in reality, there is no substantiality to the Two Vehicles; it is only by means of the Two Vehicles that they come to know the faults of birth and death and perceive the bliss of nirvāṇa.

By means of this vision, one is then able to know for oneself: what is severed and what is not severed; what is true and what is not true; what is cultivated and what is not cultivated; and what is attained and what is not attained.

“Good son! Just as that infant conceives the notion of gold within what is not gold, so too does the Tathāgata speak of purity within the impure; because the Tathāgata has attained the ultimate truth, there is no falsehood in this.”

Just as that infant perceives what is not an ox or a horse as being an ox or a horse, so too there may be sentient beings who perceive what is not the true path as being the true path. The Tathāgata likewise speaks of the non-path as the path; although there is truly no path within the non-path, because it can produce subtle causes and conditions for the arising of the path, he speaks of the non-path as the path.

Just as that infant conceives the notion of a male or female child regarding a wooden figure, so too does the Tathāgata; though he knows they are not sentient beings, he speaks of them using the notion of "sentient beings," yet in reality, there is no characteristic of a sentient being whatsoever.
If the Buddha-Tathāgata were to say that there are no sentient beings, all sentient beings would fall into wrong views; therefore, the Tathāgata says that there are sentient beings.
Those who form the notion of "sentient beings" regarding sentient beings are unable to shatter the mark of sentient beings.

If one can shatter the mark of sentient beings regarding sentient beings, one will then be able to attain Great Parinirvāṇa. Because one has attained such Great Nirvāṇa, one ceases weeping; this is called the practice of an infant.
"Good son!
If there are men or women who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain these five practices, you should know that such persons will certainly attain these five practices."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I too shall certainly attain these five practices.”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Not only you have attained these five practices; now, ninety-three thousand people in this assembly have likewise attained these five practices, just as you have.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-one.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, Part One At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
“O son of good family!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra in such a manner, they will attain ten kinds of meritorious qualities that are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they are inconceivable and cause those who hear of them to be struck with wonder. They are neither internal nor external, neither difficult nor easy, neither possessing marks nor lacking marks, neither worldly dharmas nor devoid of characteristics—things that do not exist in the world.
What are these ten? There are five; what are the five? First, one is able to hear that which was not previously heard;

second, having heard it, one is able to derive benefit from it; third, one is able to sever the mind of doubt and confusion; fourth, the mind of wisdom is upright and without crookedness; fifth, one is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. These are the five matters.
What is it that one has not heard but is now able to hear?

It is this most profound and subtle treasury: that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; that there is no distinction between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; that the nature and characteristics of the Three Jewels are eternal, blissful, self, and pure; and that among all Buddhas, none ever enter final nirvana, for they abide eternally and are unchanging.
The Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is neither existent nor non-existent; neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither with outflows nor without outflows;
neither form nor non-form; neither name nor non-name; neither characteristic nor non-characteristic;
neither existent nor non-existent; neither a thing nor a non-thing; neither cause nor fruit. It is not...
It is neither dependent nor independent; neither luminous nor dark; neither emerging nor non-emerging;
neither permanent nor impermanent; neither annihilated nor non-annihilated; neither beginning nor end; neither past, nor future, nor present;
neither the aggregates (*skandha*) nor not the aggregates; neither the sense-bases (*āyatana*) nor not the sense-bases; neither the elements (*dhātu*) nor...
Neither the elements nor the twelve links of dependent origination, yet not non-twelve-links-of-dependent-origination—
such dharmas as these are profoundly deep and subtle, which one has never heard before, yet now is able to hear.

Furthermore, there are things not heard, namely: all the scriptures of external paths, the four Vedas, the Vyākaraṇa, the Vaiśeṣika treatises, the Sāṃkhya treatises, all incantations, medical prescriptions, and arts; as well as eclipses of the sun and moon, the movements and transformations of the constellations, and the records of maps and prophecies.
In such sūtras as these, the meaning of the secret has never before been heard; now it is known through this sūtra.
Furthermore, among the eleven divisions of the scriptures—with the exception of the Vaipulya—there is likewise no such profound and secret meaning; now it is known through this sūtra.
"Good son! This is called 'being able to hear what was previously unheard. Regarding 'benefit after having heard':
if one can listen to and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will be able to fully comprehend the profound meanings and flavors of all Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras."
It is like a man or a woman who, looking into a bright and clear mirror, sees their own form and image with perfect clarity.
The mirror of the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise; when a bodhisattva holds it, they are able to clearly perceive the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
It is also like a person in a dark room who, by holding a great torch, sees all objects clearly;
the torch of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise, for when a bodhisattva holds it, they are able to perceive the profound and subtle meaning of the Mahāyāna.
It is also like the rising sun, which possesses a thousand rays of light capable of illuminating the dark recesses of all mountains and enabling all people to see objects from afar.
This sun of pure wisdom of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise; it illuminates the profound depths of the Mahāyāna and enables those of the two vehicles to see the Buddha-way from afar.
Why is this? Because they are able to hear and accept this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Good son!
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who hear and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they will come to know the names of all dharmas.
If they can further transcribe it, recite it with fluency, explain it extensively for others, and contemplate its meaning, they will then understand the principles and meanings of all dharmas.
"Good son!
Those who merely listen to and receive it know only the names, but do not understand their meaning;
if they can write it down, accept and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, and contemplate its meaning, then they will be able to understand the meaning."
Furthermore, good son!
Those who hear this sutra hear that there is buddha-nature, yet they have not yet attained the vision of it;
however, those who copy, read, recite, extensively explain it to others, and contemplate its meaning shall indeed see it.
Those who listen to this sutra may hear the name of *dāna*, yet they are not yet able to see the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

However, those who copy, read, recite, extensively explain it to others, and contemplate its meaning will be able to see the perfection of giving; this applies likewise to all the perfections up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Good son!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he will know the Dharma and know its meaning, possessing the two kinds of unimpeded knowledge. Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as among devas, māras, brahmās, and the entire world, he shall attain fearlessness. He will expound and analyze the twelve divisions of the sūtras, explaining their meanings without error. Without hearing them from another, he will be able to know them for himself, drawing near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Good son! Having heard this, it can bring about benefit.
Regarding 'the severing of doubt,' there are two kinds of doubt: [the doubt concerning the teacher and the doubt concerning the teaching]."
The first is doubt regarding names; the second is doubt regarding meanings.
Those who listen to this sutra sever the mind that doubts names;
those who contemplate its meaning sever the mind that doubts meanings.
Furthermore, good son,
there are five kinds of doubt:
first, doubting whether the Buddha has definitely entered parinirvāṇa or not;
Second, they doubt whether the Buddha is eternally abiding;
third, they doubt whether the Buddha is true bliss;
fourth, they doubt whether the Buddha is true purity.
Fifth, those who doubt whether the Buddha is truly the Self will have that doubt eternally severed if they listen to this sutra;
those who copy, read, recite, extensively explain it to others, or contemplate its meaning will have four doubts eternally severed.
Furthermore, good son, there are three kinds of doubt: first, doubting whether the śrāvaka exists or does not exist;
[the second is doubting whether the pratyekabuddha exists or does not exist; and the third is doubting whether the Buddha exists or does not exist.]
Second, they doubt whether the Pratyekabuddha vehicle exists or does not exist;
third, they doubt whether the Buddha vehicle exists or does not exist.
For those who hear this sutra, these three doubts will be forever extinguished without remainder.
By copying, reciting, reading, explaining it extensively for others, and contemplating its meaning, one will be able to understand that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, good son!

If there are sentient beings who have not heard such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra as this, their minds will harbor many doubts—namely, regarding whether things are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or unpleasant, pure or impure, self or non-self, life or no-life, sentient being or non-sentient being, ultimate or non-ultimate, the next world or beyond the world, existent or non-existent, suffering or not suffering, accumulation or not accumulation, the path or not the path, cessation or not cessation, dharma or non-dharma, wholesome or unwholesome, empty or non-empty. Those who hear this sūtra shall forever sever all such doubts.
Furthermore, good son!
If there are those who have not heard such a sutra as this, they will further harbor various and numerous doubts, namely: "Is form the self?"
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the self?
Is it the eye that sees,
or is it the self that sees?
Does consciousness cognize? Do I cognize?
Does form experience retribution?
Is it the self that receives retribution?
Or is it up to consciousness that receives retribution?
Is it the self that receives retribution?
Does form go to another world?
Does the self go to another world?
And so on, up to consciousness, it is the same.
Does the law of birth and death have a beginning and an end,
or is it without beginning and without end?
Those who listen to this sutra shall likewise attain the eternal severance of such doubts.

Furthermore, there may be those who harbor doubts: "Do icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave offenses, those who have committed the five heinous crimes, and those who slander the Vaipulya sutras—beings such as these—possess the Buddha-nature?"
"Is there no Buddha-nature?"—for those who hear this sutra, such doubts as these shall all be forever severed.
Furthermore, there are others who doubt: "Is the world finite?"
Is the world infinite?
Are there worlds in the ten directions?
Or are there no worlds in the ten directions?
Those who hear this sutra will likewise attain the permanent severance of such doubts; this is called being able to sever the mind of doubt and confusion.
"One whose mind of wisdom is upright and free from crookedness": if the mind harbors doubt, then what one perceives will not be correct.
If all ordinary beings do not hear this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, their views will be deviant and crooked; even the views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise crooked.
What is meant by the "perversion seen by all ordinary beings"?
It is to perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity within that which is subject to outflows (sāsrava);
and to perceive impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self in the Tathāgata.
They perceive the existence of sentient beings, a life-span, and cognitive vision;
they reckon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to be nirvana;
and they see Mahesvara as possessing the Eightfold Noble Path.
There are views of existence and views of annihilation;
such views as these are called crooked and deviant.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and practices the noble conduct, they will then be able to sever and eliminate such crookedness.
What is meant by the deviant and crooked views of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?

They see the Bodhisattva descending from Tuṣita, transforming himself into one riding a white elephant, and entering the mother’s womb; they see that his father is named Śuddhodana and his mother is named Māyā.

In the city of Kapilavastu, his gestation having reached full term, he was born after ten months. Before he had even touched the ground, Śakra received him in his arms; the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda spat forth water to bathe him; the great yakṣa king Maṇibhadra held a precious parasol and stood in attendance behind him; the earth goddess manifested flowers to receive his feet; and he walked seven paces in each of the four directions.
Upon arriving at the temple of the gods, all the divine images rose to welcome him.
The seer Asita took the child in his arms to examine his marks; having completed the examination, he was overcome with great sorrow and lamented that he would not live to see the rise of the Buddha.
He went to his teachers to study writing, arithmetic, archery and defense, divination and prophecy, and various arts and skills.
Remaining within the deep palace, he was entertained and provided with pleasure by sixty thousand court ladies.

He went out of the city to travel and observe, reaching the Kapilavastu Garden; on the way, he saw an old man and even a śramaṇa walking in religious robes. Upon returning to the palace, he saw that the bodies and features of the court ladies were like withered bones, and all the palaces were no different from burial mounds.

Disgusted with worldly life, he fled the city at midnight and went to the great seers Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma, where he heard their teachings on the sphere of consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having heard this, he contemplated that state as impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self; then, departing for the foot of a tree, he fully practiced asceticism for six full years.

Knowing that these ascetic practices could not lead to the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he then went to the river Ārīvatī to bathe and accepted the milk-gruel offered by the cowherd girl. Having accepted it, he proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree, where he defeated Māra Pāpīyas and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
From turning the Wheel of Dharma for the five bhikṣus at Vārāṇasī until entering parinirvāṇa here in the city of Kuśinagara—
such views as these are called the crooked views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears and receives this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
they completely sever and eliminate views such as these.
If one can copy, read, recite with fluency, explain to others, and contemplate its meaning, then one will attain upright views free from crookedness. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra in this way, they know with certainty that from immeasurable kalpas ago, the bodhisattva has never descended from Tuṣita to enter his mother’s womb, nor has he entered parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara; this is called the upright view of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

To be able to know the profound and secret meaning of the Tathāgata refers to what is called the Great Parinirvāṇa: that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; that after repenting for the four grave prohibitions, removing the mind that slanders the Dharma, exhausting the five heinous crimes, and extinguishing the icchantika state, one subsequently attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is termed the profoundly deep and secret meaning.
Furthermore, good son,
what is meant by the meaning of "profound"?
Although one knows that sentient beings truly have no self, yet the fruits of karma are not lost in the future.
Although one knows that the five aggregates cease and perish here, the karma of good and evil never perishes;
although there are various karmas, there is no agent who performs them;
although there is a destination reached, there is no goer.
Although there are fetters, there is no one who is bound;
although there is nirvana, there is no one who attains extinction.
This is called the profound and secret meaning.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijñāguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the principle of ‘hearing what has not been heard’ is not so.”

Why is this? If a phenomenon exists, it must necessarily exist; if a phenomenon does not exist, it must necessarily not exist. That which is non-existent should not arise, and that which exists should not perish.
If one hears it, then one has heard; if one does not hear it, then one has not heard. How can you say that one hears what was not previously heard?
World-Honored One!
If it cannot be heard, that is non-hearing; if it has already been heard, then there is no further hearing.
Why is this? Because it has already been attained through hearing.
How can it be said that one hears what has not been heard?
It is like a traveler: when he has arrived, he no longer travels; when he is traveling, he has not yet arrived.
It is also like that which has already arisen does not arise again, and that which has not arisen does not arise.
Having attained, one does not attain; not having attained, one does not not-attain.
Having heard, one does not hear; not having heard, one does not not-hear—it is likewise so.
World-Honored One!

If those who have not heard were to hear, then all sentient beings who have not yet attained bodhi should immediately possess it; those who have not yet attained nirvana should likewise attain it; and those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature should see the Buddha-nature. Why, then, do you further say that although a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage sees the Buddha-nature, they have not yet attained clear realization?
World-Honored One!
If there is such a thing as hearing what has not been heard, from whom did the Tathāgata hear it in the past?
If you say he did hear it, why does the Tathāgata further state in the Āgamas that he had no teacher?

If the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through that which is neither heard nor not heard, then all sentient beings would also attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through that which is neither heard nor not heard.
If the Tathāgata had not heard this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and yet seen the Buddha-nature, then all sentient beings, even without hearing this sūtra, should likewise have attained the vision of it.
"Bhagavān!
As for all forms (rūpa), some are visible and some are invisible.
Sound (śabda) is likewise: some are audible and some are inaudible."
This Great Nirvana is neither form nor sound; how then can it be said that it may be seen or heard? World-Honored One!

That which has already perished in the past cannot be heard; that which has not yet arrived in the future cannot be heard; at the very moment of listening in the present, it is not yet called "hearing"; and once the hearing is over and the sound has ceased, it can no longer be heard.

This Great Nirvāṇa is neither of the past, the future, nor the present. If it does not belong to the three periods of time, it cannot be spoken of; if it cannot be spoken of, it cannot be heard. How then can it be said that a bodhisattva cultivates this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and hears what has never been heard before?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāpāla-Ābhāsvara-Guṇarāja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
