The bones accumulated by each and every sentient being within a single kalpa would equal Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha; the milk they have drunk would equal the waters of the four oceans; the blood shed from their bodies would exceed the waters of the four oceans; and the tears shed while wailing for deceased parents, siblings, wives, children, and kinsmen would exceed the waters of the four great seas. Even if one were to take all the grasses and trees upon the earth and use them as four-inch counting sticks to enumerate one’s parents, they could not be fully counted. The suffering endured throughout immeasurable kalpas—whether in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts—is beyond calculation. One might easily exhaust this great earth by reducing it to the size of jujube pits, yet birth and death are difficult to end.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate all sentient beings in this way, they undergo immeasurable suffering due to these causes and conditions of desire; yet, because of this very suffering inherent in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the Bodhisattvas do not lose their mindfulness and wisdom.
"Good son! It is like this:
suppose there were a great multitude in the world filling an area of twenty-five li, and a king commanded an official:
'Carry a bowl of oil through the midst of them without spilling a drop; if you lose even a single drop, I shall have your life taken.'"
He further dispatched another man who followed behind with a drawn sword to terrify him.

Having received the king’s command, the minister maintained his resolve with all his heart as he passed through the midst of that great multitude. Although he beheld the five kinds of perverse desires that were pleasing to the mind, he constantly thought to himself:
"If I become negligent and become attached to those perverse desires, I shall abandon what I hold fast to, and my life will not be preserved."

"Because of these causes and conditions of fear, that person does not spill even a single drop of oil. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not lose mindfulness or wisdom within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Because he does not lose them, although he encounters the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), his mind does not become attached to them. If he sees pure forms, he does not give rise to the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), but observes only the mark of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*); this applies likewise even to the marks of consciousness (*vijñāna*). He does not construct the mark of arising, nor the mark of cessation, nor the mark of cause; he contemplates the mark of conditioned combination (*saṃyoga-lakṣaṇa*). At that time, the Bodhisattva’s five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are purified; because the faculties are purified, he is complete in the precept of guarding the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-śīla*)."
The five faculties of all ordinary beings are impure and cannot be properly maintained; this is called "outflow from the faculties" (*indriyāsrava*).
Bodhisattvas have eternally severed these, and are therefore without outflows (*anāsrava*). The Tathāgata has uprooted them and eternally severed their very root; therefore, they are not outflows.
"Furthermore, good son! There is also the abandonment of outflows (*āsrava*).
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva desires the fruit of Buddhahood, which is unsurpassed ambrosia (*amṛta*), he abandons evil outflows."
What is meant by "detachment"?

If one can practice the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra—by copying it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, explaining and expounding it, and contemplating its meaning—this is called detachment. Why is this so?
"Good son!
Among all the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I do not see any that can bring about freedom from evil outflows like this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Good son!"
It is like a skilled master who instructs his disciples; among those disciples, there are some who receive the instruction and do not commit evil in their minds.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa is also like this, for he does not commit evil in his mind.
"Good son!

It is like a skillful incantation in the world; if one hears it but once, for seven years thereafter, they will not be affected by any poison, nor can snakes bite them. If there is one who recites it, until the end of their life, no evils shall exist."
Good son! This Great Nirvana is also like this: if there are sentient beings who hear it but once, after seven kalpas they shall not fall into the evil realms.

If there are those who copy, read, recite, explain, or contemplate its meaning, they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and purify their vision of the Buddha-nature, just as that holy king obtained the taste of ambrosia.
Good son! This Great Nirvāṇa possesses such immeasurable merits as these. Good son!

If there are those who can copy this sutra, read and recite it, explain and expound it for others, and contemplate its meaning, you should know that such persons are truly my disciples; they have well received my teachings, they are what I behold, and they are what I keep in mind. Such persons truly know that I do not enter parinirvāṇa.

Wherever such a person dwells—whether in a city or town, a village, a mountain forest or wilderness, a house, field, or estate, or a multi-storied pavilion, hall, or temple—I too shall dwell there constantly and never depart. For the sake of such a person, I will always act as a recipient of their offerings, appearing either as a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, a brāhmaṇa, a brahmacārī, or a poor beggar.
"How may this person know that the Tathāgata has accepted the gift they have offered?

Good son, if this person, while sleeping at night in a dream, sees the image of a Buddha, or the image of a deva, the image of a śramaṇa, the image of a king, a noble cakravartin king, or a lion king; or the form of a lotus flower, or the form of an udumbara flower; or sees a great mountain, or the waters of the great ocean, or sees the sun and moon; or sees the image of a white elephant or a white horse; or sees their father and mother; or obtains flowers, fruits, or treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; or obtains the five products of the cow—at that time, one should know that it is the Tathāgata who has accepted the gift they have offered."
Having awakened, he experiences joy and bliss, and immediately obtains all manner of necessary things; his mind does not dwell on evil, and he delights in cultivating wholesome dharmas. Good son!
This Great Nirvāṇa is fully capable of accomplishing such immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, and boundless merits.
“Good son, you should now believe and accept my words:
if there are good sons or good daughters who wish to see me, who wish to pay homage to me, who wish to see me as identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
who wish to attain the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi), who wish to see the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and who wish to practice the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.”
The Lion King’s Samādhi: Desiring to destroy the eight māras— the eight māras being the so-called four māras,
as well as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity— those who wish to attain the bliss of humans and devas should see those who receive,
uphold, copy, read, recite, and explain the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra to others.

One who contemplates the meaning should go to those [teachers], draw near to them, rely upon them, and seek instruction from them; they should provide for them with offerings, reverence, respect, and praise,
and attend to them by washing their hands and feet, preparing their bedding and seats, and supplying the four requisites so that they lack for nothing.

If someone comes from afar, one should go ten yojanas along the way to welcome them; for the sake of this sutra, whatever precious things one possesses should be offered to them, and if such things are lacking, one should even sell one's own body.
Why is this? This sutra is difficult to encounter, surpassing even the udumbara flower.
"O son of good family!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable and boundless nayutas of kalpas ago, there was a world named Sahā. In that world, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who proclaimed this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the great assembly.
At that time, I heard from a spiritual friend that the Buddha was about to preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa for the great assembly.

Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy, and I wished to make an offering. Being poor and possessing nothing, I intended to sell myself; however, due to my meager merit, no one would buy me, so I was about to return home.
Seeing a man on the road, he spoke to him, saying:
"I wish to sell myself; would you be able to buy me?
The man replied:
"My household has a task that no one else is capable of performing; if you are able to do it, I shall purchase you.
I immediately asked, "What kind of task is it that no one is capable of performing?"
The man replied: "I have a malignant disease;
a skilled physician has prescribed medicine that requires me to consume three *liang* of human flesh daily.
If you can provide me with three *liang* of your own flesh every day, I shall give you five gold coins."
Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy, and I spoke again:
"Give me some money and lend me seven days; once my business is concluded, I shall return to you immediately."
The man replied: "Seven days will not do;
if you can truly manage it so, I shall grant you one day.
O son of good family!

At that time, I immediately took that money and returned to where the Buddha was; I prostrated myself with my head at his feet, offered him everything I possessed as a tribute, and thereafter listened to and received this sutra with a sincere heart.
At that time, I was dull-witted; although I had heard the sutra, I could only master the words and phrases of a single verse:
“The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa, Having forever severed birth and death.”
"If one listens with a sincere heart, one will always obtain immeasurable joy.
Having received these verses, he immediately returned to the house of that sick person.
"Good son!

Although I gave you two or three pieces of meat every day at that time, because of the causal conditions of recollecting the verses, I did not feel it as pain; I did not cease giving them day after day for a full month."
"Good son! By these causes and conditions, his illness was cured; my body was restored to its original state, free from any sores or wounds.
At that time, seeing my body complete and intact, I immediately resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
"If even the power of a single verse can be such as this, how much more so for one who fully receives, maintains, reads, and recites it?
Seeing that this sutra possesses such benefits, I have redoubled my resolve, vowing to attain the path of Buddhahood in the future, with the name Śākyamuni."
"Good son!
By the power of the causal conditions of this single verse, I am able today, amidst this great assembly, to proclaim it in its entirety for the sake of all devas and humans."
"Good son!

For these reasons, this Great Nirvāṇa is inconceivable; it accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit and is the profound, secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. For this reason, those who are able to receive and uphold it will sever and abandon evil outflows."

That which is called "evil" refers to wicked elephants, wicked horses, wicked oxen, and wicked dogs; the dwelling places of venomous snakes; treacherous lands of thorns; precipices and steep cliffs; violent waters and swirling eddies; wicked people and wicked countries; wicked cities and wicked houses; and wicked associates. Regarding such things as these: if they act as causes for outflows (*āsrava*), the Bodhisattva immediately abandons them;
if they do not so act, he does not distance himself from them. If they increase the outflows, he then abandons them;
if they do not cause them to increase, he does not abandon them. If they produce unwholesome dharmas, he then abandons them; if they can produce wholesome dharmas, he does not abandon them.
What is meant by "detachment"?
It is not to carry weapons or staves, but to always distance oneself through the skillful means of right wisdom; therefore, it is called detachment through right wisdom.

To give rise to wholesome dharmas, one must abandon unwholesome dharmas; the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates his own body as being like a disease, like a sore, like an abscess, like an enemy, and like an arrow piercing the body—it is a great mass of suffering and the root of all evils.
Although this body is thus impure, the Bodhisattva nevertheless gazes upon it and nurtures it.

Why is this? It is not for the sake of craving the body, but for the sake of wholesome dharmas; for the sake of nirvāṇa and not for the sake of saṃsāra; for the sake of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and not for the sake of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity; for the sake of the path to bodhi and not for the sake of the path of existence; for the sake of the One Vehicle and not for the sake of the Three Vehicles; for the sake of the subtle and wondrous body endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and not for the sake of even the body of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and for the sake of being a Dharma-wheel-turning King and not for the sake of being a wheel-turning monarch.
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always protect his body. Why is this?

If one does not protect one’s body and life, then one’s life will not be preserved; if life is not preserved, one will be unable to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, or contemplate its meaning. For this reason, a bodhisattva should skillfully protect the body; by means of this principle, the bodhisattva becomes free from all evil outflows (*āsrava*).

Good son! It is like one who wishes to cross over and must carefully protect their raft; like a traveler on the road who carefully protects a fine horse; like a farmer planting crops who carefully protects the manure; like one seeking to neutralize poison who carefully protects a venomous snake; like a person protecting a *caṇḍāla* for the sake of wealth; like one guarding a strong warrior to destroy bandits; like a person in the cold cherishing fire; or like a leper seeking a poisonous medicine.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although he sees that this body is filled with immeasurable impurities, because he wishes to receive and uphold the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he still carefully protects it so that it does not fail or diminish.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates a vicious elephant and an evil spiritual friend as being equal and without distinction. Why is this?
Because both equally destroy the body.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva feels no fear toward evil elephants and the like, yet gives rise to a sense of dread toward evil associates. Why is this?
Because while these evil elephants and such can only destroy the body and cannot destroy the mind, evil associates destroy both.
These evil elephants and the like destroy only a single body, whereas an evil spiritual friend destroys immeasurable bodies of goodness and immeasurable minds of goodness.
These evil elephants and the like can only destroy the impure and foul-smelling body, whereas an evil spiritual friend can destroy both the pure body and the pure mind.
While such evil elephants and the like can destroy only the physical body, an evil spiritual friend destroys the Dharma-body.
One killed by an evil elephant does not necessarily fall into the three evil realms, but one killed by an evil friend will certainly go to the three evil realms.
While such evil elephants and the like are merely enemies to the body, an evil spiritual friend (pāpamitra) is an enemy to the wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should always remain far removed from all evil spiritual friends.
Ordinary worldlings do not depart from such outflows; therefore, outflows arise.
When Bodhisattvas depart from them, outflows do not arise.
If even Bodhisattvas have no outflows in this way, how much less so for the Tathāgata?
Therefore, it is not an outflow (*āsrava*).
What is the "proximate outflow"?

All ordinary worldlings accept and take up clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for the sake of physical and mental pleasure; seeking such things, they commit various evils, unaware of their past or future, and transmigrate through the three realms of existence. For this reason, it is called an outflow.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives such faults, he immediately distances himself from them. When he requires robes, he accepts them only at the proper time; he does not do so for the sake of his body, but solely for the sake of the Dharma. He does not increase arrogance, but keeps his mind perpetually humble. He does not accept them for adornment, but for the sake of modesty, and to ward off cold and heat, as well as evil winds, torrential rains, and the bites and stings of harmful insects, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and vipers.

Although he receives food and drink, his mind is free from greedy attachment; it is not for the sake of his body, but always for the sake of the True Dharma; not for the sake of skin or flesh, but solely for the sake of sentient beings; not out of pride, but for the sake of physical strength; not to cause harm to others, but to treat the ulcer of hunger. Even when obtaining superior flavors, his mind remains free from greedy attachment; his receiving of dwellings and lodgings is likewise thus.
One does not allow the fetters of greed and pride to dwell in the mind; one takes up a dwelling as a refuge for Bodhi to ward off the thieves of the fetters and to block the winds and rains of evil.
Those who seek medicine do so with a mind free from greed and pride, solely for the sake of the True Dharma and not for the sake of life, but for the sake of eternal life.
Good son! It is like a person suffering from an ulcer who applies ghee and parched flour to it and wraps it with cloth.
He applies the ghee and flour to draw out the pus and blood; he scatters medicinal powder upon it so that the ulcer may heal; and he stays in a deep room to protect against the evil winds.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: because he views the body as a wound, he covers it with clothing; for the pus of the nine orifices, he seeks out food and drink; for protection against evil winds and rain, he accepts and takes up a dwelling; and when the four poisons flare up, he seeks out medicine.
The Bodhisattva accepts the four kinds of offerings for the sake of the path to enlightenment, not for the sake of his own life. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects as follows:

"If I do not accept these four kinds of offerings, my body will perish and fail to attain stability; if it lacks stability, I shall not be able to endure suffering; if I cannot endure suffering, I shall be unable to cultivate wholesome dharmas; but if I can endure suffering, I shall be able to cultivate immeasurable wholesome dharmas."

If I am unable to endure various sufferings, I will give rise to a mind of hatred toward painful sensations, a mind of greedy attachment toward pleasant sensations, and if I seek pleasure but do not obtain it, ignorance will arise.
Therefore, while ordinary beings give rise to outflows (*āsrava*) regarding the four types of offerings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to observe them deeply and does not give rise to outflows.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is called "without outflows" (*anāsrava*); how then could the Tathāgata be called "with outflows"?
For this reason, the Tathāgata is not said to possess outflows (*āsrava*).
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 22. *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 23.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Ten, Part Three: The Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Radiant and All-Illuminating.
"Furthermore, good son!

Although all ordinary beings may skillfully guard their bodies, their minds still give rise to three kinds of evil thoughts; for this reason, even if they sever their afflictions and attain birth in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, they will nonetheless fall back again into the three evil realms.
"Good son!
It is like a person crossing the great ocean who, when on the verge of reaching the other shore, sinks into the water and dies.
Ordinary people are just like this: when they are about to exhaust the three realms of existence, they fall back into the three miserable paths."
Why is this? Because there is no wholesome awakening.
What is wholesome awakening?
Regarding the so-called six objects of mindfulness:

ordinary persons possess weak and inferior wholesome minds while unwholesome states blaze intensely. Because their wholesome minds are weak, their wisdom is meager; because their wisdom is meager, they increase the various outflows (*āsrava*).

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with the pure eye of wisdom, perceives the faults of the three types of awakening; he knows that these three awakenings possess various afflictions and constantly act as enemies to sentient beings within the context of the three vehicles.

Due to these three causes and conditions for delusion, immeasurable ordinary beings fail to see the Buddha-nature; throughout immeasurable kalpas, they give rise to inverted views, claiming that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, lacks permanence, bliss, and self, and possesses only purity, and that the Tathāgata ultimately enters into parinirvāṇa.
All sentient beings are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; yet, due to their inverted minds, they speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

In reality there are no three vehicles, yet due to their inverted minds, they speak of the existence of three vehicles. The path of one reality is true and not false, yet due to their inverted minds, they say there is no single reality.
These three evil thoughts are constantly censured by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; these three evil thoughts constantly harm oneself or may also harm others.

When these three perceptions exist, all manner of evils constantly follow after one; these three perceptions are themselves the three fetters, which bind sentient beings to the boundless cycle of birth and death.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly performs such observations regarding the three types of thoughts.

At times, due to certain causes and conditions, a bodhisattva may encounter the thought of desire; however, they should remain silent and not accept it, just as a person who is handsome and pure does not accept any filth or impurity;
or like a red-hot iron ball, which no one would take up.
Just as a Brahmin by nature does not accept beef;
just as a person who is full does not accept foul food;
and just as a Wheel-Turning King does not sit on the same seat as any outcaste (caṇḍāla).
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s loathing of the three perceptions, their non-acceptance and non-savoring, is likewise so. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Sentient beings know me to be a field of merit; how could I accept such unwholesome dharmas?
If I were to accept these unwholesome thoughts, I would no longer be fit to serve as a field of merit for sentient beings."
I myself do not say that I am a field of merit; it is when sentient beings see my appearance that they say, "I am one.
If I were now to give rise to such an evil thought, I would be deceiving all sentient beings.
Because of my past deceptions, I have wandered through birth and death for immeasurable eons and fallen into the three evil realms.
If I were to receive the faithful offerings of others with an evil mind, all devas and humans, as well as the seers possessing the five supernormal powers, would bear witness to it and reprove me.
If I were to receive the faithful offerings of others with unwholesome thoughts, I would cause the donor's karmic fruit to diminish or even become void of reward.
If I were to accept the gifts of a benefactor with an evil mind, I would become an enemy to that donor.
All these donors have always regarded me as their own infant; how could I deceive them and give rise to thoughts of enmity toward them? Why is this so?
Or because it causes the donor to fail to obtain the fruit of their reward, or to obtain only a meager reward.

I always refer to myself as one who has left the household life; now, one who has left the household life should not give rise to evil, for if one gives rise to evil, they are not one who has left the household life.
For one who has left the household life, body and speech must be in accord; if they are not in accord, one is not truly a renunciant.

I have abandoned my parents, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, and friends to leave home and cultivate the Way. This is precisely the time for cultivating wholesome thoughts, not the time for cultivating unwholesome thoughts.
It is like a person who enters the ocean to seek jewels, yet instead of taking genuine gems, takes only glass;
or like a person who abandons exquisite music to play amidst filth and excrement.
It is like abandoning a precious woman to consort with a maidservant;
like discarding a golden vessel to use a clay bowl;
like casting away nectar to consume poisonous medicine.
It is like abandoning a long-time friend and a skilled, virtuous physician to follow a hostile and wicked physician, seeking and taking his medicine.

"I am just like this: having abandoned the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma, I have instead consumed the various evil thoughts of the Māra-enemy."
A human body is as difficult to obtain as the udumbara flower, yet I have now obtained it;
a Tathāgata is even more difficult to encounter than the udumbara flower, yet I have now encountered him;
the pure jewel of the Dharma is difficult to see or hear, yet I have now heard it.
It is like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.

Human life does not pause, passing faster than water over a mountain; though one exists today, tomorrow is difficult to guarantee. Why, then, do you indulge your mind and allow it to dwell in unwholesome dharmas?
Vigorous youth does not endure, being like a galloping horse; how can one rely upon it to give rise to arrogance?

It is like an evil spirit waiting to seek out a person's faults; the four great evil spirits are likewise, constantly coming to seek out my own failings. How could I allow unwholesome thoughts to arise?
It is like a dilapidated house or a collapsing dwelling;
my life is likewise. How could I give rise to evil?
I am called a śramaṇa; a śramaṇa is one who awakens to what is wholesome.
"I have now given rise to unwholesome thoughts; how can I truly be called a śramaṇa?
I am named 'one who has left the home life,' and those who have left the home life are said to cultivate the path of goodness;
yet I now practice evil—how can I be called one who has left the home life?"
I am now called a true Brahmin; a Brahmin is one who practices pure conduct.
Since I am now engaging in impure and evil thoughts, how can I be called a Brahmin?
I am now also called one of the great Kṣatriya clan; those of the Kṣatriya clan are able to eliminate enemies.
Since I am currently unable to eliminate evil enemies, how can I be entitled to the name of the Kṣatriya clan?
"I am called a bhikṣu; one who is a bhikṣu is named for having destroyed afflictions.
If I do not now destroy evil thoughts and afflictions, how can I be entitled to the name 'bhikṣu'?"
There are six things in the world that are difficult to encounter, which I have now attained; how could I allow unwholesome thoughts to dwell in my mind? What are these six?

First, a Buddha appearing in the world is difficult to encounter; second, hearing the True Dharma is difficult; third, the arising of a sense of dread is difficult; fourth, being born in a central land is difficult; fifth, obtaining a human body is difficult; and sixth, having all faculties complete is difficult.
"These six things are difficult to obtain, yet they have now been obtained; therefore, one should not give rise to evil thoughts.

At that time, the Bodhisattva practices this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and constantly and diligently observes these various evil minds. Because all ordinary worldlings do not see the faults and calamities of such evil minds, they undergo the three types of perception, which is called "undergoing outflows" (āsrava).

Having seen this, the Bodhisattva does not accept it, does not cling to it, relinquishes it without guarding it, and relying on the Eightfold Noble Path, pushes it away so that it departs and cuts it off so that it is severed. For this reason, the Bodhisattva has no outflows (āsrava); how then could one say that the Tathāgata has outflows?
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not subject to outflows (*āsrava*).

Furthermore, son of good family, when ordinary persons encounter physical or mental suffering and distress, they give rise to various evils. Whether they contract a physical illness or a mental affliction, they cause their body, speech, and mind to commit various evils; because of committing these evils, they transmigrate through the three realms of existence and undergo all manner of suffering.
Why is this? Because ordinary persons lack mindfulness and wisdom, they give rise to various outflows; these are called the outflows of mindfulness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly reflects upon himself:

"Since countless kalpas past, I have committed various evils with this body and mind; by these causes and conditions, I have wandered through birth and death within the three evil realms, fully experiencing manifold sufferings, which has ultimately caused me to stray from the true path of the Three Vehicles."
Because of these evil causes and conditions, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great fear within his own body and mind; he abandons all evils and proceeds toward the wholesome path. Good son!

It is as if there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket and ordered a man to tend to them—feeding them, providing for their rest and movement, and washing their bodies—and declared: "If you cause even one snake to become angry, I shall execute you by the law in the marketplace."
At that time, having heard the king’s urgent command, the man was filled with terror and abandoned the chest to flee.
The king then dispatched five *caṇḍālas* to follow him with drawn swords; when the man looked back and saw the five men behind him, he hurried away even more swiftly.
At that time, the five men used a wicked stratagem; they concealed the knives they were carrying and secretly dispatched one man to feign friendship, saying to him:
"You should return."
The man did not believe them and fled to a village, wishing to hide himself.

Once he had entered the village, he peered into the various houses but saw no one; he inspected the jars and vessels, finding them all empty and devoid of anything. Seeing no people and unable to find any goods, he sat down upon the ground, when he heard a voice from the air: "Alas, O man!"
"This settlement is desolate and devoid of inhabitants.
Tonight, six great bandits will arrive; if you should encounter them, your life will not be spared. How then shall you manage to escape them?"
At that time, the man’s terror increased even further, and he abandoned [the previous path] and departed.
On the way, he encountered a river with a swift current; as there were no boats or rafts, out of fear he immediately gathered various kinds of grass and wood to make a raft.
He further reflected:
"If I remain here, I shall be harmed by the venomous snake, the five caṇḍālas, the one who feigns friendship, and the six great bandits."
"If I cross this river, I cannot rely upon this raft; I shall surely drown and die.
It would be better to drown and die than to be harmed by those snake-thieves.
He then pushed the grass raft into the water, leaned his body upon it, and with hands clutching and feet treading, he cut across the current to the other side.
Having reached the other shore, they dwell in peace and freedom from affliction; their minds are serene and their fears are eliminated.

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear, receive, and uphold the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they contemplate the body as being like a casket and the earth, water, fire, and wind elements as being like four venomous snakes—those with venom in their sight, venom in their touch, venom in their breath, and venom in their bite. Because all sentient beings encounter these four poisons, they lose their lives."

The four great elements of sentient beings are likewise thus: sometimes they are harmful when seen, sometimes harmful when touched, sometimes harmful through their breath, and sometimes harmful when bitten; by these causes and conditions, they remain far removed from all that is wholesome.
Furthermore, good son!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the four venomous snakes have four castes, namely: kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, vaiśya, and śūdra.

These four great serpents are likewise thus; they possess four natures: the nature of solidity, the nature of moisture, the nature of heat, and the nature of motion. Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates these four great elements as being of the same nature as the four venomous snakes.
Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates these four great elements as being like four venomous snakes.
How does he contemplate them?
These four poisonous snakes constantly watch for an opportunity, wondering: "When shall we look upon him?
When shall we touch him?
When shall we bite him?"
When will they bite?
The four great venomous snakes are likewise; they constantly watch for sentient beings to find their vulnerabilities.
If one is killed by these four snakes, one will ultimately not fall into the three evil realms.
If one is slain by the four great elements, one will inevitably fall into the three evil realms; of this there is no doubt.
Although these four poisonous snakes may be cared for and nourished, they still seek to kill people;
the four great elements are likewise: though they are constantly provided for, they also constantly lead people to commit various evils.
Just as any one of these four poisonous snakes can kill a person if it becomes enraged, so too is the nature of the four great elements:
if even one of them becomes disturbed, it can likewise harm a person.
Although these four venomous snakes dwell in the same place, their four minds are each distinct;
likewise, the four great poisonous snakes are also thus—though they occupy the same location, their natures are each different.
Although these four venomous snakes may be treated with respect, they are difficult to approach;
likewise, the four great venomous snakes are also difficult to approach, even if one treats them with respect.
When these four poisonous snakes harm a person, there may be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who can treat them with mantras and medicines;
however, when the four great elements kill a person, even if there were śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others with divine mantras and excellent medicines, they would be unable to cure it.
Just as a person who cherishes themselves, upon smelling the foul odor of four venomous snakes, immediately distances himself from them;
so too do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, upon smelling the stench of the four great elements, immediately distance themselves from them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further contemplated the four great poisonous snakes; giving rise to great fear, he fled from them and cultivated the Eightfold Noble Path.
"The five caṇḍālas are the five aggregates."
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla?
A caṇḍāla is one who constantly causes the separation of loved ones for noble persons and brings together those who harbor enmity and hatred.
The five aggregates are likewise; they cause people to greedily approach unwholesome dharmas and to distance themselves from all purely wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a caṇḍāla who adorns himself with various weapons—whether swords, shields, bows, arrows, armor, or spears—which can harm others.
The five aggregates are likewise: they are firmly adorned with various afflictions, which harm ignorant people and cause them to fall into the various realms of existence.
Good son! It is like a *caṇḍāla*, who seizes the opportunity to harm anyone who has committed a transgression.
The five aggregates are likewise; they possess the faults of various fetters and can constantly harm people.
For this reason, the bodhisattva deeply contemplates the five aggregates as being like caṇḍālas.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like outcasts (*caṇḍāla*):
just as an outcast has no heart of compassion and harms both enemies and kin alike, so too are the five aggregates;
they have no heart of compassion and harm both the good and the evil alike.
Just as a caṇḍāla distresses all people, so too are the five aggregates; by means of the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they constantly distress all sentient beings in saṃsāra.
For this reason, the bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like outcastes (caṇḍāla):
just as an outcaste person constantly harbors a harmful mind,
so too do the five aggregates constantly harbor minds of affliction and harm through the various fetters (saṃyojana).
Just as a person who lacks feet, weapons, and attendants will surely be killed by a *caṇḍāla*, so it is with sentient beings:
lacking feet, lacking weapons, and lacking attendants, they are plundered and harmed by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

The feet are called the precepts, the sword is called wisdom, and the attendants are called virtuous friends; because these three things are absent, one is harmed by the thieves of the five aggregates.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes that the five aggregates are worse than a caṇḍāla.

Why is this? If sentient beings are killed by the five *caṇḍālas*, they do not fall into hell; however, those killed by the aggregates (*skandha*) fall into hell. For this reason, the Bodhisattva regards the aggregates as more harmful than the *caṇḍālas*.
Having made this contemplation, he made this vow:
"I would rather attend upon a *caṇḍāla* for the rest of my life than attend upon the five aggregates for even a moment.
A *caṇḍāla* can only harm the deluded people of the desire realm; [the five aggregates, however, cause suffering in all realms]."
These thieves of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) universally harm the ordinary beings of the three realms.
A caṇḍāla can only slaughter those who have committed crimes;
these thieves of the five aggregates, however, do not distinguish whether beings are guilty or innocent, but are able to harm them all.
A caṇḍāla does not harm the elderly, women, or children;
however, this thief of the five aggregates harms all sentient beings without distinction, whether they be old or young, or female.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates that these aggregates (skandhas) are more dangerous than a caṇḍāla; for this reason, he makes this vow: "I would rather dwell near a caṇḍāla for the rest of my life than be near the five aggregates for even a moment."
Furthermore, good son!
A caṇḍāla harms only others and never harms himself;
the thief of the five aggregates harms both himself and others, exceeding even the caṇḍāla in its wickedness.
A caṇḍāla may be ransomed through kind words, money, or precious goods;
the five aggregates are not like this, for they cannot be forcibly liberated by means of kind inducements, money, or precious goods.
A caṇḍāla does not necessarily kill at all times during the four periods of the day;
the five aggregates are not like this, for they constantly harm all sentient beings in every moment of thought.
A caṇḍāla can be escaped from by fleeing to another location; [the five aggregates cannot].
The five aggregates are not like that; they pervade all places and there is no escape.
Although a caṇḍāla may harm others, he does not follow them after the harm has been done;
the five aggregates are not like that, for once they have killed a sentient being, they pursue and never leave it.
Therefore, a bodhisattva would rather dwell near a caṇḍāla for the rest of their life than dwell with the five aggregates even for a moment.
A person of wisdom, through skillful means, attains liberation from the five aggregates.

Skillful means consist of the Eightfold Noble Path, the Six Pāramitās, and the Four Immeasurable Minds; by means of these skillful means, one attains liberation, such that body and mind are no longer harmed by the five aggregates.
Why is this? Because the body is like a vajra and the mind is like space, the body and mind are difficult to destroy or corrupt.
For this reason, when a bodhisattva observes that the aggregates (skandhas) give rise to various unwholesome dharmas, they conceive great fear and cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is also like that man who, fearing the four venomous snakes and the five caṇḍālas, proceeds along the road without looking back or lingering.
That which feigns intimacy and friendliness is called craving.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply contemplates the fetter of craving as an enemy feigning friendship: if one knows it for what it truly is, it can do no harm; but if one fails to recognize it, one will certainly be harmed by it.

Craving is likewise so; if one knows its nature, it cannot cause sentient beings to revolve within the suffering of birth and death, but if one does not know it, they will cycle through the six realms of existence and undergo all manner of suffering.
Why is this? Because the affliction of craving is difficult to abandon.

It is like a false friend who feigns intimacy and is hard to distance oneself from; such a false friend constantly watches for one's vulnerability to cause separation from what is loved and union with what is hated.
Craving is likewise; it causes people to distance themselves from all wholesome dharmas and draw near to all unwholesome dharmas.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas deeply contemplate craving as being like a deceitful enemy masquerading as a friend.

Because of seeing and not seeing, and hearing and not hearing: just as an ordinary person sees the faults of birth and death, yet although they possess wisdom, because it is covered by ignorance, they later fail to see them again.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise: though they see, they do not truly see; though they hear, they do not truly hear.
Why is this? It is because of their attachment to craving.
Why is this? Because one perceives the faults of birth and death, one cannot swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards this fetter of craving as an enemy feigning friendship.
What is meant by the signs of an enemy feigning intimacy?

It is like an enemy who, being unreal, falsely manifests the appearance of reality; who, being unapproachable, falsely manifests the appearance of approachability; who, being truly unwholesome, falsely manifests the appearance of wholesomeness; and who, being truly unloved, falsely manifests the appearance of love.
Why is this? Because it constantly watches for a person's vulnerability, desiring to cause them harm.

Craving is also like this: it constantly deceives sentient beings by feigning reality where there is none, feigning proximity where there is none, feigning goodness where there is none, and feigning affection where there is none; it perpetually deludes all beings, causing them to revolve in birth and death.
For this reason, the bodhisattva contemplates craving as an enemy feigning friendship.
An enemy feigning friendship deceives because one perceives only their body and speech, but does not see their heart;
craving is likewise: it is merely deceptive and ultimately unobtainable, and for this reason it deludes all sentient beings.
An enemy who feigns friendship has both a beginning and an end, and is thus easy to distance oneself from;
affection is not like this, having neither beginning nor end, and is therefore difficult to distance oneself from.
An enemy who feigns intimacy is difficult to recognize when at a distance, but easy to recognize when near;
affection is not like this—it is difficult to recognize even when near, how much more so when far away?
For this reason, a bodhisattva regards craving as worse than a deceitful friend.

Because all sentient beings are bound by the fetter of craving, they distance themselves from Great Nirvana and draw near to birth and death; they distance themselves from permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and draw near to impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity. Therefore, in various sūtras, I have described it as one of the three stains.

Regarding present affairs, because of ignorance, one does not see their faults and harms; thus, one cannot abandon those who are affectionate, hateful, or deceitfully friendly, and ultimately cannot harm those who possess wisdom.

Therefore, the bodhisattva deeply contemplates this craving and gives rise to great fear; he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, just as that man, fearing the four venomous snakes, the five caṇḍālas, and the one who feigned friendship, pressed on along the road without turning back.
"The empty village is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates the internal six sense bases as empty and non-existent, just like an empty village. It is like that terrified person who, having entered the village, does not see even a single inhabitant; he searches everywhere through the jars and vessels but does not find a single thing."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; he contemplates the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as empty and non-existent, seeing not even a single atom of reality in sentient beings. Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates the internal six sense bases as empty and non-existent, like that deserted village.
"Good son!
When a band of thieves gazes from afar at that empty village, they never conceive the notion that it is empty space.

Ordinary people are just like this: they do not conceive the notion of emptiness regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Because they cannot conceive the notion of emptiness, they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing immeasurable suffering."
"Good son!

When a band of thieves arrives, one gives rise to the perception of emptiness; the Bodhisattva is likewise, for he contemplates these six sense bases and constantly gives rise to the perception of emptiness. Because he gives rise to the perception of emptiness, he does not transmigrate through birth and death to undergo suffering."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is always free from inversion regarding these six sense bases; because they are free from inversion, they no longer transmigrate through birth and death.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as a band of thieves entering this empty village finds peace and security, so too do the thieves of the afflictions find peace and security upon entering these six sense bases.
Just as a thief dwelling in an empty village has no fear, so too are the bandits of the afflictions; dwelling within these six sense bases, they likewise have no fear.

Just as that empty village is the dwelling place of lions, tigers, wolves, and various other evil beasts, so too are these six internal sense bases the dwelling place of all manner of evil beasts that are the afflictions.
Therefore, the bodhisattva deeply contemplates that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are empty and non-existent, being purely abodes for all that is unwholesome.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as empty and non-existent, like an empty village."

Why is this? Because it is deceptive and unreal; because one perceives existence where there is emptiness and nothingness; because one perceives pleasure where there is truly no pleasure; and because one perceives a person where there is truly no person.

The six internal sense bases are likewise thus: though empty and non-existent, one forms the perception of existence; though truly there is no pleasure, one forms the perception of pleasure; though truly there is no person, one forms the perception of a person. Only the wise person can know this and attain its reality.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as an empty village may at times have people and at times have no people, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are not like this;
they are invariably devoid of a person.
Why is this? Because their nature is eternally empty; that which is known by the wise is not seen with the eyes.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as being full of many harms, and cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path without ceasing or resting, just like that person who, fearing the four poisonous snakes, the five caṇḍālas, the one feigning intimacy, and the six great thieves, clings to the correct path.
"The six great thieves are the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-bāhyaviṣaya*).
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates these six sense objects as being like six great thieves. Why is this?
Because they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas.
Just as six great bandits can plunder all the wealth and treasures of the people, so too are these six thieves of the sense objects; they likewise plunder the wholesome wealth of all sentient beings.

Just as six great bandits, upon entering a person’s house, are able to plunder everything currently within it, making no distinction between the good and the bad, causing even the most wealthy to suddenly fall into poverty.

These thieves of the six sense objects are likewise; if they enter the faculties of a person, they can plunder all wholesome dharmas. Once wholesome dharmas are exhausted, one becomes impoverished and destitute, becoming an icchantika. Therefore, a bodhisattva contemplates the six sense objects with careful attention as being like six great thieves.
Furthermore, good son!
Just as when the six great thieves wish to plunder a person, they must rely on an insider; if there is no insider, they will simply turn back midway.

These thieves of the six sense objects are likewise; they desire to plunder the wholesome dharmas only when there are internal factors within sentient beings, such as their perceptions and views, and characteristics such as permanence, bliss, self, purity, and non-emptiness.
If there are no such internal signs within, the evil thieves of the six sense-objects cannot plunder any wholesome dharmas.

A person of wisdom has no such signs internally, whereas ordinary beings do; therefore, the six sense-objects constantly come to invade and seize the wealth of wholesome dharmas, for because they do not guard them well, they are plundered by them.

"Guardian" refers to wisdom; a person possessing wisdom is able to provide excellent protection and thus is not robbed. For this reason, the Bodhisattva contemplates these six sense objects as being no different from the six great thieves.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as the six great thieves can cause physical and mental suffering and affliction to the people, so too are these thieves of the six sense-objects; they constantly cause physical and mental suffering and affliction to sentient beings."
The six great thieves can only plunder the wealth and goods of people in the present;
these thieves of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) constantly plunder the wholesome wealth of sentient beings across the three periods of time.
The six great thieves find joy in the night; [the thieves of the six sense-objects find joy] in the darkness of ignorance.
The six objects of sensory desire, which are like evil bandits, are likewise thus: they find joy only while dwelling in the darkness of ignorance.
Just as these six great bandits can only be restrained by kings, so too can the six evil bandits of the sensory objects be restrained only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Whenever these six great thieves intend to plunder, they do not discriminate between the handsome and the ugly, the noble lineage and the lowly, the wise and the learned, or the wealthy and the poor;

the evil thieves of the six sense-objects are likewise, for when they intend to plunder the wholesome dharmas, they do not discriminate between the handsome and so forth, down to the poor and the lowly.
Although various kings may sever the hands and feet of these six great thieves, they are still unable to cause their minds to cease [their depredations];

the evil thieves of the six sense-objects are likewise: although *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, and *anāgāmins* may sever their hands and feet, they cannot prevent them from plundering wholesome dharmas.
Just as a valiant and courageous person is able to subdue these six great thieves, so too do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas likewise subdue the evil thieves of the six sense-objects.
For example, if a person has many clans and a flourishing circle of kinsmen, they will not be plundered by the six thieves;
sentient beings are likewise: if they have a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they will not be plundered by the evil thieves of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
These six great thieves can only steal and plunder when they encounter people or objects;
the six sense-objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) are not like this, for whether one sees or knows, hears or smells, touches or perceives, they are all capable of plundering.
The six great thieves can only plunder the wealth of persons within the desire realm, but they cannot plunder those in the form and formless realms;
the evil thieves of the six sense objects, however, are not like this, for they can plunder all the treasures of goodness throughout the three realms.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva carefully contemplates that the six sense objects are more dangerous than those six thieves. Having made this contemplation, he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path and proceeds directly forward without turning back.
This is like that terrified person who, fearing the four venomous snakes, the five outcasts, the one deceiver, and the six great thieves, abandoned the empty village and set out upon the road.
“Encountering a river along the way is itself affliction (*kleśa*).
How does a bodhisattva contemplate this affliction as being like a great river?
Just as that swift river can sweep away even a fragrant elephant;”
The swift river of afflictions is likewise; it can sweep away even the pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, the bodhisattva deeply contemplates afflictions as being like a swift river.
Because its depth is difficult to fathom, it is called a "river";
because its boundaries cannot be found, it is called "great. Within it dwell many kinds of evil fish, and the great river of afflictions is just the same.
Because only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to reach its bottom, it is called "extremely deep.
Because only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can reach its boundaries, it is called "vast and great.
Because it constantly harms all deluded sentient beings, it is called "evil fish."
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates these afflictions as being like a great river.

Just as the waters of a great river can cause all grasses, trees, and forests to grow, so too does the great river of afflictions cause the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) of sentient beings to flourish; thus, the Bodhisattva contemplates these afflictions as being like a great river.
For example, it is like a person who falls into a great river and has no sense of shame or remorse;
sentient beings are likewise, falling into the river of afflictions without shame or remorse.
Just as one who falls into the river may die before reaching its bottom; so it is with these beings.
Falling into the river of afflictions is likewise so: without reaching its bottom, one revolves through the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

What is called the "bottom" is the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*); if there are those who do not cultivate such a mark of emptiness, it should be known that such persons cannot achieve liberation from the twenty-five states of existence. Because all sentient beings are unable to skillfully cultivate emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*), they are constantly swept away by the swift current of afflictions.
Just as that great river can only destroy the body but cannot sweep away all wholesome dharmas, the great river of afflictions is not like this;
it can destroy all wholesome dharmas of both body and mind.
That great violent river can only sweep away those within the desire realm;
the great river of afflictions, however, can sweep away those among the humans and devas of the three realms.
As for the great rivers of the world, one may reach the other shore by embracing them with the hands and treading upon them with the feet.
The great river of afflictions can only be crossed by Bodhisattvas through the six *pāramitās*.
Just as the waters of a great river are difficult to cross,
so too is the great river of afflictions difficult to cross.
Why is it called "difficult to cross"?
Even the great Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet been able to cross it completely; only the Buddhas have finally crossed it. For this reason, it is called "difficult to cross."
For example, if a person were being swept away by a river, they would be unable to practice even a hair’s breadth of wholesome dharma;
so it is with sentient beings: those who are swept away and submerged by the river of afflictions likewise cannot practice wholesome dharmas.
Just as when a person falls into a river and is being swept away by the current, another who possesses strength can pull them out and rescue them;
yet when one has fallen into the river of afflictions as an icchantika, neither śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, nor even the Buddhas are able to rescue them.
When the great rivers of the world reach the end of a kalpa, the seven suns shine simultaneously and can cause them to dry up;

the great river of afflictions is not like this, for even though śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment, they cannot dry it up. Therefore, the bodhisattva regards all afflictions as being like a turbulent river.

"It is, for example, like that man who, fearing the four venomous snakes, the five caṇḍālas, the one who feigns intimacy, and the six great thieves, abandoned the deserted village and proceeded along the road until he reached a river, where he gathered grass to make a raft."

The Bodhisattva is likewise: fearing the four great serpents of the elements, the Cāṇḍālas of the five aggregates, the deceptive intimacy of craving, the empty village of the six sense bases, and the evil bandits of the six sense objects; having reached the river of afflictions, he cultivates morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the six pāramitās, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as his boat and raft. Relying upon and riding this raft, he crosses the river of afflictions, reaches the other shore, and dwells eternally in the bliss of nirvāṇa.
A Bodhisattva practicing the Great Parinirvāṇa reflects thus:
"If I am unable to endure such physical suffering and mental suffering, I shall not be able to enable all sentient beings to cross the river of afflictions."
Reflecting thus, although there were such physical and mental sufferings, he silently endured them; because he endured them, no outflows (āsrava) arose.
If even a bodhisattva has no outflows in this way, how much less could a Buddha, a Tathāgata, have any outflows?
Therefore, the Buddhas are not said to possess outflows (*sāsrava*).
Why, then, are the Tathāgatas not without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
It is because the Tathāgatas constantly act within the midst of that which possesses outflows.

The outflows (āsrava) are precisely the twenty-five states of existence; therefore, while śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings say that the Buddha possesses outflows, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are truly without outflows.
"Good son! For these reasons, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have no fixed characteristics. Good son!"
"Therefore, those who commit the four grave offenses, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and the icchantikas—all of these are indefinite.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijñā-Āryaguṇarāja addressed [the Buddha], saying: "So it is, so it is."
Just as the holy teachings state, all dharmas are entirely indeterminate.
Because they are indeterminate, one should know that the Tathāgata likewise does not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa.
As the Buddha previously taught, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, is there "Nirvāṇa" or "Great Nirvāṇa" within what is heard and what is not heard?
What is Nirvāṇa?
"What is the Great Parinirvāṇa?
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! If there are bodhisattvas who have attained the dhāraṇī of mindfulness, they are then able to inquire as you have done, good son!"

Just as people in the world speak of an ocean and a great ocean, a river and a great river, a mountain and a great mountain, a land and a great land, a city and a great city, a sentient being and a great sentient being, a king and a great king, a person and a great person, a deva and a deva among devas, a path and a great path, so it is with nirvāṇa: there is nirvāṇa and there is great nirvāṇa.
"What is nirvana? Good son!
It is like a person who, being hungry, obtains a small amount of food and drink; this is called peace and happiness, and such peace and happiness is also called nirvana."
Just as one who recovers from illness is called "at ease and happy," such peace and happiness is also called *nirvāṇa*.
Just as a person who is terrified finds peace and happiness upon finding a place of refuge, such peace and happiness is also called *nirvāṇa*.
Just as a poor person who obtains the seven precious treasures attains peace and happiness, such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa.
Just as a person who contemplates bones and does not give rise to craving attains peace and happiness, such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa.
Such a nirvāṇa cannot be called Mahāparinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because it is characterized by hunger and thirst, illness, fear, poverty, and the arising of craving and attachment, it is merely called nirvāṇa, not Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Good son!

Whether it be ordinary persons or śrāvakas, if they sever the fetters of the desire realm—whether by means of the mundane path or the noble path—they attain peace and happiness. Such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa, but it cannot be called Mahāparinirvāṇa.

If one can sever the fetters of the first dhyāna, up to and including those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one then attains peace and bliss; such peace and bliss is also called nirvāṇa, but it cannot be called the Great Nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because afflictions arise again due to the presence of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
What is meant by "affliction-habitual-tendencies"?

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the residual habit-energies of affliction (*kleśa-vāsanā*), namely: "my body," "my robe," "I go," "I come," "I speak," and "I hear. When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter Nirvāṇa, the nature of Nirvāṇa is without self (*anātman*) and without pleasure (*asukha*), possessing only permanence (*nitya*) and purity (*śuci*); this is precisely what is called the residual habit-energy of affliction.
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha possess distinct characteristics, and the Tathāgata ultimately enters parinirvāṇa.

However, the nirvāṇa attained by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is equal and without distinction. For this reason, that which is attained by the two vehicles is not the Great Nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because it is devoid of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Only that which possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity can be named Great Nirvana.
Good son! Just as there is a place capable of receiving all waters, which is called the great ocean;
so too, wherever śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Tathāgatas enter, that is named Great Nirvāṇa.

The four dhyānas, the three samādhis, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the ten totalities—whosoever is able to encompass such immeasurable wholesome dharmas as these is said to possess Great Nirvāṇa.
“Good son! It is like a river whose bottom cannot be reached even by the foremost fragrant elephant; it is therefore called ‘great.
When śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage do not see the Buddha-nature, that is called ‘nirvāṇa,’ but not ‘Mahāparinirvāṇa.’”
If one can clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, then it is called Great Nirvana.
As for this Great Nirvana, only the Great Elephant King can fathom its depths; the Great Elephant King refers to all Buddhas.
"Good son!
If even Mahānāgas, Baktra-demons, and great strongmen cannot ascend it after a long period of time, only then is it called a 'great mountain'."
That which cannot be seen by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the nāgas and mahābalas—this is what is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Wherever a minor king resides is called a small city; where a wheel-turning sage-king (cakravartin) resides is called a great city.
The abodes of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—those numbering eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, and ten thousand—are called "nirvāṇa.
However, the abode of the Unsurpassed Lord of Dharma, the Holy King, is alone entitled to be named Mahāparinirvāṇa; for this reason, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Good son!
For example, if there is a person who sees the fourfold army and feels no fear, you should know that this person is called a 'Great Being.

If there are sentient beings who feel no fear toward the three evil realms, afflictions, or evil karma, and are able to extensively deliver sentient beings therein, you should know that such persons have attained Great Nirvana."

If there is one who can provide for their parents, show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, cultivate wholesome dharmas, speak with sincerity and without deception, endure all evils, and give alms to the poor and destitute, such a person is called a great man.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: possessing great compassion and pitying all beings, he is like a parent to all sentient beings; able to ferry them across the river of birth and death, he universally reveals to all beings the Way of the Single Reality—this is what is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
“Good son! ‘Great Name’ is inconceivable;

that which is inconceivable cannot be believed by any sentient beings, and this is precisely what is called Mahāparinirvāṇa. It is named Great Nirvāṇa because it is perceived only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.”
For what reasons and conditions is it further called "Great"?
Because it is attained only after immeasurable causes and conditions, it is called "Great. Good son!
Just as things obtained by many causes and conditions in the world are called "great," so too is Nirvana;
because it is obtained through many causes and conditions, it is called "great."
Why is it further called Great Nirvāṇa?
Because it possesses the Great Self (mahātman), it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Although Nirvāṇa is without self, because it is characterized by great sovereignty, it is called the Great Self.
What is meant by "great sovereignty"?
There are eight forms of sovereignty, which are called the "Self. What are these eight?
First, they are able to manifest a single body as many bodies, with the number and size of these bodies being like fine motes of dust, filling immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
The body of the Tathāgata is in truth not composed of atoms; because of his sovereignty, he manifests a body of atoms. Such sovereignty is the Great Self.
Second, he manifests a single atom-sized body that fills the trichiliocosm, yet the body of the Tathāgata in truth does not fill the trichiliocosm.
Why is this? Because it is unimpeded and because it is directly sovereign, it fills the trichiliocosm; such sovereignty is called the "Great Self."

"Third, he is able to lift his body—which fills this trichiliocosm—and fly through the air, passing beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers without any obstruction."
The body of the Tathāgata is in truth neither light nor heavy; because of its sovereignty, it can manifest as light or heavy.
Such sovereignty is called the Great Self. Fourth, through sovereignty, one attains mastery.
What is mastery?
The Tathāgata dwells with a single mind, unmoving, yet manifests infinite forms and types of beings, each causing them to possess a mind.
At times, the Tathāgata may perform a single act, yet causes sentient beings to accomplish it individually.
The body of the Tathāgata dwells eternally in a single land, yet causes it to be seen by all in other lands.
Such mastery is called the Great Self.
"Fifth, because of mastery over the faculties."
What is meant by mastery over the faculties?
It is that with a single faculty, the Tathāgata is likewise able to see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, distinguish tastes, perceive tangibles, and know mental phenomena.
The six sense faculties of the Tathāgata likewise do not see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, distinguish tastes, feel tangibles, or cognize dharmas.
Because they possess mastery, they cause the faculties to be sovereign; such sovereignty is called the Great Self.
"Sixth, because of mastery, he attains all dharmas, yet the Tathāgata’s mind has no notion of attainment.
Why is this? Because there is nothing to be attained."
If something were existent, it could be called "attainment"; since in reality nothing exists, how can it be called attainment?

If the Tathāgata were to conceive the notion of attainment, then the Buddhas would not attain *nirvāṇa*. It is because there is no attainment that one is said to "attain" *nirvāṇa*; because of mastery, one attains all dharmas; and because of attaining all dharmas, one is called the "Great Self."
"Seventh, because of mastery in exposition.

When the Tathāgata expounds the meaning of a single verse, even after the passage of immeasurable kalpas, the meaning is not exhausted—whether it concerns morality, concentration, generosity, or wisdom. At that time, the Tathāgata does not give rise to the thought, 'I am speaking' or 'He is listening.
Nor does he give rise to the notion of a 'verse,' for although people of the world consider four lines to be a verse, it is called a 'verse' only in accordance with worldly convention."
The nature of all dharmas is likewise ineffable; it is through sovereign mastery that the Tathāgata expounds it, and because he expounds it, it is called the "Great Self.
Eighth, the Tathāgata pervades all places, just like space.

The nature of space cannot be perceived; likewise, the Tathāgata is truly invisible, yet by virtue of his sovereign power, he causes all to see him. Such sovereignty is called the "Great Self" (Mahātman), and such a Great Self is called Great Nirvāṇa. For this reason, it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a treasure trove that contains many rare and extraordinary things, complete with a hundred varieties; therefore, it is called a 'great treasury.
The profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is also like this: containing many wonders and being complete without deficiency, it is named Mahāparinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, good son!
That which is boundless is called "great"; because nirvāṇa is boundless, it is therefore called "great.
Furthermore, good son!
Because it possesses great bliss, it is called Great Nirvana.
Nirvana itself has no [inherent] bliss;
it is called Great Nirvana because it possesses four kinds of bliss.
What are the four?
First, because all pleasures have been severed; for that which does not sever pleasure is called suffering, and if there is suffering, it cannot be called great bliss.
Because pleasure has been severed, there is no suffering; being without suffering and without pleasure is what is called "Great Pleasure" (mahāsukha).
The nature of nirvāṇa is without suffering and without pleasure; therefore, nirvāṇa is named Great Pleasure, and for this reason it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son, there are two kinds of joy:
first, that of ordinary beings; second, that of the Buddhas.
The pleasures of ordinary beings are impermanent and subject to decay; therefore, they possess no true pleasure.
The Buddhas possess eternal bliss that never changes; for this reason, it is called Great Bliss.
Furthermore, good son!
There are three kinds of feeling:
first, painful feeling; second, pleasant feeling; and third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also suffering.
Although nirvana is equally neither painful nor pleasant, it is called "great bliss" (mahāsukha); because it is great bliss, it is named Great Nirvana.
Second, because it is great tranquility, it is named great bliss.
The nature of nirvāṇa is great tranquility. Why is this?
Because it is far removed from all clamorous phenomena; it is called "Great Nirvāṇa" because of its great tranquility.
"Third, because they possess all-knowledge, it is called Great Bliss.
That which does not possess all-knowledge is not called Great Bliss;
because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess all-knowledge, it is called Great Bliss."
Because it is great bliss, it is called Great Nirvana.
Fourth, because the body is indestructible, it is called great bliss;
if the body were destructible, it would not be called bliss.
The body of the Tathāgata is adamantine and indestructible; it is not a body of afflictions nor a body of impermanence, and is therefore called Great Bliss.
Because it is Great Bliss, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
“Good son! Worldly names may have causes and conditions, or they may lack causes and conditions.
Those with causes and conditions are like Śāriputra: his mother’s name was Śārī, and because he was named after his mother, he is called Śāriputra.”
For example, the practitioner Māṭhara was born in the country of Māṭhara; he was named after the country, and thus he was called the practitioner Māṭhara.
Likewise, as for Maudgalyāyana, "Maudgalyāyana" is his clan name; he was named after his clan, and thus he was called Maudgalyāyana.
Just as I was born into the Gautama clan and am thus named Gautama after that clan;
or as the ascetic Viśākha, whose name Viśākha is derived from the name of a lunar mansion, is named Viśākha after that constellation.
For example, one who has six fingers is called a "six-fingered person" because of those six fingers;
likewise, one who is a slave to the Buddha or a slave to a deva is called a "Buddha-slave" or a "deva-slave" because of the Buddha or the deva.
Because they are born from moisture, they are called "moisture-born.
Just as because of sound one names them *kakkara*, *kukkula*, or *tattara*.
Names such as these are names based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Those without causes and conditions are, for example, "lotus," "earth," "water," "fire," "wind," and "space."

It is like the *mandapa*, which has one name but two realities: first, it is called a hall; second, it is called a drinking-hall (*pānaka-śālā*). Even when no drink is being consumed, it is still appropriately named a *mandapa*.
For example, that which is called *sarvacarma* is termed "snake-canopy," yet it is not actually a snake-canopy; this is called being "without cause," as one forcibly establishes a name.
Or, for instance, *tilapīḍaka* is called "oil-eater," yet he does not actually eat oil; the name "oil-eater" is forcibly established for him.
This is called being without cause, yet forcibly establishing a name. Good son!
This Great Nirvana is also like this; it has no causes or conditions, yet a name is forcibly established for it.
"Good son!
For example, space is not called 'great space' because of a small space.
Nirvāṇa is likewise; it is not called 'Great Nirvāṇa' because of small characteristics."
"Good son!
For example, there is a dharma that cannot be measured and cannot be conceived; therefore, it is called 'Great.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: because it cannot be measured and cannot be conceived, it is named Mahāparinirvāṇa."
It is called Great Nirvana because it is pure.
What is meant by purity?
There are four kinds of purity.
What are the four?
First, the twenty-five existents are termed "impure"; because they can be permanently severed, they are termed "pure," and purity is precisely nirvāṇa.

Thus, nirvāṇa may also be called "existent," yet this nirvāṇa is in reality not existent; it is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, conform to worldly convention that they speak of nirvāṇa as existing.
For example, among worldly people, one might call someone who is not one's father "father," or someone who is not one's mother "mother"; though they are not actually parents, they are called parents.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: in accordance with worldly convention, it is said that all Buddhas possess Great Nirvāṇa.
Second, because their karma is pure.
All ordinary beings have impure karma and therefore lack nirvana;
the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have pure karma and are thus called "Greatly Pure. Because they are Greatly Pure, they are called "Great Nirvana."
Third, because the body is pure.
If the body were impermanent, it would be called impure;
the Tathāgata’s body is permanent and is therefore called the Great Purity. Because it is the Great Purity, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Fourth, because the mind is pure: if the mind has outflows (*āsrava*), it is called impure;
the Buddha’s mind is without outflows, and is therefore called "Great Purity. Because it is Great Purity, it is called Great Nirvana.
"Good son! This is called the good man or good woman practicing this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and fully accomplishing the merits of the first stage."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-three;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Tenth Chapter, Part Four: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Radiant Universal Illumination Sovereign Virtue King.
"Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa and achieve the fulfillment of the second merit?"
"Good son!
