When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa, that which was previously unattained is now attained; that which was previously unseen is now seen; that which was previously unheard is now heard; that which was previously unreached is now reached; and that which was previously unknown is now known."
What is meant by "that which was previously unattained but is now attained"?
It refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which were previously unattained but are now attained.
There are two kinds of these powers:
The first is internal, and the second is external.
That which is called external is shared with non-Buddhists.
The internal, moreover, is twofold:
The first are those of the two vehicles, and the second are bodhisattvas.
The supernormal powers attained by bodhisattvas through the practice of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
What is meant by "not shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas"?
The supernatural transformations produced by those of the Two Vehicles are such that when they focus their minds on one thing, they cannot produce many.
The Bodhisattva is not like this; within a single moment of mind, he is able to fully manifest bodies in the five realms of existence. Why is this?
It is because he has attained the power of this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; thus, it is said that what was previously unattainable is now attained.
Furthermore, how is it that what was previously unattained is now attained?
It refers to attaining mastery over the body and attaining mastery over the mind. Why is this so?
All ordinary beings lack mastery over their own body and mind; either the mind follows the body, or the body follows the mind.
What is meant by "the mind following the body"?

For example, when a person is intoxicated, as long as the wine remains within their body, their body moves and their mind moves accordingly; likewise, when the body is weary, the mind becomes weary accordingly. This is what is meant by "the mind follows the body."
Furthermore, it is like an infant: as its body is small and immature, its mind is likewise small; as an adult’s body is large, their mind is likewise large.
It is also like a person whose body is coarse and rough, who constantly thinks of obtaining oil to moisten and soften it—this is what is called the mind following the body.
"What is meant by 'the body follows the mind'?

It refers to going, coming, sitting, lying down, practicing, giving, observing precepts, and practicing patience. When one is afflicted by sorrow, the body becomes emaciated; when one is joyful, the body becomes plump and radiant; when one is terrified, the body trembles; when one listens to the Dharma with single-minded focus, the body becomes serene and pleased; and when one weeps in grief, tears flow profusely. This is what is meant by 'the body follows the mind'."
The Bodhisattva is not like this; he attains mastery over both body and mind, which is called "that which was previously unattained is now attained.
Furthermore, good son!

The physical manifestations assumed by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva are like motes of dust; with these minute bodies, they are able to reach all immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without any obstruction, yet their minds remain constantly in samādhi, never wavering from the start. This is called "the mind does not follow the body."
"This is also called 'that which was previously unattainable but is now attained.
Why is it further called 'that which was previously unattainable but is now attained'?

It is because that which all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others cannot reach, the bodhisattva can reach; for this reason, it is called 'that which was previously unattainable but is now attained.'"

Although all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others may employ their supernormal powers, they cannot transform their bodies into subtle particles to pervade immeasurable Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; when the bodies of these śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas move, their minds likewise move along with them.
The Bodhisattva is not like this; although his mind does not move, there is nowhere his body does not reach—this is called "the Bodhisattva’s mind does not follow the body.
Furthermore, good son!
The transformation body of a bodhisattva is like a trichiliocosm; with this great body, he enters the body of a single atom, yet at that time his mind does not become small accordingly.

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can manifest transformation bodies as vast as the trichiliocosm, they cannot place such a massive body into a single minute particle; since they cannot even accomplish this much, how much less could they cause the mind not to move in accordance with it?
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mind not following the body.
Furthermore, son of good family!

With a single voice, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to hear it, yet his mind never thinks, "I shall cause this voice to pervade all worlds so that sentient beings who have not heard it before may now hear it."
Furthermore, this bodhisattva does not say from the outset, "I have caused sentient beings to hear what they have never heard before.

If a bodhisattva were to say, "It is because of my teaching of the Dharma that sentient beings hear what they had not heard," one should know that such a person will ultimately be unable to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Why is this? Because the thought, "Sentient beings have not heard it; I shall speak it," is a mind of birth and death. All bodhisattvas have already exhausted such a mind; for this reason, the body and mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva do not follow after one another.
"Good son!

The bodies and minds of all ordinary beings follow one another; it is not so for Bodhisattvas. For the sake of transforming sentient beings, although they manifest small bodies, their minds are likewise not small."
Why is this? Because the nature of the minds of all bodhisattvas is eternally vast; thus, although they manifest great bodies, their minds do not become greater.
What is meant by a "great body"?
The body is like the trichiliocosm;
how can one have a small mind and practice the conduct of an infant?
For this reason, the mind does not follow the body.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having already for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas abstained from wine, yet their minds may still be stirred; their hearts may shed tears despite the absence of sorrow or suffering; and their bodies may tremble despite the absence of fear. For this reason, it should be known that the body and mind of a bodhisattva are autonomous and do not necessarily follow one another.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests only a single body, yet all sentient beings perceive it differently.
Furthermore, good son,
how is it that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa hears what he has never heard before?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva first grasps the characteristics of sounds—namely, the sounds of elephants and horses, the sounds of carts and people, the sounds of conch shells and drums, the sounds of flutes and pipes, and the sounds of singing and weeping—and practices them. Through such practice, they are able to hear all the sounds of the hells throughout immeasurable trichiliocosm worlds.
Furthermore, through further cultivation, he attains a distinct faculty of the ear, which differs from the divine ear of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?

The pure supernormal power of the ear attained by those of the Two Vehicles, if it relies on the pure and subtle four great elements of the first dhyāna, can hear only the sounds of the first dhyāna but not those of the second; the same applies up to the fourth dhyāna. Although they may at one time hear all the sounds within a trichiliocosm, they cannot hear the sounds of worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless Ganges Rivers.
For this reason, the ear-faculty attained by a bodhisattva differs from that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; because of this difference, what was previously unheard is now heard.

Although they hear sounds, their minds from the very beginning possess no characteristic of hearing sound; they do not form notions of existence, permanence, pleasure, self, purity, a master, dependence, agency, causality, fixedness, or result. For this reason, these Bodhisattvas and others, who previously had not heard it, now hear it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijña-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If it is as the Buddha has taught—that no fixed characteristics are established and no characteristics of fruition are established—then this meaning is not so."
Why is this? The Tathāgata previously declared that if a person hears even a single phrase or a single word of this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
how is it that the Tathāgata now speaks again of there being no certainty and no fruit?
If one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, that is precisely a mark of certainty and a mark of fruition;
how then can you say there is no certainty and no fruition?
Because one hears evil sounds, an evil mind arises; because an evil mind arises, one reaches the three miserable realms. If one reaches the three miserable realms, this is a fixed result;
how then can you say there is no fixity and no result?
At that time, the Tathāgata praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
To be able to ask such a question:

if the Buddhas were to say that all sounds have a fixed characteristic of fruition, then that would not be the mark of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; it would be the mark of Māra, the mark of birth-and-death, and a mark far removed from Nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, in whatever they proclaim, do not have a fixed characteristic of fruition. Good son!

For example, when one sees the reflection of a person's face in a blade, it appears long if the blade is held vertically and wide if held horizontally. If there were a fixed characteristic [to the reflection], how could it appear long when vertical and wide when horizontal?
For this reason, whatever the Buddha-World-Honored Ones have proclaimed, there is no fixed characteristic of a result. Good son!
Nirvana is truly not the fruit of sound; if nirvana were the fruit of sound, one should know that nirvana would not be an eternal dharma.
Good son! For example, in the world, phenomena arise from causes: where there is a cause, there is an effect; where there is no cause, there is no effect.
Because the cause is impermanent, the effect is also impermanent.
Why is this? Because the cause also acts as the fruit, and the fruit also acts as the cause; for this reason, all dharmas lack a fixed characteristic.
If nirvana were produced from a cause, then because the cause is impermanent, the fruit would also be impermanent.
However, this nirvana does not arise from causes, and its essence is not an effect;
therefore, it is eternal. Good son!
For this reason, the essence of nirvana is neither fixed nor an effect.
“Good son! As for nirvana, it can be called ‘certainty’ and it can also be called ‘fruit.
What is meant by certainty?

The nirvana possessed by all Buddhas is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is definitive. It is free from birth, aging, and decay; therefore, it is definitive. Even those such as icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave offenses, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and those who have committed the five heinous crimes—by relinquishing their former [afflictive] minds—they will certainly attain it; therefore, it is definitive.
“Good son! As you have said, if a person hears even a single word or a single phrase of my teaching on the Great Nirvana and thereby attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Regarding this meaning, you have not yet fully understood it.
You should listen attentively; I shall further analyze it for you. Good son!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing even a single word or a single phrase of the Great Nirvana, do not form the notion of words, do not form the notion of phrases, do not form the notion of hearing, do not form the notion of the Buddha, and do not form the notion of preaching—such a meaning is called the "markless mark. Because of this markless mark, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son!
As for what you have said—that one reaches the three miserable realms because of hearing evil sounds—this is not so. Why is that?
It is not because of evil sounds that one arrives at the three miserable realms; one should know that this result is actually due to an evil mind. Why is this so?

There are sons and daughters of good family who, although they hear evil sounds, do not give rise to an evil mind. Therefore, one should know that it is not because of evil sounds that one is born within the three miserable realms.
Sentient beings, however, give rise to the three evil destinies because their afflictions and fetters cause malevolent thoughts to proliferate, not because of evil sounds.
If sound possessed a fixed nature, then all who heard it would necessarily give rise to malevolent thoughts.
There are those for whom [anger] arises and those for whom it does not; therefore, one should know that sound has no fixed characteristic.
Because it lacks a fixed characteristic, even though one is conditioned by it, one does not give rise to an evil mind.
“World-Honored One!
If sound has no fixed nature, how is it that a bodhisattva hears now what they have not heard before? “Good son!
Sound has no fixed characteristic; that which was not heard in the past is now being heard by the bodhisattvas. For this reason, I say: "That which was not heard in the past is now being heard."
“Good son! How is it that what was previously unseen is now seen? Good son!”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, they first apprehend the signs of illumination—namely, the light of the sun, moon, and stars; the radiance of blazing fires, lamps, and candles; the brilliance of jewels and fire; and the glow of medicinal herbs. Through such cultivation, they attain a faculty of the eye that is extraordinary, surpassing that which is attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is the difference?

The pure divine eye attained by those of the Two Vehicles, if it relies on the eye-faculty composed of the four great elements of the desire realm, cannot see the first dhyāna; if it relies on the first dhyāna, it cannot see the higher stages, and so on until even its own eye cannot be seen. If they wish to see more, the limit is at most the trichiliocosm.

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not cultivate the divine eye; he sees all exquisite physical forms as being entirely skeletal in nature. Although he perceives the forms within worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, he does not conceive them as forms, nor as permanent phenomena, nor as signs of existence, nor as substantial entities, nor as signs of names and so forth. He perceives them only as signs of causes and conditions, and does not form any conceptualized view of them.
It does not say that this eye possesses a subtle and pure characteristic; rather, it perceives only the characteristics of conditions and non-conditions.
What are these conditions?
Form is the condition for the eye. If form were not a condition, ordinary beings would not give rise to the perception of seeing form.
For this reason, form is called a causal condition (*pratyaya*).
That which is not a causal condition is such that even though a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives it, they do not give rise to the mark of form; therefore, it is not a condition.
For this reason, the pure divine eye attained by a bodhisattva differs from that attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Because of this difference, they simultaneously see all the Buddhas currently present throughout the worlds of the ten directions; this is called what the bodhisattva has not seen before but now beholds.
Because of this difference, one is able to see subtle atoms, which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot see.
Because of this difference, although one sees one's own eyes, there is from the outset no characteristic of seeing; rather, one sees the characteristic of impermanence.

One sees that the body of an ordinary person is filled with the thirty-six impure substances, as clearly as observing an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand; for this reason, what was previously unseen is now seen.

If one perceives the physical characteristics of sentient beings, one then knows the capacities for the Great or Small Vehicles of that person; by merely touching their robes, one also knows the distinctions between the wholesome and unwholesome faculties of that person. For this reason, what was previously unknown is now known.
Because of this single vision, that which was previously unknown is now known; because of this knowledge, that which was previously unseen is now seen.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
How does a bodhisattva come to know what was previously unknown?

Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the minds of ordinary beings characterized by greed, anger, and delusion, they do not initially form the notions of mind or mental factors, nor the notions of sentient beings or material things; rather, they cultivate the mark of ultimate emptiness, the primary truth.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas constantly and skillfully cultivate the characteristic of emptiness.
By cultivating emptiness, that which was previously unknown is now known.
What is meant by "knowing"?

It is to know that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; it is to know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and because of this Buddha-nature, even those such as the icchantikas who have abandoned their original resolve shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
All such matters as these are beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet can be known by bodhisattvas; for this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known.
Furthermore, good son, how is it that what was previously unknown is now known?

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he recollects the various lineages, parents, brothers, wives, children, retinues, friends, and enemies of all sentient beings in past lives; within a single thought-moment, he attains a distinguished wisdom that differs from the wisdom of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is the difference?

The wisdom possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas recalls all sentient beings of the past—their castes, parents, and even their enemies—and forms mental images of them as having those specific characteristics of caste through to enemy.

The Bodhisattva is not like this; although he may contemplate his past lineage, parents, and even enemies, he never gives rise to the conceptual marks of lineage, parents, or enemies. He constantly dwells in the mark of the Dharma-nature and the mark of empty stillness. This is called that which the Bodhisattva did not previously know, but now knows.
Furthermore, good son,
how is it that what was previously unknown is now known?

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he attains the knowledge of others' minds, which differs from that attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is the difference?
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know the minds of human beings with a single moment of wisdom, they are unable to know the minds of those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, or devas.

The Bodhisattva is not so; in a single thought-moment, he thoroughly knows the minds of sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence. This is called that which the Bodhisattva did not previously know, but now knows.
Furthermore, good son!

There is yet another form of knowledge: within a single moment of mind, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the initial mind of a srotāpanna, proceeding sequentially through to the sixteenth mind. For this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known.
This is the second merit fully accomplished by a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the Mahāparinirvāṇa to fully accomplish the third merit?
"Good son!
When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, he relinquishes compassion and attains compassion; at the time he attains compassion, it does not arise from causes and conditions.
What is meant by 'relinquishing compassion and attaining compassion'?"
"Good son! 'Loving-kindness' refers to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas relinquish conventional loving-kindness, they attain ultimate loving-kindness (*paramārtha-satya*); this ultimate loving-kindness is not obtained through conditions."
Furthermore, how is it that one relinquishes loving-kindness and yet attains loving-kindness?
If loving-kindness can be relinquished, it is called the loving-kindness of ordinary beings;
if loving-kindness can be attained, it is called the objectless loving-kindness of a bodhisattva.

One abandons the compassion of icchantikas, the compassion of those who have committed the four grave offenses, the compassion of those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and the compassion of those who commit the five heinous crimes; instead, one attains the compassion of pity, the compassion of the Tathāgata, the compassion of the World-Honored One, and the compassion that is without cause or condition.
What, furthermore, is meant by "abandoning compassion and attaining compassion"?

It means abandoning the compassion directed toward eunuchs, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, and women; it also means abandoning the compassion directed toward butchers, meat-sellers, hunters, poultry and pig breeders, and others such as these; and it further means abandoning the compassion of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, in order to attain the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) of all bodhisattvas.
One does not perceive one's own compassion, nor does one perceive the compassion of others; one does not perceive the observance of precepts, nor does one perceive their violation.
Although one perceives one's own pity, one does not perceive sentient beings.
Although there is the sensation of suffering, one does not perceive a feeler. Why?
Because one cultivates the foremost ultimate truth.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, which achieves and fulfills the third merit.
Furthermore, good son,
how does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa to achieve and fulfill the fourth merit?
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Great Parinirvāṇa and achieves the fulfillment of the fourth merit, there are ten matters.
What are these ten?"

First, their roots are deep and difficult to uproot; second, they give rise to the conviction within themselves; third, they do not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit; fourth, they cultivate pure Buddha-lands; fifth, they eliminate all that remains [of afflictions]; sixth, they sever the conditions of karma; seventh, they cultivate a pure body; eighth, they thoroughly understand all conditions; ninth, they remain free from all enemies; and tenth, they abandon the two extremes.
What is meant by "the roots are deep and difficult to uproot"?
That which is called a "root" is named heedfulness (*apramāda*). Of what root is this heedfulness?
This is what is called the root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Good son! All the roots of goodness of all Buddhas are rooted in non-heedlessness (*apramāda*); because of this non-heedlessness, all other roots of goodness increase further and further. Because it is able to cause all roots of goodness to grow, it is the most preeminent among all virtues.
"Noble son!
Just as among all footprints the footprint of an elephant is supreme, so too is the dharma of heedfulness; it is the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas."
Good son! Just as among all forms of light, the sunlight is the foremost;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as among all kings, the wheel-turning sage king is the most supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son! Just as among all flowing waters the four great rivers are supreme, so too is the dharma of heedfulness:
it is the highest and most excellent among all wholesome dharmas."
"Good son! Just as among all mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, is the foremost;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence the foremost among all wholesome dharmas."
Good son! Just as among flowers born of water, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son!
Just as among flowers that grow on land, the pāriyātra flower is the most supreme;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence, for it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas."
Good son! Just as among all beasts the lion is the foremost,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as among all flying birds, the king of golden-winged birds (garuḍa) is the most supreme;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence (apramāda), for it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma).
“Good son! Just as among those with great bodies, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, is the most preeminent;
so too is the dharma of non-heedlessness, for it is the most preeminent among all wholesome dharmas.”
Good son! Just as among all sentient beings—whether two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, or legless—the Tathāgata is the most supreme;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence, for it is the most supreme and highest among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as among all assemblies, the Buddha and the Sangha are supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most preeminent and supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as within the Buddha-dharma, the dharma of Great Nirvana is the most supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son! For this reason, the root of heedfulness is deep, firm, and difficult to uproot.
How is it that through heedfulness one attains growth?"

These are the faculty of faith, the faculty of ethical discipline, the faculty of generosity, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of patience, the faculty of learning, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of spiritual friends. Such faculties increase through heedfulness; because they have increased, they become deep-rooted and difficult to uproot.
For this reason, it is said that the roots of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa are deep and difficult to uproot.
"How does one form the perception of certainty regarding the body?"
One gives rise to a resolute mind regarding one's own person, thinking:
"In future lives, this body of mine will certainly become a vessel for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

The mind is also like this: it does not become narrow or limited; it does not undergo change; it does not become the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; it does not become the mind of Māra, nor the mind that seeks its own pleasure, nor the mind that delights in birth and death; rather, it constantly seeks the mind of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.

This is called the bodhisattva generating a mind of certainty within himself, thinking: "In a future life, I shall become a vessel for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa and generates the perception of certainty within himself.
"How does a bodhisattva not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit?
What is a field of merit?
Outsiders, those who observe the precepts, and those up to the Buddhas—these are called fields of merit."
If one should think:
"Such persons as these are true fields of merit," you should know that such a mind is narrow and inferior.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive all immeasurable sentient beings as none other than fields of merit.
Why is this? Because they have skillfully cultivated the foundations of mindfulness with diverse aspects.
There is another foundation of mindfulness: for one who practices it well, they observe that among all sentient beings there is neither the observance of precepts nor their violation.
They constantly contemplate what has been taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones: although there are four kinds of giving, all yield pure retribution.
What are the four?
First, the donor is pure while the recipient is impure; second, the donor is impure while the recipient is pure; third, both the donor and the recipient are pure.
The fourth is when both the giver and the recipient are impure.
What is meant by the gift being pure while the recipient is impure?

It refers to a donor who possesses precepts, learning, and wisdom, and understands that there is merit in giving as well as its karmic fruit; whereas the recipient violates the precepts, is exclusively attached to false views, and does not believe in the fruit of giving. This is called a pure gift with an impure recipient.
"What is meant by the recipient being pure while the donor is impure?

It refers to a donor who violates the precepts and is exclusively attached to false views, claiming that there is no such thing as wise giving or its karmic fruit; whereas the recipient upholds the precepts, possesses extensive learning and wisdom, and knows that there is indeed giving and the fruit of giving. This is called the donor being impure and the recipient being pure."
"What is meant by 'both the giver and the receiver being pure'?

When both the giver and the receiver possess ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom, and understand both the act of giving and the karmic fruition of giving—this is called the purity of both the giver and the receiver."
"What is meant by 'both being impure'?
It refers to when both the giver and the receiver have broken the precepts and hold wrong views, claiming that there is no such thing as giving nor any karmic retribution for giving.
If this is the case, how can one further say that a pure retribution is obtained?"
Because there is neither giving nor retribution, it is called "pure. Good son!
If there is one who does not perceive giving or the retribution of giving, you should know that such a person is not said to have broken the precepts, nor are they solely attached to wrong views.
If one follows the Śrāvaka teachings and claims that neither giving nor the karmic retribution of giving is seen, this is called breaking the precepts and holding wrong views.
However, if one follows such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and does not perceive giving or the karmic retribution of giving, this is called upholding the precepts and holding right views.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have a distinct application of mindfulness; through its cultivation, they do not perceive sentient beings who maintain precepts or break precepts, nor givers, recipients, or the karmic rewards of giving. For this reason, it is called "upholding the precepts with right view."
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit.
What is meant by "purifying the Buddha-land"?

It is when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings; he abandons all thoughts of killing and harm, and with these roots of goodness, vows to share them with all sentient beings, wishing that all beings may attain long life, possess great power, and achieve great supernormal faculties.

By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings within that land shall possess long lifespans, great power, and attain great supernormal faculties.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abandons the mind of stealing. By means of these roots of goodness, he vows to share them with all sentient beings, and prays that the lands of all buddha-fields shall consist entirely of the seven treasures, and that sentient beings shall be wealthy and sufficient, so that they may enjoy their desires freely."

By the power of the causes and conditions of these vows, at the time he attains Buddhahood in a future age, the land he obtains shall consist entirely of the seven treasures; sentient beings shall be wealthy and prosperous, and they shall enjoy all their desires to their heart's content.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abandons the mind of lustful desire. By means of these roots of goodness, he makes this vow: 'May I share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands be free from the minds of greed, anger, and delusion, and may there be none among them who suffer from hunger or thirst.'"

By the power of the causes and conditions of these vows, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, the sentient beings in his land will be far removed from greed, hatred, and delusion, and none shall suffer the afflictions of hunger or thirst.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, he abandons the mind of false speech. By means of these roots of goodness, he vows to share them with all sentient beings, wishing that in all Buddha-lands there shall always be flowering trees, fruit trees, and incense trees, and that all sentient beings therein may obtain sublime voices."

By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all lands shall always possess flowering trees, fruit trees, and fragrant trees; and all sentient beings therein shall obtain pure and sublime voices.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, he remains far removed from divisive speech. By means of these roots of goodness, he makes a vow to share them with all sentient beings, wishing that all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands may always be in harmony and fellowship, expounding and discussing the True Dharma."

By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, all sentient beings within that land shall dwell in complete harmony and together discourse upon the essentials of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he distances himself from harsh speech. By means of these roots of goodness, he makes this vow: 'May I share them with all sentient beings; may the ground of the Buddhas' lands be as level as the palm of a hand, free from sand, gravel, tiles, stones, thorns, and wicked brambles; and may the minds of all sentient beings therein be impartial.'"

By the power of the causes and conditions of these vows, at the time he attains Buddhahood in a future world, all the lands of his realm shall be as level as the palm of a hand, free from sand, gravel, thorns, and harsh brambles; and the minds of all sentient beings therein shall be impartial and equal.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abstains from meaningless speech. By means of these roots of goodness, he vows to share them with all sentient beings, and prays that all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands shall be free from suffering and affliction."
By the power of the causes and conditions of these vows, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, none of the sentient beings within his land shall experience any suffering or affliction.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, he remains far removed from greed and envy. By means of these roots of goodness, he vows to share them with all sentient beings, and prays that all sentient beings in all buddha-lands shall be free from greed, envy, malice, harm, and false views."

By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, at the time he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings within his land shall be entirely free from greed, envy, malice, and wrong views.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he remains far removed from affliction and harm. By means of these roots of goodness, he makes a vow to share them with all sentient beings, wishing that all beings in every Buddha-land may together cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion, and attain the stage of the 'Only Son' (Ekaputraka-bhūmi)."

By the power of the causes and conditions of these vows, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings throughout that world shall together cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion, and attain the stage of regarding all as one's only child.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, they remain far removed from false views. By means of these roots of goodness, they vow to share them with all sentient beings, and pray that all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands may fully attain the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."

By the power of these causes and conditions of his vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future world, all sentient beings therein shall be able to receive, uphold, and practice the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of a pure buddha-field.
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva eliminate what remains?
There are three kinds of remainders:
first, the remainder of the retribution of afflictions; second, remaining karma; and third, remaining existence.”
Good son! What is meant by the residual retribution of afflictions?
If there are sentient beings who habitually indulge in sensual desire, because that retribution has ripened, they fall into hell.

Emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal—namely, a pigeon, a sparrow, a mandarin duck, a parrot, a *jīvajīvaka* bird, a *śārika* bird, a blue jay, a fish, a turtle, a monkey, a roe deer, or a stag. If one subsequently attains a human body, one receives the form of a eunuch, a woman, one with two sexual organs, one without sexual organs, or a prostitute; or if one leaves the household life and violates the first grave precept—these are called residual retributions (*avaśeṣa-vipāka*).
"Furthermore, good son!
If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of earnest devotion, habitually practice and draw near to anger, they will fall into hell because that retribution has ripened."

Emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal, namely a venomous snake—possessing four kinds of venom: the venom of sight, the venom of touch, the venom of biting, and the venom of breath—or belongs to the species of lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, cats, wildcats, hawks, or falcons. If one obtains a human body, one is fully possessed of the sixteen evil codes of conduct; or if one leaves the household life and violates the second grave precept, these are called residual retributions.
"Furthermore, good son! If there are those who practice foolishness, when the retribution for that karma ripens, they fall into hell.

Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—namely, the forms of elephants, pigs, oxen, sheep, water buffaloes, fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and so forth. If they obtain a human body, they will be deaf, blind, mute, or crippled; their faculties will be incomplete, and they will be unable to receive the Dharma. Even if they manage to leave the household life, their faculties will be dull and obtuse, and they will take pleasure in violating the heavy precepts, even down to the theft of five coins. This is called 'residual retribution.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
If there are those who cultivate arrogance, when the retribution for this ripens, they fall into hell.

Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—namely, dung-worms, camels, donkeys, dogs, or horses. If they are born among humans, they receive the status of slaves or servants, or become poor beggars; or, even if they manage to leave the household life, they are constantly held in contempt by sentient beings and violate the fourth precept. This is called the residual retribution."
These and others like them are called the residual retributions of afflictions.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, they completely eliminate all such residual retributions.
"What are residual karmas?

They refer to the karma of all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), the karma of all *śrāvakas*, the karma for receiving seven more existences of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the karma for receiving two more existences of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and the karma for receiving existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). These are called residual karmas."
In this way, through the cultivation of the Great Nirvana, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva completely eliminates all other karmas.
What, then, are these "remaining existences"?

When an Arhat attains the fruit of Arhatship, or a Pratyekabuddha attains the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, they revolve through these two fruits without karma or fetters; this is called "remaining existence" (avaśeṣabhava).

These three kinds of dharmas with remainder are eliminated by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva through the cultivation of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s elimination of what remains.
“What is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the pure body?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the precept against killing with five kinds of mind, namely: inferior, middling, superior, superior-middling, and supreme-superior; this applies likewise even up to right view.”
These fifty states of mind are called the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment;
when these fifty states of mind are fully perfected and established with certainty, they are called "fulfillment.
These one hundred states of mind are called the "one hundred merits."
One hundred merits are fully possessed to form a single mark.
In this manner, proceeding successively, one fully achieves the thirty-two marks, which is called the pure body.
For this reason, one further cultivates the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); for there are sentient beings in the world who serve eighty deities.
What are the eighty? They are:

the twelve days, the twelve great devas, the five major planets, the Northern Dipper, Aśvina, the deva of the path, Brahmāvatī, Śrī-devī, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the earth deva, the wind deva, the water deva, the fire deva, Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Kumāra, the eight-armed deva (Viṣṇu), Maheśvara, Bhañjara, Haritī, the Four Heavenly Kings, the deva of writing, and Vasu. These are called the eighty.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he cultivates the eighty minor marks to adorn himself; this is called the pure body of a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Because these eighty marks are that in which all sentient beings place their faith and submission; therefore, while the bodhisattva’s body remains unmoving as he cultivates the eighty marks, he causes those sentient beings to see it each according to their own inclinations. Having seen it, they revere him with devotion, and each gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate a pure body. "Good son!

It is like a person who wishes to invite a great king; they must first adorn their residence, making it utterly pure, and prepare various kinds of a hundred-flavored delicacies, after which the king will accept the invitation to their abode."

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: wishing to request the Dharma-wheel King of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he must first cultivate his body until it is utterly pure; only then shall the Unsurpassed Dharma King take up residence therein.
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must cultivate a pure body. Good son!
It is like a person who wishes to consume ambrosia; they must first purify their body.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: desiring to partake of the unsurpassed ambrosial flavor of the Dharma, which is the Prajñāpāramitā, he must first purify his body with the eighty minor marks.
"Good son!
It is like a fine vessel of gold or silver filled with pure water; both its interior and exterior are pure.
The physical body of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise pure: when it contains the water of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, both its interior and exterior are pure."
"Good son!
It is like the pure white garments of Vārāṇasī, which easily take on dye. Why is this? Because..."
Because its nature is pure and white, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: because his body is pure, he swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the pure body.
How does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully know all conditions?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perceive the mark of form, does not perceive the condition of form, does not perceive the substance of form, does not perceive the arising of form, does not perceive the cessation of form, does not perceive a single mark, does not perceive diverse marks, does not perceive a seer, does not perceive characteristics, and does not perceive a receiver.
Why is this? Because they thoroughly understand causes and conditions.
As it is with form, so it is with all phenomena; this is called a bodhisattva’s thorough knowledge of all conditions.
"How does a bodhisattva remain free from all enemies?
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are the enemies of a bodhisattva; because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly remains far removed from them, this is called a bodhisattva destroying all enemies."
A Bodhisattva dwelling in the fifth stage does not regard the various afflictions as enemies. Why is this?
It is because it is due to afflictions that the Bodhisattva takes birth; and because there is birth, he is able to successively transform and teach sentient beings.
For this reason, they are not called enemies.
Who, then, are the enemies?
They are those who slander the Vaipulya sutras.
As Bodhisattvas are born into successive lives, they do not fear the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; they fear only those who slander the Vaipulya sutras.

All Bodhisattvas have eight kinds of Māras who are called "enemies. To distance oneself from these eight Māras is called "leaving the enemies behind," and this is what is meant by a Bodhisattva leaving behind all enemies.
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from the two extremes?
The so-called ‘two extremes’ refer to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) and the affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā-kleśa*).
A bodhisattva constantly remains detached from the twenty-five states of existence and the affliction of craving; this is called a bodhisattva remaining far removed from the two extremes.”
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the Great Parinirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the fourth merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vairocana-āryaguṇarāja said:
"As the Buddha has taught, if there is a Bodhisattva who cultivates the Great Parinirvāṇa, they shall completely perform these ten kinds of meritorious deeds."
"For what reason does the Tathāgata cultivate only these nine matters and not cultivate a pure land?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
In the past, I also constantly cultivated these ten matters.

Among all bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas, there are none who have not cultivated these ten matters; it is impossible for any Buddha, World-Honored One, to appear within a world that is filled with impurity.
"Good son, you must not now say that the Buddhas appear in impure worlds; you should know that such a thought is unwholesome and narrow-minded.
You should know this now: I have, in truth, never appeared within the realm of Jambudvīpa."
For example, it would be devoid of reason for someone to say that this world alone possesses the sun and moon, while other worlds have neither sun nor moon.
If there is a bodhisattva who speaks these words: "This buddha-world is defiled and impure, while the buddha-lands of other directions are pure, magnificent, and beautiful," it is likewise so.
"Good son!
To the west of this Sahā world, passing through as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in thirty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Invincible (Anabhibhūta)."
For what reason is that land named Invincible?
All the magnificent and beautiful things within that land are entirely equal and without distinction, just like the Western World of Peace and Bliss, and also like the Eastern World of the Full Moon.
I appear in the world in that land, and for the sake of transforming sentient beings, I manifest the turning of the wheel of Dharma here in Jambudvīpa.
It is not only my own body that manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma herein; all Buddhas likewise turn the wheel of Dharma within this realm.
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not fail to practice these ten matters.
Son of Good Family!
By virtue of his vows, the Bodhisattva Maitreya shall, in a future age, cause this world to be pure and magnificently adorned.
For this reason, all the worlds of all Buddhas are without exception adorned and purified.
"Furthermore, good son,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplish the fifth merit?
Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa and fully accomplishes the fifth merit, there are five matters.
What are these five?

First, the faculties are fully intact; second, one is not born in a borderland; third, one is cherished by the devas; fourth, one is constantly revered by celestial māras, śramaṇas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others; fifth, one attains the knowledge of past lives.
“By the power of the causal conditions of this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the Bodhisattva fulfills these five kinds of meritorious qualities.
The Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Radiant and All-Illuminating, said:

“As the Buddha has taught, if a good man or a good woman practices giving, they will fully accomplish these five kinds of meritorious qualities. Why, then, do you now say that one obtains these five things by means of the Mahāparinirvāṇa?”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
The meanings of such matters as these differ; I shall now analyze and explain them for you.

Giving results in five ways: it is indeterminate, impermanent, impure, non-superior, and not distinct; it is not untainted (anāsrava), and it cannot benefit, bring peace and happiness to, or have compassion for all sentient beings.

If the five matters obtained through such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra are definitive, permanent, pure, supreme, distinct, and untainted, then they can benefit, bring peace and happiness to, and have compassion for all sentient beings.

Good son! Just as giving provides relief from hunger and thirst, so too can the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra cause all sentient beings to be completely free from the disease of craving for the twenty-five states of existence.
The causal conditions of giving cause birth and death to continue in succession, whereas the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra can cause birth and death to be severed so that they no longer continue.
Because of giving, one undergoes the dharmas of ordinary beings; because of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, one attains the status of a bodhisattva.
The causal conditions of giving can sever all suffering and distress of poverty, while the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra can sever all poverty of wholesome dharmas.
The causal conditions of giving possess both parts and fruits; however, through the Great Nirvāṇa, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which has neither parts nor fruits.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the fifth merit. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva, by practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplish the sixth merit?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa attains the vajra-samādhi; dwelling securely within it, he is able to completely shatter and disperse all dharmas.

One perceives that all phenomena are impermanent, characterized by instability, and the causes and conditions of terror; they are like sickness, suffering, calamity, and plunder; they perish and disintegrate moment by moment, lacking any reality; and that everything is the realm of Māra, devoid of any visible characteristic.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, although they bestow gifts upon sentient beings, they do not perceive even a single sentient being.

For the sake of sentient beings, they diligently cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), and so on up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); it is likewise in this manner.
If a bodhisattva sees a single sentient being who is unable to ultimately fulfill and accomplish the dāna-pāramitā, up to and including the fulfillment of the prajñā-pāramitā.
"Good son! It is like a vajra:
wherever it is aimed, there is nothing it does not shatter, yet this vajra itself suffers no fracture or loss.
The Vajrasamādhi is also like this: whatever dharma it is aimed at, there is nothing it does not shatter, yet this samādhi itself suffers no fracture or loss."
"Good son!
Just as among all jewels the diamond is the most supreme, so too is the vajra-samādhi attained by a bodhisattva; it is the foremost among all samādhis."
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this samādhi, all other samādhis come to be subsumed within it. Good son!

Just as all minor kings come to submit to and join the retinue of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), so too it is with all samādhis; they all come to submit to and join the retinue of the vajra-samādhi.
Good son!

It is like a person who is an enemy of the state and is detested by all people; if someone were to kill him, there would be no one among the people of the world who did not praise that person’s merit.
The Vajra-samādhi is likewise; when a bodhisattva cultivates it, they can destroy all enemies among sentient beings, and for this reason, it is always honored and revered by all samādhis.
Good son!
It is like a person whose strength is so robust that no one can match him; yet there is another person who is able to subdue him—one should know that such a person is praised by the world.
The Vajra-samādhi is likewise; its power is able to crush and subdue those dharmas that are difficult to subdue. For this reason, all samādhis come to take refuge in and submit to it.
"Good son!
It is like a person who bathes in the great ocean; you should know that such a person has already used the waters of all rivers, springs, and ponds.
In the same way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates this vajra-samādhi, you should know that they have already cultivated all other samādhis."
"Good son!
Within Mount Gandhamādana there is a spring named Anavatapta; that spring possesses water endowed with the eight qualities, and those who drink it are free from all suffering of illness."
The Vajra-samādhi is also like this: it is endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path; when a bodhisattva practices it, they sever all afflictions, sores, and grave illnesses. Good son!
Just as when a person makes offerings to Maheśvara, one should know that this person has already made offerings to all the devas;
so too it is with the Vajra-samādhi: if someone practices it, one should know that they have already practiced all other samādhis.
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in such a vajra-samādhi, they see all phenomena without obstruction, as if observing an āmalaka fruit in the palm of their hand. Although the bodhisattva attains such vision, they ultimately do not form the conceptual thought that they are seeing all phenomena."
"Good son!
It is like a person sitting at the crossroads who sees all sentient beings coming, going, sitting, and lying down.
The Vajra-samādhi is also like this: it perceives the arising and ceasing, the appearing and disappearing, of all dharmas."
"Good son!
It is like a high mountain: if someone climbs it and looks afar, all directions become clearly visible.
The mountain of the diamond-like samādhi is also like this: when a bodhisattva ascends it, they look afar and there are no dharmas that are not clearly understood."

Good son! It is like the month of spring when the heavens send down sweet rain; the drops are so fine and dense that there is no space between them, and one with clear vision sees them with perfect clarity.

The Bodhisattva is likewise; having attained the pure eye of the vajra-samādhi, he sees all worlds in the eastern direction from afar. Within them, whether lands are forming or decaying, he perceives them all clearly and without obstruction; this is also the case for the ten directions.
"Good son!
Just as when seven suns appear simultaneously from Mount Yugandhara, all the trees and forests upon that mountain are completely consumed by fire;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva who cultivates the Vajra-samādhi—all forests of afflictions are instantly extinguished."
"Good son!
For example, although a diamond can shatter all material things, it never gives rise to the thought, 'I am able to shatter them.
The Diamond Samādhi is also like this: once a bodhisattva has cultivated it, they can destroy afflictions, yet they never give rise to the thought, 'I am able to destroy the fetters.'"
Good son!

For example, the great earth can support all things, yet it never gives rise to the thought, "I have the power to support them. Fire does not think, "I am able to burn things"; water does not think, "I am able to moisten and soak"; wind does not think, "I am able to move things"; space does not think, "I am able to contain and receive"; and nirvāṇa likewise does not give rise to the thought, "I cause sentient beings to attain liberation."
The Vajra-samādhi is likewise: although it can eliminate all afflictions, from the outset it has no thought, saying, "I am able to eliminate them.

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi, in a single thought-moment they transform their body to become like that of a Buddha, appearing in immeasurable numbers throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Yet, although this bodhisattva performs such transformations, his mind is from the very beginning free of any thought of pride.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"Who possesses such a samādhi that they can perform such transformations?
Only a bodhisattva who dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi is able to do so.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi, in a single thought-moment they travel throughout Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions and then return to their original place.
Although he possesses such power, he does not think or say, "I am able to do this.
Why is that? It is because of the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi, they are able, within a single thought-moment, to sever all the afflictions of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; yet, from the very beginning, their mind harbors no conceptualization of severing the afflictions of those sentient beings.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi.
When a bodhisattva abides in this Vajra Samādhi, whatever they proclaim with a single voice, all sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
Manifesting a single color, all sentient beings each perceive various forms and appearances.
Abiding in one place without moving their bodies, they are able to cause sentient beings to see them from their respective directions.

He expounds a single dharma—whether it be the *dhātus* or the *āyatanas*—and all sentient beings each hear it according to their own fundamental understanding. When a Bodhisattva dwells in such a samādhi, although he perceives sentient beings, his mind from the outset has no perception of sentient beings;

although he perceives men and women, there is no perception of men and women; although he perceives form-dharmas, there is no perception of form; even when perceiving consciousness, there is no perception of consciousness; although he perceives day and night, there is no perception of day and night; although he perceives all things, there is no perception of all things; although he perceives all afflictions and fetters, there is no perception of any afflictions or fetters; although he perceives the Eightfold Noble Path, there is no perception of the Noble Path; although he perceives bodhi, there is no perception of bodhi; and although he perceives nirvāṇa, there is no perception of nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Good son!
Because all dharmas are fundamentally without marks.
By the power of this samādhi, the bodhisattva perceives all dharmas as being, from the very beginning, without marks.
For what reason is it called the Vajra Samādhi? Good son!

For example, just as the color of a vajra is not fixed when it is in the sunlight, so too is the Vajra Samādhi; its manifestation among the great assembly is likewise not fixed. Therefore, it is called the Vajra Samādhi.
"Good son!

For example, just as no person in the world can appraise the value of a vajra, so too it is with the Vajra Samādhi; all its merits cannot be measured by any among gods or humans. Therefore, it is further named the Vajra Samādhi."
"Good son!
For example, if a poor person obtains a vajra jewel, they will be able to remain far removed from poverty, suffering, and the malevolent spirits and evil poisons.

It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: upon attaining this samādhi, they are able to remain far removed from the various sufferings of afflictions and the malevolent spirits and evil poisons of Māra; therefore, it is further named the Vajra Samādhi."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the sixth merit.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 24; *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 25.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Ten, Part Five: The Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Radiant and All-Pervading.
"Furthermore, good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by practicing the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, fully accomplish the seventh merit?
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he reflects as follows:
"What dharmas can serve as the proximate cause for Great Parinirvāṇa?
The Bodhisattva then knew that there are four kinds of dharmas that serve as the proximate cause for Great Nirvāṇa.
If it is said that diligently practicing all ascetic austerities is the proximate cause for Great Nirvāṇa, this meaning is not correct. Why is this so?
It is impossible to attain Nirvāṇa apart from these four dharmas.
What are the four?

First, associating with virtuous friends; second, listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; third, reflecting with focused mindfulness; and fourth, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
"Good son!

It is like a person who encounters various ailments—whether feverish or cold, chronic exhaustion, dysentery, malaria, or the toxic influences of malevolent spirits—who goes to a skilled physician. The skilled physician then prescribes medicine for him according to each specific illness."
This person sincerely and properly receives the physician’s instructions, compiles the medicine according to those instructions, and takes it as prescribed.

Having taken it, the illness is cured and the body attains peace and happiness. Those who are ill are like the bodhisattvas; the great skilled physician is like the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); what the skilled physician says is like the Vaipulya sutras; properly receiving the physician’s instructions is like skillfully contemplating the meaning of the Vaipulya sutras; compiling the medicine according to the instructions is like practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) in accordance with the Dharma; the curing of the illness is like the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa*); and the attainment of peace and happiness is like attaining *nirvāṇa*, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Good son!
It is like a king who, wishing to rule according to the Dharma and to bring peace and happiness to his people, consults his wise ministers, asking, 'What is the law?
The ministers then explain it to him by means of the ancient laws of former kings."

Having heard this, the king practiced it with sincere faith and governed the country according to the Dharma; thus, there were no enemies or adversaries, and for this reason, the people lived in peace, happiness, and freedom from affliction. Good son!

The king is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas; the wise ministers are a metaphor for the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). The methods of governance taught by the wise ministers to the king are a metaphor for the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). Once the king has heard them and practices them with sincere faith, this is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas who focus their minds to contemplate the profound meanings contained within the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Governing the kingdom according to the Dharma is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas practicing according to the Dharma—namely, the six *pāramitās*. Because they are able to cultivate the six *pāramitās*, they have no enemies; this is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas who have already abandoned the bandits of all fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*). Their attainment of peace and happiness is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas attaining the great *nirvāṇa* of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
“Good son! It is like a person who has contracted a malignant leprosy, and a spiritual friend says to him:
‘If you can reach the edge of Mount Sumeru, your illness may be cured.’”
"Why is this? Because there is an excellent medicine there, its flavor like nectar; if one can take it, no illness will fail to be cured.
Having developed sincere faith in these words, the man went to that mountain, gathered and consumed the nectar, and his illness was healed, his body attaining peace and happiness.

Those with leprosy represent all ordinary beings; spiritual friends represent all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the like; wholehearted faith and acceptance represent the four immeasurable minds; Mount Sumeru represents the Eightfold Noble Path; the flavor of ambrosia represents Buddha-nature; the healing of the leprosy represents the departure from afflictions; and the attainment of peace and happiness represents the attainment of Nirvana’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Good son! It is like a man who keeps disciples who are clever and of great wisdom; this man teaches them day and night, never wearying.
The bodhisattvas are also like this: whether all sentient beings have faith or lack faith, they constantly teach and transform them without ever becoming tired or weary."
"Good son! A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) refers to those among bodhisattvas, buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and humans who believe in the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings."
For what reason is one called a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra)?

A good spiritual friend is one who can teach sentient beings to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome actions and to practice the ten wholesome actions; for this reason, they are called a good spiritual friend.
Furthermore, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) teaches in accordance with the Dharma and acts in accordance with what they teach.
What is meant by "teaching in accordance with the Dharma" and "acting in accordance with what one teaches"?

To refrain from killing oneself and to teach others not to kill, and so on, up to practicing right view oneself and teaching others right view—if one can act in this way, one may be called a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
One cultivates enlightenment for oneself and is also able to teach others to practice enlightenment; for this reason, such a person is called a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*).

One is able to personally cultivate faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, and is also able to teach others to cultivate faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom; again, for this reason, such a person is called a "good spiritual friend."
A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is so called because they possess wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma).
What are these wholesome qualities?

They do not seek their own pleasure in the deeds they perform, but always seek happiness for the sake of sentient beings; when they see the faults of others, they do not proclaim their shortcomings; and their mouths constantly proclaim only pure and wholesome matters. For these reasons, they are called spiritual friends.
“Good son! Just as the moon in the sky gradually waxes from the first day until the fifteenth day, so too is the spiritual friend:
he causes those who are training to gradually distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas and to increase wholesome dharmas.”

Good son! If there are those who draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), even if they originally lack ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they will immediately possess them; and if they are not yet complete, they will attain further increase and expansion.

Why is this? Because by associating with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), and through that association, one further attains a thorough understanding of the profound meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

If one is able to hear the profound meaning of these twelve divisions of the sutras, this is called "hearing the Dharma. Hearing the Dharma refers to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; hearing the Vaipulya sūtras is called truly hearing the Dharma. Truly hearing the Dharma is precisely hearing and receiving the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Within the Mahāparinirvāṇa, one hears that there is Buddha-nature and that the Tathāgata ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa; therefore, this is called listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion. Listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion is called the Eightfold Noble Path, for it is by means of the Eightfold Noble Path that one can sever greed, anger, and delusion; thus, it is called "hearing the Dharma."
Now, those who listen to the Dharma are called the eleven kinds of emptiness; by means of these various forms of emptiness, they do not construct conceptual signs regarding any phenomena.
Furthermore, those who listen to the Dharma are called those who have first resolved their minds, up to and including those whose minds are ultimately directed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"One attains great nirvana by means of the initial resolve, not because of hearing [the Dharma], but because of cultivation. Good son!"
For example, just as a sick person cannot be cured merely by hearing the physician’s instructions or the names of medicines, but can only recover by actually taking them;

so too, although one may hear the twelvefold profound law of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), one cannot thereby sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). It is only by means of binding the mind to mindfulness (*manasikāra*) and through skillful reflection that one can eliminate and sever them. This is called the third [stage of] binding the mind to mindfulness and reflection.
Furthermore, by what meaning is it called "contemplation with fixed mindfulness"?
It refers to the three samādhis:
the emptiness samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi.

"Emptiness" means not perceiving a single reality within the twenty-five existences; "non-action" means not forming aspirations or seeking anything within the twenty-five existences; and "signlessness" means being without the ten signs, namely: the sign of form, the sign of sound, the sign of fragrance, the sign of taste, the sign of touch, the sign of arising, the sign of abiding, the sign of cessation, the sign of male, and the sign of female. One who cultivates these three samādhis is called a bodhisattva who binds the mind in contemplation.
What is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma?

Practicing in accordance with the Dharma means practicing the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, knowing the true characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and—just like the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas—attaining parinirvāṇa within the same single path.

The Dharma is precisely that which is permanent, blissful, self, and pure; it is without birth or aging, without illness or death, without hunger or thirst, without suffering or vexation, and without falling back or perishing.
"Good son!
One who understands the profound meaning of the Great Nirvana knows that the Buddhas never ultimately enter into parinirvāṇa. Good son!"
The foremost true spiritual friend is the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Why is this? Because they constantly guide and discipline others through three kinds of skillful means.
What are these three?
First, ultimate gentle speech; second, ultimate reproach; and third, gentle speech combined with reproach.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are truly and authentically spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, good son!
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are great physicians, they are called "good spiritual friends. Why is this?
Because they know the illness, know the medicine, and prescribe medicine according to the illness.
It is like a skilled physician who is proficient in the eight branches of medical science and first observes the symptoms of the disease.
There are three kinds of such symptoms.
What are the three?
They are wind, heat, and water.
To those with wind disorders, one should administer clarified butter (sarpis).
To those with feverish diseases, he gives rock honey;
to those with water-retaining diseases, he gives ginger decoction.
Because he knows the root of the disease and administers medicine so that they recover, he is called a skilled physician.
The Buddha and the bodhisattvas are likewise in this regard; they know that there are three kinds of illnesses among ordinary people:
first, desire; second, hatred; and third, delusion.

For those with the affliction of greed, they teach the contemplation of the skeletal form; for those with the affliction of anger, they contemplate the form of loving-kindness and compassion; for those with the affliction of ignorance, they contemplate the marks of the twelvefold dependent origination.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "virtuous friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
"Good son! Just as a great shipmaster is called a 'great shipmaster' because he skillfully ferries people across, so too are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
they likewise ferry all sentient beings across the great ocean of birth and death."
For this reason, they are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Furthermore, noble son,
it is because through the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings are enabled to fully cultivate and attain the roots of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-mūla*).
"Good son!
For example, the Snowy Mountains are the source of all kinds of subtle and supreme medicinal roots.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise; they are the source of all roots of goodness."
For this reason, they are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*). Good son!

Within the Snowy Mountains there is a superior fragrant medicine named *Saha*. If someone sees it, they will attain immeasurable longevity and be free from the suffering of illness; though the four poisons may exist, they cannot cause them harm. If anyone touches it, their lifespan will increase to a full one hundred and twenty years; if anyone contemplates it, they will attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
Why is this? It is because of the power of the medicine.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise: if anyone sees them, they immediately sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), and though the four Māras may exist, they cannot disturb or confuse them; if anyone touches them, their life cannot be cut short prematurely, and they shall neither be born nor die, neither fall back nor sink away.
What is called "contact" (sparśa) is this: if one listens to and receives the sublime Dharma in the presence of a Buddha, and if one possesses mindfulness, one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra). Good son!
It is like Mount Gandhamādana, where there is the Lake Anavatapta; because of this lake, there are four great rivers, namely the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sītā, and the Vakṣu.
The sentient beings of the world constantly say:
"If there is one who has committed offenses, by bathing in these four rivers, all their sins shall be extinguished.
You should know that these words are false and unreal; setting these aside, what then is real?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are indeed the reality.
Why is this so? Because if one draws near to them, one shall attain the eradication of all transgressions.
For this reason, they are called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like the great earth:
