when all medicinal herbs, trees, forests, the hundred grains, sugarcane, and varieties of flowers and fruits face imminent death from a scorching drought, the Nanda and Upananda Dragon Kings, out of compassion for sentient beings, emerge from the great ocean and send down sweet rain, so that all forests, the hundred grains, and grasses and trees are moistened and restored to life.

It is the same for all sentient beings: when their roots of goodness are about to perish, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion and descend from the ocean of wisdom to rain down the nectar of immortality, enabling all sentient beings to fully regain the ten virtuous dharmas.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*). Good son!

It is like a skilled physician who is proficient in the eight branches of medicine; when he sees patients, he does not consider their lineage, whether they are handsome or ugly, nor their wealth and treasures, but treats them all. Therefore, the world calls him a great physician.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise; seeing that sentient beings suffer from the disease of afflictions, they do not regard their lineage, their physical beauty or ugliness, nor their wealth and treasures, but give rise to a heart of compassion and preach the Dharma for them all. Once sentient beings have heard it, the disease of their afflictions is eliminated.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of associating with such virtuous friends, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
"How does a bodhisattva, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa?

Because all sentient beings hear the Dharma, they possess the faculty of faith; because they possess the faculty of faith, they delight in practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and they attain the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, one should know that the attainment of all wholesome dharmas is due to the power of the causal condition of hearing the Dharma."
"Good son!

It is like an elder who has an only son, whom he sends to another country to trade for necessities. He shows him the places where the roads are passable and where they are blocked, and further admonishes him:
'If you encounter a courtesan, be careful not to become intimate with her; if you do become intimate, you will lose your body and life, as well as your wealth and treasures.'"
"Nor should you associate with those who are base and evil.
His son respectfully obeyed his father’s instructions; his body and mind were at peace and he acquired much wealth and treasure.

It is likewise with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who expounds the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; he demonstrates to all sentient beings and the fourfold assembly the paths that are open and those that are obstructed, so that by hearing the Dharma, these sentient beings distance themselves from all evils and become fully endowed with wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Good son! It is like a bright mirror reflecting a person’s facial features; there is nothing that is not clearly revealed.
The mirror that clarifies the Dharma is also like this: when someone looks into it, they see their good and evil clearly, without any obscuration.
For this reason, through the causal conditions of listening to the Dharma, one attains proximity to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good son!

It is like a merchant who wishes to reach an island of jewels but does not know the way; someone shows him the path, and following those instructions, he reaches the island of jewels and obtains many precious treasures beyond measure.

All sentient beings are likewise: desiring to reach the place of goodness to gather the jewels of the Way, they do not know where the path is passable or obstructed. The Bodhisattva shows it to them, and by following him, sentient beings reach the place of goodness and obtain the jewel of supreme, great Nirvana.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Good son! It is like a drunken elephant, crazed, savage, and violent, intent on killing many."
There is an elephant trainer who, using a large iron hook, hooks and strikes the elephant’s head; immediately it becomes tamed and obedient, and its evil intentions are entirely exhausted.

All sentient beings are likewise: because they are intoxicated by greed, anger, and ignorance, they wish to commit many evils. The various Bodhisattvas, using the hook of hearing the Dharma, strike them so that they are made to abide [in virtue], never again able to give rise to an evil mind.
For this reason, through the causes and conditions of listening to the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, in various sūtras I have said:

"If my disciples listen to and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures with single-minded devotion, they will leave behind the five hindrances and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. By cultivating these seven factors of enlightenment, they shall draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa."
"Because they listen to the Dharma, those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) are free from all terrors. Why is this?

When the elder Sudatta was afflicted by a grave illness, his mind was filled with great sorrow and fear; however, upon hearing Śāriputra explain that a *srotāpanna* possesses four merits and ten kinds of consolation, his terror was immediately dispelled."
For this reason, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because it opens the eye of the Dharma.
In the world there are three kinds of people:
first, those who are sightless; second, those with one eye; and third, those with two eyes.

Those who are sightless never hear the Dharma. Those with one eye, though they may hear the Dharma for a time, do not maintain it in their minds. Those with two eyes listen and receive it with single-minded devotion, practicing according to what they have heard.
By means of listening to the Dharma, one comes to know these three types of persons in the world.
For this reason, through the causal condition of listening to the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Good son!

Just as in the past, when I was in the city of Kuśinagara and the Venerable Śāriputra was afflicted by the suffering of illness, I then entrusted the bhikṣu Ānanda with the task of extensively expounding the Dharma for him."
When Śāriputra heard of this matter, he told his four disciples:
"Carry my couch to where the Buddha is; I wish to hear the Dharma.
Thereupon, the four disciples together carried him there.
Having heard the Dharma, by the power of hearing the Dharma, their suffering was alleviated and their bodies attained tranquility.
For this reason, through the causal conditions of listening to the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"How does a bodhisattva, by contemplating causes and conditions, draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa?
Through this contemplation, the mind attains liberation. Why is this?"
All sentient beings are constantly bound by the five desires; yet, through contemplation, they all attain liberation.
For this reason, the causal condition of contemplation brings one close to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son!

All sentient beings are constantly deluded by the four dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. By means of contemplation, they come to see that all phenomena are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; having seen this, the four inversions are immediately severed.
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son,
all dharmas have four characteristics.
What are these four? First, the characteristic of birth; second, the characteristic of aging; third, the characteristic of illness; and fourth, the characteristic of extinction.
By means of these four characteristics, all ordinary beings from the stage of a common person up to a *srotāpanna* are made to experience great suffering and affliction.
If one can maintain mindfulness and engage in correct reflection, even when encountering these four, suffering will not arise.
For this reason, through the causal conditions of reflection, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son!
No wholesome dharmas whatsoever are obtained without depending on reflection. Why is this?

Although some may listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, if they do not contemplate it, they will ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son!

If there are sentient beings who have unchanging faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and give rise to reverence, you should know that this is entirely due to the power of the causes and conditions of focused mindfulness and contemplation; through this, they are able to sever all afflictions.
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
"How does a bodhisattva practice in accordance with the Dharma? Good son!
To sever all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas is called the bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is meant by practicing in accordance with the Dharma?

It is to see that all dharmas are empty and non-existent, impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity. Because of this vision, one would rather sacrifice body and life than violate the prohibitive precepts; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is practice in accordance with the Dharma?
There are two kinds of cultivation:
first, the real; second, the unreal.
That which is unreal refers to not knowing the characteristics of nirvāṇa, buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the true mark, and space; this is called the unreal.
What is reality?
To be able to know the characteristics of nirvāṇa, buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the true mark, space, and so forth—this is called reality.
What is meant by knowing the characteristics of nirvāṇa?
There are eight matters regarding the characteristics of nirvāṇa. What are these eight?
First is exhaustion, second is goodness, third is reality, fourth is truth, fifth is constancy, sixth is bliss, seventh is self, and eighth is purity; these are called nirvana.
Furthermore, there are eight things.
What are these eight? First, liberation;
second, the nature of goodness; third, unreality; fourth, lack of truth; fifth, impermanence; sixth, absence of bliss; seventh, absence of self; eighth, absence of purity.
Furthermore, there are six characteristics:
first, liberation; second, the nature of goodness; third, unreality; fourth, lack of authenticity; fifth, peace and bliss; and sixth, purity.
If there are sentient beings who, relying on the mundane path, sever their afflictions, then such nirvana would involve eight matters of unreal liberation. Why is this?

Because it is not permanent, and because it is impermanent, it lacks substantiality; because it lacks substantiality, it lacks reality. Although afflictions are severed, they arise again; thus, it is impermanent, without self, without bliss, and without purity. These are called the eight aspects of nirvāṇa-liberation.
What are the six characteristics?
Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have severed their afflictions, they are called "liberated"; yet because they have not yet attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are called "unreal."
Because it is not real, it is called "untrue.
Because one shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age, it is therefore called "impermanent."
Because one has attained the untainted Noble Eightfold Path, it is called "pure bliss. Good son!
If one knows in this way, this is knowing nirvana; it is not termed buddha-nature, Tathāgata, Dharma, Saṃgha, true reality, or empty space.
“How does a bodhisattva know the buddha-nature?
There are six aspects of the buddha-nature. What are these six?”
First, permanence; second, purity; third, reality; fourth, goodness; fifth, that which should be seen; sixth, truth.
Furthermore, there are seven matters:
the first is that which can be realized, while the remaining six are as stated above. This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of buddha-nature.
“How does a bodhisattva know the marks of the Tathāgata?

The Tathāgata is the mark of awakening, the mark of excellence; he is permanence, bliss, self, and purity; he is liberation, reality, the manifestation of the path, and visible. This is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the marks of the Tathāgata.”
“How does a bodhisattva know the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)?

Phenomena may be wholesome or unwholesome, permanent or impermanent, pleasant or unpleasant, self or non-self, pure or impure, known or unknown, understood or not understood, real or unreal, cultivated or uncultivated, a teacher or not a teacher, and true or untrue—this is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena.”
"How does a bodhisattva know the characteristics of the Saṃgha?
If the Saṃgha were characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, these would be the characteristics of its disciples;
they would be visible characteristics that are virtuous, real, yet unreal."
Why is this? Because all śrāvakas shall attain the Buddha-way.
For what reason is it called "true"?
Because they have awakened to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
this is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of the Saṃgha.
"How does a bodhisattva know the true characteristic (bhūtalakṣaṇa)?"

As for the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): whether it be permanence or impermanence, pleasure or suffering, self or non-self, purity or impurity, good or evil, existence or non-existence, nirvāṇa or non-nirvāṇa, liberation or non-liberation, knowledge or ignorance, abandonment or non-abandonment, realization or non-realization, cultivation or non-cultivation, seeing or non-seeing—these are called the true mark. It is not, however, nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, or space. It is because the bodhisattva practices this Great Nirvāṇa that he comes to know the distinct characteristics among these dharmas: nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the true mark, and space.
“Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sutra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he does not perceive empty space. Why is this?
Because it is not seen by the five eyes of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, only the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) can see it;
since there is no dharma to be seen within what the wisdom eye perceives, this is called "seeing."

If that which is called "emptiness" is a non-entity, then such emptiness would be termed "real. Because it is real, it is termed "perpetually non-existent. Because it is perpetually non-existent, there is no pleasure, self, or purity.
"Good son!
'Emptiness' refers to the non-existence of dharmas; the non-existence of dharmas is called emptiness.
It is like how, in the world, the absence of things is called empty. The nature of space is also like this: because it possesses nothing, it is named 'empty space.'"
Good son! The nature of sentient beings and the nature of empty space both lack any substantial nature. Why is this so?
It is as if someone were to say that one must first eliminate existing things and then create space; yet this space is truly not something that can be created.
Why? Because it is non-existent.
Because it does not exist, one should know that emptiness does not exist.
This nature of space, if it were something that could be produced, would be called impermanent; if it were impermanent, it would not be called space.
Good son!
Just as people in the world say that space is colorless, unobstructed, eternal, and immutable, for this reason the world refers to the dharma of space as the fifth great element.
Good son! This space is in reality devoid of intrinsic nature; it is called "space" because of its luminosity, yet in truth there is no space.
It is just as with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): though it has no inherent nature, it is said to exist for the sake of sentient beings.

Good son! The essence of nirvāṇa is likewise thus: it has no place of abiding; it is simply the place where all Buddhas sever the afflictions, and is therefore called nirvāṇa. Nirvāṇa is itself permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Although nirvāṇa is blissful, it is not the experience of sensory pleasure; rather, it is the bliss of supreme, wondrous, and tranquil extinction.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, possess two kinds of bliss:
first, the bliss of quiescent extinction; second, the bliss of awakening and cognition.
The essence of the true mark possesses three kinds of bliss:
The first is the pleasure of sensation; the second is the pleasure of quiescence; the third is the pleasure of awakening.
The Buddha-nature is a single pleasure because it is to be seen; when one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is called the pleasure of bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijña-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the place where afflictions are severed were Nirvāṇa, this would not be so.”

Why is this? When the Tathāgata first attained the Way of Buddhahood in the past and went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River, at that time Māra and his retinue arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The time for Nirvana has arrived; why do you not enter it?
The Buddha told the Māra King:

"I have not yet had many disciples who are learned, who well maintain the precepts, who are intelligent and sharp-witted, and who are able to transform sentient beings; for this reason, I do not enter."

If it is said that the place where afflictions are severed and extinguished is nirvana, then since the Bodhisattvas and others have already severed their afflictions over immeasurable kalpas, why are they not called "nirvana"?
Since both are states of cessation, for what reason is it said that only the Buddhas possess this while Bodhisattvas do not?
If the severance of afflictions were not itself nirvāṇa, why did the Tathāgata formerly tell the Brahmin Jāti, saying:
"This very body of mine is now nirvāṇa"?
In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, Māra again entreated him, saying:

"Tathāgata, in the past you did not enter nirvāṇa because you had not yet had disciples who were learned, observant of the precepts, intelligent, of sharp wisdom, and capable of transforming sentient beings."
"Now that they are all complete, why do you not enter [Nirvana]?
The Tathāgata then addressed Māra, saying:
"Do not give rise to thoughts of anxiety or delay; three months hence, I shall enter Nirvana."
“World-Honored One!
If extinction were not nirvāṇa, for what reason did the Tathāgata set a time for himself that he would enter parinirvāṇa in three months?
World-Honored One!”

If the severance of afflictions were itself nirvana, then when the Tathāgata first severed his afflictions at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree in the past, that would have been nirvana; why then did he say that three months hence he would enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
If at that time it were already nirvana, why did you speak to the Mallas of Kuśinagara, saying that you would enter parinirvāṇa during the last watch of the night?
"The Tathāgata is truthful; how could he utter such false words?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vairocana-āryaguṇarāja, saying: "Good son!
If it is said that the Tathāgata possesses a broad and long tongue, one should know that throughout immeasurable kalpas the Tathāgata has already abandoned false speech.
Whatever words all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak are truthful and without falsehood.
"Good son! As you have said, regarding Māra Pāpīyas’s request in the past for me to enter parinirvāṇa, good son!
That Māra-king truly did not know the definitive characteristics of nirvāṇa."
Why is this? Pāpīyān thinks that not transforming sentient beings and remaining in silence is itself nirvāṇa. Good son!
For example, when people of the world see someone who does not speak and performs no actions, they say that this person is no different from one who is dead.
Māra Pāpīyān is just like this; thinking that the Tathāgata does not transform sentient beings and remains silent without speaking, he concludes that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata does not say that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are without distinction; he speaks only of the non-distinction between the two dharmas of permanence and purity."
"Good son!

The Buddha does not say that the Buddha, the Buddha-nature, and nirvana are indistinguishable in their characteristics; he speaks only of their being indistinguishable in their permanence, constancy, and immutability."
"Good son!
The Buddha does not say that nirvāṇa and the true mark have no difference; he only says that they are eternally present, real, unchanging, and without distinction."
"Good son!

At that time, my śrāvaka disciples will give rise to disputes and litigation, just like the evil bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī. They will violate my teachings, frequently transgressing the prohibitions and precepts; they will accept impure things and greedily seek gain and offerings."

In the presence of laypeople, he praised himself, claiming, "I have attained the state free from outflows," ranging from the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship. He disparaged others and failed to show reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the Vinaya, or his preceptor.
The Master previously told me that such items as these were permitted by the Buddha to be kept, while such items as those were not permitted by the Buddha to be kept.
I also said that such items as these were indeed not permitted by me, yet he contradicted my words, saying that such items as these were in fact permitted by the Buddha.
Since such evil people do not believe my words, for their sake I have told Pāpīyān: "Do not be distressed; three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"Good son!
Because of such evil bhikṣus, the śrāvakas and disciples under training do not see my body nor hear my Dharma, and they consequently say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa."
Only the Bodhisattvas are able to see my body and constantly hear my Dharma; for this reason, I do not say that I enter Nirvana.
Although my śrāvaka disciples may speak of the Tathāgata’s Nirvana, in truth, I do not enter Nirvana.
"Good son!

If any of my śrāvaka disciples should say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that such a person is not my disciple; they are a partisan of Māra, an evil person of false views, and do not possess right view."

If one says that the Tathāgata does not enter nirvāṇa, you should know that such a person is truly my disciple, not a partisan of Māra; they are a person of right view, not one who is evil or heterodox.
“Good son, from the beginning, I have never seen among my disciples anyone who said that the Tathāgata does not transform sentient beings, but remains in silence, which they call parinirvāṇa.”
Good son! It is like a householder who has many sons; having departed for another land, before he has yet returned, all his sons believe that their father is already dead.
Yet that elder was not actually dead; rather, his sons were deluded and all perceived him as having died.

It is the same with my śrāvaka disciples: because they do not see me, they claim that the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara. But I have not, in fact, entered parinirvāṇa; yet the śrāvaka disciples conceive the notion of my parinirvāṇa.

Good son! It is like a bright lamp that someone covers; those who do not know this say the lamp has already been extinguished, yet the bright flame has in fact not been extinguished at all. Because they do not know, they give rise to the perception of extinction.

The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: although they possess the eye of wisdom, it is obscured by afflictions, causing their minds to become inverted; thus they do not see my true body and instead give rise to the notion that I have entered parinirvāṇa, yet in reality, I do not pass into extinction.

“Good son! It is like a person born blind who does not see the sun or the moon; because they do not see them, they do not know the characteristics of day and night or light and darkness. Because they do not know these things, they then say that the reality of the sun and moon does not exist.”
The sun and moon truly exist, yet the blind do not see them; because they do not see them, they give rise to perverted conceptions and claim that there are no sun or moon.

The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: like those born blind who do not see the Tathāgata, they then say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa. In reality, the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa; it is only because of their perverted conceptions that they give rise to such a thought.

Good son! It is like clouds and mist obscuring the sun and moon; a foolish person then says that the sun and moon do not exist. Yet the sun and moon truly exist; it is simply because they are obscured that sentient beings do not see them.
The śrāvaka disciples are likewise; because their eye of wisdom is shrouded by various afflictions, they do not see the Tathāgata and thus say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
"Good son! This is merely the Tathāgata manifesting the conduct of an infant; it is not his final nirvāṇa. Good son!"

Just as in Jambudvīpa, when the sun sets, sentient beings do not see it because it is obstructed by the Black Mountains; yet the nature of the sun does not actually set, though sentient beings, failing to see it, conceive the notion that it has set.

The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: because they are obstructed by the mountains of various afflictions, they do not see my body; and because they do not see it, they conceive the notion that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, yet I am in truth not proceeding toward parinirvāṇa.
"Therefore, in the city of Vaiśālī, I said to Pāpīyān: 'Three months from now, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
O son of good family!

The Tathāgata clearly foresaw that the roots of goodness of Kāśyapa Bodhisattva would ripen three months hence, and he also foresaw that Subhadra of Mount Gandhamādana would come to my presence after completing his summer retreat; for these reasons, I told Māra Pāpīyān that three months from now I would enter parinirvāṇa."
"Good son!

There are five hundred Mallas who, at the end of three months, shall likewise resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, I have told Pāpīyas that after three months I shall enter *parinirvāṇa*."
"Good son!

For the sake of Cunda and his companions, as well as the five hundred Licchavis and the woman Āmrapālī, whose roots of goodness for the unsurpassed path will mature in three months from now, I have told Pāpīyān that in three months I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"Good son!

Sunakṣatra was closely associated with the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others; though I preached the Dharma to him for twelve full years, that man held wrong views and neither believed nor accepted it. Knowing that the roots of this person's wrong views would certainly be severed in three months, I said to Pāpīyān for this reason: 'In three months' time, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"
“Good son! For what reason did I, in the past, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, tell Māra Pāpīyān that I would not enter parinirvāṇa because I did not yet have many disciples of great wisdom?”
At that time, I desired to turn the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī for the sake of the five bhikṣus;
furthermore, I desired to do so for the sake of those five bhikṣus, namely Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Subhūti.
Next, he further desired to [benefit] fifty people, such as the householder Ugga;
next, he further desired to [benefit] immeasurable humans and devas, such as King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha.
Next, he wished to do so for the five hundred bhikṣus who were disciples of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa;
next, he wished to do so for the two brothers, Nadī Kāśyapa and Gayā Kāśyapa, along with their five hundred disciples.
Furthermore, I wish to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the other two hundred and fifty bhikṣus;
for this reason, I told the Māra Pāpīyān that I would not enter parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! There is a nirvāṇa that is not the Great Nirvāṇa.
What is nirvāṇa that is not the Great Nirvāṇa?
To sever the afflictions without seeing the Buddha-nature is called nirvana, not Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Because one does not see the Buddha-nature, there is no permanence and no self; there is only bliss and purity.
For this reason, although one may sever the afflictions, it cannot be called Great Parinirvāṇa.
If one perceives the Buddha-nature and is thereby able to sever the afflictions, this is what is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Because one perceives the Buddha-nature, it is designated as "permanence, bliss, self, and purity"; for this reason, the severing of afflictions is also termed "Great Parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! ‘Nir’ means ‘no,’ and ‘vāṇa’ means ‘weaving. The meaning of ‘not weaving’ is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, ‘vāṇa’ also means ‘covering. The meaning of ‘not covering’ is likewise called nirvāṇa.”
"Parinirvāṇa" means going and coming; that which neither goes nor comes is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Parinirvāṇa" means grasping; the meaning of non-grasping is called *nirvāṇa*. "Parinirvāṇa" means instability;
the state of being definitively free from instability is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Paṇa" signifies "new" and "old"; that which is devoid of the meaning of new and old is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Paṇa" signifies "obstruction"; that which is devoid of the meaning of obstruction is called *nirvāṇa*. Good son!
The disciples of Udraka Rāmaputra and others say that "pā" means "characteristic," and the meaning of being without characteristics is called *nirvāṇa*.
Good son, "pā" means "existence," and the meaning of non-existence is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Parinirvāṇa" means "conjunction"; the meaning of being without conjunction is called nirvāṇa.
"Parin" refers to suffering; the meaning of being without suffering is called nirvāṇa. Good son!
The severing of afflictions is not called *nirvāṇa*; rather, the non-arising of afflictions is called *nirvāṇa*.

Good son! When the afflictions do not arise within the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, this is called *nirvāṇa*; that which possesses wisdom unimpeded regarding all phenomena is what constitutes a Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is none other than ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas; this is called buddha-nature.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata’s body and mind pervades immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable lands without any obstruction; this is called space.
The Tathāgata abides eternally without change; this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not, in reality, enter ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra, fully accomplishing the seventh merit. Furthermore, O son of good family:
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplish the eighth merit? Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa eliminates five things, distances himself from five things, accomplishes six things, cultivates five things, guards one thing, draws near to four things, and faithfully accords with the one reality; thus his mind is well-liberated and his wisdom is well-liberated.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva eliminate and sever the five things?
They are the so-called five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
What is the meaning of the term "aggregate" (*skandha*)?

It refers to that which causes the continuity of birth and death for sentient beings, never allowing them to be free from their heavy burden; it is characterized by dispersal and aggregation, and is subsumed within the three periods of time. When one seeks its underlying principle, it is ultimately unfindable. For these reasons, it is called an "aggregate."
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives the aggregate of form, he does not perceive its characteristics. Why is this?
Because when one investigates its nature within the ten types of form, it is entirely unfindable; it is only for the sake of the world that it is spoken of as an "aggregate."
There are one hundred and eight feelings; although the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is perceived, from the outset there is no characteristic of feeling. Why is this?

Although feelings number one hundred and eight, in principle they have no fixed reality. Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not perceive the aggregate of feeling; the same applies to perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply perceives that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are the very root from which afflictions arise; for this reason, he employs skillful means to bring them to cessation.
"How does the Bodhisattva remain far removed from these five things?"
These are the five views. What are the five?
First, the view of a self-identity; second, the view of extremes; third, wrong view; fourth, attachment to precepts and rituals; and fifth, attachment to views.
Based on these five views, sixty-two views arise; because of these various views, birth and death continue without end. Therefore, the bodhisattva guards against them and does not approach them.
"How does a bodhisattva accomplish the six matters?
They are the six applications of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti-sthānāni*). What are the six? "

First is mindfulness of the Buddha; second is mindfulness of the Dharma; third is mindfulness of the Sangha; fourth is mindfulness of the devas; fifth is mindfulness of giving; and sixth is mindfulness of precepts. These are called the six matters accomplished by a bodhisattva.
“How does a bodhisattva cultivate the five matters?
They are the so-called five concentrations:

first, the concentration of knowledge; second, the concentration of tranquility; third, the concentration of experiencing physical and mental bliss; fourth, the concentration of no-bliss; and fifth, the Śūraṅgama concentration.”
By cultivating these five kinds of concentrated mind, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, the Bodhisattva practices with diligent effort.
"How does the Bodhisattva guard one thing?
This refers to the bodhicitta.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and diligently protects this bodhicitta, just as an ordinary person protects an only son, just as one who is blind protects their remaining eye, and just as one traveling through a wilderness protects their guide.

The Bodhisattva’s protection of the bodhicitta is likewise so; because of protecting such a bodhicitta, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and because of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one comes to possess eternity, bliss, self, and purity, which is precisely the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa. Therefore, the Bodhisattva protects this one dharma.
“What are the four things with which a bodhisattva should associate?
They are the four immeasurable minds. What are these four?”
First is great loving-kindness, second is great compassion, third is great sympathetic joy, and fourth is great equanimity.
By means of these four states of mind, one can cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta; therefore, the Bodhisattva fixes his mind upon and draws near to them.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s faith and compliance with the single reality?
A bodhisattva understands that all sentient beings ultimately return to the one path; this ‘one path’ refers to the Mahāyāna.”
For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas divide [the teachings] into three; therefore, the Bodhisattva believes and complies with them without opposition.
What is meant by "the Bodhisattva’s mind being well-liberated"?
Because greed, hatred, and deluded thoughts have been forever severed and extinguished, this is called the Bodhisattva’s mind being well-liberated.
What is the Bodhisattva’s wisdom being well-liberated?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows all phenomena without obstruction, this is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom of excellent liberation.
Through the liberation of wisdom, that which was previously unheard is now heard; that which was previously unseen is now seen; and that which was previously unattained is now attained.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijña-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for what the Buddha has said regarding the liberation of the mind, this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally unconditioned. Why is that so?
This nature of the mind is not bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, or delusion.
If it is fundamentally unbound, how can one say that the mind is "well-liberated"?
World-Honored One!
If the intrinsic nature of the mind is not bound by the fetter of greed, by what causes and conditions could it be bound?
It is like milking a horn; since it originally lacks the characteristic of milk, no amount of effort can cause milk to emerge.
One who milks a cow cannot do so by this method; though little effort is applied, much milk flows forth.
The mind is also like this: if it was originally without greed, how can there now be greed?
If greed were originally non-existent and only came into being later, then all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—who originally lacked the characteristic of greed—should now all possess it.
World-Honored One!
It is like a barren woman who originally lacks the characteristic of having a child; even if she applies effort and countless causes and conditions, a child cannot be obtained.
The mind is also like this: fundamentally it has no characteristic of greed; although various conditions are created, greed has no basis to arise.
World-Honored One!
It is like rubbing wet wood together—the fire cannot be obtained.
The mind is also like this: though one searches for it with great effort, greed cannot be found.
How, then, World-Honored One, can the fetter of greed bind the mind?
It is like pressing sand: oil cannot be obtained.
The mind is likewise; even though one presses it, greed cannot be found.
One should know that greed and the mind are two distinct principles; even if greed were present, how could it defile the mind?
World-Honored One!
It is as if someone were to try to drive a stake into empty space; it could never remain fixed there.
To place greed within the mind is likewise: through all manner of causes and conditions, one cannot cause greed to bind the mind.
“World-Honored One!
If a mind free from greed is called liberation, why do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not extract thorns from empty space?
World-Honored One!”
The mind of the past is not called liberation;
the mind of the future likewise has no liberation;
the mind of the present does not coexist with the Path.
"What kind of worldly mind, World-Honored One, is said to attain liberation?
Just as a lamp of the past cannot extinguish darkness, a lamp of the future will not extinguish darkness, and a lamp of the present likewise does not extinguish darkness."
Why is this? Because light and darkness cannot coexist.
The mind is likewise; how then can it be said that the mind attains liberation?
“World-Honored One!
Greed also exists. If greed did not exist, then when one sees the form of a woman, greed should not arise.
Since greed arises because of the form of a woman, one should know that this greed truly exists. Because greed exists, one falls into the three evil realms.”
World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who, upon seeing a painted image of a woman, also gives rise to desire; because desire has arisen, they incur various kinds of offenses.
If there were originally no desire, how could one see a painting and give rise to desire?
If the mind is free from greed, why does the Tathāgata say that the bodhisattva’s mind attains liberation?
If the mind possesses greed, why does it arise only after seeing signs, and not arise when signs are not seen?
I now clearly see that there are evil retributions; one should know that greed exists, and the same is true for hatred and delusion.
World-Honored One!

It is like sentient beings who possess bodies but have no self, yet ordinary people recklessly conceive the notion of a self (*ātman*). Although they harbor this notion of a self, they do not fall into the three evil realms.
"How is it, World-Honored One, that one who is lustful gives rise to the perception of a woman where there is no mark of a woman, and thereby falls into the three evil realms?

For example, World-Honored One, it is like rubbing wood together to produce fire; yet the nature of this fire does not exist within the various conditions [of the wood]. By what causes and conditions does it arise?"
World-Honored One!

Greed is likewise: there is no greed within form, nor is there greed within odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena. How then can greed arise with respect to form, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?
If greed is entirely absent within all conditions, why do sentient beings alone give rise to greed,
while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not?
World-Honored One!
The mind is also not fixed; if the mind were fixed, there would be no greed, hatred, or delusion.
If it is not fixed, how can you say that the mind attains liberation?
Greed is also not fixed; if it were not fixed, how could it cause one to be born in the three evil realms?
Both the greedy person and the object of greed are both not fixed.

Why is this? Because when both take the same form as their object, one may give rise to greed, another to hatred, and another to delusion. Therefore, both the greedy person and the objective realm are indeterminate. If both are indeterminate, for what reason does the Tathāgata say that when a bodhisattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, the mind attains liberation?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
The mind is neither bound by the fetter of greed nor is it unbound; it is neither liberated nor unliberated; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither present, nor past, nor future.
Why is this? Son of good family!
It is because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature.
"Good son! There are certain non-Buddhists who speak thus:

'When causes and conditions combine, a fruit arises. If that which was originally devoid of the nature of arising within the various conditions could nevertheless give rise [to a fruit], then empty space, which does not arise, should likewise produce a fruit.'"
Space does not arise because it is not a cause; rather, because the nature of the fruit already exists within the various conditions, the fruit is produced through their convergence. Why is this so?
It is like Devadatta, who, when wishing to build a wall, takes clay and earth but does not take pigments;
yet when wishing to create a painted image, he gathers pigments but does not take grass or wood.
In making clothing, one takes thread, not mud or wood;
in building a house, one takes mud, not thread or silk.

Because people select these materials, one should know that each is capable of producing its own specific fruit. Since they are capable of producing their respective fruits, one should know that the nature of the effect must already exist within the cause. If this nature did not exist, then all things could arise from within a single object.
If something can be grasped, produced, or brought forth, one should know that there must first be a fruit within it.
If there were no fruit, people would not grasp it, produce it, or bring it forth.
Only space is without grasping and without action, and thus it is able to give rise to all phenomena.
Because there is a cause, it is like a nyagrodha seed producing a nyagrodha tree, as there is clarified butter within milk, cloth within thread, and a jar within clay.
"Good son, all ordinary beings, blinded by ignorance, make this definitive statement: 'Form has the meaning of attachment, and the mind has the nature of greed.
They further say:

'The mind of an ordinary being possesses both the nature of greed and the nature of liberation; when it encounters the causes and conditions of greed, the mind gives rise to greed, and if it encounters the conditions for liberation, the mind becomes liberated.'"
Although this was said, the meaning is not so.
There are some ordinary persons who further say:
"Within all causes, there is absolutely no fruit."
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the subtle; second, the gross.
The subtle is eternal, while the gross is impermanent.
"From subtle causes they transform into coarse causes; from these coarse causes they further transform into fruits.
Because the coarse is impermanent, the fruit is also impermanent. "Good son!"
There are certain ordinary persons who further say:
"The mind has no cause, and greed also has no cause; it is simply due to the passage of time that the greedy mind arises.
Such individuals, because they are unable to understand the causes and conditions of the mind, transmigrate through the six destinies and undergo birth and death in their entirety.
“Good son! It is like a dog in a collar that has been tied to a pillar; it circles the pillar all day long and cannot escape.
All ordinary worldlings are just the same: bound by the collar of ignorance to the pillar of birth and death, they circle through the twenty-five states of existence and cannot escape.”
Good son! It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine; having emerged from it, he enters it once again.
It is like a person whose illness has been cured, yet returns to the causes of that illness.
It is like a person traveling on a road who, upon reaching an open and desolate place, returns again after having already passed through it;
or like one who has washed clean, yet smears mud over themselves once more.

All ordinary beings are likewise: they have already attained liberation from the sphere of nothingness, yet because they have not yet attained liberation from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they return once more to the three evil realms.
Why is this? All ordinary beings contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate causes and conditions, just as a dog chases a clod of earth but does not chase the person who threw it.

Ordinary beings are likewise; they contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate causes and conditions. Because they do not contemplate them, they fall back from the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception into the three evil destinies.

“Good son! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively declare that the effect exists within the cause, that the effect does not exist within the cause, that it both exists and does not exist within the cause, or that it neither exists nor does not exist within the cause.”

If one claims that within the cause there is already a fixed fruit, or a fixed absence of fruit, or a fixed presence and absence of fruit, or a fixed state that is neither present nor absent, know that such persons are all companions of Māra, belonging to Māra, and are those who cherish [false views].
Such people who cherish [false views] cannot eternally sever the fetters of birth and death; they do not understand the characteristics of the mind nor the characteristics of craving.
Good son! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest the Middle Way. Why is this?
Although it is said that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, this is not a fixed determination.

Why is this so? Because consciousness arises due to the eye, due to forms, due to light, due to the mind, and due to attention; yet this consciousness is definitely not located within the eye, within forms, within light, within the mind, or within attention. It is neither in between them, nor existent, nor non-existent. Because it arises from conditions, it is called "existent"; because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is called "non-existent. Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
"Good son!

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively declare that the mind possesses a nature of purity or a nature of impurity; for the nature of purity and impurity has no place of abiding within the mind."
Because greed arises from conditions, it is said not to be non-existent; because there is fundamentally no nature of greed, it is said not to be existent.
Good son! Due to causes and conditions, the mind gives rise to greed; due to causes and conditions, the mind attains liberation.
Good son! There are two kinds of causes and conditions:
first, those that follow saṃsāra; second, those that follow mahāparinirvāṇa.

“Good son! Due to certain causes and conditions, the mind arises together with greed and perishes together with greed; there is that which arises together with greed but does not perish with greed; there is that which does not arise together with greed but perishes together with greed; and there is that which neither arises together with greed nor perishes together with greed.”
"What is meant by 'the mind arises together with greed and ceases together with greed'? Good son!
If there is an ordinary person who has not yet severed the mind of greed and cultivates the mind of greed, such a person’s mind arises together with greed and ceases together with greed."
All sentient beings do not sever their greedy minds; the mind arises together with greed and the mind ceases together with greed.

Just as all sentient beings in the desire realm possess the dhyāna of the "taste of the first stage," whether they cultivate it or not, it is always accomplished; when they encounter the necessary conditions, they immediately attain it. What are called "conditions" refers to the calamity of fire.
All ordinary beings are likewise: whether they cultivate [the path] or do not cultivate it, their minds arise together with greed and their minds cease together with greed.
Why is this? Because they have not severed greed.
"What is meant by 'the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed'?

When a disciple of the Śrāvaka school gives rise to a greedy mind due to certain causes and conditions, they cultivate the contemplation of the white bones out of fear of that greedy mind; this is called 'the mind arising together with greed but not ceasing together with greed.'"

Furthermore, there are states of mind that arise together with greed but do not cease together with greed. For example, when a śrāvaka has not yet realized the four fruits of the path, a greedy mind arises due to certain causes and conditions; however, upon realizing the four fruits, that greedy mind ceases. This is called a mind that arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed.
"How is it that it arises together with greed but ceases together with greed?"

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having already severed the mind of greed, manifests as if possessing greed for the sake of sentient beings, he is thereby able to cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to inquire about and receive the wholesome Dharma, bringing them to full accomplishment; this is called "not arising together with greed, but perishing together with greed."
"What is meant by 'arising not together with greed' and 'ceasing not together with greed'?

This refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas, as well as Bodhisattvas other than those on the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi); these are said to arise not together with greed and cease not together with greed."
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not definitively teach that the nature of the mind is inherently pure, nor that its nature is inherently impure.
"Good son, this mind does not combine with the fetter of greed, nor does it combine with hatred or delusion."
Good son!

For example, although the sun and moon may be obscured by smoke, dust, clouds, mist, or Rāhu, and because of these conditions sentient beings are unable to see them, the nature of the sun and moon remains forever unadulterated by those five types of obscurations, even though they cannot be seen.
The mind is also like this: due to causes and conditions, the fetter of greed arises.
Although sentient beings say that the mind is conjoined with greed, the nature of the mind in reality is not conjoined with it.

If it is a mind of greed, it is the nature of greed; if it is non-greedy, it is the nature of non-greed. A non-greedy mind cannot become greedy, and a mind bound by the fetter of greed cannot become non-greedy.
Good son! For this reason, the fetter of lust cannot defile the mind.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have forever destroyed the fetter of lust; therefore, it is said that their minds have attained liberation.
All sentient beings give rise to the fetter of greed due to causes and conditions, yet their minds attain liberation from those same causes and conditions.
"Good son! It is like a place in the Snowy Mountains that is so steep and precipitous that neither humans nor monkeys can travel there."
Furthermore, there are places where monkeys can travel but humans cannot;
and there are places where both humans and monkeys can travel. Good son!
Regarding those places where humans and monkeys can travel: suppose there were hunters who used pure sticky resin, placing it upon a table to catch monkeys.

Because the monkey was foolish, it went over and touched it with its hand; once it had touched it, its hand became stuck. Desiring to free its hand, it stepped on it with its foot, and its foot likewise became attached.
Desiring to free his feet, he bit them with his mouth, but his mouth became stuck as well; thus, at all five places, he could not escape.
Thereupon, the hunter pierced him with a staff and carried him home on his back.
The perilous region of the Snowy Mountains is a metaphor for the true path attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the monkeys are a metaphor for all ordinary beings;
and the hunter is a metaphor for Māra Pāpīyan.
The sticky glue is a metaphor for the fetters of greed and desire.
The fact that neither the man nor the monkey can proceed is a metaphor for how neither ordinary worldlings nor Māra Pāpīyān can advance.

The fact that the monkey can walk where humans cannot is a metaphor for those among the non-Buddhists who possess wisdom; even though various evil Māras employ the five desires, they are unable to bind them.

Regarding those who can both walk like humans and monkeys: all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and Māra Pāpīyān constantly dwell within birth and death and are unable to practice. Ordinary people are bound by the five desires, allowing Māra Pāpīyān to take them away at will, just as that hunter uses sticky resin to capture a monkey and carries it home on his shoulder.
“Good son! It is like a king who, when dwelling within his own realm, experiences peace and happiness in body and mind; yet if he enters another’s realm, he encounters manifold sufferings.

All sentient beings are likewise: if they can abide within their own sphere, they attain peace and happiness; but if they enter another’s sphere, they encounter evil Māras and undergo various afflictions.”
One's own domain refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the domain of others refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). What is meant by being "bound to Māra"?

There are sentient beings who perceive the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent; they perceive suffering as happiness and happiness as suffering; they perceive the impure as pure and the pure as impure; they perceive non-self as self and the self as non-self; they perceive what is not true liberation as liberation and true liberation as non-liberation; they perceive what is not a vehicle (*yāna*) as a vehicle and a vehicle as not a vehicle. Such persons are called "bound to Māra. Those bound to Māra have minds that are not pure.
Furthermore, good son!

If one perceives all phenomena as truly existent, possessing fixed characteristics both in their general and specific aspects, you should know that such a person, when seeing form, constructs the characteristic of form;

likewise, up to seeing consciousness, they construct the characteristic of consciousness. Seeing a man as the characteristic of a man, seeing a woman as the characteristic of a woman, seeing a day as the characteristic of a day, seeing a month as the characteristic of a month, seeing a year as the characteristic of a year, seeing the aggregates (*skandha*) as the characteristic of the aggregates, seeing the sense-bases (*āyatana*) as the characteristic of the sense-bases, and seeing the elements (*dhātu*) as the characteristic of the elements—one who sees in this manner is said to be bound to Māra.
Those who are bound to Māra have impure minds.
Furthermore, son of good family, if one perceives:

"I am form," "form is in me," "I am in form," or "form belongs to me"; and so on, up to perceiving: "I am consciousness," "consciousness is in me," "I am in consciousness," or "consciousness belongs to me"—one who views things in this way is bound to Māra and is not my disciple.
"Good son!

My śrāvaka disciples have abandoned the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures and instead cultivate various non-Buddhist texts; they do not practice the dharma of renunciation and quiescence, but devote themselves entirely to worldly, household affairs."
What is meant by "householder affairs"?

It refers to accepting and possessing all manner of impure things—slaves, fields and houses, elephants, horses, carriages, camels, donkeys, chickens, dogs, monkeys, pigs, sheep, and various kinds of grain and wheat; remaining distant from the Teacher and the Saṃgha, associating with laypeople, and contravening the holy teachings by saying to laypeople:
"The Buddha permits bhikṣus to accept and possess various kinds of impure things."
This is called practicing the affairs of a householder.

There are certain disciples who do not seek *nirvāṇa*, but only for the sake of profit and sustenance. They draw near to and listen to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, yet they consume the property of the *caityas* and the community of monks—as well as the communal robes and food—as if it were their own. They are stingy regarding the households of others, and they cultivate intimacy with kings and princes. They practice divination for good or ill and calculate the movements of celestial bodies to predict abundance or scarcity. They engage in games such as *weiqi*, *liubo*, *chupu*, and *touhu*. They associate with *bhikṣuṇīs* and young maidens, keep two *śrāmaṇeras*, and constantly frequent the homes of butchers, hunters, and wine-sellers, as well as the dwellings of *caṇḍālas*. They engage in various kinds of trade, prepare their own food by hand, and act as messengers for neighboring states to convey messages and decrees. You should know that such persons are the retinue of Māra and are not my disciples.
For these reasons, the mind arises together with greed and ceases together with greed.
This applies likewise, up to the deluded mind, which arises and ceases together [with delusion]. "Good son!
For these reasons, the nature of the mind is neither impure nor non-impure; therefore, I say that the mind attains liberation.

If there are those who do not accept or store any impure things, but for the sake of Great Nirvana uphold, recite, transcribe, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures, you should know that such individuals are truly my disciples. They do not enter the realm of the evil Māra Pāpīyān, but are instead practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Because they practice them, they do not arise with greed, nor do they perish with greed. This is called a Bodhisattva practicing the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Great Nirvana, fully accomplishing the eighth merit.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Five The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
Scroll Twenty-Six Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Sixth Part of Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhāsa-udgata-guṇarāja.
"Furthermore, good son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra, fully accomplish the ninth merit?
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, five things will first be fully accomplished.
What are these five?"
First is faith, second is a straightforward mind, third is ethical discipline, fourth is associating with virtuous friends, and fifth is extensive learning.
What is meant by "faith"?

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas believe in the Three Jewels and that giving has its karmic fruit; they believe in the Two Truths and that the path of the One Vehicle has no other destination. Yet, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to swiftly attain liberation, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas differentiate it into three.
To believe in the ultimate truth and to believe in skillful means—this is called faith.
Such faith cannot be destroyed by any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or any sentient beings whatsoever.
By virtue of this faith, one attains the nature of a noble being (ārya).
Whether one practices giving extensively or only slightly, all such acts bring one close to Great Parinirvāṇa and prevent one from falling back into the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra).
The same applies to morality, learning, and wisdom.
This is called faith.
Although one possesses this faith, one does not perceive it; this is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa, accomplishing the first matter.
"What is the straightforward mind?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains a sincere and upright mind toward all sentient beings.
While all sentient beings may become deceitful and crooked when encountering various causes and conditions, the bodhisattva is not so."
Why is this? Because they skillfully understand that all phenomena arise solely from causes and conditions.
Although Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive the various evils and transgressions of sentient beings, they never speak of them.
Why is this? For fear that afflictions might arise; if afflictions arise, one falls into the evil realms.
Thus, if a bodhisattva sees even a slight act of goodness in sentient beings, they praise it.
What is meant by "good"?
It refers to the Buddha-nature.
By praising the Buddha-nature, one causes all sentient beings to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhā-Abhirūpa-Guṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas praise the Buddha-nature, thereby causing immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? When the Tathāgata first expounded the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, he spoke of three types:
first, if a patient obtains a skilled physician, medicine, and a caregiver, the illness can be easily cured; however, if these are not obtained, it cannot be healed.
Second, whether they obtain it or not, none can be cured;
third, whether they obtain it or not, all can be cured.

All sentient beings are likewise: if they encounter virtuous friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas, and hear the exposition of the wondrous Dharma, they will then give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; if they do not encounter such, they cannot give rise to it—namely, those at the stages of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha*.

"Second, there are those who, even though they encounter virtuous friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas, and hear the exposition of the sublime Dharma, are nonetheless unable to give rise [to the aspiration for enlightenment]; if they do not encounter them, they likewise cannot give rise to it—these are called icchantikas."
"Third, whether they encounter [favorable conditions] or not, all are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; these are what are called Bodhisattvas."

If it is said that those who encounter [the teaching] and those who do not all equally resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, why does the Tathāgata now say that he causes sentient beings to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by praising the Buddha-nature?
“World-Honored One!

If one encounters good friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, hears the exposition of the sublime Dharma, or does not encounter them, yet in all such cases is unable to give rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, you should know that this principle is likewise not so.”
Why is this? Because such persons shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Even those who are icchantikas, by virtue of their buddha-nature, shall all likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whether they hear [the teaching] or not.
World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, what is meant by the term *icchantika*?
It refers to one who has severed the roots of goodness.
This meaning is likewise not so.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-nature is never severed.
Since the principle of Buddha-nature is thus indestructible, why does the Buddha say that one may sever all roots of goodness?
As the Buddha formerly taught in the twelve divisions of the scriptures, there are two kinds of goodness:
first, the permanent; second, the impermanent.
That which is permanent is not severed; that which is impermanent is severed.
Since the impermanent can be severed, one falls into hell.
Since the permanent cannot be severed, why is it not prevented? If the Buddha-nature is not severed, how is it that one is not an icchantika?
Why does the Tathāgata speak in this way, referring to them as icchantikas?
World-Honored One,

if it is by means of the Buddha-nature that one gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for what reason does the Tathāgata extensively preach the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings?
World-Honored One!
It is like the four rivers that flow from Lake Anavatapta.
If any devas, humans, or Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, were to say that these rivers do not enter the great ocean but instead return to their source, such a thing is impossible.

The bodhicitta is also like this: for those who possess the buddha-nature, whether they hear [the Dharma] or not, whether they observe the precepts or not, whether they practice giving or not, whether they cultivate [virtue] or not, and whether they possess wisdom or not, all shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
It is like Mount Udayana, from which the sun rises in the center and reaches due south.
If the sun were to think, ‘I shall not go to the west, but shall return to the east,’ such a thing is impossible.”

The Buddha-nature is likewise: it is impossible that one who does not hear [the Dharma], does not observe the precepts, does not practice giving, does not cultivate [wholesome qualities], and lacks wisdom should fail to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, say that the nature of cause and effect is neither existent nor non-existent, such a meaning is likewise not so.
Why is this? Because...”
If there were no nature of curd within milk, then there would be no curd.
If the seed of a nyagrodha tree lacked the nature of being fifty feet tall, it could not produce a substance fifty feet in height.
If there were no tree of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the Buddha-nature, how could the tree of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* be produced?
"For this reason, the cause and effect that have been explained are neither existent nor non-existent. How can such a meaning be consistent?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
There are two kinds of people in the world who are exceedingly rare, like the udumbara flower:
first, those who do not practice unwholesome dharmas; second, those who are able to repent when they have committed an offense. Such persons are truly rare."
Furthermore, there are two types of people:
first, those who do kindness; second, those who acknowledge kindness.
Furthermore, there are two types of people:
The first is to inquire about and receive new teachings; the second is to review the old so as not to forget them.
Furthermore, there are two other types of persons:
the first is one who creates the new; the second is one who cultivates the old.
Furthermore, there are two types of persons:
first, those who delight in hearing the Dharma; second, those who delight in preaching the Dharma.
Again, there are two types of persons:
First, one who is skilled in posing questions and challenges; second, one who is skilled in providing answers.
The one skilled in posing questions and challenges is you;
the one skilled in providing answers is the Tathāgata.

"Good son! Because of this excellent inquiry, you shall immediately be able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; you shall be able to wither the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination; you shall be able to cross over the vast river of birth and death; you shall be able to wage war against the Māra Pāpīyas; and you shall be able to topple the victorious banner erected by Pāpīyas."
"Good son!

As I previously stated, there are three kinds of sick people who, whether they encounter a skilled physician, excellent nurses, and good medicine, or do not encounter them, all find their illnesses cured. What is the meaning of this?"
Whether one attains it or not, it is said that their lifespan is fixed. Why is this?

Because such a person has already cultivated the three kinds of goodness—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—throughout immeasurable lifetimes; by virtue of having cultivated these three kinds of goodness, they attain a fixed lifespan.
For example, the people of Uttarakuru have a lifespan of one thousand years.
Should anyone among them fall ill, whether they obtain a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and nursing care, or do not obtain them, all will recover.
Why is this? Because they have attained a fixed lifespan. "Good son!

As I have said, if a sick person encounters a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and proper nursing, the illness will be cured; if they do not encounter these, it will not be cured. What is the meaning of this?
"Good son! For such a person, the lifespan is not fixed.
Although their life has not yet reached its full term, there are nine causes and conditions that can cause them to die prematurely."
What are the nine?
First, knowing that food is unwholesome, one nevertheless eats it;
second, eating too much; [and so forth].
Third, eating again when previous food has not yet been digested;
fourth, failing to attend to the timely evacuation of excrement and urine;
fifth, failing to follow the physician’s instructions during illness.
Sixth, not following the instructions of those who visit the sick;
seventh, forcibly enduring [impurities] without vomiting them out;
eighth, traveling at night, whereby evil spirits strike one because of such nighttime wandering.
Ninth is excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse.
For this reason, I say that if a sick person encounters medicine and a physician, the illness may be cured; if they do not encounter them, it cannot be healed.
"Good son!
As I have previously stated, that those who encounter [a physician] and those who do not are both incurable—what does this mean?
There are people whose life-span has reached its end; for them, whether they encounter [a physician] or not, they are entirely beyond cure."
Why is this? Because his life has come to an end.
For this reason, I say that a sick person will not recover, whether they encounter medical treatment and medicine or do not encounter them.

Sentient beings are likewise: those who have resolved their minds toward Bodhi will all surely achieve accomplishment, whether they encounter virtuous friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas from whom they inquire and receive the profound Dharma, or whether they do not encounter them.
Why is this? It is because they are able to give rise to the bodhicitta.

Just as the people of Uttarakuru obtain a fixed lifespan, so too, as I have taught, from the stage of srotāpanna up to the pratyekabuddha, if they hear the profound Dharma spoken by good friends, Buddhas, or bodhisattvas, they will then give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; however, if they do not encounter Buddhas or bodhisattvas and hear the teaching of the profound Dharma, they will be unable to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Just as an uncertain lifespan may be cut short due to nine causes and conditions, so it is with the sick person who recovers from illness upon encountering a physician and medicine, yet fails to recover if such is not encountered. For this reason, I say that when one encounters a Buddha or Bodhisattva and hears the profound Dharma being taught, one is able to resolve to attain enlightenment; if one does not encounter them, one cannot so resolve.

"As I have previously stated, whether one encounters virtuous friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas and hears them expound the profound Dharma, or does not encounter them, neither case allows for the arousal [of the bodhicitta]. What is the meaning of this?"
"Good son!

As for those who are icchantikas, whether they encounter good friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas who preach the profound Dharma, or do not encounter them, they are alike unable to abandon the mind of an icchantika."
Why is this? Because they have severed the wholesome dharmas.
Even those who are icchantikas can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? If one is able to give rise to the bodhicitta, then one is no longer called an icchantika. Good son!
For what reason do you say that icchantikas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

In truth, those who are icchantikas cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they are like one whose life has ended, who, even if they encounter a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and attentive caregivers, cannot recover.
Why is this? Because their life has come to an end.
"Good son!..."
"Icchantika" means "faith," and "tī" means "not possessing. Because they do not possess faith, they are called icchantikas.
Since the Buddha-nature is not faith and sentient beings do not possess it, how could it be severed by their lack of possession?
"Icchantika" means "one who possesses skillful means," while "ti" means "lacking. Because they lack the cultivation of skillful means, they are called icchantikas.

Since buddha-nature is not something produced by the cultivation of skillful means, and sentient beings do not possess it [as a result of such cultivation], how could it be severed simply because it is not possessed?
"Icchantika" means "lacking progress" (iccha) and "lacking attainment" (tanti). Because they lack progress, they are called icchantikas.

Since buddha-nature is not something that can be progressed toward, and sentient beings do not possess it [as a separate entity], how could it be severed given that it is not something to be possessed?
"Icchantika" means "thought" (smṛti), and "iccha" means "lacking. Because they lack thought, they are called icchantikas.
Buddha-nature is not thought, and sentient beings do not possess it; since it is not something possessed, how could it be severed?
"Icchantika" means "fixed" (niyata) and "lacking" (iccha). Because they lack fixedness, they are called icchantikas.
Since buddha-nature is not fixed and sentient beings do not possess it [in a fixed manner], how could it be severed because of such non-possession?
"Icchantika" means "wisdom," and "iccha" means "lacking. Because they lack wisdom, they are called icchantikas.
Since Buddha-nature is not wisdom and sentient beings do not possess it [as such], how can it be severed when it is already lacking?
*Ikṣaṇa* means "impermanent goodness," and *iti* means "incomplete.
Because they lack the perfection of impermanent goodness, they are called *icchantikas*.
The Buddha-nature is permanent; it is neither good nor non-good.
Why is this? Because wholesome dharmas are necessarily attained through skillful means (*upāya*).
This Buddha-nature, however, is not attained through skillful means; therefore, it is not wholesome.
For what reason, then, is it also called "not unwholesome"?
Because it is able to attain wholesome fruits, and these wholesome fruits are precisely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, as for wholesome dharmas, they are attained after having been produced; however, this Buddha-nature is not something attained after being produced, and for this reason, it is not wholesome.
Because they have severed all wholesome dharmas acquired through birth, they are called icchantikas. "Good son!
As you have said, if an icchantika possesses the Buddha-nature, why does it not prevent the retribution of hell?"
"Good son! Within those of single-minded attachment (icchantika), there is no Buddha-nature. Good son!"

It is like a king who, hearing the sound of a lute, finds its tone pure and exquisite; his mind becomes deeply attached to it, and with joy, delight, and affection, he cannot bear to let go. He then asks his ministers:
"From where does such a wondrous sound emerge?"
The minister replied,
"Such a wondrous sound issues from the lute.
The king spoke again:
"Bring this sound here.
At that time, the minister immediately took the lute and placed it before the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know that this is the sound."
The king said to the lute, "Produce sound! Produce sound!
Yet the lute produced no sound at all.

At that time, the great king immediately severed its strings, yet the sound still did not emerge; he took its skin and wood and split them all apart, searching for the source of the sound but was utterly unable to find it.
At that time, the Great King became angry with the minister and said,
"How can you utter such a falsehood?
The minister addressed the King:
"Now, regarding the production of sound, the Dharma is not like that.
It is through various conditions and skillful means that sound is produced.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it has no fixed location, yet through skillful means it can be seen; because it can be seen, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
