Those who are icchantikas do not see the Buddha-nature; how then could they prevent the retribution of the three evil paths? Good son!
If an icchantika believes that the Buddha-nature exists, you should know that such a person will not fall into the three evil paths, nor would they be called an icchantika.
Because they do not have confidence that they possess the Buddha-nature, they fall into the three evil realms; because they fall into the three evil realms, they are called icchantikas. "Good son!
As you have said, if milk lacked the nature of curd, it would not produce curd."
If the seed of the *nyagrodha* tree lacked the nature of being five *zhang* tall, it would not possess the substance of being five *zhang* tall.
Foolish people speak in this way, but the wise never utter such words.
Why is this? Because they lack intrinsic nature. Good son!
If there were the nature of curd within milk, it should not require the power of various conditions once again. Good son!
Just as when water and milk are mixed together, even if left for a month, they will ultimately never become curd.
If one drops a single drop of *pāka* tree sap into it, it immediately turns into curd.
If curd were already inherently present, why would it need to depend on conditions?
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: because it relies upon various conditions, it can be seen; because it relies upon various conditions, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If something is established only after depending upon various conditions, it is devoid of intrinsic nature; because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, one is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son!
For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly praises the goodness of others and does not litigate their faults, it is called the mind of straightforwardness.
Furthermore, son of good family!
What is the upright mind of a bodhisattva?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva never commits evil; should they have a transgression, they immediately repent. They never conceal it from their teachers or fellow students, but feel shame and self-reproach, not daring to commit it again. They conceive a sense of extreme gravity regarding even minor offenses.
If one is questioned, they answer that they have indeed committed the offense.
When asked again whether this offense is good or not good,
they answer that it is not good.
He asked again, "Is this offense wholesome or unwholesome?
He replied, "It is unwholesome.
He asked again, "Is this offense the fruit of what is wholesome or the fruit of what is unwholesome?"
He replied, "This is indeed a transgression; it is truly not a wholesome fruit.
He asked again, "By whom was this transgression created?
Could it have been committed by the Buddhas, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha?"
He replied, "It was not the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha that did this; it was my own doing, for it was constructed and accumulated by my afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because of my straightforward mind, I believe in the existence of Buddha-nature; because I believe in Buddha-nature, I cannot be called an icchantika."

Because they possess a straightforward mind, they are called disciples of the Buddha; even if they receive from sentient beings tens of millions of various offerings—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—this is not considered much, for this is called the bodhisattva’s mind of integrity and straightforwardness.
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate and purify the precepts?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva upholds the prohibitive precepts not for the sake of rebirth in heaven, nor out of fear, nor even to adopt the 'dog-precepts,' 'chicken-precepts,' 'ox-precepts,' or 'pheasant-precepts. He does not break the precepts, nor does he make them deficient, nor blemished, nor mixed, nor like those of the śrāvakas. He upholds the bodhisattva-mahāsattva precepts, the śīla-pāramitā precepts, and attains the complete precepts without giving rise to arrogance; this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa, fulfilling the third precept."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s close association with virtuous friends?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly teaches sentient beings the path of goodness and does not teach the path of evil; he explains that the path of evil does not yield wholesome fruits."
"Good son!
My body is the true and virtuous spiritual friend for all sentient beings; therefore, I am able to sever all the false views held by the brahmin Pukara."
"Good son!
If there are sentient beings who draw near to me, even if they possess the causes and conditions for birth in the hells, they will immediately attain birth in the heavens.
For example, those such as Sunakṣatra were destined to fall into hell, but because they saw me, they were able to sever the causes and conditions for hell and were born in the Form Realm Heavens."
Although there are those such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, they are not called true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they give rise to the causes and conditions for the mind of an icchantika.
"Good son!
In the past, when I was dwelling in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, Śāriputra instructed two disciples: one to contemplate white bones, and the other to practice counting the breaths."
Having practiced for many years without attaining certainty, he gave rise to wrong views because of these circumstances, saying:
"There is no nirvana, nor are there any outflow-free dharmas; even if they did exist, I should have attained them."
"Why is this? Because I am able to properly uphold the precepts I have received.
At that time, seeing that this bhikṣu had conceived such a wrong thought, I called Śāriputra and rebuked him:
"You do not teach well; how can you preach the Dharma in such a distorted manner to these two disciples?
These two disciples differ in their natures: one is a washerman, and the other is a goldsmith."
"The son of a goldsmith should have been taught counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*), and the washerman should have been taught the contemplation of bones (*aśubhabhāvanā*).
Because you taught them incorrectly, you have caused these two men to give rise to evil and heterodox views."
At that time, I preached the Dharma to these two individuals according to their needs; having heard it, they both attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Therefore, I am the true spiritual friend for all sentient beings, whereas Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others are not.
If sentient beings possess extremely heavy fetters and encounter me, I shall employ skillful means to sever them for them.
For example, my younger brother Nanda possessed extremely heavy desire; I employed various kinds of skillful means to eliminate and sever it for him.
Aṅgulimāla possessed intense hatred, yet upon seeing me, his hatred was immediately stilled.
King Ajātaśatru possessed profound ignorance, yet upon seeing me, his deluded mind was instantly extinguished.
For example, the householder Vāsiṣka had cultivated and perfected extremely heavy afflictions over immeasurable kalpas, yet they were immediately severed and extinguished simply by seeing me.
Even if there were a base and lowly person who approached me and became my disciple, by virtue of this cause and condition, all humans and devas would respect and cherish them.
Śrīgupta’s false views were rampant; however, because he encountered me, his false views were immediately extinguished.
Because he encountered me, he severed the causes for rebirth in hell and created the conditions for birth in heaven, just as a breath [can extinguish] a *caṇḍāla*.
When his life was about to end, because he saw me, he regained his lifespan, just like Kauśika.
When his mind was deranged and confused, because he saw me, he regained his original state of mind, just like Śrī-Gautamī.
The son of a butcher constantly cultivated evil deeds, yet because he beheld me, he immediately abandoned them, like the bhikṣu Cāṇḍāla.
Because of seeing me, he would rather sacrifice his own body and life than violate the prohibitive precepts, like the bhikṣu Tṛṇabandha.
For this reason, while the bhikṣu Ānanda says that half of the holy life constitutes a "good spiritual friend," I say it is not so; only the complete holy life is called a "good spiritual friend."
This is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa and fulfilling the fourth [requirement]: having a virtuous spiritual friend.
How does a bodhisattva fulfill extensive learning?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, copies, recites, reads, and provides detailed explanations of the twelve divisions of the scriptures; this is called a bodhisattva fulfilling extensive learning.
Excluding eleven divisions of the canon, if one upholds, recites, transcribes, and explains only the Vaipulya, such a person is also called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning.

Excluding the twelve divisions of the scriptures, if one can uphold this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra, transcribing, reciting, and explaining it in detail, this is called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning.
Setting aside the complete body of these sutras, if one can receive and uphold even a single four-line verse;

and setting aside this verse as well, if one can receive and uphold that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and his nature is unchanging—this is called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning.
Setting aside this matter, if one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, one is also called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning.
Why is this? Because dharmas have no intrinsic nature.
Although the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas, he never speaks of anything at all.
This is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa and accomplishing the fifth perfection of extensive learning.

“Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, fully accomplish these five matters, they are able to do what is difficult to do, endure what is difficult to endure, and give what is difficult to give.”
What is it for a bodhisattva to be able to perform what is difficult to do?

If they hear that by eating a single sesame seed one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they believe these words, they shall constantly eat only a single sesame seed for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

If one hears that by entering fire one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and for immeasurable kalpas remains within the Avīci Hell amidst masses of blazing flames, this is called the bodhisattva’s ability to perform what is difficult to do.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s ability to endure what is difficult to endure?

If one hears that through the causes and conditions of undergoing suffering—such as being struck with hands, staves, swords, or stones—one will attain great *nirvāṇa*, then one should accept such physical suffering throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas without regarding it as hardship; this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to endure what is difficult to endure.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to give what is difficult to give?

If they hear that one can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by giving away kingdoms, cities, wives, children, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains to others, they immediately, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, give away all their kingdoms, cities, wives, children, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains to others; this is called a bodhisattva being able to give what is difficult to give.
Although a bodhisattva is able to perform what is difficult to do, he never thinks, "This is my doing";
it is the same when he is able to give what is difficult to give. Good son!

It is like parents who have but one son; they love him most deeply and provide him with fine garments and exquisite, delicious food, nourishing him according to the season so that he lacks for nothing.
If that child, in the presence of his parents, should give rise to a mind of contempt and insult them with harsh speech,
the parents, out of love, would feel no anger or resentment, nor would they think, "I am providing this child with clothing and food."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he regards all sentient beings as if they were his only child. If the child falls ill, the parents also fall ill; they diligently seek out medicine and treat them with care. Once the illness has been cured, they never give rise to the thought: "I have treated this child's suffering."

The Bodhisattva is likewise: seeing sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and preaches the Dharma for them; because they have heard the Dharma, their afflictions are severed. Once the afflictions are severed, he never thinks to himself, "I have severed the afflictions for these sentient beings."
If one gives rise to such a thought, one will ultimately never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
One should only maintain this thought: "There is not a single sentient being for whom I have preached the Dharma to cause them to sever their afflictions."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas harbor neither anger nor delight toward sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they have skillfully cultivated the samādhi of emptiness.
If a bodhisattva cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, toward whom could they give rise to anger or joy? Good son!
For example, when a mountain forest is consumed by a fierce fire, or its trees are cut down by people, or swept away by water, would those trees feel anger or joy toward anyone?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, having neither anger nor delight toward sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they cultivate the samādhi of emptiness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijñā-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are all dharmas empty by their very nature?”
It is empty because it is the emptiness of emptiness.
If things were empty by their own nature, one should not need to cultivate emptiness before perceiving emptiness.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that one perceives emptiness by means of cultivating emptiness?
"If the nature were not itself empty, then even by practicing emptiness, one could not make it empty.
"Good son! The nature of all dharmas is fundamentally empty from the beginning."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena (dharmas) is unattainable. Good son!
The nature of form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended.
What is the nature of form?

The nature of form is not earth, water, fire, or wind, yet it is not separate from earth, water, fire, or wind; it is not blue, yellow, red, or white, yet it is not separate from blue, yellow, red, or white; it is neither existent nor non-existent. How, then, can one say that form has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Because their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended, they are said to be empty.
All phenomena are likewise; because they continue in a semblance of succession, ordinary people, having perceived them, claim that the nature of all phenomena is not empty and quiescent.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with five things, they therefore perceive that the nature of dharmas is fundamentally empty and quiescent. Good son!

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who perceive the nature of all dharmas as not empty, you should know that such persons are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas; they cannot practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they cannot enter Great Parinirvāṇa, and they cannot manifestly behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—they are the retinue of Māra.
"Good son!
The nature of all dharmas is fundamentally empty; furthermore, it is because bodhisattvas practice emptiness that they perceive the emptiness of all dharmas.
Good son!"
Just as the nature of all phenomena is impermanent, cessation can bring them to an end.
If they were not impermanent, cessation would be unable to extinguish them.
Conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of arising, so arising can produce them; they possess the characteristic of cessation, so cessation can extinguish them.
Because all dharmas possess the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), suffering can cause one to suffer.
Son of good family!

Just as the nature of salt is salty and can make other things salty, the nature of rock honey is sweet and can make other things sweet, the nature of fermented wine is sour and can make other things sour, the nature of ginger is pungent and can make other things pungent, the *harītakī* fruit is bitter and can make other things bitter, the *āmra* fruit is astringent and can make other things astringent, and the nature of poison is harmful and can cause other things to be harmed; so too, the nature of nectar (*amṛta*) causes people not to die, and if it is mixed with other substances, those others likewise do not die.
The Bodhisattva’s cultivation of emptiness is likewise so: by cultivating emptiness, one perceives that the nature of all phenomena is entirely empty and quiescent.
The Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Universally Radiant Light, further said:
“World-Honored One!

If salt could make that which is not salty become salty, and if the cultivation of the emptiness samādhi were likewise so, one should know that this concentration is neither wholesome nor sublime, for its nature is inverted.
"If the samādhi of emptiness perceives only emptiness, it must be a non-existent dharma;
what, then, is there to be seen? "Good son!
This samādhi of emptiness perceives dharmas that are not empty and is able to render them empty and quiescent, yet it is not a perversion."
Just as salt makes that which is not salty become salty, so too is this samādhi of emptiness: it makes that which is not empty become empty.
Good son! Greed has the nature of existence; it does not have the nature of emptiness.
If greed were empty, sentient beings should not fall into hell because of this cause and condition;
if they do fall into hell, how could the nature of greed be empty?
"Good son! The nature of form exists.
What is the nature of form?"
This is what is called perversion.
Because of perversion, sentient beings give rise to craving.
If the nature of form were not perverted, how could it cause sentient beings to give rise to craving?
Because greed arises, one should know that the nature of form is not non-existent.
For this reason, practicing the samādhi of emptiness is not a perversion. Good son!
All ordinary beings, upon seeing a woman, immediately give rise to the perception of her as a woman.

It is not so for a Bodhisattva; although they see a woman, they do not give rise to the perception of her as a woman. Because they do not give rise to such perceptions, craving does not arise; and because craving does not arise, they are not inverted.
Because worldly people perceive the appearance of a woman, the Bodhisattva speaks accordingly of the existence of women.
If, when seeing a man, one were to say it is a woman, that would be a perversion.
Therefore, I said to Jāti:
"O Brahmin, if you take day for night, that is an inversion;
if you take night for day, that too is an inversion."
"Day is characterized as day, and night is characterized as night; how can this be called a perversion? Good son!

All Bodhisattvas dwelling in the nine stages perceive that dharmas have an intrinsic nature. Because of this perception, they do not see the Buddha-nature. If one were to see the Buddha-nature, one would no longer see the intrinsic nature of any dharma."
Because one cultivates this samādhi of emptiness in such a manner, one does not perceive the nature of dharmas; because one does not perceive it, one perceives the Buddha-nature.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have two kinds of teaching:
first, the existence of nature; second, the absence of nature.
For the sake of sentient beings, one speaks of the existence of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); for the sake of the noble ones (ārya), one speaks of the non-existence of the nature of phenomena.
Because those who do not see emptiness perceive phenomena as empty, they cultivate the samādhi of emptiness so that they may attain the vision of emptiness.
The nature of dharmas is also cultivated as emptiness, and is therefore empty.
For this reason, one cultivates emptiness and perceives emptiness. Good son!
"You say that you see emptiness, yet emptiness is a non-existent dharma; what, then, is it that is seen?
Good son! It is so, it is so;
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly sees nothing at all."
That which has nothing to be seen is that which has nothing existing; that which has nothing existing is all dharmas.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, they see nothing at all within all dharmas.

If there is one who sees, they do not see the Buddha-nature; they cannot cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā and cannot enter into Mahāparinirvāṇa. For this reason, the Bodhisattva perceives that the nature of all dharmas is non-existent.

“Good son! A bodhisattva does not see emptiness solely by means of the samādhi of seeing; the *prajñāpāramitā* is also empty, the *dhyānapāramitā* is also empty, the *vīryapāramitā* is also empty, the *kṣāntipāramitā* is also empty, the *śīlapāramitā* is also empty, and the *dānapāramitā* is also empty. Form is empty, the eye is empty, and consciousness is empty; even the Tathāgata is empty and Great Parinirvāṇa is also empty. Therefore, the bodhisattva sees that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely empty.”
Therefore, while I was in the city of Kapilavastu, I said to Ānanda:
"Do not be distressed, nor grieve, lament, or weep.
Ānanda then replied:
“O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
My entire retinue has now perished; how could I not be filled with grief and weeping?

You, Tathāgata, were born in this city together with me and belong to the same Śākya clan as our kinsmen and relatives. Why is it that you alone feel no sorrow or affliction, and your radiant countenance appears even more brilliant?”
"Good son! I spoke again, saying: 'Ānanda!'"
"You see that Kapila exists as a reality, but I see that all is empty and quiescent, such that nothing at all exists.
You see all the Śākyas as your kinsmen, but because I cultivate emptiness, I see nothing at all."
"Because of these causes and conditions, you have given rise to sorrow and suffering, yet the appearance of my body becomes even more radiant.

Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practice this Samādhi of Emptiness in such a manner, they do not give rise to grief or affliction; this is called the Bodhisattva practicing the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa and fully accomplishing the ninth merit.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva, by practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, become fully endowed with the final tenth merit? Good son!

The Bodhisattva cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, enters Great Nirvana—which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure—and for the sake of all sentient beings, he expounds and analyzes the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, revealing the Buddha-nature.
If those who are srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas have faith in these words, they shall all enter into mahāparinirvāṇa.
"If one does not believe, they will wander through birth and death.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Noble Virtue King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of sentient beings will fail to give rise to reverence for this sutra? "Good son!

After my parinirvāṇa, there will be śrāvaka disciples who are foolish and violate the precepts, who delight in inciting strife, who abandon the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and who instead read, recite, and study various non-Buddhist texts, verses, and manuscripts; they accept and store all kinds of impure things, claiming that these are permitted by the Buddha."
Such a person trades fine sandalwood for common wood, exchanges gold for brass, silver for pewter, silk for coarse woolen cloth, and barter the flavor of nectar for foul poison.
What is meant by "trading sandalwood for common wood"?

It refers to when my disciples, for the sake of making offerings, expound the sutras and the Dharma to laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Yet these laypeople are indolent and have no desire to listen; they sit in high places while the bhikṣus sit below, and even though the disciples provide them with various kinds of delicacies and food and drink, the laypeople still refuse to listen. This is called trading sandalwood for common wood.
What is meant by trading gold for brass?
Brass is a metaphor for visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; gold is a metaphor for the precepts.
When my disciples, on account of visible forms, break the precepts they have received, this is called trading gold for brass.
What is meant by exchanging silver for white tin?
Silver is a metaphor for the ten wholesome actions, while white tin is a metaphor for the ten unwholesome actions.
When my disciples abandon the ten wholesome actions and practice the ten unwholesome dharmas, this is called exchanging silver for white tin.
What is meant by "exchanging silk for coarse woolen cloth"?
Coarse woolen cloth is a metaphor for shamelessness and lack of remorse; silk is a metaphor for shame and remorse.
When my disciples abandon shame and remorse and instead practice shamelessness and lack of remorse, this is called exchanging silk for coarse woolen cloth.
What is meant by "exchanging ambrosia for poison"?
Poison is a metaphor for various kinds of gain and offerings; ambrosia is a metaphor for all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
When my disciples, for the sake of gain and offerings, praise themselves before laypeople, claiming they have attained the untainted, this is called exchanging ambrosia for poison.
"Because of such evil bhikṣus as these, this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra will be widely circulated throughout Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there will be certain disciples who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and extensively expound this sūtra, and they shall be killed by such evil bhikṣus."
At that time, wicked bhikṣus gathered together and established a severe regulation:
"If there be anyone who receives, upholds, copies, reads, recites, or explains the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, none shall dwell, sit, converse, or speak with them."
Why is this? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was not spoken by the Buddha; it was composed by those with false views, and those with false views are none other than the six teachers.
The scriptures of these six teachers are not the scriptures of the Buddha.
Why is this so? Because all Buddhas have taught that all phenomena are impermanent, without self, without bliss, and without purity.
If one were to say that phenomena are permanent, blissful, self, and pure, how could that possibly be a sutra spoken by the Buddha?

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas permit the bhikṣus to possess various kinds of items, whereas the Six Teachers proclaim that their disciples must not possess any items at all; regarding such a principle, how could it possibly be the teaching of the Buddha?

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas did not prohibit their disciples from consuming the five flavors of beef or eating meat; yet the Six Heretics did not permit the consumption of the five kinds of salt, the five kinds of beef-flavors, or fat and blood. If [the prohibition of these] were true, how could it be considered the authentic scripture of the Buddha?

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have taught the Three Vehicles, yet this sutra speaks exclusively of the One Vehicle, namely the Great Nirvana; how can such words be considered the authentic scripture of the Buddha?

"All Buddhas ultimately enter parinirvāṇa; yet this sutra says that the Buddha is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, and does not enter parinirvāṇa. This sutra is not included among the twelve divisions of the canon; it is a teaching of Māra, not a teaching of the Buddha."
"Good son! Although such a person is my disciple, they are unable to believe in or accord with this Nirvāṇa Sūtra. Good son!"
At that time, if there are sentient beings who believe in this sutra even for a single half-verse, you should know that such persons are truly my disciples.
By virtue of such faith, they immediately perceive the Buddha-nature and enter into nirvana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Radiant Illumination, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
The Tathāgata has today skillfully revealed and taught the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
World-Honored One!

Because of this, I have attained understanding of even a single phrase or half-phrase of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; by virtue of understanding that one phrase or half-phrase, I perceive a small portion of the Buddha-nature.
"As the Buddha has taught, I too shall attain entry into Great Parinirvāṇa.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the tenth merit.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 26;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 27.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, Part One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire assembly:
"O sons of good family!
If you have any doubts as to whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, whether there is Dharma or no Dharma, whether there is Saṅgha or no Saṅgha,
whether there is suffering or no suffering, whether there is origination or no origination, whether there is cessation or no cessation,
whether there is the path or no path, whether there is reality or no reality, whether there is a self or no self...
Pleasure and the absence of pleasure; purity and the absence of purity; permanence and impermanence;
vehicles and the absence of vehicles; nature and the absence of nature; sentient beings and the absence of sentient beings;
existence and non-existence; reality and unreality; cause and the absence of cause; fruit and the absence of fruit.
Regarding that which is conditioned and unconditioned, karma and non-karma, and retribution and non-retribution—
now ask me whatever you wish, and I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son!
Truly, I do not see anyone—whether a deva, a human, a Māra, a Brahmā, a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa—who comes to question me and whom I am unable to answer."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Siṃhanāda. He rose from his seat, composed his countenance and adjusted his robes, stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I have just wished to ask a question; will the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, again grant me the opportunity to speak?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

"You all should now give rise to deep reverence, respect, and praise for this bodhisattva; you should make offerings to him with various kinds of incense, flowers, music, garlands, banners, canopies, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and dwellings such as houses and halls, and you should welcome him when he arrives and see him off when he departs."
Why is this? Because these people have already deeply planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas and have perfected their merit; therefore, they now wish to deliver the lion’s roar before me.

“Good son! Just as the lion king, knowing his own physical strength, the sharpness of his fangs and claws, and with his four paws planted firmly on the ground, dwells securely in his rocky cave, shaking his tail and letting out a roar—if anyone can possess all such characteristics, you should know that they are indeed capable of the lion’s roar.”
The true lion king emerges from his den at dawn, stretches and yawns, surveys the four directions, and lets out a thunderous roar for eleven purposes.

What are these eleven? First, because he wishes to destroy those who are not actually lions but falsely pretend to be so; second, because he wishes to test his own strength; third, because he wishes to purify his dwelling place; fourth, so that his offspring may know their domain; fifth, so that the herd may be free from fear; sixth, so that those who are sleeping may be awakened; seventh, so that all heedless beasts may become diligent; eighth, so that the various beasts may come to rely upon him; ninth, because he wishes to tame the great fragrant elephants; tenth, because he wishes to instruct his offspring; and eleventh, because he wishes to adorn his own retinue.

When all birds and beasts hear the lion’s roar, those belonging to the watery realm sink into the deep abysses, those that move on land hide in their burrows and caves, those that fly fall to the ground, and the great fragrant elephants are so terrified they lose control and void their excrement.
"O sons of good family!
Just as that jackal, though it may follow a lion for a hundred years, can never produce the lion’s roar;
whereas a lion cub, having reached the age of three years, is able to roar like the lion king."

“Good son! The Tathāgata’s perfectly awakened wisdom is his fangs and claws; his body is perfected through the four bases of psychic power and the six pāramitās; he is fierce with the ten powers; he has great compassion as his tail; he dwells securely in the pure cave-dwelling of the four dhyānas; and for the sake of all sentient beings, he roars the lion’s roar, crushing and destroying the armies of Māra.”

He manifests the ten powers to the assembly, opens the sphere of the Buddha’s practice, and serves as a refuge for those with false views; he comforts the multitudes terrified by birth and death, awakens sentient beings sleeping in ignorance, and inspires those who commit evil deeds to feel remorse.
He reveals this to all sentient beings who hold false views, so that they may know the six teachers do not possess the lion’s roar;
to shatter the prideful minds of Pūraṇa and the others; to cause those of the two vehicles to give rise to a sense of remorse;
to instruct the bodhisattvas of the five abodes to generate a mind of great power; and for the sake of the fourfold assembly who possess right view.
Because he feels no fear toward the fourfold assemblies of those with wrong views, he stretches out his limbs and emerges from the cave-dwelling of noble conduct,
brahminic conduct, and celestial conduct; he yawns in order to cause those sentient beings to break their arrogance,
and he gazes in the four directions in order to cause those sentient beings to give rise to wholesome dharmas.
He plants his four paws firmly upon the ground so that sentient beings may attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge;
he utters the lion’s roar so that sentient beings may fully abide in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
The Lion’s Roar means definitive teaching: all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and immutable. Good son!

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas may follow the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they are nonetheless unable to utter the lion’s roar.
If Bodhisattvas of the ten stages can practice these three spheres of conduct, you should know that they are then able to roar the lion’s roar.
Sons of good family!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lion’s Roar now wishes to let out such a great lion’s roar; therefore, you all should, with deep resolve, make offerings to him, revere him, honor him, and praise him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāmin, saying:
"Good son! If you wish to ask a question, you may do so as you please."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the Buddha-nature?”
For what reason is it called "Buddha-nature"?
For what reason is it further named "permanence, bliss, self, and purity"?
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not perceive the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings?
In what dharmas do Bodhisattvas of the ten stages dwell such that they see them unclearly?
In what dharmas does the Buddha dwell such that he sees them clearly?
With what kind of eyes do Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see them unclearly?
"With what eye does the Buddha see with perfect clarity?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can inquire about and seek instruction regarding the Dharma, they will be fully endowed with two kinds of adornment:
first, wisdom; second, merit.

If there is a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these two kinds of adornment, they will know the Buddha-nature and also understand what is called the Buddha-nature; furthermore, they will be able to know by what eye the bodhisattvas of the ten stages see, and by what eye the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘adornment with wisdom’?”
"What is called the adornment of merit?
Good son, as for the adornment of wisdom, it refers to that which extends from the first stage through to the tenth stage; this is called the adornment of wisdom."
The adornment of merit refers to the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, which is not yet the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the adornment of wisdom refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"Adornment of merit refers to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the nine stages.

Furthermore, son of good family, the adornment of merit is conditioned, outflowing, subject to existence, characterized by retribution, obstructive, and impermanent; it is the dharma of ordinary worldlings."
The adornment of wisdom is unconditioned, untainted, non-existent, without karmic retribution, unimpeded, and eternally abiding.

Good son! You now possess these two adornments; therefore, you are able to inquire about this profound and wondrous meaning. I, too, possess these two adornments, and am thus able to answer this meaning.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these two kinds of adornment, then one should not ask about one kind or two kinds.”
Why does the World-Honored One say that one can answer regarding "one kind" or "two kinds"?
For what reason?
Because all dharmas possess neither one nor two kinds.
"One kind or two kinds— this is the mark of an ordinary person.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If a bodhisattva lacks the two kinds of adornment, they will be unable to know the one kind or the two kinds.
If a bodhisattva possesses the two adornments, they will be able to understand and know the one kind and the two kinds.
If it is said that all phenomena are neither one nor two, this meaning is not tenable. Why?
If there were no "one" or "two," how could one say that all phenomena are neither one nor two?
"Good son!
If one says that 'one' and 'two' are the marks of ordinary beings, then such a person is called a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes and is not an ordinary being. Why is this?
The first is called nirvana; the second is called birth-and-death.
Why is the first called nirvana?
Because it is eternal.
For what reason are these two called birth and death?
Because of craving and ignorance.
One who is eternally in nirvana does not possess the characteristics of an ordinary person.
Furthermore, the two states of birth and death are not the characteristics of ordinary beings.
For this reason, one who is endowed with both types of adornment is able to question and answer.
"Good son!..."
As for your question regarding what constitutes the Buddha-nature:
listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son!
Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called wisdom.
That which is called 'emptiness' does not perceive emptiness or non-emptiness."
The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness, permanence and impermanence, suffering and happiness, and self and non-self.
Emptiness refers to all of birth and death; non-emptiness refers to Great Nirvana.
This extends even to non-self, which is birth and death, while self refers to Great Nirvana.
To perceive all things as empty while not perceiving them as non-empty is not called the Middle Way;
likewise, to perceive all things as selfless while not perceiving a self is not called the Middle Way. That which is called the Middle Way is named Buddha-nature.
For this reason, the Buddha-nature is eternal and unchanging; yet because it is shrouded by ignorance, sentient beings are unable to perceive it.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive all things as empty, but do not perceive that which is non-empty;
they even perceive all things as selfless, but do not perceive the Self.

For this reason, one does not attain the emptiness of the ultimate truth; because one does not attain the emptiness of the ultimate truth, one does not practice the Middle Way; and because there is no Middle Way, one does not perceive the Buddha-nature.
Good son! There are three kinds of those who do not perceive the Middle Way:
first, those whose practice is exclusively pleasant; second, those whose practice is exclusively painful; and third, those whose practice is both painful and pleasant.

Regarding those who practice for the sake of meditative bliss: it refers to Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, out of compassion for all sentient beings, experience even while dwelling in the Avīci Hell a joy comparable to that of the Third Dhyāna.
Those who practice asceticism exclusively are called ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Those who practice both suffering and pleasure are called *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*; these *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* engage in both suffering and pleasure while maintaining the notion that they constitute the Middle Way.
For this reason, although the Buddha-nature exists, one is unable to see it.
Regarding your question as to why it is called "Buddha-nature," O son of good family: [The Buddha continued:
"O son of good family!"
Buddha-nature is the seed of the Middle Way within the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, good son!
There are three kinds of paths: namely, the inferior, the superior, and the intermediate.
The inferior path is to mistakenly perceive the impermanent Brahma-heaven as permanent.
The superior path is to mistakenly perceive the impermanent cycle of birth and death as permanent.
The Three Jewels are eternal, yet people erroneously calculate them to be impermanent.
Why are they called "supreme"?
Because they enable one to attain the most supreme *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The middle is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); it perceives impermanence as impermanent and permanence as permanent.
This emptiness of the ultimate truth is not termed "inferior. Why is this?
Because it is not attained by any ordinary person,
it is not called "superior. Why is this?
This is because it is neither low.
The path cultivated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is neither high nor low; for this reason, it is called the Middle Way.
"Furthermore, good son!
Regarding the fundamental limit of birth and death, there are two kinds:
first, ignorance; second, craving for existence."
Between these two extremes lies the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is called the Middle Way. Because this Middle Way can destroy birth and death, it is termed "middle."
For this reason, the Dharma of the Middle Way is called Buddha-nature; therefore, Buddha-nature is permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

Because sentient beings are unable to see it, they perceive it as impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; yet in reality, Buddha-nature is not impermanent, without bliss, without self, or without purity.
Good son! It is like a poor man who has a treasury of jewels in his house, yet he does not see it; because he does not see it, there is for him no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity.
A spiritual friend spoke to him, saying:
"Within your own home there is a treasury of gold and jewels; why then are you so impoverished and distressed, lacking permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"
He then employs skillful means to enable them to see it.
Because they have seen it, these people immediately attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Buddha-nature is also like this: sentient beings do not see it; because they do not see it, there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity.

There are spiritual friends—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—who, through the power of skillful means, provide various instructions and exhortations to enable sentient beings to behold them; by virtue of this vision, sentient beings immediately attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Furthermore, good son!
When sentient beings give rise to views, there are generally two kinds:
first, the view of permanence (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi); second, the view of annihilation (uccheda-dṛṣṭi)."
These two views are not called the Middle Way; rather, neither permanence nor annihilation is called the Middle Way.
This state of neither permanence nor annihilation is precisely the wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination; such contemplative wisdom is termed Buddha-nature.
Although those of the two vehicles contemplate causes and conditions, they still cannot be said to possess Buddha-nature.
Although Buddha-nature is eternal, because all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to perceive it.
Furthermore, they have not yet been able to cross the river of the twelve links of dependent origination, remaining like hares or horses. Why is this?
Because they have not seen the Buddha-nature.
"Good son!

This wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination is itself the seed of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination are called the Buddha-nature."
Good son! For example, the cucumber is called "the fever. Why is this?
Because they can act as the causal conditions for feverish diseases,
the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so,
O son of good family!
Buddha-nature has causes and the cause of causes; it has fruits and the fruit of fruits.

That which is the cause is the twelve links of dependent origination; that which is the cause of causes is wisdom. That which is the fruit is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that which is the fruit of fruits is the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa.

Good son! For example, ignorance is the cause and the various formations are the result; formations are the cause and consciousness is the result. By this principle, the essence of that ignorance is both the cause and the cause-of-the-cause, while consciousness is both the result and the result-of-the-result.
The Buddha-nature is also like this. Good son!

For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination do not emerge and do not perish; they are neither eternal nor discontinuous; they are neither one nor two; they neither come nor go; and they are neither cause nor effect.
Good son! That which is cause but not fruit is like the Buddha-nature; that which is fruit but not cause is like Great Nirvana;
that which is both cause and fruit is like the dharmas produced by the twelve links of dependent origination.
That which is neither cause nor effect is called Buddha-nature.
Because it is neither cause nor effect, it is eternal and unchanging.

For this reason, I have said in my sutras that the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination is extremely profound; it is beyond knowledge and vision, inconceivable, and is the realm of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, not something that can be attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
For what reason is it so profoundly deep?

The karmic actions of sentient beings neither persist nor cease, yet they obtain their retributive fruits; though perishing moment by moment, nothing is lost; though there is no agent, there is the performance of action; though there is no experiencer, there is the retributive fruit; and though the experiencer has perished, the fruit does not perish—it exists through the conjunction of that which lacks deliberative cognition.

Although all sentient beings act in accordance with the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not perceive or know them; because they do not perceive or know them, there is no beginning or end. Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see only the end but not the beginning, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see both the beginning and the end.
For this reason, the Buddhas clearly perceive the Buddha-nature. Good son!
All sentient beings are unable to see the twelve links of dependent origination; therefore, they revolve in saṃsāra.
Good son! Just as a silkworm makes a cocoon and is born and dies within it, so it is with all sentient beings.
Because they do not see the Buddha-nature, they create the karma of afflictions for themselves, wandering through birth and death like a bouncing ball.
"Good son! For this reason, I have said in various sūtras:
'If there is anyone who sees the twelve links of dependent origination, that person sees the Dharma.'"
One who sees the Dharma is one who sees the Buddha; the Buddha is none other than the Buddha-nature.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas take this as their nature.
“Good son! There are four kinds of wisdom for contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination:
first, the inferior; second, the middling; third, the superior; and fourth, the supreme.
Those of inferior wisdom who contemplate do not perceive the Buddha-nature; because they do not perceive it, they attain the path of the śrāvaka.
Those of middling wisdom who contemplate do not perceive the Buddha-nature; because they do not perceive it, they attain the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Those with superior wisdom who observe see indistinctly; because they see indistinctly, they abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Those with the most superior wisdom who observe see clearly; therefore, they attain the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination are called the Buddha-nature.
The Buddha-nature is the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); ultimate emptiness is called the Middle Way; the Middle Way is called the Buddha; and the Buddha is called Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if there is no difference between a Buddha and the Buddha-nature, for what purpose would all sentient beings cultivate the Path?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! As you have asked, this meaning is not so."
Although there is no difference between a Buddha and Buddha-nature, all sentient beings have not yet fully realized it.

Good son! For example, suppose there is a person who, with an evil mind, harms his mother; having committed the harm, he feels remorse. Although his three karmas are now virtuous, this person is still called a person of the hells.
Why is this? Because such a person is certain to fall into hell.
Although this person lacks the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of hell, they are nevertheless still designated as a "person of hell."
"Good son! For this reason, I have said in various sūtras:
'If one sees someone practicing wholesome deeds, it is called seeing devas and humans.'"
One who practices evil is said to see hell.
Why is this? Because they will certainly undergo retribution.
"Good son! Because all sentient beings will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Although all sentient beings truly do not yet possess the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, for this reason I have spoken these verses in this sutra:"
"‘What existed originally is now non-existent; what was non-existent originally is now existent.
That a dharma exists throughout the three periods of time—such a thing is impossible. Good son!..."
Existence is of three kinds:
first, future existence; second, present existence; and third, past existence.
That all sentient beings shall, in a future life, possess *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called the Buddha-nature.
All sentient beings currently possess afflictions and various fetters; therefore, in the present, they do not have the thirty-two marks or eighty minor characteristics.
All sentient beings, however, severed their afflictions in past lives; therefore, in the present, they are able to perceive the Buddha-nature.
For this reason, I have always proclaimed that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, even including those such as the icchantikas.
Although icchantikas lack wholesome dharmas, Buddha-nature is itself wholesome; because it will exist in the future, icchantikas also all possess Buddha-nature.
Why is this? Because those such as the icchantikas will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son!
For example, suppose there is a person who has milk and curd in their house, and someone asks them:
"Do you have ghee? They reply:
"I have curd, which is not yet butter; however, because it will certainly become butter through skillful means, I say that there is butter.
It is the same for sentient beings: they all possess the mind, and whoever possesses the mind will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I have always proclaimed that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
"Good son! There are two kinds of ultimate reality:
First is the ultimate of adornment, and second is the ultimate of consummation.
First is the ultimate of the mundane, and second is the ultimate of the supramundane.
The ultimate of adornment refers to the six pāramitās.

That which is ultimate and final is the One Vehicle attained by all sentient beings; this One Vehicle is called Buddha-nature. For this reason, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that all sentient beings possess the One Vehicle, yet because they are shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to see it.
"Good son!

Just as the inhabitants of this world cannot see the Northern Continent of Uttarakuru or the Heaven of the Thirty-three because they are concealed by the fruits of their retribution, so too is the Buddha-nature:
it is not seen by sentient beings because it is concealed by the various fetters."
Furthermore, good son!
Buddha-nature is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; its nature is like clarified butter (ghṛta), and it is the mother of all Buddhas.
By the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all Buddhas possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
All sentient beings possess the Śūraṅgama Samādhi as well; however, because they do not practice it, they are unable to see it, and for this reason, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! The Śūraṅgama Samādhi has five names: first, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
second, Prajñāpāramitā; third, the Vajra Samādhi; fourth, the Siṃhanāda Samādhi; and fifth, Buddha-nature.
According to its various functions, it receives different names in various contexts. Good son!

Just as a single samādhi receives various names—such as when dhyāna is called the "four dhyānas," the faculty is called the "faculty of concentration," the power is called the "power of concentration," awakening is called "concentration-awakening," and correctness is called "right concentration."
The eight awakenings of a great man are called the awakening of concentration; the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is likewise so. "Good son!
All sentient beings are fully endowed with three kinds of concentration, namely: superior, middling, and inferior."
The "superior" refers to the Buddha-nature; for this reason it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

The "middling" refers to all sentient beings being fully endowed with the first dhyāna, which they are able to cultivate when the necessary conditions are present, but cannot cultivate when such conditions are absent.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions:

first, the calamity of fire; second, the severing of the fetters of the desire realm. For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings fully possess the intermediate state of meditative concentration.

The "lower determination" refers to the mental factors (*caitasika*) among the ten universal mental states (*mahābhūmika*). For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings are fully endowed with the lower determination.

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; however, because it is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are unable to perceive it. Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) perceive the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), they do not know that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma. For this reason, it is said that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, though perceiving Buddha-nature, do so without clarity.
"Good son!

'Śūra' means 'all-encompassing ultimate,' and 'aṅga' means 'firm. That which is all-encompassing, ultimate, and has attained firmness is called Śūraṅgama. For this reason, it is said that the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is named Buddha-nature."
“Good son! At one time, while I was staying by the Nairañjanā River, I said to Ānanda:
‘I wish to bathe now; you should fetch my robe and the bathing powder.’”

Once I had entered the water, all the birds and creatures of the water and land came to observe me. At that time, five hundred brahmins also arrived at the riverbank; having reached my location, they said to one another:
"How has he come to possess a body of vajra?"
"If only Gautama would not speak of the view of annihilationism, I would accept his instruction on the method of fasting.
"Good son! At that time, by means of my knowledge of others' minds, I knew what this brahmin was thinking and said to him:"
"What do you mean when you say that I teach the view of annihilationism?
That brahmin replied,
"Gautama, you have previously stated in various sūtras that all sentient beings are entirely without a self."
Since it has been stated that there is no self, how can you say it is not the view of annihilationism?
If there is no self, who is it that observes the precepts,
and who is it that violates them?
The Buddha said:
"I do not say that all sentient beings are entirely without a self; I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Is this Buddha-nature not indeed the self?"
For this reason, I do not speak of the view of annihilationism.
Because all sentient beings do not see the Buddha-nature, they perceive it as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; it is in this sense that one speaks of the view of annihilationism.

At that time, when the various brahmins heard it said that the Buddha-nature is precisely the self, they immediately resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and subsequently left the household life to cultivate the path to enlightenment.
All birds and creatures of the water and land also gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi; having given rise to this mind, they immediately attained the relinquishment of their bodies. Good son!
This Buddha-nature is truly not the self; it is for the sake of sentient beings that it is spoken of as the self. "Good son!
Because the Tathāgata has specific causes and conditions, he speaks of non-self as the self; yet in reality there is no self. Although he speaks in this way, there is no falsehood."
"Good son!
Due to specific causes and conditions, I speak of the self as non-self, yet in reality there is a self.
For the sake of the world, although I speak of non-self, there is no falsehood."
The Buddha-nature is without self, yet the Tathāgata speaks of a self because it is eternal.
The Tathāgata is the self, yet he speaks of non-self because he has attained mastery.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, which is like that of the Vajrapāṇi, for what reason are all sentient beings unable to see it?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!

For example, although material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) possess distinctions such as blue, yellow, red, and white, as well as qualities and forms such as long and short, a blind person does not see them."
Although it is not seen, one cannot say that there is no quality of blue, yellow, red, white, long, or short. Why is this?
Because although the blind do not see it, those with eyes do.
The Buddha-nature is also like this: although all sentient beings cannot see it, because bodhisattvas in the ten stages see a small portion of it, the Tathāgata sees it in its entirety.
What the bodhisattvas in the ten stages perceive of the Buddha-nature is like seeing forms at night; what the Tathāgata perceives is like seeing forms by day.

Good son! It is like a blind person who cannot clearly perceive forms; when a skilled and virtuous physician treats his eyes, through the power of the medicine, he comes to see them with perfect clarity.

It is the same for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages: although they see the Buddha-nature, they cannot perceive it clearly; however, by the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they are able to attain clear perception.
“Good son!

If there is a person who perceives all dharmas as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure, yet perceives that which is not all dharmas as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure—such a person does not see the Buddha-nature.”
"All" refers to birth and death; "not-all" refers to the Triple Gem.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; they likewise perceive that which is not-all as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure. For this reason, they do not see the Buddha-nature.

Bodhisattvas of the ten stages perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; they do not perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity even partially within any phenomenon. For this reason, within ten parts, they perceive but one part.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; they do not perceive any phenomenon as permanent, blissful, self, or pure. For this reason, they behold the Buddha-nature as clearly as one gazes at an āmalaka fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
For this reason, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is called "ultimate. Good son!
It is like the new moon: although it cannot be seen, one cannot say that it does not exist.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; although all ordinary beings do not perceive it, one cannot say that they lack the Buddha-nature.
"Good son, the Buddha-nature consists of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness."

Because all sentient beings possess three kinds of destruction of afflictions, they are subsequently able to see those who are icchantikas; having destroyed the icchantika-nature, they are then able to attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
For this reason, I have always proclaimed that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
"Good son! The twelve links of dependent origination are shared equally by all sentient beings; they are both internal and external."
What are these twelve?
Afflictions of the past are called ignorance (*avidyā*); karmic actions of the past are called formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Within the present life, the initial entry into the womb is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The five stages of entering the womb, during which the four sense faculties are not yet complete, are called name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
When the four sense faculties are complete but it is not yet termed "contact" (sparśa), this is called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
Not yet distinguishing between suffering and pleasure is called contact (*sparśa*).
Being habituated to a single craving is called feeling (*vedanā*).
Cultivating intimacy with the five desires is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The internal and external pursuit of desire is called *upādāna* (clinging).
The arising of bodily, verbal, and mental karma for the sake of internal and external things is called *bhava* (becoming).
Consciousness in the present life is called future birth (*jāti*).
Present name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and sensation are called old age, sickness, death, and so forth in the future world.
This is called the twelve links of dependent origination. Good son!
Although all sentient beings possess these twelve links of dependent origination, some may not have them complete.
For instance, if one dies during the stage of the kalala, the twelve links will not be present.
From birth through to old age and death, one attains the full twelve [links].

Sentient beings in the form realm lack the three types of feeling, the three types of contact, and the three types of craving; yet, because they are free from old age and sickness, they may also be said to possess the full twelve.
Sentient beings in the formless realm lack form and even lack old age and sickness; yet they can still be said to be complete with the twelve [links].
Because these are necessarily attained, it is said that sentient beings equally possess the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Good son!
The Buddha-nature is also like this; because all sentient beings will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I therefore say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature."
“Good son! On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called ‘Patience. If a cow eats it, it produces clarified butter (ghṛta).

There is also another kind of grass; if a cow eats that, no clarified butter is produced. Yet, although no clarified butter is produced, one cannot say that the Snowy Mountains do not contain the grass of patience.”

The Buddha-nature is also like this: the Snowy Mountains are named the Tathāgata; the kṣānti-grass is named the Great Parinirvāṇa; and the other grasses are the twelve divisions of the scriptures. If sentient beings can listen to, receive, inquire about, and consult regarding the Mahāparinirvāṇa, they will then see the Buddha-nature.
Although it is not mentioned among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, one cannot say that the Buddha-nature does not exist.

Son of good family! The Buddha-nature is both form and non-form, neither form nor non-form; it is both characteristic and non-characteristic, neither characteristic nor non-characteristic; it is both one and non-one, neither one nor non-one; it is neither eternal nor annihilated, neither non-eternal nor non-annihilated; it is both existent and non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent; it is both exhausted and non-exhausted, neither exhausted nor non-exhausted; it is both cause and fruit, neither cause nor fruit; it is both meaning and non-meaning, neither meaning nor non-meaning; it is both letter and non-letter, neither letter nor non-letter.
What is form? It is the vajra-body. What is non-form?
The eighteen unique qualities are not material phenomena because they are not of the nature of form.
Why are they neither form nor non-form?
Because both form and non-form lack fixed characteristics.
What is meant by "marks"?
It refers to the thirty-two marks.
What is meant by "non-marks"?
Because the characteristics of all sentient beings do not manifest.
Why is it neither characteristic nor non-characteristic?
Because characteristics and non-characteristics are not fixed.
What is meant by "one"?
It is because all sentient beings are of the single vehicle (ekayāna).
What is meant by "not one"?
Because the three vehicles are taught.
Why is it neither one nor not one?
Because the dharmas are innumerable.
Why is it not eternal?
Because it is seen to arise from conditions.
Why is it not annihilated?
Because it is free from the view of annihilationism.
Why is it neither eternal nor annihilated?
Because it has no beginning or end.
What is meant by "existence"?
It is because all sentient beings possess it.
What is meant by "non-existence"?
Because it is seen through skillful means.
Why is it neither existent nor non-existent?
Because its nature is like space.
What is meant by "exhaustion"?
It is because one has attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
What is meant by "non-exhaustion"?
Because it is eternal.
Why is it neither exhausted nor non-exhausted?
Because all characteristics of exhaustion have been severed.
What is the cause?
It is because it is a revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*). What is the fruit?
Because the fruit is determinate.
Why is it neither cause nor fruit?
Because it is eternal.
What is meant by "meaning"?
It is because one is able to fully grasp all meanings without obstruction.
What is meant by "non-meaning"?
Because it is inexpressible.
Why is it neither meaning nor non-meaning?
Because it is ultimately empty.
What is meant by "syllable" (akṣara)?
It is because there is a name. What is meant by "non-syllable"?
Because names are nameless.
Why is it neither a word nor not a word?
Because all words have been severed.
Why is it neither suffering nor pleasure?
Because all sensations have been severed.
Why is it not-self?
Because they have not yet fully attained the eight masteries.
Why is it not "non-non-self"? Because it is eternal.
Why is it neither self nor non-self?
Because there is no agent and no recipient. Why is it empty?
Because it is emptiness in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Why is it not empty?
Because it is eternal.
What is meant by being neither empty nor non-empty?
It is because it can serve as the seed for wholesome dharmas. "Good son!..."
If there are those who can contemplate and understand such meanings as these from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, you should know that such persons see the Buddha-nature.
This Buddha-nature is inconceivable; it is the realm of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Good son!

The Buddha-nature is not the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; it is not that which was originally non-existent and now exists, nor is it that which already exists and then returns to non-existence. It is through virtuous causes and conditions that sentient beings perceive it."
For example, when black iron enters fire it becomes red, and upon emerging and cooling it returns to black; yet this blackness is neither internal nor external—it exists due to causes and conditions.
The Buddha-nature is also like this: when the fire of the afflictions of all sentient beings is extinguished, they are then able to hear and see it. Good son!

Just as when a seed has perished, a sprout is then able to arise, yet the nature of this sprout is neither internal nor external; even up to the flowers and fruits, it is likewise so—they exist by virtue of conditions.
"Good son! This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
Buddhahood is likewise; it is entirely accomplished through immeasurable and boundless merits."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One,
how many dharmas must a bodhisattva fully accomplish so that he may see the Buddha-nature, yet not see it with clarity?"
“How many dharmas do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, fulfill to attain clear vision?
“Good son, there are ten dharmas that a bodhisattva fully accomplishes; although such a one sees the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.”
What are the ten? First, fewness of desires;

second, contentment; third, tranquility; fourth, diligence; fifth, right mindfulness; sixth, right concentration; seventh, right wisdom; eighth, liberation; ninth, praising liberation; and tenth, teaching and transforming sentient beings through the Great Nirvana.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between having few desires and being content?”
“Good son! One who has few desires does not seek or take;
one who is content does not feel regret when obtaining little.”
One who has few desires has little that they wish for;
one who is content does not harbor anxiety or affliction in their mind regarding matters of the Dharma. Good son!
There are three kinds of desire:
first, evil desire; second, great desire; and third, the desire for desire.
As for evil desire, it is when a bhikṣu gives rise to covetousness in his mind:

"I wish to be the foremost leader among all the great assemblies, causing all the Sangha to follow behind me, and causing the fourfold assembly to all provide offerings, pay homage, praise, and show respect to me."
May I first preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly, causing all to believe and accept my words.
May kings, ministers, and elders all show me respect, so that I may obtain in great abundance robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and excellent dwellings.
To have desire for birth and death is called evil desire.
What is great desire?
It is when a bhikṣu gives rise to a mind of desire:
"How may I cause the fourfold assembly to know that I have attained the first stage up to the tenth stage,
and have realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"Shall I attain the fruit of arhatship down to the fruit of srotāpanna?
Shall I attain the four dhyānas down to the four types of unimpeded knowledge?
To seek these things for the sake of gain and honor is called great desire.

Regarding sensual desire: if there is a bhikṣu who desires to be born in the Brahma Heaven, the Māra Heaven, the Īśvara Heaven, or as a Cakravartin King; or who desires to attain mastery among kṣatriyas, householders, or brahmins.
To act for the sake of gain and offerings is called the desire for sensual pleasure.
To be unhindered by these three kinds of evil desires is called having few desires.
"Desire" refers to the twenty-five types of craving; to be free from these twenty-five cravings is called having few desires.
Not seeking after desired things in the future is called having few desires;
obtaining them without attachment is called contentment.
Not seeking honor and respect is called having few desires.
To not accumulate [possessions] is called contentment. "Good son!

There are those who have few desires but are not called contented; there are those who are contented but are not called having few desires; there are those who both have few desires and are contented; and there are those who are neither contented nor have few desires."
One who has few desires refers to a srotāpanna;
one who is contented refers to a pratyekabuddha;
one who has both few desires and is contented refers to an arhat.
Those who have few desires yet do not know contentment are what are called bodhisattvas.
Good son, there are furthermore two kinds of those who have few desires and know contentment:
The first is wholesome; the second is unwholesome.
The unwholesome refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); the wholesome refers to noble ones (*ārya*) and bodhisattvas.

Although all noble ones have attained the fruits of the Path, they do not proclaim them themselves. Because they do not proclaim them, their minds are free from affliction and resentment; this is called contentment.
Good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and desire to see the Buddha-nature therefore cultivate few desires and contentment.
"What is tranquility?
There are two kinds of tranquility:
first, tranquility of mind; second, tranquility of body."
One whose body is tranquil never commits the three kinds of evil through the body;
one whose mind is tranquil likewise does not commit the three kinds of evil through the mind.
This is what is called the tranquility of body and mind.
One whose body is tranquil never associates with the fourfold assembly nor participates in any of their affairs;
one whose mind is tranquil never cultivates greed, anger, or delusion.
This is what is called the tranquility of body and mind.
There may be a bhikṣu whose body is tranquil but whose mind is not tranquil;
there may be one whose mind is tranquil but whose body is not tranquil;
and there may be one whose both body and mind are tranquil.
Furthermore, there are those for whom both body and mind are not tranquil, and those for whom the body is tranquil but the mind is not.

For instance, there may be a bhikṣu who sits in meditation in a quiet place, far removed from the fourfold assembly, yet whose mind constantly accumulates greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called "the body is tranquil but the mind is not tranquil."

Regarding "the mind is tranquil while the body is not tranquil": there may be a bhikṣu who, though associating with the fourfold assembly, kings, and ministers, has severed greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called "the mind is tranquil while the body is not tranquil."
Those whose body and mind are tranquil refer to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
those whose body and mind are not tranquil refer to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Why is this?

Although the body and mind of ordinary persons may be tranquil, they are unable to deeply contemplate impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity. For this reason, ordinary persons are unable to bring stillness to the actions of their body, speech, and mind.
Those who are icchantikas, who have committed the four grave offenses, or who have committed the five heinous crimes—such persons cannot be said to possess tranquility of body and mind.
What, then, is diligence?
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, to distance himself from all unwholesome deeds, and to cultivate all wholesome deeds, this is called diligence.
This practitioner of diligent effort binds their mindfulness to six objects, namely: the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, generosity, and the devas; this is called right mindfulness.
The samādhi attained by one who possesses right mindfulness is called right concentration.
The contemplation of all phenomena as being like empty space by one who possesses right concentration is called right wisdom.
One who possesses right wisdom is far removed from all afflictions and fetters; this is called liberation.
One who has attained liberation extols liberation for the sake of all sentient beings, declaring that this liberation is eternal and unchanging; this is called praising liberation.
Liberation is itself the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa; Nirvāṇa is the extinguishing of the fires of the various fetters of affliction.
Furthermore, Nirvāṇa is called a dwelling place.
Why is this? Because it can ward off the evil winds and rains of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* is called the refuge; why is this?
Because it is able to transcend all fears.
Furthermore, nirvana is called an island. Why is this?
Because it cannot be swept away by the four violent rivers.
What are these four? First, the flood of desire; second, the flood of existence; third, the flood of views; and fourth, the flood of ignorance. For this reason, nirvāṇa is called an island.
Furthermore, nirvāṇa is called the ultimate refuge.
Why? Because it enables one to attain all ultimate bliss.
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fulfill and possess these ten dharmas, although they see the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
"Furthermore, good son!
Those who have left the household life have four kinds of illnesses; for this reason, they do not attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
What are these four illnesses?
They are the four evil desires:
