First is the desire for clothing, second is the desire for food, third is the desire for bedding, and fourth is the desire for existence;

these are called the four evil desires. There are four excellent medicines for the diseases of those who have left the household life that can cure these ailments: namely, wearing rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) can cure a bhikṣu’s evil desire for clothing; begging for alms can destroy the evil desire for food; dwelling under trees can destroy the evil desire for bedding; and tranquility of body and mind can destroy a bhikṣu’s evil desire for existence.
To eliminate these four ailments by means of these four medicines is called the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*).
Such a noble practice is termed having few desires and being content.
There are four kinds of bliss for one who is tranquil.
What are these four?
First, the joy of renunciation; second, the joy of tranquility; third, the joy of eternal cessation; and fourth, the ultimate joy.
Attaining these four joys is called tranquility.
Because one possesses the four kinds of diligence, it is called diligence;
because one possesses the four foundations of mindfulness, it is called right mindfulness;
and because one possesses the four dhyānas, it is called right concentration.
Because one perceives the reality of the Four Noble Truths, it is called "Right Wisdom";
because one eternally severs all fetters of affliction, it is called "Liberation";
and because one censures and explains the faults of all afflictions, it is called "Praising Liberation."
"Good son!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in and fulfill these ten dharmas, although they see the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
Furthermore, good son!"
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having heard this sutra, draws near to and cultivates it while remaining far removed from all worldly affairs, this is called having few desires.
Having already left the household life, they do not give rise to a mind of regret; this is called contentment.
Having attained contentment, one dwells near secluded places, far removed from clamor and bustle; this is called tranquility.
Those who lack contentment do not delight in seclusion, whereas those who possess contentment always rejoice in empty stillness. In such a place of empty stillness, they constantly reflect:
"The entire world claims that I have attained the fruits of the śramaṇa path, yet I have in fact not yet attained them. How could I now deceive and delude others?"
Having formed this thought, one diligently cultivates the fruits of the śramaṇa path; this is called diligence.
To draw near to and cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa is called right mindfulness.
To act in accordance with the divine conduct is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
To abide securely in this concentration with right view and right knowledge is called right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*).
One who possesses right view and knowledge is able to attain detachment from the fetters and bonds of affliction; this is called liberation (*vimukti*).
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, for the sake of sentient beings, extol and praise nirvana; this is called praising liberation.
Good son, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell securely in these ten dharmas, although they see the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
"Furthermore, noble son! As for 'having few desires':

if there is a bhikṣu who dwells in a secluded place, sitting upright without lying down; or who dwells at the foot of a tree, or among burial mounds, or in the open air; who sits upon whatever grassy ground is available; who eats by begging for alms, being content with whatever he obtains;
or who eats in a single sitting, not exceeding one meal;..."
To maintain only the three robes— the rag robe and the woolen robe—
is called having few desires.
Having practiced these matters, for the mind to feel no regret is called contentment.
Cultivating the samādhi of emptiness is called tranquility.
Having attained the four fruits, one’s mind does not cease its pursuit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called diligence.
To bind the mind in contemplation that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging is called right mindfulness.
To cultivate the eight liberations is called right concentration.
To attain the four analytical knowledges is called right wisdom.
To be far removed from the seven outflows is called liberation.
To extol nirvana as being devoid of the ten characteristics is called praising liberation.
The ten characteristics are: birth, old age, sickness, death, form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and impermanence.
To be far removed from these ten characteristics is called Great Nirvāṇa. Good son!
This is what is meant by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, while dwelling securely in and fully possessing these ten dharmas, perceives the Buddha-nature yet does not see it clearly.
"Furthermore, good son!
Out of excessive desire, they associate with kings, ministers, elders, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, falsely claiming, 'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat.
For the sake of gain and offerings, they engage in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and even the acts of defecation and urination."
If one sees a donor, one still practices respect and engages them with welcoming speech.
To destroy evil desires is called "having few desires.
Although one may not yet have destroyed all fetters and afflictions, being able to act in accordance with the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata is called "contentment."
"Good son!
These two dharmas are the proximate causes and conditions for mindfulness and concentration; they are constantly praised by teachers, patriarchs, and fellow students.
I, too, have always extolled and lauded these two dharmas throughout various sūtras."
If one can be fully endowed with these two dharmas, then one will draw near to the gate of Great Nirvāṇa and the five kinds of bliss;
this is called tranquility. To firmly uphold the precepts is called diligence.
To possess a sense of shame and remorse is called right mindfulness.
Not perceiving the characteristics of the mind is called right concentration.
Not seeking the nature, marks, causes, or conditions of all phenomena is called right wisdom.
Because there are no marks, afflictions are severed; this is called liberation.
To extol such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is called praising liberation.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abiding in ten dharmas; although he sees the Buddha-nature, he does not see it clearly. Good son!"
As you have said, by what eye do Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature yet not clearly?
And by what eye do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see the Buddha-nature and see it clearly?
"Good son! Because it is seen with the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus), it is not clearly perceived;
because it is seen with the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus), it is clearly perceived."
Because of practicing for the sake of bodhi, one does not see clearly;
because there is no practice, one sees clearly.
Although one sees while abiding in the ten stages (bhūmis), it is not clear.
Because it abides and yet does not abide, it is seen with perfect clarity.
Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the cause of wisdom, they see without full clarity;
because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have severed both cause and effect, their vision is perfectly clear.
Complete awakening is called buddha-nature; because bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet attained complete awakening, they see it but do not perceive it clearly.
Good son! There are two kinds of seeing:
first, seeing with the eyes; second, seeing through hearing.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive the Buddha-nature with their own eyes, as if looking at an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of their hand.

Because the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes hear of and see the Buddha-nature, they do not perceive it clearly; these Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes can only know for themselves that they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet they cannot know that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
“Good son! Furthermore, there is ‘seeing with the eyes’: the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature with their eyes.
Furthermore, there is ‘seeing by hearing’: all sentient beings, up to those in the ninth stage, hear and see the Buddha-nature.”
If a bodhisattva hears that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature but does not give rise to faith in their heart, this is not called "hearing and seeing.

Good son! If there are good men or good women who wish to see the Tathāgata, they should cultivate the twelve divisions of the scriptures, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, and explaining them.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Since all sentient beings are unable to know the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s mind, how should they contemplate it so that they may come to know it?”
“Good son! All sentient beings truly cannot know the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata. If they wish to observe and thereby come to know them, there are two causes and conditions:
first, seeing with the eyes; second, seeing through hearing.”
If one perceives all the bodily actions of the Tathāgata, one should know that this is the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes.
If one contemplates all the verbal actions of the Tathāgata, one should know that this is the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing through hearing."
If one sees that in physical appearance there is no being among all sentient beings who is his equal, one should know that this is the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes.
If one hears that his voice is subtle, wondrous, and most supreme, unlike any voice possessed by sentient beings, one should know that this is the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing through hearing."
If one sees the supernatural powers manifested by the Tathāgata, is it for the sake of sentient beings, or for the sake of gain and offerings?
If it is for the sake of sentient beings and not for the sake of gain and offerings, one should know that this is indeed the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes.
Furthermore, when observing the Tathāgata using his knowledge of others' minds to contemplate sentient beings, does he speak for the sake of gain and offerings?
Does he preach for the sake of sentient beings?
If he preaches for sentient beings and not for the sake of gain or sustenance, you should know that he is indeed the Tathāgata; this is what is meant by "hearing and seeing.
How could the Tathāgata receive such a body?
For what reason does one receive a body?
For whom does one receive a body?
This is called seeing with the eyes.
If one contemplates the Tathāgata, how does he preach the Dharma?
For what purpose does he preach the Dharma?
For whom does he preach the Dharma?
This is called "seeing through hearing.
If one does not become angry when subjected to the evil deeds of the body, know that this person is a Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes.
If one does not become resentful when subjected to the evil deeds of speech, know that this person is a Tathāgata; this is called "seeing through hearing."

If one sees the Bodhisattva at the time of his birth, taking seven steps in each of the ten directions; the great generals of the spirits, Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra, holding banners and canopies; the shaking of immeasurable and boundless worlds; the golden light shining brilliantly, filling all of space; the Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda bathing the Bodhisattva’s body with their supernormal powers; the forms of various devas receiving him with prostrations; and the seer Asita joining his palms in reverent respect.

In the prime of his youth, he renounced desire as if discarding mucus or spittle; he was not deluded by worldly pleasures and left the household life to cultivate the Way, delighting in quietude and seclusion. To shatter false views, he practiced austerities for six years; toward all sentient beings he was impartial and without duality, his mind constantly abiding in meditative concentration without the slightest distraction. His body was adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and wherever he traveled, even desolate ruins became level. His robes remained four inches away from his body without falling, and when walking, he gazed straight ahead without looking to the left or right. Regarding the food he consumed, no item was ever left uneaten, and at the places where he sat or rose, the grass remained undisturbed.
To teach the Dharma for the sake of taming sentient beings, his mind is free from pride; this is called "seeing with the eyes.
Furthermore, upon hearing that the Bodhisattva had taken seven steps and proclaimed these words:
"This present body of mine is the very last," [this is also seeing with the eyes].
The seer Asita joined his palms and said:
"Great King, you should know that Prince Siddhārtha will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he will never remain at home as a wheel-turning monarch."
Why is this? Because his marks are clearly manifest.
The marks of a wheel-turning sage king are not so clearly manifest.
"Prince Siddhārtha’s physical marks are radiant and prominent; therefore, he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having witnessed old age, sickness, and death, he further spoke these words:

"All sentient beings are most pitiable, for they are constantly pursued by such birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet they fail to perceive this and perpetually dwell in suffering; I shall bring an end to it."
From the five-attainment seer Ārāḍa, he received the meditative attainment of non-perception; having mastered it, he later declared it to be incorrect.
From the seer Udraka, he received the meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having mastered it, he declared that it was not *nirvāṇa*, but rather a phenomenon of saṃsāra.
Having practiced austerities for six years without attaining anything, he spoke these words:

"The cultivation of these austerities is empty and yields no result. If this were the truth, I should have attained it; because it is false and illusory, I have gained nothing. This is called a perverted artifice, not the Right Path."
After he had attained enlightenment, Brahmā entreated him, saying:
"I pray that the Tathāgata will extensively open the gate of ambrosia for sentient beings and preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā King!
All sentient beings are constantly obscured and covered by afflictions; they are unable to receive my words of the True Dharma.
Brahmā King spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are of three kinds: namely, those of sharp faculties, those of middling faculties, and those of dull faculties.
Those of sharp faculties are able to receive [the teaching]; we only pray that you will speak for them.”
The Buddha said:
"Brahmā King!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"I shall now open the gate of ambrosia for all sentient beings.
Thereupon, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the True Dharma and proclaimed the Middle Way.
All sentient beings do not sever their fetters, yet it is not that they cannot sever them; they neither sever nor do not sever, and for this reason it is called the Middle Way.
They do not deliver sentient beings, yet it is not that they cannot deliver them; this is called the Middle Way.
Neither that all things are established nor that they are not established—this is called the Middle Way.
In whatever one speaks, not claiming oneself to be the teacher and not claiming others to be disciples—this is called the Middle Way.
To speak not for the sake of profit, yet not failing to attain the fruit—this is called the Middle Way.
It is right speech, truthful speech, timely speech, and genuine speech; words are never uttered in vain, being subtle and supreme.
Such dharmas as these are called "hearing and seeing. Good son!
The characteristics of the Tathāgata’s mind are in truth invisible.
"If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to see the Tathāgata, they should rely upon these two kinds of causes and conditions.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 27; *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 28.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven, Part Two: The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As previously stated, the simile of the mango fruit illustrates four kinds of persons.
There is one who acts with subtlety, yet whose mind is not upright or sincere.”
There are those whose minds are subtle but whose conduct is not upright and true;
there are those whose minds are subtle and whose conduct is also upright and true;
and there are those whose minds are not subtle and whose conduct is not upright and true.
"How can these first two kinds be known?
As the Buddha has said, although one relies upon these two, they cannot be known.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
the analogy of the mango fruit regarding these two kinds of persons is indeed difficult to discern.”
Because they are difficult to know, I have said in my sūtras: "One should live together with them;
if one does not know them while living together, one should dwell with them for a long time;
if one still does not know them after dwelling for a long time, one should discern them through wisdom."
If wisdom does not know, one should observe deeply;
through such observation, one then knows those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them. Good son!
Endowed with these four matters—dwelling together, living for a long time, wisdom, and observation—one can then know whether one maintains the precepts or violates them. Good son!
There are two kinds of precepts, and the observance of precepts is likewise twofold:
first, ultimate precepts; second, non-ultimate precepts.

If there is someone who receives and maintains the prohibitive precepts due to causes and conditions, the wise should observe whether this person’s observance of the precepts is for the sake of gain and offerings.
Is it the ultimate upholding? Good son!
The precepts of the Tathāgata have no causes or conditions; therefore, they are named the ultimate precepts.

For this reason, although a bodhisattva may be harmed by evil sentient beings, they do not give rise to anger or resentment; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to have achieved ultimate and consummate upholding of the precepts.
"Good son!
Once in the past, I was dwelling together with Śāriputra and five hundred disciples in the great city of Campā in the kingdom of Magadha."

At that time, there was a hunter pursuing a pigeon. Terrified, the pigeon reached the shadow of Śāriputra and continued to tremble like a plantain tree; however, upon entering my shadow, its body and mind became peaceful and secure, and its fear was dispelled.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, maintains the precepts to the ultimate degree; even his shadow possesses such power. Good son!
If one does not perfect the precepts, one cannot even attain the stage of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, let alone attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, for the sake of gain and offerings; second, for the sake of the True Dharma.

If one upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of gain and offerings, you should know that such precepts do not perceive the Buddha-nature or the Tathāgata. Although one hears the names of the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata, it cannot yet be called 'hearing and seeing.'"

If one upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of the True Dharma, you should know that these precepts enable one to see the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes" and is also called "seeing through hearing."
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, those whose roots are deep and difficult to uproot; second, those whose roots are shallow and easily moved.
If one can cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, this is called having deep roots that are difficult to uproot.
If one does not cultivate these three samādhis, even if one practices them for the sake of the twenty-five states of existence, this is called having shallow roots that are easily shaken.
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, for oneself; second, for sentient beings.
Regarding those who act for the sake of sentient beings, they are able to perceive the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of people who uphold the precepts:
first, those who naturally uphold them by their own nature; second, those who require instruction and admonition from others.

If, after having received the precepts, one does not lose or violate them for the first time throughout immeasurable lifetimes, yet encounters an evil land, meets with evil associates, or lives during an evil time or age, hearing false and evil teachings and dwelling together with those of wrong views.

At that time, although there was no formal method for receiving the precepts, they practiced and maintained them as originally intended without any transgression; this is called "maintaining by nature.

If one encounters a teacher or a sangha and receives the precepts through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the ritual of fourfold proclamation), then even after having received the precepts, one must rely on the instruction and admonition of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), various teachers, fellow students, and virtuous friends to understand what to advance toward and what to refrain from, and to listen to and preach the Dharma while maintaining all proper dignified deportment; this is called "requiring the instructions of others."
"Good son!
One whose nature is capable of upholding [the precepts] sees the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata with their eyes; this is also called 'seeing through hearing.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts:"
There are two types of precepts: first, the śrāvaka precepts; second, the bodhisattva precepts.
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, these are called the bodhisattva precepts.
If one contemplates white bones and even attains the fruit of Arhatship, this is called the precept of the Śrāvaka.
If there are those who uphold the precepts of the Śrāvaka, it should be known that such persons do not see the Buddha-nature nor the Tathāgata.

If there are those who receive and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts, you should know that such persons shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and will be able to perceive the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, and Nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions does one receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, it is because the mind feels no regret.”
Why does one not feel regret?
Because one experiences pleasure.
Why does one experience pleasure?
It is for the sake of detachment. Why detachment?
It is for the sake of peace and security.
Why is there peace and security?
It is for the sake of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Why is there meditative concentration?
It is for the sake of knowing and seeing reality.
Why is it for the sake of knowing and seeing reality?
It is for the sake of seeing the various faults and afflictions of birth and death.
For what reason does one perceive the faults and afflictions of birth and death?
It is for the sake of the mind being free from craving and attachment.
For what reason is the mind free from craving and attachment?
It is for the sake of attaining liberation.
Why is it for the sake of attaining liberation?
It is for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, great parinirvāṇa.
For what reason is it for the sake of attaining Great Parinirvāṇa?
It is for the sake of attaining the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For what reason is it for the sake of attaining permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
It is for the sake of attaining that which is neither born nor extinguished.
Why is it for the sake of attaining that which is neither born nor extinguished?
It is for the sake of perceiving the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, by their very nature, Bodhisattvas are able to maintain ultimate pure precepts. Good son!
Although a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts does not make a vow to seek a mind free from regret, a mind free from regret is naturally attained.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Although they do not seek pleasure, nor do they dwell in the peace and security of true knowledge and vision, yet seeing the faults of birth and death, their minds do not become attached.
Liberation, nirvana, permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as non-arising and non-ceasing, are naturally attained upon seeing the Buddha-nature.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!

If one attains the fruit of non-regret because of upholding the precepts, and attains the fruit of nirvāṇa because of liberation, then the precepts would be without cause, and nirvāṇa would be without fruit.”
If precepts were without cause, they would be termed eternal.
Since Nirvana has a cause, it is impermanent.
If that were so, then Nirvana would be something that originally did not exist but now exists.
If something was originally non-existent and now exists, it is impermanent, just like lighting a lamp.
If nirvāṇa were likewise so, how could it be designated as self, bliss, and purity?
The Buddha said,
"Good man! Excellent, excellent!"
Because you have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past, you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such profound meanings.
Son of good family!
You have not lost your original resolve, which is why you ask in this way.
I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the city of Vārāṇasī, named Śubhavyūha.

At that time, for three hundred million years, that Buddha expounded such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra as this. I and you were both present at that assembly, and I questioned that Buddha regarding this matter.
At that time, for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata entered into samādhi and did not yet answer this matter.
"Excellent, Great Being!
You are indeed able to recall such a past event."
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall speak for you.
The precepts also have a cause, namely, listening to the True Dharma.
Listening to the True Dharma also has a cause, namely, associating with virtuous friends.
Associating with virtuous friends also has its cause, which is faith.
Faith itself also has its cause; there are two kinds of causes:
first, listening to the Dharma; second, contemplating its meaning.
"Good son!
Faith is caused by hearing the Dharma, and hearing the Dharma is caused by faith.
These two dharmas are both causes and causes of causes, and both fruits and fruits of fruits."
Good son! It is like a Nirgrantha standing with his feet apart and holding up a jar; they are mutually cause and effect and cannot be separated from one another. Good son!
Just as ignorance conditions volitional formations and volitional formations condition ignorance,
so too this ignorance and these volitional formations are both causes and the cause of causes, as well as effects and the effect of effects.

Up to birth as the condition for old age and death, and old age and death as the condition for birth: this birth and old age and death are both causes and causes of causes, and both fruits and fruits of fruits.
Good son! Birth can give rise to dharmas, but it cannot give rise to itself. Because it does not give rise to itself, it arises by means of "the birth of birth" (*jāti-jāti*).
The "birth of birth" cannot give rise to itself; it further relies upon "birth" in order to arise.
Therefore, the two births are both causes and causes of causes, and both fruits and fruits of fruits.
Son of good family,
faith and listening to the Dharma are likewise so.
“Good son! This which is the fruit and not the cause is called Great Nirvāṇa.
For what reason is it called the fruit?
Because it is the supreme fruit, the fruit of the śramaṇa, the fruit of the brāhmaṇa, because it severs birth and death, and because it destroys the afflictions, it is therefore called a "fruit."
Because it is reviled by all afflictions (*kleśa*), Nirvāṇa is called the fruit; afflictions, therefore, are called the "transgressions of transgressions.
Good son! Nirvāṇa has no cause, yet its essence is the fruit.

Why is this? Because it is without arising or ceasing; because it is without anything produced; because it is not conditioned; because it is unconditioned; because it is eternal and immutable; because it has no location; and because it has no beginning or end.
Good son! If nirvana had a cause, it could not be called nirvana. "Nir" (槃) signifies cause;
"vāṇa" (般涅) signifies non-existence. Because there is no cause, it is called nirvana.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"As the Buddha has taught that nirvāṇa is without cause, this meaning is not so.
If one says it is non-existent, it would accord with six meanings:"
First, it is called "non-existent" because it is ultimately non-existent, such as when all phenomena are said to be without self (*anātman*) and without what belongs to a self (*anātmīya*).
Second, it is called "non-existent" because it is non-existent at certain times, such as when people of the world say that a river or pond has no water, or that there are no sun or moon.
Third, because it is minimal, it is called "non-existent," just as people in the world say that food with little salt is "saltless," or that sweet juice with little sweetness is "sweetness-less."

Fourth, because there is no receiving, it is called "non-existent. For example, a *caṇḍāla* cannot receive or uphold the Dharma of a *brāhmaṇa*; therefore, he is called one who is "without *brāhmaṇa*-hood."

Fifth, because they embrace unwholesome dharmas, they are said to be "non-existent. As people of the world say, those who embrace unwholesome dharmas are not called śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; therefore, it is said that there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Sixth, because it is not opposed [to its counterpart], it is called "non-existent"; for example, the absence of white is called black, and the absence of clarity is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
“World-Honored One!
Nirvāṇa is also like this; because at times it is without cause, it is called nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Regarding these six meanings you have now explained, why do you not cite that which is ultimately non-existent as a metaphor for nirvana,
but instead take that which is non-existent at certain times?
"Good son!
The essence of nirvāṇa is ultimately without cause, just like non-self and that which belongs to no self.
Good son!"
Worldly dharmas and nirvana are ultimately not counterparts; therefore, these six matters cannot serve as analogies. Good son!

All dharmas are entirely without self, yet this nirvana truly possesses a self. For this reason, nirvana has no cause, yet its essence is the fruit. That which is the cause but not the fruit is called Buddha-nature.
Because it is not produced by causes, this cause is not a fruit.
Since it is not a fruit of the śramaṇa, it is called "not a fruit.
Why is it called a cause?
Because it is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*). Good son,
there are two kinds of causes:
First is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), and second is the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
That which can produce a phenomenon is called the productive cause;
because a lamp can reveal objects, it is called the revealing cause.
The various fetters of affliction are called the productive cause;
the parents of sentient beings are called the revealing cause.
For example, seeds and the like are called the productive cause.
Earth, water, manure, and so forth are called the "revealing causes" (vijñapti-hetu).
Furthermore, there are "generative causes" (janana-hetu), namely the six pāramitās and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there is a revealing cause, namely, the Buddha-nature and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there is a revealing cause, namely, the six pāramitās and the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there is the producing cause, namely the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there is the revealing cause, namely the Eightfold Noble Path and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, there is a cause for birth, namely, faith and the six pāramitās.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, regarding the seeing of the Tathāgata and the Buddha-nature, what is the meaning of this? World-Honored One, the body of the Tathāgata has no marks;

it is neither long nor short, neither white nor black, it has no location, it does not abide within the three realms, it is not a conditioned phenomenon, and it is not cognizable by visual consciousness. How, then, can it be seen?
"The Buddha-nature is also like this.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
The Buddha-body is of two kinds:
first, the eternal; second, the impermanent.
The impermanent is that which is manifested through skillful means for the purpose of delivering all sentient beings; this is what is called "seeing with the eyes."
That which is permanent is the liberation-body of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One; it is called "seen with the eyes" and also called "seen by hearing.
Buddha-nature likewise has two aspects:
first, that which is visible; second, that which is invisible.
Those who can be seen are the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Those who cannot be seen are all sentient beings.
As for "seeing with the eyes," this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, seeing with their own eyes the Buddha-nature possessed by all sentient beings.
Regarding those who hear and see: all sentient beings and bodhisattvas of the ninth stage hear that there is buddha-nature, the body of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds:
first, it is form; second, it is non-form.
Form is the liberation of the Tathāgata; that which is non-form is because the Tathāgata has forever severed all marks of form.
There are two kinds of Buddha-nature:
first, that which is form; second, that which is non-form.

"Form" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; "non-form" refers to ordinary beings up to bodhisattvas of the ten stages. Because bodhisattvas of the ten stages do not see it with complete clarity, it is called "non-form."
Good son! The Buddha-nature is further of two kinds:
first, that which is form; second, that which is non-form.
"Form" refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; "non-form" refers to all sentient beings.
"Form" is that which is seen with the eyes; "non-form" is that which is seen through hearing.

“Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external; although it is neither internal nor external, it is not lost or destroyed, and for this reason it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One!”
As the Buddha has taught, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, just as there is curd within milk.
The Buddha-nature of the Vajrapāṇi and the Buddhas is like pure *sarpis* (clarified butter). Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
I do not say that there is curd within milk; rather, because curd is produced from milk, I say that there is curd."
“World-Honored One!
All phenomena that arise each have their own proper season. “Good son!

At the time of milk, there is no curd, nor is there fresh butter, clarified butter, or the finest cream; all sentient beings likewise call it milk, and for this reason I say that there is no curd within the milk.
If it were truly existent, why could it not have two names? For example, because a person possesses two skills, they are called both a goldsmith and an ironworker. It is also like this:

when there is curd, there is no milk, nor fresh butter, nor clarified butter, nor the essence of ghee (amṛta); yet sentient beings still call it "curd," rather than calling it milk, or fresh butter, or clarified butter, or the essence of ghee. It is just so.
Good son! There are two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause (hetu-hetu); second, the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu).
The direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*) is like milk producing curd; the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is like yeast, warmth, and so forth.
Because it arises from milk, it is said that the nature of curd exists within the milk.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If milk lacks the nature of curd, and that [nature] is likewise absent in the horn, why does it not arise from the horn?”
“Good son! Even from a horn, curd is produced. Why is this?
I also say that there are two types of causal conditions:
first, fermentation; second, warmth.
Because the nature of curdled milk is warm, it can also produce yogurt.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If curd could be produced from horns, why would those seeking curd seek milk instead of taking the horns?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! For this reason, I speak of the direct cause and the conditional cause."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"If it were the case that the nature of curd did not originally exist within milk and only comes to be now,
then since the āmalaka tree originally did not exist within milk, why does it not grow there?"
"Because both are non-existent. "Good son!
Milk can also produce the *āmra* tree."
If one were to water it with milk, it would grow five feet in a single night; for this reason, I speak of two causes.
Good son, if all phenomena were produced from a single cause, one could raise the objection: "Why is it that the mango tree cannot be produced from within milk?"
Good son! It is like the four great elements, which act as the causes and conditions for all material forms; yet these forms are each distinct, their differences being manifold.
For this reason, the *āmra* tree does not grow from within milk.
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of causes: the direct cause and the contributory cause.
Of these, to which cause does the buddha-nature of sentient beings belong?”
“Good son! The Buddha-nature of sentient beings also has two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause (dharmatā-hetu); second, the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu).”
"The direct cause refers to all sentient beings; the conditional cause refers to the six pāramitās.
Siṃhanāda said, "World-Honored One!"
I now know with certainty that milk possesses the nature of curd. Why is this?
I observe that in the world, those who seek curd take only milk and never water; therefore, one should know that milk possesses the nature of curd.
“Good son! As you have asked, this meaning is not so. Why is that?
"All sentient beings, desiring to see their own reflections, immediately take up a blade.
The Lion’s Roar said,
"World-Honored One!"
For this reason, milk possesses the nature of curd.
If a sword did not possess the reflection of a face, why would one take up the sword?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If this face were definitively present within this blade, why would it appear distorted—appearing long when held vertically and wide when held horizontally?
If it were one’s own face, why would it appear elongated?”
If it were another's face, how could it be called one's own facial reflection?
If one sees another's face because of one's own face, why does one not see the reflections of donkeys and horses?
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
Because the eye-light reaches that object, one sees the length of the face.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! This light of the eyes does not actually reach that place."
Why is this? Because those near and far can see [the object] simultaneously, yet they do not see any objects situated between them. Good son!
If light reaches that place and can be seen, then all sentient beings would see the fire; why then is it not burned?
It is like a person seeing a white object from afar—they should not give rise to doubt as to whether it is a crane.
Is it a banner?
Is it a person?
Or is it a tree?
If light reaches [the object], how is it that one can see things within crystal or fish and stones in a deep pool?
If one sees without [light] reaching [the object], why is it that one can see things within crystal but cannot see the forms beyond a wall?
Therefore, if one says that the eye-light reaches the object and sees the elder, this meaning is not so. Good son!
As you have said, if there is curd within milk, why is it that the person who sells milk takes only the price for the milk and does not demand the value of the curd?
When one sells a weanling horse, one takes only the price for the horse and does not demand payment for the colt.
Good son! Because people in the world have no offspring, they seek to marry a wife.
If a woman is pregnant, one must not say she is a girl.
If one were to say she is a girl because she possesses the nature of a child, and thus she ought to be betrothed, this reasoning is incorrect.
Why is this? If there is the nature of a son, there should also be a grandson; if there is a grandson, he is [the same as] a brother. Why is this?
Because they are born from the same womb.
Therefore, I say that a woman lacks the nature of producing a son.
If there were the nature of curd within her milk, why would the five flavors not be perceived all at once?

If there were already within the seed of a tree the five-fathom substance of a nyagrodha tree, why is it that the differences in the color and form of its sprouts, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are not seen all at once?

Good son! The color of milk differs at different times, its taste differs, and its result differs; even up to the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta), it is likewise so. How, then, can one say that milk possesses the nature of curd?
“Good son! It is like a person who intends to consume ghee tomorrow but already finds it foul today.
To say that the nature of curd definitely exists within milk is just like this.”
Good son! It is like a person who possesses a pen, paper, and ink, and combines them to form characters.
Yet within this paper there were originally no characters; because they were originally non-existent, they are produced through the conjunction of conditions.
If they existed inherently from the beginning, what need would there be for various conditions?
For example, when blue and yellow combine to produce green, one should know that these two originally lack the nature of being conditions [for one another];
if they existed inherently from the beginning, why would they need to be combined?
Good son! It is like sentient beings who obtain life because of food, yet within this food there is truly no life.
If life were inherently present, then before it was eaten, the food itself should be life.
"Good son!
All dharmas fundamentally have no intrinsic nature. For this reason, I speak these verses:
'Originally non-existent, now existent; Originally existent, now non-existent.'"
"It is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time. "Good son!
All dharmas arise because of causes and conditions, and they cease because of causes and conditions."
"Good son!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature within, then all sentient beings should possess the Buddha-body just as I do now.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither broken nor destroyed; it cannot be pulled or seized, and it is neither bound nor fettered."
Just as there is space within all sentient beings—indeed, all sentient beings possess space—because it is without obstruction, each does not perceive for themselves that they possess this space.

If sentient beings were without space, there would be no coming or going, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, nor would there be birth or growth. For this reason, I have stated in my sutras that all sentient beings possess the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*); this space-element is what is called "space."
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: bodhisattvas of the ten stages can see but a small portion of it, as if looking at a diamond jewel.
Good son! The buddha-nature of sentient beings is the realm of all Buddhas; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Because all sentient beings do not see the Buddha-nature, they are constantly bound by afflictions and wander through birth and death.
Because they see the Buddha-nature, they cannot be bound by the fetters of affliction; they are liberated from birth and death and attain Great Nirvana.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings possess the nature of Buddhahood, just as milk possesses the nature of curd.”
If milk lacked the nature of curd, why would the Buddha have taught that there are two kinds of causes: first, the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*), and second, the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*)?
As for the contributory cause, these are: first, fermentation; second, warmth.
"Because space has no intrinsic nature, it has no conditions or causes.
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
"If the nature of curd were definitively present within milk, why would it require conditions and causes?
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
Because there is an existent nature, one must rely on conditions as causes. Why is this?
It is because one wishes to clearly perceive; thus, the condition as cause is precisely the revealing cause.
World-Honored One!
It is like various objects already existing in the darkness; one uses a lamp to illuminate them for the sake of seeing them.
If they did not exist from the beginning, what would the lamp illuminate?
Just as a pot exists within clay, it requires such conditions as a person, water, a wheel, a rope, and a staff to serve as its completing causes (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*).
Likewise, the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree requires earth, water, and fertilizer to serve as its completing causes.
The warmth of the fermenting agent within milk is likewise so; it must function as a "revealing cause" (*vyañjaka-hetu*).

Therefore, although the nature [of curd] exists beforehand, it must depend upon a revealing cause before it can be perceived. For this reason, one knows with certainty that the nature of curd exists beforehand within the milk.
“Good son! If there were a fixed nature of curd within milk, it would be a revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*).
If it were a revealing cause, why would it need to be revealed further?”
Good son! If this is a cause of illumination and its nature is to illuminate, it should constantly illuminate itself;
if it cannot illuminate itself, how can it illuminate others?
If it is claimed that the revealing cause (jñāpaka-hetu) possesses two natures—
first, self-revealing, and second, revealing others— this meaning is not tenable. Why is this so?
If the "revealing cause" (*vyakti-hetu*) is a single dharma, how can there be two?
If there were two, then milk should also be twofold.
If there are no two characteristics within the milk, why should the revealing cause alone possess two?
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As worldly people say, ‘I am with eight people,’ so too is the cause of realization (pariniṣpattihetu): it realizes itself and realizes others.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If the revealing cause were such as you describe, it would not be a revealing cause."
Why is this? Because that which counts can count its own form and the forms of others; thus, one may speak of "eight.

Yet this nature of form lacks the characteristic of cognition (*vijñapti*) within itself. Since it lacks the characteristic of cognition, it must rely upon the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*) to then count its own and others' [forms].
Therefore, the cause of illumination cannot illuminate itself, nor can it illuminate others. Good son,
if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what reason do they cultivate immeasurable merits?
If one says that cultivation is the cause of manifestation (*vyañjana-hetu*), it is already the same as [the case of] curd turning sour.
If one says that the fruit definitely exists within the cause, then morality, concentration, and wisdom would have no growth.
I observe that worldly people originally possess no precepts, meditative concentration, or wisdom; only after receiving them from a teacher do these qualities gradually increase.

If you claim that the teacher’s instruction is the "revealing cause" (了因), then at the very moment the teacher gives the instruction, the recipient would still not yet possess precepts, concentration, or wisdom.
"If it were something already understood, it would have been understood as non-existent; how then could one understand precepts, concentration, and wisdom so that they may increase?
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, "World-Honored One!"

"If there were no revealing cause, how could one say that there is milk and there is curd? "Good son! There are generally three ways in which people in the world respond to difficult questions: [1] responding by means of a different principle; [2] responding by means of a different meaning; and [3] responding by means of a different time. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "What is meant by 'responding by means of a different principle'? It is when a person asks about a certain principle, yet the respondent answers by means of another principle. For example, if someone asks, 'Is the self eternal? the respondent answers, 'The self is not eternal. Why? Because it is subject to birth and death. Furthermore, if someone asks, 'Does the Tathāgata exist after death? the respondent answers, 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death. Why? Because he has entered parinirvāṇa. This is called responding by means of a different principle. What is meant by 'responding by means of a different meaning'? It is when a person asks about a certain meaning, yet the respondent answers by means of another meaning. For example, if someone asks, 'Does the Tathāgata exist after death? the respondent answers, 'The Tathāgata exists after death. Why? Because he possesses the power of the Dharma-body. Furthermore, if someone asks, 'Is the self eternal? the respondent answers, 'The self is eternal. Why? Because it is free from birth and death. This is called responding by means of a different meaning. What is meant by 'responding by means of a different time'? It is when a person asks about a certain time, yet the respondent answers by referring to another time. For example, if someone asks, 'Is the self eternal? the respondent answers, 'If you have attained the fruit of Arhatship, then the self is eternal. Why? Because one is free from birth and death. Furthermore, if someone asks, 'Does the Tathāgata exist after death? the respondent answers, 'If one has not yet attained the fruit of Arhatship, then the Tathāgata exists after death. Why? Because he has not yet entered parinirvāṇa. This is called responding by means of a different time. Good son! If there were no revealing cause, how could one say that there is milk and there is curd? First is the answer by turning the question back: as previously stated, for what reason is it called "precept"?
It is because there is no regret, and so forth, up to the attainment of great *nirvāṇa*.
Second is the answer by silence: for example, when a certain Brahmin came and asked me, "Am I eternal? [I remained silent].
At that time, I remained silent.
Third is the answer by way of doubt: as in this sutra, if there were two causes of manifestation, why could there not be two [manifestations] within milk?
"Good son! I shall now answer you in turn.

Just as people of the world say that one who possesses milk or curd does so because they will certainly obtain them, and are therefore said to 'have' milk or 'have' curd; the Buddha-nature is likewise: sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature because they will see it in the future."
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has spoken, this meaning is not so.”
The past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; how, then, can they be called "existent"?
If you claim that what is "to come" is called "existent," this meaning is not tenable.
It is like people in the world who, seeing that they have no children, say, "I have no children."
“If all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature, why do you say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

The past is said to exist; for example, when planting an orange tree, the sprout arises as the seed perishes. The sprout is already sweet, and this remains so until the fruit is produced; once it has ripened, it becomes sour.
"Good son!

This sour taste does not exist within the seed, the sprout, or even the developing fruit; rather, as it matures according to its original nature, the color, form, and characteristics give rise to the sour taste. Although this sour taste was originally non-existent and now exists, even though it was originally non-existent and now exists, it does not arise without depending on its original cause."
In this way, although the primary substance has passed away, it is still designated as "existent.
For this reason, the past is called existent.
Furthermore, why is the future also called existent?
For example, suppose there is a person planting sesame seeds, and someone asks him,
"For what purpose are you planting these? He replies:
"There is oil.
In reality, there was no oil yet; only after the sesame has ripened, the seeds are harvested, parched and steamed, then pounded and pressed, can oil finally be extracted.
One should know that this person is not speaking falsely.
For this reason, it is called "existence in the future.
Furthermore, why is it also called "existence in the past"?
"Good son!
It is like a person who, in private and out of sight, reviles the king; though years pass by, the king eventually hears of it.
Having heard it, he immediately asks:"
"Why do you revile me?
He replied, "Great King."
I do not revile. Why?
Because that which reviles has already ceased.
The king said, "When one reviles another, both 'I' and the body exist; how can you say they have been extinguished?
For this reason, he lost his life.
"Good son! These two do not truly exist, yet the fruit is not extinguished; this is called 'existence in the past.
Furthermore, what is called 'existence in the future'?"
For example, suppose a person goes to a potter and asks, "Do you have any jars?
and the potter replies, "I have jars.
Although that potter does not actually have any jars yet, because he possesses clay, he says, "I have jars. You should know that this person is not speaking falsely.
The presence of curd within milk, and the Buddha-nature within sentient beings, is also like this.
Those who wish to see the Buddha-nature should observe its timing, season, form, and color; therefore, when I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, it is truly not false.
Siṃhanāda said:
"If all sentient beings lack buddha-nature, how can they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Because of the true cause, sentient beings are enabled to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What is this true cause?
It is what is called buddha-nature.
World-Honored One!
If there were no nyagrodha tree for the nyagrodha seed, why would it be called a "nyagrodha seed" and not a "khadira seed"?
World-Honored One!
Just as one of the Gautama clan cannot be called of the Atiya clan, and one of the Atiya clan likewise cannot be called of the Gautama clan;
so it is with the son of Nyagrodha—he cannot be called the son of Khadirani, nor can the son of Khadirani be called the son of Nyagrodha.
Just as the World-Honored One could not abandon his Gautama lineage, so too is the buddha-nature of sentient beings; for this reason, one should know that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If one says that the nyagrodha tree exists within the seed, this meaning is not so."
If it exists, why is it not seen?
Good son! Just as with worldly objects, there are cases where they cannot be perceived due to the presence of causes and conditions.
What is meant by "causes and conditions"?
It refers to that which is distant and invisible, such as the tracks of birds in the sky;
and that which is near and invisible, such as the eyelashes of a person.
It is not seen because it is destroyed, like one whose sense organs have failed;
it is not seen because of distracted thoughts, like a mind that is not single-minded;
it is not seen because it is subtle, like minute particles of dust.
One does not see because of obstruction, as with stars behind clouds;
one does not see because of multiplicity, as with hemp in a heap of rice;
and one does not see because of similarity, as with beans in a heap of beans.
The nyagrodha tree is not like these eight kinds of causes and conditions; if it were such, why would it not be seen?
If you say it is not seen because of subtle obstructions, this argument is not tenable.
Why is this? Because the characteristics of a tree are coarse.
If one says its nature is subtle, how could it grow?
If you say that it cannot be seen because of obstructions, then it should never be seen.
Originally there was no coarse characteristic, yet now a coarse one is seen.

One should know that this coarseness originally lacks its own nature; originally there was no nature of seeing, yet now it can be seen. One should know that this seeing, too, originally lacks its own nature.
"It is the same with you: originally there was no tree, yet now there is one; what fault could there be in this?
Siṃhanāda said, "As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of causes:"
First is the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*), and second is the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*).
Because the *nyagrodha* seed uses earth, water, and manure as its revealing causes, it causes that which is subtle to become coarse.
The Buddha said,
"Good son! If it were originally existent, what need would there be for a revealing cause?"
If there is no inherent nature from the beginning, what is it that is realized through realization?
If a coarse characteristic was originally absent within a nyagrodha tree, yet arises through the power of a realizing cause, why does it not likewise arise as a khadira tree?
Because both are non-existent.
Son of good family!
If the subtle were not visible, then the coarse should be visible.
For example, a single atom is invisible, yet when many atoms combine, they should become visible.
In the same way, the coarse [form] within the seed should be visible. Why is this?

Within this [seed] already exist sprouts, stems, flowers, and fruits; within each fruit there are immeasurable seeds, and within each seed there are immeasurable trees. Therefore, it is called "gross. Because this grossness exists, it ought to be visible.
"Good son!

If the *nyagrodha* seed possessed the nature of a *nyagrodha* tree at the time it was produced, then since we see with our own eyes that this seed can be burned by fire, such a nature of being burned should also have existed inherently from the beginning.
If it had existed inherently from the beginning, the tree would not have been able to grow."
If all phenomena inherently possessed arising and ceasing, why would arising necessarily precede ceasing rather than occurring simultaneously?
For this reason, one should know that they lack intrinsic nature.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If the nyagrodha seed originally lacks the nature of a tree yet produces a tree, why does this seed not produce oil?”
"Because both are non-existent.
"Good son! In this same way, oil can also be produced from the seeds; although it lacks an inherent nature, it exists by virtue of causes and conditions."
The Lion’s Roar asked,
“Why is it not called sesame oil?
[The Buddha replied,] “Good son!
It is not because of the sesame seeds. Good son!
Just as fire arises from the condition of fire and water arises from the condition of water, although both arise from conditions, they cannot exist within one another.
The seed of the nyagrodha tree and sesame oil are also like this: although both arise from conditions, they do not produce one another.
The nature of the nyagrodha seed is to cure cold disorders.
As for sesame oil, its nature is to treat wind disorders. Good son!
It is like sugarcane, which arises due to causes and conditions.
“Crystallized honey and black honey, though originating from the same source, differ in their appearance; crystallized honey treats heat, while black honey treats cold.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One!”

If milk lacked the nature of curd, sesame seeds lacked the nature of oil, the *nyagrodha* seed lacked the nature of a tree, and clay lacked the nature of a jar, such that all sentient beings lacked the Buddha-nature—contrary to what the Buddha previously taught that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and therefore shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—then this principle would be untenable.
Why is this? Because humans and devas lack an inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

Because they lack an inherent nature, a human can become a deva and a deva can become a human; this occurs through the causal conditions of karma (*karmahetu-pratyaya*), not by way of an inherent nature.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by virtue of karmic causes and conditions.
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what reason do those such as the icchantikas sever all roots of goodness and fall into hell?
If the bodhicitta were the buddha-nature, then those such as the icchantikas should not be able to sever it;
if it can be severed, how can one say that the buddha-nature is eternal?
If it were impermanent, it would not be called Buddha-nature.
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why is it called "the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment"?
Why speak of those who are *vibhāṣa* (regressing) and those who are *avivarta* (non-regressing)?
"World-Honored One, you should know that those who are *apratiprasrabdha* (irreversible) possess no Buddha-nature.

World-Honored One, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva single-mindedly inclines toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, possessing great kindness and great compassion, sees the faults and afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, and the defilements; contemplates Great Nirvāṇa as being free from the various faults of birth, old age, death, and afflictions; and has faith in the Triple Gem and the retribution of karmic actions while upholding the prohibitive precepts—such dharmas as these are called 'Buddha-nature.'"
If the Buddha-nature existed apart from these dharmas, why would it require these dharmas to serve as causes and conditions?
World-Honored One!

For example, milk does not depend on external conditions to inevitably become curd, whereas fresh butter is not like that; it must await causes and conditions, namely human effort, a water vessel, and a churning rope.
Sentient beings are also like this: those who possess the Buddha-nature should attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi apart from causes and conditions.

If it were definitively existent, for what reason would practitioners, upon seeing the sufferings of the three evil realms and the experiences of birth, old age, sickness, and death, give rise to a regressive mind?
Furthermore, it would not be necessary to cultivate the six pāramitās; one should immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as milk becomes curd without depending on external conditions.
Nevertheless, it is not without relying on the six pāramitās that one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, one should know that sentient beings all lack buddha-nature.
As the Buddha previously stated that the Sangha Jewel is permanent, if it is permanent, then it is not impermanent;
if it is not impermanent, how can it attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"World-Honored One, if the Saṃgha were permanent, why do you further say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature? World-Honored One,

if sentient beings have had neither the bodhicitta nor the mind for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the very beginning, but only acquire them later, then the Buddha-nature of sentient beings should likewise be such— that it was originally non-existent and only comes into being later."
"For this reason, all sentient beings would have no Buddha-nature.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
You have long understood the meaning of buddha-nature; it is for the sake of sentient beings that you ask such a question.
All sentient beings truly possess buddha-nature."
As for your statement that if sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they should not have those who first resolve to attain enlightenment— good son,
the mind is not Buddha-nature. Why is this?
The mind is impermanent, whereas the Buddha-nature is eternal.
As for your question, "Why is there a regressing mind?
in truth, there is no such thing as a regressing mind.
If the mind were subject to regression, one would ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is because attainment is delayed that it is termed "regression.
This bodhicitta, in reality, is not the Buddha-nature.
Why is this? Because those such as the icchantikas sever their roots of goodness and fall into hell.
If the bodhicitta were itself the Buddha-nature, then these icchantikas could not be called icchantikas.
The bodhicitta, moreover, cannot be called impermanent.
Therefore, it is certain that the bodhicitta is truly not the Buddha-nature. "Good son!
As for your statement that if sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they should not depend on conditions—just as milk becomes curd—that is not the case.
Why? If one says that five conditions produce clarified butter (*sarpis*), you should know that Buddha-nature is likewise so.

For example, among various stones there may be gold, silver, copper, and iron; though they all derive from the four great elements and share the same name and substance, that which is produced from each is distinct.
It must depend upon various conditions—the merit of sentient beings, the furnace, and human effort—before it can be produced; therefore, one should know that there was originally no nature of gold.

The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not called "Buddha" [in itself]; rather, through the harmony and combination of various meritorious causes and conditions, one perceives the Buddha-nature and subsequently attains Buddhahood.
As for your question, "If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not see it?"—
this argument is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because the various causes and conditions have not yet converged,
son of good family,
for this reason I speak of two kinds of causes: the direct cause and the conditional cause.
The direct cause is called the Buddha-nature; the conditional cause is the arousal of the bodhicitta.
By means of these two causes and conditions, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as gold is extracted from stone.
“Good son! As for your statement that the Saṃgha is eternal while all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature, good son!
‘Saṃgha’ means harmony; there are two kinds of harmony:”
The first is worldly harmony; the second is ultimate harmony.
Worldly harmony refers to the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas; ultimate harmony refers to the Saṃgha of Bodhisattvas.
The worldly Sangha is impermanent, whereas the Buddha-nature is permanent.
Just as the Buddha-nature is permanent, so too is the Dharma-Sangha.

Furthermore, there is a Sangha that refers to the harmony of the Dharma; this harmony of the Dharma refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Since the twelve divisions of the scriptures are permanent, I say that the Dharma and the Sangha are permanent.

Good son! The Sangha is named "harmony" (saṃgha). Harmony is named the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda). Within the twelve links of dependent origination there is also the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu), and the twelve links of dependent origination are eternal.
The Buddha-nature is also like this; therefore, I say that the Saṃgha possesses Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, "Saṃgha" refers to the harmony of all Buddhas; for this reason, I say that the Saṃgha possesses Buddha-nature.
“Good son! As for what you said—that if sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why is it that some regress while others do not?
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain this for you.
Noble son,
there are thirteen dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regresses.
What are the thirteen?
First, lack of faith in the mind;
second, the absence of a [resolute] mind.
Third is doubt;
fourth is stinginess regarding one's body and wealth;
fifth is the arising of great fear toward nirvāṇa, thinking, "How can I cause sentient beings to undergo eternal extinction?"
Sixth, the mind is unable to endure;
seventh, the mind is not pliant;
eighth, there is sorrow and affliction.
Ninth, lack of joy;
tenth, negligence;
eleventh, disparaging oneself.
Twelfth, they perceive their own afflictions as being incapable of being destroyed;
thirteenth, they take no pleasure in advancing toward the dharmas of bodhi. Good son!
These are called the thirteen dharmas that cause bodhisattvas to regress from enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that destroy the bodhicitta. What are these six?

First, stinginess regarding the Dharma; second, giving rise to unwholesome thoughts toward sentient beings; third, associating with evil friends; fourth, lacking diligent effort; fifth, being conceited and arrogant; sixth, engaging in worldly occupations.
These six dharmas are able to destroy the bodhicitta. Good son!

There are those who hear that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are the teachers of gods and humans, the most supreme and peerless among all sentient beings, surpassing the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.

With the Dharma-eye clear and bright, seeing all phenomena without obstruction, he is able to deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of suffering; having heard this, he immediately makes a great vow:
"If there is such a person as this in the world, may I also attain it."
By these causes and conditions, they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or else they resolve their minds upon *bodhicitta* through being instructed by others.
Or, having heard that a bodhisattva practices austerities for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) before finally attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they reflect upon hearing this:
"I am currently unable to endure such austerities; how could I possibly attain it?"
"For this reason, there is regression.
Good son, furthermore,
there are five dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta."

What are these five? First, taking pleasure in leaving the household life as a non-Buddhist renunciant; second, failing to cultivate a heart of great compassion; third, delighting in seeking out the faults and evils of Dharma masters; fourth, constantly taking pleasure in remaining within the cycle of birth and death; and fifth, having no joy in receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, or explaining the twelve divisions of the scriptures. These are called the five dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there are two things that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta. What are these two?
First, craving and delighting in the five desires; second, being unable to revere and respect the Triple Gem.
For these and other such reasons, one may regress from the bodhicitta.
What, then, is called the non-regressing mind?

It is when someone hears that the Buddha can deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and that by practicing naturally without consulting a teacher, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"If the path to enlightenment can be attained, I shall cultivate it and surely achieve it.
For this reason, I resolve upon the mind of bodhicitta; whatever merit I have performed, whether much or little, I dedicate entirely toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, making this vow:

'May I always be able to draw near to the Buddhas and their disciples, always hear the profound Dharma, possess all five sensory faculties intact, and never lose this mind even when encountering suffering or hardship.'"
Furthermore, I vow that all Buddhas and their disciples shall always give rise to a heart of joy toward me and be endowed with the five roots of goodness.

If sentient beings were to hack at my body, sever my hands and feet, or cut off my head, eyes, limbs, and joints, I would instead conceive great compassion for those people and feel deep personal rejoicing. Such individuals serve as causes and conditions for my growth toward Bodhi; if it were not for them, by what means could I achieve Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
He further made this vow:

"May I never obtain a body that is rootless, possesses both genders, or is female; may I not be subject to others, nor encounter an evil master, nor be under the rule of an evil king, nor be born in an evil land. If I obtain a fine body of noble lineage, may I possess abundant wealth and treasures without becoming arrogant. May I always hear the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and receive, uphold, recite, transcribe, and explain them."
If I preach anything for the sake of sentient beings, may those who receive it have respectful faith and no doubt, never giving rise to ill will toward me.
It would be better to hear little but understand much of the meaning and flavor, than to wish to hear much while failing to comprehend the meaning.

May you take the mind as your teacher, rather than being taught by the mind; may your actions of body, speech, and mind not associate with evil; may you be able to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings; may your physical discipline, mind, and wisdom remain unmoving like mountains; and desiring to uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma, may you give rise to no stinginess regarding your body, life, or wealth.

One does not perform meritorious deeds with impure things; one sustains oneself through right livelihood with a mind free from deceit and flattery; one constantly bears in mind those who have shown kindness and repays even small favors with great gratitude.

One skillfully masters all worldly arts and crafts, is proficient in the various dialects and customs of sentient beings, recites and transcribes the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and never gives rise to a mind of indolence or laziness.
If there are sentient beings who do not delight in hearing [the Dharma], he employs skillful means to guide and receive them, causing them to take pleasure in hearing it.

His speech is always gentle, and his mouth never utters evil; he can bring harmony to those who are divided and cause those with sorrow and fear to be free from sorrow and fear. In an age of famine, he causes abundance to be attained; in an age of disease, he acts as a great King of Physicians. Possessing sovereign mastery over the wealth required for medicines and treatments, he ensures that all who are ill are completely healed.
During the kalpa of weapons, one shall possess great power to sever their violence so that none remain;

one shall be able to sever the various fears of sentient beings—namely, those of death, imprisonment, being beaten or struck, water and fire, kings and thieves, poverty, violation of precepts, ill repute, and the evil realms—and all such fears shall be utterly severed.

May I give rise to deep reverence for my parents, teachers, and elders; may I conceive a heart of great compassion toward those who harbor enmity or hatred; may I constantly cultivate the six recollections, the gate of the samādhi of emptiness, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, and the observation of arising and ceasing; may I practice the mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation, the celestial conduct, the Brahma-conduct, and the noble conduct; may I attain the Vajra-samādhi and the Śūraṅgama-samādhi; and even in places where the Triple Gem is absent, may I spontaneously attain a heart of tranquility.
When your body and mind undergo great suffering, do not lose the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta; do not give rise to contentment with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

Where the Three Jewels do not exist, they always go forth as monastics within the teachings of non-Buddhist paths; yet, in order to destroy false views, they do not practice those paths, thereby attaining mastery over phenomena and mastery over the mind.

Having clearly perceived conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), I am terrified of the fruits of the paths of the two vehicles (*śrāvakayāna* and *pratyekabuddhayāna*), just as one who cherishes life fears the loss of that body; for the sake of sentient beings, I delight in dwelling within the three evil realms.

Just as sentient beings who delight in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven would, for the sake of each and every person, undergo the sufferings of hell for immeasurable eons without their minds giving rise to regret;
and seeing others obtain benefit, they do not give rise to envy, but always produce joy as if they themselves had obtained pleasure.

If one encounters the Triple Gem, one should make offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, dwellings, medicine, lamps, flowers and incense, music, banners and canopies, and the seven precious jewels.
If one receives the Buddha’s precepts, one shall uphold them with firm resolve, never giving rise to thoughts of violation.

Upon hearing of the difficult practices and ascetic austerities of a bodhisattva, one’s heart shall rejoice without regret. One shall personally recognize the events of past lives and never again commit karma born of greed, hatred, or delusion.
"One does not accumulate causes and conditions for the sake of karmic retribution, nor does one give rise to greedy attachment toward present pleasures.
"Good son! If there are those who can make such a vow, they are called bodhisattvas who never fall back or lose the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta)."

They are also called donors; they are able to see the Tathāgata and clearly understand the Buddha-nature; they are able to discipline sentient beings and deliver them from birth and death; they are well able to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma; and they are able to attain the fulfillment of the six pāramitās.
"Good son! For this reason, the mind of non-retrogression is not called Buddha-nature. Good son!"
You must not, on account of having a regressive mind, claim that all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature.

It is like two people who both hear that in another land there is a mountain of seven treasures, with clear springs whose water is sweet and delicious; those who can reach it will forever end their poverty, and those who drink its water will increase their lifespan by ten thousand years. However, the road is remote and filled with many perils and obstacles.
Then those two persons both desired to go together; one person prepared various provisions for the journey, while the other went empty-handed, carrying nothing at all.
As they proceeded forward, they encountered a man on the road who was carrying a great abundance of treasures and was fully equipped with the seven precious gems.
