The two men then stepped forward and asked:
"Virtuous one!
Is it true that in that land there are mountains made of the seven treasures?"
The man replied: "It is indeed true and not false;

I have already obtained the treasure and drunk its water. My only concern is that the road is perilous and beset by many bandits, and it is a wasteland of salt and thorns, lacking both water and grass. Of those who go, there are ten million, but very few reach their destination."
Having heard this, one person immediately felt regret and spoke these words:
"The road is so vast and distant, with many hardships; those who go are countless, yet those who reach their destination are few. How could I possibly arrive there?"
"My current property is sufficient for my own support; if I were to travel this road, I might lose my life. If my life is not preserved, where is my long life?
Another person said again, "If there is someone who can pass through, I too can pass through."
If one reaches the goal, one will obtain what is wished for, gather precious treasures, and drink sweet water;
if one does not reach it, death shall be the appointed end.

At that time, of the two men, one regretted it and turned back, while the other proceeded forward to that mountain. There he obtained much wealth and treasure, drank the water as he had wished, and taking his entire haul with him, returned to his dwelling to support his parents and provide for his kinsmen.
At that time, the one who had regretted his departure and returned saw this occurrence and felt a burning heat arise within his heart:
"Since he has already gone and returned, why do I remain here?
He immediately prepared himself and set out upon the road.

The mountain of seven treasures is a metaphor for the Great Nirvana; the sweet water is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature; the two men are metaphors for two bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds on the Way; the perilous and evil road is a metaphor for birth and death; the person encountered is a metaphor for the Buddha, the World-Honored One; the presence of thieves is a metaphor for the four māras; the salty wasteland and thorns are metaphors for all afflictions (*kleśa*); the absence of water and grass is a metaphor for not cultivating the path to Bodhi; the man who returns is a metaphor for a regressive bodhisattva; and the one who goes straight ahead is a metaphor for a non-regressive bodhisattva.
"Good son!

The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is eternally abiding and unchanging, just like that perilous path; one cannot say that because people regret and turn back, the path itself becomes impermanent. The Buddha-nature is also like this."
"Noble son! Within the path to enlightenment, there is ultimately no such thing as falling back. Noble son!"

Just as the one who had previously repented saw his former companion return with treasures, possessing power and autonomy, providing for his parents, supporting his kinsmen, and enjoying great peace and happiness.

Having seen this, a feverish heat arose within his heart; he immediately arrayed himself once more and returned by that path, disregarding his own body and life and enduring all manner of hardships, until he finally reached those mountains of the seven treasures. It was the same for the Bodhisattvas who had regressed.
"Good son!

All sentient beings will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, I have stated in my sūtras that all sentient beings—even those who commit the five heinous crimes, violate the four grave prohibitions, or are icchantikas—possess Buddha-nature."
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
In what way do bodhisattvas have regression or non-regression?”

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, they are called ‘non-retrogressive,’ called a ‘bodhisattva-mahāsattva,’ called ‘immovable,’ called ‘one who has compassion for all sentient beings,’ called ‘superior to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,’ and called ‘an avaivartika.’”
"Good son!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the precepts without wavering and his mind of giving does not shift, abiding securely in truthful speech like Mount Sumeru, by these karmic conditions he attains the mark of level soles, like the bottom of a casket."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva provides offerings and support with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma to their parents, preceptors, teachers, and even down to animals, through these karmic conditions, they attain the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet."
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva refrains from killing and stealing, and always gives rise to joy toward their parents and teachers, by these karmic conditions they attain three marks:
first, fingers that are slender and long; second, heels that are long; and third, a body that is square and straight."
These three marks arise from the same karmic conditions.

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings, by virtue of this karmic condition, he obtains webbed fingers like those of a white goose king."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when their parents, teachers, or elders are suffering from illness, washes and wipes them with their own hands, holds them, and massages them, through these karmic conditions, they attain softness of hand and foot."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the precepts, hears the Dharma, and practices giving without weariness, by these karmic conditions, he attains well-proportioned ankles and calves, with the hairs of his body all pointing upward."
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva listens to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and expounds the true teaching, by these karmic conditions, he obtains calves like those of a deer king.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not give rise to a harmful mind toward sentient beings, is moderate in food and drink, always delights in giving, and provides medicine for the sick, by these karmic conditions, his body becomes perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree.”
His hands reach below his knees when he stands, he has a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head (uṣṇīṣa), and his cranial mark is invisible.

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva provides protection for those who are terrified and gives clothing to those who are naked and barefoot, by these karmic conditions he attains the mark of the concealed organ (kośagatavastiguhyatā)."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva associates with the wise, stays far away from fools, delights in skillful inquiry and response, and sweeps and repairs the roads—by virtue of these karmic conditions, his skin becomes fine and soft, and the hairs on his body curl to the right."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly bestows upon others clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, and lamps, by virtue of these karmic conditions, they will obtain a golden-colored body that is perpetually radiant."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing generosity, is able to relinquish their most cherished possessions without stinginess, and does not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit, by virtue of these karmic conditions, they attain the mark of the seven parts of the body being full."
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when practicing giving, does not give rise to doubt in his mind, by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains a soft and supple voice.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and uses it for giving, by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains full clavicles, an upper body like that of a lion, and arms and elbows that are well-proportioned and slender."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva stays far away from divisive speech, harsh words, and a mind of malice, by reason of these karmic conditions, they obtain forty teeth that are white, pure, even, and closely set.”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates great loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, by virtue of these karmic conditions, they attain the mark of two tusks.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly makes this vow:
'Should anyone come seeking something, I shall give it to them according to their wishes.'"
"By these karmic conditions, he obtains cheeks like those of a lion.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva provides whatever food and drink sentient beings require, by these karmic conditions, he obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors."
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva personally cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action and also transforms others through them, by these karmic conditions, they obtain a broad and long tongue.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not speak of others' shortcomings and does not slander the true Dharma, by these karmic conditions, they obtain the Brahma-voice."
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, upon seeing those who are hostile or hateful, gives rise to a mind of joy, through these karmic conditions, he obtains eyelashes of deep blue color.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not conceal the virtues of others but praises their goodness, through these karmic conditions, he obtains the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.”
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the karmic causes and conditions for these thirty-two marks, they shall attain the non-retrogressive mind of enlightenment.”
“Good son, all sentient beings are inconceivable; the realm of the Buddhas, karmic fruition, and Buddha-nature are likewise inconceivable.”
Why is this? These four dharmas are all eternal; because they are eternal, they are inconceivable.
All sentient beings are shrouded and obstructed by afflictions, and for this reason, they are called "eternal."
Because it severs the afflictions of eternalism and nihilism, it is called impermanence.
If one were to say that all sentient beings are permanent, for what reason would they cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to sever all suffering?
If all sufferings are severed, they are termed impermanent; the bliss thus received is termed permanent.
Therefore, I say that all sentient beings, being shrouded and obstructed by afflictions, do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they do not attain nirvana.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 28. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 29.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
In the eleventh chapter, "The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda," part three,
Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, all dharmas have two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause (hetu-hetu), and second, the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu).
By means of these two causes, there should be neither bondage nor liberation.
These five aggregates arise and perish from moment to moment. Given such arising and perishing, who is there to be bound or liberated?
World-Honored One!

Based on these five aggregates, subsequent five aggregates arise; these aggregates perish of their own accord and do not pass over to those subsequent aggregates. Although they do not pass over to them, they are nonetheless able to give rise to those subsequent aggregates.
Just as a sprout arises from a seed, yet the seed does not migrate into the sprout; although it does not migrate into the sprout, it is nonetheless able to produce it.
Sentient beings are likewise. How, then, can there be bondage and liberation?
“Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.”

Good son! It is like a person who, when casting off life and undergoing great suffering, is surrounded by kinsmen who wail and lament in distress; that person is terrified and knows no one on whom to rely for rescue.

Although he possesses the five sensory faculties, they have no power of cognition; his limbs tremble and convulse, unable to be sustained; his body is cold and hollow, and his vital warmth is about to be extinguished, as he beholds the signs of the retribution for the good and evil deeds he previously cultivated.
"Good son!

Just as when the sun is about to set, the shadows of mountains, hills, and mounds appear to shift toward the east and cannot logically travel to the west, so too it is with the karmic fruits of sentient beings.
When this aggregate ceases, that aggregate arises in succession, just as when a lamp is lit darkness is extinguished, and when the lamp is extinguished darkness arises."

Good son! It is like a wax seal being pressed into clay: as the seal and the clay meet, the seal disappears and the impression is formed. Yet this wax seal does not transform and remain within the clay, nor does the impression emerge from the clay, nor does it come from any other place; rather, by means of the causal conditions of the seal, this impression arises.
When the aggregates of the present life cease, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise; yet these present aggregates never transform into the five aggregates of the intermediate state.
Furthermore, the five aggregates of the intermediate state do not arise from themselves, nor do they come from elsewhere.
Because the aggregates of the present existence manifest, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise; it is like a seal impressing clay: when the seal is removed, the impression is formed.
Although the names do not differ, the temporal stages are each distinct.
Therefore, I say that the five aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava) are not seen by the fleshly eye, but are seen by the divine eye.
Within this intermediate state, there are three kinds of nutriment:
first, the nutriment of volition (manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra); second, the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra); and third, the nutriment of mental intention (vijñānāhāra).
There are two kinds of intermediate state (antarābhava):
first, the result of wholesome karma, and second, the result of unwholesome karma.
Due to wholesome karma, one attains wholesome vitarka and vicāra.
Due to evil karma, one acquires evil thoughts and observations.
At the time when the parents unite in sexual intercourse, following the conditions of their karma, they move toward the place of rebirth, conceiving love for the mother and hatred for the father.
When the father’s semen is emitted, [the intermediate being] claims it as its own; having seen this, the mind rejoices and gives rise to delight.

By means of these three kinds of afflictive conditions, the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) perish and the five aggregates of the subsequent birth arise, just as when a seal is pressed into clay: the seal perishes and the impression is formed.
At the time of birth, the sense faculties may be complete or incomplete. When those with complete faculties see forms, they give rise to greed; because greed arises, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because of madness, greed arises; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Due to the two causes and conditions of craving and ignorance, all perceived objects are entirely inverted: one perceives the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, the suffering as happiness, and the impure as pure.
Due to the four inversions, one performs wholesome and unwholesome deeds; afflictions produce karma, and karma produces afflictions—this is called bondage.
For this reason, it is termed the arising of the five aggregates.

If this person is able to draw near to the Buddha, his disciples, and various virtuous friends, they will then hear and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Because they have heard the Dharma, they contemplate wholesome objects; because they contemplate wholesome objects, they attain great wisdom. That which is called great wisdom is right knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*). Because they have attained knowledge and vision, they give rise to a mind of remorse regarding birth and death; because they give rise to a mind of remorse, they do not produce delight; because they do not produce delight, they are able to destroy the mind of greed; because they destroy the mind of greed, they cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path; because they cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, they attain the state where there is no birth and death; and because there is no birth and death, they are said to have attained liberation.
Just as fire that encounters no fuel is called "extinguished," because one has extinguished birth and death, it is called "Nirvana.
For this reason, it is termed the "extinction of the five aggregates."
Siṃhanāda said: "In space there are no thorns; how can one speak of pulling them out?
The aggregates have no binder; how can they be bound?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

By means of the fetters of affliction, the five aggregates are bound. Apart from the five aggregates, there are no separate afflictions; apart from afflictions, there are no separate five aggregates.”
Good son! Just as a pillar supports a house—there is no pillar apart from the house, and no house apart from the pillar—so it is with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings.
Because of the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called "bound"; because of the absence of afflictions, they are called "liberated."

"Good son! Just as the three acts of clenching a fist, joining the palms, and tying a knot involve no distinct phenomena other than the arising and ceasing of joining and dispersing, so it is with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings:
because of the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called 'bondage'; because of the absence of afflictions, they are called 'liberation'."

Good son! As it is said regarding name-and-form, bondage, and sentient beings: if name-and-form ceases, there are no sentient beings; apart from name-and-form, there is no separate sentient being; and apart from sentient beings, there is no separate name-and-form. Thus, it is called "name-and-form binding sentient beings," and it is also called "sentient beings binding name-and-form."
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!

Just as the eye does not see itself, a finger does not touch itself, a blade does not cut itself, and feeling does not feel itself, why does the Tathāgata say that name-and-form is bound by name-and-form?”
Why is it said that "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is itself the sentient being,
and that the sentient being is itself name-and-form?
If one says that name-and-form binds the sentient being, then it is simply name-and-form binding name-and-form.
The Buddha said,
“Good son! Just as when two hands are joined together, there is no other separate dharma that comes to join them.”
Name and form are likewise thus. For this reason, I say that name and form bind sentient beings.
If one is separated from name and form, one attains liberation; therefore, I say that sentient beings are liberated.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If name-and-form were that which binds, then all Arhats, who have not yet abandoned name-and-form, would also be bound.”
“Good son! There are two kinds of liberation:
first, the severance of the seed; second, the severance of the fruit.”

What is called "the severance of the seed" refers to the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*). Arhats and others have already severed the afflictions; their various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are withered and destroyed, and therefore the fetter of the seed cannot bind them.

Because they have not yet severed the fruits [of affliction], they are said to be bound by those fruits; all Arhats do not perceive the Buddha-nature, and because they do not perceive it, they do not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, it may be said that they are bound by the fruit, but one cannot say they are bound by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Good son! It is like lighting a lamp: as long as the oil is not exhausted, the light will not be extinguished; if the oil is exhausted, its extinction is certain.
"Good son! That which is called 'oil' is a metaphor for all afflictions (*kleśa*), and the lamp is a metaphor for sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings possess the oil of afflictions, they do not enter *nirvāṇa*; if they succeed in severing it, they then enter *nirvāṇa*."
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
The lamp and the oil have two distinct natures.”
The afflictions of sentient beings are not like this; sentient beings are themselves the afflictions, and the afflictions are themselves sentient beings.
Sentient beings are called the five aggregates, and the five aggregates are called sentient beings.
“The five aggregates are called afflictions, and afflictions are called the five aggregates; why, then, does the Tathāgata liken them to a lamp?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
There are eight kinds of similes: first, the concordant simile;

second, the inverse simile; third, the manifest simile; fourth, the non-simile; fifth, the prior simile; sixth, the posterior simile; seventh, the prior-and-posterior simile; and eighth, the pervasive simile.

What is the analogy of conformity? As it is said in the Sūtra: "When the heavens send down great rain, the ditches become full; because the ditches are full, the small pools become full; because the small pools are full, the large pools become full; because the large pools are full, the small springs become full; because the small springs are full, the large springs become full; because the large springs are full, the small lakes become full; because the small lakes are full, the large lakes become full; because the large lakes are full, the small rivers become full; because the small rivers are full, the large rivers become full; and because the large rivers are full, the great ocean becomes full."

The Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is also like this: when sentient beings fulfill the precepts, because the precepts are fulfilled, the mind of non-regret is fulfilled; because the mind of non-regret is fulfilled, joy is fulfilled; because joy is fulfilled, detachment is fulfilled; because detachment is fulfilled, tranquility is fulfilled; because tranquility is fulfilled, samādhi is fulfilled; because samādhi is fulfilled, right knowledge and vision are fulfilled; because right knowledge and vision are fulfilled, disenchantment is fulfilled; because disenchantment is fulfilled, revulsion is fulfilled; because revulsion is fulfilled, liberation is fulfilled; because liberation is fulfilled, nirvāṇa is fulfilled. This is called an analogy of progressive sequence.

"What is the analogy in reverse? The great ocean has its source in the great rivers; the great rivers have their source in the small rivers; the small rivers have their source in the large ponds; the large ponds have their source in the small ponds; the small ponds have their source in the large springs; the large springs have their source in the small springs; the small springs have their source in the large pits; the large pits have their source in the small pits; the small pits have their source in the ditches and canals; and the ditches and canals have their source in the heavy rains."

Nirvana has a root, which is called liberation; liberation has a root, which is called reproach; reproach has a root, which is called wearying detachment; wearying detachment has a root, which is called right knowledge and vision; right knowledge and vision have a root, which is called samādhi; samādhi has a root, which is called tranquility; tranquility has a root, which is called seclusion; seclusion has a root, which is called a joyful mind; a joyful mind has a root, which is called freedom from regret; freedom from regret has a root, which is called upholding the precepts; upholding the precepts has a root, which is called the rain of Dharma. This is called the analogy of reverse order.
"What is an analogy based on direct observation?
As it is said in the sūtras, the nature of the minds of sentient beings is like that of a monkey; the nature of a monkey is to abandon one thing and seize another.

The nature of the minds of sentient beings is likewise: they grasp at and become attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, never remaining still for even a moment. This is called an analogy based on direct observation."
"What is meant by 'not being an analogy'?
It is as when I formerly told King Prasenajit:
'Great King!'"
A trusted person came from each of the four directions, each saying:
"Great King!
Four great mountains are coming from the four directions, intending to harm the people."
“If the King were to hear this, what plan would he devise?
The King replied,
“World-Honored One!
"If this should come to pass, there will be no place for escape; you must simply focus your mind on observing the precepts and practicing generosity.
I then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
When I speak of the four mountains, they are precisely the birth, aging, sickness, and death of sentient beings.
Birth, aging, sickness, and death constantly come to afflict people.
Why, Great King, do you not cultivate precepts and practice giving?
The King said:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of fruit is obtained through observing the precepts and practicing giving?"
I said: "Great King! You shall experience much happiness among humans and devas."
The King said:
"World-Honored One!
If the Nyagrodha tree were to observe the precepts and practice giving, would it also receive peace and security among humans and devas?"
I said: "Great King!
The nyagrodha tree cannot uphold the precepts or practice giving; if it were able to do so, there would be no difference between it and those who receive [the fruit]."
This is called a non-example.
"What is the prior example?
In my sūtras it is said: For instance, there was a person who was so attached to exquisite flowers that while gathering them, he was swept away by water."
Sentient beings are likewise: craving and receiving the five desires, they are swept away and submerged by the waters of birth and death; this is called the first analogy.
"What is the subsequent analogy?
As stated in the *Dharmapada*:
"Do not disregard even a minor transgression, thinking it will bring no calamity.
Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel."
"This is called the subsequent simile.
What is the preceding and subsequent simile?
It is like the plantain tree, which dies as soon as it bears fruit; the fool who receives nourishment is likewise. It is like a mule that conceives, whose life is not long preserved."
"What is the universal analogy?

As it is said in the Sūtra: 'In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is the Pārijātaka tree; its roots penetrate the earth to a depth of five yojanas, it is one hundred yojanas high, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all directions. When the leaves ripen, they turn yellow.'"
When the devas see this, joy arises in their hearts, thinking: "These leaves will surely fall before long.
When the leaves have fallen, they again feel joy, thinking: "This branch will surely change color before long."
When the branches have changed color, he again feels joy, thinking: "This color will not last long; it will surely produce buds.
Having seen this, he rejoices again, thinking: "These buds will not last long; they will surely produce beaks."
Having seen this, they rejoice again, thinking: "This beak will surely open and split before long.

When it opens and splits, its fragrance pervades fifty yojanas and its radiance shines afar for eighty yojanas; at that time, the various devas spend the three months of the summer season there below, enjoying themselves.
"Good son!
My disciples are also like this: the yellowing of the leaves is a metaphor for my disciples' desire to leave the household life;
the falling of the leaves is a metaphor for my disciples shaving off their hair and beards."
The change in its color is a metaphor for my disciples receiving full ordination through the white-fourfold formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
The initial formation of a blister is a metaphor for my disciples giving rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The mouth is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas of the ten stages who have attained the vision of the Buddha-nature;
the opening and splitting [of the seed] is a metaphor for the bodhisattva attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Perfume" is a metaphor for the immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions who uphold the prohibitive precepts;
"light" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s name, which is unimpeded and pervades the ten directions.
The three months of summer are a metaphor for the three samādhis.
The thirty-three devas experiencing happiness is a metaphor for all Buddhas attaining permanence, bliss, self, and purity within Great Nirvāṇa.
This is called the "universal analogy.
Good son, when citing analogies, it is not necessary to take them in their entirety; one may take a small portion, a large portion, or take them in full.
To say that the Tathāgata’s face is like the full moon is called a partial description. Good son!
It is, for example, as if there were someone who had never seen milk before, and then asked another person:
"What kind of substance is milk?
That person replied,
"It is like water, honey, or a conch shell."
"Water has the characteristic of moisture, honey has the characteristic of sweetness, and the conch shell has the characteristic of color.
Although these three analogies are cited, they do not yet constitute the reality of milk. Good son!"
When I speak of the analogy of the lamp, it is likewise used to illustrate sentient beings.
Good son! Just as there is no river apart from water, so it is with sentient beings; apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate sentient being.
"Good son!
Just as there is no separate vehicle apart from the carriage body, wheels, axle, spokes, and rim, so it is with sentient beings.
Good son!"

If you wish to understand how this corresponds to the analogy of the lamp, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now explain it. The wick is a metaphor for the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*);

the oil is a metaphor for craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the light is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*); the dispelling of darkness is a metaphor for destroying ignorance (*avidyā*); and the heat is a metaphor for the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

Just as when the oil of a lamp is exhausted, its bright flame is extinguished, so too when a sentient being’s craving is exhausted, they perceive the Buddha-nature; though possessing name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), they cannot be bound by them.
Even while dwelling within the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), they are not defiled by those states of existence.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Since the five aggregates of sentient beings are empty and non-existent, who is there to receive the teaching and cultivate the Path?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

All sentient beings possess a mind of mindfulness, a mind of wisdom, a mind of resolve, a mind of diligent effort, a mind of faith, and a mind of concentration. Although such dharmas arise and perish from moment to moment, they nevertheless continue in a similar succession without interruption; therefore, it is called the cultivation of the path.”
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Since all such dharmas perish moment by moment, and these momentary perishing dharmas also continue in a similar succession, how are they to be cultivated?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Just as a lamp, though it perishes moment by moment, possesses light that dispels darkness, so too are all dharmas such as mindfulness."
Good son! Just as the food consumed by sentient beings, though perishing moment by moment, still causes those who are hungry to become fully satiated;
and just as a superior medicine, though perishing moment by moment, is nevertheless able to cure disease.
Although the light of the sun and moon perishes moment by moment, it can still cause forests, trees, and grasses to grow.
Noble son, as for what you asked:
"If they perish moment by moment, how can there be growth?"
Because the mind is uninterrupted, it is called "growth. Good son!
It is like a person reciting a book: the words and phrases being recited cannot occur simultaneously; what precedes does not reach the middle, and the middle does not reach the end.
The person, the characters, and the mental conceptions all perish from moment to moment; yet, through long cultivation, one attains proficiency. Good son!

It is like a goldsmith who, from his first practice until his hair turns white, although each moment perishes and what precedes does not reach what follows, because of accumulated habit, his work becomes exquisite. For this reason, he is called a skilled goldsmith. The recitation and study of the scriptures is also like this.
"Good son! It is like a seed:

the earth does not instruct it, 'You must produce a sprout,' yet by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the sprout arises spontaneously; even so, the flower does not instruct it, 'You must produce a fruit,' yet by the nature of phenomena, the fruit arises spontaneously. The cultivation of the path by sentient beings is likewise."
Good son! It is like the method of counting:
one does not reach two, and two does not reach three; yet, although each moment ceases, it reaches a thousand or ten thousand. The practice of the path by sentient beings is also like this.
"Good son!

Just as a lamp extinguishes moment by moment, the flame that first extinguishes does not instruct the subsequent flame, saying: 'I shall extinguish myself so that you may arise and destroy all darkness.
Good son!"
For example, as soon as a calf is born, it seeks milk; the wisdom that seeks milk is not actually taught by anyone. Although it perishes moment by moment, it is hungry at first and satiated later.
Therefore, one should know that [the subsequent state] is not identical [to the preceding]; if they were identical, there would be no arising of difference.
The cultivation of the path by sentient beings is also like this: although there is no increase at first, because of long-term cultivation, one is then able to destroy all afflictions.
Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, once a person who has attained the fruit of a srotāpanna has realized that fruition, even if they are born in an evil land, they still maintain the precepts, refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, and drinking intoxicants.
The aggregates of a srotāpanna are extinguished right here and do not reach an evil land.
The cultivation of the path is likewise; it does not lead to an evil land.
If they are similar [to those who fall into evil realms], why is it that they are not born in pure and wondrous lands?
"If the aggregates of an evil country are not the aggregates of a srotāpanna, how can one avoid committing evil karma?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."

Although a srotāpanna may be born in an evil land, he never loses the name "srotāpanna"; yet his aggregates (skandhas) are not similar [to those of others]. For this reason, I have cited the calf as a metaphor.
Although a srotāpanna may be born in an evil land, by the power of the Path, he does not commit evil deeds. Good son!
It is like Mount Gandhamādana, where there dwells a lion king; because of this, all birds and beasts vanish from sight, and none dare approach this mountain.
Sometimes when a king goes into the Snowy Mountains, all the birds and beasts still do not remain there.
It is the same with a stream-enterer (srotāpanna): although they do not practice the Path, by the power of the Path they do not commit any evil deeds.
Good son!
It is like a person who consumes ambrosia; although the ambrosia itself perishes, by its power it can cause this person to be neither born nor to die.
"Good son!

It is like Mount Sumeru, which has a supreme and wondrous medicine named Laṅgali. If a person takes it, although it perishes moment by moment, by the power of the medicine, they do not encounter illness or suffering."
"Good son!
It is like the place where a wheel-turning monarch sits; even though the king is not present, no one dares to approach it. Why is this?
By virtue of the King’s majestic power, it is likewise with the *srotāpanna*: although born in an evil land and not practicing the Path, by the power of the Path, they do not commit evil deeds.
Good son! The aggregates of a srotāpanna cease here; although he is born with different aggregates, he nevertheless does not lose the aggregates of a srotāpanna. Good son!

For example, when sentient beings, for the sake of fruit, perform much labor upon a seed—applying manure and providing irrigation—if the seed perishes before the fruit is obtained, it can still be said that they obtain the fruit by means of the seed; the aggregates (*skandha*) of a *srotāpanna* are likewise.
"Good son! It is like a man of immense wealth who has an only son who has already passed away; that son’s own son is, moreover, in another land."

That man suddenly and unexpectedly passed away; having heard this, the grandson returned to take possession of the estate. Although he knew that the wealth and goods were not his own making, there was no one to prevent him from taking them.
Why is this? Because their lineage is one.
The aggregates of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) are likewise so.
Siṃhanāda said: “As the Buddha spoke in verse:
‘If a bhikṣu cultivates virtue, concentration, and wisdom.’”
"You should know that this is non-retrogression, drawing near to Great Nirvāṇa.
"World-Honored One, how does one cultivate precepts?
How does one cultivate concentration?"
"What is the cultivation of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."

If there are those who uphold the prohibitive precepts solely for their own benefit—seeking the pleasures of humans and devas—and not for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, nor for the protection of the unsurpassed True Dharma; but rather for the sake of gain and offerings, out of fear of the three evil realms, or for the sake of life, physical vigor, peace, and unimpeded eloquence; or out of dread of royal law, ill repute, and foul rumors, or for the sake of worldly affairs—if they protect the precepts in such a manner, it cannot be called the cultivation of the precepts.
Good son! What is called the true cultivation of the precepts?

When upholding the precepts, if one does so for the sake of liberating all sentient beings and protecting the True Dharma—in order to deliver those not yet delivered, to liberate those not yet liberated, to provide refuge to those without refuge, and to lead those who have not entered nirvana to enter it—when cultivating in this manner, one does not perceive the precepts, does not perceive the characteristics of the precepts, does not perceive a holder of the precepts, does not perceive the karmic fruit, and does not contemplate transgression.
"Good son!
If one can act in this way, it is called the cultivation of precepts.
Furthermore, what is called the cultivation of samādhi?"

When practicing samādhi, if one does so for the sake of one's own liberation or for gain and offerings, rather than for the sake of sentient beings or for the protection of the Dharma; or if one practices samādhi out of a desire to see the faults of greed, impure food, and the like—the impurity of the nine orifices of men and women, their quarrels, beatings, stabbings, and mutual slaughter—then such practice of samādhi is not truly called the cultivation of samādhi.
Good son! What, furthermore, is called the true cultivation of samādhi?

If, for the sake of sentient beings, one cultivates samādhi, attaining a mind of equanimity toward all beings; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the dharma of non-retrogression; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the noble mind; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the Mahāyāna; desiring to protect and uphold the unsurpassed Dharma; for the sake of causing sentient beings not to regress from Bodhi; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain Śūraṅgama; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain Vajra-samādhi; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain dhāraṇī; for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid); and for the sake of causing sentient beings to see the Buddha-nature—when performing such practices, one does not perceive the samādhi, does not perceive the characteristics of samādhi, does not perceive the practitioner, and does not perceive the karmic fruit.
"Good son!
If one can act in this way, it is called the cultivation of samādhi.
Furthermore, what is called the cultivation of wisdom?
If there are those who practice and reflect thus:
"If I cultivate such wisdom, I shall attain liberation and cross over the three evil realms;
who else can benefit all sentient beings?"
Who can deliver beings from the path of birth and death?

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. I am now able to sever the fetters of all afflictions and shall certainly attain the fruit of liberation; therefore, I must diligently cultivate wisdom, swiftly sever my afflictions, and quickly achieve deliverance.
"One who practices in this manner cannot be said to be practicing wisdom.
What, then, is called true practice?
A wise person, when contemplating birth, old age, death, and suffering, perceives that all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and do not know how to practice the unsurpassed Right Path."

"May this body of mine fully take the place of sentient beings in receiving great suffering and affliction; may all the poverty, lowliness, and precept-breaking minds of sentient beings, as well as their karma of greed, hatred, and delusion, all come to gather upon my own body."

May all sentient beings not give rise to greedy grasping and not be bound by name-and-form; may all sentient beings quickly cross over birth and death, while I alone remain within it without weariness; may all beings attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When practicing in this way, one does not perceive wisdom, nor the characteristics of wisdom; one does not perceive a practitioner, nor the karmic fruit. This is what is called the cultivation of wisdom.
"Good son!
One who cultivates such morality, concentration, and wisdom is called a bodhisattva.
One who cannot thus cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom is called a śrāvaka."
"Furthermore, good son!
What is meant by 'cultivating the precepts'?
It is when one is able to destroy the sixteen evil codes of conduct of all sentient beings."
What are the sixteen?
First, for the sake of profit, they fatten lambs and then sell them after they have grown plump.
Second, for the sake of profit, they purchase animals and slaughter them.
Third, for the sake of profit, they feed and raise pigs until they are fat, then sell them.
Fourth, for the sake of profit, they purchase [animals] and slaughter them.
Fifth, for the sake of profit, they feed and raise calves until they are fat, then sell them.
Sixth, for the sake of profit, one buys [animals] and slaughters them.
Seventh, for the sake of profit, one raises chickens until they are fat, and once they are fat, sells them on.
Eighth, for the sake of profit, one buys [animals] and slaughters them.
Ninth, those who fish with hooks;
tenth, hunters;
eleventh, plunderers.
Twelfth, the executioner;
thirteenth, snaring birds;
fourteenth, double-tongued speech.
Fifteenth are the hell-wardens;
sixteenth are the spell-bound dragons.
To be able to bring about the permanent severance of these sixteen types of evil karma for the sake of sentient beings is called the cultivation of precepts.
What is the cultivation of concentration?

It is the ability to sever all worldly samādhis—namely, the "bodiless" (anātmaka) samādhi, which causes sentient beings to give rise to perverted thoughts and claim it is *nirvāṇa*; the "boundless mind" (*anantacitta*) samādhi; the "pure accumulation" (*śuddharāśi*) samādhi; the "limit of the world" (*lokānta*) samādhi; the "severance of the world" (*lokaccheda*) samādhi; the "nature of the world" (*lokasvabhāva*) samādhi; the "hero of the world" (*lokapuruṣa*) samādhi; and the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*) samādhi. Such concentrations as these cause sentient beings to give rise to perverted thoughts and claim they are *nirvāṇa*. If one can permanently sever such samādhis, this is called the cultivation of concentration.
Furthermore, what is meant by "cultivating wisdom"?
It is that which can destroy all evil views in the world. All sentient beings possess such evil views, namely: "Form is the self, and it also belongs to the self."
The self is within form, and form is within the self; this applies likewise up to consciousness.
The permanent is the self; when form ceases, the self remains.
Form is the self; when form ceases, the self ceases.
Furthermore, some say:
"The agent is called 'self,' and the recipient is called 'form' (rūpa). Others say:
"The agent is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and the experiencer is called the self (ātman).
Furthermore, some say:
"There is no agent and no experiencer; things arise and perish of themselves, entirely without causes and conditions."
Again, some say:
"There is no agent and no recipient; all things are created by Īśvara.
Again, others say:
"There is no agent and no recipient; everything is produced by the power of time.
Furthermore, some say:
"Both agent and recipient are non-existent; the five great elements, such as earth and so forth, are what are called sentient beings."
"Good son! If one can destroy such evil views of all sentient beings, this is what is called cultivating wisdom. Good son!"
The cultivation of precepts is for the sake of the tranquility of the body. The cultivation of samādhi is for the sake of the tranquility of the mind.

The cultivation of wisdom is for the sake of destroying doubt; the destruction of doubt is the cultivation of the Path; the cultivation of the Path is for the sake of seeing the Buddha-nature; the seeing of the Buddha-nature is for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa. The attainment of Great Nirvāṇa is for the sake of severing for all sentient beings all birth-and-death, all afflictions, all states of existence (*bhava*), all realms (*dhātu*), and all truths (*satya*). From the severing of birth-and-death up to the severing of the truths, it is for the sake of attaining the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, if that which is neither born nor extinguished is called Great Nirvāṇa, then birth is likewise neither born nor extinguished; why, then, cannot it be called nirvāṇa?”
“Good son! It is so, it is so.
It is just as you have said.”
"Although this birth is neither produced nor extinguished, it nonetheless has a beginning and an end.
"World-Honored One!

This dharma of birth and death likewise has no beginning or end. If there is no beginning or end, it is called 'eternal'; what is eternal is precisely nirvāṇa. Why, then, is birth and death not called nirvāṇa?"
“Good son! These phenomena of birth and death all possess causes and effects; because they possess causes and effects, they cannot be called nirvana. Why is this?
"Because the essence of nirvāṇa has neither cause nor effect.
Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
Indeed, Nirvana also possesses causes and effects.
As the Buddha has said:
"By cause one is born in heaven; by cause one falls into the evil realms."
"Nirvāṇa arises from causes; therefore, all things possess causes.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus in the past:
"I shall now explain the fruits of the śramaṇa path."
What is called a "śramaṇa" refers to one who is able to fully cultivate ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The "path" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, and the "fruit of the śramaṇa" refers to nirvāṇa.
"World-Honored One!
Since Nirvāṇa is thus, is it not a fruit?
Why do you say that the essence of Nirvāṇa has neither cause nor fruit?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
That which I have proclaimed as the cause of nirvāṇa is what is called buddha-nature. The nature of buddha-nature does not give rise to nirvāṇa; therefore, I say that nirvāṇa has no cause.”
"It is called the 'Great Fruit' because it can destroy afflictions; it is called 'fruitless' because it does not arise from the Path. Therefore, Nirvana has neither cause nor fruit.
Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
Is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings shared collectively by all,
or does each possess it individually?
If it were shared collectively, then when one person attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all sentient beings should likewise attain it simultaneously.
“World-Honored One!
It is like twenty people who share a single enemy; if one person is able to eliminate him, the remaining nineteen will likewise all be freed from him.
The Buddha-nature is also like this: when one person attains it, the others should likewise attain it.”
If each were distinct, then it would be impermanent.
Why? Because it could be calculated and enumerated.

However, the Buddha has taught that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither one nor two. If each possessed it as a distinct entity, it would not be right to say that all Buddhas are equal, nor would it be right to say that the buddha-nature is like space.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither one nor two; it is as equal as space among all Buddhas, and all sentient beings possess it in common.”
If there are those who can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, you should know that such persons will attain clear vision. Good son!
On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Patience"; if a cow eats it, it becomes ghee. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
Siṃhanāda said: "As the Buddha has taught, is the grass of patience one,
or many?"
If there were only one, the ox would have finished eating it all.
If there were many, how could you say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this?
As the Buddha has taught, if there are those who cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, they will see the Buddha-nature; this meaning, however, is not so.
Why is this? If the Way were singular, like the kṣānti-grass, it would necessarily come to an end; if it were to come to an end, once one person had cultivated it, others would have no share in it.
“If the path were manifold, how could it be said that one has fully cultivated it, and why would it not be called the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñā-jñāna)?
The Buddha said, “Good son!”
It is like a level road upon which all sentient beings travel without obstruction.

Along the way there is a tree whose shade is cool and refreshing; travelers rest beneath it to halt their journey. Yet the shade of that tree remains constantly without shifting, neither decaying nor perishing, and there is no one who can carry it away.
The road is a metaphor for the Noble Path, and the enclosures are a metaphor for the Buddha-nature. Good son!

It is like a great city that has but a single gate; although many people pass through it coming and going, there is no one at all who can create an obstacle, nor is there anyone who can destroy or demolish it to carry it away.
"Good son!
It is like a bridge by which people pass; no one can obstruct, hinder, destroy, or carry it away.
Good son!"

For example, just as a skilled physician treats all manner of illnesses without anyone being able to prevent him from treating this one while setting aside that one, so too it is with the Noble Path and Buddha-nature.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
The meanings of the various analogies you have cited are not as such.”
Why is this? If one is ahead on the road, they will obstruct those behind; how then can it be said that there are no obstructions?
This applies to all other cases as well.
“If the Buddha-nature of the Noble Path were such as you describe, then when one person practices it,
they should obstruct others. The Buddha said, “Good man!
What you have said is not consistent with the meaning.
The path I used as a metaphor is a partial analogy, not a complete one. Good son!
The worldly path involves obstructions and distinctions between this and that, lacking any state of equality. The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is not like this;

it enables sentient beings to be without obstruction, equal and non-dual, devoid of spatial distinctions such as "this" and "that. Such a right path serves as the *vyakty-hetu* (revealing cause) for the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings, but does not act as the *janaka-hetu* (producing cause).
It is like a bright lamp that illuminates objects. Good son!

All sentient beings are equally possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*), which conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). One cannot say that when one person’s ignorance conditions their formations, others should consequently be without them.
All sentient beings possess ignorance, which conditions volitional formations; therefore, it is said that the twelve links of dependent origination are equal for all.

The untainted, right path cultivated by sentient beings is likewise so: it equally severs the afflictions, the four modes of birth, the various realms, and the path of existence of all beings. For this reason, it is called "equality."
Those who have realized it possess mutual knowledge and vision without any obstruction; for this reason, it is named the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowing). Siṃhanāda said:

"The bodies of all sentient beings are not of one kind—there are celestial bodies, human bodies, and the bodies of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings. Since there are thus many different types of bodies that are not one, how can you say that the Buddha-nature is one?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

It is like a person who puts poison into milk; even the clarified butter (ghṛta) produced from it will all be poisonous. What is called milk is not yet curd, and what is called curd is not yet milk; even so it is with everything up to the clarified butter.”

Although the names have changed, the poisonous nature is not lost; it is present throughout all five flavors, and it is exactly so in every case—even if one consumes *sarpis* (clarified butter), it can still kill a person, yet in truth, no poison was ever placed within that *sarpis*.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; although they dwell within the five realms of existence and receive diverse bodies, this buddha-nature remains eternally one and unchanging.
Siṃhanāda said, “World-Honored One!
Among the sixteen great nations, there are six great cities.
Namely, Śrāvastī, Vārāṇasī, Campā, Vaiśālī, Sāketa, and Rājagṛha; these six cities are the greatest in the world.
"For what reason has the Tathāgata forsaken [great cities] and entered parinirvāṇa here in this borderland city of Kuśinagara, which is wretched, evil, extremely humble, narrow, and small?
"O son of good family!"
You should not say that the outskirts of the city of Kuśinagara are inferior, wretched, most desolate, and cramped; rather, you should say that this city is adorned with subtle and sublime merits.
Why is this? Because it is the sphere of practice for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Good son!

It is like the house of a lowly person: if a king were to pass by, he should praise it, saying, "This house is magnificent and endowed with excellent qualities; it is worthy of having the Great King turn his carriage to visit."
"Good son!

It is like a person with a grave illness who takes a foul and inferior medicine; once he has taken it and his illness is cured, he should immediately rejoice and praise it, saying, 'This medicine is supreme and most wonderful, for it has been able to cure my illness.'"
"Good son!

It is like a person traveling by boat upon the great ocean whose vessel suddenly breaks apart and leaves them with nothing to rely upon; because they lean against a corpse, they reach the other shore. Having reached the other shore, they should feel great joy and offer praise, saying: 'I am indebted to this corpse for meeting it, and thus I have attained safety.'"
The city of Kuśinagara is likewise so; it is a place where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have practiced. How can you say it is a remote, wicked, sordid, and cramped little town?

“Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was an eon named Good Awakening (Sujñāna). At that time, there was a holy king of the Kauśika clan who possessed the seven treasures and was endowed with a thousand sons.”

When that king first founded this city, it was twelve yojanas in circumference and breadth, adorned with the seven treasures. The land abounded in rivers, whose waters were pure, soft, and sweet; these included the Nairañjanā River, the Airāvatī River, the Hiraṇyavatī River, the Vāgvatī River, and the Vipāśā River—rivers such as these numbering five hundred.
On both banks of this river, the trees were lush and flourishing, with flowers and fruits that were fresh and pure.
At that time, the lifespan of the people was immeasurable.
After a hundred years had passed, the Wheel-Turning Sage King made this proclamation:
"As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena are entirely impermanent.
If one can cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas, one will be able to sever such great suffering of impermanence."
When the people heard this, they all together reverently practiced the Dharma of the ten wholesome actions.

At that time, having heard the name of the Buddha and upheld the ten wholesome actions, I contemplated and cultivated them, and for the first time, I gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having generated this mind, he further used these teachings to instruct immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, saying that all phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay.
Therefore, I now continue here as well to speak of how all phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay, while teaching only that the Buddha-body is the eternally abiding dharma.
I recall the causal conditions of my past conduct; for this reason, I have now come here to enter parinirvāṇa, desiring also to repay the kindness this land has shown me in the past.
For this reason, I have stated in my sutras that those who are my kinsmen are able to repay the kindness they receive.
"Furthermore, good son!

In the past, when the lifespan of sentient beings was immeasurable, this city was named Kuśāvatī; it was fifty yojanas in circumference and extent. At that time, the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa lived so close together that a rooster could fly from one to another."
There was a wheel-turning king named Sudarśana, who possessed the seven treasures, was endowed with a thousand sons, and ruled over the four continents.
The eldest crown prince contemplated the True Dharma and attained the state of a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King saw that his crown prince had become a Pratyekabuddha, whose dignified deportment was composed and whose supernatural powers were rare and marvelous.

Having witnessed this, he immediately renounced the royal throne as if discarding phlegm or saliva, and went forth into homelessness among these *śāla* trees. For eighty thousand years he cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and for eighty thousand years each, he cultivated the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
"Good son! If you wish to know who that noble King Sudarśana was at that time, it was none other than myself.
Therefore, I now constantly delight in dwelling and practicing these four dharmas; these four dharmas are called samādhi."
For this reason, the body of the Tathāgata is eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Good son!
By these causes and conditions, I have now come to this city of Kuśinagara, among the śāla trees, to enter right samādhi.

“Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, this city was then named Kapilavastu. In that city there was a king named Śuddhodana; the king’s queen was named Māyā, and the king had a son named Siddhārtha.”
At that time, the prince, without relying on a teacher’s instruction, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through his own natural contemplation.
He had two disciples:
the first was named Śāriputra, and the second was named Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
My attendant disciple was named Ānanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One was expounding this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra between the twin trees.
I was present at the assembly and participated in these matters, hearing that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Having heard this matter, he immediately attained non-retrogression regarding Bodhi and promptly made this vow:

"I vow that when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, my parents, my land, my name, my disciples, and those who serve me, as well as my preaching and teaching of the Dharma, shall be equal to and no different from those of the World-Honored One in the present."
For these reasons, I have now come here to proclaim and expound the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
"Good son, when I first left home and had not yet attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, King Bimbisāra sent an envoy who said:
'If Prince Siddhārtha becomes a holy wheel-turning monarch, I shall become his subject.'"

If you do not delight in the household life and have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I pray that you will first come here to this city of Rājagṛha to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, and accept my offerings.
At that time, I remained silent and accepted his invitation. Good son!

When I had first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and was traveling toward the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a Brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan by the name of Eḷeyya on the banks of the river Erāvaṇī, who, together with five hundred disciples, was seeking the unsurpassed path. For the sake of these people, I went there to preach the Dharma.
Kāśyapa said: "Gautama!

I am now advanced in years, having reached one hundred and twenty. All the people of the kingdom of Magadha, as well as its great king Bimbisāra, all believe that I have already realized the fruit of arhatship."
If I were now to listen to and receive the Dharma in your presence, all the people might give rise to perverted thoughts, thinking: "Is the Venerable Kāśyapa not an Arhat?"
"I pray that Gautama may quickly depart for another place; if these people come to know for certain that Gautama’s merit surpasses mine, we shall have no further means to receive offerings."
I then replied: "Kāśyapa!
If you do not harbor intense resentment toward me, please allow me to stay for one night; I shall depart early tomorrow morning."
Kāśyapa said: "Gautama!
My mind harbors no other thoughts; I hold you in deep affection and high esteem."
"However, there is a venomous dragon in my dwelling whose nature is fierce and impetuous;
I fear it might harm you. I said, "Kāśyapa!..."
"The poison among poisons is none other than the three poisons, which I have now severed.
As for the poisons of the world, I have no fear of them.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If you can indeed remain undaunted, excellent! You may stay.
Son of good family!
At that time, I intentionally manifested the eighteen transformations for Kāśyapa, as described in the sutras.
At that time, Kāśyapa and his assembly of five hundred followers, having seen and heard this, realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, Kāśyapa had two younger brothers:
one named Gayākāśyapa and the other named Nadīkāśyapa; their teachers and disciples, along with their retinues, also numbered five hundred, and they too all realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, when the six heretical teachers of Rājagṛha heard of this matter, they conceived great malice toward me.

I then accepted the King’s invitation and traveled to Rājagṛha; before I had even reached the midpoint of the road, the King came out with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers to welcome me, and I preached the Dharma for them.

Upon hearing the Dharma, eighty-six thousand devas of the desire realm resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the twelve thousand followers in King Bimbisāra’s retinue attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*; and immeasurable sentient beings achieved the mind of patience (*kṣānti*).

Having entered the city, I led Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, along with their retinue of two hundred and fifty people, to renounce their original intentions and leave the household life to study the Path; I then remained there to receive the King’s offerings.
The six heretical teachers gathered together and went to the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was an elder in that city named Sudatta who had gone to Rājagṛha to betroth a wife for his son. Having reached that city, he stayed as a guest in the house of the elder Sandhāna.
Then, at midnight, this elder rose and addressed his kinsmen:
"Sirs, you should rise; quickly adorn yourselves together, sweep and clean the house, and prepare the various delicacies."
Having heard this, Sudatta immediately reflected to himself:
"Is it not that he wishes to invite King Māgadha?
Or is there a marriage celebration or some festive gathering?"
Having reflected thus, he immediately stepped forward and asked,
"Great Being!
Do you wish to invite King Bimbisāra of Magadha?"
"Is there a wedding feast or some joyful gathering?
Why is your urgent business so unsettled?
The elder replied:
"No, householder! I have invited the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, for tomorrow.
When the elder Sudatta first heard the name of the Buddha, the hairs on his body all stood on end; he then immediately asked:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
The elder replied,
"Have you not heard?
In the city of Kapilavastu, there was a son of the Śākya clan named Siddhārtha, of the Gautama lineage, whose father’s name was Śuddhodana.
Not long after his birth, physiognomists divined that he would certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), like an amra fruit already held in his hand.

With no desire for or attachment to [worldly life], he renounced it and left home; without a teacher, he awakened by himself and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with greed, hatred, and delusion exhausted.
Eternally abiding and unchanging, neither born nor extinguished, it is free from sorrow and fear.
Toward all sentient beings, its mind is impartial, just as parents regard their only child with equal affection.
He is the most supreme among all beings of body and mind; though he excels all, he is free from arrogance, and his mind remains unchanged whether anointed or cut.

His wisdom penetrates all things without obstruction, and he is fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the five wisdoms, the samādhis, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness; therefore, he is called a Buddha.
"Knowing that you have accepted my invitation, I was in such a hurry that I had no leisure to look upon you.
Sudatta said, "Excellent, Great Being!"
"The one called 'Buddha' possesses unsurpassed merit; where is he now?
The elder replied, "He is currently here in the great city of Rājagṛha, dwelling at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery."

At that time, Sudatta single-mindedly recollected all the merits of the Buddha—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the five wisdoms, the samādhis, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness. While he was reflecting thus, suddenly there was a brilliant light; its radiance was so fierce and intense that it was like the midday sun. He immediately followed the light out and arrived beneath the city gate.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the gate opened of its own accord.
Having passed through the gate, there was a shrine to a deity on the road; as Sudatta passed by, he paid his respects with prostrations, whereupon it immediately became dark again.
His heart was filled with fear and he wished to return to his dwelling place; at that time, a heavenly deity at the city gate addressed Sudatta, saying:
"If you, O benevolent one, go to where the Tathāgata is, you will obtain great and manifold benefits."
Sudatta asked, "What is this 'excellent benefit'?
He replied:
"O Householder!

Suppose there were someone who gave to a single person a hundred sets of genuine jewel necklaces, a hundred fine horses, a hundred fragrant elephants, and a hundred jeweled chariots; furthermore, a hundred figures cast from gold, each as handsome as a woman adorned with necklaces and inlaid with various jewels; and a hundred magnificent palaces and halls with intricate carvings and engravings, along with a hundred golden platters filled with silver grain and a hundred silver platters filled with golden grain—were such things given to one person, and this process repeated until every person in Jambudvīpa had received them, the merit obtained would not equal that of a person who resolves their mind and takes a single step toward the presence of the Tathāgata."
Sudatta said: "Good man! Who are you?"
He replied, "Householder!
I am the son of the brahmin Viśeṣacintin; I was your spiritual friend in the past."

Because in the past I saw Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my heart was filled with joy; having cast off this body, I was reborn as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, specifically charged with guarding this city of Rājagṛha.

Because I gave rise to a heart of joy by prostrating before Śāriputra and the others, I have already obtained such a wondrous and excellent body; how much more so when I shall behold the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, and pay him homage and make offerings?
After the elder Sudatta heard these words, he immediately returned by the same path to where I was.
Upon arrival, he bowed his head at my feet in respectful salutation; I then preached the Dharma to him according to what was appropriate for him.
Upon hearing this, the elder attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; having realized this fruit, he further entreated me, saying:
"The Tathāgata is greatly compassionate; I pray that you will deign to visit Śrāvastī and accept my humble offering."
I then asked: "In your city of Śrāvastī, is there a vihāra that might accommodate us?
Sudatta replied:
"If the Buddha would look upon me with compassion and deign to grant his presence, I shall exhaust myself to prepare and establish [the assembly].
"Good son! At that time, I accepted the invitation in silence."
Having received my permission, the elder Sudatta addressed me, saying:

"I have never before performed such a task. I only pray that the Tathāgata will dispatch Śāriputra to instruct me in the proper rites; I shall then attend to him and command those who assist in the construction."
"Then Śāriputra and Sudatta traveled together in a single carriage toward the city of Śrāvastī.
By means of my supernatural power, we arrived at our destination after one day and one night."
Then Sudatta said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable One!
Outside this great city, where is there a plot of land that is neither too near nor too far, abounding in springs and ponds, with fine groves of trees, flowers, and fruits, lush, pure, and secluded?"
"I shall, within this place, construct a vihāra for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus.

Śāriputra said, "Prince Jeta’s Grove is neither too near nor too far; it is pure and secluded, with many springs and ponds, and trees, flowers, and fruits available in all seasons. This location is most excellent and suitable for establishing a vihāra."
When Sudatta heard these words, he immediately went to the great elder Jeta and said to him:
"I now wish to construct a monastery for the Unsurpassed Dharma King; I pray that you will grant me the use of your grove for this purpose."
"I now wish to purchase it; would you be able to grant it to me?
Jeta replied, "Even if one were to cover the entire ground with pure gold, I still would not give it."
Sudatta said, "Excellent, Jeta!
The forest land belongs to me; you may now take the gold."
Jeta replied, "I do not sell my garden; why would I take gold? Sudatta said:
"If you cannot resolve this yourselves, we should go together to the place of the magistrate.
Then the two elders went together to the magistrate's location.
The magistrate said:
"The garden belongs to Sudatta; Jeta has taken the gold.

Thereupon, the elder Sudatta immediately dispatched people to load carts and horses to carry it and gather it to spread upon the ground. Within a single day, only five hundred paces remained where the gold had not yet been fully covered.
Jeta said, "If you,
Elder, regret it, I will allow you to stop as you please.
Sudatta replied:
"I do not regret it.
He thought to himself, "From which treasury shall I draw enough gold?
Then Jeta thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is truly unsurpassed; the sublime Dharma he proclaims is pure and unstained, which is why this person regards wealth as so insignificant."
He then said to Sudatta:
"For the remaining areas that have not yet been covered, I do not require any more gold; please grant me this instead.
I shall personally construct a gate tower for the Buddha so that the Tathāgata may always pass through it when entering or leaving."

The elder Jeta himself constructed the gate pavilion, while the elder Sudatta established a great residence within seven days, sufficient for three hundred people, with sixty-three secluded meditation cells and separate quarters for winter rooms and summer halls.
The kitchen, the bathhouse, the place for washing feet, and the large and small latrines were all fully prepared.
Once everything was set up, he took hold of an incense burner and, facing toward Rājagṛha from afar, spoke these words:
"All that is required has been prepared; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion and pity, will accept this dwelling place for the sake of all sentient beings."

"At that time, I knew the mind of this elder through profound insight; immediately, together with the great assembly, I departed from Rājagṛha and, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and stretch his arm, arrived at the Jeta Grove, the Saṃghārāma of Sudatta, in Śrāvastī."
Once I had arrived, the elder Sudatta offered me that which he had prepared for my use.
Having accepted it, I then took up residence therein.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle 29.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: The Lion’s Roar of the Bodhisattva, Part Four.
At that time, the six heretical teachers became filled with jealousy; they all gathered together and went to King Prasenajit, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should know that your realm is pure, peaceful, and tranquil—truly a place for renunciants to dwell. For this reason, we have come here for this very purpose."
"Your Majesty governs with righteousness and removes the sufferings of the people.
Yet the śramaṇa Gautama is both young in years and shallow in his studies; he has no mastery of the arts of the Way.
There are elders of long-standing virtue already in this kingdom who, relying on their royal lineage, do not show him respect."
If one belongs to the royal caste, the law dictates that they should govern the people; if they renounce the world, they should honor those of long-standing virtue.
Great King, listen well: the śramaṇa Gautama was not truly born into a royal lineage. If the śramaṇa Gautama had parents, how could he have robbed others of their parents?
"Great King!
In my sutras it is said that after a thousand years have passed, a deceptive phantom of an ill omen shall appear; this refers to none other than the śramaṇa Gautama."

Therefore, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has neither father nor mother; if he had parents, how could he say that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, uncreated, and without a recipient?
By means of illusory arts, they deceive and delude sentient beings; the foolish believe and accept them, while the wise abandon them.
Great King!

A king is indeed the parent of the world, like a scale, like the earth, like the wind, like fire, like a path, like a river, like a bridge, like a lamp, like the sun, and like the moon. He adjudicates affairs according to the Dharma, making no distinction between enemy and kin.
"The śramaṇa Gautama will not allow us to live; wherever we go, he pursues us and will not let us be.
We pray only that Your Majesty will permit us to compete with that Gautama in the power of their spiritual paths."
"If he defeats me, I shall belong to him;
if I defeat him, he shall belong to me.
The King said:
"Venerable ones!
Each of you has your own rules of conduct, and the places where you reside are likewise different.
I now know for certain that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, will cause you no hindrance."
The six teachers replied:
"How can there be no harm?
The śramaṇa Gautama has used the methods of illusion and sorcery to entice and deceive the people and brahmins until they have all been brought to submission."
"If Your Majesty would permit me to compete with you in the power of our paths, your good reputation will spread throughout the eight directions;
if you do not, ill repute will fill the roads.
The King said:
"Venerable One!

Because you do not yet know that the Tathāgata’s power of the Way and his majestic spiritual authority are so sublime, you seek to test him; were you to know for certain, I fear you would not be able."
"Great King! Have you now already accepted the illusion of Gautama?
We pray only that Your Majesty will deign to listen and consider this, and not slight us."
"Constructing arguments with empty words is not as good as verifying them through reality.
The King said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
The disciples of the six teachers departed with joy.

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and came to where I was; he prostrated himself in respectful salutation, circumambulated me three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed me, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The six teachers have recently sought to compare their spiritual powers with mine; without due consideration, I have already granted them my consent.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
Excellent, excellent!
You should simply establish monasteries throughout every part of this country. Why is that?
"If I were to compete with him in spiritual power, those among his assembly who would be converted would be many; this place is narrow and small—how could it accommodate them? "Good son!
At that time, for the sake of the six teachers, from the first day until the fifteenth day, I manifested great and rare supernatural transformations.
At that moment, immeasurable sentient beings resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to faith and ceased all doubt toward the Triple Gem.
The followers of the six teachers were immeasurable in number; they shattered their minds of false views and left the household life to enter the True Dharma.

Immeasurable sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive mind within Bodhi; immeasurable sentient beings attained various dharanis and samadhi-gates; and immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of srotapanna up to the fruit of arhat.
