At that time, the six heretical teachers felt deep shame and remorse in their hearts; they went together in a procession to the city of Vārāṇasī and taught the people there to believe in and accept their false doctrines, saying, "The śramaṇa Gautama speaks only of empty matters."
"Good son!
At that time, acting as my mother, I was dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven under the Pārijātaka tree, observing the rains retreat and preaching the Dharma.
At that moment, the six heretical teachers were filled with great joy and cried out:"
"Excellent! Gautama’s magical arts have now vanished," he said,
while further teaching immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to increase their false views.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assembly addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable One!
In this Jambudvīpa, wrong views are increasing; sentient beings are pitiable, for they walk in great darkness."
I pray that the Venerable One, upon reaching that celestial realm, shall bow his head to the World-Honored One and speak on my behalf as follows:
"It is like a calf, not long since born; if it does not obtain milk, its certain death is beyond doubt."
"We sentient beings are likewise; we only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and return to dwell here.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana silently gave his consent and, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, went to that heavenly realm. Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The fourfold assembly throughout Jambudvīpa thirsts for and yearns for the Tathāgata, longing to see him and hear the Dharma."
King Bimbisāra, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assembly bow their heads at your feet.
All sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa have increased in wrong views and walk in great darkness; they are truly to be pitied.
It is like a calf that has been born not long ago; if it does not receive milk, it will surely die without a doubt.
We are just the same. We only pray that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, will return once more to this Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Return now quickly to Jambudvīpa and inform the various kings and the fourfold assembly that seven days from now I shall descend again."
"For the sake of the six teachers, I shall again go to that city of Vārāṇasī.

After seven days had passed, surrounded by Śakra, Brahmā, Māra, and immeasurable sons of gods, as well as all the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, I went to the city of Vārāṇasī. There, I let out a great lion’s roar and spoke these words:
"Only within my Dharma are there true śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; all phenomena are impermanent and without self, nirvāṇa is tranquil, and it is free from all faults and evils."
"If it is said that there are other dharmas wherein there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and wherein there is permanence, a self, and nirvāṇa, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the six teachers said to one another:
"If there were truly no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas within our teachings, how could we receive the offerings of the world?"
"Then the six teachers again gathered together and went to Vaiśālī.
'O son of good family!
Once, while I was staying in the Āmra Grove at Vaiśālī, the woman Āmrapālī, knowing that I was there, wished to come to my place.'"
At that time, I told the bhikṣus:
"You should contemplate the foundations of mindfulness and skillfully cultivate wisdom; according to what you practice, let your minds not be negligent."
What is called the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness?
If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the internal body and does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self;
who contemplates the external body and the internal-external body, and does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self.
Contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena is likewise; this is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
What is meant by "cultivating wisdom"?
If a bhikṣu perceives suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path in accordance with reality, this is called a bhikṣu cultivating wisdom.
What is called "non-negligence of mind"?

If a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of relinquishment, and mindfulness of the devas, this is called a bhikṣu whose mind is not negligent.

Then the woman Āmrapālī came to where I was, prostrated with her head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and having completed her respectful salutation, withdrew to sit on one side.
"Good son!
At that time, I preached the Dharma to the woman Āmrapālī according to her needs. Having heard it, the woman gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At that time, five hundred Licchavis from that city came to where I was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and having completed their acts of reverence, withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, I further preached the Dharma to the Licchavi youths as was appropriate for them, saying:
"Good sons, one who is heedless has five kinds of results. What are these five?"

First, one will not attain mastery over wealth and profit; second, a bad reputation will spread abroad; third, one will take no pleasure in giving wisdom and alms to the destitute; fourth, one will take no pleasure in seeing the fourfold assembly; and fifth, one will not obtain the body of a deva.
"Good sons, through heedfulness, one can give rise to both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
If there are those who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should diligently cultivate the dharma of heedfulness."
Furthermore, those who are heedless experience thirteen kinds of retributive results. What are these thirteen? First, they delight in performing worldly tasks;

second, they delight in speaking useless words; third, they constantly delight in long bouts of sleep; fourth, they delight in discussing worldly affairs; fifth, they constantly delight in associating with evil friends; sixth, they are always indolent and lazy; seventh, they are constantly held in contempt by others; eighth, though they hear something, they soon forget it; ninth, they delight in dwelling in remote borderlands; tenth, they are unable to subdue their sense faculties; eleventh, they do not know moderation in eating; twelfth, they do not delight in emptiness and stillness; thirteenth, their views are incorrect. These are called the thirteen.
"Good son!
As for those who are heedless, even though they may be near the Buddha and his disciples, they remain far indeed.
The Licchavi youths said:
"We know ourselves to be heedless people. Why is this?
Had we not been heedless, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, would have appeared in our land."
At that time, there was a son of a brahmin in the great assembly named Ajita, who said to the Licchavis:
"Excellent, excellent!
Just as you have said, King Bimbisāra has already attained great benefit."
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has appeared in this land, just as a wondrous lotus flower grows in a great pond; though it grows in the water, the water cannot defile it.
O sons of the Licchavis!
The Buddha is likewise; although he is born in that land, he is not obstructed by worldly dharmas.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, neither emerge nor enter; for the sake of sentient beings they appear in the world, yet they are not obstructed by worldly dharmas.
You yourselves are deluded and addicted to the five desires; you do not know to draw near and go to the place where the Tathāgata dwells. For this reason, you are called heedless people.
It is not that the Buddha’s appearance in the kingdom of Magadha is itself named "heedlessness."
"Why is this? The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is like the sun and the moon; he does not appear in the world for the sake of only one or two people.
When the Licchavis heard these words, they immediately resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and further spoke thus:
“Excellent, excellent, Anabhibhū!
You have spoken these most skillful and sublime words with great eloquence.”
Then the Licchavis each removed one garment from their own bodies and offered it to Ajita.
Having accepted them, Ajita presented them to me, saying again:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I obtained these garments from the Licchavis; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, will accept what I have offered.
At that time, out of pity for him who was without superior, I immediately accepted them.
Then all the Licchavis simultaneously joined their palms and spoke these words:
"We pray that the Tathāgata will dwell for a time in this land and accept our humble offerings."
At that time, I accepted the Licchavis' invitation in silence.
When the six heretical teachers heard of this matter, they consulted among themselves and went together to the city of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, I again went to Vārāṇasī and stayed by the banks of the Varanā River.

At that time, there was a son of a householder in Vārāṇasī named Ratnayaśas, who was addicted to the five desires and did not realize the impermanence of things. Because I had arrived, he spontaneously attained the dharma of the meditation on white bones; he saw his palace, its halls, and the court ladies all as white bones. His heart was filled with terror, regarding them as a sword or a venomous snake, as a thief or a fire. He immediately left his residence and came to where I was, speaking along the way: "Śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"I am now being pursued by bandits; I am filled with great fear and dread, and pray that you will rescue me.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are peaceful and free from fear.
The son of the elder said,
"If within the Three Jewels there is nothing to fear, then I too shall now attain fearlessness."
I immediately granted him permission to leave the household life to pursue the Way.

At that time, the son of the elder had fifty companions who, hearing from afar that Ratnayaśas had grown weary of desire and left the household life, immediately joined together in harmony and likewise left the household life.
Having heard this, the six teachers traveled on from place to place until they reached the great city of Campā.

At that time, all the people of the great kingdom of Campā were devoted to the followers of the six teachers; they had never before heard the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, and many among them committed extremely evil deeds.
At that time, for the sake of sentient beings, I went to the city of Campā.
At that time, there was a great elder in that city who had no heir; he served the six teachers in hopes of obtaining a son. Not long thereafter, his wife became pregnant.
Having learned this, the elder went to the six teachers and said with joy:
"My wife is pregnant; will it be a boy or a girl?"
The six teachers replied,
"She will certainly be a girl.
Upon hearing this, the elder felt deep distress in his heart.
Furthermore, a friend came and said to the householder,
"For what reason are you so distressed?
The householder replied:

"My wife is pregnant, and as we do not yet know whether it will be a boy or a girl, I have questioned the six masters. According to what the six masters told me, based on their methods of physiognomy, the child born will certainly be a girl."

Upon hearing these words, I reflected that I am advanced in years and possess immeasurable wealth; yet if he were not a male, there would be no one to whom I could entrust it, and for this reason I am grieved.
The acquaintance spoke again:
"You lack wisdom; have you not heard before whose disciples the brothers Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his followers were?"
Is it the Buddha,
or the six teachers?
If the six teachers were all-knowing, why did Kāśyapa abandon them and not serve them, but instead become a disciple of the Buddha?

Furthermore, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, as well as kings such as Bimbisāra and their queens such as Mallikā, and elders of various lands such as Sudatta—are these people not disciples of the Buddha?

Are not such beings as the yakṣas of the wilderness, King Ajātaśatru, the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla, and Aṅgulimāla—who possessed such fierce malice that he sought to harm his own mother—subdued by the Tathāgata?
"Elder! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is called a Buddha because his knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena are unimpeded.
He is called the Tathāgata because his speech is non-dual."
Because he has severed all afflictions, he is called an Arhat.
What the World-Honored One has taught is ultimately without duality;
the Six Teachers are not so—how can they be trusted?
"The Tathāgata now dwells nearby; if you wish to know the truth, you should go to where the Buddha is.

At that time, the elder immediately accompanied this person to my place, prostrated with his head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and spoke these words:
"The World-Honored One is equal toward all sentient beings without distinction; he regards enemies and kin as one and the same."
"I am bound by the fetters of craving; thus, I have not yet been able to maintain equanimity toward enemies and kin alike.
I now wish to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding worldly matters, yet out of deep shame and fear, I have not dared to speak."
“World-Honored One!
My wife is pregnant, and the six teachers have prophesied that she will certainly give birth to a girl.
What do you say of this? The Buddha said:
“Householder!
Your wife is pregnant; there is no doubt that it will be a son.
Once the child is born, his merit and virtue will be beyond compare.”
At that time, having heard my words, the elder was filled with great joy and returned home.
At that moment, the six heretical teachers, hearing my profound prediction that the child would certainly be a boy and possess great merit and virtue, were [filled with envy].
Conceiving jealousy, she mixed poisonous drugs with mango fruits, took them to the house, and said to the elder: "How wonderful!

Gautama has skillfully explained the signs. Your wife, as she approaches her time of delivery, may take this medicine; once she has taken it, the child will be handsome and the mother will suffer no harm."
The elder joyfully accepted the poison and gave it to his wife to take; having taken it, she died immediately.
The six teachers were delighted and, traveling throughout the city, proclaimed in a loud voice:
"The śramaṇa Gautama predicted that this elder’s wife would give birth to a son, and that the child's merit and virtue would be unsurpassed in the world."
"The child has not yet been born, and the mother has already lost her life.

At that time, the elder again conceived a lack of faith in me; he then followed worldly custom, enshrouding the body in a coffin and carrying it outside the city, where he piled up a great quantity of dry wood and cremated it with fire.
"With my eye of the Way, I clearly perceive this matter; I call for Ānanda and command him, 'Bring me my robe, for I wish to go there to destroy false views.
At that time, Vaiśravaṇa Deva addressed the Great General Maṇibhadra, saying:
'The Tathāgata now wishes to go to that cemetery. You should go quickly to level and sweep the ground, prepare a lion throne, and seek out exquisite flowers and incense to adorn the site.'"
At that time, the six heretical teachers saw me approaching from afar and said to one another:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has come to this cemetery; does he wish to eat flesh?"
At that time, many laymen (*upāsaka*) who had not yet attained the Dharma-eye felt deep shame and said to me:
"That woman has already died; we pray that you do not go."
At that time, Ānanda said to the assembly:
"Wait but a moment; before long, the Tathāgata shall extensively expound and reveal the realm of all Buddhas.
When I arrived and sat upon the lion throne, the elder Nanda spoke these words:
"What you call 'non-duality' may indeed be named the World-Honored One.
Since your mother has already passed away, how could she have given birth to a son? I said:
"Householder!
At that time, you did not ask at all about the length of your mother's life;
you asked only whether the child she carried would be a boy or a girl."
"The speech of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is non-dual; therefore, you should know that you will certainly obtain a son.
At that moment, the corpse was consumed by fire until its belly split open, and from within it emerged a child, sitting upright amidst the flames like a ruddy sheldrake upon a lotus pedestal.
When the six teachers saw this, they spoke again, saying:
"A sorcerer is Gautama; he is skilled in the arts of illusion.
When the elder saw this, his heart was filled with joy once more, and he rebuked the six teachers:
"If you say it is an illusion, why do you not create one yourself?
At that time, I immediately told Jīvaka:
"Go into the fire and bring this child back here."
As Jīva was about to go, the six masters pulled him back and said to him:
"The illusory arts employed by the śramaṇa Gautama are not necessarily always effective; they may sometimes succeed and sometimes fail. If they fail, you might instead be burned or harmed."
"How can you now believe and accept his words? Jīvaka replied,
"If even the fierce fires of the Avīci Hell cannot burn one whom the Tathāgata has sent there, how much less so the fires of this world?"
At that time, Jīvaka stepped forward and entered the mass of fire as if entering the cool waters of a great river; he took up the child, returned to my presence, and handed the child over to me.
Having accepted the child, I said to the elder:
"The lifespan of all sentient beings is uncertain, like a bubble upon the water.
If sentient beings possess the karmic fruits of grave deeds, fire cannot burn them, nor can poison harm them."
"This is the karmic fruit of this child's own actions;
it was not done by me. Then the elder said, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"If this child is to fulfill his natural lifespan, I pray that the Tathāgata will grant him a name.
The Buddha said,
"O Householder!"
"This child was born from within a fierce fire; since the fire was named Jyotiṣka, he should be named Jyotiṣka.
At that time, witnessing my spiritual transformations within the assembly, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the six teachers, having failed to find a place to set foot throughout the six cities, came back with shame and bowed heads to this city of Kuśinagara.
Having arrived there, they cried out these words:
"All people should know that the śramaṇa Gautama is a great master of illusion who has deceived and deluded the world throughout the six great cities."
It is like a magician who conjures four kinds of troops— namely, chariot troops, cavalry, elephant troops, and infantry—
and further conjures various kinds of necklaces, city walls, palaces, houses, rivers, ponds, and trees.
The śramaṇa Gautama is also like this, manifesting illusory forms of royal bodies.

For the sake of preaching the Dharma, he may manifest as the body of a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a male, a female, a small body, or a large body; or he may manifest as the body of an animal, a ghost, or a spirit. At times he speaks of impermanence, and at times he speaks of permanence; at times he speaks of suffering, and at times he speaks of pleasure; at times he speaks of a self, and at times he speaks of no-self; at times he speaks of purity, and at times he speaks of impurity; at times he speaks of existence, and at times he speaks of non-existence. Because all that he does is illusory, it is called a "phantasm."
Just as one obtains fruit according to the seed from which it sprang, so it is with the Śramaṇa Gautama.
Since Māyā, his mother who gave birth to him, was an illusion, her son cannot be anything other than an illusion.

The śramaṇa Gautama possesses no true knowledge or vision; even though the various brahmins have practiced asceticism for years and accumulated merit over many ages, and have maintained their prohibitions and precepts, they still say that he does not yet possess true knowledge and vision.
How much less so for Gautama, who is young, of shallow learning, and has not practiced asceticism; how could he possess true knowledge and vision?
Even if he were to complete seven years of ascetic practice, his insight would still not be extensive, let alone when his cultivation falls short of six years.
"Those fools, lacking wisdom, believe and accept his teachings, just as a great illusionist deceives and deludes the ignorant; the śramaṇa Gautama is exactly like this.
O son of good family!
"In this way, these six teachers greatly increase false views among sentient beings within this city.

'Good son! Seeing this matter, my heart gave rise to compassion. By means of my supernatural power, I summoned the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, who gathered like clouds in this forest, filling it completely for forty yojanas on all sides; now, in the midst of this assembly, I utter the Great Lion’s Roar.'"
"Good son!
Although one may say much in an empty place, it cannot be called a 'lion’s roar.
Only within this great assembly of wise people can it truly be called a Great Lion’s Roar."
The Lion’s Roar proclaims that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; it speaks only of the Tathāgata as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
At that time, the six teachers spoke again, saying:
"If Gautama has a self, we also have a self.
That which is called 'self' is the seer; this is named the self."
"Gotama! It is just as if a person were to see an object in a mirror; I am also like this.
The mirror is a metaphor for the eye, and the seer is a metaphor for the self."
The Buddha told the six teachers:
"If you say that what sees is called the 'self,' this meaning is not so. Why is that?"
Regarding the analogy you have cited, when a person faces a single direction, all six sense faculties are simultaneously active.
If there were a fixed self that perceives through the eye, why does it not likewise attend to all objects simultaneously within a single faculty?
If a single faculty cannot simultaneously hear and see the six objects, one should know that there is no self.
As for the analogy of the direction cited, even after a hundred years, what the observer sees through it remains no different.

If the visual faculty were thus, there would likewise be no difference when one is advanced in years and the faculties have matured; yet because people turn toward different objects, they see both internally and externally.
If the visual faculty were thus, it should also perceive both the internal and external simultaneously.
"If it is not seen, how can there be a self?
The six teachers spoke again:
"Gautama!..."
"If there is no self, who is it that sees? The Buddha said,
"When there is form, light, mind, and the eye— through the conjunction of these four, it is called 'seeing'."
Within this, there is in reality neither a seer nor an experiencer.
Sentient beings, due to their inversions, claim that there is a seer and an experiencer.
For this reason, what all sentient beings perceive is inverted, while what the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive is true.
"O Six Teachers!
If you say that form is the self, this is also not so. Why is that?"
Form is truly not the self.
If form were the self, one would not be subject to obtaining an ugly appearance; why, then, are there distinctions among the four castes, rather than all being of a single kind, such as the Brahmins?
Why is it that you are subject to others and lack self-mastery?
Why are your faculties deficient and your birth incomplete?
Why do you not take on the bodies of the various devas?
And why do they undergo the various bodies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts?
If one cannot obtain these forms at will, one should know that there is certainly no self.

Because there is no self, it is called impermanent; because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is empty; because it is empty, it is a perversion. Due to this perversion, all sentient beings revolve in birth and death; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
"O Six Teachers!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has forever severed the bonds of form up to the bonds of consciousness; therefore, he is called Eternal, Blissful, Self, and Pure.
Furthermore, form is itself dependent origination; that which is dependently originated is called non-self, and that which is non-self is called suffering and emptiness."

"The body of the Tathāgata is not produced by causes and conditions; because it is not produced by causes and conditions, it is said that there is a self. If there is a self, then it is eternal, blissful, and pure.
The six teachers spoke again:
"Gautama!..."
"Form is also not self, and so on, up to consciousness is also not self.
The self pervades all places, just like space.
The Buddha said:
"If it were omnipresent, one should not say, 'I have never seen it before.
If one has never seen it before, then one knows that this seeing was originally non-existent and now exists; if it was originally non-existent and now exists, it is called impermanent."
If it were impermanent, how could you say it is pervasive?

If it were pervasive, it should possess bodies within all five realms of existence; if it possessed bodies, each would have to undergo its own retribution. If each were to undergo its own retribution, how could you say that one transmigrates to receive the states of humans and devas?
Regarding your statement that [the self] is pervasive: is it one or many?
If my self were one, then there would be no distinction between father and son, enemy and friend, or neutral person.
If my faculties were manifold, then the five faculties of all sentient beings would necessarily be equal, and their karma and wisdom would likewise be so.
If this were the case, why speak of faculties being either complete or incomplete?
“What is the distinction between wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and the difference between the ignorant and the wise? “Gautama!
The self of sentient beings has no limit.”
Dharma and non-Dharma have their respective boundaries.
If sentient beings practice Dharma, they obtain a good body; if they engage in non-Dharma, they obtain an evil body.
For this reason, the karmic fruits of sentient beings cannot be without distinction.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If dharma and non-dharma were as you say, then I would not be all-pervading."
If I were omnipresent, then I would have to be present everywhere.
If that were the case, those who cultivate goodness would also possess evil, and those who commit evil deeds would also possess goodness.
"If it were not so, how could you say it is 'pervasive'? "Gautama!
It is like a single room where a hundred thousand lamps are lit; each illuminates itself without obstructing the others."
"It is the same for the 'self' of sentient beings: the cultivation of good and the commission of evil do not intermingle. "Good son!
If you say that the self is like a lamp, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? The light of that lamp exists dependent upon conditions; as the lamp increases, the light also increases.
The "self" of sentient beings is not like this: the light issues from the lamp and resides in a different location.
The self of sentient beings cannot be like this, emerging from the body and dwelling in a separate location.
That light of a lamp coexists with darkness. Why is this?
It is like lighting a single lamp in a dark room: at first, illumination is not clear, but when many lamps are lit, it becomes distinct.
If the first lamp had destroyed the darkness, there would be no need for subsequent lamps; if subsequent lamps are required, one should know that the initial light coexisted with the darkness.
“Gautama! If there is no self, who performs good and evil deeds?
The Buddha said:
"If the self were the agent, how could it be called eternal?
If it were eternal, how could it sometimes perform good and sometimes perform evil?"
If one says that there are times when one performs good or evil deeds, how can one further claim that the self is infinite?
If the self were the agent, for what reason would it continue to practice unwholesome dharmas?
If I were the agent and the knower, why would I give rise to doubt regarding the non-existence of a self in sentient beings?
For this reason, within the teachings of the non-Buddhists, there is certainly no such thing as a self.
If one speaks of "self," it is none other than the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because his body is boundless, because he is free from the net of doubt, and because he neither acts nor undergoes [the results of action], he is therefore called "eternal."
Because it is neither born nor extinguished, it is called bliss.
Because it is free from the defilements of affliction, it is called purity.
Because it is devoid of the ten marks, it is called emptiness.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and pure; he is empty and devoid of all marks.
The non-Buddhists said:
"If you say that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, yet empty because he lacks marks—"
"You should know that the Dharma taught by Gautama is not empty; therefore, I shall now receive and uphold it with the highest reverence.
At that time, immeasurable numbers of non-Buddhists developed faith in the Buddha’s Dharma and left the household life to become monks.
“Good son! For these reasons, I let out a great lion’s roar here between the twin śāla trees.
This ‘lion’s roar’ is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.”
"Good son!
The pair in the east destroys impermanence and attains permanence. ...
And so on, until the pair in the north destroys impurity and attains purity."
"Good son!
Herein, these sentient beings, for the sake of the twin trees, protect the śāla grove so that outsiders do not take its branches and leaves, nor cut them down or destroy them."
I am also like this; for the sake of four dharmas, I cause my disciples to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
What are these four?
They are permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These four pairs of trees are under the jurisdiction of the Four Heavenly Kings; because I have been protected by the Four Kings in the maintenance of my Dharma, I entered parinirvāṇa therein.
O son of good family!
The twin śāla trees are always lush with flowers and fruit, and they constantly benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
I am also like this, constantly able to benefit śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The flower is a metaphor for the self, and the fruit is a metaphor for bliss; by this meaning, I have entered the Great Samādhi of Quiescence here between these twin śāla trees, and this Great Samādhi of Quiescence is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa in the second month?”

“Good son! The second month is called spring; it is the month of spring’s warmth when all things grow and flourish. Roots and seedlings are planted, flowers and fruits bloom in abundance, rivers overflow with water, and the hundred beasts conceive and give birth.”

At that time, sentient beings mostly gave rise to the notion of permanence; in order to shatter such a mind of permanence among sentient beings, it was taught that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, while it was taught only that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Good son! Among the six seasons, the early winter is withered and parched, such that the multitude finds no joy in it.
The spring sun is warm and moistening, which people greedily cherish.
In order to destroy the worldly pleasure of sentient beings, he expounds eternal bliss.
It is the same for self and purity: in order to destroy the worldly self and worldly purity, the Tathāgata speaks of the true self and purity of the Tathāgata.
The mention of "the second month" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s two kinds of *dharmakāya*.
"Not delighting in winter" means that the wise do not delight in the Tathāgata’s impermanence or his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
The joy of the second month is a metaphor for the wise person’s love and delight in the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity.
Planting seeds is a metaphor for sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma, rejoice and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thereby planting various roots of goodness.
The river is a metaphor for the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions coming to me to inquire about and receive this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
The various beasts giving birth to their young is a metaphor for my disciples generating various roots of goodness.
The flowers are a metaphor for the seven factors of enlightenment;
the fruit is a metaphor for the four fruits of the spiritual life.
For this reason, I shall enter great parinirvāṇa in the second month.
Siṃhanāda said:

"The Tathāgata’s birth, renunciation, attainment of enlightenment, and turning of the wondrous Wheel of Dharma all occurred on the eighth day; for what reason was his parinirvāṇa alone on the fifteenth day?"
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
Just as the moon on the fifteenth day has neither waning nor waxing, so too it is with all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; they enter Great Nirvāṇa without waning or waxing.
For this reason, they enter Parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day.
Good son, when the moon is at its fullness on the fifteenth day, there are eleven qualities.

What are these eleven? First, it can dispel darkness; second, it enables sentient beings to distinguish the path from what is not the path; third, it enables sentient beings to discern the deviant from the correct regarding the path; fourth, it removes oppressive heat and brings the joy of coolness; fifth, it can destroy the haughty minds of fireflies; sixth, it quiets all thoughts of robbery and theft; seventh, it removes the fear of wild beasts from sentient beings; eighth, it causes the *utpala* flowers to bloom; ninth, it causes the lotuses to close; tenth, it inspires the mind of the practitioner to advance along the path; and eleventh, it causes all sentient beings to delight in the five desires and obtain much happiness.
“Good son! The full moon of the Tathāgata is also like this: first, it destroys the great darkness of ignorance; second, it proclaims the right path and the deviant paths;

third, it reveals the treacherous dangers of birth and death and the level rectitude of nirvāṇa; fourth, it causes people to distance themselves from the fevers of greed, anger, and delusion; fifth, it destroys the ignorance of external paths; sixth, it destroys the thieves of the fetters of affliction; seventh, it eliminates the mind that fears the five hindrances; eighth, it causes the minds of sentient beings to blossom as they plant roots of goodness; ninth, it covers over the minds of sentient beings’ five desires; tenth, it inspires sentient beings to initiate the practice of advancing toward great nirvāṇa; and eleventh, it causes all sentient beings to delight in cultivating liberation.”
For this reason, although on the fifteenth day I enter great parinirvāṇa, in truth I do not enter nirvāṇa.
Among my disciples, foolish and wicked people will certainly say that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa.
It is like a woman who has many sons; that mother leaves her home and travels to another land, and during the time before she returns, each of her sons says, "My mother is dead."
"Yet this mother has not truly died.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
“What kind of bhikṣu can adorn these twin śāla trees? “Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who receives, maintains, reads, and recites the twelve divisions of the sūtras, correcting their phrasing and penetrating their profound meaning; who explains them for others as being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; and who, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, expounds the holy life—such a bhikṣu can adorn the twin śāla trees.”
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the bhikṣu Ānanda is that very person.”

Why is this? The bhikṣu Ānanda receives, maintains, reads, and recites the twelve divisions of the sūtras, expounding the correct words and correct meanings for others, just as one pours water from one vessel and places it into another.
The bhikṣu Ānanda was also like this: having heard from the Buddha, he would repeat it exactly as he had heard it. "Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who has attained the pure divine eye and sees everything within the trichiliocosm of the ten directions as clearly as looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand, such a bhikṣu can also adorn the twin śāla trees."
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Aniruddha is that very person.”
Why is this? Aniruddha, with his divine eye, clearly perceives everything within the trichiliocosm, even including those in the intermediate state (antarābhava), without any obstruction.

“Good son! If there is a bhikṣu who has few desires and is content, whose mind delights in tranquility, and who diligently practices vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and the liberation of wisdom—such a bhikṣu is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.”
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is that very person.”
"Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has skillfully cultivated such dharmas as having few desires and being content. "Good son!"

If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and not for the sake of gain or sustenance, cultivates and masters the Samādhi of Non-contention, the Noble Practices, and the Practice of Emptiness—such a bhikṣu is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Subhūti is precisely that person.”
"Why is this? Subhūti has skillfully cultivated the noble practice of non-contention and the practice of emptiness. "Good son!"

If there is a bhikṣu who has skillfully cultivated supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such that within a single thought-moment he can perform various miraculous transformations, and with a single mind he can certainly produce two effects—namely, water and fire—a bhikṣu such as this is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is thus, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is precisely that person.”
Why is this? It is because Maudgalyāyana has skillfully cultivated the supernormal powers and immeasurable transformations. "Good son!..."

If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates great wisdom, sharp wisdom, swift wisdom, liberating wisdom, profound wisdom, vast wisdom, boundless wisdom, unsurpassed wisdom, and true wisdom, and who fully accomplishes such faculties of wisdom (prajñendriya), his mind will be without discrimination toward enemies or kin.

If, upon hearing that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is impermanent, one’s mind does not grieve; and if, upon hearing that he is eternally abiding and does not enter nirvāṇa, one does not give rise to joy—such a bhikṣu is then able to adorn the twin śāla trees.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Śāriputra is that very person.”
Why is this? It is because Śāriputra is well able to accomplish and fully possess such great wisdom as this. "Good son!..."

If there is a bhikṣu who can declare that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, who attains an adamantine body without limit, who is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, whose body and mind are unimpeded, and who attains the eight masteries—such a bhikṣu is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then only the Tathāgata is that person.”

Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is adamantine and boundless, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; his body and mind are unimpeded, for he possesses the eight masteries.
World-Honored One!
Only the Tathāgata is able to adorn these twin śāla trees; were he not present, they would not be dignified.
We pray that out of great compassion, for the sake of this adornment, you will remain forever here in this śāla grove.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
All dharmas are by nature non-abiding; why do you say, ‘I pray that the Tathāgata abide’?”
Good son! Generally speaking, that which is called "abiding" refers to material phenomena (rūpa-dharma); because they arise from causes and conditions, they are called "abiding.
Since there is no place for causes and conditions, it is therefore called "abiding in non-abiding."
The Tathāgata has already severed all bonds of form; how, then, could one say that the Tathāgata dwells?
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Good son!
Abiding is called pride; because of pride, one does not attain liberation. Because one does not attain liberation, it is called "abiding. Who possesses this pride?
From where does it come?
Therefore, it is called "dwelling in non-dwelling.
The Tathāgata has forever severed all pride; how then can one say, "May the Tathāgata dwell"?
To "dwell" is a term for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); since the Tathāgata has already severed conditioned phenomena, he does not dwell.

Dwelling is called the dharma of emptiness; the Tathāgata has already severed such dharmas of emptiness, and for this reason has attained permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Why, then, do you say, "May the Tathāgata dwell"?

"Dwelling" refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). Since the Tathāgata has already severed these twenty-five states of existence, why do you say, "May the Tathāgata dwell"?

Those who dwell are all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); the noble ones (*ārya*) neither go, nor come, nor dwell. Since the Tathāgata has already severed the marks of going, coming, and dwelling, how can you say he dwells?
Now, that which is "non-abiding" is called the "boundless body. Since the body is boundless, how can you say, "I pray only that the Tathāgata will abide in the Śāla grove"?
If he were to abide in this grove, then he would possess a bounded body; if he has a bounded body, then he is impermanent. Yet the Tathāgata is eternal—how then can you say he abides?
That which is non-abiding is called space; the nature of the Tathāgata is identical to space—how, then, can it be said to abide?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding is called the Vajra-samādhi; the Vajra-samādhi destroys all abidings, and the Vajra-samādhi is itself the Tathāgata—how, then, can it be said to abide?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding is called an illusion; since the Tathāgata is identical to an illusion, how can one say he abides?
Moreover, non-abiding is termed being without beginning or end; since the nature of the Tathāgata has no beginning or end, how can one say he abides?
Furthermore, "non-abiding" is called the boundless *dharmadhātu*. Since the boundless *dharmadhātu* is itself the Tathāgata, how can one say that he abides?

Moreover, "non-abiding" is called the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* knows all phenomena without attachment; because it is without attachment, it is named *Śūraṅgama*. The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; how then can one say that he abides?

Furthermore, "non-abiding" refers to the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*). Since the Tathāgata has perfected this power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible, how could one say that he abides?

Moreover, "non-abiding" refers to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). If the perfection of giving were to abide, then one would not be able to reach the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); for this reason, the perfection of giving is called non-abiding.
If the Tathāgata does not even abide in the *prajñāpāramitā*, how can one wish to say that the Tathāgata eternally dwells in the *śāla* grove?

Furthermore, that which is "non-abiding" is called the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If the Tathāgata were to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, he would be unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is what is meant by "abiding in non-abiding."
Furthermore, "non-abiding" refers to the boundless realm of sentient beings; the Tathāgata reaches every part of this boundless realm of all sentient beings, yet remains nowhere.

Furthermore, "non-abiding" means having no dwelling place; having no dwelling place means non-existence; non-existence means non-arising; non-arising means non-death; non-death means signlessness; signlessness means non-binding; non-binding means non-attachment; non-attachment means outflowlessness (*anāsrava*); outflowlessness is goodness; goodness is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the unconditioned is Great Nirvāṇa; Great Nirvāṇa is permanence; permanence is self (*ātman*); self is purity; purity is bliss; and permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the Tathāgata.
"Good son! Just as space does not abide in the east, the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below,
so too the Tathāgata does not abide in the east, the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below."
Good son! If anyone were to say that evil deeds of body, speech, and mind result in wholesome fruits, such a thing is impossible.
Likewise, it is also impossible for wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind to result in unwholesome fruits.
If one were to say that ordinary beings can see the Buddha-nature while Bodhisattvas of the ten stages cannot, this is also impossible.

Likewise, it is impossible for those of the icchantika class, those who have committed the five heinous crimes, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, or those who violate the four grave prohibitions to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
It is impossible for a Bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage to fall into the three evil realms due to the causes and conditions of afflictions.
It is also impossible for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while in the body of a real woman.
That the icchantikas are eternal while the Three Jewels are impermanent is impossible;
likewise, that the Tathāgata dwells in the city of Kuśinagara is also impossible. Good son!

"The Tathāgata has now entered the cave of profound meditative concentration through the Great Samādhi in this city of Kuśinagara; because the multitude does not see him, it is called 'entering Nirvāṇa.
Siṃhanāda asked, "For what reason does the Tathāgata enter the cave of meditative concentration?"
"Good son, it is because they wish to deliver all sentient beings; to cause those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them;
and to cause those who have already planted roots of goodness to increase them."
To cause unripened virtuous fruits to ripen;
to teach those whose fruits have already ripened so that they may proceed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and to cause those who disparage wholesome dharmas to give rise to respect for them.
It is to cause those who are heedless to abandon their heedlessness;
it is to engage in discourse with Mañjuśrī and other great fragrant elephants;
and it is because he wishes to transform those who delight in recitation so that they come to cherish meditative concentration deeply.
It is for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings through the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, and the celestial conduct;
it is for the sake of contemplating the profound treasury of the unshared Dharma;
and it is because he wishes to rebuke disciples who are negligent.
The Tathāgata is eternally tranquil and yet still delights in meditative concentration; how much more so should you, whose afflictions are not yet exhausted, refrain from giving rise to negligence?
This is for the purpose of rebuking those wicked bhikṣus who accept and store the eight kinds of impure things and who possess neither few desires nor contentment;
and it is to cause sentient beings to revere the dharma of meditative concentration they have heard.
"For this reason and by these causes and conditions, one enters the cave of meditative concentration.
The Lion’s Roar said,
"World-Honored One!"
The concentration of signlessness is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Nirvāṇa is named "signless.
For what reason and by what causal conditions is it named "signless"?
“Good son! Because it is devoid of the ten characteristics. What are these ten?
These are the so-called marks of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, arising, abiding, and perishing, as well as the marks of male and female; these are called the ten marks.
Because it lacks such characteristics, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).

Good son! One who clings to signs gives rise to delusion; because of delusion, craving arises; because of craving, one is bound; because of being bound, one undergoes birth; because of birth, there is death; and because of death, there is impermanence.

One who does not cling to signs does not give rise to delusion; because delusion does not arise, there is no craving; because there is no craving, there is no bondage; because there is no bondage, one does not undergo birth; because one does not undergo birth, there is no death; because there is no death, it is called "eternal. For this reason, nirvana is named "eternal."
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of bhikṣu is able to sever the ten signs?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
If there is a bhikṣu who repeatedly cultivates the three marks, he will sever the ten marks.”
Repeatedly cultivating the sign of samādhi-concentration, repeatedly cultivating the sign of wisdom, and repeatedly cultivating the sign of equanimity—these are called the three signs.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
What are called the characteristics of concentration, wisdom, and equanimity?”
Regarding "concentration is samādhi": all sentient beings possess samādhi; why then do you say that one must practice samādhi?
If the mind is fixed upon a single object, it is called samādhi; if it attends to other conditions, it is not called samādhi.
If it is not fixed, it is not omniscience; if it is not omniscience, how can it be called "fixed"?

If one attains samādhi through a single practice, then all other practices would not be samādhi; if they are not samādhi, they are not omniscience; and if they are not omniscience, how can they be called samādhi?
"The two characteristics of wisdom and relinquishment are likewise thus.
The Buddha said: "Good son!"
As you have said, that which takes a single object as its condition is called samādhi, while other conditions are not called samādhi; this is not so. Why is that?
In this way, because other conditions likewise share a single object, the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are also thus.
Furthermore, the claim that sentient beings possess samādhi from the outset and do not need to cultivate it is also incorrect.
Why is this? That which is called samādhi is known as the "excellent samādhi. Since it does not yet truly exist within any sentient being, how can you say that there is no need to cultivate it?

Abiding in such a wholesome samādhi, one contemplates all dharmas as having the characteristic of wholesome wisdom; not perceiving any distinct characteristic between the samādhi and wisdom is called the characteristic of relinquishment.
"Furthermore, good son!
If one grasps the marks of form but is unable to contemplate the marks of form as permanent or impermanent, this is called samādhi.
If one is able to contemplate the marks of form as permanent or impermanent, this is called the mark of wisdom."
To contemplate all phenomena with equanimity through samādhi and wisdom is called the mark of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Good son!
It is like a skilled charioteer driving a team of four horses; when the speed is appropriately regulated, this appropriate regulation of speed is called the mark of equanimity.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: if samādhi is predominant, he cultivates wisdom; if wisdom is predominant, he cultivates samādhi.
When samādhi and wisdom are equal, this is called equanimity (upekṣā).
"Good son!
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess great power of wisdom but little power of samādhi; for this reason, they cannot clearly perceive the Buddha-nature.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess great power of samādhi but little power of wisdom; by these causes and conditions, they do not see the Buddha-nature."

Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the equality of meditative concentration and wisdom, they clearly perceive the Buddha-nature with complete and unimpeded clarity, as if looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of their hand.
To see the Buddha-nature is called "the relinquishing of marks."
Śamatha is called "able to extinguish," because it can extinguish all afflictions and fetters;
furthermore, śamatha is called "able to discipline," because it can discipline the faculties from being evil and unwholesome;
furthermore, śamatha is called "quiescence," because it can cause the three karmas to become quiescent.
Furthermore, *śamatha* is called "detachment," for it enables sentient beings to distance themselves from the five desires;
furthermore, *śamatha* is called "purification," for it can purify the three turbid dharmas of greed, hatred, and delusion.
For these reasons, it is termed the characteristic of concentration (*samādhi*).
Vipassanā is called right view; it is also called clear seeing, capable seeing, universal seeing, sequential seeing, and seeing of specific characteristics; this is what is meant by wisdom.
Upekṣā is called equanimity; it is also called non-contention, non-contemplation, and non-exertion—this is termed relinquishment (upekṣā).
“Good son! There are two kinds of śamatha:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.”
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, those who have attained accomplishment; second, those who have not.
Those who have attained accomplishment are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Those who do not achieve [this] are the so-called śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
Furthermore, there are three types:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
The inferior refers to ordinary worldlings; the middling refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the superior refers to buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, regression; second, abiding; third, progress; and fourth, the ability to bring great benefit.
Furthermore, there are five kinds,
namely the five wisdoms (pañca-jñāna) samādhis. What are these five?

First is the samādhi of non-nourishment; second is the samādhi of faultlessness; third is the samādhi of the single-minded purity of body and mind; fourth is the samādhi of the mutual joy of cause and effect; fifth is the samādhi of constant mindfulness.

Furthermore, there are six kinds: first, the samādhi of contemplating the skeleton; second, the samādhi of loving-kindness; third, the samādhi of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination; fourth, the samādhi of ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing); fifth, the samādhi of right mindfulness regarding vitarka and vicāra; and sixth, the samādhi of contemplating birth, cessation, abiding, and change.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds, namely the seven factors of enlightenment:

first, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; second, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena; third, the factor of enlightenment of energy; fourth, the factor of enlightenment of joy; fifth, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; sixth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration; and seventh, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds: first, the samādhi of the srotāpanna;

second, the samādhi of the sakṛdāgāmin; third, the samādhi of the anāgāmin; fourth, the samādhi of the arhat; fifth, the samādhi of the pratyekabuddha; sixth, the samādhi of the bodhisattva; and seventh, the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s awakening and realization.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds, namely the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) of samādhi: first, the liberation-samādhi of perceiving external forms while possessing internal perception of form;

second, the liberation-samādhi of perceiving external forms while lacking internal perception of form; third, the liberation-samādhi of personally realizing the pure liberation; fourth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds, namely the nine successive concentrations (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*):
the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the samādhi of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, there are ten kinds, namely the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) samādhis.

What are the ten? First, the samādhi of the all-pervading earth; second, the samādhi of the all-pervading water; third, the samādhi of the all-pervading wind; fourth, the samādhi of the all-pervading blue; fifth, the samādhi of the all-pervading yellow; sixth, the samādhi of the all-pervading red; seventh, the samādhi of the all-pervading white; eighth, the samādhi of the all-pervading space; ninth, the samādhi of the all-pervading consciousness; and tenth, the samādhi of the all-pervading non-existence.
Furthermore, there are countless varieties, namely those of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Good son, these are called the characteristics of samādhi. "Good son!
Wisdom is of two kinds:
first, mundane; second, supramundane.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
The first is *prajñā*, the second is *vipaśyanā*, and the third is *jñāna*.
*Prajñā* refers to all sentient beings; *vipaśyanā* refers to all noble ones (*ārya*); and *jñāna* refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, *prajñā* is called "discerning characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), *vipaśyanā* is called "comprehensive characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and *jñāna* is called "deconstructing characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-bhañjana*).
There are also four kinds, namely, the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
“Good son! One cultivates śamatha for three reasons.
What are these three?
First, for the sake of non-negligence; second, for the sake of adorning great wisdom; third, for the sake of attaining mastery.
Furthermore, one cultivates vipaśyanā for three reasons.
What are the three?
First, for the sake of contemplating the evil retributions of birth and death; second, for the desire to increase all roots of goodness; third, for the purpose of destroying all afflictions.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 30. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 31.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
In the eleventh chapter, "The Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva," part five,
the Lion’s Roar said:
"World-Honored One!
"As it is said in the sutras: 'If vipaśyanā can destroy the afflictions, for what reason does one further cultivate śamatha?
The Buddha replied: 'Good son!'"
As for your statement that vipaśyanā destroys the afflictions, this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions; and when afflictions exist, there is no wisdom. How, then, can you say that vipaśyanā is able to destroy the afflictions?
Good son! For example, when there is light, there is no darkness; when there is darkness, there is no light.
If someone were to say that light can destroy darkness, such a thing is impossible.
Good son! Who possesses wisdom?
Who possesses afflictions?
Yet it is said that wisdom can destroy afflictions;
if it did not exist, there would be nothing to destroy. Good son!
If it is said that wisdom can destroy afflictions, does it destroy them by reaching them or by not reaching them?
If it destroys them without reaching them, then ordinary beings should also be able to destroy them.
If it were to break upon reaching [the object], it should break at the first moment of contact; if it does not break at the first moment, it will not break later either.
If it breaks as soon as it arrives, then it has not actually reached [the object]; how then can you say that wisdom is able to break [it]?
If it is claimed that [insight] can destroy [afflictions] whether it reaches them or not, this meaning is incorrect.
Furthermore, regarding the Vipassanā that destroys afflictions, does it act alone to destroy them?
Is it broken because of companions?
If it could be broken by one alone, why would a bodhisattva cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?
If it is broken because of companions, one should know that it cannot be broken when alone.

If one cannot do it alone, one cannot do it with a companion; just as a single blind person cannot see forms, even if accompanied by a multitude of blind people, they still cannot see—so too is vipassanā.

“Good son! Just as the earth has the nature of solidity, fire the nature of heat, water the nature of moisture, and wind the nature of motion—yet these natures, from the solidity of earth to the motion of wind, are not produced by causes and conditions; their nature is simply so of itself.”
Just as the nature of the four great elements is such, so too are the afflictions;
their nature is inherently severed. If they are already severed, why say that wisdom can sever them?
For this reason, vipaśyanā is definitively unable to destroy the various afflictions.
Good son! Just as the nature of salt is salty and makes other things salty,
and the nature of honey is sweet and makes other things sweet;
The nature of water is moisture, which causes other things to become moist;
the nature of wisdom is cessation, which causes phenomena to cease.
This interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? If a phenomenon is without cessation, how could wisdom forcibly cause it to cease?
If one were to say that just as salt’s pungency causes other things to become pungent, so too does the cessation of wisdom cause other phenomena to cease, this is also not the case.
Why is this? Because the nature of wisdom perishes from moment to moment.
If it perishes from moment to moment, how can one say that it is able to extinguish other dharmas?
For this reason, the nature of wisdom does not destroy afflictions.
"Good son! All dharmas have two kinds of cessation: [the cessation of arising and the cessation of non-arising]."
The first is extinction by nature; the second is ultimate extinction.
If it were extinction by nature, how could one say that wisdom is able to extinguish it?
If one says that wisdom can burn away afflictions as fire burns objects, this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? Just as when fire burns an object there remains some residual ash,
if wisdom were like that, there would necessarily be some remaining residue.
Just as when an axe fells a tree, the place where it was cut can be seen;
if wisdom were like that, what would there be to see?
If wisdom could cause the afflictions to depart, those afflictions should appear elsewhere, just as the non-Buddhists appeared at Kuśinagara after departing from the six great cities.
If afflictions do not manifest elsewhere, then one knows that wisdom cannot cause them to depart.
Good son! If the nature of all dharmas is itself empty, who could cause them to arise?
Who can cause them to cease?
They arise and cease differently, without a creator. Good son!
If one cultivates meditative concentration, one attains such correct knowledge and correct view; for this reason, I have said in my sutras:
"If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates meditative concentration, he is able to see the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
"Good son! If one does not cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one cannot even comprehend worldly matters, let alone those that transcend the world.

One who lacks concentration will stumble and fall on level ground; their mind will attend to different phenomena, their mouth will utter different words, their ears will hear different sounds, their mind will understand different meanings, they will wish to compose different characters, their hands will write different scripts, they will wish to travel by different paths, and their body will traverse different tracks."
"If there are those who practice the samādhi of meditative concentration, they will obtain great benefit, even unto Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
'Good son!'"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are endowed with two dharmas are able to bring great benefit:
first, concentration; second, wisdom. Good son!
Just as when cutting *kuśa* grass, it snaps if pulled too forcefully;
so it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates these two dharmas. Good son!
Just as when pulling out a firm piece of wood, one first moves it with the hand and then it is easily extracted;
so too it is with the bodhisattva’s concentration and wisdom: first one moves with concentration, and subsequently one extracts with wisdom.
"Good son!
Just as when washing a soiled garment, first using lye and afterwards using clear water, the garment becomes bright and clean;
the meditative concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva are likewise."
"Good son!
Just as one first recites and then understands the meaning,
so it is with the concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva."
"Good son!
It is like a valiant man who first firmly adorns himself with armor and weapons before entering the fray; he is then able to destroy the enemy thieves.
The samādhi and wisdom of a bodhisattva are also like this."
Good son! It is like a skilled craftsman who, using tongs and a crucible, freely and at will stirs and melts gold;
the meditative concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva are also like this.
"Good son! Just as a clear mirror reflects the image of a face,
so too are the concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva."
"Good son!
Just as one first levels the ground and then sows the seeds, and first receives instruction from a teacher and later contemplates its meaning;
so too it is with the concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva."
For this reason, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate these two dharmas, they are able to bring about great benefit. "Good son!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate these two dharmas, they discipline and regulate the five faculties and endure all sufferings—namely, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, being struck, beaten, reviled, or insulted; being bitten by fierce beasts or stung by mosquitoes and gadflies. They constantly restrain their minds so as not to let them become lax, do not practice unrighteousness for the sake of gain and offerings, cannot be defiled by adventitious afflictions, and are not deluded by various false and heterodox views. They are always able to remain far removed from all evil thoughts and reflections, and before long they will achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they desire to achieve [enlightenment] for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates these two dharmas, the violent winds of the four inversions cannot shake him, just as Mount Sumeru cannot be moved despite being buffeted by the four winds;
he cannot be uprooted by non-Buddhist teachers or false masters, just as Śakra’s banner cannot be shifted."

They cannot be deceived by various heterodox arts and are constantly endowed with the subtle, supreme peace and bliss. They are able to understand the profound and secret meaning of the Tathāgata; they do not rejoice when experiencing pleasure and do not grieve when encountering suffering. Honored and praised by devas and worldlings alike, they clearly perceive both birth-and-death and that which is beyond birth-and-death. Being well-versed in understanding the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), their bodies possess the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; this is what is called the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa.

“Good son! The characteristic of concentration is called the samādhi of emptiness; the characteristic of wisdom is called the samādhi of wishlessness; the characteristic of equanimity is called the samādhi of signlessness.”
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who well knows the time for concentration, the time for wisdom, and the time for equanimity, as well as knowing what is not the [proper] time, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the path to enlightenment."
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva know the proper time and the improper time?”

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to great arrogance because of experiencing pleasure, or gives rise to arrogance because of preaching the Dharma, or gives rise to arrogance because of diligent effort, or gives rise to arrogance when understanding the meaning or engaging in skillful questioning and answering, or gives rise to arrogance because of associating with evil associates, or gives rise to arrogance because of giving away highly valued objects, or gives rise to arrogance because of the merit of worldly wholesome dharmas, or gives rise to arrogance because of being honored by those who are wealthy and noble—know that at such times it is inappropriate to cultivate wisdom; rather, one should cultivate meditative concentration. This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the timely and the untimely.”

If there is a bodhisattva who diligently practices with vigor, yet has not attained the benefit of the bliss of nirvana, and because of this lack of attainment gives rise to a mind of regret; or because of dull faculties is unable to subdue the five sensory organs; or because the power of various defilements and afflictions is so prevalent that he suspects his own precepts have become weakened—then one should know that at such a time it is inappropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), but rather one should cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*). This is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the appropriate and inappropriate times.
"Good son!

If a bodhisattva’s two dharmas of concentration and wisdom are unequal, you should know that at such a time it is inappropriate to cultivate equanimity; if the two dharmas are equal, then it is appropriate to cultivate it. This is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the timely and the untimely."
"Good son!

If there are bodhisattvas who, while practicing concentration and wisdom, give rise to afflictions, you should know that at such a time it is not appropriate for them to practice equanimity; rather, they should recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures."

Mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of the heavens, and mindfulness of relinquishment—this is called the cultivation of relinquishment. Good son!
If there is a bodhisattva who practices these three aspects of the Dharma, by these causes and conditions they will attain formless nirvana.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
Because it is devoid of the ten marks, it is called Great Nirvana.”

Regarding that which is signless (*animitta*), for what further reasons is it called unborn (*ajāta*), unarisen (*anutpanna*), unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), a dwelling (*layana*), an island (*dvīpa*), a refuge (*śaraṇa*), peace (*kṣema*), extinction (*nirvāṇa*), cessation (*upaśama*), free from all sickness and suffering (*vigata-vyādhi-duḥkha*), and non-existent (*akiṃcana*)?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Because there are no causes or conditions, it is called 'unborn'."
Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called "without emergence.
Because there is no creation of karma, it is called "without action.
Because it does not enter into the five views, it is called a "dwelling."
Because it is free from the four floods, it is called an island.
Because it tames sentient beings, it is called a refuge.
Because it destroys the thieves of the fetters, it is called peace and security.
Because the fires of all fetters have been extinguished, it is called "extinction" (nirvāṇa).
Because it is free from applied and sustained thought, it is called "nirvāṇa.
Because it is far removed from clamor and bustle, it is called "quiescence."
Because one has forever severed the certainty of death, it is called "freedom from illness.
Because all things are non-existent, it is called "non-possession. Good son!
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, they immediately attain clear and penetrating vision of the Buddha-nature.
Siṃha-nāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
“By accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva see such signless nirvāṇa up to non-existence?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they are able to clearly perceive nirvāṇa, from its signlessness up to its non-existence. What are these ten?
First, the full possession of faith.
What is meant by being fully endowed with faith?

It is to have deep faith that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are eternal; that the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest through skillful means; and that all sentient beings, including those of the icchantika nature, possess the Buddha-nature.

Not believing that the Tathāgata undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death; that he practiced asceticism; that Devadatta truly caused a schism in the Saṃgha and drew blood from the Buddha's body; or that the Tathāgata will ultimately enter parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma will be extinguished—this is called a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of faith.
"Second is the fulfillment of pure precepts.
What is meant by the fulfillment of pure precepts? Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who claims his precepts are pure, yet although he does not engage in physical union with that woman, when seeing her he utters mocking words or engages in playful jesting, such a bodhisattva has fulfilled the conditions for desire; he has violated the pure precepts, defiled the holy life, and rendered the precepts impure. He cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who claims his precepts are pure; yet, although he does not physically unite with that woman nor engage in flirtatious jesting or laughter, he hears from behind a wall the various sounds of the woman’s necklaces, bracelets, and bangles, and his mind gives rise to attachment. Such a bodhisattva has fulfilled the dharma of desire, violated the pure precepts, brought disgrace upon the holy life, and rendered the precepts defiled; he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who claims his precepts are pure; although he does not engage in physical union with women, nor converse with them in jest, nor listen to their voices, yet when he sees a man pursuing a woman, or a woman pursuing a man, he immediately gives rise to lustful attachment. Such a bodhisattva has accomplished the dharma of desire, has violated the pure precepts, has defiled the holy life, and has rendered the precepts impure; he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who claim their precepts are pure; yet, although they do not engage in physical union with women, nor engage in flirtatious conversation, nor listen to their voices, nor see men and women following one another, they do so for the sake of being born in heaven to experience the pleasures of the five senses. Such bodhisattvas have accomplished the dharma of desire, thereby violating the pure precepts, defiling the holy life, and making the precepts impure; they cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who maintains pure precepts, yet does not do so for the sake of the precepts themselves, nor for the sake of the śīla-pāramitā, nor for the sake of sentient beings, nor for the sake of gain and offerings, nor for the sake of bodhi, nor for the sake of nirvāṇa, nor for the sake of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but solely for the sake of the supreme ultimate truth—good son!"
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of pure precepts.
"Third is to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). As for a spiritual friend:
if there is one who can expound faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom, causing others to receive and practice them, this is called a Bodhisattva’s spiritual friend."
"Fourth is delighting in tranquility.
As for tranquility, it refers to the tranquility of body and mind.
To contemplate the profound realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) of all dharmas is called tranquility."
"Fifth is diligence (*vīrya*).
As for diligence, it means binding the mind to contemplate the Four Noble Truths; even if one's head were on fire, one would never relinquish this effort—this is called diligence."
"Sixth is the perfection of mindfulness.

As for the perfection of mindfulness, it refers to mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of the devas, and mindfulness of renunciation; this is called the perfection of mindfulness."
"Seventh is gentle speech.
Gentle speech refers to truthful speech, exquisite speech, greeting others with kindness before they speak, timely speech, and authentic speech; this is called gentle speech."
“Eighth is the protection of the Dharma.

As for the protection of the Dharma, it means to cherish and delight in the True Dharma, constantly delighting in its exposition, recitation, transcription, contemplation of its meaning, and its wide proclamation and dissemination so that it may spread. If one sees someone transcribing, explaining, reciting, praising, or contemplating its meaning, one provides them with the necessities of life—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—as offerings. For the sake of protecting the Dharma, one does not begrudge even body or life; this is called the protection of the Dharma.”

"Ninth, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees fellow students or fellow practitioners of the precepts who are in need, he seeks from others whatever is required to provide for them—be it bowls, dyed robes, requisites for nursing the sick, clothing, food and drink, bedding, or dwellings—and supplies them with these things."
"Tenth is the perfection of wisdom.
Wisdom consists in contemplating that the Tathāgata is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature."

To contemplate the two aspects of phenomena—namely, emptiness and non-emptiness; permanence and impermanence; bliss and non-bliss; self and non-self; purity and impurity; that some phenomena can be severed while others cannot; that some phenomena arise from conditions, some are seen through conditions, some are fruits of conditions, and some are not fruits of conditions—is called the perfection of wisdom.
