“Good son! This is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with ten dharmas, whereby one is able to clearly perceive the signlessness of nirvāṇa.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously told Cunda: ‘You have now already seen the Buddha-nature, attained Great Nirvana, and accomplished Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’”
What is the meaning of this, World-Honored One? As it is said in the sutras:

if one gives to an animal, one receives a hundredfold reward; if one gives to an icchantika, one receives a thousandfold reward; if one gives to a precept-keeper, one receives a hundred-thousandfold reward; if one gives to a non-Buddhist who has severed the afflictions, one receives immeasurable reward; if one makes offerings to those on the four stages of approach and the four fruits up to a pratyekabuddha, one receives immeasurable reward; and if one gives to a non-retrogressive bodhisattva, a bodhisattva in his final body, or a Tathāgata, World-Honored One, the resulting merit and reward is immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable.
If the Mahāsattva Cunda were to receive such immeasurable retribution, that retribution would be inexhaustible; when, then, would he attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
World-Honored One!

The sūtras further state that if a person performs wholesome or unwholesome karma with a resolute mind, they will certainly obtain its retribution—whether to be experienced in the present life, in the next birth, or in subsequent lives.
Cunda’s wholesome karma was performed with a sincere and earnest mind; you should know that this karma will certainly result in its retribution.
If it must inevitably be experienced as retribution, how can he attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"How, furthermore, can one see the Buddha-nature?
World-Honored One!
In the sutras it is further taught that giving to three kinds of people yields inexhaustible retribution:"
First, the sick person; second, one's parents; third, the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If all sentient beings were such that they possessed no karma pertaining to the desire realm, they would immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Karma pertaining to the realm of form and the formless realm is likewise so.
World-Honored One!
As it says in a verse of the *Dharmapada*:
"Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts,
is there any place on earth where one can escape and not receive the results of one's karma.
Furthermore, Aniruddha said:
“World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, by giving a single meal as an offering, for eighty thousand kalpas I did not fall into the three evil realms.
World-Honored One!
"If even the gift of a single meal yields such a reward, how much more so for Cunda, who with a faithful heart has given to the Buddha, fully accomplishing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
World-Honored One!"

If the retribution for wholesome fruits cannot be exhausted, how can the offenses of slandering the Vaipulya sutras, committing the five heinous crimes, violating the four grave prohibitions, or the transgressions of an icchantika ever be exhausted?
"If they cannot be exhausted, how can one perceive the Buddha-nature and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!

Only two kinds of people can attain immeasurable and boundless merit—incalculable and ineffable—which enables them to dry up the torrential river of drifting through birth and death, to subdue demonic enemies and topple the banners of Māra, and to turn the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel of the Tathāgata:
first, those who ask well; second, those who answer well."
"Good son! Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of karma is the most profound. Good son!"
There are sentient beings who, regarding the conditions of karma, have minds that are dismissive and lack faith; it is for the sake of delivering them that I speak thus.
Good son! All actions performed are either light or heavy, and each of these two types of karma—light and heavy—further possesses two aspects.
The first is determinate, and the second is indeterminate.
Good son! Some people say:
"Evil karma has no fruit.
If one says that evil karma definitely has fruit, how is it that by merely blowing air upon a caṇḍāla, one could be reborn in heaven,
or that Aṅgulimāla could attain the fruit of liberation?"
For this reason, you should know that there are actions whose results are certain to be obtained and those whose results are not certain to be obtained.
It is to eliminate such false views that I have spoken these words in the sūtras: "There is no action performed that does not bear fruit."
“Good son! There are heavy karmas that can be made light, and there are light karmas that can be made heavy.
This applies not to all people, but only to the foolish and the wise; therefore, you should know that not all karma necessarily results in a fixed fruit.”
Although it is not necessarily attained, it is also not unattainable. Good son!
All sentient beings are of two kinds:
First are the wise, and second are the ignorant.
A person of wisdom, by the power of their insight, can cause the most heavy karma of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life.
"Those who are foolish receive the heavy retribution of hell for the light karma of their present lives.
Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
"If it were so, then one should not seek the pure brahmacarya or the fruit of liberation.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If all karma were destined to yield its fruit, then one would not need to seek the holy life (brahmacarya) and liberation.
Because it is not fixed, one cultivates the holy life and the fruit of liberation.
"Noble son!
If one can distance oneself from all unwholesome karma, one will obtain wholesome fruits.
If one distances oneself from wholesome karma, one will obtain unwholesome fruits."
If all karma were destined to yield its fruit, then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path; yet if the Path is not cultivated, there is no liberation.
The reason all noble ones cultivate the Path is to destroy fixed karma and obtain light retribution, for indeterminate karma does not have a [fixed] retribution.
If all karma were destined to yield its fruit, then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path; for it is impossible that anyone could attain liberation without cultivating the Noble Path.
It is likewise impossible that one who has not attained liberation could attain nirvana. Good son!
If all karma were to necessarily yield its fruit, then the purely wholesome karma performed in a single lifetime would cause one to experience peace and happiness forever thereafter.
If the extremely heavy evil karma committed in a single lifetime must also result in the perpetual experience of great suffering and affliction,
then if such were the nature of karmic fruition, there would be no cultivation of the path, nor liberation, nor nirvana.

If humans were born as humans and brahmins were born as brahmins, then there would be no such thing as low castes or low-born people; humans would remain eternally human, and brahmins would remain eternally brahmins.
If one performs an action in childhood, it should be experienced in childhood; it should not be experienced in middle age or old age.

If one commits an evil deed in old age that leads to rebirth in hell, the experience should not occur immediately upon the first body in hell, but rather should wait until one is old before being experienced.
If one does not kill during old age, one should not obtain longevity in one's prime; if there were no longevity in one's prime, how could one reach old age?
For karma is never lost.
If karma is never lost, how can there be the cultivation of the path and nirvana?
Good son! There are two kinds of karma: determinate and indeterminate.
Determinate karma is of two types:
First is the certainty of retribution (*vipāka-niyama*), and second is the certainty of time (*kāla-niyama*).
There are cases where the retribution is certain but the time is uncertain; when conditions converge, one experiences it.

Or there is experience at three times, namely: experience in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), experience in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and experience in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
"Good son!

If one performs deeds such as good or evil with a concentrated mind, and after having performed them, gives rise to deep faith and joy, and further makes vows to make offerings to the Triple Gem, this is called determinate karma."
“Good son! The roots of goodness of the wise are firm and deep, and thus difficult to shake; for this reason, they can cause heavy karma to become light.
The foolish person’s unwholesomeness is profound and deep, and thus can cause light karma to result in a heavy retribution.”
For this reason, all karmas are not termed "fixed.
Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess no karma for the hells, they give rise to great vows to be born within the hells for the sake of sentient beings.
"Good son!
In the past, when the lifespan of sentient beings was one hundred years, as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River underwent retribution in the hells.
Having seen this, I immediately made a great vow to take on a body in the hells."
At that time, the Bodhisattva truly had no such karma; rather, for the sake of sentient beings, he underwent the retribution of the hells.

During that time, while in the hells for immeasurable years, he extensively expounded and analyzed the twelve divisions of the sutras for all the offenders. Having heard them, those people destroyed their evil karmic results, causing the hells to become empty, with the sole exception of the icchantikas. This is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva undergoing this evil karma neither in the present life, nor in a future life, nor in a subsequent rebirth.
"Furthermore, good son!
Within this Bhadrakalpa, immeasurable sentient beings fall among the animals to undergo the fruits of their evil karma.

Having seen this, I again made a vow; desiring to preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, I have taken the bodies of various creatures—such as deer, bears, monkeys, nāgas, snakes, garuḍas, birds, pigeons, fish, turtles, rabbits, elephants, oxen, and horses."
"Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly has no such evil karma of an animal; rather, by the power of great vows for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests the reception of this body. This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva not receiving this evil karma in the present, future, or subsequent lives."
"Furthermore, good son!

Within this Bhadrakalpa, there are again immeasurable and boundless sentient beings born among the hungry ghosts (preta). Some eat vomit, fat, flesh, pus, blood, excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva; their lifespans last for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, and they have never even heard the name of water, let alone having seen it with their own eyes and being able to drink it."
If one sees water from afar and goes toward it with the intent to reach it, upon arrival it transforms into fierce flames, pus, and blood;
or sometimes it does not transform, but many people appear holding spears and lances to block, seize, and restrain one, not allowing one to proceed;
or when rain falls from the sky, it turns into fire upon reaching the body—these are called the retributions of evil karma.
"Good son!

Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas truly have no such fruits of evil karma, they make vows to take on such bodies for the sake of transforming sentient beings and enabling them to attain liberation. This is called a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives."

“Good son! During this Bhadrakalpa, I was born into a family of butchers, where I raised chickens, pigs, oxen, and sheep; I practiced hunting with snares and nets and trapping with traps; I lived in the dwellings of caṇḍālas and committed robbery and theft.”

In truth, a bodhisattva has no such evil karma; rather, in order to deliver sentient beings and enable them to attain liberation, they assume such a body through the power of their great vows. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva not experiencing such evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.

“Good son! Within this Bhadrakalpa, you shall again be born in a borderland where you will frequently give rise to greed, anger, and delusion; you will practice what is contrary to the Dharma, lack faith in the Three Jewels and the retribution of future lives, and fail to show reverence to your parents, elders, seniors, and those of long standing.”
"Good son!

At that time, the bodhisattva truly has no such karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, he is born therein through the power of his great vows. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives."

“Good son! Within this Bhadrakalpa, you will again receive a female body, an evil body, a body of greed, a body of hatred, a body of delusion, a body of envy, a body of stinginess, a body of illusion, a body of deception, and a body shrouded by the hindrances.”
"Good son!

At that time, the bodhisattva likewise possesses no such karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, he vows by the power of his great vow to be born therein. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives."
“Good son! During this Bhadrakalpa, I have received the bodies of eunuchs, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, and those with indeterminate organs. Good son!”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas truly possess no such evil physical karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, they vow by the power of their great vows to be born therein. This is called the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.

“Good son! During this Bhadrakalpa, I again practiced the teachings of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas. I believed and accepted their doctrine: that there is no giving, no sacrifice, and no retribution for giving or sacrificing; no good or evil karma, and no retribution for good or evil karma; no present world nor future world; no ‘this’ nor ‘that’; no noble ones; no transformation bodies; and no path to nirvana.”
“Good son!

A bodhisattva truly possesses no such evil karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, he accepts these false dharmas through the power of his great vows. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not experience this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.”

“Good son! I recall that in the past, Devadatta and I were both caravan leaders, each with five hundred merchants of our own. For the sake of profit, we went out to the great ocean to gather precious jewels.”
Due to the conditions of their evil karma, they encountered a violent storm on the road that blew their ship apart, and all their companions perished.
At that time, because of the karmic retribution for not having committed murder and the causal condition of longevity, Devadatta and I were both blown by the wind onto dry land.
At that time, Devadatta, out of greed and attachment for his treasures, was overcome with great sorrow and suffering, and broke into loud weeping.
I then said to him: "Devadatta!..."
"There is no need to weep.
Devadatta then said to me:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
It is, for example, like a person who, impoverished and suffering from distress, goes to a cemetery and grasps a corpse with his hand, saying:
"I pray that you will now bestow upon me the pleasure of death, and I shall bestow upon you my life of poverty."
At that moment, the corpse immediately sat up and spoke to the poor man, saying:
"Good son! You yourself must endure this life of poverty; I am now exceedingly happy. Such is the joy of death; truly, I do not rejoice in your birth into poverty."
"However, today I have neither the joy of death nor even wealth; how could I not weep?
I then comforted him: "Do not grieve for now.
I have two pearls here, each of incalculable value; I shall divide one of them to bestow upon you as a gift."
I immediately divided it and gave it to him, speaking further:
"Only one who possesses life can obtain this treasure; if one lacks life, who could possibly obtain it?"
"At that time, being exhausted, I went beneath a tree to rest and fell asleep.
Devadatta’s greed was so intense that, for the sake of the remaining single jewel, he conceived an evil intent, gouged out my eyes, and plundered my jewel."
At that time, I was afflicted with sores and groaned in pain; then a woman came to where I was and asked me,
"Venerable sir,
for what reason do you groan in such a manner?"
I then explained my past life to her in detail.
Having heard this, the woman asked me again:
"What is your name?"
I then replied:
"It is called 'Truthful Speech'.
The woman said:
"How do you know that you speak the truth?
I then made this vow:
"If I now harbor any ill will toward Devadatta, may my eyes become thus forever blind."
"If it has not [permanently] ceased, you shall regain your sight.
Having spoken these words, his eyes were restored to their former state.
"O son of good family!"
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s teaching on retribution in the present life. “Good son!
I recall that in the past, I was born in the city of Pūṇḍravardhana in South India, into a family of Brahmins.”
At that time there was a king named Karapu, whose nature was violent and cruel, arrogant and conceited; though young and of handsome appearance, he was deeply addicted to the five desires.
At that time, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I was practicing silent meditation outside that city.

Then, during the spring when the trees were in full bloom, the king, together with his retinue, palace ladies, and court beauties, went out of the city to sightsee; beneath the trees, he indulged himself in the five desires.
Those palace ladies abandoned the king’s pleasure excursion and came to where I was.
At that time, wishing to sever their craving, I preached the Dharma for them.
Just then, the king arrived; upon seeing me, he immediately conceived an evil thought and questioned me, saying:
"Have you now attained the fruit of arhatship? I replied, "I have not."
He spoke again:
"Have you attained the fruit of non-returning? I replied:
"No," he replied, and spoke again:
"If you have not yet attained these two fruits, you are fully possessed of the afflictions of desire; how then can you look upon my women with such self-indulgence?"
I then replied: "Great King!
You should know that although I have not yet severed the fetter of greed, my inner mind is truly free from attachment."
The King said, "Fool!

In this world there are various seers who subsist on air and eat fruit; yet they still feel greed when they see beautiful forms. How much more so for you, in the prime of your youth and not yet having severed your desires—how could you possibly remain free from greed upon seeing such forms?"
I said: "Great King!
Seeing forms without attachment is truly not due to inhaling vital energy or eating fruits; it arises entirely from fixing the mind upon impermanence and impurity."
The King said:
"If one disparages others and gives rise to slander, how can they be said to practice the pure precepts? I replied:
"Great King!
If one possesses a jealous mind, then there is slander.
I have no jealous mind; how can you say that I am slandering?"
The king said,
"Venerable Sir!
What is meant by 'precept'?"
“Great King!
Patience is called precept.
The king said:
"If patience constitutes your precept, I shall cut off your ears; if you can endure it, I shall know that you uphold the precept.
He then cut off his ears.
At that time, though his ears were severed, his facial expression remained unchanged.
At that time, the king’s ministers, having witnessed this event, immediately admonished the king, saying:
"A Great Being such as this should not be subjected to harm.
The king addressed his ministers:
"How do you know that he is a Great Being?
The ministers replied,
"We saw that his countenance did not change even when he was undergoing suffering."
The king spoke again, saying,
"I shall test him further to see whether he changes or remains unchanged.
He then cut off his nose and severed his hands and feet.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had already cultivated compassion and pity for suffering sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless eons;
yet, the Four Heavenly Kings, harboring anger and resentment in their hearts, rained down sand, gravel, and stones.
Having seen this, the king was filled with great fear; he came once more to my place, knelt down for a long time, and said:
"I only pray that you will have compassion for me and accept my repentance."
I said: "Great King!
My mind is free from anger, just as it is free from greed."
The King said:
"Venerable Sir!
How can it be known that the mind is free from anger and resentment?"
I then made this vow:
"If it is true that I am free from anger and resentment, may this body of mine be restored to its former state.
Having made this aspiration, my body was immediately restored; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s teaching on retribution in the present life.
“Good son! It is the same for wholesome karma that results in birth-retribution or subsequent retribution, as well as for unwholesome karma.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all karmas receive their retribution in the present life.”
Regarding unwholesome and evil karma that yields retribution in the present life: it is like a king who commits an evil act and the heavens send down a rain of calamity;

or as when a person points out the location of a bear to a hunter or shows a deer with the color of a jewel, and his hand falls off. This is called the experiencing of the fruit of retribution for evil karma in the present life.
Retribution in the present life refers to those such as icchantikas, or those who have committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes.
Retribution in future lives refers to those who maintain the precepts and make profound vows, aspiring that in future worlds they may always obtain such a body of pure precepts.
If there are sentient beings whose lifespan is one hundred years, or eighty years, you shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King during that time to teach and transform sentient beings.
Good son!
If karma were destined to yield only retribution in the present life, then it could not yield retribution in future lives.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the karma for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, that karma cannot yield retribution in the present life.
If karma does not receive these three kinds of retribution, it is called "indeterminate. Good son!

If one says that all karmas definitely receive retribution, then there can be no cultivation of the holy life, nor liberation and nirvana. You should know that such a person is not my disciple, but a follower of Māra.
If one says that various karmas are both determinate and indeterminate: those that are determinate are [karma] to be experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives;
those that are indeterminate are experienced when conditions converge, and not experienced when they do not converge.
For this reason, there must be the holy life (brahmacarya), liberation, and nirvana; you should know that such a person is truly my disciple and not a follower of Māra.
"Good son!
All sentient beings have more indeterminate karma and less determinate karma. For this reason, there is the cultivation of the Path.
Because of the cultivation of the Path, even heavy determinate karma can be made to be experienced lightly, while indeterminate karma does not result in retribution in the present life."
“Good son! There are two kinds of people:

first, those who transform indeterminate karma into determinate retribution; those who transform retribution to be experienced in the present life into retribution to be experienced in a future life; those who transform light retribution into heavy retribution; and those who should have received retribution among humans instead receive it in hell.”

Second, that which is fixed in timing becomes indefinite: that which was to be experienced in a future life is turned into being experienced in the present; heavy retribution is made light; and that which was to be experienced in hell becomes a light experience among humans.
Thus, between these two persons—one foolish and one wise—the wise person’s offense is lightened, while the foolish person’s is made heavy. Good son!
It is like two men who have committed an offense against the king: he with many kinsmen has his crime lightened, whereas he with few kinsmen, though his crime should have been light, becomes heavier.

It is the same for the foolish and the wise: because the wise have performed much wholesome karma, they experience heavy [retribution] as light; because the foolish have performed little wholesome karma, they experience light [retribution] as heavy.
Good son!
It is like two men, one stout and strong and the other emaciated and weak; both sink into deep mud, yet the stout one is able to emerge while the weak one sinks.
"Good son!

It is like two people who both consume poison; one possesses the power of mantras and agada medicine, while the other has none. The one who relies on the mantras and medicine cannot be harmed by the poison, whereas the one without the mantras and medicine dies immediately upon consuming it."
Good son!

It is like two people who have both drunk much liquid; one has a powerful digestive fire while the other’s is weak. He whose digestive fire is strong can digest it, whereas he whose digestive fire is weak suffers from it as an ailment.

Good son! It is like two men who have been imprisoned by a king; one possesses wisdom and the other is foolish. The wise man is able to attain liberation, while the foolish person has no prospect of release.
Good son!

It is like two people traveling together along a perilous path: one has eyes, while the other is blind. The person with eyes passes straight through without harm, whereas the blind one falls and tumbles into a deep pit.
Good son!
It is like two people who both drink wine; one eats much, while the other eats little. The one who eats much suffers no harm when drinking, whereas the one who eats little falls ill from drinking.

Good son! It is like two men who both face an enemy army: one is fully equipped and adorned with armor and weapons, while the other is bare-bodied. The one possessing weapons is able to defeat the enemy, whereas the one who is bare-bodied cannot even exert himself.

Furthermore, there were two people whose clothes were defiled by excrement and filth; one noticed it and washed them immediately, while the other noticed it but did not wash them. The one who washed them had clean and pure clothes, whereas the one who did not wash them saw their grime and filth increase day by day.

Furthermore, there were two people traveling together in a carriage; one had a spare axle, while the other did not. The one with a spare axle proceeded according to his will, whereas the one without a spare axle could not move from his place.

Furthermore, there were two people traveling together on a desolate road; one was provided with provisions, while the other went empty-handed. The one with provisions was able to cross the perilous terrain, whereas the one who went empty-handed could not pass through.

Furthermore, there were two men who were robbed by bandits; one possessed a treasure storehouse while the other had none. The one with the treasure storehouse felt no sorrow or distress in his heart, whereas the one without the storehouse was filled with grief and affliction.
"It is the same for the foolish and the wise: those who possess a treasury of merit receive heavy karma lightly;
those who lack a treasury of merit receive light karma heavily.
Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, not all karma necessarily yields a fixed fruit, nor do all sentient beings necessarily undergo its retribution.
World-Honored One!”
"How is it that some sentient beings experience light retribution in the present life for what would otherwise be heavy retribution in hell,
while others experience heavy retribution in the present life for what would otherwise be light?
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, those with wisdom; second, those who are ignorant.
Those who are able to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom are called wise."
If one is unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, such a person is called a fool.
What is meant by not cultivating the body?
If one is unable to restrain the five sensory faculties, this is called not cultivating the body.
To be unable to uphold the seven kinds of pure precepts is called not cultivating morality.
Because the mind is not disciplined, it is called not cultivating the mind.
Not cultivating noble conduct is called not cultivating wisdom.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body cannot fulfill the essence of pure precepts.
One who does not cultivate the precepts accepts and keeps the eight kinds of impure objects.
One who does not cultivate the mind is unable to practice the three kinds of marks.
One who does not cultivate wisdom does not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to contemplate the body, unable to contemplate form (*rūpa*) or the characteristics of form, and unable to contemplate the characteristics of the body; they do not know the enumeration of the body, nor do they know that this body moves from here to there. They give rise to the notion of "body" within what is not the body, and produce the notion of "form" within what is not form. Therefore, being greedily attached to the self-body and the enumeration of the body is called "not cultivating the body."
Regarding those who do not cultivate the precepts: if one receives inferior precepts, it is not called cultivating the precepts.

To observe partial precepts for the sake of self-benefit or self-discipline, rather than universally for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings, or for the purpose of upholding the unsurpassed True Dharma, but instead for the sake of being born in the heavens to experience the pleasures of the five desires—this is not called cultivating the precepts.

One who does not cultivate the mind, if their mind is distracted, will be unable to focus single-mindedly on its own domain. "One's own domain" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; "another's domain" refers to the five sensual desires.
If one cannot cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called not cultivating the mind.
If one does not skillfully guard the mind amidst evil deeds, this is called not cultivating wisdom.
"Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to deeply contemplate that this body is impermanent, unstable, fragile, perishing moment by moment, and the realm of Māra."
Those who do not cultivate ethical discipline cannot fulfill the perfection of morality (śīla-pāramitā).
Those who do not cultivate the mind cannot fulfill the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Those who do not cultivate wisdom cannot fulfill the perfection of insight (prajñā-pāramitā).
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is greedily attached to the self-body and the body belonging to the self, [thinking]: "My body is eternal and constant, without change.
One who does not cultivate precepts commits the ten unwholesome karmas for the sake of their own body.
One who does not cultivate the mind cannot restrain the mind amidst evil karma.
One who does not cultivate wisdom, because they do not restrain the mind, cannot discern dharmas such as the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body does not sever the view of self.
One who does not cultivate ethical discipline does not sever the clinging to precepts and rituals.
One who does not cultivate the mind commits actions of greed and hatred, heading toward hell.
One who does not cultivate wisdom does not sever the mind of delusion.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to contemplate that although the body may be free of fault, it is nonetheless a constant source of enmity.
“Good son! It is like a man who has an enemy constantly pursuing him, watching for an opportunity to strike;
once the wise man has become aware of this, he binds his mind in careful protection, for if he does not protect himself carefully, he will be harmed by that enemy.”

The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise; they must constantly be sustained and nourished with water, food, drink, cold, and warmth. If they are not thus protected, guarded, and cherished, they will immediately disintegrate and perish.
Good son!

It is like a brahmin who serves the god of fire, constantly offering incense and flowers, praising, prostrating, making offerings, and attending to him for a full hundred years; yet if he should touch it even once, it immediately burns the person's hand.
Although this fire receives such offerings, it never for a single moment repays the kindness of its provider.

The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise; even if they are supplied with fine incense, flowers, necklaces, clothing, food, drink, bedding, and medicine for many years, should they encounter internal or external adverse conditions, they will immediately perish and utterly fail to remember the kindness of the food and clothing provided in the past.
"Good son!
It is like a king who keeps four venomous snakes, places them in a single basket, and entrusts them to a man, commanding him to look after and nourish them.
Among these four snakes, if even one should give rise to anger, it can kill the person."
This person is terrified and constantly seeks food and drink, guarding them at all times.
The four great poisonous snakes that are the four elements (*mahābhūta*) of all sentient beings are just like this: if even one of them becomes enraged, it can destroy the body.

"Good son! It is like a person who has been ill for a long time; they should with a sincere heart seek out a physician for treatment. If they do not diligently seek rescue, they will surely die without doubt.
The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise: one should always collect the mind and not allow it to become negligent; if one is negligent, the body will immediately perish."
Good son! It is like an unbaked clay jar, which cannot endure wind and rain, nor being struck, beaten, or pressed;
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise, unable to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, wind and rain, or being struck, bound, and reviled.
"Good son!
Just as one must always carefully protect an abscess before it has ripened so that no one touches it— for if someone were to touch it, there would be great pain—
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise."
"Good son!
Just as a mule that conceives brings ruin upon its own body, so too is it with the bodies of all sentient beings: when there is wind or cold within, the body immediately suffers harm."
Good son, it is like the plantain tree: when it bears fruit, it withers;
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise. Good son!
It is also like the plantain tree, which has no solid core within;
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise. Good son!
Just as snakes and mongooses each harbor constant feelings of enmity toward one another,
so it is with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of sentient beings. Good son!
Just as the king of geese does not delight in cemeteries,
so too the bodhisattva does not crave or take pleasure in the cemetery that is the body. Good son!
Just as a *caṇḍāla* who, for seven generations in succession, does not abandon his trade, is therefore held in contempt by others;
so too is this body’s seed: its seeds of semen and blood are ultimately impure, and because of this impurity, it is held in contempt and rebuked by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

“Good son! This body is not like Mount Malaya, which produces sandalwood; nor can it produce blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), *campaka* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, or *vārṣika* flowers. Its nine orifices constantly flow with impurities such as pus and blood; its place of birth is foul-smelling and filthy, ugly and loathsome, and it always dwells together with various worms.”
Good son!
For example, although there may be a most excellent and pure garden in the world, once a corpse enters it, it becomes impure; everyone abandons it together and no longer gives rise to attachment.
The same applies to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): although it is pure and subtle, because it involves a physical body, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas collectively renounce it. "Good son!
If there are those who cannot perform such contemplation, they are said to be those who do not cultivate the body and do not cultivate precepts."
"Good son!
If one cannot perceive that the precepts are the ladder for all wholesome dharmas, nor the root of all wholesome dharmas—just as the earth is the foundation from which all trees grow;
nor that they are the leader of these roots of goodness, just as a merchant leader guides a multitude of merchants;"
Precepts are the supreme banner of all wholesome dharmas, like the victory banner erected by Śakra, Lord of Devas;
precepts can forever sever all evil karma and the three evil realms, healing the maladies of evil like a medicinal tree;

precepts are the provisions for the perilous path of birth and death; precepts are the armor and weapons for crushing fetters and destroying thieves; precepts are the efficacious mantra for extinguishing the venomous snakes of the fetters; precepts are the bridge for crossing over the conduct of evil karma.
If there are those who cannot contemplate in this manner, they are said to be not cultivating the precepts.
Those who do not cultivate the mind are unable to observe the mind; it is flighty and restless, difficult to grasp and difficult to tame, galloping and running wild like a great, vicious elephant;
its moments of thought are as swift as a flash of lightning.
Restless and unceasing, like a monkey, and like a phantom or a mirage, these are the root of all evils.
The five desires are difficult to satisfy, like fire obtaining fuel;
they are also like the great ocean, which swallows up all flowing streams.
Like Mount Mandara, where grasses and trees abound;
yet one cannot discern that birth and death are illusory, becoming entangled in delusion and bringing about affliction, like a fish swallowing a hook;
always leading the way while various karmas follow in its wake, just as a mother oyster shell leads her offspring.
Attached to the five desires and taking no pleasure in nirvana, they are like camels that eat honey until they die;
heedless of the straw, they are deeply attached to present pleasures and do not contemplate future faults, like oxen greedy for the sprouts who fear neither the whip nor the cudgel.
They gallop and roam throughout the twenty-five realms of existence like a swift wind blowing through *tūla* cotton;
they seek what ought not to be sought with insatiable craving, like ignorant people seeking the fire of heatlessness; they constantly delight in birth and death and take no pleasure in liberation;
they are like the *nimba* worm, which delights in the *nimba* tree, being deluded and attached to the foul stench of birth and death.
It is like a prisoner who takes pleasure in the daughter of a jailer;
or like a pig in a latrine who delights in dwelling amidst impurity.
If one is unable to contemplate in this manner, it is called failing to cultivate the mind.

"One who does not cultivate wisdom does not perceive that wisdom possesses great power: it can destroy evil karma like the golden-winged garuḍa; it can dispel the darkness of ignorance like the light of the sun; it can uproot the trees of the aggregates like water washing away objects;
and it can incinerate false views like a fierce fire."
Wisdom is the root of all wholesome dharmas and the seed of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If there are those who cannot contemplate in this manner, they are not said to be cultivating wisdom.

“Good son! Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), if one perceives the body, the characteristics of the body, the cause of the body, the fruit of the body, the collection of the body, the oneness of the body, the duality of the body, this body, that body, the cessation of the body, the equality of the body, the cultivation of the body, or a cultivator—if there is such a perception, it is called not cultivating the body.”

“Good son! If one perceives the precepts, the characteristics of the precepts, the causes of the precepts, the fruits of the precepts, superior precepts, inferior precepts, the accumulation of precepts, the unity of precepts, the duality of precepts, these precepts, those precepts, the cessation of precepts, the equality of precepts, the cultivation of precepts, the cultivator, or the precept-pāramitā—if one has such perceptions, it is called not cultivating the precepts.”

"If one perceives the mind, the characteristics of the mind, the causes of the mind, the fruits of the mind, the accumulation of the mind, the mind and its mental factors, the unity of the mind, the duality of the mind, this mind, that mind, the cessation of the mind, the equality of the mind, the cultivation of the mind, the cultivator, the superior, middling, and inferior minds, or wholesome and unwholesome minds—if one has such views, it is called not cultivating the mind."

“Good son, if one perceives wisdom, the characteristics of wisdom, the causes of wisdom, the fruits of wisdom, the accumulation of wisdom, the unity of wisdom, the duality of wisdom, this wisdom, that wisdom, the cessation of wisdom, the equality of wisdom, superior, middling, or inferior wisdom, dull wisdom or sharp wisdom, the cultivation of wisdom, or the cultivator—if there is such a perception, it is called not cultivating wisdom.”

“Good son, if there are those who do not cultivate the body, precepts, mind, or wisdom, such persons will receive great retribution for even minor evil karma. Out of fear, they constantly give rise to this thought:
‘I belong to hell; I am performing the deeds of hell.’”
"Even though they hear the wise describe the sufferings of hell, they constantly think:
'As iron strikes iron, stone strikes stone, wood strikes wood, and fire-worms delight in fire, so too does the body in hell resemble hell itself.'"
"If it is like hell, what suffering could there be?
It is like a fly that, being stuck by saliva, cannot escape;
this person is just the same, unable to extricate himself from even a minor transgression.

If the mind initially feels no remorse and cannot cultivate goodness, but instead conceals its flaws, then even though one possesses all past wholesome karma, it will be entirely defiled by these transgressions; consequently, whatever light retribution was to be experienced in the present life will be transformed into the extremely heavy evil fruits of hell.
"Good son!

It is like a small vessel of water into which one *śoṇa* of salt is placed; its taste becomes so salty and bitter that it is difficult to drink. The sinful karma of this person is also just like this."

Good son! It is like a person who owes another a single coin; because he cannot repay it, his body is bound and he undergoes manifold sufferings. The karmic offenses of such a person are likewise thus.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does this person cause light retribution to manifest as suffering experienced in hell?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! If all sentient beings possess five conditions, they will cause a present light retribution to be transformed into suffering experienced in hell.”
What are these five? First, because of ignorance;

second, because their roots of goodness are meager; third, because their evil karma is deep and heavy; fourth, because they do not repent; and fifth, because they do not cultivate their original wholesome karma.
Furthermore, there are five things: first, the cultivation of unwholesome karma;

second, the absence of the wealth of precepts; third, being far removed from all roots of goodness; fourth, failing to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; and fifth, associating with evil associates.
“Good son! For this reason, it can cause what would be a light retribution in the present life to become a heavy suffering in hell.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of person can transform the retribution of the hells so that it is experienced as light in the present life? “Good son!”

If there are those who cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom as previously described, and are able to contemplate all phenomena as being identical to empty space—neither perceiving wisdom nor the wise person, neither perceiving delusion nor the deluded person, and neither perceiving cultivation nor the one who cultivates—they are called wise persons.
Such a person is able to cultivate the precepts of body, speech, and mind, as well as wisdom; this person can cause the retribution of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life.
Even if such a person commits extremely grave evil karma, through contemplation and observation they can render it slight, thinking to themselves:
"Though my karma is heavy, it is not equal to the power of wholesome karma."
For example, even a hundred catties of cotton flowers can never equal a single ounce of pure gold.
It is like throwing one sheng of salt into the Ganges River; the water has no salty taste, and those who drink it do not perceive it.
It is like a person of great wealth who, though he owes others millions of treasures, cannot be bound or made to suffer; just as a great fragrant elephant can break iron chains and depart at will.
A person of wisdom is likewise: they constantly reflect, "My power of goodness is great, while my evil karma is weak;
I am able to confess and repent to eliminate sinful karma and cultivate wisdom."
"The power of wisdom is great, while the power of ignorance is slight.

Having reflected thus, he draws near to virtuous friends, cultivates right view, and receives, maintains, recites, copies, and explains the twelve divisions of the scriptures. When he sees others who receive, maintain, recite, copy, and explain them, he conceives a heart of reverence and honors them by providing food, clothing, dwellings, bedding, medicine for illness, flowers, and incense. He praises and respects them, speaking of their virtues wherever he goes and never mentioning their faults.

They made offerings to the Triple Gem and reverently believed in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, [affirming that] the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging, and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Such a person can cause the heavy retribution of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life. Good son!
For this reason, it is not the case that all karma has a fixed fruit, nor is it the case that all sentient beings must necessarily undergo [retribution].
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 31; The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 32,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Sixth Part of Chapter Eleven:
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all karma does not necessarily yield its fruit, and if all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and ought to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, for what cause and condition do all sentient beings fail to attain this Great Parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, they would certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; why then is it necessary to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?
“World-Honored One!

As it is said in this sutra, there are sick people who, if they obtain medicine, a caregiver, and food and drink appropriate to their illness, will all be completely cured—even if they do not obtain them [in this life].”

All sentient beings are likewise: if they encounter śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, buddhas, bodhisattvas, or various spiritual friends, and if they hear the teaching of the Dharma, they cultivate the noble path.
Even those who do not encounter, hear, or practice the Path shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
"Because of the Buddha-nature, World-Honored One!

It is like the sun and moon, which nothing can obstruct so as to prevent them from reaching the edge of Mount Āṭavika; or like the four great rivers, which cannot fail to reach the great ocean; or like those of icchantika nature, who cannot fail to go to hell."
All sentient beings are likewise thus; there is nothing that can obstruct them from attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
"Because of the Buddha-nature, World-Honored One!

For this reason, all sentient beings do not need to cultivate the Path; by the power of the Buddha-nature, they should attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, rather than by the power of practicing the Noble Path."
World-Honored One!

If those who are icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave offenses, or those who have committed the five heinous crimes were unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then one must certainly practice and cultivate [the path].
Because one will certainly attain it by virtue of the Buddha-nature, it is not something attained only after practicing cultivation.
World-Honored One!
It is like a magnet; although it is far from the iron, by its power, the iron follows it.
"The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; therefore, there is no need to diligently practice the Path.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Good son!
It is like seven kinds of people on the banks of the Ganges who enter the river—whether for bathing, out of fear of bandits, or to gather flowers.
The first person sinks as soon as he enters the water.
Why is this? Because he is weak and lacks strength, and has not practiced swimming.
As for the second person, although he sinks and then emerges, once emerged he sinks again.
Why is this? Because his physical strength is great, he is able to emerge; yet because he has not practiced swimming, he sinks back down after emerging.
The third person, having sunk, immediately emerges; once emerged, he does not sink again.
Why is this? He sinks because his body is heavy, but he emerges because his strength is great; and because he was previously practiced in floating, once emerged, he remains afloat.
As for the fourth person: having entered, he immediately sinks; having sunk, he emerges again; having emerged, he stands still and surveys the four quarters.

Why is this? Because of his heaviness he sinks; because of his great strength he emerges again; because he has practiced swimming he remains afloat; and because he does not know the way out, he surveys the four quarters.

As for the fifth person, having entered, he immediately sinks; having sunk, he emerges; having emerged, he stands still; having stood still, he observes the directions; having observed them, he departs. Why is this?
Out of fear.
As for the sixth person, having entered, he immediately departs and stays in the shallow part. Why is this?

Because they observe whether the bandits are near or far, the seventh person, having reached the other shore, ascends a great mountain; he is no longer afraid, is free from all hostile bandits, and experiences great happiness.

“Good son! The great river of birth and death is likewise thus. There are seven kinds of people who, fearing the thieves of affliction, resolve to cross the great river of birth and death; they leave the household life, shave their heads, and don the dharma robes.”

Having already left the household life, he associated with evil friends, followed their teachings, and listened to and accepted false doctrines. These so-called sentient beings are nothing but the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the five aggregates are themselves called the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). When a sentient being dies, the five great elements are forever severed. Since the five great elements are severed, what need is there to cultivate various karmas of good and evil? Therefore, one should know that neither good nor evil exists, nor do the retributions for good and evil.
Such a person is called an icchantika.
An icchantika is one who has severed the roots of goodness; because they have severed the roots of goodness, they sink into the river of birth and death and are unable to emerge from it.
Why is this? Because their evil karma is heavy and they lack the power of faith, like the first person by the side of the Ganges.
Good son, those who are icchantikas have six causes and conditions that cause them to sink into the three evil realms and be unable to emerge.
What are the six? First, because malevolent thoughts are intense;

second, because one does not perceive future lives; third, because one delights in practicing afflictions; fourth, because one distances oneself from roots of goodness; fifth, because one is obstructed by evil karma; and sixth, because one associates with evil friends.
Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to fall into the three evil realms.

What are these five? First, committing unrighteous acts toward a bhikṣu; second, committing unrighteous acts toward a bhikṣuṇī; third, using the property of the Saṃgha for one's own private purposes; fourth, committing unrighteous acts toward one’s mother; and fifth, giving rise to disputes and accusations against one another within the five divisions of the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to fall into the three evil realms.

What are these five? First, constantly preaching that there are no fruits of good or evil; second, killing sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta; third, delighting in speaking of the faults of Dharma teachers; fourth, preaching what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma, and preaching what is the Dharma as being not the Dharma; and fifth, listening to and receiving the teachings for the purpose of seeking out faults in the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are three matters by which one sinks into the three evil realms. What are these three?

First, the notion that the Tathāgata is impermanent and eternally extinguished; second, the notion that the True Dharma is impermanent and subject to change; and third, the notion that the Jewel of the Saṃgha can be destroyed. Because of these, one constantly sinks into the three evil realms.
"As for the second person, they have resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; however, because they have severed their roots of goodness, they sink and cannot emerge.
What is meant by 'emerging' is that by drawing near to virtuous friends, one attains faith."

This so-called "faith" refers to believing in giving and the fruits of giving; believing in goodness and the fruits of goodness; believing in evil and the fruits of evil; and believing in birth, death, suffering, impermanence, and decay—this is what is called faith.
Having attained faith, they cultivate pure precepts, uphold, recite, transcribe, and explain them; they constantly delight in giving and skillfully cultivate wisdom.
Yet, because their faculties are dull and they encounter evil friends, they are unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, and instead listen to and accept false teachings;
or, encountering an evil time and dwelling in an evil land, they sever all roots of goodness.
Because they have severed their roots of goodness, they are constantly submerged in birth and death, like the second person by the side of the Ganges.

"The third person is one who has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; yet because they have severed their roots of goodness, they sink within it. By associating with virtuous friends, they are said to emerge. They place faith in the Tathāgata as the All-Knowing One, eternal, constant, and unchanging, who for the sake of sentient beings preaches the Unsurpassed Way. They believe that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and that the Tathāgata does not perish, nor do the Dharma and the Sangha, which likewise never undergo destruction."
Those such as the icchantikas who do not sever their [defiled] dharmas can never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they must first distance themselves from them before they can finally attain it.

Out of faith, they cultivate pure precepts; having cultivated the precepts, they receive, uphold, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures, widely proclaiming and disseminating them for the sake of all sentient beings. They delight in giving and cultivate wisdom; because their faculties are sharp, they abide firmly in faith and wisdom with minds that never regress, like the third person by the side of the Ganges River.

"The fourth person is one who has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, yet sinks within it because they have severed their roots of goodness. Because they draw near to virtuous friends, they attain faith; this is called 'emerging. Having attained faith, they receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures; for the sake of sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate them. They delight in giving and cultivate wisdom. Because their faculties are sharp, they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom, with no regression in mind. They look out across the four directions; these four directions refer to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. This is like the fourth person by the side of the Ganges."

"The fifth person is one who has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; however, because he had severed his roots of goodness, he sank within it. By associating with virtuous friends, he attained faith, which is called 'emerging. Because of this faith, he received, upheld, recited, copied, and explained the twelve divisions of the scriptures, widely proclaiming and disseminating them for the sake of sentient beings. Delighting in wise giving and cultivating wisdom, and because of his sharp faculties, he remained steadfast in faith and wisdom with a mind free from regression. Having no regression, he then moved forward; 'moving forward' refers to the *pratyekabuddha*. Although he can cross over himself, he does not reach [the benefit of] all sentient beings; this is called 'going,' like the fifth person by the side of the Ganges."

"The sixth person is one who has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; however, because he had severed his roots of goodness, he sank within it. By associating with virtuous friends, he attained faith. Because he attained faith, he is said to have 'emerged. On account of this faith, he received, upheld, recited, copied, and explained the twelve divisions of the scriptures; for the sake of sentient beings, he widely proclaimed and disseminated them. Delighting in giving and cultivating wisdom, and because his faculties were sharp, he remained steadfastly established in faith and wisdom. With no regression in mind, having reached the state of non-regression, he then moved forward until he reached shallow water. Having reached shallow water, he stayed there and did not depart. One who stays and does not depart is called a Bodhisattva; desiring to deliver all sentient beings, he dwells in contemplation of afflictions, just like the sixth man by the side of the Ganges."

"As for the seventh person: he resolves to cross the great river of birth and death, but because he has severed his roots of goodness, he sinks within it. By associating with virtuous friends, he attains faith; having attained faith, this is called 'emerging. Because of that faith, he upholds, recites, copies, and explains the twelve divisions of the scriptures; for the sake of sentient beings, he widely proclaims and disseminates them. He delights in giving and cultivates wisdom. Because his faculties are sharp, he abides firmly in faith and wisdom, and his mind does not regress. Having no regression, he immediately moves forward; having moved forward, he reaches the other shore, ascends the great high mountain, leaves all terrors behind, and experiences much peace and happiness."

Good son! The mountain on the other shore is a metaphor for the Tathāgata; experiencing peace and bliss is a metaphor for the Buddha’s eternal abiding; and the great high mountain is a metaphor for Great Nirvāṇa.
“Good son! These people along the banks of the Ganges all possess hands and feet, yet they are unable to cross over.

All sentient beings are likewise: although there truly exist the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Sangha-jewel; although the Tathāgata constantly teaches the essential meaning of all dharmas, including the Eightfold Noble Path and Great Parinirvāṇa, sentient beings are entirely unable to attain them.”
This is not my fault, nor is it the fault of the Noble Path or of sentient beings.
You should know that this is entirely the fault and evil of the afflictions; for this reason, all sentient beings do not attain nirvāṇa.
"Good son!
It is like a skilled physician who diagnoses an illness and prescribes medicine; if the patient does not take it, it is not the fault of the physician.
Good son!"
Suppose there is a donor who gives all that he possesses to all people; if there are those who do not accept it, this is not the fault of the donor. Good son!
It is like the rising of the sun, which illuminates all darkness; if a blind person cannot see the road, it is not the fault of the sun.
"Good son!
Just as the waters of the Ganges can remove thirst and exhaustion, yet if those who are thirsty do not drink, it is not the fault of the water.
Good son!"
It is like the great earth, which universally produces fruits and grains, being impartial and without distinction; if a farmer does not sow, it is not the fault of the earth. Good son!

In the same way, the Tathāgata universally expounds and analyzes the twelve divisions of the scriptures for the sake of all sentient beings; if sentient beings do not accept them, it is not the fault of the Tathāgata.
"Good son!
If one cultivates the path, one immediately attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son!"
As for your statement that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and should therefore attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just like a magnet—
excellent, excellent!
By virtue of the causal power of the Buddha-nature, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
therefore, it is incorrect to say that the cultivation of the Noble Path is unnecessary.

Good son! It is like a person traveling through a vast wilderness who, overcome by thirst and exhaustion, encounters a well. Although the well is deep and dark and he does not see water, he should know that it must certainly be there.
This person uses skillful means to seek out a jar and a rope; only when drawing water does he see it.
The Buddha-nature is likewise: although all sentient beings possess it, they must cultivate the untainted noble path before they can perceive it.
Good son! Just as when there is sesame one can see oil, yet it cannot be seen apart from various skillful means, so it is with sugarcane. Good son!
Just as the Heaven of the Thirty-three and Uttarakuru are existent phenomena, yet cannot be seen if one lacks wholesome karma and the power of supernatural faculties.
The roots of grasses and underground water within the earth are not seen by sentient beings because they are covered by the earth.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; because one does not cultivate the Noble Path, it cannot be seen.

“Good son! As you have said, there are patients in the world who, whether they encounter a skilled physician who attends to them with excellent medicine and appropriate food and drink according to their illness, or do not encounter such things, all recover from their ailments.”
"Good son! I have taught this meaning for the sake of bodhisattvas dwelling in the sixth stage. Good son!"

For example, just as space is neither internal nor external to sentient beings, and because it is neither internal nor external, it is without obstruction; so too is the buddha-nature of sentient beings.
Good son! It is like a person whose wealth is in a distant land; although it is not present before them for their immediate use, when someone asks about it, they say, "I have it."
Why is this? Because it definitely exists.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it is neither this nor that, yet because it will certainly be attained, one says that all possess it.
Good son! For example, when sentient beings create various karmas—whether wholesome or unwholesome—they are neither internal nor external.

Likewise, the nature of karma is neither existent nor non-existent; furthermore, it is not that what was previously non-existent now exists, nor does it arise without cause. It is not the case that one creates this and another receives it, or that one creates this and another receives it, or that another creates and another receives it.
There is no agent and no recipient; rather, when the conditions of time and season harmonize, the fruit of retribution is obtained.

The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it is not that it was originally non-existent and now exists; it is neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent, neither this nor that; it does not come from another place, nor is it without causes and conditions, nor is it something that all sentient beings fail to see. It is only when the various Bodhisattvas encounter the harmonization of the conditions of time and season that they are able to see it.

As for "the right time," it refers to when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva of the ten stages cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path and attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; at that moment, they attain vision, which is not called "making."
“Good son! As for your statement that it is like a magnet, this meaning is not so. Why is that?
Stone does not attract iron.
Why is this? Because it lacks the karma of intention.
"Good son!
Because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises; because one phenomenon is absent, another phenomenon perishes. There is no agent of creation, nor is there any agent of destruction."
Good son! It is like a fierce fire that cannot actually burn the wood; rather, when the fire arises and the wood is destroyed, it is called "burning the wood. Good son!

For example, just as sunflowers turn toward the sun, these sunflowers likewise possess no mind of reverence, no consciousness, and no karma; they simply revolve of their own accord due to the nature of phenomena.

Good son! It is like the plantain tree, which grows because of thunder; this tree has no ears, no mind, no mentation, and no consciousness. Because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon grows; because one phenomenon is absent, another phenomenon perishes.

Good son! It is like the aśoka tree: when a woman touches it, its flowers bloom. This tree has no mind and no sensation of touch; yet because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises, and because one phenomenon ceases, another phenomenon perishes.
"Good son!

It is like a tangerine tree that, upon receiving a *śīrṣa* [seed/essence], produces many fruits; yet this tangerine tree has no mind and no sensation. Because a different dharma exists, another dharma flourishes; because a different dharma is absent, another dharma perishes."
"Good son!

Just as a pomegranate tree bears abundant fruit because of the brick dust, bone fragments, and manure, yet the pomegranate tree has no intention or contact [with them]; so too, because of the existence of one phenomenon, another phenomenon arises, and because of the non-existence of one phenomenon, another phenomenon perishes."
Good son! The magnet attracting iron is likewise so: because a distinct phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises; because a distinct phenomenon is absent, another phenomenon perishes.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it cannot "suck up" anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son!

Ignorance cannot suck up formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor can formative forces suck up consciousness (*vijñāna*); yet it is still called "ignorance conditions formative forces" and "formative forces condition consciousness. Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the dharma-realm remains eternally abiding.
“Good son! If it is said that the Buddha-nature dwells within sentient beings, good son!”
The nature of permanence has no abiding place; if there were a place of abiding, it would be impermanent. Good son!
Just as the twelve links of dependent origination have no fixed place of abiding, if they had a place of abiding, the twelve links of dependent origination could not be called permanent.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata likewise has no place of abiding; the Dharma-realm, the Dharma-base, the Dharma-aggregates, and empty space—all have no place of abiding.
Buddha-nature is also like this, having no place of abiding whatsoever.
Good son! It is like the four great elements:

although their powers are equal, some are solid, some are hot, some are moist, and some are mobile; some are heavy, some are light, some are red, some are white, some are yellow, and some are black. Yet these four great elements possess no karma, for they are distinct from the dharma-realm and thus do not resemble one another.
The Buddha-nature is also like this; because it is distinct from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it manifests when the time arrives. Good son!

Because all sentient beings do not regress from their Buddha-nature, it is said that they "possess" it. Because they are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*), because they will possess it in the future, because they will certainly attain it, and because they will certainly see it, for these reasons it is said that all sentient beings universally possess Buddha-nature.
“Good son! It is like a king who said to a great minister, ‘Lead an elephant before some blind men to show it to them.
At that time, having received the king’s command, the minister gathered many blind men and showed the elephant to them.”
Then those blind men each felt with their hands, and the minister returned and reported to the king, saying:
"I have finished showing them.
Thereupon, the great king summoned the blind men and questioned each one individually:
"Did you see the elephant?
Each of the blind men replied,
"I have seen it."
The king asked,
"What kind of creature is an elephant?
Those who had touched its tusks replied, "The shape of an elephant is like the root of a radish."
He who touched its ears said the elephant was like a winnowing basket;
he who touched its head said the elephant was like a rock;
he who touched its trunk said the elephant was like a pestle.
Those who touched its legs said the elephant was like a wooden mortar;
those who touched its back said it was like a bed;
those who touched its belly said it was like a large jar.
Those who touched its tail said that the elephant was like a rope.
Good son! Like those blind men, they did not describe the essence of the elephant, yet it was not that they did not describe it at all.
If all these various features are not the elephant itself, then apart from them, there is no other elephant. Good son!

The king is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; the minister is a metaphor for the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; the elephant is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature; and the blind man is a metaphor for all sentient beings shrouded in ignorance.
"When these sentient beings have heard the Buddha’s teaching, some may say:
'Form is the Buddha-nature. Why is this?'"
Although this form perishes, it continues in successive succession; therefore, one obtains the thirty-two marks of the unsurpassed Tathāgata.
The form of the Tathāgata is eternal, for the form of the Tathāgata is eternally uninterrupted. For this reason, form is called the Buddha-nature.

For example, it is like genuine gold: although its form may change, its color remains ever the same. Whether it is fashioned into a bracelet, a hairpin, or a basin, its yellow hue never undergoes any alteration.
"The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: although its substance is impermanent, its form is permanent; for this reason, it is said that form is the Buddha-nature.
Or there are those who say:
"Feeling is the Buddha-nature."

Why is this? Because by means of sensation as a condition, one attains the true bliss of the Tathāgata; the "sensation" of the Tathāgata refers to ultimate sensation and sensation in the primary sense.
Although the nature of sentient beings' sensations is impermanent, their succession continues without interruption; therefore, they attain the eternal sensation of the Tathāgata.
For example, there may be a person whose clan name is Kauśika; although the person is impermanent, the clan name is eternal, remaining unchanged throughout thousands of millions of generations.
"The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; for this reason, it is said that sensation (*vedanā*) is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the Buddha-nature."
Why is this? Because through the condition of perception (*saṃjñā*), one attains the Tathāgata’s perception of reality.

The perception of the Tathāgata is called the "perception of non-perception. This perception of non-perception is neither the perception of a sentient being nor the perception of male or female; it is also not the perception of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it the perception of annihilation. Although the perceptions of sentient beings are impermanent, because these perceptions continue in succession without interruption, one thereby attains the Tathāgata’s eternal and constant perception.
Good son! It is like the twelve links of dependent origination for sentient beings: although the sentient beings perish, the dependent origination remains constant.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; for this reason, it is said that conceptualization is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Volitional action (*saṃskāra*) is the Buddha-nature. Why is this so?"
Practice is called "life span"; by virtue of the causes and conditions of life span, one attains the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding life span.
Although the life spans of sentient beings are impermanent, because their lives continue in succession without interruption, they attain the Tathāgata’s true and eternal life span.
Good son! It is like the twelve divisions of the scriptures: although those who hear them and those who preach them are impermanent, these scriptures exist eternally and remain unchanging.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; for this reason it is said that conduct is the buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Consciousness is the buddha-nature."
By reason of consciousness as a condition, one attains the Tathāgata’s mind of equality.
Although the mental consciousness of sentient beings is impermanent, because consciousness continues in succession without interruption, one attains the Tathāgata’s truly eternal mind.
Just as heat is the nature of fire, although fire is impermanent, heat is not impermanent.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; for this reason, consciousness is said to be the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Apart from the aggregates (skandhas) there is a self; this self is the Buddha-nature. Why is this so?"
By virtue of these causes and conditions, I have attained the Tathāgata’s eight kinds of mastery.

There are certain non-Buddhists who claim that coming and going, seeing and hearing, sorrow and joy, and speech constitute the self; they hold that although such characteristics of a self are impermanent, the Tathāgata’s self is truly eternal.
"Good son!
Just as the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, though impermanent, are called 'constant,' so too is the buddha-nature of sentient beings.
Good son!"
Just as those blind men each described the elephant; although they did not grasp the reality, it was not that they were not describing the elephant.
It is the same with those who speak of the Buddha-nature: it is not identical to the six dharmas, yet it is not separate from the six dharmas.
"Good son! For this reason, I say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not form, yet is not separate from form; and so on, up to: it is not self, yet is not separate from self.
Good son!"
Although various non-Buddhists claim there is a self, in reality there is no self.
What sentient beings call the "self" is simply the five aggregates; apart from these aggregates, there is no separate self.
Good son! It is like a lotus flower, which is composed of its stalk, petals, filaments, and pericarp; apart from these, there is no other flower. The "self" of sentient beings is also like this.
Good son! For example, when walls, grass, and wood are combined, they are called a "house"; apart from these, there is no separate house.
Just as when *khatāra* trees, *palaśa* trees, *nyagrodha* trees, and *udumbara* trees are combined, they form a "forest"; apart from these, there is no separate forest.
For example, it is like an army composed of chariots, elephants, cavalry, and infantry; apart from these, there is no separate army.
It is like a variegated silk fabric made from the combination of threads of five colors; apart from these, there is no separate fabric.
Just as the four castes combined are called the "great assembly," and there is no separate assembly apart from them, so it is with the sentient being and the self:
apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate self.
Good son! That which is the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding is called the Self.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is boundless and unimpeded, neither arising nor ceasing; having attained the eight masteries, it is called the Self.
Sentient beings truly lack such a self or anything belonging to a self; rather, because they will certainly and ultimately attain the supreme ultimate emptiness, it is called Buddha-nature.
“Good son! Great loving-kindness and great compassion are called the Buddha-nature. Why is this?

Great kindness and great compassion always follow the bodhisattva like a shadow follows a form; all sentient beings will certainly attain great kindness and great compassion, and for this reason it is said that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
Great kindness and great compassion are called buddha-nature; buddha-nature is called the Tathāgata.
Great joy and great equanimity are called buddha-nature. Why is this?
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot relinquish the twenty-five states of existence, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain it, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
