Great joy and great equanimity are the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature" is termed great faith. Why is this so?
Because of their faith, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fulfill the *dāna-pāramitā* through to the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Since all sentient beings will certainly attain great faith, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Great faith is itself the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata; and the Buddha-nature is called the Stage of the Only Son.
Why is this? Because by virtue of the causal conditions of the Stage of the Only Son, the Bodhisattva attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain the stage of being an only son, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The stage of being an only son is itself Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called the fourth power.
Why is this? It is because, by means of the conditions of the fourth power, a bodhisattva is then able to teach and transform sentient beings."
Because all sentient beings will certainly and inevitably attain the fourth power, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The fourth power is itself Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called the twelve links of dependent origination. Why is this?
Because by means of causes and conditions, the Tathāgata eternally abides."
All sentient beings certainly possess these twelve links of dependent origination; therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).

By reason of these four unimpeded knowledges, one speaks with unimpeded mastery over words and meanings; because of this unimpeded mastery over words and meanings, one is able to transform sentient beings."
The four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are themselves the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.

"Buddha-nature" is named the "Culminating Samādhi" (*mūrdhan-samādhi*); because one cultivates this Culminating Samādhi, one is able to comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas. Therefore, it is said that the Culminating Samādhi is called the Buddha-nature.
Bodhisattvas in the ten stages who cultivate this samādhi have not yet attained its full perfection; thus, although they see the Buddha-nature, they do so without clarity.
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain it, it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
“Good son, because all sentient beings will certainly attain the various dharmas as described above, it is for this reason that it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.”

"Good son! If I were to say that form is the Buddha-nature, sentient beings, upon hearing this, would give rise to perverted views. Because of these perverted views, at the end of their lives they would be reborn in the Avīci Hell."

The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma in order to sever [the cycle of] the hells; for this reason, he does not say that form is the Buddha-nature, and the same applies even to his teaching regarding consciousness. "Good son!
If there were sentient beings who fully realized their Buddha-nature, they would have no need to cultivate the Path;
yet even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, by cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, only see the Buddha-nature slightly—how much less could those who do not practice it ever perceive it?
"Good son!

Just as Mañjuśrī and other bodhisattvas have cultivated the noble path for immeasurable eons and thereby fully understood the Buddha-nature, how could śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possibly know the Buddha-nature?"

If there are sentient beings who wish to clearly understand the Buddha-nature, they should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, explain, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Furthermore, upon seeing anyone who receives, upholds, or even praises such a sūtra, they should provide them with excellent dwellings, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness; moreover, they should further praise, prostrate to, and inquire after their well-being.

Good son, if there are those who, throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds in the past, have drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, deeply planting roots of goodness, only then will they be able to hear the name of this sutra.
"Good son!

The Buddha-nature is inconceivable; the Treasures of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are also inconceivable; and that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature yet are unable to know it—this too is inconceivable."
The Tathāgata’s dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are also inconceivable; that all sentient beings are able to believe in such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, there are all sentient beings who are able to believe in such an inconceivable Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.”
“World-Honored One!

Among this great assembly, there are eighty-five thousand *koṭis* of people who do not give rise to faith in this sutra. Therefore, those who are able to believe in this sutra are called inconceivable.”
“Good son! These people shall likewise certainly attain faith in this sutra in future ages, perceive the Buddha-nature, and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a non-retrogressive bodhisattva know for himself that he possesses the resolve of non-retrogression?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should test his own mind through ascetic practices: he may eat a single sesame seed per day for seven days; likewise, he may do the same for seven days each with polished rice, mung beans, hemp seeds, millet, and white beans.”
When eating a single sesame seed, he reflected:
"Such ascetic practices are entirely without benefit.
If one can perform even that which is of no benefit, how much more so should one perform that which is beneficial?"
"Because he is able to endure what is unbeneficial with a mind that does not retreat or waver, he will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

While practicing such asceticism for days on end, all his skin and flesh became emaciated and shriveled like a raw gourd cut off and left in the sun; his eyes were sunken like stars at the bottom of a well; his ribs protruded as his flesh was exhausted, like a dilapidated thatched hut; his vertebrae appeared one after another like a string of bricks; and the place where he sat was like a horse's hoofprint.
When he wished to sit, he would prostrate; when he wished to rise, he would lie flat. Although he endured such unbeneficial suffering, he did not retreat from the mind of bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

In order to destroy all suffering and bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to relinquish internal and external wealth, as well as their own bodies and lives, just as they would discard blades of straw.

If one can disregard this body and life, such a bodhisattva knows for themselves that they will certainly possess a non-retrogressive mind and that they will definitely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, for the sake of the Dharma, a bodhisattva carves his own body to serve as a lamp; he wraps his skin and flesh with cotton cloth, pours ghee and oil over it, and burns it to form a wick."
At that time, the bodhisattva undergoes such great suffering; he rebukes his own mind and says:
"Such suffering as this does not even constitute one-hundred-thousand-millionth part of the suffering in the hells."

Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have undergone great suffering and affliction to no avail; if you cannot endure this slight hardship now, how will you be able to save suffering sentient beings within the hells?
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, his body does not perceive suffering, and his mind does not retreat, waver, or turn back.
At that time, the Bodhisattva should deeply know for himself: 'I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
Good son!

At that time, although the Bodhisattva was still fully possessed of afflictions and had not yet severed them, for the sake of the Dharma’s causal conditions, he was able to give his head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, blood, and flesh to sentient beings; he even drove nails into his body, threw himself from cliffs, and leapt into fire.

At that time, although the bodhisattva undergoes such immeasurable sufferings, if his mind does not retreat, does not waver, and does not turn back, the bodhisattva should know: "I now certainly possess a non-retreating mind; I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Good son! In order to destroy the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva vows to take the body of a coarse and large animal, offering his own flesh and blood to them. When sentient beings take it, he further gives rise to compassion; at that time, the bodhisattva holds his breath and does not pant, manifesting the appearance of death so that those who take it do not conceive the thought of doubt regarding the act of killing.”
Although a bodhisattva may take the body of an animal, he never performs the karma of an animal.
Why is this? Good son!
Once a bodhisattva has attained the non-retrogressive mind, they will never again commit karma that leads to the three evil realms.

If, in future lives, there should be even a minute particle of karmic retribution for evil deeds whose timing of experience is not fixed, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva will accept it all on behalf of sentient beings through the power of their great vows.

It is like a sick person possessed by a spirit dwelling within their body; through the power of a mantra, the spirit’s form immediately manifests, speaking or rejoicing, becoming angry or reviling, or weeping and wailing.

The karma of the three evil realms in future ages for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas is likewise so; when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas receive the body of a bear, they constantly expound the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Or he may take the body of a *kapiñjala* bird to preach the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

Thus, he takes the bodies of a *gotra*, a deer, a rabbit, an elephant, a ram, a monkey, a white dove, a garuḍa, a dragon, a snake, and so forth. When taking such bodies among the animals, he never commits the evil karma of an animal; rather, he constantly expounds the True Dharma for other animals and sentient beings, causing them to hear the Dharma and swiftly attain liberation from their animal bodies.
At that time, although the bodhisattva has received the body of an animal, he does not commit evil deeds; one should know that he certainly possesses a non-regressive mind.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters starving sentient beings during a famine, he manifests as a tortoise or a fish many *yojanas* in length and makes this vow:

"May all sentient beings, when they take my flesh, have it grow back as soon as it is taken. By eating my flesh, may they be freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst, and may they all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The Bodhisattva made this vow:

"If there be any who, because of me, are freed from hunger and thirst, may they, in future ages, swiftly attain liberation from the suffering of hunger and thirst within the twenty-five realms of existence."
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva undergoes such suffering and their mind does not retreat, you should know that they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva encounters those suffering from illness during an age of pestilence, they reflect:

'Just as the King of Medicine Trees, if there are those who are ill, can cure their diseases by taking its roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, or pith, may my body likewise be so: if there are those who are ill, whether they hear my voice, touch my body, or consume my flesh and blood, even down to my marrow, may their illnesses all be completely cured;
and when sentient beings eat my flesh, may they not give rise to an evil mind as if eating the flesh of their own children.'"
“Once I have cured their illness, I shall constantly preach the Dharma for them, wishing that they may believe and accept it, contemplate it, and teach it to others.

Furthermore, good son, although a bodhisattva who is fully possessed of afflictions undergoes physical suffering, his mind does not regress, waver, or change; you should know that he will certainly attain the non-regressive mind and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, good son!
If there are sentient beings afflicted by spirits, when the Bodhisattva sees them, he immediately says:
'May I take on the body of a spirit—a large body, a powerful body, and a body with many retinues—so that they may hear and see me, and their illness may be cured. "
“Furthermore, good son, for the sake of sentient beings, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas diligently practice asceticism; although they possess afflictions, these do not defile their minds.”
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they do not seek the fruits of those six pāramitās.
When practicing the unsurpassed six pāramitās, they make this vow:

"I now bestow these six pāramitās upon all sentient beings; once each and every sentient being has received my gift, may they all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I myself shall also diligently practice austerities for the sake of the six pāramitās and undergo various sufferings; while undergoing these sufferings, I vow that my mind of bodhi shall never regress."
"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow, it is called the mark of non-retrogression from awakening.
Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable. Why is this?

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas deeply understand that birth and death abound with many faults and transgressions, and they perceive that Great Nirvāṇa possesses great merit. For the sake of all sentient beings, they remain within birth and death and undergo various sufferings, yet their minds never regress; this is called the inconceivability of a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to compassion without any external cause or condition; he truly receives no favor yet constantly bestows favors, and though he bestows favors, he seeks no recompense. For this reason, he is further named "inconceivable."
Furthermore, good son!

There may be sentient beings who practice various ascetic austerities for their own benefit, whereas the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices austerities for the sake of benefiting others; this is called self-benefit, and for this reason, it is further termed inconceivable.

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva, while still possessing afflictions, cultivates a mind of equanimity in order to destroy the various sufferings experienced by both enemies and kin; for this reason, it is also called inconceivable."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva encounters sentient beings who are evil or unwholesome, he may reprimand them, speak to them gently, expel them, or abandon them. Toward those of a wicked nature, he may manifest gentleness; toward those who are arrogant, he may manifest great arrogance, yet in his inner mind he is truly free of arrogance. This is called the inconceivable skillful means of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva possesses few material goods despite being fully endowed with afflictions, yet the seekers are many, his mind does not narrow or shrink; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world, a bodhisattva, knowing the virtues of the Buddha, takes birth in a remote borderland for the sake of sentient beings—appearing as if blind, deaf, lame, or paralyzed. This is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva deeply understands all the transgressions and faults of sentient beings; for the sake of their deliverance, he constantly associates with them. Although he accords with their inclinations, he remains unstained by their defilements; for this reason, he is further called "inconceivable."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva clearly knows and perceives that there is no mark of a sentient being, no defilement of afflictions, and no one who cultivates the path to leave afflictions behind. Although for the sake of enlightenment there is no practice of enlightenment, nor any one who accomplishes the practice of enlightenment; although there is neither the experience of suffering nor the destruction of suffering, yet he is able to perform the practice of enlightenment to destroy the suffering of sentient beings. For this reason, it is further called inconceivable."
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva receives his final body and dwells in Tuṣita Heaven, this too is called inconceivable.

Why is this? Among the heavens of the desire realm, Tuṣita Heaven is the most excellent. Those in the lower heavens have minds that are negligent and indolent, while those in the higher heavens have dull faculties; for this reason, it is called supreme.
By practicing generosity and observing ethical discipline, one attains a body in the upper or lower realms;
by practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, one attains a body in Tuṣita.
All Bodhisattvas revile and destroy all forms of existence (bhava); they never perform the karma for Tuṣita Heaven nor receive a body in that heaven.

Why is this? Because even when Bodhisattvas dwell in other realms of existence, they are still able to teach and bring sentient beings to maturity; yet, though they manifest with desire within the desire realm, they are actually free from any mind of desire. For this reason, they are further called "inconceivable."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are born in the Tuṣita Heaven, they possess three things that are superior:
first, longevity; second, physical form; and third, renown.
Although Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not truly seek longevity, physical form, or renown, they obtain these superior qualities despite having no seeking mind.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply delights in *nirvāṇa*, yet because his conditions and causes are also superior, he is further called "inconceivable.

Although these three matters of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva are thus superior to those of the devas, the devas and others never give rise toward him to thoughts of anger, envy, or arrogance; they always give rise to thoughts of joy. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva does not harbor arrogance toward the devas; for this reason, he is further called "inconceivable."
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not create karma for the life-span, yet possesses an ultimate lifespan in that heaven; this is called "superiority of life.
Furthermore, he has no karma for form, yet his wondrous physical body is filled with pervasive radiance; this is called "superiority of form."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in those celestial palaces, they take no pleasure in the five desires but engage solely in Dharma activities; therefore, their fame fills the ten directions, and this is called "superior renown."
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.
"When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways; for this reason, it is further called inconceivable."

Why is this? When the Bodhisattva descended, the devas of the desire and form realms all came to attend upon and escort him; they raised a great sound to praise the Bodhisattva, and by the wind from their mouths, they caused the earth to tremble.

Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas who are elephant-kings among men; these elephant-kings among men are called dragon-kings (*nāgarāja*). When a dragon-king first enters the womb, various dragon-kings dwelling beneath this earth experience either fear or joy; for this reason, the great earth shakes in six ways, and for this reason it is further called inconceivable.

"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the time of entering the womb, the time of abiding therein, and the time of emerging; he knows the father and knows the mother, yet remains undefiled by impurity, like the blue sapphire gem in the topknot of Śakra. For this reason, he is further named 'Inconceivable.'"
“Good son! The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise thus, inconceivable. Good son!”
For example, the great ocean possesses eight inconceivable qualities.
What are these eight? First, it gradually deepens;

second, its depth is difficult to fathom; third, it has a single uniform salty taste; fourth, its tides do not exceed their limits; fifth, it contains various treasuries of jewels; sixth, large-bodied beings dwell within it; seventh, it does not harbor dead corpses; and eighth, when all the myriad streams and heavy rains pour into it, it neither increases nor decreases.
"Good son! There are three matters by which it gradually becomes ever more profound.
What are these three?"

First, the power of the merit of sentient beings; second, traveling with the wind; third, because the river water flows in. Furthermore, there are likewise three reasons each for neither increasing nor decreasing.
"This subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise possessed of eight inconceivable qualities.
The first is that it becomes progressively deeper. That is to say:

the Upāsaka precepts, the Śrāmaṇera precepts, the Bhikṣu precepts, the Bodhisattva precepts; the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva; and the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This Nirvāṇa Sūtra expounds such dharmas as these, which is called 'progressively deepening. For this reason, this sūtra is named 'Progressively Deep.'"
"Second, it is profoundly difficult to fathom its depths.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is neither born nor extinguished; he does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor does he turn the wheel of the Dharma; he neither eats nor receives, nor does he practice giving. For this reason, he is named Constant, Blissful, Self, and Pure."

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. This Buddha-nature is not form, yet it is not separate from form; it is not sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from consciousness. It is eternal and visible; it is a cause of realization, not a cause of creation.

From the stream-enterer up to the pratyekabuddha, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet they possess neither afflictions nor a place of abiding. Although they lack afflictions, this is not called "permanence"; for this reason, it is called "profound."
Furthermore, there is a profound depth in this sutra: at times it speaks of a self, and at times it speaks of non-self;
at times it speaks of permanence, and at times it speaks of impermanence; at times it speaks of purity, and at times it speaks of impurity;
at times it speaks of bliss, and at times it speaks of suffering; at times it speaks of emptiness, and at times it speaks of non-emptiness; or...
Some say that all exists, while others say that all is non-existent; some speak of the three vehicles, while others speak of the one vehicle;

some say that the five aggregates are themselves the Buddha-nature, as are the diamond-like samādhi, the middle way, the śūraṅgama samādhi, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ultimate emptiness, and compassion and equanimity.
Regarding all sentient beings, it possesses the wisdom of the crown of the head and the mind of faith; it knows the faculties and powers, and possesses unimpeded wisdom regarding all dharmas.
Although the Buddha-nature exists, it does not declare it to be fixed; for this reason, it is called "profound."
"Third is the single flavor (*ekarasa*).

All sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they all share the same vehicle, the same liberation, the same cause, the same fruit, and the same nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). All shall attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is called the single flavor."
"Fourth, the tide does not overstep its limit.
Likewise, in the sutras it is ordained that bhikṣus must not accept or store the eight kinds of impure things.

If my disciples are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and analyze this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they would rather lose their lives than ever violate these precepts; this is called 'the tide not overstepping its limit.'"
"Fifth, there are various treasuries of jewels. This sutra is itself an immeasurable treasury of jewels.

What is called 'jewels' refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; the conduct of infants, the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, and the celestial conduct; all skillful means; the Buddha-nature of sentient beings; the merits of bodhisattvas, Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas; the six pāramitās; immeasurable samādhis; and immeasurable wisdom—these are called the treasury of jewels."
"Sixth is the dwelling place of beings with great bodies. 'Beings with great bodies' refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

they are called 'great beings' because of their great wisdom. They are called 'beings with great bodies' because of their great body, great mind, great adornment, great subduing, great skillful means, great preaching of the Dharma, great power, great retinue, great supernormal powers, and great compassion; because they are eternally unchanging; because all sentient beings have no hindrance before them; and because they accommodate and receive all sentient beings. This is called the dwelling place of beings with great bodies."
"Seventh, one does not allow a corpse to remain overnight.

A 'corpse' refers to those who are icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution, or those who slander the Vaipulya sutras; those who preach what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, or preach the Dharma as not the Dharma; those who accept and store the eight kinds of impure things; those who use the property of the Buddha or the property of the Sangha according to their own whims; or those who commit unlawful acts against bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—these are called corpses."
This *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is free from such things as these; therefore, it is called "not harboring a corpse.
Eighth is "neither increasing nor decreasing.

Because it is boundless, because it has no beginning or end, because it is not form, because it is not a conditioned product, because it is eternally abiding, because it is neither born nor extinguished, because all sentient beings are entirely equal, and because the nature of all phenomena is of one single nature—it is called "without increase or decrease. For this reason, this sūtra possesses eight inconceivable qualities, like that great ocean.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is said that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished and is therefore called ‘profound,’ yet all sentient beings have four kinds of birth:”
Egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth—these four modes of birth are all present among human beings.

For example, the bhikṣu Śiśumāra, the bhikṣu Upaśiśumāra, the mother of the householder Mṛgāra, the mother of the householder Nyagrodha, and the mother of the householder Pañcāla each had five hundred sons born from eggs; one should know that egg-birth exists among humans.
Regarding those born from moisture, as the Buddha has said: "In the past, when I was practicing as a bodhisattva, I was King Mūrdhaja and King Hastija;
and as is now being taught, there were the women Āmrapālī and Kāpālikā. One should know that among human beings, there are also those born from moisture.
At the beginning of the kalpa, all sentient beings were born by transformation.
Since the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has attained the eight masteries, for what reason and by what causes and conditions was he not born by transformation?
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Although all sentient beings are born through the four modes of birth, once they have attained the noble Dharma, they no longer undergo birth from eggs or moisture as they did before."
"Good son!
At the beginning of the kalpa, all sentient beings were born through transformation; at that time, no Buddha appeared in the world.
Good son!"
If there are sentient beings who encounter the suffering of illness, they require a physician and medicine.

At the beginning of the kalpa, sentient beings were born by transformation; although they possessed afflictions, their illnesses had not yet manifested, and for this reason the Tathāgata did not appear in that world.
At the beginning of a kalpa, the bodies and minds of sentient beings were not yet fit vessels; therefore, the Tathāgata does not appear in that world. Good son!
All the undertakings of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, surpass those of all other sentient beings—namely, his lineage, his retinue, and his parents.
Because of his preeminence, all who hear what he teaches believe and accept it; therefore, the Tathāgata does not undergo transformation birth (*upapāduka*).
Good son! Among all sentient beings, the father performs the karma of a son, and the son performs the karma of a father.

If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, were to receive a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), he would have no parents; if he had no parents, how could he cause all sentient beings to perform various wholesome deeds?
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept transformation bodies. Good son,
within the True Dharma of the Buddha, there are two kinds of protection:
There are two kinds: internal and external.
Internal protection refers to the precepts and prohibitions; external protection refers to one's clan, relatives, and kinsmen.
If the Buddha-Tathāgata were to accept a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), he would lack external protection; therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a transformation body.

Good son! There are those who give rise to arrogance by relying on their lineage; because the Tathāgata wishes to destroy such pride, he is born into a noble family and does not accept a manifested body.
"Good son!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has true parents: his father is named Śuddhodana and his mother is named Māyā. Yet sentient beings still say he is an illusion; how then could he receive a body born by transformation?"
If [the Tathāgata] were to receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), how could there be *śarīra* relics of the pulverized body?

It is for the sake of increasing the merit and virtue of sentient beings that the Tathāgata pulverizes his body so they may make offerings; therefore, the Tathāgata does not receive a transformation body.
"All Buddhas are entirely without transformation-birth; why then am I alone made to receive a transformation-body?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and praised the Buddha in verse:
"The Tathāgata is a mass of immeasurable merit; I am now unable to proclaim it fully."
Now, for the sake of sentient beings, I shall expound but a single portion; I pray only that you will compassionately listen to my words.
Sentient beings wander in the darkness of ignorance, fully experiencing boundless hundreds of kinds of suffering;
the World-Honored One is able to cause them to be far removed from these, and for this reason he is called the Greatly Compassionate One by the world.
Sentient beings wander back and forth on the rope of birth and death; Through heedlessness and delusion, they lack peace and joy.
The Tathāgata can bestow peace and joy upon all; Therefore, he forever severs the rope of birth and death.
Because the Buddha is able to bestow peace and happiness upon all beings, he does not crave his own pleasure;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he practices asceticism—therefore, the world offers him worship.
Seeing others suffer, his body trembles; though dwelling in hell, he feels no pain.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he undergoes great suffering; therefore, it is unsurpassed and immeasurable.
The Tathāgata practiced austerities for the sake of the multitudes, Accomplishing and perfecting the six pāramitās;
His mind remained unshaken amidst the winds of evil, And thus he surpassed all great beings of the world.
Sentient beings constantly desire peace and happiness, yet they do not know how to cultivate the causes of peace and happiness;
the Tathāgata can teach them to practice these, just as a compassionate father loves his only son.
The Buddha beholds the afflictions of sentient beings; his mind suffers as a mother pities a sick child.
He constantly contemplates all skillful means to bring them freedom from illness; for this reason, he subjects this body to others.
All sentient beings undergo various sufferings, yet their minds are inverted, taking them for pleasure;
the Tathāgata expounds the truth of suffering and pleasure, and is therefore titled the Greatly Compassionate One.
The world dwells entirely within the shell of ignorance; no one possesses the beak of wisdom capable of breaking it.
Only the Tathāgata’s beak of wisdom can peck it apart; for this reason, he is called the Greatest Son.
Not encompassed by the three periods of time, Devoid of names and conventional designations,
Awakened to the profoundly deep meaning of nirvāṇa— For this reason, the Buddha is called the Great Awakened One.
There is a river with swirling eddies that submerges sentient beings; blinded by ignorance, they do not know how to escape.
The Tathāgata has crossed over himself and is able to ferry others across; for this reason, he is called the Buddha, the Great Captain.
Able to know all causes and effects, And likewise thoroughly penetrating the path to cessation,
Constantly bestowing the medicine for the suffering of sentient beings— Therefore, the world calls him the Great King of Physicians.
The heterodox teachers with their false views preach asceticism, claiming that through this one may attain unsurpassed bliss;
the Tathāgata proclaims the practice of true bliss, which enables sentient beings to experience happiness.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, destroys false paths and reveals to sentient beings the true and correct way;
those who walk this path attain peace and happiness, and for this reason the Buddha is called the Guide.
Not created by self, nor created by another, Nor produced by both together, nor without cause—
The Tathāgata’s teaching on the matter of painful sensation Surpasses all those of the non-Buddhists.
Having fully accomplished the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, you likewise teach sentient beings through these dharmas;
when bestowing the gift of Dharma, you are free from envy or stinginess—therefore, the Buddha’s compassion is called "without conditions."
Without fabrication and without causal conditions, one attains that which is causeless and devoid of karmic retribution;
therefore, all the wise proclaim that the Tathāgata seeks no reward.
Though constantly associating with those in the world who act with negligence, his person is not defiled by negligence;
therefore he is called "Inconceivable," for the eight worldly dharmas cannot defile him.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has neither enemy nor friend; therefore, his mind is always impartial.
I roar the lion’s roar in praise of his great compassion, for he can roar the immeasurable lion’s roar.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-two;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, Part One.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings; he can tame those who are untamed, purify those who are impure, provide refuge to those without refuge, and bring liberation to those not yet liberated. Having attained the eight masteries, he acts as the Great Physician and serves as the Great King of Medicine.

The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was a son of the Buddha when he was a bodhisattva; after leaving the household life, he received, upheld, recited, and expounded upon the twelve divisions of the sūtras, destroyed the fetters of the desire realm, and attained the four dhyānas.
Why did the Tathāgata prophesy that Sunakṣatra is an icchantika, a person of the lowest station who shall dwell in hell for an eon and is incurable?
Why did the Tathāgata not first expound the True Dharma to him and only later [declare him] a bodhisattva?
“If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cannot save the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, how can he be said to possess great compassion and great skillful means?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
For example, suppose there were parents who had only three sons.
One of these sons possessed a mind of faith and compliance; he was respectful toward his parents, possessed keen faculties and wisdom, and was able to understand worldly matters with great speed.
The second son did not respect his parents and lacked a heart of faith and obedience; however, possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, he was able to quickly understand worldly matters.
The third son did not respect his parents and lacked a heart of faith and obedience; moreover, he had dull faculties and no wisdom.
When parents wish to provide instruction, whom should they instruct first?
Whom should they love most?
And whom should they first teach to understand the affairs of the world?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
One should first instruct those who possess faith and obedience, who revere their parents, and who have sharp faculties, wisdom, and knowledge of worldly affairs.”
Next, as for the second and even the third [son], although those two sons lacked faith and a heart of reverence, he nevertheless taught them in succession out of compassion.
“Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise.
His three sons represent, respectively: first, the bodhisattva; second, the śrāvaka; and third, the icchantika.”
The subtle meanings within the sūtras of the twelve divisions of the canon have already been explained by me for the bodhisattvas;
the shallow and mundane meanings have been taught for the śrāvakas;

and the worldly meanings have been taught for icchantikas and those who have committed the five heinous crimes—though these offer no benefit in the present life, they are spoken out of compassion so as to produce the seeds of all virtues for future lives.

Good son! It is like three kinds of fields: the first has easy access for irrigation channels and is free from sand, gravel, shards, stones, thorns, and brambles; by sowing one seed, one obtains a hundredfold.
Second, although there are no pebbles, shards, stones, or thorns, and the irrigation channels are not difficult to traverse, the harvest is reduced by half.
Third, where the irrigation channels are difficult to traverse and there are many pebbles, shards, stones, and thorns, one obtains only what was sown, because of the abundance of straw and chaff.
"Good son!
In the spring months, in which field does a farmer first sow?
"World-Honored One!"
"First one plants in the first field, next in the second field, and finally in the third.
"The first is a metaphor for the bodhisattva, the next for the śrāvaka, and the last for the icchantika."
"Good son!
It is like three jars: one is intact, the second is leaking, and the third is broken. If one wishes to store milk, curd, water, or ghee, which one would one use first?"
“World-Honored One!
One should first employ those that are complete, next those that have leaks, and finally even those that are broken.
“Those that are complete and pure are a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas and the Saṃgha; those with leaks are a metaphor for the Śrāvakas; and those that are broken are a metaphor for the icchantikas.”
Good son! It is like three sick people who come together to a physician: one is easily cured, the second is difficult to cure, and the third is incurable. Good son!
“If a physician were to treat them, whom should he treat first?
“World-Honored One,
he should first treat the one who is easiest, then the second, and finally the third.”
Why is this? Because they are one's kinsmen.
"Those who are easy to treat are a metaphor for the community of Bodhisattvas."
Those who are difficult to cure are likened to the śrāvaka-saṃgha;

those who are incurable are likened to icchantikas—though they lack wholesome fruits in the present life, [the Buddha] out of compassion plants the seeds for various wholesome qualities for them in future lives.
Good son! It is like a great king who has three kinds of horses:

first, those that are well-trained, vigorous, and of great strength; second, those that are untrained but have full teeth and great strength; and third, those that are untrained, emaciated and old, and lacking in strength.
“O King, if you were to ride them, whom would you mount first?
“World-Honored One!
I should mount the one that is well-trained, strong, and powerful first; then use the second, and finally use the third.”
“Good son! The well-trained, powerful ox is a metaphor for the bodhisattva-saṃgha;
the second is a metaphor for the śrāvaka-saṃgha.”

The third type is likened to an icchantika; although they provide no benefit in the present life, out of compassion, [the Buddha] plants the seeds for all manner of wholesome roots for their future lives.

Good son! It is like when three people come at the time of a great giving: the first is of noble birth, intelligent, and observant of the precepts; the second is of middle-class birth, of dull faculties, and observant of the precepts; the third is of low birth, of dull faculties, and violates the precepts.
"Good son! To whom should this great donor first give?
"World-Honored One!"
"One should first bestow [the gift] upon the son of a noble family who possesses sharp faculties and maintains the precepts; next, one should reach the second; and finally, the third.
"The first is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; the second is a metaphor for the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; and the third is a metaphor for the icchantika."
"Good son!
Just as a great lion exerts its full strength when killing a fragrant elephant, it does so likewise when killing a rabbit, without conceiving a thought of contempt.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are also like this: when they expound the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas and icchantikas alike, their application of effort is no different."
"Good son!
At one time I was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra served as my attendant.
During the first watch of the night, I expounded the essentials of the Dharma for Śakra, the Lord of Devas."
It is the duty of a disciple to sleep after his teacher; at that time, because I had sat for a long duration, Sunakṣatra conceived an evil thought.
Furthermore, when the young boys and girls of Rājagṛha cried and would not stop, their parents would say to them:
"If you do not stop, we shall hand you over to the spirit Bakula."
At that time, Sunakṣatra was instead seized and held captive, and he said to me:
"Enter the meditation chamber quickly; Bakula is coming. I said:
“Foolish man, have you not always heard that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is fearless?
At that time, Śakra spoke to me, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Will such people as these also be able to enter into the Buddha-dharma?
I then said to him: "Kauśika!
"Such a person as this shall enter the Buddha-dharma, possesses the Buddha-nature, and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Although I preached the Dharma for this Śunakṣatra, he had no mind whatsoever to believe or accept it.
“Good son! At one time, while I was in the city of Śivapura in the kingdom of Kāśī, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra served as my attendant.
At that time, I wished to enter that city to beg for alms; immeasurable sentient beings, with hearts empty and yearning, desired to see my footprints.”
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra followed closely behind me and attempted to destroy [my reputation], yet he was unable to do so;
instead, he caused sentient beings to give rise to unwholesome thoughts.
After I had entered the city, I saw a Nirgrantha at a tavern, crouching on the ground with his back hunched, eating dregs of wine.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra said:
"World-Honored One!
If there are any arhats in the world, this person is the most supreme."
"Why is this? Because what this person says is that there is neither cause nor effect. I said:
"O fool, have you not always heard that an Arhat does not drink alcohol, does not harm others, does not deceive, does not steal, and does not engage in sexual misconduct?"
This person has murdered his parents and consumed wine dregs; how can you say he is an Arhat?
When this person abandons his body, he will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
"An Arhat has eternally severed the three evil destinies; how can you say that this person is an Arhat?
Sunaksatra then replied, "The nature of the four great elements may still be transformed, but to claim that this man will certainly fall into Avīci—that is impossible."
I said, "Foolish man,
have you not always heard that the truthful words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are non-dual?
Although I preached the Dharma for this Śunakṣatra, he was utterly devoid of any mind to believe or accept it.
“Good son, at one time I was staying in the city of Rājagṛha together with the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra. At that time, there was in the city a Nirgrantha named Duḥkha who constantly said:
‘The afflictions of sentient beings have no cause and no condition; the liberation of sentient beings likewise has no cause or condition.’”
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there are arhats in the world, Kṛtaka is the foremost."
I said: "Foolish man, you have perversely attained the state of a Nirgrantha; you are truly not an Arhat, nor can you understand the path of an Arhat.
Sunakṣatra spoke again:
"For what reason does an Arhat give rise to jealousy toward another Arhat? I replied:
"Foolish man, I do not give rise to jealousy toward an Arhat; it is you yourself who have conceived this evil and false view."
"If you say that this Kudu is an Arhat, then seven days from now he shall suffer from abdominal pain due to indigestion and die; having died, he shall be reborn among the hungry ghosts who eat vomit.
His fellow students shall carry his corpse and place it in the cold forest."
At that time, Sunakṣatra went to where the Nirgrantha Kṛtaka was and said to him: "Elder!
Do you know now?"
"Śramaṇa Gautama has predicted that in seven days you shall suffer from abdominal pain caused by undigested food and die; having died, you shall be reborn among the hungry ghosts who consume vomit;
your fellow students and teachers shall carry your corpse and place it in the cold forest."
"Elder! Reflect well and employ every means to cause Gautama to fall into falsehood.

When Kṛtaka heard these words, he immediately undertook a fast from the first day until the sixth; when the seventh day was completed, he consumed black honey, and having consumed the black honey, he drank cold water; having drunk the cold water, his belly ached and he died.

When the funeral rites were completed, his fellow students carried his corpse to the forest of cold ashes (śītavana) and placed it there. Immediately, he took on the form of a hungry ghost who feeds upon vomit and remained by the side of his own corpse.

Having heard of this matter, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra went to the forest of cold ashes and saw that Kṛtaka had assumed the body of a suffering being, taking the form of one who feeds upon vomit, crouching on the ground with his back hunched beside his corpse.
Sunakṣatra asked,
"Venerable sir, are you dead?
Kṛtaka replied:
"I have already died.
"How did you die? He replied:
“He died from abdominal pain.
[The king asked: “Who carried out your corpse? He replied:
“Fellow student.
“Where did you put it? He replied:
“Foolish man, do you not recognize this as the Śītavana cemetery?
“What kind of body have I obtained?
He replied:
"I have obtained the body of a *vāntāśana* (vomit-eating) spirit. Sunakṣatra!
Listen attentively to the Tathāgata’s well-spoken words, his truthful words, his timely words, his meaningful words, and his words of Dharma."
"Sunakṣatra! Such true words as these have issued from the mouth of the Tathāgata; why did you not believe them at that time?
If there are sentient beings who do not believe the true words of the Tathāgata, they too shall receive a body such as this one of mine."
At that time, Sunakṣatra returned to me and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
After the death of the Nirgrantha Kṛtaka, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
I said: "Foolish man, an Arhat has no place of rebirth; how can you say that Kṛtaka was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three?"
“World-Honored One!
It is indeed as you have said; the Nirgrantha Kṛtaka was not reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, but has now received the body of a hungry ghost who consumes vomit.”
I said: "Foolish man, the truthful words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are non-dual; it is impossible for a Tathāgata to speak with two different accounts."
Sujāta immediately replied,
"Although the Tathāgata spoke thus at that time, I did not give rise to faith in these matters at all.
"Good son," I have also constantly preached the true Dharma for the bhikṣu Sujāta, yet he has utterly lacked any mind to believe and accept it.

“Good son! Although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra recited and studied the twelve divisions of the scriptures and attained the four dhyānas, he did not understand the meaning of even a single verse, a single phrase, or a single word; having associated with evil friends, he fell away from the four dhyānas.”
Having lost the four dhyānas, he gave rise to evil and false views and spoke thus:
"There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no nirvāṇa.
The śramaṇa Gautama is skilled in the science of marks; for this reason, he is able to know the minds of others."
At that time, I said to Sunaksatra:

"The Dharma I teach is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its words are skillful, its characters and meanings are authentic and true, what is spoken is unadulterated, and it fully accomplishes the pure holy life."
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra further said:
"Although the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma for me, I truly maintain that there is neither cause nor effect.
O son of good family!
"If you do not believe such a matter, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra is currently nearby at the Nairañjanā River; you may go together with me to question him.

At that time, the Tathāgata immediately went with Kāśyapa to Sunakṣatra’s location. When the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra saw the Tathāgata from afar, he immediately gave rise to an evil and heterodox mind; because of that evil mind, his body sank down alive and fell into the Avīci Hell.

“Good son! Although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra entered the immeasurable treasury of jewels that is the Buddha-dharma, he obtained nothing at all; he did not gain the benefit of even a single dharma, because of his negligence and because of evil associates.”
It is, for example, like a person who enters the great ocean and sees many various jewels, yet obtains nothing because of negligence.
Or again, it is like entering the sea and seeing a heap of jewels, yet killing oneself, or being slain by rākṣasas or malevolent spirits.
The bhikṣu Śunakṣatra was just like this: having entered the Buddha-dharma, he was killed by evil associates, who were like rākṣasa demons.
O son of good family!
Therefore, out of compassion, the Tathāgata constantly says that Sunakṣatra is full of negligence.
Good son! If one is originally poor, although one may feel compassion for such a person, that compassion will be slight.
If one who was originally immensely wealthy later loses their property, the compassion one feels for that person is profound;
the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra is just like this. Having mastered and recited the twelve divisions of the scriptures and attained the four dhyānas, he subsequently fell away from them—this is truly pitiable.
Therefore, I say that the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was full of negligence; because of his great negligence, he severed all roots of goodness.

Among my disciples, those who have seen or heard of him cannot fail to give rise to a heart of profound compassion for this person, just as one would feel for a man who was once immensely wealthy but later lost all his fortune.
For many years, I have constantly followed and associated with Sunakṣatra, yet he has conceived an evil and heterodox mind; because of that evil heterodoxy, he does not abandon his wrong views.
"Good son!

Since the distant past, I have observed that this Sunakṣatra possessed even the slightest root of goodness, as small as a hair or a filament; for this reason, I never prophesied that he had severed his roots of goodness, was an icchantika, a base person, or one who would dwell in hell for kalpas."

Because he proclaims that there is no cause and no effect, and that there is no such thing as karmic action, he is then designated as one who has severed his roots of goodness—a *icchantika*, a base person who shall dwell in hell for eons.
Good son! It is like a person who has fallen into a privy.
A good friend reaches in with his hand; if he finds the hair of the head, he wishes to pull him out, but after searching for a long time without success, he finally desists.

I am likewise; seeking even the slightest root of goodness in Sunakṣatra, I wish to rescue him, yet though I search all day long, I do not find so much as a hair’s breadth of it. For this reason, I cannot deliver him from hell.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason did the Tathāgata prophesy that he would fall into the Avīci Hell?”

“Good son! The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra has many followers, all of whom claim that Sunakṣatra is an arhat and one who has attained the fruit of the Path. Because I wish to destroy their evil and heterodox minds, I have declared that Sunakṣatra, due to his negligence, will fall into hell.”
"Good son!
You should now know that what the Tathāgata has spoken is true and without duality. Why is this?"
If the Buddha has prophesied that one shall fall into hell, it is impossible that they would not fall there.
As for the predictions made by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there are two possibilities:
they may be false or they may be true.
For example, when Maudgalyāyana was in the kingdom of Magadha, he announced to all the people that after seven days the heavens would send down rain, yet in the end it did not rain;
he further predicted that a cow would give birth to a white calf, but at the time of delivery, she instead gave birth to a brindled calf;
and he predicted the birth of a son, but later a daughter was born.

“Good son! The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra constantly preached to immeasurable sentient beings that there are no results of good or evil in anything; at that time, he forever severed all roots of goodness until not even so much as a hair’s breadth remained.”
"Good son!
I have long known that this bhikṣu Śunakṣatra would sever his roots of goodness; nevertheless, I continued to dwell with him for a full twenty years, supporting and associating with him."

If I were to cast them far away and not keep them close at hand, these people would cause immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil deeds; this is called the Tathāgata’s fifth power of understanding.
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions do those of the icchantika class lack wholesome dharmas? “Good son!
Because those who are icchantikas have severed their roots of goodness.

Although all sentient beings possess the five faculties, such as faith, the icchantikas have eternally cut them off; for this reason, one incurs the sin of killing even by slaying an ant, yet there is no sin of killing when one kills an icchantika.
“World-Honored One!
Since those of icchantika nature ultimately possess no wholesome dharmas, is it for this reason that they are called icchantikas?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is. "World-Honored One!
All sentient beings possess three kinds of goodness, namely: those of the past, the future, and the present."
"Even those who are icchantikas cannot sever future wholesome dharmas; why, then, do you say that one who severs all wholesome dharmas is called an icchantika? "Good son!..."
There are two kinds of severance:
first, cessation in the present; second, the obstruction of the future by the present.
The icchantikas possess both forms of severance; therefore, I say that they have severed all roots of goodness.
Good son!

It is like a person who has sunk into a latrine; though there remains only the tip of a single hair that has not yet submerged, even though that single hair-tip remains above, it cannot support the body.
The icchantikas are also like this: although they will possess roots of goodness in future lives, they cannot rescue themselves from the sufferings of hell.
While they may be rescued in future ages, there is nothing that can be done for them in the present life; therefore, they are called "those who cannot be saved."
By means of the causes and conditions of buddha-nature, one can attain salvation; for buddha-nature is neither past, nor future, nor present, and therefore buddha-nature cannot be severed.
"Just as rotten seeds cannot produce sprouts, so it is with those who possess the icchantika nature.
"World-Honored One!
Those who possess the icchantika nature do not sever their Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is itself wholesome. Why, then, do you say that they have severed all goodness?"
“Good son! If sentient beings possessed the Buddha-nature within the present life, they could not be called icchantikas.
Just as with sentient beings in the world, the self-nature and the Buddha-nature are eternal and are not encompassed by the three periods of time.”
If it were encompassed within the three periods of time, it would be called impermanent.
Because the Buddha-nature exists in the future and will be seen, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
For this reason, it is only when Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are fully adorned that they obtain a slight vision of it.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha-nature is eternal, just like space; for what reason does the Tathāgata say it is ‘in the future’?”

If the Tathāgata were to say that those who are icchantikas possess no wholesome dharmas, how could it be that these icchantikas do not give rise to feelings of love and affection toward their fellow students, teachers, parents, kinsmen, wives, and children?
"If they were thus born, would that not be good?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Good son, you have asked this question well.
The Buddha-nature is like space; it is neither past, nor future, nor present.”
All sentient beings have three kinds of bodies, namely: those of the past, the future, and the present.
Sentient beings will, in the future, attain a body fully adorned and pure, through which they shall perceive the Buddha-nature; therefore, I say that the Buddha-nature is "future."
"Good son!

For the sake of sentient beings, I sometimes speak of causes as effects, and sometimes speak of effects as causes. Therefore, in the sutras it is said that life is food, seeing forms is contact, and because the future body is pure, it is called Buddha-nature."
“World-Honored One!
If the meaning is as the Buddha has explained it, for what reason do you say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature? “Good son!”
Although the Buddha-nature of sentient beings does not exist in the present, it cannot be said to be non-existent.
It is like the nature of space: although it does not exist in the present, it cannot be said to be non-existent.
Although all sentient beings are impermanent, this Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, in this sutra I have said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external, just as space is neither internal nor external.
If space possessed an interior or an exterior, space could not be called "one" or "permanent," nor could it be said to exist everywhere.
Although empty space is neither internal nor external, yet all sentient beings possess it; the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise so.
As for what you said—that those of the icchantika class possess wholesome dharmas—this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? If those who are icchantikas possess any physical, verbal, or mental karma—whether it be karma of grasping, seeking, giving, or understanding—all such karma is exclusively wrong karma.
Why is this? Because they do not seek cause and effect. Good son!
"Just as the harītakī fruit—its roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—are all bitter, so too are the karmic actions of an icchantika.

'Good son, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of beings; therefore, he is well able to distinguish the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings. He knows that this person will transform from inferior to middling, that this person will transform from middling to superior, that this person will transform from superior to middling, and that this person will transform from middling to inferior. For this reason, you should know that the nature of the faculties of beings is not fixed. Because it is not fixed, one may sever the roots of goodness, yet having severed them, they may grow back again.'"

If the faculties and natures of sentient beings were fixed, their afflictions would never cease once severed, nor would they arise again after having been severed; furthermore, one should not say that those of the icchantika class fall into hell for a lifespan of one kalpa.
“Good son! For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas have no fixed characteristics.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of beings; you must surely know that Sunakṣatra will sever his roots of goodness.
For what reason did you permit him to leave the household life?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

When I first left the household life in the past, my younger brother Nanda, my cousin Ānanda, Devadatta, and my son Rāhula—all such as these followed me to leave the household life and practice the Way. Had I not permitted Sunakṣatra to leave the household life, he would have been next in line to inherit the royal throne; with his power and autonomy, he would have destroyed the Buddha-Dharma. For this reason, I permitted him to leave the household life and practice the Way.”
"Good son! If the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra had not left the household life, he would likewise have severed his roots of goodness and would have been of no benefit whatsoever for immeasurable ages.

Now that he has left the household life, although he has severed his roots of goodness, he is able to receive and uphold the precepts, to offer service and respect to the elders, the seniors, and those of virtuous character, and to cultivate the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; this is called a 'wholesome cause.'"

In this way, wholesome causes can give rise to wholesome dharmas; once wholesome dharmas have arisen, one is able to cultivate the Path; having cultivated the Path, one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, I permitted Sunakṣatra to go forth as a monk.
Good son! Had I not permitted the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra to leave the household life and receive the precepts, I could not have been called a Tathāgata endowed with the ten powers.

“Good son! The Buddha observes that sentient beings are endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas. Although such a person possesses these two types of dharmas, before long they will be able to sever all roots of goodness and become possessed of roots of unwholesomeness.”

Why is this? Because such sentient beings do not associate with virtuous friends, do not listen to the true Dharma, do not engage in correct reflection, and do not act in accordance with the Dharma; by these causes and conditions, they are able to sever their roots of goodness and become possessed of unwholesome roots.
"Good son!

The Tathāgata further knows that whether in this present life or in future lives—whether in youth, middle age, or old age—this person shall draw near to virtuous friends and hear and receive the True Dharma of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; at that time, they will be able to regenerate their roots of goodness."
"Good son!
It is like a spring not far from a village, whose water is sweet and possesses the eight meritorious qualities.
Suppose there is a person suffering from heat and thirst who wishes to go to that spring."
A wise person observing this thirsty man will know for certain, without doubt, that he will reach the place where water is.
Why? Because there is no other path.
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, observes all sentient beings in this very same way; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to be 'endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of earth from the ground, placed it upon his fingernail, and said to Kāśyapa:
"Is this earth more, or [the earth of the great earth]?"
“Is the earth and soil of the worlds in the ten directions much?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, the soil upon the World-Honored One’s fingernail cannot be compared to all the soil that exists throughout the ten directions.”
“Good son! There are those who, having abandoned their bodies, again obtain human bodies;

having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, they receive human bodies with all faculties intact, are born in a central land, possess perfect right faith, are able to cultivate the Path, and having cultivated the Path, are able to attain liberation; and having attained liberation, are able to enter nirvāṇa—such as the amount of dust on a fingernail.

Having abandoned the human body, they obtain the bodies of the three evil realms; having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, they obtain yet more bodies of the three evil realms. With their faculties incomplete, they are born in borderlands, believing in heterodox and inverted views, and practicing false paths; thus they fail to attain liberation, permanence, bliss, or nirvana—just like the amount of earth found throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"Good son!

Uphold the prohibitive precepts with diligent and tireless effort; do not commit the four grave offenses, do not perform the five heinous acts, do not misappropriate the property of the Saṃgha, do not become an icchantika, and do not sever the roots of goodness. Believe in such sūtras on nirvāṇa as these, which are as rare as the dust upon a fingernail."

Those who violate the precepts and are indolent, those who commit the four grave offenses, those who commit the five heinous crimes, those who misappropriate the property of the Sangha, those who become icchantikas, and those who sever all roots of goodness—such as those who do not believe in this sutra—are as numerous as all the particles of earth in the worlds of the ten directions.
“Good son!
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows such superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings; for this reason, the Buddha is said to possess the power of knowing faculties.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with this power of knowing the faculties; therefore, he is able to know the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings, as well as their distinctions of sharpness and dullness.”
He knows the faculties of sentient beings in the present age, and he also knows the faculties of sentient beings in the future.
Such beings, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, will speak thus:
"The Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa," or "He has not ultimately entered parinirvāṇa"; or they will say that there is a self, or that there is no self.
I may have an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or I may not have an intermediate state; I may speak of falling back (*parihāṇi*), or I may speak of no falling back;
I may say that the body of the Tathāgata is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), or I may say that the body of the Tathāgata is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
some may say that the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are conditioned phenomena, while others say that dependent origination is unconditioned.
Regarding the Dharma, some say that the mind is permanent, while others say it is impermanent;
some say that the enjoyment of the five sensory pleasures can obstruct the Noble Path, while others say it does not;

some say that the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) belongs only to the desire realm, while others say it belongs to all three realms; or some say that giving is exclusively a mental action (manas-karman), or...
Some say that it is precisely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); some say there are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
some say there are no three unconditioned phenomena; furthermore, some say there is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), while others say there is no derived matter;
some say there is non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), while others say there is no non-manifest form.
Regarding form (*rūpa*), some say there are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), while others say there are no mental factors;
some say there are five kinds of existence (*bhava*), while others say there are six kinds of existence;
some say that the eightfold precepts of the fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) and the lay follower’s precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*) are fully obtained through formal reception, while others say they are not.
Regarding the full reception [of precepts]: some say that even after a bhikṣu has committed the four grave offenses (pārājika), the bhikṣu-precepts still remain;

others say they no longer remain. Some say that those who have attained the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat all attain the Buddha-way; others say they do not. Or it is said that buddha-nature exists within sentient beings.

Some say that buddha-nature exists apart from sentient beings; some say that even those who have committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or who are icchantikas all possess buddha-nature, while others say they do not;
some say there are Buddhas of the ten directions, while others say there are no Buddhas of the ten directions—just as the Tathāgata has fully realized.
“Since you have accomplished the power of the faculty of knowledge, why do you not give a definitive teaching today?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Good son!...”
This meaning is not known by visual consciousness, nor even by mental consciousness; it is that which can be known only by wisdom.
If there is one who possesses such wisdom, toward that person I shall never make a duality; this is also called my teaching of non-duality.
To those who lack wisdom, I speak with indeterminacy, yet those lacking wisdom likewise claim that I speak indeterminately.
Son of good family!

All the virtuous deeds of the Tathāgata are for the sake of taming all sentient beings; they are like the medical prescriptions of a master physician, which are entirely for the purpose of curing all suffering from disease.
"Good son!

For the sake of the land, for the sake of the season, for the sake of the words of others, for the sake of various individuals, and for the sake of the diverse faculties of beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, makes two kinds of explanations regarding a single dharma; he speaks of immeasurable names for a single named dharma, speaks of immeasurable names for a single meaning, and speaks of immeasurable names for immeasurable meanings."
How is it that a single name expresses immeasurable names?

Just as with *nirvāṇa*, it is also called *nirvāṇa*, also called "non-arising," also called "non-issuance," also called "unconditioned," also called "the uncreated," also called "refuge," also called "cave-dwelling," also called "liberation," also called "light," also called "lamp-light," also called "the further shore," also called "fearlessness," also called "non-retrogression," also called "abiding in peace," also called "quiescence," also called "signless," also called "non-dual," also called "single practice," also called "coolness," also called "darkness-free," also called "unimpeded," also called "without strife," also called "unturbid," also called "vast," also called "ambrosia," and also called "auspiciousness. Thus, what is a single name is made into immeasurable names.
"What is meant by 'one meaning expressed through immeasurable names'?

It is like Śakra, who is also called Śakra, also called Kauśika, also called Vāsava, also called Purandara, also called Maghavan, also called Indra, also called Sahasrākṣa, also called Śacīpati, also called Vajrin, also called Ratnaśikhin, and also called Ratnadhvaja; this is what is meant by one meaning expressed through immeasurable names."
"How is it that immeasurable meanings are expressed by immeasurable names?
For example, the Buddha-Tathāgata is called 'Tathāgata,' where the meaning differs from the name;
he is also called 'Arhat,' where the meaning differs from the name."
He is also called Samyaksaṃbuddha; these are different names with different meanings.

He is also called the Boatman, the Guide, the Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha), the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna), the Great Lion King, the Śramaṇa, and the Brāhmaṇa. And so forth.
He is named Tranquility; he is also named Benefactor; he is also named One Who Has Reached the Further Shore; he is also named Great King of Physicians;
he is also named Great Elephant King; he is also named Great Dragon King; he is also named Bestower of Eyes; he is also named Great Malla;
he is also named Great Fearlessness; he is also named Heap of Jewels; and he is also named Caravan Leader.

He is also called "One Who Has Attained Liberation," "Great Being," "Teacher of Gods and Humans," "Great Pundarika," "Solitary Without Equal," "Great Field of Merit," "Ocean of Great Wisdom," "Formless One," and "Endowed with the Eight Knowledges"— all such names as these.
The meanings differ and the names differ.
Good son! This is called explaining immeasurable names within immeasurable meanings.

Furthermore, there is another principle: that a single meaning is expressed by immeasurable names. For example, as with the aggregates (*skandha*), they are called "aggregates," and they are also called "inversions" (*viparyāsa*), "truths" (*satya*), "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), "the four nutriments" (*āhāra*), "the four stations of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*), "existence" (*bhava*), "the path" (*mārga*), "time" (*kāla*), "sentient beings" (*sattva*), "the world" (*loka*), "the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*), the "three cultivations"—namely, body, precepts, and mind— "cause and effect" (*hetu-phala*), "afflictions" (*kleśa*), "liberation" (*vimukti*), "the twelve links of dependent origination" (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), "śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas," "hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas," and "the past, present, and future. This is what is meant by saying that a single meaning is expressed by immeasurable names.

“Good son! For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, explains the detailed within the concise and the concise within the detailed; he explains the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and explains the conventional truth as the ultimate truth.”
What is meant by "explaining the concise within the extensive"?
It is as when he addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now proclaim the twelve links of dependent origination.
What are the twelve links of dependent origination?
Regarding what is called cause and effect:
what is meant by "briefly stating the middle and explaining it extensively"?

It is as when [the Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus: "I now proclaim suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. 'Suffering' refers to immeasurable sufferings; 'its origin' refers to immeasurable afflictions; 'its cessation' refers to immeasurable liberations; and 'the path' refers to immeasurable skillful means."
What is meant by explaining the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
It is, for example, as when [the Buddha] told the bhikṣus: "In this body of mine, there are now old age, sickness, and death.
What is meant by explaining the conventional truth as the ultimate truth?
As it was said to Kauṇḍinya: "Because you have realized the Dharma, you shall be named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Therefore, because he acts according to the person, according to the intention, and according to the time, he is called the Tathāgata who possesses the power of knowing the faculties of others.
Good son, if I were to provide a definitive explanation regarding such matters as these, then I could not be called a Tathāgata who possesses the power of knowing the faculties.
“Good son, a person of wisdom should know that what a fragrant elephant can carry cannot be borne by a donkey.
The practices of all sentient beings are immeasurable; therefore, the Tathāgata preaches immeasurable teachings in various ways.”
Why is this? Because sentient beings possess many afflictions.
If the Tathāgata were to teach only a single practice, he could not be said to have fully accomplished the power of knowing the faculties of others.

Therefore, in other sūtras I have said that five kinds of sentient beings should not be taught five kinds of dharmas: one should not praise right faith to those who lack faith; one should not praise the observance of precepts to those who violate them; one should not praise giving to those who are stingy and greedy; one should not praise extensive learning to those who are indolent; and one should not praise wisdom to those who are ignorant and deluded.

Why is this? If a wise person were to explain these five matters to these five types of people, one should know that such a speaker would not possess the power of fully knowing the faculties of others, nor could they be called one who has compassion for sentient beings.
Why is this? Because when these five types of people hear this matter, they give rise to lack of faith, malevolence, and anger;

due to these causes and conditions, they will undergo the retribution of suffering for immeasurable lifetimes. For this reason, they are not called those who have compassion for sentient beings and are endowed with the power of the faculties.
Therefore, I previously told Śāriputra in another sutra:
