"Be careful not to preach the Dharma extensively to those of sharp faculties, nor preach it concisely to those of dull faculties."
Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One!
I spoke only out of compassion; it was not because I possess the full power of the faculties."
“Good son! The teaching of the Dharma, both extensive and concise, is the realm of the Buddhas; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Good son!”

As you have said, regarding those disciples who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, each offer divergent explanations: these people all rely on inverted causes and conditions and fail to attain right view; for this reason, they are unable to benefit themselves or others.

Good son! These sentient beings do not possess a single nature, a single practice, a single faculty, a single land, or a single spiritual friend. Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims various essential teachings for them. For this reason, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, reveal and expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings.
"Good son!
When the Tathāgata speaks these twelve divisions of the sūtras, it is not for his own benefit, but solely for the benefit of others.
Therefore, the fifth power of the Tathāgata is called the power of understanding."

By virtue of these two powers, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows that this person is able to sever their roots of goodness in the present life, while that person is able to sever their roots of goodness in a future life; and that this person is able to attain liberation in the present life, while that person is able to attain liberation in a future life.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the Supreme Warrior.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 33. *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 34.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve, Part Two: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa. "Good son!
If one says that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate nirvāṇa or has not entered ultimate nirvāṇa, such a person speaks thus because they do not understand the intention of the Tathāgata. Good son!

In this Fragrant Mountain dwell fifty-three thousand sages; all of them, under the past Buddha Kāśyapa, cultivated various merits but had not yet attained the Right Path, and they have remained in the presence of the Buddhas to hear and receive the True Dharma.
Desiring to act for the sake of such people as these, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, saying:
"After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
When the devas heard this, the sound was transmitted from one to another until it reached Mount Gandhamādana.
Upon hearing this, the sages immediately gave rise to a sense of regret and spoke these words:
"How is it that we, having been born among human beings, have not drawn near to the Buddha?"
"The appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world is extremely rare, like the udumbara flower; I shall now go to the presence of the World-Honored One to hear and receive the True Dharma.
"O son of good family!"
At that time, fifty-three thousand seers came to where I was, and I then taught them the Dharma as was appropriate:
"O Great Beings!
Form is impermanent."
Why is this? Because the causes and conditions of form (*rūpa*) are impermanent; since it arises from impermanent causes, how could form be permanent?
This applies likewise up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the various seers immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship. "Good son!

In Kuśinagara there were three hundred thousand Mallas who were without any master or protector; they relied on their own arrogance and self-indulgence, as well as their physical strength, vitality, and wealth, their minds being crazed and intoxicated with disorder."
"Good son!
For the sake of subduing those Mallas, I said to Maudgalyāyana:
'You must subdue such Mallas as these.'"

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, out of reverence for and compliance with my instruction, engaged in various forms of teaching and transformation for five years, yet he was unable to cause even a single Malla to accept the Dharma and attain subduing.
For this reason, I again spoke to Ānanda for the sake of those Mallas, saying:
"After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
O son of good family!
When the Mallas had heard these words, they gathered together and leveled the roads.

After three months had passed, I traveled from the kingdom of Vaiśālī to the city of Kuśinagara; seeing the Mallas from afar along the way, I immediately transformed myself into the likeness of a śramaṇa and went to where the Mallas were, speaking to them thus: "O youths!"
"What are you doing? Having heard this, all the wrestlers gave rise to resentment and spoke these words:
"O Śramaṇa!..."
"Why do you now claim that we are but children? I then said to them:
"If this great assembly of three hundred thousand people, exerting all the strength of their bodies, cannot move even this insignificant small stone, how can they not be called children?"
The Mallas said:
"If you consider us to be children, you should know that you yourself are the true adult.
O son of good family!
At that time, I dug out this stone with two toes of my feet.
When those strongmen saw this, they conceived a sense of inferiority toward themselves and spoke again, saying:
"O Śramaṇa!..."
"Can you now move this rock aside so that the path is cleared?
I asked the youth,
"For what reason and by what cause are you preparing and clearing this road?"
The Mallas said: "Śramaṇa!
Do you not know?"
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni shall travel by this path to the Śāla grove to enter parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, we are leveling and clearing it.
At that time, I praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
young man!
Since you have already conceived such a virtuous mind, I shall remove this rock for you."
At that time, I lifted a great stone with my hand and hurled it upward until it reached the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
When the Mallas saw the stone suspended in the air, they were all struck with terror and immediately sought to scatter in the four directions.
I spoke again, saying:
"O Mallas, you should not now give rise to a heart of fear and each desire to disperse.
The Mallas said:
“‘Śramaṇa! If you can rescue and protect me, I shall abide in peace.
At that time, I again took the stone with my hand and placed it in my right palm.”
Having seen this, the Malla felt joy arise in his heart and spoke again, saying:
"Śramaṇa! Is this stone eternal?"
"Is this impermanent?
At that time, I blew upon it with my mouth, and the stone immediately shattered and crumbled like fine dust.
Having seen this, the strongman cried out:
"Śramaṇa! This stone is impermanent.
Immediately, a sense of shame arose within him, and he reproached himself:
"How is it that we, relying on our sovereignty, physical beauty, strength, lifespan, and wealth, give rise to such arrogance?
Knowing their thoughts, I immediately relinquished my manifested form, restored my original appearance, and preached the Dharma for them.
Upon seeing this, all the Mallas conceived the aspiration for Bodhi. "Good son!
In Kuśinagara there was a craftsman named Cunda, who had previously made a great vow before the Buddha Kāśyapa:”
"When the Tathāgata Śākyamuni enters parinirvāṇa, I shall be the last to offer him food and drink.
For this reason, while in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, I entrusted my final instructions to the bhikṣu Upamāna:
"Good son!..."
After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara.
You should go and inform Cunda so that he may know this.

"Good son! In the city of Rājagṛha, there is a rishi with the five supernormal powers named Subhadra, who is one hundred and twenty years old. He constantly claims to be an omniscient person and has given rise to great arrogance. Having already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past, I, for the sake of subduing him, told Ānanda:
'After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"

Having heard this, Subhadra will come to me and give rise to a mind of faith and reverence; I shall then preach various dharmas for him, and upon hearing them, he will attain the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya).

“Good son! King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha had a crown prince named Ajātaśatru. Due to the causes and conditions of his karma, he conceived a mind of perversity and rebellion, desiring to harm his father, yet he could find no opportunity.”

At that time, the wicked man Devadatta, due to the causal conditions of his past karma, again conceived unwholesome thoughts toward me and desired to harm me; he immediately cultivated the five supernormal powers and attained them before long, becoming close friends with Prince Sudarśana.

For the sake of the crown prince, he manifested various supernatural feats: exiting through what was not a gate and entering through a gate; exiting through a gate and entering through what was not a gate; and at times manifesting the bodies of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, and women.

Upon seeing him, Prince Sudarśana immediately gave rise to a heart of affection, a heart of joy, and a heart of reverent faith; for this reason, he prepared various kinds of offerings and made them to him, and further addressed him, saying:
"O Great Master, O Holy One!"
"I now wish to see the Mandārava flowers.
Thereupon, Devadatta went at once to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and sought them from the devas there; however, because his merit was exhausted, no one gave him any.
Having failed to obtain the flowers, he thought to himself:
"The mandārava tree is devoid of self or what belongs to a self; if I were to take them myself, what sin could there be?"
As he stepped forward intending to seize him, he immediately lost his supernormal powers and saw himself once again in Rājagṛha.
Feeling shame and remorse, he was unable to see Prince Sudarśana again, and he further thought:
"I shall now go to where the Tathāgata is and seek out the great assembly."
"If the Buddha would grant me permission, I shall instruct and command Śāriputra and the others according to my will.
At that time, Devadatta came to me and spoke these words:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will entrust this great assembly to me; I shall teach and transform them through various methods of preaching the Dharma, so that they may be subdued."
I said to that foolish man:
"Śāriputra and the others are of brilliant wisdom and great insight, trusted and revered by the world;
yet I would not entrust the great assembly even to them, let alone to you, a foolish man who eats spittle."
At that time, Devadatta again conceived an even more intense malice toward me and spoke these words:
"Gautama! Although you now subdue the great assembly, your power shall not endure for long; you shall soon see yourself destroyed."

Having spoken these words, the great earth immediately shook in six ways; Devadatta fell to the ground at once, and a violent wind arose from his side, blowing up dust and soil to defile and cover him.
Having seen these evil omens, Devadatta spoke again, saying:
"If this very body of mine must enter the Avīci Hell in this present life, I shall certainly take revenge upon such a great enemy."
Then Devadatta immediately rose and went to where Prince Sudarśana was. Upon seeing him, Sudarśana asked:
"Noble one!
Why is your countenance so haggard and why do you have such an expression of sorrow?"
Devadatta said, "I have always been this way; do you not know it?
Sudarśana replied:
"Please tell us your intention; what are the causes and conditions for this?
Devadatta replied, "I am now extremely close and affectionate with you, yet outsiders revile you as being irrational. Having heard this matter, how could I not be distressed?"
Prince Sudarśana spoke again, saying,
"How did the people of the country insult and humiliate me?
Devadatta replied:
"The people of the country revile you as 'Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru).
Sudarśana spoke again:
"For what reason are they calling me 'Unborn Enemy'?"
"Who gave this name?
Devadatta replied, "Before you were born,
all the physiognomists said that once this child is born, he shall kill his father."
For this reason, all outsiders have called you "The Unborn Enemy" (Ajātaśatru),
while all those within the palace, out of a desire to protect your mind,
call you "Good Vision" (Sudarśana). When Queen Vaidehī heard these words, she took you from the high tower where you were born and cast you upon the ground, thereby breaking one of your fingers.
For this reason, people will again call you Pāṭaliputra.
Having heard this, my heart was filled with grief and distress, yet I could not bring myself to tell you of it.
Devadatta, through various such evil deeds, instructed him to kill his father, saying:
"If you kill your father, I too shall be able to kill the śramaṇa Gautama."
Prince Sudarśana questioned a great minister named Varṣākāra:
"For what reason did the Great King establish my name as Ajātaśatru?
The minister then explained the matter from beginning to end, exactly as Devadatta had described it.
Upon hearing this, Susīma immediately had his father, the king, arrested by his ministers and confined outside the city, where he was guarded by the fourfold army.
When Queen Vaidehī heard of these events, she went at once to the king’s location, but the guards blocked her way and would not allow her to enter.
At that time, the queen gave rise to a mind of anger and began to revile him.
Then the guards immediately informed the prince:
"Great King!..."
"Does my lady wish to go and see her father, the King? I wonder if he will grant her audience?
Upon hearing this, Sudarśana again gave rise to anger and resentment; he immediately went to his mother's quarters, seized her hair, drew his sword, and was about to strike her.
At that time, Jīvaka addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
Since the establishment of the kingdom, even those whose crimes are most grave have not been subject to such punishment as this, much less one's own mother who gave birth to you."
Upon hearing these words, Prince Sudarśana released him for the sake of Jīvaka.
He then cut off his father the king’s clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions; after seven days had passed, the king’s life came to an end.

After Prince Sudarśana had witnessed his father’s death, he finally gave rise to a sense of remorse; however, the minister Vṛṣṭika again addressed him with various evil and heterodox doctrines, saying:
"O Great King!..."
"All karmic actions are entirely without fault; for what reason, then, do you now give rise to a mind of regret?
Jīvaka replied again, "Great King!"
You should know that such an action involves two kinds of offenses:
first, the murder of one's father, the King; second, the murder of a Srotāpanna.
Regarding such a crime, there is no one other than a Buddha who can eliminate it.
King Sudarśana said:
"The Tathāgata is pure and free from all defilement; how can we, who are sinful people, behold him?
O son of good family!
Knowing this matter, I told Ānanda:
"After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, Sudarśana immediately came to my presence; I preached the Dharma for him, whereby his grave offenses were lightened and he attained rootless faith.
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and therefore speak thus:
'The Tathāgata definitively teaches that there is ultimate nirvāṇa.'"
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who possess the true meaning; second, those who are merely nominal.”
The nominal bodhisattvas, hearing that I shall enter parinirvāṇa in three months, all conceived a mind of retreat and spoke thus:
"If the Tathāgata is impermanent and does not abide, for what purpose should we undergo such great suffering and affliction throughout immeasurable lifetimes for his sake?"
Even the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who has fully accomplished and perfected immeasurable merits, cannot destroy such a Mara of Death; how much less could those like us possibly destroy it?
"Good son! For this reason, I speak these words for such bodhisattvas:
'The Tathāgata eternally abides and is subject to no change.'"
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and definitively declare that the Tathāgata will never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! There are sentient beings who give rise to the view of annihilationism and speak thus:
‘After the bodies of all sentient beings have perished, there is no one who experiences the results of their good and evil karma.’”
For such people, I speak these words:
"The retribution of good and evil deeds truly has one who experiences it.
How is it known that it exists?
"Good son!

In a past age, in Kuśinagara, there was a king named Sudarśana. He spent eighty-four thousand years as a youth, eighty-four thousand years as a crown prince, and another eighty-four thousand years upon ascending the throne."
Sitting in solitude, he reflected thus:
"Sentient beings have meager merit and short lifespans; they are constantly pursued by the four enemies, yet they remain unaware of this and continue to be heedless."
"Therefore, I shall leave the household life to practice the Way and sever the four enemies:
birth, old age, sickness, and death.
He then commanded his officials to construct a hall made of the seven treasures outside the city.
Having done so, he then addressed his ministers, officials, palace ladies, consorts, sons, and retinue:
"You should know that I wish to leave the household life; will you grant me your permission?"
At that time, the great minister and his retinue each spoke these words:
"Excellent, Great King!
Now is precisely the right time."
At that time, King Sudarśana, taking a single attendant, dwelt alone in the hall for another eighty-four thousand years, cultivating a mind of loving-kindness.

By reason of this compassion, he will successively become a Wheel-Turning Sage King for eighty-four thousand future lifetimes, a Śakra Devendra for thirty lifetimes, and various minor kings for immeasurable lifetimes.
"Good son! At that time, do you think that King Sudarśana was someone else?
Do not hold such a view; he was none other than myself."
"Good son!
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively teaches that there is a self and that there is what belongs to a self."
"Furthermore, at one time I spoke for the sake of all sentient beings, saying:

'The self is precisely nature; that is to say, internal and external causes and conditions, the twelve links of dependent origination, sentient beings, the five aggregates, the realm of mind, the world, merit, karmic actions, Maheśvara, and the age—these are what are called the self.'"
"When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed that the Tathāgata definitely taught that a self exists. Good son,
at another time, there was a bhikṣu who came to me and spoke as follows:"
“World-Honored One!
What is called ‘self,’ and who is this self?”
"For what reason is there a 'self'?
At that time, I immediately spoke to the bhikṣu, saying: "Bhikṣu!..."
There is no self, nor anything belonging to a self.
The eye is originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence.

At the time of its arising, it comes from nowhere; at the time of its cessation, it goes nowhere. Although there are karmic fruits, there is no agent; there is no one who casts off the aggregates, nor anyone who receives them.
Regarding what you have asked, "What is the self?
the self is precisely the life-span (*āyus*). Who is this self?
This is precisely karma.
For what reason is there a "self"?
This is precisely craving.
"Monks! Just as when two hands clap together, a sound arises from between them, so too am I:
by reason of the three conditions—sentient beings, karma, and craving—I am designated as 'self'."
"Monks! For all sentient beings, form is not the self; the self does not exist within form, nor does form exist within the self. This applies likewise, even unto consciousness."
"O Bhikṣus!

Although the various non-Buddhists claim there is a self, it never exists apart from the aggregates (skandhas). It is impossible that there could be a self distinct from and separate from the aggregates."
All sentient beings act like illusions and transformations, like a mirage in the heat.
Bhikṣus! The five aggregates are all impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity.
"Good son!
At that time, there were many immeasurable bhikṣus who, contemplating these five aggregates as being without self or what belongs to a self, attained the fruit of arhatship."
“Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively teaches non-self. Good son!”
In the sūtras, I have further stated:
"The convergence of three factors results in the acquisition of this body:
first, the father; second, the mother; and third, the intermediate state being (antarābhava)."
"Through the conjunction of these three, one receives this body.
At other times, he further says:
"Anāgāmin-saints attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, or they enter parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (antarābhava)."
Or again, it may be said:
"The sense faculties of the intermediate state body are fully complete and clear; all are caused by past karma, like refined clarified butter (sarpis).
O son of good family!
I have sometimes said:
"The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) experienced by evil sentient beings is like the coarse, rough woolen cloth of the world;
the intermediate state experienced by purely virtuous sentient beings is like the white cotton cloth produced in Vārāṇasī."
When my disciples heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed that the Tathāgata taught the existence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"O son of good family!
Furthermore, for the sake of those sentient beings who have committed the heinous crimes of immediate retribution, I have spoken these words:"
"One who commits the five heinous crimes casts off their body and enters directly into the Avīci Hell.
I further said:
"The bhikṣu Dharmaruci, upon casting off his body, entered directly into the Avīci Hell, with no place to rest or stay along the way."
I further said to that brahmin Vatsa: "Brahmin!
If there were an intermediate state (antarābhava), then there would be six states of existence."
I further said:
"Formless sentient beings have no intermediate state (antarābhava).
Good son, when my disciples heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed: "The Buddha has definitively stated that there is no intermediate state."
"Good son! In the sūtras, I have further spoken of falling back. Why is this?
Because of the immeasurable indolence and laziness of certain bhikṣus who do not cultivate the Path, five types of regression are taught:

first, delighting in many affairs; second, delighting in talking about worldly matters; third, delighting in sleep; fourth, delighting in associating with householders; and fifth, delighting in frequent wandering. By these causes and conditions, bhikṣus are caused to regress.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions for falling back:
first, internal; second, external.
Although an Arhat has abandoned internal causes, he has not abandoned external causes; due to external conditions, afflictions arise, and because afflictions arise, he then falls back.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Gautika who fell back six times; having fallen, he felt shame and remorse, and practicing with renewed diligence, he attained it on the seventh attempt. Having attained it, he feared losing it and took his own life with a knife.
Furthermore, I have sometimes spoken of "occasional liberation," or of the six types of arhats and so forth.
When my disciples hear these teachings, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively stated that there is falling away from the fruit.
“Good son! The sutras further state:
For example, once wood has been charred, it can never become wood again; likewise, once a jar is broken, it no longer serves the function of a jar.
Afflictions are also like this: once severed by an Arhat, they never arise again.”
It is also taught that there are three causes for the arising of afflictions in sentient beings:
first, not having severed the afflictions; second, the presence of causal conditions that prevent their severance; and third, unwholesome reflection.
However, for an Arhat, there are no two such causes and conditions—namely, the severance of afflictions and the absence of unwholesome reflection. Good son!
When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively stated there is no falling back.
“Good son! In the sutras, I have taught that there are two kinds of the Tathāgata’s body:
first, the birth-body (janma-kāya), and second, the dharma-body (dharma-kāya).”
What is called the "birth-body" (janmakāya) is precisely the body manifested through skillful means (upāya).

Of such a body, one may say that it undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death; that it is long or short, black or white; that it is this or that; and that it is either a learner (śaikṣa) or one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively stated that the Buddha-body is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

[They claim] that the Dharma-body is indeed permanence, bliss, self, and purity, forever free from all birth, old age, sickness, and death; it is neither white nor black, neither long nor short, neither this nor that, and neither a learner (*śaikṣa*) nor one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, [the Dharma] remains eternally abiding and immovable, without change or alteration.

Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively stated that the Buddha-body is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
“Good son! In my sutras I have said:
‘What is called the twelve links of dependent origination?’”

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises clinging; from clinging arises becoming; from becoming arises birth; and from birth come old age, death, sorrow, and suffering.

"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are definitively conditioned."
On another occasion, I instructed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination are eternally abiding.
O sons of good family!..."
There are twelve links of dependent origination that do not arise from conditions, and there are those that do arise from conditions.

There are things that are not the twelve links of dependent origination yet arise from conditions; there are also things that are the twelve links of dependent origination yet do not arise from conditions, as well as things that are neither the twelve links of dependent origination nor arise from conditions.
Those that are the twelve links but not produced from conditions refer to the twelve factors in the future life.
Those that are produced from conditions but are not the twelve links refer to the five aggregates possessed by an Arhat.
There are things that arise from conditions and are also the twelve links of dependent origination; these refer to the five aggregates belonging to ordinary persons.
There are things that neither arise from conditions nor are the twelve links of dependent origination; these refer to space and nirvana.

"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are definitively unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."
“Good son! In my sutras I have said:

‘When all sentient beings perform good or evil deeds and cast off their bodies, the four great elements immediately disintegrate at that moment; those whose karma is purely good, their minds ascend, while those whose karma is purely evil, their minds descend.’”
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says the mind is definitely permanent.
Good son!"
At one time, I spoke these words to King Bimbisāra:
"Great King!
You should know that form is impermanent."
Why is this? Because it arises from impermanent causes.
If this form arises from impermanent causes, how could a wise person say that it is permanent?
If form were permanent, it should not undergo disintegration or destruction, nor give rise to various forms of suffering and affliction.
Now we see that this form is dispersed, extinguished, and destroyed; therefore, one should know that form is impermanent, and so it is for all [the aggregates] up to consciousness.
“Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says the mind is definitively severed. Good son!”
In my sūtras, I have said:

"My disciples may accept various fragrant flowers, gold, silver, precious objects, wives, children, male and female servants, and the eight impure things; yet they still attain the Right Path, and having attained the Right Path, they do not abandon it."
When my disciples heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and declared definitively: "The Tathāgata says that experiencing the five desires does not obstruct the Noble Path.
Furthermore, at another time, I again made this statement:
"It is impossible for a person living at home to attain the Right Path."
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says the acceptance of the five desires definitely obstructs the right path."
“Good son! In my sūtras I have said:
‘To be far removed from afflictions yet not yet to have attained liberation is like practicing the worldly supreme dharma (laukikāgradharma) within the desire realm.’”
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says the foremost dharma exists only in the desire realm."
Furthermore, I have said:
"The stage of Heat, the stage of Summits, the stage of Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma exist within the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna."
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has taught such a Dharma as existing within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, I have said:

"Various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who have previously attained the severance of the afflictions of the four dhyānas, and who have cultivated the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), and who contemplate the Four Noble Truths, shall attain the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says the foremost dharma resides in the formless realm.
Good son, in my sutras I have said:
'Among the four kinds of giving, there are three kinds of purity.'"
First, the donor has faith in the cause, the result, and the act of giving, while the recipient lacks faith in the cause, the result, and the act of giving;
second, the recipient has faith in the cause, the result, and the act of giving, while the donor lacks faith in the cause, the result, and the act of giving;
third, both the donor and the recipient possess faith.
"Fourth, there is the case where neither the donor nor the recipient has faith.
Among these four kinds of giving, the first three are pure.
When my disciples heard this teaching, they failed to understand my intention and proclaimed, "The Tathāgata says that giving depends solely on the mind."
"Good son, at another time I also spoke thus:
'When a donor gives, they give with five things.
What are these five?'"

First, the gift of physical beauty; second, the gift of strength; third, the gift of peace; fourth, the gift of life; and fifth, the gift of eloquence. By these causes and conditions, the donor likewise obtains five kinds of retributive fruits.
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said that giving is itself the five aggregates.
Good son! At one time, I proclaimed:"
"Nirvana is detachment; it is the eternal exhaustion of afflictions, extinguished without remainder.
It is like the extinction of a lamp, after which no further phenomena arise; nirvana is likewise."
That which is called "space" is simply non-existence; for example, because there is nothing within it, like that which exists in the world, it is named "space.
The cessation not through the condition of wisdom is likewise simply non-existence.
If it were to exist, there would have to be causes and conditions for its existence.
Because there are causes and conditions, there would have to be its exhaustion and cessation.
Since it does not exist, there is no exhaustion or cessation.
"When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed that the Buddha taught there are no three and no unconditioned phenomena.
Son of good family, at one time, for the sake of Maudgalyāyana, I spoke these words:
'Maudgalyāyana!'"

Now, Nirvana is the very words and phrases; it is the footprint; it is the ultimate state; it is fearlessness; it is the Great Teacher; it is the Great Fruit; it is ultimate wisdom; it is the great patience and unimpeded samādhi; it is the Great Dharma-realm; it is the flavor of ambrosia; and it is difficult to perceive.
"Maudgalyāyana!
If one were to say that there is no nirvāṇa, how could those who give rise to slander fall into hell?
"Good son! [The Buddha continued: "Good son!"
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed, "The Tathāgata says that there is nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, on another occasion, I spoke thus to Maudgalyāyana:
"Maudgalyāyana!..."
The eye is not solid, and so it is with everything down to the body; because they are all not solid, they are called "empty space.
The place where food descends, circulates, and is digested, as well as all sounds, are likewise called "empty space."
"When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed that the Tathāgata definitively taught that unconditioned space exists.
Furthermore, on another occasion, I said to Maudgalyāyana:
'Maudgalyāyana!'"

When a person who has not yet attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* abides in the stage of *kṣānti*, they sever the retributions of the three evil realms; one should know that these are extinguished not through the condition of wisdom.

“When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively teaches the existence of cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
‘Good son! [This is not so.]’”
On another occasion, I said to the bhikṣu Bāṣpa:
"Bāṣpa! If a bhikṣu contemplates form—whether past, future, or present; whether near or far; whether coarse or subtle—all such forms are not the self, nor do they belong to the self."
"If there is a bhikṣu who, having contemplated in this way,
is able to sever craving for form," Bāpā said again,
"What is called 'form'?"
I said: "The four great elements are called 'form' (rūpa), and the four aggregates are called 'name' (nāma).
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed: "The Tathāgata has definitively stated that form is the four great elements."
“Good son, I have further said:
‘For example, because of a mirror, an image appears. Form is also like this;

it is produced by the four great elements—namely, coarse and fine, rough and smooth, blue, yellow, red, and white, long, short, square, round, oblique angles, light and heavy, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist. These are called derived forms, which are like echoes and images.’”

When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says: "If there are the four great elements, then there is derived matter," or that "there may be the four great elements without derived matter."
“Good son! Once in the past, Prince Bodhi spoke these words:
‘If a bhikṣu who upholds the prohibitive precepts should give rise to an evil thought, you should know that at that moment he loses his bhikṣu-precepts.’”
At that time, I spoke these words:
"Prince Bodhi! There are seven kinds of precepts;
they arise from body and speech and consist of non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa)."

Because of this unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) as a causal condition, even though the mind may dwell within the states of evil or the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not called a loss of precepts; it is still called "maintaining the precepts.
For what reason is it called unmanifest form?
"It is not a cause distinct from form, nor does it produce a result that is a distinct form.
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said there is 'unmanifested form' (avijñapti-rūpa)."
“Good son! In another sutra I have said this:
‘Precepts are that which restrain evil dharmas; if one does not commit evil, this is called upholding the precepts.’”

"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively declared that there is no such thing as 'unmanifest form' (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Good son, in the sūtras I have made this statement:
'The aggregates of form through to consciousness of the noble ones all arise from the causal conditions of ignorance.'"
All ordinary beings are likewise thus: from ignorance arises craving; one should know that this craving is itself ignorance.
From craving arises grasping; one should know that this grasping is itself ignorance and craving.
From grasping arises becoming; this becoming is itself ignorance, craving, and grasping.
From birth arises sensation; one should know that this sensation is itself the formations and existence.

From the conditions of sensation arise name-and-form, ignorance, craving, grasping, formations, sensation, contact, consciousness, the six sense bases, and so forth. Therefore, sensation is itself the twelve links of dependent origination.
“Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says there are no mental factors (caitasika).
Good son, in the sūtras I have made such a statement as this:”
"From the four factors of the eye, forms, light, and unwholesome desire, visual consciousness arises.
What is called 'unwholesome desire' is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
When the nature of desire seeks [its object], it is termed craving (*tṛṣṇā*)."
With craving as condition, there is grasping; grasping is termed karma.

With karma as condition, there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact; with contact as condition, there arise perception, feeling, craving, faith, energy, concentration, and wisdom.
"Such dharmas as these arise because of contact, yet they are not contact itself. "Good son!
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says there are mental factors (caitta)."
“Good son! At times I teach that there is only one existence;
at other times I teach two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, up to twenty-five.”
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed that the Tathāgata said there are five *bhavas*, or that there are six *bhavas*.
"Good son, once in the past, when I was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu, Śreṇika Bimbisāra came to where I was and spoke these words:
'What is meant by the term upāsaka? "
I then spoke for him:
"If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who possesses all their faculties intact and receives the three refuges, they are called an upāsaka."
Śreṇika Mānava said:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a ‘one-part upāsaka’?”
I said: "Māṇava!
If one receives the three refuges and receives a single precept, this is called a 'one-part' upāsaka."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says the Upāsaka precepts cannot be obtained unless they are received in their entirety.
Good son!..."
At one time I was staying by the banks of the Ganges. At that time, Kātyāyana came to where I was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
I instruct sentient beings to receive the precepts of the fast, whether for one day, or one night, or one period, or even for a single thought-moment. Do such people fulfill the fast?"
I said: "Bhikṣu! This person has attained merit, but it is not called attaining the fast."

When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed: "The Tathāgata says that the eight precepts of the fast can only be attained by receiving them in their entirety. "Good son!
In the sūtras, I have spoken thus:
"If a bhikṣu commits the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer called a bhikṣu; he is termed a 'broken bhikṣu' or a 'lost bhikṣu,' and can no longer produce the seeds of the sprouts of goodness."
For example, a scorched seed does not produce fruit; likewise, if the crown of a tāla tree is severed or destroyed, it will no longer bear fruit.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense is just like this.

When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has said: "Once the bhikṣus have committed a grave transgression, they lose the bhikṣu precepts."
“Good son! In a sutra, I spoke for the sake of Cunda: ‘There are four kinds of bhikṣus:

first, those who have ultimately reached the Way; second, those who show the Way; third, those who receive the Way; and fourth, those who defile the Way. One who commits the four grave offenses is precisely one who defiles the Way.’”

"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has said that even after committing the four pārājika offenses, bhikṣus do not lose their prohibitive precepts."
“Good son! In a sutra, I told the bhikṣus:

‘There is one vehicle, one path, one practice, and one object. In this way, from the one vehicle up to the one object, these can bring great tranquility to sentient beings, forever severing all bonds, grief, suffering, and the causes of suffering, leading all beings to reach the single existence.’”

"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has said that those from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat all attain the path of Buddhahood."
"Good son! In a sutra I have said:
'The srotāpanna, having gone back and forth seven times between the human realm and the heavens, attains parinirvāṇa.'"
The Sakṛdāgāmin, having experienced one more birth among gods or humans, then attains parinirvāṇa.
As for the Anāgāmin, there are five types: some attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, up to those who attain parinirvāṇa by flowing upwards.

There are two kinds of arhats: first, those of the present, and second, those of the future; those of the present sever the afflictions and the five aggregates, and those of the future likewise sever the afflictions and the five aggregates.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata says that those from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat cannot attain the Buddha-way.
“Good son! In this sutra, I have said:
‘The Buddha-nature possesses six things:’”
"First, it is eternal; second, it is real; third, it is true; fourth, it is good; fifth, it is pure; sixth, it is visible.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from the sentient beings themselves.
“Good son! I have also said:

‘The buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space; space is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither internal nor external; it is not comprised of form, sound, odor, taste, or touch—and the buddha-nature is likewise.’”

“When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said that the buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from the sentient beings themselves. Good son!
I have further said:

"The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like a treasure trove within the house of a poor woman, a diamond jewel upon the forehead of a strongman, and a spring of ambrosia belonging to a wheel-turning sage king."
“When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said: ‘The buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings. Good son!
I have further said:
"Those who commit the four grave offenses, icchantikas, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and those who commit the five heinous crimes—all possess Buddha-nature."
"Thus, these sentient beings possess no wholesome dharmas at all, whereas the Buddha-nature is wholesome.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from the sentient beings themselves.
“Good son! I have also further said:
‘Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-nature.’”
Why is this? Because apart from sentient beings, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, I spoke the parable of the elephant to King Prasenajit: it is like the blind men describing an elephant; although they do not grasp the elephant itself, they do not describe something other than the elephant.
When sentient beings speak of form, up to and including consciousness, as being the Buddha-nature, it is likewise so: although these are not the Buddha-nature, they are not without the Buddha-nature.
Just as I spoke the analogy of the lute for the king, the Buddha-nature is also like this.
“Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and offer various interpretations.

It is like a blind man asking about milk; the Buddha-nature is just like that. For these reasons, some say that even those who have committed the four grave offenses, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas—all possess the Buddha-nature—while others say they do not.”
“Good son, in various sūtras I have said:

‘It is impossible for one person’s appearance in the world not to benefit many people; it is impossible for two wheel-turning kings to appear in a single land, or for two Buddhas to appear in a single world-system.’”
"It is impossible for there to be [only] one set of four continents, eight sets of the Four Heavenly Kings, and so on, up to two sets of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Nevertheless, I have taught:
"From Jambudvīpa down to the Avīci Hell, and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Buddha has said there are no Buddhas of the ten directions.
Yet, I have also taught in various Mahāyāna sūtras that there are Buddhas of the ten directions."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 34 [and] Scroll 35.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, Part Three. "Good son!
Such disputes and contentions are the realm of the Buddha; they are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."

If a person gives rise to doubt regarding this, they are still able to destroy immeasurable afflictions as vast as Mount Sumeru; however, if one develops a fixed conviction within this, it is called attachment.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by attachment?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! If such a person—

whether hearing from another, seeking it out in the sūtras themselves, or being intentionally instructed by another— is unable to relinquish the objects to which they are attached, this is called ‘clinging.’”
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
Is such attachment considered wholesome?"
"Is this unwholesome? "Good son,
such attachment is not called wholesome."
"Why is this? Because they are unable to destroy the net of all doubts.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Since such a person has been free from doubt from the very beginning, why do you say that they have not destroyed the net of doubt? “Good son!
"Indeed, that which is 'not doubting' is itself doubt.
"World-Honored One!
If there is someone who says that a srotāpanna does not fall into the three evil realms, should this person also be said to be attached to names and to have doubt?"
“Good son! This may be called certainty; it cannot be called doubt. Why is this?
"Good son!
It is like a person who first sees a man and a tree; later, while traveling at night, he sees a stump from afar and immediately gives rise to a doubtful thought: 'Is it a man?'"
"A tree? "Good son!
It is like a person who first sees a bhikṣu or a brahmacārin, and later, while on the road, sees a bhikṣu from afar and immediately gives rise to a doubt, thinking: 'Is this a śramaṇa?'"
"Is this a brahmin? "Good son!
It is like a person who first sees a cow and a water buffalo, and later sees a cow from afar; he then gives rise to a doubt, thinking: 'Is that a cow?'"
"Is this a water buffalo? Good son!
All sentient beings first perceive two things, and only afterwards does doubt arise."
Why is this? Because the mind does not understand.
I do not say that a srotāpanna falls into the three evil realms or does not fall into the three evil realms; for what reason, then, would such a person give rise to doubt?
Kāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, one must first see something before one can have doubt regarding it.”
There are those who, when they have not yet seen two kinds of things, likewise give rise to doubt.
What are these? They are what is called nirvāṇa.
"Bhagavān!
It is like a person who encounters turbid water on a road; having never seen it before, they also give rise to doubt: 'Is this water deep?
Or is it shallow?'"
“Since this person has not yet seen it, how can they give rise to doubt?
“Good son! That which is called nirvana is precisely the cessation of suffering.”
That which is not nirvana is suffering.
All sentient beings perceive two kinds of things: they see what is suffering and what is not suffering.

What is "suffering" and "not suffering" consists of hunger and thirst, cold and heat, anger and joy, illness and health, old age and vigor, birth and death, bondage and liberation, separation from loved ones, and encountering those one hates.
When sentient beings see this, they immediately give rise to doubt: "Will there ever come a time when such suffering and affliction are utterly transcended?
For this reason, sentient beings harbor doubts regarding nirvana.
If you think that this person has not previously seen turbid water and yet harbors doubt,
that argument is incorrect. Why is this so?
"This person previously saw it in another place; therefore, even though this is a place he has never been to before, he again gives rise to doubt.
"World-Honored One!
When this person previously saw the deep and shallow places, he did not give rise to doubt; for what reason does he now again give rise to doubt?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! It is because you have not yet practiced that you give rise to doubt.”
"Therefore, I said that because of a lack of understanding, there is doubt.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught, doubt is itself attachment, and attachment is itself doubt.
To whom does this refer? "Good son!
"One who has severed the roots of goodness. Kāśyapa said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of people are able to sever their roots of goodness? "Good son!
If there are those who are clever, wise, and of sharp faculties, they are able to discern well."

One who distances themselves from virtuous friends, does not listen to the true Dharma, engages in improper reflection, and does not abide according to the Dharma—such a person is able to sever their roots of goodness.
Free from these four matters, one reflects within the mind:
"There is no object to be given. Why is this so?"
Giving consists in the relinquishing of material wealth. If giving were to have a retribution, one should know that the donor would always remain impoverished. Why is this?
Because the fruit resembles its seed; therefore, it is said that there is neither cause nor fruit.
"If one speaks in this way of there being neither cause nor effect, this is called severing the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, one might think:

'The donor, the recipient, and the gift—these three things are impermanent and do not abide. If they do not abide, how can it be said that "this is the donor," "this is the recipient," or "this is the gift"? "
"If there is no recipient, how can one obtain a fruit?
For this reason, there is neither cause nor fruit.
If one speaks thus of the non-existence of cause and fruit, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Again, he reflects thus:

"When a donor gives a gift, there are five ways of giving; after the recipient has received it, they may sometimes perform wholesome deeds or unwholesome deeds, yet the donor likewise does not obtain the fruit of either the wholesome or the unwholesome."
Just as in worldly phenomena, a fruit is produced from a seed, and that fruit in turn becomes a seed;

so too, the donor is the cause and the recipient is the fruit. Yet, this recipient cannot, by means of these wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, cause the donor to obtain [the result]. For this reason, there is neither cause nor fruit.
"If one speaks in this way, denying cause and effect, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Furthermore, they harbor this thought:
'There is no gift to be given.'"
Why is this? Because the object given is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If it is indeterminate, how can it yield a wholesome fruit of retribution?
The absence of the fruits of good and evil is precisely what is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If wealth were indeterminate, one should know that there would be no retribution for good or evil; therefore, there would be no giving, no cause, and no fruit.
"If one speaks in this way of there being neither cause nor effect, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Furthermore, they form this thought:
'The donor is simply the mind.'"
If it is the mind, it is invisible and non-resistant, and is not a material phenomenon (rūpa-dharma). If it is not material, how can it be given?
Therefore, there is no giving, no cause, and no fruit.
"If one speaks in this way of no cause and no effect, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Furthermore, they may think:
'If a donor makes offerings for the sake of images of Buddhas or deities, or for deceased parents, there is no recipient; and if there is no recipient, there should be no karmic retribution.'"
"If there is no retribution, this constitutes the absence of cause; if there is no cause, this constitutes the absence of fruit.
If one speaks thus of the absence of cause and the absence of fruit, you should know that such a person is capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Again, he thought: "There is no father and no mother.
If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings and give rise to them, then logically they should produce them constantly, without interruption."
Why is this? Because [the cause] exists eternally.
Yet, it does not arise eternally; therefore, one should know that there are no parents.
"Again, he thinks:
'There is no father and no mother. Why is this?'"

If the bodies of sentient beings existed because of their parents, then a single person should possess both male and female organs; yet since no such person exists, one should know that sentient beings do not exist because of their parents.
"Furthermore, he reflects:
'Sentient beings are not born solely because of their parents. Why is this? "
When one observes sentient beings with the eyes, they do not resemble their parents in terms of body, form, mind, deportment, or movement; therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings.
Again, he thought:
"In all the world there are four kinds of non-existence:
first, that which has not yet arisen is called non-existent, such as when a lump of clay has not yet served the function of a jar."
Second, that which is non-existent after having ceased is called "non-existence," such as when a jar has been destroyed; this is termed non-existence.
Third, mutual non-existence due to difference, such as there being no horse within a cow, and no cow within a horse.
The fourth is that which is ultimately non-existent, such as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise.
The parents of sentient beings are likewise like this, sharing these four types of non-existence.
If one claims that parents are the cause of sentient beings, then when the parents die, the child does not necessarily die; therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings.
Again, he thought: "If it were said that parents are the cause of sentient beings, then sentient beings should always be born from parents.
Yet there are also those born by transformation and those born from moisture; therefore, one should know that sentient beings are not produced solely through parents as their cause."
Again, he had this thought:
"There are sentient beings who grow and develop without depending on parents.
For example, when a peacock hears the sound of thunder, it immediately becomes pregnant."
Furthermore, it is like the blue jay (*nīlāṇḍa*), which becomes pregnant simply by drinking the urine of the male;
or like the *jīvajīvaka* bird, which becomes pregnant upon seeing the male dance.
When he thinks this, if he does not encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), you should know that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
He further thinks:
"In all the worlds, there are no fruits of good or evil."
Why is this? There are sentient beings who possess the ten wholesome dharmas, delight in giving, and diligently cultivate merit.

Yet these people may likewise suffer from diseases gathering in their bodies, meet with premature death in the prime of life, lose their wealth and property, and endure manifold sorrows and sufferings.
There are those who commit the ten non-virtuous actions, being stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous; they are lazy and indolent, and do not cultivate various virtues;
yet their bodies remain at ease and free from illness, they live out their full lifespans, possess abundant wealth and treasures, and are free from all sorrows and sufferings.
"Therefore, you should know that there are no fruits of good or evil. Again, he thought:
"I have also heard various sages say that there are those who cultivate goodness, yet at the end of their lives, they mostly fall into the three evil realms."
‘There are those who commit evil deeds yet, at the end of their lives, are reborn among humans or devas;
therefore, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil.
Again, they think thus:

"All noble ones have two kinds of teachings: some say that killing results in a wholesome karmic retribution, while others say that killing results in an unwholesome karmic retribution; therefore, one should know that the teachings of the noble ones are not fixed."
"If the Noble Ones are not fixed, how can I be fixed?
Therefore, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil. He further thought:
"There are no noble ones (ārya) in all the worlds. Why is this?

If one says that a noble one should have attained the right path, yet all sentient beings cultivate the right path while still possessing afflictions (kleśa), then it should be known that for such a person, the right path and the afflictions exist simultaneously. If they exist simultaneously, it should be known that the right path cannot destroy the fetters (saṃyojana)."
If one were to cultivate the path while devoid of afflictions, what would this right path accomplish?
Therefore, for one who possesses afflictions, the path cannot destroy them;
yet for one who lacks afflictions, the path is useless.
"Therefore, you should know that there are no noble ones (ārya) in the entire world.
He further thought:
"Ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, up to birth conditioning old age and death; these twelve links of dependent origination are shared equally by all sentient beings."

The Noble Eightfold Path is equal in its nature; it should likewise be such that when one person attains it, all should attain it, and when one person cultivates it, all suffering should be extinguished.
Why is this? Because they are equal to afflictions.
Yet now it is not attained; therefore, one should know that there is no true path.
"Furthermore, he thought:

'The Noble Ones all share the same dharmas as ordinary people, namely: eating and drinking, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; sleeping; laughing and smiling; hunger and thirst; cold and heat; sorrow and fear.'"
If one were the same as an ordinary person regarding such matters, it should be known that the noble ones have not attained the noble path;
if they have attained the noble path, they ought to have eternally severed such matters.
"If such matters as these are not severed, one should know that there is no Path.
He further thought:

"The Noble One has a body and experiences the pleasures of the five desires; he likewise insults and beats others, feels envy and pride toward people, and undergoes suffering and joy while performing good and evil deeds. For these reasons, I know there is no Noble One."
"If there were one who possessed the Way, they should sever these matters; since these matters are not severed, one should know that there is no Way.
He further thought:
"One who possesses great compassion is called a sage."
For what reason is one called a "Noble One" (ārya)?
It is because of the causal conditions of the Path that one is called a Noble One.
If the nature of the Path is compassionate, then it should naturally take pity upon all sentient beings; this does not depend on having practiced [the path] first before such compassion is attained.
"If there were no compassion, why would the sages, having attained the noble path, be able to feel pity?
Therefore, one should know that the noble path does not exist in the world.
He further thought:

"All four great elements are not born from causes; all sentient beings equally possess this nature of the four great elements, yet one does not observe whether these sentient beings should reach this limit or should not reach that."
"If there were a noble path, its nature should be such;
yet now it is not so. Therefore, one should know that there are no noble ones in the world. He further thought:
"If all noble ones possessed a single nirvāṇa, one should know that there would then be no noble ones at all.
Why is this? Because it cannot be apprehended."
The principle of the eternally abiding dharma cannot be apprehended; it is neither to be grasped nor abandoned.
If the nirvana of the various sages were manifold, it would be impermanent. Why is this so?
Because it is a phenomenon that can be enumerated:
if *nirvāṇa* were one, then when one person attains it, everyone should attain it.
If *nirvāṇa* were many, it would then have limits; if it had limits, how could it be called eternal?
If someone were to say that the essence of nirvāṇa is one while liberations are many— just as a canopy is one while its ribs and spokes are many—
this meaning is not correct. Why is this so?
That which is attained individually is not attained by all.
Because it has limits, it must be impermanent.
If it is impermanent, how can it be called nirvana?
"If nirvāṇa does not exist, who would be a noble one (ārya)?
Therefore, one should know that there are no noble ones. He further thought:
“The Way of the Sage is not attained through causes and conditions.
If the Way of the Sage were not attained through causes and conditions, why would everyone not become a sage?”
"If all people were non-noble ones, one should know that there would then be no noble ones, nor any noble path.
He further thought: "The Noble One has taught that right view has two causes and conditions:"
First, hearing the Dharma from others; second, internal reflection for oneself.

Regarding these two causes and conditions, if they arise from conditions, that which arises from them must itself arise from conditions. If this process continues in such a succession, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
"If these two things were not produced from conditions, why would all sentient beings not obtain them?
When one contemplates in this way, one is able to sever the roots of goodness. "Good son!..."
If there are sentient beings who deeply perceive such a state as being without cause and without effect, these people are able to sever the five faculties, beginning with faith.

Good son! Those who sever their roots of goodness are not inferior, dull-witted, or ignorant persons; they are also not among the devas or within the three evil realms. The same applies to those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When will such a person be able to regenerate their roots of goodness?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! This person will regenerate roots of goodness at two times: when first entering hell and when emerging from hell."
Good son! There are three kinds of goodness: past, present, and future.
If it is of the past, its nature has already ceased; although the cause has been extinguished, the retribution has not yet matured. Therefore, it is not called the severance of past results.
"Because one severs the causes of the three periods of time, it is called 'severing.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If one severs the causes of the three periods of time, it is called severing the roots of goodness.
A person who has severed the roots of goodness nonetheless possesses Buddha-nature.
Is such Buddha-nature of the past, of the present, of the future, or does it pervade all three periods of time?
If it were of the past, how could it be called eternal?
Since the Buddha-nature is also eternal, one should know that it is not of the past.
If it were of the future, how could it be called eternal?
For what reason does the Buddha say that all sentient beings will certainly and inevitably attain it?
If they will certainly attain it, why speak of severance?
If it exists in the present, how can it be permanent?
Why, then, do you say that it must necessarily be visible?
The Tathāgata has also taught that there are six qualities of the Buddha-nature:
first, permanence; second, truth; third, reality; fourth, goodness; fifth, purity; and sixth, visibility.
If those who have severed their roots of goodness still possess the Buddha-nature, then they cannot be called "those who have severed their roots of goodness.
If they lack the Buddha-nature, why do you further say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature?
“If you say that the Buddha-nature both exists and is severed, why does the Tathāgata further declare it to be permanent?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, employs four kinds of answers:
first, the categorical answer; second, the analytical answer; third, the answer according with the question; and fourth, the answer by setting aside the question.
“Good son! What is a categorical answer?
For example, if one asks: ‘Does evil karma yield a wholesome fruit?’”
Is it an unwholesome fruit?
This should be answered definitively as "it obtains an unwholesome fruit";
the same applies to wholesome [fruits].
If one asks whether the Tathāgata possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*),
one should definitively answer that he does possess all-knowledge.
If one asks whether the Buddha-dharma is pure, [one should definitively answer that it is].
In this case, one should categorically answer that they are certainly pure.
If asked whether the disciples of the Tathāgata abide in accordance with the Dharma,
one should categorically answer that there are those who abide in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called a categorical answer.
What is a discriminative answer?
It is as when I teach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
What are the four?
They are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
What is the truth of suffering?
Because there are eight types of suffering, it is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
What is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)?
Because it is the cause of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is named the Truth of Origination.
What is the truth of cessation?
Because greed, hatred, and delusion are ultimately exhausted, it is called the truth of cessation.
What is the truth of the path?
Because of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, it is called the Truth of the Path.
This is known as the analytical answer.
What is the answer according to the question?
As I have taught, all phenomena are impermanent.
Furthermore, someone may ask:
"For the sake of what phenomenon does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speak of impermanence?"
He replied:
"The Tathāgata taught that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent; the same applies to non-self (*anātman*).
As I have stated, all phenomena burn others.
He asked again:
"For the sake of what dharma does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, say that all things are burned?
He replied:
“The Tathāgata has taught that greed, anger, and delusion burn everything. “Good son!

The Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, great kindness and great compassion, three foundations of mindfulness, the eighty trillion samādhi-gates such as Śūraṅgama, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the thirty-five thousand samādhi-gates such as the Five Wisdom Seals, the vajra-samādhi and other samādhi-gates numbering four thousand two hundred, and the immeasurable and boundless samādhis of skillful means—such dharmas as these are the Buddha and the Buddha-nature.”
Thus, the Buddha-nature possesses seven attributes:
first, permanence; second, selfhood; third, bliss; fourth, purity; fifth, truth; sixth, reality; and seventh, goodness. This is called the analytical answer.
“Good son! For a bodhisattva in his final birth, there are six aspects of the Buddha-nature:
first, permanence; second, purity; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, goodness; and sixth, being seen only slightly. This is called the analytical answer.”

"As you previously asked regarding those who have severed their roots of goodness having Buddha-nature: such persons also possess the Tathāgata-Buddha-nature and also possess the Buddha-nature of future bodies. Because these two types of Buddha-nature are obstructed from manifesting in the future, they are designated as 'non-existent'."
Because it is ultimately attained, it is called "existent.
This is known as the analytical answer.

"The Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is neither past, nor present, nor future; however, because the buddha-nature of the final body is slightly visible in the present and the future, it is designated as 'present.'"
Because they have not yet fully realized [this] vision, they are called "future.
When the Tathāgata had not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha-nature, as a cause, was likewise past, present, and future.
The fruit is not so; some belong to the three periods of time, while others do not.
Because the Buddha-nature of a Bodhisattva in his final body is a cause, it likewise belongs to the past, present, and future; the fruit is also like this.
This is called the analytical answer.
"The Buddha-nature of a Bodhisattva in the ninth stage has six aspects:
first, permanence; second, goodness; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, purity; and sixth, visibility."
Because the Buddha-nature is a cause, it is also past, present, and future;
its fruit is likewise so.
This is called an analytical answer.
"For Bodhisattvas dwelling in the eighth stage down to the sixth stage, the Buddha-nature possesses five attributes:
first, it is true; second, it is real; third, it is pure; fourth, it is good; and fifth, it is visible."
Because the Buddha-nature is a cause, it pertains to the past, present, and future; its fruit is likewise so.
This is called an analytical answer.
Regarding the five aspects of the Buddha-nature for Bodhisattvas from the fifth stage down to the first:
First, the True; second, the Real; third, the Pure; fourth, the Visible; and fifth, the Good and the Unwholesome.
Son of good family!

Because these five kinds of Buddha-nature, six kinds of Buddha-nature, and seven kinds of Buddha-nature will certainly be attained by those who have severed their roots of goodness, it can be said that they exist.
This is called an analytical answer.

"If someone were to say that those who have severed their roots of goodness definitely possess the Buddha-nature, or that they definitely lack the Buddha-nature, this is called a question to be set aside."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that not answering is what is called a ‘set-aside’ answer.”
"For what reason does the Tathāgata now answer by means of what is called 'setting aside' (sthāpanīya)?
"Good son! It is not that I say one sets it aside and does not answer; rather, I speak of answering by way of setting aside."
Good son! Such setting aside of the question is further of two kinds:
first, cessation; second, non-attachment.
"For this reason, it is called a 'set-aside' answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, how is it that the cause is past,
present, and future, while the fruit is also past, present, and future, yet is not [simply] past, present, and future?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The five aggregates are of two kinds:
The first is cause and the second is effect.
These five aggregates as cause belong to the past, present, and future.
These five aggregates as effect also belong to the past, present, and future, and yet they do not belong to the past, present, or future.
"Good son!
All fetters, such as ignorance and afflictions, are entirely the Buddha-nature. Why is this?"
Because the Buddha-nature is the cause, one attains the wholesome five aggregates through ignorance, volitional formations, and all afflictions; this is called the Buddha-nature.
From these wholesome five aggregates, one proceeds until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I have previously stated in the sutras that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like milk mixed with blood;
"blood" refers to all afflictions such as ignorance and volitional formations, while "milk" refers to the wholesome five aggregates.
Therefore, I say that one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the various afflictions and the five aggregates of goodness.
Just as the bodies of sentient beings are all accomplished from semen and blood, so too is the Buddha-nature.
For those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin and have severed a small portion of afflictions, the Buddha-nature is like milk.
For those who have attained the stage of Anāgāmin, the Buddha-nature is like curd.
Arhats are like fresh butter;
from Pratyekabuddhas up to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, they are like processed butter;
the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is like clarified butter (ghṛta).
"Good son!
Because present afflictions act as obstacles, they cause sentient beings to be unable to see it.
It is like the kṣānti-grass found on Mount Gandhamādana, which not all oxen are able to eat."
"Buddha-nature is also like this;
this is called an analytical answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the five kinds, six kinds, and seven kinds of Buddha-nature exist only in the future, why do you say that those who have severed their roots of goodness possess Buddha-nature?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! Just as all sentient beings have past karma, and because of this karma, sentient beings receive its retribution in the present.”
There is future karma which, because it has not yet arisen, will never produce its fruit; however, there are present afflictions.

If there were no afflictions, all sentient beings would clearly perceive their Buddha-nature. Therefore, those who have severed their roots of goodness are able to sever them due to the causes and conditions of present-world afflictions.
“By virtue of the causal conditions of the power of the Buddha-nature in the future, they will again give rise to roots of goodness.
Kāśyapa said,
“World-Honored One!”
"How can future [dharmas] produce roots of goodness?
"Good son, it is like a lamp or the sun: although they have not yet arisen, they are nonetheless able to dispel darkness."
"The future birth that can produce the future Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
This is called an analytical answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is said that the five aggregates are the Buddha-nature, why do you say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! For what reason have you lost your composure in this way?
Did I not previously state that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the Middle Way?”
Kāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!
It is not that I have truly lost my way; rather, it is because sentient beings cannot understand this Middle Way that I have posed this question.”
“Good son! That sentient beings do not understand is itself the Middle Way.
At times they understand, and at times they do not understand.”
"Good son!
For the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain understanding and liberation, I say that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external. Why is this?"
Ordinary beings may say that the Buddha-nature dwells within the five aggregates, like fruit inside a vessel;
or they may say it exists apart from the aggregates, like empty space.
For this reason, the Tathāgata teaches the Middle Way.
