Good son!"

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who greatly delight in teaching and transforming others; their minds are preoccupied with such activities and they are unable to attain meditative concentration. For this reason, they do not attain nirvana in the present life. Good son!
As you have asked: for what causes and conditions do some abandon the body of the desire realm and attain *nirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), while others do not in the form realm?
Good son! This person contemplates that there are two types of causal conditions for the afflictions of the desire realm:
The first is internal and the second is external.
Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are no external causes and conditions.
Furthermore, within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there are two kinds of craving:
The first is craving for sense-desire (*kāmarāga*) and the second is craving for form (*rūparāga*).
One contemplates these two cravings and reproaches them with a sincere mind; having thus reproached them, one attains entry into *nirvāṇa*.

Within this realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one is able to reproach all coarse afflictions (*kleśa*), namely stinginess, greed, anger, envy, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*); by these causes and conditions, one is able to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, the path of the desire realm is courageous and robust by nature.
Why is this? Because it attains the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].
Therefore, there is parinirvāṇa in the interim within the desire realm, but not within the form realm. Good son!
There are three kinds of parinirvāṇa in the interim, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior [type] attains nirvana after casting off the body, without yet having departed from the desire realm.
The middling [type] attains nirvana after first departing from the desire realm, but before reaching the form realm.
The inferior [type] attains nirvana after having departed from the desire realm and reached the limit of the form realm.
This person is like a crocodile that stays still after having obtained food.
What is meant by "abiding"?
Because one dwells in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), having attained a physical body, it is therefore called "abiding.
Because one does not receive [the body of] the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—whether as a human, deva, hell-being, animal, or hungry ghost—it is therefore called "abiding."
Having already severed immeasurable fetters of affliction, because a small remainder still persists, it is therefore called "abiding.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called "abiding"?
Because one ultimately never engages in activities shared with ordinary worldlings, it is therefore called "abiding."
Because one is oneself fearless and does not cause others to fear, it is called "abiding.
Because one is far removed from the two types of craving, as well as stinginess, greed, and anger, it is called "abiding. "Good son!
Those who have reached the other shore are likened to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas; they are like the divine tortoise that can travel both on land and in water.
For what reason and by what conditions are they compared to a tortoise?

Because they skillfully conceal their five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*), so too do Arhats and even all Buddhas skillfully cover their five sense-faculties; for this reason, they are likened to a turtle.
As for the terms "water" and "land," water is a metaphor for the mundane world (*saṃsāra*), and land is a metaphor for that which transcends the world (*lokottara*).

These noble ones are likewise thus; because they are able to contemplate all evil afflictions, they reach the other shore, and for this reason they are likened to those who travel both by water and by land.
“Good son! Just as the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River, though they bear the names of fish, turtles, and so forth, do not depart from the water;

likewise, within this subtle and wondrous Great Nirvana, from the icchantika up to the Buddhas, though there are various different names, they likewise do not depart from the water of the Buddha-nature.”
"Good son!

For these seven types of sentient beings, whether it be wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, the path of skillful means or the path of liberation, the sequential path or cause and fruit—all are the Buddha-nature. This is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a cause, there is an effect; if there is no cause, there is no effect.”
Nirvana is called the fruit; because it is eternal, it has no cause.
If it has no cause, how can it be called a fruit?
Furthermore, this Nirvana is also called the śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa.
"What is a śramaṇa?
What is the fruit of the śramaṇa?
"O son of good family!"
In all worlds there are seven kinds of fruits:

first, the fruit of skillful means; second, the fruit of repaying kindness; third, the fruit of intimacy; fourth, the fruit of remnants; fifth, the fruit of equality; sixth, the fruit of retribution; and seventh, the fruit of detachment.

Regarding the fruit of skillful means (*upāya-phala*): it is like people in the world who, having harvested much grain in the autumn, say to one another that they have obtained the fruit of skillful means.
This "fruit of skillful means" is termed the fruit of karmic action (*karma-phala*).
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause is what is called the seed.
The remote cause refers to water, manure, and human labor;
this is called the fruit of skillful means.
As for the fruit of repaying kindness, it is like when people of the world make offerings to their parents, and the parents both say:
"I have now attained the fruit of being nurtured.
That a child is able to repay their kindness is called "fruit.
Such a fruit likewise has two kinds of causes:
The first is the proximate cause, and the second is the remote cause.
The proximate cause is the parents' past karma of pure goodness;
the remote cause is the filial son who is born.
This is called the fruit of repaying kindness.

Regarding the "fruit of intimacy": for example, suppose there is a person who associates with virtuous friends and attains the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat. That person declares:
"I have now attained the retribution of the fruit of intimacy."
Regarding such a fruit, there are two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate is faith, and the remote is the virtuous friend.
This is called the fruit of association.
As for the "remaining fruits," such as obtaining a third body through the practice of non-killing, resulting in increased longevity and years of life—this is called the remaining fruit.
Such fruits have two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause is the purity of body, speech, and mind.
The distant [result] refers to the prolongation of life and the increase of longevity;
this is called the residual fruit (*avaśeṣa-phala*).
"The fruit of equality" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Such fruits also have two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause refers to sentient beings practicing the ten wholesome actions.
The distant cause refers to the so-called three calamities;
this is called the fruit of equality.
As for the fruit of retribution: suppose a person, having obtained a pure body, cultivates the purity of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; that person would then say:
"I have obtained the fruit of retribution.
Regarding such a fruit, there are two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause refers to the purity of body, speech, and mind in the present.
The remote cause refers to the purity of body, speech, and mind in the past.
This is called the fruit of retribution.
"The fruit of separation" is nirvana, which is the departure from all afflictions and all wholesome karma.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes for this nirvana:
The first is the proximate cause; the second is the remote cause.
The proximate cause refers to the three gates of liberation.
The remote cause refers to the wholesome dharmas cultivated throughout immeasurable lifetimes.

“Good son! Just as in worldly dharmas there are those spoken of as productive causes (*janaka-hetu*) and those spoken of as revealing causes (*paridīpaka-hetu*), so too it is with supramundane dharmas; they are likewise spoken of as both productive causes and revealing causes.”
Good son! The three gates of liberation and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can act as the non-arising cause for all afflictions, and they also act as the revealing cause for nirvana.
Good son! By being far removed from afflictions, one then clearly perceives nirvana; therefore, nirvana possesses only the cause of manifestation and lacks a cause of production.
“Good son! Regarding what you have asked: ‘What is a śramaṇa?
What are the fruits of śramaṇaship?’”
"Good son!

'Śramaṇa' refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, and the 'fruit of śramaṇaship' refers to the ultimate and permanent severance of all greed, hatred, and delusion through that path; these are called śramaṇaship and the fruit of śramaṇaship."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition is the Eightfold Noble Path called śramaṇatā?”
“Good son! What the world calls ‘śramaṇa’ means ‘destitution,’ while ‘na’ means ‘path. Such a path cuts off all destitution and cuts off all paths.”
For this reason, the Eightfold Noble Path is called *śramaṇatva*.
Because one attains the fruits from within this path, they are called the fruits of the *śramaṇa*. Good son!
Furthermore, regarding the term *śramaṇa*: just as those people in the world who delight in tranquility are also called *śramaṇas*, so too is this Path.
It enables the practitioner to abandon the evil wrong livelihoods of body, speech, and mind, thereby attaining the bliss of stillness; for this reason, it is called *śramaṇa*.
"Good son! Just as a person of low status in the world can become a superior person, he is called a śramaṇa.
This Path is likewise; because it can cause those of low status to become superior persons, it is therefore named 'śramaṇatā'."
Good son! Those Arhats who cultivate this path attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya; for this reason, they are said to have reached the other shore.

The fruit of arhatship is precisely the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and the fivefold dharma-body—namely, precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Because one reaches the other shore by means of these five factors, it is called "reaching the other shore."
Having reached the further shore, he declared of himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Good son! Because this Arhat has forever severed the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time, he declares of himself: 'Birth has been exhausted.
Furthermore, because he has also severed the fruits of the five aggregates within the triple world, he further says: 'Birth has been exhausted.'"
Because the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that was cultivated has reached its ultimate consummation, he therefore proclaims: "The holy life is established.
Furthermore, having relinquished the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*), it is also called "established.
Since what was originally sought has been attained today, he therefore proclaims: "What was to be done has been accomplished" (*kṛta-kṛtya*).
Having cultivated the path and attained the fruit, one also says, "It is already accomplished.

Because of having obtained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one proclaims: "Birth has been exhausted for me; all fetters of existence have been eliminated."
For this reason, they are called Arhats who have reached the other shore.
As it is with the Arhats, so it is with the Pratyekabuddhas.

When Bodhisattvas and Buddhas fully accomplish the six pāramitās, they are said to have reached the other shore; once these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are said to be fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
Why is this? Because one attains the fruit of the six pāramitās; because one has attained the fruit, it is called "complete. "Good son!

These seven types of sentient beings do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom; being unable to practice these four matters, they are able to commit the five heinous crimes, sever their roots of goodness, violate the four grave prohibitions, and slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. For this reason, they are called those who are "perpetually submerged."
"Good son!

Among these seven kinds of people, those who are able to draw near to spiritual friends, listen to and receive the Tathāgata’s true Dharma with a sincere heart, reflect upon it well within themselves, abide according to the Dharma, and diligently cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom—for this reason, they are called those who cross the river of birth and death to reach the other shore."
If one says that an icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called attachment;
if one says they do not attain it, this is called falsehood.
“Good son! Of these seven kinds of persons, there may be one person who possesses all seven, or there may be seven persons each possessing one.
Good son!”

If there is a person whose mind and speech differ from their thoughts, and they claim that an icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should know that such a person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;

if a person’s mind and speech differ from their thoughts, and they claim that an icchantika does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this person is likewise called a slanderer of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"Good son!
If someone says that the eightfold noble path is attained by ordinary persons, that person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
if someone says that the eightfold noble path is not attained by ordinary persons, that person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
"Good son!

If there are those who say that all sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature, or that they definitely lack Buddha-nature, such people are also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
"Good son!

For this reason, I have said in the sūtras that there are two kinds of people who slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha: first, those who do not believe due to a mind of hatred; second, those who, though they believe, do not understand the meaning."
Good son! If a person possesses faith but lacks wisdom, that person will increase ignorance.
If one possesses wisdom but lacks faith, that person will increase false views.
"Good son! Because of their minds of anger and resentment, those who lack faith say that there are no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha Jewels.
Those who have faith but lack wisdom misunderstand the meaning in a perverted way, causing those who hear the Dharma to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
"Good son!

For this reason, I say that it is because of a mind of anger that those who lack faith, and because of a lack of wisdom that those who possess faith, are able to slander the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha."
"Good son!

If there is one who says that icchantikas and others, having not yet produced wholesome dharmas, immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, if there is another who says that an icchantika person abandons the state of being an icchantika and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within a different body, this person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

Furthermore, if it is said that an icchantika can give rise to roots of goodness, and having given rise to them, continues them without interruption until attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then one may say that the icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; one should know that such a person does not slander the Triple Gem.
"Good son!

If there is one who says that all sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature—which is permanent, blissful, self, and pure—and that it cannot be seen because it does not arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions, you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

If there is one who says that all sentient beings have no Buddha-nature at all, being like the horns of a rabbit, produced through expedient means, originally non-existent but now existing, and having existed, returning to non-existence, you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
If someone were to say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent like space nor non-existent like a rabbit’s horn—
for what reason?
Because space is eternal and the rabbit’s horn is non-existent— it can therefore be said that it both exists and does not exist.
Because it exists, one refutes the horns of a rabbit; because it does not exist, one refutes empty space. One who speaks in this manner does not slander the Triple Gem. "Good son!

As for the Buddha-nature, it is not called a single dharma, nor ten dharmas, nor a hundred dharmas, nor a thousand dharmas, nor ten thousand dharmas. Before one has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all that is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate is entirely termed 'Buddha-nature.'"
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of the fruit within the cause, and speaks of the cause within the fruit; this is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention.

Because he speaks according to his intention, he is named Tathāgata; because he speaks according to his intention, he is named Arhat; because he speaks according to his intention, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 36; The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 37.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva Chapter, Part Twelve, Section Five.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
"As the Buddha has taught, the buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space. Why is it said to be 'like empty space'?
"Good son, the nature of empty space is neither past, nor future, nor present; the buddha-nature is likewise."
Good son! Space is not of the past. Why is this?
Because the present does not exist.
If dharmas were present, one could speak of the past; however, since the present does not exist, there is neither the past nor the present. Why is this?
Because there is no future.
If a dharma were in the future, it could be said to be in the present; however, since there is no future, there is neither the present nor the future. Why is this?
Because there is no present or past;
if there were a present or past, then there would be a future. Since there is no present or past, there is no future.
For this reason, the nature of space is not subsumed within the three periods of time. Good son!
Because space is non-existent, the three periods of time do not exist; it is not because space exists that the three periods of time are absent.
Just as a flower in the sky does not exist and therefore has no existence in the three periods of time, so too is space:
because it does not exist, it has no existence in the three periods of time.
"Good son! That which is without substance is space; the Buddha-nature is also like this, good son!"
Because space is non-existent, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time. Good son!
The Tathāgata has already attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; all Buddha-nature and all Buddha-dharmas are eternal and unchanging.
For this reason, there are no three periods of time, being just like empty space.
Good son! Because space is non-existent, it is neither internal nor external;
because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is neither internal nor external.
Therefore, it is said that buddha-nature is like empty space. Good son!
Just as in the world, that which has no obstruction is called empty space.
The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and is without any obstruction regarding all Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like empty space.
"For these reasons, I say that the Buddha-nature is like empty space.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata, buddha-nature, and nirvāṇa are not subsumed within the three periods of time, yet they are called "existent.
Space, likewise, is not subsumed within the three periods of time; for what reason, then, can it not be called "existent"?
The Buddha said: "Good son!
That which is not nirvana is called nirvana; that which is not a Tathāgata is called a Tathāgata; that which is not buddha-nature is called buddha-nature."
What is meant by "non-nirvana"?
It refers to all afflictions and conditioned phenomena; it is called nirvana because it destroys such conditioned afflictions.

Those who are not Tathāgatas refer to those ranging from icchantikas up to pratyekabuddhas; it is for the sake of destroying such icchantikas and others up to pratyekabuddhas that one is called a Tathāgata.
That which is not Buddha-nature refers to all walls, tiles, stones, and insentient things; apart from such insentient things, that is called Buddha-nature.
"Good son!
Throughout all worlds, there is nothing that is not empty space confronting empty space.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the world, there is nothing that does not have a counterpart to the four great elements, yet they are still called ‘existent.
Since space has no counterpart, why can it not be called existent?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If you say that nirvana is not subsumed within the three periods of time, and that space is likewise so, this meaning is not correct."

Why is this? Because *nirvāṇa* exists; it can be seen and realized. It is form, a footprint, and a textual passage; it is existence, a characteristic, a condition, and a place of refuge; it is tranquility, radiance, security, and the further shore. For these reasons, it is designated as not being subsumed within the three periods of time.
The nature of space does not possess such dharmas; therefore, it is called "non-existent.
If there were any dharma apart from such dharmas, it would necessarily be subsumed within the three periods of time.
If space were the same as a phenomenon that exists, it could not be excluded from being subsumed within the three periods of time. Good son!
As people of the world say, space is called formless, non-obstructive, and invisible; if it is formless, non-obstructive, and invisible, then it is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*).

If space were of the same nature as mental phenomena (*caitasika-dharma*), it could not fail to be subsumed within the three periods of time. If it were subsumed within the three periods of time, it would be one of the four aggregates (*skandha*). Therefore, apart from the four aggregates, space does not exist.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The various non-Buddhists say that space is itself light, and if it is light, it is a material phenomenon (rūpa-dharma)."
If space were such that it were a material phenomenon (rūpadharma), it would be impermanent; being impermanent, it would be subsumed within the three periods of time.
Why, then, do the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim that it is not included within the three periods of time?
If it were subsumed within the three periods of time, it would not be empty space; yet one might also say that empty space is eternal. Good son!
Furthermore, some say that empty space is a place of abiding, and if there is a place of abiding, it is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).

Furthermore, all locations are impermanent and subsumed within the three periods of time; space, however, is permanent and not subsumed within the three periods of time. If one speaks of "locations," one should know that space does not exist therein.

Furthermore, there are those who say: "Space is sequential; if it is sequential, it is a numerical phenomenon (saṃkhyā-dharma); if it can be numbered, it is subsumed within the three periods of time; if it is subsumed within the three periods of time, how can you say it is eternal?"
"Good son!
Furthermore, it is said that space is not apart from three dharmas:
first, emptiness; second, reality; and third, both emptiness and reality."
If one says that emptiness is this [the self], one should know that space is an impermanent phenomenon. Why?
Because it does not exist in reality.
If one says that [the self] is truly real, one should know that space is likewise impermanent.
Why? Because there is no [substantiality] in the place of space.
If emptiness were truly existent, one should know that space would likewise be impermanent.
Why? Because both are non-existent.
Therefore, space is called "non-existent. Good son! It is as if one were to say that space is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);

for example, it is as if one were to say that space is created by removing trees or removing houses, that space is leveled, that space is covered, that space is elevated, or that the color of space is painted like the water of the great ocean; thus, space is a conditioned phenomenon.
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, like an earthen jar; if space were likewise, it should also be impermanent. Good son!
People of the world say that among all phenomena, that which is unimpeded is called space."
Regarding this state of non-obstruction within the locus of all phenomena:
does it exist in its entirety, or does it exist partially?
If it exists in its entirety, one should know that there would be no space in other locations.
If it were divisible, it would be a phenomenon that can be counted as "this" or "that"; if it can be counted, one should know it is impermanent. Good son!
If someone says that unimpeded space merges with existence, or further says that space resides within things like fruit inside a vessel—both of these views are incorrect.
Why is this? If one speaks of "conjunction," there are three types:
first, conjunction through different actions, such as flying birds gathering in a tree;
Second, the conjunction of common karma, like two rams butting heads;
third, the conjunction of what has already conjoined with further conjunction, like two pairs of fingers joined together in one place.
If one speaks of the conjunction of distinct karmas, there are two types of distinction:
First is the activity of matter, and second is the activity of space.
If the activity of space were to conjoin with matter, then space would be impermanent.
If the activity of matter were to conjoin with space, then matter would not be all-pervading; and if it were not all-pervading, it too would be impermanent.
If it is claimed that space is eternal and, being by nature immovable, unites with moving objects, this meaning is not tenable. Why?
Because if space were eternal, objects would also have to be eternal.
If things were impermanent, then emptiness would also be impermanent.
To say that empty space is both permanent and impermanent is impossible.
If it were to combine with collective karma, this principle would not hold true.
Why is this? Space is called "pervasive.

If it were to combine with karma, then karma too would have to be pervasive. If it were pervasive, it would have to pervade all things; if it pervaded all things, it would have to combine with all things. Thus, one could not speak of there being both combination and non-combination.
If it is argued that they have already conjoined, like two fingers joined together, this is not the case.
Why? Because there was no prior conjunction, and conjunction occurs only subsequently.
That which did not previously exist but subsequently comes into being is an impermanent phenomenon; therefore, one cannot say that space has already combined or is in the process of combining.
Just as worldly phenomena that did not previously exist but subsequently come into being are impermanent entities, so it is with this.
If space were thus, it too would be impermanent.
If you say that space exists within objects, like fruit inside a vessel, this argument is not tenable. Why is this so?
If space were like this, prior to the existence of a vessel, where would it abide?
If it had a place of abiding, then space would be manifold.
If it were manifold, how could one say it is eternal, singular, and all-pervasive?
If space were to exist apart from emptiness, then material objects would likewise exist apart from space; therefore, one should know that space does not exist. Good son!
If someone were to say that the location where a finger points is called "space," one should know that space is an impermanent phenomenon. Why is this?
Because the finger has four sides; if it has four sides, one should know that space also has four sides.
All eternal dharmas have no location whatsoever; because space has a location, it is impermanent.
If it were impermanent, it would not be separate from the five aggregates; yet if it were separated from the five aggregates, it would be nothing at all.
“Good son! If there is a phenomenon that abides by means of causes and conditions, you should know that such a phenomenon is called impermanent. Good son!”
For example, just as all sentient beings and trees abide because of the earth, and since the earth is impermanent, the things that depend upon the earth are successively impermanent. Good son!
Just as earth depends on water, because water is impermanent, earth is also impermanent.
Just as water depends on wind, because wind is impermanent, water is also impermanent.
Wind depends upon space; because space is impermanent, wind is also impermanent.
If it is impermanent, how can you say that space is permanent and omnipresent?
Because space is non-existent, it is not of the past, future, or present; likewise, because a rabbit’s horn is a non-entity, it is not of the past, future, or present.
Therefore, I say that because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
because space is non-existent, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time. Good son!
I never dispute with the world. Why is this?
When worldly wisdom says something exists, I also say it exists; when worldly wisdom says something does not exist, I also say it does not exist.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One,
how many dharmas must a bodhisattva-mahāsattva fulfill so as not to contend with the world?”
"Are you not defiled by worldly dharmas?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they do not contend with the world and are not defiled by worldly phenomena.

What are these ten? First, faith; second, possessing ethical discipline; third, associating with virtuous friends; fourth, internal reflection; fifth, being fully possessed of diligence; sixth, being fully possessed of right mindfulness; seventh, being fully possessed of wisdom; eighth, being fully possessed of right speech; ninth, delighting in the true Dharma; and tenth, compassion for sentient beings.
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these ten dharmas, he does not contend with the world and is not defiled by worldly dharmas, just like an utpala flower."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, when worldly wisdom says something exists, I also say it exists; when worldly wisdom says something does not exist, I also say it does not exist.”
"What is meant by the existence or non-existence of worldly knowledge?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
If worldly wisdom says that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and so on up to consciousness being likewise—
O son of good family!
This is called what the worldly wise say exists, and I also say it exists.
"Good son!
The wise of the world say that form lacks permanence, bliss, self, and purity; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Good son!"
"This is what those who possess worldly wisdom call 'non-existent,' and I also say it is non-existent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The wise of the world—namely the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all noble ones—hold that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. How then can the Tathāgata say that the Buddha’s form-body is eternal and unchanging?
The wise of the world say that such things do not exist; why then does the Tathāgata say they exist?
If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks in this way, how can it be said that he does not contend with the world?
Is he not defiled by worldly dharmas?

The Tathāgata has already abandoned the three kinds of inversion—namely, inversion of perception, inversion of mind, and inversion of view—and thus he should declare that the Buddha’s form is truly impermanent. Yet now you say it is permanent; how can this be called being free from inversion and not contending with the world?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! The form of ordinary beings arises from afflictions; therefore, wisdom declares that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.”
"The form of the Tathāgata is far removed from afflictions; therefore, it is said to be permanent, eternal, and unchanging.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, "World-Honored One!"
"How is it that form arises from afflictions?
"Good son, there are three kinds of afflictions: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)."
The wise should contemplate the faults and transgressions inherent in these three outflows.
Why is this? Because once one has recognized these faults, one is able to distance oneself from them.
It is like a physician who first examines the patient's pulse, identifies the location of the illness, and only then administers medicine.
Good son! It is like a person leading a blind man into a thicket of brambles, then abandoning him there and returning home.
A blind person will find it extremely difficult to emerge from there later on, and even if they should emerge, their body will be utterly destroyed.
So too it is with ordinary worldlings: unable to know or see the faults of the three outflows (*āsrava*), they follow after them in their course.
One who perceives it thus is able to distance themselves from it; having recognized their transgressions, even though they must undergo the retribution, that retribution will be slight.
Good son, there are four kinds of people:

First, when the action is heavy, the retribution received is light; second, when the action is light, the retribution received is heavy; third, when the action is heavy, the retribution received is also heavy; fourth, when the action is light, the retribution received is also light.
"Good son! If a person can contemplate the faults and transgressions of the afflictions, that person’s karma and the resulting retribution will both be light.
Good son!"
A person of wisdom reflects thus:
"I should distance myself from such outflows, and furthermore, I should not commit such base and evil deeds. Why is this?"
Because I have not yet attained liberation from the retributions of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas,
if I cultivate the Path, I shall, by the power of this, destroy all sufferings.
Having observed this, that person’s greed, hatred, and delusion become weakened.
Seeing that greed, hatred, and delusion have been lightened, their mind becomes joyful, and they further think:

"That I am now thus is entirely due to the power of the causes and conditions of practicing the Path; it has enabled me to leave unwholesome dharmas behind and draw near to wholesome dharmas. Therefore, having now beheld the Right Path, I ought to apply myself with diligence to its cultivation."

By means of this, that person diligently cultivates the power of the Path, thereby distancing themselves from immeasurable evil afflictions and escaping the retributions of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
Therefore, I have said in the sūtras that one should contemplate all outflowing afflictions (*āsrava*) as well as the causes of these outflows. Why is this?
If a person of wisdom contemplates only the outflows without contemplating their causes, they will be unable to sever those afflictions.
Why is this? Because the wise observe that outflows arise from these causes; if I now sever the causes, the outflows will not arise. Good son!
Just as that physician first eliminates the cause of the disease so that the illness does not arise, so too is it for the wise person who first eliminates the causes of affliction.

A person of wisdom should first contemplate the causes and then contemplate the retributive effects; they know that from wholesome causes wholesome fruits arise, and they know that from unwholesome causes unwholesome fruits arise.
Having contemplated the retribution of results, one distances oneself from evil causes.

Having contemplated the retribution of results, one should next contemplate the gravity of the afflictions (*kleśa*); having contemplated their gravity, one first abandons the heavy ones; once the heavy ones have been abandoned, the light ones will depart of their own accord.

“Good son! If a wise person knows afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, that person will at that time diligently cultivate the Path, without ceasing or regretting, associating with virtuous friends, and listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart, for the sake of extinguishing all such afflictions.”
"Good son!
It is like a sick person who knows for himself that his illness is light and will certainly be cured; even if he obtains bitter medicine, he takes it without regret.
A person of wisdom is also like this: they diligently cultivate the Noble Path with joy and without sorrow, never ceasing and never regretting."
"Good son!

If a person can know afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, and diligently cultivates the Noble Path for the sake of eliminating afflictions, that person will not be born from afflictions; the same applies to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

If one cannot understand afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, and does not diligently cultivate the Path, such a person will arise from afflictions; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
"Good son!

One who knows afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity or lightness of afflictions, and who practices the Path for the sake of severing afflictions, is himself the Tathāgata. For these reasons, the form of the Tathāgata is permanent, and so on, up to his consciousness being permanent."
"Good son!

One who does not know afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, and thus cannot cultivate the Path, is a worldling. Therefore, for a worldling, form is impermanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent."
"Good son!
The wise of the world, all noble ones, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas speak of these two meanings; I, too, likewise speak of these two meanings."
"Therefore, I say that I do not dispute with the wise of the world, nor am I defiled by worldly dharmas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

“As the Buddha has taught, there are three outflows (*āsrava*). What are they called: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Regarding the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*): internal evil thoughts and reflections, conditioned by external objects, give rise to the outflow of desire.
Therefore, in the past, while I was in Rājagṛha, I said to Ānanda: "Ānanda!..."
"You have now received these verses spoken by this woman; these verses were indeed proclaimed by the Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, all internal evil thoughts and external conditions are called "desire," and this is termed the "outflow of desire" (kāma-āsrava).

Regarding "with outflows" (*sāsrava*): the form and formless realms, internal unwholesome dharmas, and external conditions—excluding the external conditions and internal applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the desire realm—are called "with outflows."

Regarding the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*): being unable to clearly understand "self" and "what belongs to self," and failing to distinguish between the internal and the external, is called the outflow of ignorance.
Good son! Ignorance is the very root of all outflows.

Why is this? Because all sentient beings, due to the causal conditions of ignorance (*avidyā*), give rise to conceptualizations and signs regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); these are called "sentient beings. This is termed a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view. By means of these causal conditions, all outflows (*āsrava*) arise. Therefore, in the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I have taught that ignorance is the cause of greed, the cause of hatred, and the cause of delusion.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!

In the past, the Tathāgata spoke in the twelve divisions of the scriptures that greed, anger, and delusion arise due to the causal condition of improper reflection; for what reason do you now say they arise from ignorance?”
“Good son! These two dharmas serve as cause and effect for one another and mutually increase each other.
Improper mental attention gives rise to ignorance, and with ignorance as a condition, improper mental attention arises.”
"Good son!
That which can give rise to and grow all afflictions is entirely termed the causes and conditions of affliction; to draw near to such causes and conditions of affliction is termed ignorance."
“Improper reflection is like a seed producing a sprout; the seed is the proximate cause, while the four great elements are the remote causes. It is the same with afflictions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“As the Buddha has taught, ignorance itself is an outflow (āsrava). Why, then, do you say that the various outflows arise because of ignorance?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
As I have taught, that which is the outflow of ignorance is internal ignorance.
That which gives rise to all outflows due to ignorance is the internal-external cause.
If one speaks of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), this is called internal inversion; it is the failure to recognize impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
If one speaks of the causes and conditions of all afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called not knowing the external self and what belongs to the self (*ātma-ātmīya*).
"If one speaks of the outflow of ignorance, it is called having neither beginning nor end; from ignorance arise the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, a person of wisdom understands the cause of the outflows (*āsrava*). What is meant by "understanding the cause of the outflows"?
"Good son! A wise person should contemplate:
by what causes and conditions do these afflictions (*kleśa*) arise?"
What kind of conduct did one perform to give rise to these afflictions?
At what time did these afflictions arise?
While dwelling with whom did these afflictions arise?
In what place does one dwell so that these afflictions arise?
Having observed what object do afflictions arise?
Receiving whose dwellings, bedding, food and drink, clothing, and medicinal requisites do afflictions arise?
For what causes and conditions do the inferior become intermediate and the intermediate become superior; how is it that inferior karma becomes intermediate and intermediate karma becomes superior?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this way, they will attain detachment from the causes and conditions for the arising of outflows (*āsrava*).
When one observes in this manner, unarisen afflictions are prevented from arising, and those already arisen are eliminated.
Therefore, I have said in the sūtras that the wise should contemplate the causes from which afflictions arise.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a single body of a sentient being can give rise to various kinds of afflictions?”
The Buddha said, "Good son!
It is like various kinds of seeds within a single vessel; once they receive water and rain, each grows forth on its own."
“Sentient beings are also like this: although the vessel is one, because of the conditions of craving, they are able to produce and grow various afflictions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, “World-Honored One!”
"How does the wise person contemplate karmic retribution? "Good son!
The wise person should contemplate that the causes and conditions of the various outflows can give rise to birth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals."

These outflows are the causes and conditions by which one obtains the bodies of humans and devas; these are themselves impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Within this vessel of a body, one encounters three kinds of suffering and three kinds of impermanence.

These outflows serve as causes and conditions that enable sentient beings to commit the five heinous crimes, undergo various evil retributions, sever their roots of goodness, violate the four grave prohibitions, and slander the Triple Gem.
"The wise person should contemplate: 'Since I have received such a body as this, I ought not to give rise to such afflictions and undergo various evil fruits.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
There is the fruit of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), yet it is further said that the wise sever all retributive fruits (*vipākaphala*).
Is the outflow-free retribution included within what is severed?
All those who have attained the Path possess the outflow-free fruit; if such wise ones seek the outflow-free fruit, why does the Buddha say that all wise ones should sever retribution?
“If they were to be severed, how could the various sages exist today?
“Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes speaks of the fruit within the cause, and sometimes speaks of the cause within the fruit.”
As worldly people say that clay is the jar or that thread is the garment, this is called "speaking of the effect within the cause.
Speaking of the cause within the effect is, for example, saying that the cow is the water and grass it consumes, or that a person is the food they eat.

I am also like this: speaking of the effect within the cause, I previously stated in the sūtras that because I move the body by means of the mind from the causal basis of the mind-body, it is called "the mind-body reaching as far as the Brahma-heaven."
This is called "speaking of the effect within the cause" and "speaking of the cause within the effect.
These six sense bases are called past karma; this is called "speaking of the cause within the effect. Good son!
For all noble ones (*ārya*), there truly exists no outflowing fruit and retribution (*anāsrava-vipāka*).
Because the fruit and retribution resulting from the cultivation of the path by all noble ones does not give rise to further outflows, it is therefore called "outflow-free fruit and retribution."
"Good son!
When a person of wisdom contemplates in this way, they immediately attain the eternal extinction of the retribution of afflictions.
Good son!"
Having observed this, the wise person cultivates the Noble Path in order to sever such afflictions and their karmic retributions. The Noble Path consists of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Having cultivated this path, one is able to extinguish all afflictions and their retributions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings obtain their retributions from afflictions; what we call afflictions is evil. The afflictions produced by these evil afflictions are likewise called evil.”
Such afflictions are of two kinds:
first, cause; second, effect.
Because the cause is evil, the effect is evil; because the effect is evil, the offspring is evil.
Just as with the nimba fruit, because its seed is bitter, the flower, fruit, stem, and leaves are all bitter.
It is like a poisonous tree; because its seed is poisonous, the fruit is likewise poisonous.

The cause is sentient beings and the fruit is also sentient beings; the cause is afflictions and the fruit is also afflictions. The cause and fruit of afflictions are themselves sentient beings, and sentient beings are themselves the cause and fruit of afflictions.
If this is the meaning, why did the Tathāgata previously use the analogy of the Snowy Mountains, which contain both poisonous weeds and the wondrous medicinal king?

If it is said that afflictions are identical to sentient beings and sentient beings are identical to afflictions, how can it be said that there is a wondrous medicinal king within the bodies of sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
Immeasurable sentient beings all share this same doubt; since you are now able to inquire and seek its resolution, I too am able to sever it.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now explain it to you in detail.
Good son! The analogy of the Snowy Mountains refers to sentient beings; the poisonous herbs refer to afflictions; and the king of wondrous medicines refers to pure brahmacarya.
“Good son!
If there are sentient beings who can cultivate such pure brahmacarya, they are said to have the wondrous King of Medicines within their bodies.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do sentient beings possess pure Brahma-conduct? “Good son!
It is just as in the world, where fruit arises from a seed; of these fruits, some are capable of acting as a cause for a seed, while others are not.
That which is capable of so acting is called the "fruit-seed."
If one cannot perform [the action], one may only be called the "fruit" and not the "seed.
It is the same for all sentient beings, who possess two kinds:
first, those who have the fruit of afflictions and are the cause of afflictions; second, those who have the fruit of afflictions but are not the cause of afflictions.
This is the fruit of affliction, not the cause of affliction; this is what is called pure brahmacarya.
"Good son! Sentient beings contemplate sensation and know it to be the proximate cause of all outflows—namely, the internal and external outflows."
Due to the condition of feeling (*vedanā*), one cannot sever all outflows (*āsrava*) nor escape the prison of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Because sentient beings, due to feeling, cling to "self" and "what belongs to self," they give rise to the inversion of mind, the inversion of perception, and the inversion of view; therefore, sentient beings should first contemplate feeling.
Feeling such as this acts as the proximate cause for all craving; therefore, a wise person who wishes to sever craving should first contemplate feeling.
Good son!
All the good and evil deeds performed by all sentient beings through the twelve links of dependent origination are rooted in the moment of sensation; for this reason, I said to Ānanda: "Ānanda!..."
"All the good and evil deeds performed by all sentient beings are occasions for feeling.
Therefore, the wise person should first contemplate feeling; having contemplated feeling, they should further contemplate: "From what causes and conditions does such feeling arise?"
If it arises from causes and conditions, from what do such causes and conditions themselves arise?
If it were to arise without a cause, why would that which lacks a cause not also give rise to non-sensation (*vedanā*)?

Furthermore, one contemplates that this sensation does not arise from the creation of Īśvara, nor from a primal spirit (*puruṣa*), nor from atoms, nor from the seasons; it does not arise from conceptualization, nor from a fundamental nature (*prakṛti*); it is not born of itself, nor born of another, nor born of both self and other, nor is it born without a cause. This sensation arises entirely from the conjunction of conditions.

The causal condition is precisely craving; within this conjunction, there is neither sensation nor non-sensation. Therefore, I shall sever this conjunction; by severing the conjunction, sensation will not arise.
“Good son! Once the wise person has contemplated the cause, they next contemplate the retribution of the fruit.
Due to sensation, sentient beings undergo the immeasurable sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and even the three realms.
Due to the condition of feeling, one experiences impermanent pleasure.
Due to the condition of feeling, one severs the roots of goodness.
Due to the condition of feeling, one attains liberation.
When one practices this contemplation, one does not create the cause for sensation.
What is meant by "not creating the cause for sensation"?
It refers to the discrimination of sensation.
What kind of sensation can act as the cause for craving?
What kind of craving can act as the cause for sensation? Good son!
If sentient beings can thus deeply contemplate the cause of craving and the cause of sensation, they will then be able to sever both "I" and "mine.
Good son! If a person can perform such contemplations as these, they should further discern: where do craving and sensation cease?

Seeing that there is even a slight place where craving, sensation, and existence are extinguished, one should know that there must also be ultimate extinction; at that time, one gives rise to faith in liberation.
Having given rise to faith, one then considers: "By what means is this state of liberation attained?"
Knowing that it proceeds from the Eightfold Path, one then practices it.
What is called the Eightfold Noble Path?
This path contemplates that feeling has three characteristics:
The first is suffering, the second is pleasure, and the third is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. These three types are all capable of increasing both body and mind.
By what causes and conditions are they able to increase them?
Contact is the causal condition.
This contact is of three kinds:
first, contact associated with ignorance; second, contact associated with clarity; and third, contact associated with neither-clarity-nor-ignorance.

What is called "contact of clarity" is the Eightfold Noble Path; the other two types of contact increase the body and mind as well as the three kinds of sensation. Therefore, I should sever the causal conditions of these two types of contact; because contact is severed, the three sensations will not arise.
Good son!
Such feeling is called both cause and fruit; the wise should contemplate it as being both cause and fruit.
What constitutes the cause?
Because feeling gives rise to craving, it is called the cause.
What is called the effect?
Because it arises from contact, it is called the effect.
Therefore, this sensation is both cause and effect.
Once the wise person has contemplated sensation in this way, they next contemplate craving; because it is the retribution of sensation, it is called craving.
The wise observe that craving is further divided into two kinds:
first, craving for food; second, craving for non-food.
Craving for food is the cause of birth, old age, sickness, death, and all forms of existence.
Regarding those who lack craving for food: they sever all forms of existence—including birth, old age, sickness, and death—as well as greed, by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Furthermore, the wise person should reflect thus:
"If I were to give rise to this craving for various kinds of food, I would be unable to sever birth, old age, sickness, and death."

Although I now covet the path of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), if I do not sever the cause of feeling (*vedanā*), I shall not be able to attain the fruit of the path of outflowlessness. Therefore, one should first sever this contact (*sparśa*); once contact is severed, feeling will naturally cease; once feeling has ceased, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) will also follow and cease.
"This is called the Eightfold Noble Path. Good son!

If there are sentient beings who can contemplate in this way, although they possess poisonous bodies, within them there is also a subtle and wondrous king of medicines, just as in the Snowy Mountains, although there are poisonous herbs, there are also sublime medicines."
"Good son!
Although such sentient beings obtain retribution from their afflictions, this retribution no longer serves as a cause for further afflictions; this is precisely what is called pure brahmacarya."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A wise person should contemplate these two things—feeling (vedanā) and craving (tṛṣṇā)—as to by what causes and conditions they arise.
One knows that they arise because of perception (saṃjñā)."

Why is this? Sentient beings do not give rise to craving when they see forms, nor do they give rise to craving when they contemplate feelings. However, if they give rise to inverted perceptions regarding form—claiming that form is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, or that feeling is eternal and unchanging—it is because of these inverted perceptions that craving, hatred, and delusion arise.
Therefore, the wise should practice contemplation. How should they contemplate?
They should form this thought: "All sentient beings who have not yet attained the Right Path possess inverted perceptions."
What is inverted perception?

It is to conceive the notion of permanence in what is impermanent, the notion of pleasure in what is suffering, the notion of purity in what is impure, and the notion of a self in phenomena that are empty.

Regarding that which is neither male nor female, neither large nor small, neither day nor night, neither month nor year, and neither clothing, nor dwelling, nor bedding—there arises the perception of them as being from a male to bedding.
This perception is of three kinds:
first, small; second, great; and third, boundless.
Due to small conditions, small perception arises; due to great conditions, great perception arises; and due to immeasurable conditions, immeasurable perception arises.
Furthermore, there is the "small perception," which refers to not yet having entered meditative absorption.
There is also the "great perception," which refers to having already entered meditative absorption.
Finally, there is the "immeasurable perception," which refers to the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, there are minor perceptions, namely all perceptions of the desire realm and so forth.
Furthermore, there are great perceptions, namely all perceptions of the form realm and so forth.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable perceptions, namely all perceptions of the formless realm and so forth.
"Because the three perceptions are extinguished, sensation naturally ceases; because perception and sensation are extinguished, it is called liberation.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, "World-Honored One!"
“The cessation of all phenomena is called liberation.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that the cessation of perception and feeling is called liberation?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Sometimes the Tathāgata speaks about sentient beings because of [the needs of] sentient beings, and those who hear it understand the Dharma.
Sometimes he speaks about sentient beings because of the Dharma, and those who hear it also understand [it as being about] sentient beings.”
What is meant by "teaching according to sentient beings so that the hearers understand the Dharma"?
It is as I previously said to Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa!..."
"When sentient beings cease, wholesome dharmas also cease.
This is called teaching by way of sentient beings, such that the listener understands the dharma.
What is it to teach concerning sentient beings by way of the dharma, such that the listener also understands sentient beings?
As I previously told Ānanda:
"I do not say that one should associate with all dharmas, nor do I say that one should not associate with all dharmas."
If, by associating with certain phenomena, wholesome qualities decline and unwholesome ones flourish, such phenomena should not be associated with.
If, by associating with certain phenomena, unwholesome qualities diminish and wholesome qualities increase, such phenomena should be associated with.
"This is called explaining [the teaching] regarding sentient beings by means of the Dharma; those who hear it also explain it regarding sentient beings. Good son!
Although the Tathāgata speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, he has thereby explained in general all that is to be abandoned."
Once the wise person has thus contemplated such a perception, they next contemplate the cause of that perception: from what does this immeasurable perception arise?
They know it arises from contact (*sparśa*).
This contact is of two kinds:
The first is contact due to affliction; the second is contact due to liberation.
That which arises dependent on ignorance is called contact due to affliction; that which arises dependent on clarity is called contact due to liberation.
"From contact with afflictions arises perverted perception; from contact with liberation arises non-perverted perception.
Having contemplated the causes of perception, one next contemplates its retribution.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If, by means of this notion of affliction, one gives rise to perverted notions, then all noble ones would in fact possess perverted notions while being without afflictions.”
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"How can a noble one possess inverted perceptions?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
All noble ones perceive an ox as an ox and likewise speak of it as an ox;
they perceive a horse as a horse and likewise speak of it as a horse.
It is the same for men and women, the large and the small, houses, vehicles, coming and going—this is called inverted perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*).
“Good son! All ordinary beings have two kinds of perceptions:
first, the perception of worldly convention; second, the perception of attachment.”
All noble ones possess only the conventional designations current in the world and have no notion of attachment.
All ordinary beings, due to their unwholesome discursive thoughts and reflections, give rise to notions of attachment toward these worldly conventions.
Because all noble ones possess skillful contemplation and observation, they do not give rise to thoughts of attachment toward worldly phenomena.
Therefore, ordinary persons are said to have "perverted perceptions," whereas noble ones, though they know [these things], are not said to have perverted perceptions.

Once the wise person has thus contemplated the cause of perception, they next contemplate its retribution: this fruit of evil perception is experienced within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.

Just as for me, because evil vitarka and vicāra have been severed, the contact of ignorance is severed; therefore, perception is severed, and because perception is severed, its retribution is also severed.
To sever such causes of perception, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
"Good son!
If there are those who can perform such contemplations as these, they may be called practitioners of pure brahmacarya.
Good son!"

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous bodies of sentient beings; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines.
"Furthermore, good son!
The wise contemplate desire; desire consists of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch.
Good son! This is the Tathāgata speaking of the fruit within the context of the cause.
From these five things, desire arises; yet in reality, they are not desire. Good son! Foolish people greedily seek to receive them;

thus, within form (*rūpa*), they give rise to perverted perceptions (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*), and so on, even within tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*) they give rise to perverted perceptions. Due to the conditions of these perverted perceptions, sensation (*vedanā*) arises. For this reason, the world says that ten kinds of perceptions arise from perverted perceptions.

Due to the conditions of desire, one undergoes evil retributions within this world; one inflicts harm upon parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others, intentionally committing what ought not to be done, without regard for body or life.
Therefore, the wise person observes that it is due to these unwholesome perceptions as causes and conditions that the mind of desire arises.

Having thus observed the cause of desire, the wise person next observes its retribution: this desire brings about many evil retributions, namely those in the hells, among hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas; this is called observing the retribution.
If these unwholesome perceptions are eliminated, the mind of desire will never arise again.

Because there is no mind of desire, one does not experience unwholesome sensations; because there are no unwholesome sensations, there is no unwholesome fruit. Therefore, I should first sever unwholesome perceptions; once unwholesome perceptions have been severed, such phenomena as these will naturally cease.
Therefore, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to extinguish unwholesome thoughts; this is called pure brahmacarya.

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous body of sentient beings, just as the snowy mountains, though containing poisonous herbs, also contain wondrous medicines.
"Furthermore, good son!
Once the wise person has contemplated desire in this way, they should next contemplate karma. Why is this?

A person of wisdom should reflect in this way: sensation, perception, contact, and desire are themselves afflictions; these afflictions can produce the karma of birth, but they do not produce the karma of feeling.
Thus, when afflictions and karma function together, there are two types: first, karma that produces birth; second, karma that produces experience. Therefore, the wise should contemplate karma.
This karma is of three kinds:
namely, that of body, speech, and mind. Good son!
The two karmas of body and speech are called both "karma" and "the fruit of karma";
the mental [karma] is called only "karma" and not "fruit," because as the cause of karma, it is designated as "karma."
Good son! The two karmas of body and speech are called external karma, while the karma of mind is called internal.
Because these three types of karma function together with the afflictions, they produce two kinds of karma: first, productive karma (*janmakarma*), and second, retributive karma (*vedanīyakarma*).
Good son! Right action (*samyak-karmānta*) is precisely mental action (*manas-karma*); occasional action refers to bodily and vocal actions.
Because it arises first, it is called mental action; because it is produced from mental action, it is called bodily and vocal action. Therefore, mental action receives the name "right."

Having contemplated karma, the wise person next contemplates the cause of karma. The cause of karma is ignorance-contact (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*). Due to ignorance-contact, sentient beings seek existence; the causal condition for seeking existence is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). By reason of craving as a causal condition, they perform the three types of karma of body, speech, and mind.
"Good son!
Having thus contemplated the causes of karma, the wise person next contemplates its retributive fruits.
There are four such fruits: first, black-black retribution; second, white-white retribution; third, variegated retribution; and fourth, neither-black-nor-white retribution."
Regarding the black-and-black retribution: when the karma is performed, it is defiled, and the retribution is also defiled.
Regarding the white-and-white retribution: when the karma is performed, it is pure, and the retribution is also pure.
Regarding "mixed karmic retribution": when the karma is performed, it is mixed, and thus the retribution is also mixed.
That which is "neither white nor black" with "neither white nor black" retribution is called untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Previously, you said that the untainted (anāsrava) has no karmic retribution; why do you now say it has a retribution that is neither white nor black?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, this meaning has two aspects:
First, that which is both a fruit and a retribution; second, that which is only a fruit and not a retribution.
The black-and-black fruit-retribution is called both a "fruit" and a "retribution.
It is called a "fruit" because it is produced from black causes, and it is called a "retribution" because it acts as the causal agent.
The same applies to pure and mixed [results].

As for the uncontaminated result, because it arises from a contaminated cause, it is called a "result" (*phala*); since it does not function as a cause for another [result], it is not called a "retribution" (*vipāka*). Therefore, it is termed a "result" and not a "retribution."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is not a black dharma; for what reason and by what conditions is it not called white?”
“Good son! Because there is no karmic retribution, it is not called ‘white.
Because it is the antidote to the black, it is called ‘white.’”

I now declare that what receives karmic retribution is called "white"; because this untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) does not receive retribution, it is not called white, but is called "quiescence" (*śānta*).

Such karmic actions have fixed places where their retribution is experienced; for instance, the ten unwholesome paths of action are fixed in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm, while the ten wholesome paths of action are fixed in the human and celestial realms.
The ten unwholesome dharmas have superior, middling, and inferior degrees.

Due to superior causes and conditions, one receives a body in hell; due to middling causes and conditions, one receives a body as an animal; and due to inferior causes and conditions, one receives a body as a hungry ghost.
Furthermore, there are four grades of human karma consisting of the ten wholesome actions:
first, inferior; second, middling; third, superior; and fourth, supreme.
Due to inferior causes and conditions, one is born in Uttarakuru.
By means of middling causes and conditions, one is born in Pūrvavideha;
by means of superior causes and conditions, one is born in Aparagoyānī;
and by means of the most superior causes and conditions, one is born in Jambudvīpa.
Having made this observation, the wise person thinks:
"How shall I sever this retribution?
He then further reflects:
"This karma arises from the contact of ignorance as its cause and condition. If I were to sever both ignorance and contact, then such karmic fruits would be extinguished and not arise.
Therefore, the wise person, in order to sever the causal conditions of the contact of ignorance, cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path; this is what is called the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).
"Good son!

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous body of sentient beings; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
After the wise person has contemplated karma and contemplated the afflictions (*kleśa*), they next contemplate the retributive fruits obtained from these two.
These two fruits are themselves suffering (*duḥkha*); once this is known as suffering, one is then able to relinquish all forms of rebirth."

The wise person further contemplates: afflictions arise from the causal conditions of afflictions; afflictions also arise from the causal conditions of karma; afflictions again give rise to karma from their causal conditions; karma gives rise to suffering from its causal conditions; afflictions arise from the causal conditions of suffering; existence arises from the causal conditions of afflictions; suffering arises from the causal conditions of existence; existence arises from the causal conditions of existence; existence arises from the causal conditions of karma; afflictions arise from the causal conditions of karma; suffering arises from the causal conditions of afflictions; and suffering gives rise to further suffering from its causal conditions.
Good son! If a wise person can practice such contemplation, you should know that this person is able to contemplate the suffering of karma. Why is this?
What has been observed above is precisely the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) of birth and death.

If a person can contemplate this twelvefold chain of dependent origination of birth and death in such a manner, it should be known that this person does not create new karma and is able to destroy past karma.

Good son! A person of wisdom contemplates the suffering of the hells, observing from one single hell up to one hundred and thirty-six locations. Within each and every hell there are various kinds of suffering, all of which arise due to the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.

Having contemplated the hells, one next contemplates the sufferings of hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth. Having performed this contemplation, one further contemplates all the various sufferings of humans and devas; such manifold sufferings as these are all produced from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
"Good son!

Although there are no great sufferings or afflictions in the heavens, their bodies are soft, supple, and smooth; yet when they perceive the five signs, they experience extreme suffering that is no different from the torments of hell."
"Good son!
The wise deeply contemplate that all the sufferings within the three realms arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
Good son!"
For example, just as a fragile earthen vessel is easily broken, so too is it with sentient beings who receive a body; once a body has been received, it is already a vessel for manifold sufferings.
For example, just as a great tree with abundant flowers and fruit can be destroyed by flocks of birds, or as a large pile of dry grass can be consumed by a small fire; so it is with this body.
Sentient beings, when receiving a body, are likewise destroyed by suffering in these eight ways. Good son!
If a wise person can contemplate these eight kinds of suffering as they are described in the Noble Practices, you should know that such a person is able to sever all sufferings.
"Good son!
Once the wise have deeply contemplated these eight sufferings, they next contemplate the cause of suffering.
The cause of suffering is craving and ignorance."
This craving and ignorance are of two kinds:
first, the seeking of the body; second, the seeking of wealth.
Both the seeking of the body and the seeking of wealth are suffering; therefore, one should know that craving and ignorance are the causes of suffering.
Good son! This craving and ignorance are of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.
Internally it is able to produce karma, and externally it is able to increase it.
Furthermore, internally it is able to produce karma, and externally it produces the fruit of karma.
Once internal craving is severed, karma is then severed.
Once external craving has been severed, its fruit is likewise severed.
Internal craving gives rise to suffering in future lives, while external craving gives rise to suffering in the present life.
The wise contemplate craving as the very cause of suffering.
Having observed the causes, one next observes the retribution of the fruit.
The retribution of suffering is precisely grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping is the name for the fruit of craving; the causal conditions of this grasping are internal and external craving, which constitute the suffering of craving.
Good son! A wise person should contemplate that craving is the condition for grasping, and grasping is the condition for craving.
If I can sever these two things—craving and grasping—then I shall not create karma and undergo manifold sufferings.
Therefore, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path in order to sever the suffering of craving.
Good son! If there is anyone who can contemplate in this manner, this is what is called the pure holy life (brahmacarya).

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous bodies of sentient beings; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines.
*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle 37 [and] Fascicle 38.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve, Part Six:
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called ‘pure brahmacarya’?
The Buddha said:
“Good son, all dharmas are [the Tathāgata].
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are not fixed in their meaning. Why is this?

The Tathāgata has at times spoken of what is wholesome and unwholesome; at other times he has spoken of it as the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness; sometimes he has spoken of it as the twelve bases, sometimes as the spiritual friend, sometimes as the twelve links of dependent origination, sometimes as sentient beings, sometimes as right view and wrong view, sometimes as the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and sometimes as the two truths. Now the Tathāgata says that all dharmas constitute the pure brahma-faring. What, then, are these "all dharmas"?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is the treasury of all wholesome dharmas.
Just as the great ocean is a repository for all manner of jewels, so too is this Nirvāṇa Sūtra; it is the secret treasury of the meaning of all words and phrases.
"Good son!
Just as Mount Sumeru is the root of all medicinal herbs, so too is this sutra; it is the very root of the bodhisattva precepts.
Good son!"
Just as space is the dwelling place for all things, so too is this sutra the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas. Good son!
