Just as a fierce wind cannot be bound, so too is this sutra; it cannot be bound by any afflictions or unwholesome dharmas. All practices of the bodhisattvas are likewise thus.
Good son! For example, just as there is nothing that can destroy a diamond, so too is this sutra; even though there may be those who are heretical, evil, and perverse, they cannot destroy it.
"Good son!
Just as there is no one who can count the sands of the Ganges River, so too it is with the meaning of this sutra; there is no one who can count it.
Good son!"
This sutra serves as a Dharma-banner for all bodhisattvas, like the banner of Śakra.
Good son! This sutra is the caravan leader who leads toward the city of Nirvāṇa, just as a great guide leads merchants toward the great ocean.
"Good son!
This sutra can serve as the light of the Dharma for all bodhisattvas, just as the sun and moon in the world are able to dispel all darkness.
Good son!"

This sutra can serve as a great and excellent medicine for sentient beings suffering from illness, just as the subtle and wondrous King of Medicines on Mount Gandhamādana can cure all diseases. Good son!
This sutra can serve as a staff for icchantikas, just as a weak person relies on it to rise up. Good son!
This sutra can serve as a bridge for all evil people, just as a worldly bridge enables everyone to cross over.

Good son! This sutra can provide cool shade for those who wander through the twenty-five states of existence and encounter the heat of afflictions, just as an umbrella in the world shields one from the scorching heat.
"Good son!
This sutra is the Great King of Fearlessness; it can destroy all afflictions and evil Māras, just as the lion king subdues all other beasts."
Good son! This sutra is a great master of divine spells, capable of destroying all demons of affliction, just as a worldly spell-master can expel malevolent spirits.
Good son! This sutra is the unsurpassed frost and hail, capable of destroying all karmic retributions of birth and death, just as worldly hail and rain destroy all fruits and crops.
Good son! This sutra serves as a great and excellent medicine for those whose eyes of precept have been impaired, just as the worldly añjana medicine effectively cures eye pain.
Good son! This sutra can sustain all wholesome dharmas, just as the earth of the world sustains all things. Good son!
This sutra is the bright mirror for sentient beings who violate the precepts, just as a worldly bright mirror reveals all forms and images.
O son of good family!
This sutra can serve as clothing for those who lack shame and remorse, just as worldly garments conceal the physical body.
"Good son! This sutra can provide great wealth and treasure for those who are poor in wholesome dharmas, just as the goddess Guṇakārandavatī benefits the destitute. Good son!"
This sutra can act as nectar for sentient beings who thirst for the Dharma, just as water of eight virtues satisfies those who are parched.
Good son! This sutra can serve as a Dharma-couch for those afflicted by afflictions, just as worldly people encounter a couch of peace and security.
"Good son!

This sutra can serve as a jeweled necklace, incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, and burning incense for bodhisattvas from the first stage up to those in the tenth dwelling. It is a vehicle that fulfills the pure lineage, surpassing all six pāramitās, and is a place of sublime bliss like the pārijātaka tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."

“Good son! This sutra is the sharp axe of adamantine wisdom that can fell all the great trees of affliction; it is the keen blade that can sever habitual tendencies; it is the courageous warrior that can crush the enmity of Māra; it is the fire of wisdom that burns the fuel of afflictions; it is the treasury of causes and conditions from which pratyekabuddhas emerge; it is the treasury of hearing from which śrāvakas are born; it is the eye of all devas; it is the right path for all humans; it is the place of refuge for all animals; it is the place of liberation for hungry ghosts; it is the unsurpassed sovereign for those in the hells; it is the unsurpassed vessel for all sentient beings of the ten directions; and it is the father and mother of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions.”
"Good son! For this reason, this sutra encompasses all dharmas.
As I have previously stated, although this sutra encompasses all dharmas, I say that the brahma-faring consists precisely of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
"Good son!

If one is apart from these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one will ultimately be unable to attain the correct fruit of a śrāvaka, up to and including the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; nor will one perceive the Buddha-nature or the fruit of the Buddha-nature. For this reason, the holy life (brahmacarya) is itself the thirty-seven factors."
Why is this? The nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is non-perverted, and thus they can destroy perversion;
their nature is not false views, and thus they can destroy false views.
“His nature is not fear, yet he is able to destroy fear;
his nature is pure conduct, yet he is able to cause sentient beings to ultimately practice the pure Brahma-faring.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since even impure dharmas can serve as causes for pure dharmas, why does the Tathāgata not declare that impure dharmas constitute the pure brahmacarya?”
“Good son! All that is with outflows (sāsrava) is inverted; therefore, that which has outflows cannot be called pure brahmacarya.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the ‘Dharma Supreme in the World’ with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! This is with outflows (sāsrava).
“World-Honored One!”
“Although it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), its nature is not inverted; why, then, is it not called pure conduct (*brahmacarya*)?

“Good son! Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is the cause of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it resembles the outflow-free; because it tends toward the outflow-free, it is not called inverted.”

Good son! The pure brahmacarya begins with the continuous succession of the resolve for awakening (bodhicitta) up until its ultimate consummation; however, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) consists of only a single moment of thought. Therefore, it cannot be designated as pure brahmacarya.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The five consciousnesses of sentient beings are also with outflows (*sāsrava*), yet they are not inverted, nor are they of a single thought-moment; for what reason are they not called pure brahma-conduct?”

“Good son! Although the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are not of a single moment, they are nevertheless outflowing (sāsrava) and inverted; because they increase all outflows, they are called ‘outflowing.’”
The substance is not real; it is inverted because of clinging to perceptions.
Why is it said that the substance is not real and that one is inverted by clinging to perceptions?
It is to perceive the idea of male or female where there is neither male nor female, and so on, even regarding houses, vehicles, jars, and clothing—it is likewise thus; this is called inversion.
"Good son! The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are by nature free from inversion; therefore, they are called the pure brahmacarya. Good son!"

If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, knows their roots, knows their causes, knows their inclusion, knows their increase, knows their masters, knows their guides, knows their excellence, knows their reality, and knows their ultimate consummation—such a bodhisattva may be called one whose pure conduct is purified.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘knowing the faculties’ up to ‘knowing the ultimate’?”
The Buddha said:
"Good man! Excellent, excellent!"
A bodhisattva raises a question for two reasons:
first, for their own knowledge; second, so that others may know.
You have already known this, yet you have requested an explanation of this matter for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings who do not yet understand. For this reason, I now praise you once again.
Excellent, excellent! Son of good family! For the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, desire is the root;

their cause is called contact with clarity (*vidyā-sparśa*); their gathering is called feeling (*vedanā*); their increase is called wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā*); their presiding factor is called mindfulness (*smṛti*); their guidance is called concentration (*samādhi*); their excellence is called wisdom (*prajñā*); their reality is called liberation (*vimukti*); and their ultimate consummation is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Good son!
A wholesome desire is the initial arousal of the mind toward enlightenment and even the very root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, I say that desire is the root."
"Noble son!
As it is said in the world, all suffering and affliction have craving as their root;
all maladies and ailments have undigested food as their basis."
"All matters of litigation have contention as their root;
all evil matters have falsehood as their root.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Previously, in this sutra, the Tathāgata taught that all wholesome dharmas have heedfulness as their root; yet now you speak of desire. What is the meaning of this?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If one speaks of the cause of arising, it is wholesome desire."
If one speaks of the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), it is heedfulness (*apramāda*).
As it is said in the world, for all fruits, the seed is their cause.
Or again, as some say, the seed is the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) and the earth is the revealing cause; the meaning here is likewise.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
In other sūtras, the Tathāgata previously stated that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the root of Buddhahood; what is the meaning of this?”
“Good son! The Tathāgata has previously taught that when sentient beings first come to know the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the Buddha is their root.
If they personally realize them for themselves, desire is the root.”
“World-Honored One!
Why is luminous contact called the cause? “Good son!
The Tathāgata sometimes explains clarity as wisdom and sometimes explains it as faith.
Good son! Because of the condition of faith, one draws near to virtuous friends; this is called contact.
To hear the true Dharma through the condition of drawing near to it is called contact (*sparśa*).
To purify body, speech, and mind by virtue of hearing the true Dharma is called contact.
Due to the purification of the three types of action, one attains right livelihood; this is called contact.
Due to right livelihood, one attains the precepts of pure faculties;
due to the precepts of pure faculties, one delights in secluded places.
Because of delighting in tranquility, one is able to engage in skillful reflection;
because of skillful reflection, one attains dwelling in accordance with the Dharma;
because of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma, one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which can destroy immeasurable evil afflictions—this is called contact.
"Good son!
'Feeling' (vedanā) is named 'appropriation. When sentient beings experience feeling, they are able to perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds; therefore, feeling is called appropriation. Good son!"

Because of the condition of sensation (*vedanā*), various afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are able to destroy them. Therefore, sensation is taken as the "appropriation" (*upādāna*).
Because of skillful reflection (*yoniso-manasikāra*), one is able to destroy the afflictions; for this reason, it is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
Why is this? Because they are diligently cultivated.

Having attained these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), if one contemplates them so as to destroy all evil afflictions (*kleśa*), it must depend upon focused mindfulness (*smṛti*). Therefore, mindfulness is taken as the primary factor.

Just as all four divisions of the worldly army follow the will of their commander-in-chief, so too it is with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they all follow the master that is mindfulness. Good son!

Once one has entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, concentration is taken as the guide.
Among these thirty-seven factors that discern the characteristics of phenomena, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the most supreme; therefore, wisdom is taken as the preeminent factor.

Having thus known the afflictions through wisdom, the afflictions are extinguished by the power of that wisdom, just as in the world four types of troops destroy an enemy, or as one or two brave and skillful warriors may do so.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are likewise thus: by the power of wisdom, they are able to destroy the afflictions; therefore, wisdom is supreme. Good son!
Although one may obtain the four dhyānas, supernatural powers, and peace and bliss through the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors, these are not called "real."
When one destroys the afflictions and realizes liberation, it is then called "real.

Although these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment involve the arousal of the mind and the cultivation of the path, and though one may thereby attain worldly happiness, supramundane happiness, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, and liberation, they still cannot be called "ultimate."
If one can sever the practices associated with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is called nirvāṇa; therefore, I say that the ultimate is precisely Great Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A mind of wholesome affection is itself desire (*chanda*).
Because one approaches a virtuous friend due to that wholesome affection, it is called contact (*sparśa*); this is what is meant by 'cause.'
Because one draws near to virtuous friends, it is called "receiving," which is termed "appropriation.
Because one is able to contemplate skillfully by drawing near to virtuous friends, it is called "increasing.
Because these four factors can cause the Path to grow—namely, aspiration, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—this is termed "predominant mastery."

Based on these three dharmas, one attains two kinds of liberation: because craving is severed, the mind attains liberation; because ignorance is severed, wisdom attains liberation. This is called the truth.
These eight dharmas ultimately result in the fruit, which is called nirvāṇa; therefore, they are termed "ultimate.

Furthermore, son of good family, "desire" refers to the arousal of the mind to leave home, and "contact" refers to the rite of the fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman); these are called the causes.
"Comprehending" refers to receiving two kinds of precepts:
first, the Prātimokṣa precepts; second, the precepts for purifying the faculties. This is called "receiving," and this is called "comprehending."
"Augmentation" refers to the cultivation of the four dhyānas.
"Mastery" refers to the fruits of srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin.
"Guidance" refers to the fruit of anāgāmin.
"Victory" refers to the fruit of arhatship;
"reality" refers to the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood;
and "ultimate" refers to the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, good son! 'Desire' is called consciousness;

'contact' is called the six sense bases; 'gathering' is called feeling; 'increase' is called ignorance; 'lord' is called name-and-form; 'guide' is called craving; 'superior' is called grasping; 'reality' is called becoming; and 'ultimate' is called birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these three dharmas—root, cause, and condition—how do they differ?”

“Good son! That which is called the ‘root’ is the initial arousal [of the thought of enlightenment]; the ‘cause’ is the uninterrupted continuity of its semblance; and the ‘increase’ is the ability to produce its semblance after having extinguished that semblance.”
Furthermore, good son!
The faculty is itself the action; the cause is itself the fruit; and the increase is itself the utility. Good son!
In future ages, although there is a retribution, because it has not yet been experienced, it is called a cause.
When it is experienced, it is called an increase.
Furthermore, good son!
The faculty (*indriya*) is seeking; attainment (*lābha*) is the cause (*hetu*); and function (*vṛtti*) is increase (*vṛddhi*). Good son!
In this sutra, the faculty is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the cause is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); and increase is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Furthermore, good son!
The faculties (indriya) are the direct cause; the cause is itself the expedient cause. From these two causes, one obtains retribution, which is called "growth."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, that which is ultimate is nirvāṇa; how, then, can such nirvāṇa be attained?”
“Good son! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās are able to cultivate the ten perceptions, you should know that such persons will be able to attain nirvāṇa.”
What are the ten? First is the perception of impermanence;

second is the perception of suffering; third is the perception of non-self; fourth is the perception of revulsion toward food; fifth is the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in; sixth is the perception of death; seventh is the perception of manifold faults and transgressions; eighth is the perception of detachment; ninth is the perception of cessation; and tenth is the perception of non-craving.
"Good son!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who cultivate these ten kinds of perceptions will ultimately and certainly attain nirvāṇa. They do not follow the minds of others, but are able to discern for themselves what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. This is called truly fulfilling the meaning of the term 'bhikṣu,' and even fulfilling the meaning of the term 'upāsikā.'"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by bodhisattvas, and even up to laywomen, cultivating the perception of impermanence?”
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who have newly resolved their minds; second, those who have already practiced the path.”
The perception of impermanence is likewise of two kinds:
first, coarse; second, subtle.
When a beginner bodhisattva contemplates the perception of impermanence, they reflect as follows:
"There are generally two kinds of things in the world:
first, internal; second, external.

Such internal things are impermanent and subject to change. I observe that when one is born, young, old, in the prime of life, aging, or at the time of death—each of these stages is distinct from the others. Therefore, one should know that internal things are impermanent."
Again, he thought:
"I see sentient beings who are perhaps plump and fresh, endowed with physical beauty and strength, moving about and pausing with ease and without hindrance."
In some instances, they see the suffering of illness, with physical strength ruined and wasted, countenances emaciated and impaired, lacking all autonomy.
In other instances, they see wealth and riches, with storehouses overflowing.
In some instances, he sees those who are impoverished and destitute in every undertaking;
in others, he sees those who have accomplished immeasurable merit;
and in yet others, he sees those who are fully possessed of immeasurable unwholesome dharmas.
Therefore, one knows with certainty that internal phenomena are impermanent.

Furthermore, observing external phenomena, one sees that at the time of the seed, the sprout, the stalk, the leaf, the flower, and the fruit, each of these stages is distinct from the others. Thus, external phenomena may be complete or incomplete; for this reason, one should know that all external things are certainly impermanent.
Having thus observed that the phenomena of the Dharma are impermanent, he further observes the Dharma as heard:

"I have heard that the devas possess and are fully endowed with supreme, wondrous bliss and sovereign supernormal powers, yet they too exhibit the five signs of decay; therefore, one should know that these are likewise impermanent."

Furthermore, I have heard that at the beginning of the kalpa, there were sentient beings who each possessed supreme and wondrous merit; their bodies were self-illuminating without depending on the sun or moon, yet through the power of impermanence, their radiance was extinguished and their merit diminished.

Furthermore, I have heard that in the past there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King who ruled over the four continents, possessed the seven treasures, and attained great sovereignty, yet he could not escape the mark of impermanence.

He further contemplates the great earth: in former times, it provided a dwelling place for immeasurable sentient beings, with not even a space the size of a chariot wheel left vacant; it was fully endowed with all manner of wondrous medicinal herbs, and its groves, trees, and fruits flourished luxuriantly. Yet, due to the meager merit of sentient beings, this great earth has lost its power, and the things produced from it have consequently become depleted and exhausted.
Therefore, one should know that all internal and external phenomena are impermanent; this is what is called coarse impermanence.
Having observed the coarse, one next observes the subtle.
What is meant by "subtle"?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all internal and external things, down to even a minute particle, and perceives that they are already impermanent in the future.
Why is this? Because it is fully endowed with and achieves the characteristic of disintegration.
If future form were not impermanent, one could not say that form possesses the distinctions of its ten temporal stages.
What are the ten stages? First, the stage of the membrane;

second, the stage of the bubble; third, the stage of the vesicle; fourth, the stage of the flesh-mass; fifth, the stage of the limbs; sixth, the stage of the infant; seventh, the stage of the child; eighth, the stage of youth; ninth, the stage of full maturity; tenth, the stage of old age and decay.

The Bodhisattva contemplates that if the membrane were not impermanent, it should not progress through the stages up to the bubble and even to full maturity; for that which is not impermanent would never reach old age.
If these various stages did not perish moment by moment, they would never gradually grow; rather, they should have grown to full completion all at once.
Since this is not the case, one should know that there is certainly a subtle impermanence occurring in every moment.
Furthermore, one sees another person whose faculties are complete and whose complexion is radiant, yet later sees them become withered and emaciated.
One then reflects: "This person certainly possesses moment-to-moment impermanence."
Furthermore, one contemplates the four great elements and the four modes of deportment.
One further contemplates the two causes of suffering within and without, namely hunger and thirst, and cold and heat.
One further contemplates these four: if they were not subject to moment-to-moment subtle impermanence, these four types of suffering could not be spoken of.
If there is a bodhisattva who can form such a thought, this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of subtle impermanence.
It is the same for internal and external forms and mental phenomena. Why is this?
Because of the activity of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

When the six sense bases are active, one may give rise to a mind of joy, or a mind of anger, or a mind of attachment, or a mind of mindfulness; these arise successively in different ways and never remain of a single kind. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena, whether material (*rūpa*) or non-material (*arūpa*), are entirely impermanent.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva, within a single thought-moment, can perceive that all phenomena arise and perish and are impermanent, this is called a bodhisattva possessing the perception of impermanence."
"Good son!
Once the wise person has cultivated the perception of impermanence, they distance themselves from the pride of permanence, the inversion of permanence, and the inversion of perception.
Next, they cultivate the perception of suffering."
For what reason and by what conditions does such suffering exist?

One deeply understands that this suffering is caused by impermanence (*anitya*). Because of impermanence, one undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death; due to the conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is termed "impermanence. Because of the condition of impermanence, one undergoes internal and external sufferings—hunger, thirst, cold, heat, flogging, and verbal abuse—and all such sufferings are caused by impermanence.
Furthermore, the wise person deeply contemplates this body as a vessel of impermanence; since this vessel is suffering, the phenomena contained within it are likewise suffering.

Good son! The wise person further contemplates that arising itself is suffering and cessation itself is suffering; because there is the arising and cessation of suffering, it is impermanent, and is neither self nor belonging to a self.
"One cultivates the perception of non-self.
Furthermore, the wise observe that suffering is impermanent and impermanence is suffering; if suffering is impermanent, how could the wise say there is a self?"
Suffering is not the self, and impermanence is likewise so.
Thus, the five aggregates are also suffering and impermanent; how can sentient beings say that there is a self?

Furthermore, when observing all phenomena, they consist of various combinations; all phenomena do not arise from a single combination, nor is a single phenomenon the result of all combinations. All combinations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), lack a single nature, lack a distinct nature, lack the nature of a substance, and lack sovereignty. If all phenomena possess such characteristics as these, how could a wise person say that there is a self?

Again, he reflects: "Among all phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon that can act as an agent; if a single phenomenon cannot act as an agent, then even the conjunction of many phenomena cannot act as an agent."
All phenomena (dharmas) are ultimately incapable of arising or ceasing in isolation; they cease through conjunction and arise through conjunction.
Once these phenomena have arisen, sentient beings, due to their inverted perceptions, claim that this is "conjunction."
Arising from a combination of conditions, the notion of a "sentient being" is a perversion of perception and lacks reality; how, then, could there be a real self?
Therefore, the wise contemplate non-self.
Furthermore, one should carefully observe for what causes and conditions sentient beings speak of a "self.
If this self were to exist, it would have to be either one or many.
If the self were one, how could there be Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, humans, devas, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, the small and the great, or the old and the young?
Therefore, we know that the self is not a single entity.
If the self were manifold, why would it be said that the self of sentient beings is one, all-pervading, and without limit?
Whether singular or plural, both are devoid of self.
Once the wise person has thus contemplated the absence of self, they next contemplate the perception of revulsion toward food.

He formed this thought: "If all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, how can one, for the sake of food, give rise to the three kinds of evil karma of body, speech, and mind?"

If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of craving food, give rise to the three kinds of unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, the wealth they acquire shall be shared by all, yet when they later experience the fruits of suffering, there will be no one to share them.
"Good son!
The wise person further contemplates that all sentient beings undergo suffering of body and mind for the sake of food and drink.
If food is obtained only through manifold sufferings, how could I possibly give rise to craving and attachment toward such food?"
Therefore, one should not give rise to a mind of craving toward food.

Furthermore, the wise person should contemplate: "It is because of food and drink that the body grows. Now that I have left the household life to receive the precepts and cultivate the Way, my purpose is to relinquish this body;
if I now crave this food, how can I ever succeed in relinquishing it?"

Having observed in this way, although he still partakes of food, it is as if he were eating the flesh of his own child in a desolate wilderness; his mind feels revulsion, finding no pleasure or sweetness in it at all.

He deeply contemplates that there are such faults in the nutriment of physical morsels (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), and next contemplates the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*), which is like a cow being flayed and devoured by immeasurable worms.
Next, contemplate the food of volition as being like a great mass of fire;
the food of consciousness is like three hundred spears. Good son!
When the wise person has contemplated the four kinds of nutriment in this way, they will ultimately never give rise to thoughts of craving or delight toward food.
If craving should still arise, they ought to contemplate its impurity. Why is this?
In order to abandon craving for food,
one skillfully cultivates the perception of impurity regarding all food, making it correspond to its various impure aspects.
Having contemplated in this way, whether one receives excellent food or poor food, one accepts it as if applying medicine to a festering wound, never giving rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
“Good son!
If a wise person can contemplate in this way, it is called accomplishing the perception of revulsion toward food.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
When a wise person contemplates food and forms the perception of it as impure,
is this a contemplation of reality or a contemplation based on conceptual understanding?”
"If it were a true contemplation, the food being contemplated would not truly be impure.
If it were a conceptual understanding, how could such a dharma be called a 'wholesome perception'?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Such a perception is both a true contemplation and a false understanding.
It is called 'true' because it can destroy the craving for food; it is called 'false understanding' because one does not see worms where there are no worms."
"Good son!
All that is with outflows is called 'empty,' yet it can also attain the real.
Good son!"
If there is a bhikṣu who resolves to go for alms, he pre-emptively forms this thought:
"I shall go for alms; may I obtain what is excellent and not what is coarse or poor; may I certainly obtain much and not what is meager; and may I obtain it quickly and not be delayed."

"A bhikṣu who acts in this way is not said to have attained the perception of revulsion toward food; the wholesome dharmas he cultivates will decline day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will gradually increase."
"Good son!
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to go on almsround, he should first make this aspiration:

'May all those who beg for food be fully satisfied; may those who give the food obtain immeasurable merit; and if I receive food, I shall use it to heal my poisonous body, cultivate wholesome dharmas, and bring benefit to the donor.'"
When one makes such a vow, the wholesome dharmas one cultivates will increase day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will gradually be extinguished. Good son!
If there is a bhikṣu who can practice in this way, you should know that this person does not eat in vain the offerings of faith from the kingdom.
“Good son! A wise person, endowed with these four perceptions, is able to cultivate the perception that the world is not to be relished, thinking thus:
‘There is no place in all the worlds where birth, aging, sickness, and death do not exist; yet there is no place where this body of mine has not been born.’”
If there were not a single place within this world where one could escape birth, old age, sickness, and death, how could I take pleasure in the world?
In all the worlds, there is no progress that does not entail decline; therefore, the world is certainly impermanent. If it is impermanent, why would a wise person delight in the world?

Each and every sentient being wanders through all worlds, fully experiencing both suffering and pleasure; though they may even attain the body of a Brahmā or reach as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, at the end of their lives they fall back again into the three evil realms.

Although they may take the form of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, at the end of their lives they are reborn in the animal realm, becoming lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, elephants, horses, oxen, or donkeys.

"Next, one contemplates the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King: though he rules over the four continents with noble status and sovereign power, when his merit is exhausted, he falls into poverty and destitution, lacking even the basic provisions of food and clothing.
Having deeply contemplated such matters, the wise person conceives the perception that the world is not to be relished.

Furthermore, the wise person observes that there are worldly phenomena—namely, houses, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, necklaces, various musical performances, wealth, and treasures—all of which are intended for the sake of leaving suffering behind;
yet these very things are themselves suffering in essence. How, then, can one seek to leave suffering by means of what is itself suffering?
"Good son!
When the wise have observed in this manner, they do not give rise to attachment or the perception of pleasure toward worldly things.
Good son!"

For example, suppose there is a person afflicted with a grave illness; although there may be various kinds of music, performers, fragrant flowers, and necklaces of pearls, they would ultimately feel no greed, attachment, or delight for them.
The wise one, having observed this, likewise reflects thus: "Good son!

The wise one deeply contemplates all worlds as not being places of refuge, not being places of liberation, not being places of tranquility, not being places of endearment, not being the further shore, and not being dharmas that are permanent, blissful, self, or pure. If I were to crave and delight in such a world, how could I ever become free from these dharmas?"
It is like a person who, disliking to dwell in darkness, seeks light, yet returns once more to the dark. Darkness is the mundane world; light is the supramundane.

If I delight in the mundane, I increase the darkness and distance myself from the light. Darkness is ignorance (*avidyā*); light is the clarity of wisdom (*jñāna*). The cause of this clarity of wisdom is precisely the perception of the world as something not to be delighted in.
Although all fetters of craving are indeed bonds, I now crave the light of wisdom and do not crave the world.
Having deeply contemplated such phenomena, the wise one fully possesses the perception that the world is not to be relished.
“Good son! A person of wisdom, having already cultivated the perception of the world’s lack of delight, next cultivates the contemplation of death.
This life-span is constantly surrounded by immeasurable enemies; it diminishes with every thought-moment and never increases.”

It is like a mountain torrent that cannot remain still; it is like the morning dew whose duration is brief; it is like a prisoner being led to the marketplace, with every step bringing him closer to death; it is like leading an ox or a sheep to the slaughterhouse.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
How does the wise person contemplate moment-to-moment extinction?”
“Good son! It is like four men, all skilled in the art of archery, who gather in one place and each shoot in a different direction, thinking together:
‘Our four arrows shall be released simultaneously and fall at the same time.’”
Furthermore, there was another person who thought to himself:
"I am able to catch these four arrows with my hands all at once before they have fallen. Good son!
"Could such a person be said to be ill?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva replied,
"Indeed he could."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Good son!”

The ghosts who travel on the earth are faster than this person; the ghosts who fly are faster than those who travel on the earth; the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings are faster than those who fly; the divine deities of the sun and moon are faster than the Four Heavenly Kings; the gods of the Heaven of Firm Speed are faster than the sun and moon; and the lifespans of sentient beings pass even more swiftly than the Heaven of Firm Speed.
"Good son!
In a single breath and a single blink, the life-span of sentient beings undergoes four hundred births and deaths.
If a wise person can contemplate life in this way, it is called being able to observe the extinction of every thought-moment."
"Good son!
The wise person contemplates that life is bound to the King of Death; if I can separate myself from such a King of Death, then I shall attain the permanent severance of impermanent life."

Furthermore, the wise observe this life-span as being like a great tree standing on the edge of a steep riverbank; it is like a person who has committed a heinous crime and faces execution with no one to pity him; it is like a lion king when he is severely famished; it is like a venomous snake when it inhales a great wind; it is like a thirsty horse guarding its water; and it is like a great malevolent ghost when his rage erupts—in this same way, the King of Death treats all living beings.
“Good son! If a wise person can practice contemplation in this manner, it is called the cultivation of the perception of death. Good son!”

The wise person further contemplates: "Even if I were to obtain a lifespan of only seven days and seven nights after leaving the household life, I would diligently cultivate the Path therein, uphold the prohibitive precepts, preach the Dharma, and transform sentient beings for their benefit. This is called the wise person’s cultivation of the perception of death.

Furthermore, one may consider seven days and seven nights as long; yet if one can obtain six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, one day, a single session, or even the duration of a single exhalation and inhalation, I shall therein diligently cultivate the Way, uphold the prohibitive precepts, preach the Dharma to transform others, and benefit sentient beings. This is called the wise person’s skillful cultivation of the perception of death.
The wise person who is endowed with the six aforementioned perceptions possesses the causes for seven perceptions.

What are these seven? First, the perception of constant cultivation; second, the perception of joyful cultivation; third, the perception of non-anger; fourth, the perception of non-envy; fifth, the perception of virtuous aspiration; sixth, the perception of non-arrogance; and seventh, the perception of mastery over samādhi.
“Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the seven perceptions, he is called a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, one who is tranquil, one who is pure, one who is liberated, a wise one, one of right view, one who has reached the other shore, a great king of physicians, a great caravan leader, and one who well understands the secrets of the Tathāgata. He also knows the seven kinds of speech of all Buddhas; he is called one of right view and knowledge, who severs the net of doubt arising from the seven kinds of speech.”
"Good son!

If a person is fully endowed with the six perceptions mentioned above, you should know that this person is able to censure the triple world, remain far removed from the triple world, extinguish the triple world, and does not give rise to attachment within the triple world; this is called the wise one being fully endowed with the ten perceptions."
"If there is a bhikṣu who possesses these ten perceptions, he shall immediately be deemed to have attained the true marks of a śramaṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa praised the Buddha before him with a verse:
"Great King of Physicians, you who have compassion for the world; Both your body and your wisdom are utterly tranquil."
Within the dharma of non-self, there is a true self; therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
There is no distinction between the initial resolve and the ultimate goal; of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
To seek to save others before one has saved oneself—to this initial resolve, I pay homage.
Having first resolved [to attain enlightenment], one becomes a teacher of humans and devas, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
such a resolve transcends the three realms, and for this reason it is called the most unsurpassed.
The Savior of the World must be entreated before he is attained; the Tathāgata acts as teacher without being requested.
The Buddha follows the world like a calf; therefore, he is named the Great Compassionate Ox.
The Tathāgata’s merits fill the ten directions; those of inferior station and lacking wisdom cannot praise them.
Now I praise his compassionate heart, as an offering for the two types of karma of body and speech.
The world constantly delights in its own benefit, yet the Tathāgata never acts for such ends;
he is able to sever the worldly karmic retributions of sentient beings—therefore, I pay homage to him who benefits both self and others.
In the world, one pursues kin and bestows benefits with greater thickness; the Tathāgata benefits all without distinction between enemy and kin.
The Buddha does not possess such characteristics as worldly people do; therefore, his mind is equal and without duality.
The world speaks of karma as being distinct from its action; the Tathāgata, however, acts without deviation from his teaching.
Having practiced all that is required to sever all conditioned formations, he is therefore named the Tathāgata.
Having already fully understood the faults of afflictions, he manifests dwelling among them for the sake of sentient beings;
though he has long attained liberation from the world, he delights in remaining within birth and death out of his compassion.
Though manifesting in celestial and human forms, compassion follows [beings] like a calf;
the Tathāgata is the mother of sentient beings, and loving-kindness is the little calf.
Personally undergoing manifold sufferings while mindful of sentient beings, When contemplating them with compassion, my mind never regrets or sinks;
With a surging heart of pity, I am unaware of my own pain— Therefore, I prostrate to the one who uproots suffering.
Although the Tathāgata has performed immeasurable merit, his actions of body, speech, and mind are ever pure;
he always acts for the sake of sentient beings and not for himself. Therefore, I pay homage to his pure karma.
The Tathāgata experiences suffering yet does not perceive it as suffering;
seeing the suffering of sentient beings as his own, though he dwells in hell for the sake of beings, he gives rise to neither the thought of suffering nor a mind of regret.
The various sufferings experienced by all sentient beings are entirely the suffering of the Tathāgata alone;
having awakened to this, his mind becomes even more firm and steadfast, and thus he is able to diligently cultivate the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha possesses a great heart of compassion of a single flavor, And regards all sentient beings with pity as if they were his own children;
Yet sentient beings do not know that the Buddha can save them, And thus they slander the Tathāgata, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Although the world is possessed of manifold afflictions, And likewise contains immeasurable faults and evils,
The Buddha, from his very first resolve, was able to destroy All such fetters and transgressions.
Only the Buddhas can praise the Buddha; Aside from the Buddha, there is no one else who can offer praise.
I now praise him with but a single dharma: That he wanders through the world with a heart of loving-kindness.
The Tathāgata’s compassion is a great mass of Dharma; this compassion can also deliver sentient beings.
It is itself the unsurpassed, true liberation, and liberation is itself Great Nirvāṇa.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 38;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 39.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: Kauṇḍinya, Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya: “Form is impermanent;

by the cessation of this form, one attains the eternally abiding form of liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent; by the cessation of these consciousnesses, one attains the eternally abiding consciousness of liberation.”
Kauṇḍinya! Form is suffering;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the form of liberation and peace. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

Kauṇḍinya! Form is itself emptiness; by the cessation of form through emptiness, one attains liberation from form that is not empty. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Kauṇḍinya! Form is without self;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the true self-nature of form that is liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Kauṇḍinya! Form is impure;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the pure form of liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

Kauṇḍinya! Form is the characteristic of birth, old age, sickness, and death; by the cessation of this form, one attains liberation—the form that is not subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

Kauṇḍinya! Form is the cause of ignorance; when that cause is extinguished, one attains liberation from form which is not caused by ignorance. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

Kauṇḍinya! Even up to form, which is a cause of birth—when that cause of form is extinguished, one attains liberation from form as a cause of birth; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Kauṇḍinya! Form is the cause of the four perversions; by extinguishing form that is subject to perversion, one attains liberation from form that is not the cause of the four perversions. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

Kauṇḍinya! Form (*rūpa*) is the cause of immeasurable unwholesome dharmas, namely: the bodies of men and women and so forth; craving for food, craving for sensual desire; greed, hatred, envy, and malicious intent; stinginess; the four nutriments—edible food, consciousness-food, volition-food, and contact-food; birth from eggs, birth from wombs, birth from moisture, and spontaneous birth; and the five desires and the five hindrances. All such dharmas as these arise because of form. By the cessation of form, one attains liberation and is no longer subject to such immeasurable unwholesome forms. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
Kauṇḍinya! Form itself is bondage;
by extinguishing the bondage of form, one attains the liberation of form that is free from bondage. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Kauṇḍinya! Form itself is a flux;
by the cessation of the fluxing form, one attains liberation through non-fluxing form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Kauṇḍinya! Form is not the refuge;
by the cessation of this form, one obtains the refuge of form that is liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Kauṇḍinya! Form is a festering sore;
by the cessation of this form, one attains liberation—the state of form free from sores. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
Kauṇḍinya! Form is not quiescent;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the quiescent form of nirvāṇa. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Kauṇḍinya! If there is anyone who can know in this way, they are called a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa; they are fully endowed with the dharmas of a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa.
Kauṇḍinya! Apart from the Buddha-dharma, there are no śramaṇas and no brāhmaṇas, nor is there any dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.

All those of external paths are false pretenders; they possess no genuine practice at all. Although they manifest outward appearances and claim that these two [categories] exist, in reality, such a thing is impossible.
Why is this? If the dharmas of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas did not exist, how could one say that there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
I constantly let out the lion’s roar within this great assembly; you, too, should likewise let out the lion’s roar within the great assembly.
At that time, there were immeasurable people among the non-Buddhists who, having heard these words, conceived thoughts of malice and anger:
"Gautama now says that within our assembly there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor is there the dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"How shall I employ extensive skillful means to say to Gautama: 'Among our assembly there are also śramaṇas and the dharma of śramaṇas; there are brahmins and the dharma of brahmins'?"
At that time, there was a brahmin among the assembly who proclaimed these words:
"O worthy ones!
The words of Gautama are no different from those of a madman."
How can one examine him?
This madman of the world may sing, dance, weep, laugh, revile, or praise; he cannot distinguish between those who are hostile and those who are kin.
The śramaṇa Gautama is also like this: sometimes he says that he was born into the family of King Śuddhodana, and sometimes he says he was not born;
sometimes he says that after being born he walked seven steps, and sometimes he says he did not walk;
sometimes he says that from childhood he practiced and studied worldly affairs, and sometimes he says that he is an omniscient person; or at times he [accepts] within the palace...
He sometimes delighted in having sons; at other times he felt weary of them, rebuking and despising them. At times he personally practiced asceticism for six years;
at other times he criticized the ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists.
Sometimes he claimed to have received teachings not heard before from Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma; at other times he said they possessed no knowledge at all. At times...
At times he says that he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* beneath the Bodhi tree;
at other times he says that he did not go to the tree and achieved nothing; at other times he says that this present body of mine is itself nirvāṇa;
or he says that the extinction of the body is nirvāṇa.
"What Gautama has said is no different from the ravings of a madman;
why then do you grieve over this? The brahmins then replied:
"O Great Being!"
How could we not be filled with sorrow now?

Since the śramaṇa Gautama first left the household life, he has preached the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. When my disciples hear this, they give rise to terror, saying: "How can sentient beings be impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure?"
They did not accept his words.

Now, Gautama has come again to this Śāla grove and preached to the great assembly the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; having heard these words, all my disciples have abandoned me to accept Gautama’s teaching, and for this reason, they have given rise to great sorrow and suffering.
At that time, there was another brahmin who spoke these words:
"O virtuous ones!
Listen attentively, listen attentively."
"It is a falsehood, not the truth, that the śramaṇa Gautama is said to cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
If he truly possessed loving-kindness and compassion, why would he instruct my disciples to receive his own dharma?"
The fruit of compassion consists in conforming to the wishes of others; now that it contradicts my own wish, how can you say it exists?
Furthermore, if anyone says that the śramaṇa Gautama is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, that too is false.
If you say that Gautama has few desires and is content, why does he now seize our profits?
If you say that his lineage is of a noble clan, this too is false; for what reason?
"From time immemorial, we have neither seen nor heard of a great lion king harming a small mouse.
If Gautama is of noble lineage, why does he now trouble and harass us?"
If you say that Gautama possesses great power, this too is false.

Why? Because from time immemorial, neither have we seen nor heard of the King of the Garuḍas contending with a crow; if his strength is so great, for what reason would he then engage in battle with me?
If it is said that Gautama possesses the knowledge of others' minds, this too is false.
Why? If he possessed such knowledge, for what reason would he not know my mind?
"O virtuous ones!
In the past, I heard this matter from ancient sages: after a hundred years have passed, a demonic illusion shall appear in the world."
"He is indeed Gautama.
Such a deceptive deceiver will soon perish right here in this Śāla grove; you should not now be filled with grief and distress."
At that time, another Nirgrantha replied:
"Venerable sir!

I am now distressed and suffering not because of the lack of offerings for myself or my disciples, but because the world is mired in ignorance and darkness, lacking the eye of wisdom; they fail to distinguish between fields of merit and non-fields of merit, abandoning the wise Brahmins of ancient lineage to instead offer worship to the young—this is what grieves me."

The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great knowledge of incantations; by the power of these incantations, he can cause a single body to become infinite bodies, and cause infinite bodies to return to being a single body, or manifest his own body as the forms of men, women, oxen, sheep, elephants, and horses.
"I have the power to destroy such incantations; once the incantations of the Śramaṇa Gautama are destroyed, you shall all receive abundant offerings and enjoy peace and happiness."
At that time, there was another brahmin who spoke thus:
"O worthy ones!
The śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with and has perfected immeasurable merits; therefore, you should not contend with him."
The great assembly replied:
"Foolish man, how can you say that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great merit?
Seven days after his birth, his mother passed away; how can this be called a mark of merit?"
The brahmin said:
"That one does not become angry when reviled and does not retaliate when struck—know that this is the mark of great merit.

That his body is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and possesses immeasurable supernormal powers—for these reasons, you should know it to be the mark of merit."

His mind is free from arrogance; he is the first to offer greetings with a welcoming disposition, his speech is gentle and never coarse or harsh. Though both his age and vigor are at their peak, his mind is not impulsive or violent. Although the kingdom possesses great wealth, he feels no attachment to it; he renounces it to leave the household life as if discarding nasal mucus or saliva. For this reason, I say that the śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
The great assembly replied:
"Excellent, worthy one!
The śramaṇa Gautama truly possesses as you have described; he has accomplished immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations, and we shall not compete with him in these matters."

The śramaṇa Gautama is of a naturally gentle disposition and cannot endure ascetic practices; having been raised in the depths of the palace, he has no experience with external affairs and can only be addressed with soft words.
He knows nothing of the arts, scriptures, or debate; let us invite him to discuss in detail the essentials of the True Dharma.
"If he defeats me, I shall serve him;
if I defeat him, he shall serve me.
At that time, many immeasurable followers of external paths gathered together and went to King Ajātaśatru of Magadha.
When the King saw them, he asked:
"Virtuous ones, from where have you come?

Each of you practices the noble path; you are renunciants who have abandoned wealth and worldly affairs. Yet all the people of my kingdom provide for you together, looking upon you with reverence and never offending you. For what reason have you come here in such a large group?"

"Virtuous ones, each of you has received different teachings and different precepts; your renunciations are not the same, and each of you has likewise gone forth to practice the Way according to your own respective rules of training. For what reason and by what causes and conditions do you now unite with one mind and live in harmony, like fallen leaves driven together in a single place by a whirlwind?"
"For what reason have you come here?
I shall always protect those who have left the household life, even at the cost of my own body and life.
At that time, all the various followers of external paths spoke thus:
“Great King!
Listen attentively.

You, Great King, are now a great bridge of the Dharma, a great whetstone of the Dharma, and a great scale of the Dharma. You are the vessel for all merit, the true nature of all merit, the path of the True Dharma, and the fertile field for seeds. You are the foundation of all lands, the great mirror of all lands, the embodiment of all the devas, and the father and mother of all the people of the realm.”
"Great King!
The treasury of merits of all the world is none other than Your Majesty’s own body.
For what reason is it called the 'Treasury of Merits'?"

When the king adjudicates state affairs, he makes no distinction between enemies and kin; his mind is impartial, like earth, water, fire, and wind. For this reason, the king is called a treasury of merit.
"Great King!

Although the lifespan of sentient beings today is short, the merit of Your Majesty is like that of the long-lived and blissful kings of old, and is also like those of King Mūrdhaja, King Sudarśana, King Kṣāntivādin, King Nahuṣa, King Yayāti, King Śibi, and King Eka-cakra. Such kings were fully endowed with wholesome dharmas; Your Majesty now is likewise so."
"Great King!

Because of you, the king, the land is peaceful and prosperous, and the people are flourishing. For this reason, all those who have left the household life yearn for this country, diligently upholding the precepts and practicing the Right Path."
"Great King!

In my sūtras I have said that if a renunciant, wherever they dwell in a kingdom, maintains the precepts with diligence and zealously cultivates the Right Path, that king also shares in the merit of practicing virtue."
"Great King!
You have already brought all other thieves and robbers under control, so that those who have left the household life have no fear at all.
Now there remains only one great evildoer, the Śramaṇa Gautama; since Your Majesty has not yet investigated him, we are deeply afraid."

That person, relying on their own noble lineage and physical perfection, and further receiving abundant offerings as a result of past acts of giving, gives rise to great arrogance based on these various factors; or, they may give rise to arrogance through the mastery of incantations. Due to these causes and conditions, they are unable to practice asceticism and instead accept and keep fine, soft clothing and bedding.
Therefore, all the wicked people of the world have gathered at my place for the sake of gain and sustenance, acting as my attendants and unable to endure ascetic practices.

By the power of incantations, they have subdued Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others; now they have come to me and dwell within the Śāla grove, proclaiming that this body is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, thereby seducing my disciples.
"Great King!

Previously, Gautama taught that there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity; I was able to endure that. But now he proclaims permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which I truly cannot endure."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to debate with that Gautama.
The King replied immediately,
"O Great Beings!"
By whom have you now been instructed, such that your minds are deranged and unstable, like surging waves, like a whirling firebrand, or like a monkey leaping from tree to tree?
This matter is shameful; when wise people hear of it, they immediately feel compassion, but when fools hear of it, they immediately break into derision.
What you have said is not the mark of one who has left the household life.
If you suffer from diseases of wind or jaundice, I possess all the medicines capable of curing them;
as for diseases caused by spirits, my elder brother Jīvaka is skilled at removing them.
You now wish to scrape Mount Sumeru with your fingernails and teeth, and you wish to bite through a diamond with your mouth.
O Great Beings!
It is like a foolish person who, seeing the lion king sleeping during his hunger, wishes to awaken him.

It is as if a person were to place a finger in the mouth of a venomous snake, or as if one wished to touch with the hand a fire covered by ashes; you all are now just like this, O sons of good family!

It is like a wild fox making the roar of a lion; it is like a mosquito competing with a golden-winged garuḍa in a race for speed; it is like a rabbit crossing the ocean wishing to reach its bottom—you all are just like this now.
If you have seen one superior to Gautama in a dream, that dream is a delusion and is not to be trusted.
O Great Beings!
Your current resolve is like that of a moth throwing itself into a great mass of fire.
"Follow my words; there is no need for further speech.
Although you have praised me as being as impartial as a scale, do not let outsiders hear these words again.
At that time, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) spoke once more:
"Great King!
Has the illusory magic performed by the śramaṇa Gautama reached you,
such that it causes Your Majesty’s mind to harbor doubt and lack faith in these holy men?"
"O Great King!
You should not treat such a Mahāsattva with contempt.
O Great King!"
Who created these things—the waxing and waning of the moon, the salty taste of the great ocean, and Mount Meru?
Is it not we Brahmins who did so?
Great King!
Have you not heard that for twelve years during the time of the seer Ajita, the waters of the Ganges remained within his ears?
Great King!

I have heard that the seer Gautama has manifested great supernatural powers, such as transforming into the body of Śakra for twelve years, and causing that body of Śakra to take the form of a ram, with a thousand female organs appearing upon that body of Śakra?
Great King!
Have you not heard how the seer Kaṇva drank up the waters of the four oceans in a single day, causing the great earth to dry?
Great King!
Have you not heard how the seer Vasu created three eyes for Maheśvara?
Great King!
Have you not heard how the seer Ārāḍa transformed the city of Kapilavastu into a mound of earth?
"Great King!
Among the brahmins there are such powerful sages as these, who can be verified in the present.
Why, then, do you treat them with such contempt?"
The King said:
"O worthy ones!

If you wish to act because you do not yet have faith, the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is currently nearby in the Śāla grove. You may go there and question him as you please; the Tathāgata will also analyze matters for you and answer in accordance with your intentions."

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, together with his retinue of followers and various non-Buddhist sects, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed his acts of reverence, withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"These non-Buddhist practitioners wish to pose questions and challenges at their own convenience; we only pray that the Tathāgata will answer them as he sees fit.
The Buddha said, "Great King, cease for now; I myself know the proper time."
At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly named Jātiśrona who spoke these words:
"Gautama! Do you say that nirvāṇa is an eternal dharma?"
"It is so, it is so, Great Brahmin! The Brahmin said:
"Gautama! If you say that nirvāṇa is eternal, this meaning is not so. Why is that?"
The phenomena of the world arise from seeds to produce fruits in an uninterrupted succession, just as a jar is produced from clay or cloth is obtained from threads.
Gautama, you constantly say that by cultivating the perception of impermanence one attains nirvana; if the cause is impermanent, how can the fruit be permanent?

Furthermore, Gautama has said that liberation from sensual desire is itself Nirvāṇa; liberation from the desire for form and the desire for the formless is itself Nirvāṇa; and the extinction of ignorance and all other afflictions is itself Nirvāṇa.
From desire up to ignorance, all afflictions are impermanent; since they are impermanent, the nirvāṇa attained because of them should also be impermanent.
Furthermore, Gautama, you say that one is born in heaven because of causes, falls into hell because of causes, and attains liberation because of causes; therefore, all phenomena arise from causes.
If liberation is attained by means of causes, how can you say it is eternal?
Gautama, you also teach that form arises from conditions and is therefore impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so, and liberation is just like this.
If it were form, one should know it is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
If there were liberation apart from the five aggregates, one should know that liberation is identical to empty space.
If it were space, one could not say that it arises from causes and conditions. Why?
Because it is permanent, unitary, and omnipresent.
Gautama also says that whatever arises from causes is suffering.
If it is suffering, why do you further say that liberation is bliss?

Gautama also says that the impermanent is suffering, and suffering is non-self. If things are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, they are impure. Since all phenomena arising from causes are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, why do you further say that *nirvāṇa* is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?
If the Gautama says that things are both eternal and non-eternal, both suffering and happiness, both self and non-self, and both pure and impure—is this not, in such a case, a dualistic discourse?
I have also heard this teaching from wise men of former times: "If a Buddha appears in the world, his words are never dual.
Yet now, Gautama speaks two words; he says, "The Buddha is none other than my own self. What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Brāhmaṇa!
As you have spoken, I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
The brahmin said, “Excellent, Gautama!”
The Buddha said,
“Brahmin! Is your nature eternal?”
"Is this impermanent?
The brahmin replied,
"My nature is permanent."
“Brahmin! Is this nature capable of acting as the cause for all internal and external phenomena? “It is so.”
"Gautama! The Buddha said, "Brahmin!"
"How does it act as a cause?

"Gautama! From *prakṛti* arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One arises ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); from ego-consciousness arise the sixteen dharmas, namely: earth, water, fire, wind, space, and the five faculties of cognition (*pañca-buddhīndriyāṇi*):"
The five sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
the five organs of action—hand, foot, mouth, voice, and the two sexual organs; and the mind as the organ of equanimity: these constitute the sixteen factors.
From these five dharmas arise form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; these constitute twenty-one dharmas.
There are three fundamental types:
first, the defiled; second, the coarse; and third, the dark.
Attachment is called craving; coarseness is called aversion; and blackness is called ignorance.
Gautama! These twenty-five dharmas all arise from their own natures.
“Brahmin! Are these great dharmas permanent or impermanent? “Gautama!”
"In my teaching, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternal, whereas the great elements and all other phenomena are impermanent. "Brahmin!
Just as in your own doctrine, the cause is eternal while the fruit is impermanent."
"But in my Dharma, although the cause is impermanent, if the fruit were permanent, what fault would there be?
Brahmin! Do you have two kinds of causes in your own Dharma?"
He replied, "There is. The Buddha said:
"What is meant by 'existence'?
The Brahmin replied:
"The first is the cause of production; the second is the cause of manifestation."
The Buddha said:
"What is the productive cause?
What is the revealing cause?"
The brahmin said:
"The productive cause is like clay giving rise to a jar; the revealing cause is like a lamp illuminating an object.
The Buddha said:
"These two kinds of causes share the same nature as causes.
If they are one and the same, could it be that a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) is made into a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*), or that a revealing cause is made into a productive cause?"
"No, Gautama," he replied.
The Buddha said:

"If it were the case that the productive cause does not function as the revealing cause, and the revealing cause does not function as the productive cause, could one still say that these possess the characteristics of a cause?
The Brahmin replied,
"Even though they do not act as each other, they nonetheless possess the characteristics of a cause."
“Brahmin! Is that which is realized by the cause of realization identical to the realization itself? “No.”
"Gautama!
The Buddha said,
"Although my Dharma attains nirvāṇa through impermanence, it is not itself impermanent."
"O Brahmin! Because they are attained through the cause of realization, they are permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Because they are attained through the cause of birth, they are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure."
Therefore, although the Tathāgata speaks of two, these two statements are not dual; for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have "non-dual speech.
As you have said—that you have heard from the wise of former times that when a Buddha appears in the world there is no dual speech—this statement is excellent.
The teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are without discrepancy; therefore, it is said that the Buddha has no dual speech.
Why is there no discrepancy?
Because where there is existence, he speaks of existence in the same way, and where there is non-existence, he speaks of non-existence in the same way; thus, they are called a single meaning.
"Brahmin! Although the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks in two words, it is for the sake of clarifying one word.
How do these two words clarify that one word?"
"Just as the two terms 'eye' and 'form' give rise to the single term 'consciousness,' so it is likewise for the mind and mental phenomena.
The brahmin said, "Gautama!"
"You are well able to discern the meaning of such words, yet I do not yet understand how the two utterances you have produced clarify a single word.
At that time, the World-Honored One then proclaimed for him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: "Brahmin!"
"The Truth of Suffering is both two and one, and so on up to the Truth of the Path, which is also both two and one.
The Brahmin said,
"World-Honored One!"
"I have already understood," he said.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"How does one know this?
The brahmin said,
"World-Honored One!"
"Regarding the Truth of Suffering, all ordinary persons have two [aspects], while noble ones have one; this applies likewise up to the Truth of the Path.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"I have understood," the brahmin said.
"World-Honored One!"

Having now heard the Dharma, I have attained right view; I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. I pray only that you, out of great compassion, will grant me permission to go forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"You should shave off the hair and beard for this Jātiśroṇa and permit him to go forth."
At that time, Kauṇḍinya immediately accepted the Buddha’s command and shaved his hair.
As soon as he applied the razor, two things fell away:
first, the beard and hair; second, the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thereupon, while still seated, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin of the Vāsiṣṭha clan who spoke these words:
"Gautama, is the nirvāṇa you speak of permanent?"
"So it is, brahmin," [the Buddha replied]. Vāseṭṭha said:
"Does Gautama not teach that the absence of afflictions is nirvāṇa?"
"So it is, brahmin," [the Buddha replied]. Vāsiṣṭha said,
"Gautama!..."
There are four kinds of things in the world that are termed "non-existent":
first, phenomena that have not yet emerged are termed non-existent, such as when a jar has not yet emerged from the clay, it is called a "non-existent jar";
second, phenomena that have already ceased are termed non-existent, such as when a jar has been destroyed, it is called a "non-existent jar."
Third, when distinct entities are mutually absent, it is termed "non-existence," such as there being no horse within a cow, and no cow within a horse;
fourth, because something is ultimately non-existent, it is termed "non-existence," such as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
"Gotama! If nirvāṇa is defined as the mere elimination of afflictions, then nirvāṇa would be non-existent.
If it were non-existent, how could you say that it possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!

Such nirvana is not a prior non-existence like that of a pot when it is still clay; nor is it a cessation-non-existence like the destruction of a pot; nor is it an absolute non-existence like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, which is equivalent to a different kind of non-existence."
Good son! As you have said, although there is no horse among oxen, one cannot say that the ox is also non-existent.
Although there is no ox among horses, one likewise cannot say that the horse is also non-existent.
Nirvana is also like this: within the afflictions there is no nirvana, and within nirvana there are no afflictions; therefore, they are called "distinct from one another" and "mutually non-existent.
Vāseṭṭha said: "Gautama!"
If you take "otherness" (anyathābhāva) to be nirvāṇa, then that which is "otherness" lacks permanence, bliss, self,
and purity. Gautama,
why do you say that nirvāṇa possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Regarding what you have said concerning ‘otherness’ being non-existent, there are three kinds of non-existence:”
That oxen and horses were previously non-existent and subsequently come into being is called "prior non-existence" (*pūrvābhāva*);
that what has already existed returns to non-existence is called "non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*);
as for "non-existence of distinct characteristics," it is as you have described.
"Good son! These three kinds of non-existence do not exist within nirvāṇa; therefore, nirvāṇa is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
It is like the illnesses of worldly people: first, feverish illness; second, wind illness; and third, cold illness."

These three kinds of diseases can be cured by three medicines: for those with feverish diseases, clarified butter (sarpis) can cure them; for those with wind diseases, oil can cure them; for those with cold-natured diseases, honey can cure them. These three medicines can thus cure these three kinds of malignant diseases.
"Good son!
There is no oil in the wind, nor is there wind in the oil; likewise, there is no coldness in honey, nor is there honey in the coldness. It is for this reason that they can treat [the ailments]."
All sentient beings are likewise thus, having three kinds of illnesses:
first, greed; second, hatred; and third, delusion.

For these three illnesses, there are three kinds of medicines: the contemplation of impurity serves as the medicine for greed; the contemplation of loving-kindness serves as the medicine for hatred; and the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination serves as the medicine for delusion.

Good son! To eliminate greed, one practices the contemplation of non-greed; to eliminate hatred, one practices the contemplation of non-hatred; to eliminate delusion, one practices the contemplation of non-delusion.
Within the three kinds of illnesses there are no three kinds of medicines, and within the three kinds of medicines there are no three kinds of illnesses. Good son!
Because there are no three medicines within the three illnesses, there is no permanence, no self, no bliss, and no purity.
"Within these three kinds of medicine there are no three kinds of illness; therefore, they may be called permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Vāsiṣṭha said:
"World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata has taught me both the permanent and the impermanent;
what is permanent, and what is impermanent?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Form is impermanent, while liberation from form is permanent; likewise, up to consciousness, it is impermanent, while liberation from consciousness is permanent. Good son!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to contemplate that form, up to and including consciousness, is impermanent, it should be known that such persons have attained the eternal Dharma.
Vāseṭṭha said:
“World-Honored One!
I have now understood the dharmas of permanence and impermanence.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, how do you understand the dharmas of permanence and impermanence?”
Vāseṭṭha said:
“World-Honored One!
I now know that my form is impermanent, yet I have attained the permanence of liberation; this applies likewise even unto consciousness.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! It is well that you have now repaid this body."
He addressed Kauṇḍinya:
“This Vāsiṣṭha has already realized the fruit of arhatship; you may now bestow upon him the three robes and the alms bowl.
Then Kauṇḍinya, following the Buddha’s instruction, bestowed the robes and the bowl upon him.
Then Vāsiṣṭha, having received the robe and bowl, spoke these words:
"Venerable Kauṇḍinya!
By means of this wretched and evil body, I have now obtained a wholesome fruit."
