"I only pray that the Venerable One will deign to go to the World-Honored One on my behalf and fully declare my heart's intent:

'I, a wicked man, have offended the Tathāgata by addressing him by his clan name, Gautama. I only pray that you will grant me repentance for this transgression; I am unable to remain long in this poisonous body and shall now enter nirvana.'"
Then Kauṇḍinya went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Vāsiṣṭha has conceived a sense of shame and remorse, saying to himself:..."

"Stubborn and ignorant as I am, I have offended the Tathāgata, who bears the clan name Gautama. I cannot remain long in this body, which is like a venomous serpent; now, wishing to extinguish this body, I entrust my repentance to you."
The Buddha said: “Kauṇḍinya!

The bhikṣu Vāśiṣṭha has already cultivated roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past. Now he accepts my words and abides according to the Dharma; because he abides according to the Dharma, he has attained the correct fruit.”
"You all should make offerings to his body.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya, having heard this from the Buddha, returned to the place where the body was and prepared the offerings.
At that time, as Vāseṭṭha was performing self-immolation, he displayed various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
When the various non-Buddhists witnessed this, they cried out in a loud voice:
"This Vāseṭṭha has already acquired the incantations and arts of the śramaṇa Gautama; before long, this man shall again surpass that śramaṇa Gautama."
At that time, there was another brahmin in the assembly named Śreṇika, who again spoke these words:
"Gautama, does a self exist?
The Tathāgata remained silent.
“Gautama, is there no self?
The Tathāgata remained silent.
When asked a second and a third time in this same manner, the Buddha remained silent each time.
Śreṇika said: “Gautama!
If all sentient beings possess a self—that which is omnipresent, unitary, and the agent—why do you, Gautama, remain silent and not answer?”
The Buddha said,
“Sṛgaya! Do you say that this ‘self’ of yours pervades all places?”
Srenika replied, "Gautama! Not only do I say this;
all those who possess omniscience speak in this same way."
The Buddha said, “Good son!

If I were omnipresent in all places, I should receive retribution for the five destinies simultaneously. If there were simultaneous reception of retribution for the five destinies, for what reason, O brahmins, would you not commit various evils in order to avoid hell?”
"By practicing various wholesome dharmas, one receives a celestial body?
Śreṇika said, "Gautama!..."
Within my Dharma, there are two kinds of self:
first, the self as a created body; second, the self as an eternal body.
For the sake of the self as a created body, one cultivates the abandonment of unwholesome dharmas so as not to enter hell, and cultivates various wholesome dharmas so as to be born in the heavens.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As you say that the self pervades all places, if this self were to exist within the body, one should know it to be impermanent; if it does not exist within the body, how can you say it is pervasive?"
“Gautama! The self that I postulate is also included within the category of the conditioned, yet it is also an eternal dharma. Gautama!”
It is like when a person’s house catches fire and burns down; once the owner has departed, one cannot say that because the house was burned, the owner was also burned.
My Dharma is likewise: although this constructed body is impermanent, at the time of its impermanence, the *ātman* departs. Therefore, the *ātman* is both all-pervading and eternal.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As you say that I am both pervasive and eternal, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? There are two kinds of pervasiveness:
first, the eternal; second, the impermanent.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, form (rūpa); second, the formless (arūpya).
Therefore, if one speaks of "all that exists," it is both permanent and impermanent, and both with form and without form.
If it is argued that because the householder is able to escape, he cannot be called impermanent, this interpretation is incorrect. Why?

Because the house is not called the master, and the master is not called the house; since they are distinct from one another in burning and distinct from one another in escaping, it is thus established.
I am not like that. Why?
Because I am form, and form is I; I am formlessness, and formlessness is I.
How can you say that when form is impermanent, you then attain liberation? Good son!
If you think that all sentient beings share one and the same self, this contradicts both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.
Why is this? Worldly dharmas are designated as father, son, mother, and daughter.

If the self were a single entity, then the father would be the son and the son would be the father; the mother would be the daughter and the daughter would be the mother; the enemy would be the relative and the relative would be the enemy; this would be that and that would be this.
"Therefore, if one were to say that all sentient beings share a single self, this would contradict both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. Śreṇika said:
"I do not say that all sentient beings share a single self; rather, I say that each individual person possesses their own self."
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If one says that each individual has a separate self, this would result in a plurality of selves; such a proposition is not tenable."

Why is this? As you previously stated, the self is omnipresent; if it were omnipresent, then the karmic faculties of all sentient beings would be identical. When Devadatta sees, Buddhadatta would also see; when Devadatta acts, Buddhadatta would also act; when Devadatta hears, Buddhadatta would also hear—and so it would be for all phenomena.
"If it were seen by devas but not seen by Buddhas, one should not say that 'I' pervade all places;
if it does not pervade, then it is impermanent. Śreṇika said, "Gautama!"
"All sentient beings are pervaded by me, whereas dharma and non-dharma do not pervade all; for this reason, the Buddha may act differently, and Devadatta may act differently."
"Therefore, Gautama!
You should not say that when the Buddha perceives, the gods must perceive; or when the Buddha hears, the gods must hear.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Are dharma and non-dharma not produced by karma?
Śreṇika replied:
“Gautama! This is produced by karma.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If dharma and non-dharma were the agents of karma, they would be identical in nature; how then could one say they are different? Why is this so?”

When the Buddha-attainer (Buddhadeva) has his sphere of activity, there is the Deva-attainer (Devadeva); when the Deva-attainer has his sphere of activity, there is the Buddha-attainer. Therefore, when the Buddha-attainer acts, the Deva-attainer also acts; the same should apply to what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
"Good son!
Therefore, if all sentient beings, dharmas, and non-dharmas were such as you describe, the retributions they obtain would likewise not differ."
"Good son! From a seed comes fruit, yet that seed never thinks or discriminates:
'I shall produce only the fruit of a Brahmin, and not the fruit of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra.'"

Why is this? Just as fruit emerges from a seed without ever obstructing these four castes, so too it is with the Dharma and non-Dharma; they cannot distinguish that "I shall produce fruit only for Buddhajīva and not for Devajīva."
One attains the fruit by becoming a deva, not by becoming a Buddha. Why?
Because karma is equal.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama!
It is like a single room with a hundred thousand lamps; although the wicks are different, their light makes no distinction."
"The difference between the wick and the lamp is a metaphor for the Dharma and non-Dharma; that there is no distinction in their light is a metaphor for the self of sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
As for your statement that you use the light of a lamp as a metaphor for the self, this meaning is not tenable. Why?
Because the room is different and the lamp is different.
This light of the lamp exists both at the edge of the wick and throughout the entire room.

If what you say regarding the self were so, then the self would have to exist at the edges of both the dharma and the non-dharma, and within the self there would also have to be both dharma and non-dharma.
If both dharma and non-dharma were devoid of a self, one could not say that they pervade all places.
If both were present together, how could the analogy of the wick and the light still be applicable?
"Good son!
If you think that the wick and the light are truly distinct entities, for what reason does the light increase and flourish as the wick grows, and why does the light perish when the wick withers?"
Therefore, one should not use the lamp and its wick as a metaphor for dharma and non-dharma, nor the lack of difference in its radiance as a metaphor for the self (ātman). Why is this?
Because these three things—dharma, non-dharma, and the self—are one and the same.
Śreṇika said: “Gautama!
Your citation of the analogy of the lamp is inauspicious.”
Why is this? If the analogy of the lamp were auspicious, I have already cited it;
if it were inauspicious, why would you state it again?
“Good son! The metaphors I have employed are neither auspicious nor inauspicious; they are spoken according to your own inclination.
These metaphors also describe both the existence of light apart from the wick and the existence of light within the wick itself.”
Your mind is not impartial; therefore, you have used the analogy of the lamp-wick for both the Dharma and non-Dharma, while using the light to represent the self.
For this reason, I challenge you: if the wick is the light, then the light exists apart from the wick;
if the Dharma is the self, then the self exists apart from the Dharma.
The unrighteous is myself, and I am the unrighteous.
Why do you now accept only one side and not the other?
Such a metaphor will bring you no good fortune.
Therefore, I now turn this very [argument] back upon you to refute you. Good son!
Such a metaphor is, in fact, no metaphor; because it is not a metaphor, it brings good fortune to me, but ill fortune to you.
"Good son!
If you think that because I am inauspicious, you too are inauspicious, this is not the case. Why is that?"

I see people in the world who use their own knives to harm themselves, yet employ what they have made for others; the analogy you have cited is just like this—it is auspicious for me, but inauspicious for you.
Srenika said: "Gautama!
You previously censured me for having an uneven mind, yet what you have now said is itself uneven."
"Why is this? Gautama, you now direct good fortune toward yourself and misfortune toward me; judging by this, it is truly unjust.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Just as my own unevenness can destroy your unevenness, you are thereby made even; thus, my unevenness is itself auspicious.
By destroying your unevenness with my unevenness and causing you to attain evenness, that is my own evenness.”
"Why is this? Because he has attained equality with all the noble ones. Śreṇika said:
"Gautama! I am always even; why do you say that you have destroyed my unevenness?
All sentient beings equally possess the self; how can you say that my self is uneven?"
“Good son! You also say that one shall undergo the hells, shall undergo the realm of hungry ghosts, shall undergo the realm of animals, and shall undergo the realms of humans and devas.”
If I had already pervaded all five realms of existence previously, why do you now say that I am about to undergo birth in various destinies?
You yourself also say that a child is born only after the union of father and mother.
If the son already existed beforehand, why do you further say that he exists only after the conjunction [of causes]?

Therefore, a single person possesses bodies in the five destinies; if the body already existed in those five locations beforehand, for what cause or condition would one create karma for the sake of that body?
Therefore, it is not equitable. Good son!
If you think that "I" am the creator, this meaning is not so.
Why is this? If the self were the agent, for what cause and condition would it create suffering for itself?
Yet, sentient beings truly experience suffering; therefore, one should know that the self is not the agent.
If one says that this suffering is not created by me and does not arise from causes, then all phenomena should likewise not arise from causes; for what reason, then, do you say "I am the creator"?

Good son! The suffering and happiness of sentient beings truly arise from causes and conditions; such suffering and happiness can produce sorrow and joy, for when there is sorrow there is no joy, and when there is joy there is no sorrow.
At times one is joyful, at other times sorrowful; how can a wise person say that this is permanent?
Son of good family!
You claim that the self is permanent; if it were permanent, why would you say there are ten distinct temporal stages?
An eternal dharma should not possess the stages from the kalala stage up to old age; even for the eternal dharma of space, there is not even a single moment, let alone ten stages. Good son!
The "self" is not the kalala stage, nor does it exist through to the stage of old age; how then can one speak of ten distinct stages?
Good son, if the self were a creator, then this self would have periods of flourishing and decline, and sentient beings likewise would have periods of flourishing and decline.
If the self were such [an agent], how could it be permanent? Good son!
If the self were the agent, why would one person be sharp while another is dull?
"Good son!
If I were an agent, then I would be able to perform bodily karma and verbal karma.
If verbal karma were that which I performed, how could one say in speech that there is no self?"
What do you mean by doubting whether [seeing] exists or does not exist?
Son of good family!
If you think that seeing exists apart from the eye, this is not the case.
Why is this? If there were a seer distinct from and independent of the eye, what need would there be for this eye? This applies likewise even to the body-faculty.
If you think that although "I" am able to see, it must depend on the eye to see, that too is not correct.
Why is this? It is like someone saying that *sumanā* flowers can burn down a great village.
How could they possibly burn it?
"Because fire has the power to burn,
so too is it with the 'view of self' that you have established. Śreṇika said:
"Gautama! Just as a person who grasps a sickle is able to cut grass, so too do I see, hear, and so forth, up to touch, by means of the five faculties. "Good son!"
Since each person’s sickle is distinct, one who grasps a sickle is able to perform an action.
Apart from the sense faculties, there is no separate self; how then can it be said that the self, by means of the sense faculties, is able to perform an action?
"Good son!
If you think that it is the sickle that can cut, I am also like this. Do I have hands?"
Are you without hands?
If you have hands, why do you not grasp it yourself?
If you are without hands, how can you say, "I am the agent"?
"Good son!
That which is able to cut the grass is the sickle; it is neither 'I' nor 'person.
If it were 'I' or 'person' that could do so, why would one rely upon the sickle?"
Good son! A person has two types of implements:
first, grasping grass; second, grasping a sickle. This sickle possesses only the efficacy of cutting.
It is the same for sentient beings perceiving phenomena: the eye is able to see forms through the arising of a combination [of conditions].
If seeing occurs through the combination of causes and conditions, how can a wise person say that there is a self?
Good son! If you think that the body acts and the self receives [the result], this meaning is not so. Why is that?
In the world, one does not see that Devadatta performs the action while Śākyamuni receives the fruit.
If you say it is not the body that acts and that "I" am not the cause for receiving [the fruit], then for what reason do you seek liberation from causes and conditions?
If your former body was not produced by causes and conditions, then after attaining liberation, you should likewise produce another body without causes;
and as it is with the body, so it should be with all afflictions.
Srenika said: "Gautama!
I have two kinds [of views]:”
The first is that which possesses consciousness; the second is that which lacks consciousness.
The self devoid of consciousness can obtain a body, while the self possessing consciousness can relinquish the body.
It is like an unbaked clay pot: once it has been fired, its original color is lost and it never returns to its former state.
"In the same way, the afflictions of a wise person, once they have been extinguished and destroyed, will never arise again.
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
Regarding that which is called "knowing," is it the wisdom that knows?
Or is it the self that knows?
If it is wisdom that knows, why do you say, "I am the knower"?
If I already knew, for what purpose would I employ skillful means to further seek knowledge?
If you think that I know by means of knowledge, that view is refuted by the analogy of the flower. Good son!
For example, a thorny tree has the inherent nature of piercing; one cannot say that the tree grasps the thorn to pierce.
Wisdom is also like this: wisdom itself is capable of knowing. Why, then, do you say that "I grasp wisdom to know"?
"Good son!
Within your Dharma, I have attained liberation; do you know that I have attained it, or do you not know that I have attained it?"
If one has not attained knowledge, it should be known that they still possess afflictions in their entirety.
If one has attained knowledge, it should be known that they already possess the five sensory faculties. Why is this?
Apart from the sense faculties, there is no separate cognition.
If one possesses all the sense faculties, how can one further be said to have attained liberation?
If you claim that this "self" is pure in nature and distinct from the five faculties, why do you say it exists pervasively throughout the five realms of existence?
For what reason do you cultivate various wholesome dharmas for the sake of liberation?
Son of good family!
It is as if someone were trying to pull out a thorn from empty space; you are just like that.
If I am already pure, why do you further say that I must sever all afflictions?
If you believe that liberation is not obtained through causes and conditions, why then do all animals not attain it as well?
Srenika said: "Gautama!
If there were no self, who would be able to recollect?"
The Buddha told Śreṇika:
"If there were a self, for what reason would it again be forgotten?
Good son!..."
"If this mindfulness were the self, for what reason would it give rise to evil thoughts, think what should not be thought, and fail to think what should be thought?
Śreṇika spoke again:
"Gautama!..."
"If there is no self, who sees and who hears?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."

Within there are the six sense bases, and without there are the six objects; through the conjunction of the internal and external, the six kinds of consciousness arise. These six kinds of consciousness receive their names based on these causes and conditions. Good son!

For example, there is a single fire: because it arises from wood, it is called "wood-fire"; because it arises from grass, it is called "grass-fire"; because it arises from chaff, it is called "chaff-fire"; and because it arises from cow dung, it is called "cow-dung-fire."
The consciousness of sentient beings is also like this: depending on the eye, depending on form, depending on light, and depending on desire, it is called "eye-consciousness. Good son!

In this way, visual consciousness does not reside in the eye, nor even within desire; rather, this consciousness arises through the conjunction of four factors, and the same applies to the mental consciousness as well.
If things arise through the combination of causes and conditions, wisdom should not say that "seeing" is the self, nor even that "touching" is the self. Good son!
For this reason, I say that from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, all dharmas are like illusions.
In what way is it like an illusion?
That which was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence. Good son!

For example, when ghee, flour, honey, ginger, black pepper, long pepper, grapes, walnuts, pomegranates, and jujubes are thus combined, it is called a "joy-pill" (*mudga-vaṭaka*); apart from this combination, there is no joy-pill.
The six internal and external sense bases are what are called sentient beings, self, persons, and individuals.
Apart from these internal and external sense bases, there is no separate sentient being, self, person, or individual.
Srenika said: "Gautama!
If there is no self, how can one say: 'I see,' 'I hear,' 'I suffer,' 'I am happy,' 'I grieve,' or 'I rejoice'?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
If one says ‘I see’ or ‘I hear’ and thereby claims there is a self, for what reason does the world further say, ‘The sin you have committed was not seen or heard by me’?”
Good son!

For example, when four types of troops are combined, they are called an "army. Although these four troops are not called one, one nevertheless says, "My army is brave and strong," or "My army has defeated the enemy."

The same applies to that which is produced by the conjunction of the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*): although it is not a single entity, one may nonetheless say, "I act," "I experience," "I see," "I hear," "I suffer," or "I am happy."
Srenika said, "Gautama! According to what you have said,
when the internal and external elements are combined, who is it that utters the voice saying, 'I act' and 'I experience'?"
The Buddha said: “Sreṇika!

From craving and ignorance as causes and conditions, karma arises; from karma, existence arises; from existence, immeasurable mental factors arise; from the mind, vitarka and vicāra arise; vitarka and vicāra move the wind; and the wind, following the mind, contacts the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips.”
Sentient beings possess inverted perceptions; from their mouths they utter words, saying, "I act," "I receive," "I see," and "I hear.
Good son! It is like the bells atop a banner: through the causal condition of the wind, they produce sounds.
When the wind is great, the sound is great; when the wind is small, the sound is small;
there is no agent. Good son!
It is like hot iron cast into water, which produces various sounds; within this, in truth, there is no agent.
Good son!
Because ordinary beings are unable to contemplate and discern such matters, they speak of a self and what belongs to a self, saying "I act" and "I experience."
Srenika said:
"If, as Gautama says, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, for what reason do you further speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! I do not say that the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and the six consciousnesses of the mind are permanent, blissful, self, and pure; rather, I proclaim that the cessation of the six consciousnesses produced by the internal and external sense bases is called ‘permanent.’”
Because it is permanent, it is called "self"; because there is a permanent self, it is called "bliss"; and because there is a permanent self and bliss, it is called "purity."
"Good son!
Sentient beings weary of suffering and sever its causes, attaining sovereign detachment; this is what is called 'self.
For these reasons, I now proclaim the permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
Śreṇika said:
“World-Honored One!
I pray only that you, out of great compassion, will proclaim it for me: how may I obtain such permanence, bliss, self, and purity?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

All those in the world have, from the very beginning, been possessed of great pride; they are able to increase their pride and further create the causes and karmic actions of pride. For this reason, they now undergo the retribution of pride and are unable to distance themselves from all afflictions to attain the permanence, bliss, self, and purity.”
"If all sentient beings wish to distance themselves from all afflictions,
they must first abandon pride. Śreṇika said,
"World-Honored One!"
So it is, so it is; it is exactly as the Holy Teaching declares.
Previously, I harbored pride, and because of that pride, I addressed the Tathāgata by his clan name, Gautama.
"I have now already abandoned such great pride; therefore, with a sincere heart, I entreat you to request the Dharma: how may I attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
O son of good family!
"If one can regard it as neither self, nor other, nor a sentient being, one remains far removed from these dharmas.
Śreṇika said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have already understood and realized it; I have attained the right Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"How can you say that you have known it, understood it, and attained the true Dharma-eye?
"World-Honored One!
That which is called 'form' belongs neither to self, nor to others, nor to sentient beings; this applies even up to consciousness."
"Observing in this way, I have attained the right eye of the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
I now greatly desire to leave the household life to practice the Way; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The Buddha said,
“Welcome, bhikṣu. Immediately,
he became fully endowed with pure brahmacarya and realized the fruit of arhatship.
Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was again a brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan who spoke as follows:
"Gautama! The body is the life-force; the body is one thing and the life-force is another."
The Tathāgata remained silent.
A second and a third time, it was likewise.
The brahmin spoke again:
“Gautama! If a person has cast off this body but has not yet attained a subsequent body, could one not say that in the interval between them, the body is one thing and the life-principle is another?
If they are indeed different, Gautama!”
"Why do you remain silent and not answer? "Good son!
I teach that body and life both arise from causes and conditions; they do not exist without causes and conditions."
"Just as it is with the body and life, so it is with all phenomena.
The brahmin spoke again: "Gautama!"
"I see that there are phenomena in the world that do not arise from causes and conditions.
The Buddha said, "Brahmin!"
"How do you see there being any phenomenon in the world that does not arise from causes and conditions?

The brahmin replied, "I see a great fire burning through a thicket of brushwood; when the wind blows, the flames are extinguished and fall elsewhere. Is this not called being without cause and condition?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!
I say that this fire also arises from causes; it does not arise without a cause."
The brahmin said:
"Gautama! When a flame is extinguished, it does not depend on fuel or charcoal; how then can you say it depends upon causes and conditions?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Although there is no firewood or charcoal, it is extinguished by means of the wind; yet because of the conditions of the wind, its flames do not cease.”
“Gautama! When a person has cast off this body but has not yet attained the next body, what serves as the causal condition for the life-span in the interval?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmin! Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) act as causes and conditions.
It is because of these two causes and conditions—ignorance and craving—that the life-span is maintained.”
"Good son!
Due to certain causes and conditions, the body is itself life, and life is itself the body;
due to certain causes and conditions, the body and life are distinct."
"A wise person should not speak categorically that the body is one thing and the life-principle is another.
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that you will analyze and explain this for me, so that I may clearly understand cause and effect.
The Buddha said, “Brahmin!”
The cause is the five aggregates, and the fruit is likewise the five aggregates. Good son!
If there are sentient beings who do not kindle fire, then there will be no smoke.
The brahmin said:
“World-Honored One!
I have already known; I have already understood.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, how do you know this?"
"How do you understand this?
"World-Honored One!

Fire is affliction (*kleśa*), which can burn within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas. Smoke is the retribution of affliction—impermanent, impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome; for these reasons, it is called smoke."

If there are sentient beings who do not produce afflictions, such persons will have no retribution for those afflictions; therefore, the Tathāgata says that if one does not kindle fire, there will be no smoke.
“World-Honored One!
I have attained right view; I only pray that you will compassionately pity me and grant me permission to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"Listen to this brahmin as he leaves the household life and receives the precepts.

At that time, having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya convened the Saṃgha, granted him permission to leave the household life, and conferred upon him full ordination (*upasampadā*). After five days had passed, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was another brahmin named Pūraṇa, who spoke again as follows:
"Gautama! Have you perceived that the world is an eternal phenomenon, and have you therefore declared it to be eternal?"
Regarding such matters: are they real or unreal?
Permanent or impermanent?

Both permanent and impermanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent? Finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite? Is the body the same as the life-principle, or is the body one thing and the life-principle another? Does the Tathāgata exist after death, or does he not exist after death, or both exist and not exist after death, or neither exist nor not exist after death?
The Buddha said: “Pūrṇa!

I do not speak of the world as permanent, empty, real, impermanent, both permanent and impermanent, neither permanent nor impermanent; as finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite; as the body being the life-force, the body being different from the life-force; or that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa he exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist.”
Pūrṇa spoke again: "Gautama!
What fault do you now perceive that you do not make such a statement?"
The Buddha said:
"Pūraṇa! If someone were to say that the world is eternal, and that this alone is true while all else is false, this is called a view."

To perceive the object of perception is called the activity of views, the karma of views, attachment to views, bondage of views, the suffering of views, the grasping of views, the fear of views, the fever of views, and the entanglement of views.

Purna! Ordinary persons are entangled by views and cannot distance themselves from birth, old age, sickness, and death; they circulate through the six realms of existence, undergoing immeasurable suffering, even up to the point of "neither going nor not going," which is likewise the case.
"Purna! I see that such views have these faults; therefore, I do not cling to them, nor do I speak of them for others.
"Gautama! [Purna said.]
"If one sees such faults as these, one neither clings to them nor speaks of them.
Gautama, what do you now see, what do you cling to, and what do you proclaim?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! That which is characterized by attachment to views is called the dharma of birth and death; because the Tathāgata has already transcended the dharmas of birth and death, he is therefore unattached. Good son!”
“The Tathāgata is called one who is able to see and able to speak; he is not called one who is attached.
“Gautama, in what way is he able to see?”
"How can one speak [of this]?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
I am able to clearly perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; I analyze and proclaim these Four Noble Truths.

Because I see them thus, I am able to remain far removed from all views, all cravings, all taints, and all conceits. Therefore, I am endowed with the pure Brahma-conduct and supreme tranquility, having attained the eternal body—a body that is neither east, west, south, nor north.
Pūrṇa said: "Gautama!
For what reason is the eternal body not [limited to] the directions of east, west, south, or north?"
The Buddha said, "Good son!
I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
What do you think, son of good family?
Suppose a great mass of fire were burning right before you; when it was burning, would you know that it was burning?
"So it is, Gautama! When this fire is extinguished, do you know that it has been extinguished?"
"So it is, Gautama! O Pūraṇa!"
If someone were to ask you where that previous mass of fire came from when it was burning,
and where it went when it was extinguished,
how would you answer?

“Gautama! If someone were to ask this, I would answer: ‘This fire arises in dependence upon various conditions; when its original conditions have been exhausted and new conditions have not yet arrived, this fire then extinguishes.’”
“If someone were to ask again, ‘Once this fire has been extinguished, to which direction has it gone?
how would you answer? “Gautama! [I would answer:]”
I would answer: "It ceases because its conditions are exhausted; it does not go to any location. "Good son!

The Tathāgata is also like this. If there is impermanent form, up to and including impermanent consciousness, they burn because of craving. That which burns is the experience of the twenty-five states of existence (pañcaviṃśati-bhava). Therefore, while it is burning, one may say that this fire is in the east, west, south, or north."

Now that craving has been extinguished, the retributive fruits of the twenty-five states of existence do not arise; because they do not arise, it cannot be said that there are directions such as east, west, south, or north. Good son!

The Tathāgata has already extinguished impermanent form up to and including impermanent consciousness; therefore, his body is eternal. If the body were eternal, one could not speak of its being in the east, west, south, or north.
Pūrṇa said, "I beg you to provide an analogy; I only wish that you would grant me your attention.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Speak as you wish.
“World-Honored One!”
Suppose there were a grove of *sāla* trees outside a large village, and within it stood a single tree that had grown before the grove itself, reaching a full hundred years of age.

At that time, the owner of the grove would water it and tend to it according to the seasons; yet the tree was ancient and decayed, its bark, branches, and leaves having all fallen away, leaving only the solid heartwood remaining.
The Tathāgata is likewise; all that is old and worn has been completely eliminated, and only the true Dharma remains.
World-Honored One!
I now deeply desire to leave the household life to cultivate the Way.
The Buddha said,
“Welcome, bhikṣu.
As soon as these words were spoken, he immediately left the household life and, with the exhaustion of the outflows, realized the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin named Viśuddha who spoke these words: "Gautama!

All sentient beings do not know what dharma it is that leads them to perceive the world as permanent, impermanent, both permanent and impermanent, neither permanent nor impermanent, and so on, up to neither thus-gone nor not thus-gone?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Because they do not know form, and so on up to because they do not know consciousness, they view the world as eternal, and so on up to neither passing away nor not passing away."
The brahmin said: "Gautama!
By knowing what dharma do sentient beings not perceive the world as eternal, up to and including neither passing away nor not passing away?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Because one knows form, and so on up to knowing consciousness, one does not perceive the world as eternal, nor even as neither-going-nor-not-going."
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will analyze and explain for me whether the world is eternal or non-eternal."
The Buddha said,
“Good son! If a person abandons the old and does not create new karma, that person is able to know the permanent and the impermanent.”
The brahmin said:
“World-Honored One!
I have already known and seen.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, how do you see it?”
"How do you know this?
"World-Honored One!
The old names are ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the new names are grasping (*upādāna*) and becoming (*bhava*)."
If a person distances themselves from this ignorance and craving, and does not produce grasping or existence, that person truly knows the permanent and the impermanent.
I have now attained the pure eye of the True Dharma and take refuge in the Triple Gem; I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya, “Grant this brahmin permission to leave the household life and receive the precepts.

Having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya led him to the midst of the Saṃgha and performed the *karmavācanā* for him so that he might go forth. Fifteen days later, his outflows were forever exhausted, and he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Nine;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Forty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen, Part Two: Kauṇḍinya.
The Brahmin Vatsa spoke again, saying: "Gautama!
"I now wish to ask a question; will you grant me the opportunity to hear it?
The Tathāgata remained silent.
A second and a third time he spoke thus, and the Tathāgata likewise remained silent.
The Vātsīputrīya spoke again:
“Gautama! I have long been your close friend; between you and me, there is no difference in principle. I wish to consult you, so why do you remain silent?”
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This brahmin is by nature refined and elegant, pure, virtuous, and straightforward; he has always come to inquire for the sake of knowledge, not to cause disturbance."
"If he should ask, you should answer according to his inclination.
The Buddha said, "Vatsa!"
"Excellent, excellent!
I shall answer according to whatever questions you have.
Ghoṭamukha said:
"Gautama! Is there goodness in the world? "It is so."
"Brahmin! Is there that which is unwholesome? "It is so."
"Brahmin!
Gautama, please explain this to me so that I may come to know wholesome and unwholesome phenomena."
The Buddha said, “Good son!
I am able to analyze and explain its meaning in detail, but for now I shall explain it to you in brief.”
"Good son! Desire is called unwholesome; one who is liberated from desire is called wholesome. It is the same for anger and delusion.
Killing is called unwholesome; non-killing is called wholesome; and this applies even up to wrong views."
"Good son!
I have now explained for you three kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as well as ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

If my disciples can thus distinguish these three kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, up to the ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, you should know that such persons are able to exhaust greed, anger, and delusion, as well as all outflows (āsrava), and sever all existence (bhava)."
The brahmin said, "Gautama!
Is there perhaps even a single bhikṣu within this Buddha-dharma who is able to exhaust such greed, hatred, and delusion, all outflows (āsrava), and all existence (bhava)?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!

Within this Dharma of the Buddha, it is not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred; rather, there are immeasurable bhikṣus who are able to exhaust such greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all outflows (āsrava) and all modes of existence (bhava)."

“Gautama! Setting aside one bhikṣu, is there perhaps even one bhikṣuṇī within this Buddha-dharma who is able to exhaust such greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all outflows (āsrava) and all existence (bhava)?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Within this Dharma of the Buddha, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but indeed immeasurable bhikṣuṇīs who are able to sever such greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all outflows (āsrava) and all modes of existence (bhava).”
The son of the cowherd said: "Gautama!

Setting aside one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī, is there perhaps even a single upāsaka in this Buddha-dharma who maintains the precepts with diligence, whose pure conduct is stainless, who has crossed to the further shore of doubt, and who has severed the web of uncertainty?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

In my Buddha-dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred; rather, there are immeasurable upāsakas who are diligent in observing the precepts and pure in their holy life (brahmacarya). Having severed the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni), they have attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin), crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and severed the net of doubt.”
The young man said: "Gautama!

Setting aside one bhikṣu, one bhikṣuṇī, and one upāsaka, is there perhaps even one upāsikā within this Buddha-dharma who maintains the precepts with diligence, whose holy life is pure, who has crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and who has severed the web of doubt?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!

In my Buddha-dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but indeed immeasurable upāsikās who, through diligent observance of the precepts and pure brahmacarya, have severed the five lower fetters, attained the stage of anāgāmin, crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and cut through the net of uncertainty."
The young man said: "Gautama!

Let us set aside one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī who have exhausted all outflows, and one upāsaka and one upāsikā who maintain the precepts with diligence, whose holy life is pure, and who have severed the net of doubt."
"In this Buddha-dharma, are there any upāsakas who enjoy the pleasures of the five desires while their minds remain free from the net of doubt?
The Buddha said, "Good son! [There are indeed such people]."
Within this Buddha-dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but rather immeasurable upāsakas who have severed the three fetters and attained the stage of srotāpanna;
and those who have attenuated greed, anger, and delusion and attained the stage of sakṛdāgāmin.
"As it is with the upāsakas, so it is also with the upāsikās.
"World-Honored One!
I would now like to offer an analogy."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Speak as you wish."
“World-Honored One!
Just as the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda send down great rain, so too is the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata; it falls equally upon upāsakas and upāsikās.”
“World-Honored One!
If various non-Buddhists wish to come forth and leave the household life, I do not know for how many months the Tathāgata tests them?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! All undergo a four-month trial, though not necessarily of one kind.
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]
"If it is not of one kind [with us], I only pray that the Great Compassionate One will grant me permission to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One told Kauṇḍinya:
"I permit this Vatsa to leave the household life and receive the precepts."

Then, having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya stood among the assembly of monks and performed the *karmavācanā* for him; fifteen days after his renunciation, he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Having attained the fruit, he further thought:
"If there is wisdom to be gained through study, I have now attained it and am fit to see the Buddha."

He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and having completed his respectful salutations, withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As for all wisdom that is acquired through learning, I have now attained it."
“I only pray that you will explain this to me again in detail, so that I may attain the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna).
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"You should diligently apply yourself with vigor to the cultivation of two dharmas:
first, śamatha; second, vipaśyanā. Good son!"
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, he should also diligently cultivate these two dharmas.
Furthermore, if he wishes to attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhat, he should likewise practice these two dharmas.
“Good son!

If there are bhikṣus who wish to attain the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the six supernormal powers, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of the summit, the ultimate knowledge, the four unhindered knowledges, the diamond-like samādhi, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising, they too should practice these two dharmas.”

"Good son! If you wish to attain the ten stages (bhūmi), the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), the patience regarding signless dharmas, the patience regarding inconceivable dharmas, the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, the celestial conduct, the bodhisattva conduct, the space-like samādhi, the wisdom-seal samādhi, the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the earth samādhi, the non-retrogressive samādhi, the Śūraṅgama samādhi, the vajra samādhi,
unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and the conduct of a Buddha, you should likewise cultivate these two dharmas."
Having heard this, the young man prostrated and departed; dwelling in the Śāla grove, he cultivated these two dharmas and before long attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, there were also immeasurable bhikṣus who wished to go to where the Buddha was. Upon seeing them, Vatsa asked,
"Venerable sirs,
where do you intend to go?"
The bhikṣus said,
"We wish to go to the place where the Buddha is.
The calf spoke again:
"Venerable sirs!

If you should go to the Buddha's presence, please announce on my behalf: 'The brahmin Vatsa, having practiced two dharmas, has attained the knowledge of one beyond training; now, to repay the Buddha's kindness, he has entered parinirvāṇa.'"
When the bhikṣus had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Vatsa has sent us this message:”
“World-Honored One!
The brahmin Ghoṭaka, having cultivated two dharmas and attained the knowledge of one beyond training, now repays the Buddha’s kindness by entering nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! The brahmin Vatsa has attained the fruit of arhatship; you should go and make offerings to his body.
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha’s command, they returned to the place where the corpse was and made extensive offerings.
The Nigaṇṭha Naṭaputta spoke again, saying:
“Gautama! Just as you have said, Gautama, that throughout immeasurable ages one performs good and evil deeds, and in the future one still receives a body of good or evil accordingly.”
This meaning is not so.
Why? Because as Gautama has said, it is due to afflictions that this body is obtained.
If the body is obtained because of afflictions, does the body come first,
or do the afflictions come first?
If the afflictions come first, by whom were they produced?
Where does it abide?
If the body existed first, how could one say that it is obtained through afflictions?
Therefore, to claim that the afflictions exist first is likewise untenable.
If the body exists prior [to consciousness], this is also untenable;
if one says they exist simultaneously, this is also untenable.

Since the meanings of priority, posteriority, and simultaneity are all untenable, I therefore say that all dharmas possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise from causes and conditions.
"Furthermore, Gautama! Solidity is the nature of earth; moisture is the nature of water;

heat is the nature of fire; motion is the nature of wind; and non-obstruction is the nature of space. These five great natures do not exist through causes and conditions. If there were even a single dharma-nature in the world that did not exist through causes and conditions, then all dharma-natures would likewise not exist through causes and conditions."
"If there is even one dharma that arises from causes and conditions, for what reason do the natures of the five great elements not arise from causes and conditions?

Gautama! That sentient beings attain liberation through both virtuous bodies and non-virtuous bodies is entirely due to their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*); it does not arise from causes and conditions."
Therefore, I say that all dharmas exist by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and are not produced through causes and conditions.
"Furthermore, Gautama!
The phenomena of the world have fixed functions and domains."
It is like a carpenter who thinks, "This wood may be used to make a carriage or a cart; it may likewise be used to make a door, a bed, or a desk. It is also like a goldsmith:

whatever he fashions, that which is placed upon the forehead is called a wreath (*mālā*); that which is worn below the neck is called a necklace (*hāra*); that which is worn on the upper arm is called a bracelet (*kaṭaka*); and that which is worn on the finger is called a ring (*aṅgulīyaka*). Because their respective uses are fixed, they are said to have a fixed nature (*niyata-svabhāva*).
"Gautama!

All sentient beings are likewise thus; because they possess the nature of the five destinies, there are those in hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas. If this is so, why do you say that [rebirth] arises from causes and conditions?"
"Furthermore, Gautama!
All sentient beings have distinct natures; for this reason, they are called 'all self-natures.
Gautama!"
Just as a land-dwelling tortoise naturally enters the water when born,
a calf, once born, is able to drink milk on its own,
and a fish, upon seeing a hook and bait, naturally swallows it.
Once a venomous snake has been born, it naturally feeds on earth.
Who could have taught it such things?
Just as a thorn, once grown, naturally has a pointed tip, and the plumage of a flying bird naturally possesses distinct colors.

The sentient beings of the world are likewise thus: there are those who are sharp and those who are dull; those who are wealthy and those who are poor; those who are handsome and those who are ugly; those who attain liberation and those who do not attain liberation. Therefore, one should know that within all phenomena, each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Furthermore, Gautama!

As you, Gautama, have stated—that greed, hatred, and delusion arise from causes and conditions, and that these three poisons have the five sensory objects as their causes and conditions—this meaning is not so."
Why is this? When sentient beings sleep, they are far removed from the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), yet they still give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.

It is the same while in the womb; even when first emerging from the womb, before they are able to distinguish between the five sensory objects or between the beautiful and the ugly, they still give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Even sages and holy ones dwelling in solitary places, where the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are absent, are still capable of giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.

Conversely, there are also people who, because of the five sensory objects, give rise to non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Therefore, it is not necessarily the case that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they exist by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Furthermore, Gautama!
I see people in this world who lack the five sense faculties, yet possess abundant wealth and great power.
Conversely, there are those whose faculties are complete, yet who are poor and lowly, lacking autonomy and serving as servants to others."
"If there are causes and conditions, why is it so? Therefore,
all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise by means of causes and conditions,
O Gautama!"

Even infants of this world are not yet able to distinguish the five sense objects; yet they sometimes laugh and sometimes cry. When they laugh, they know joy; when they cry, they know sorrow. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Gautama!
There are two worldly phenomena:
first, existence; second, non-existence.
Existence is identical to space, and non-existence is identical to a rabbit’s horn.

Regarding these two phenomena: because the first exists, it does not arise from causes and conditions; because the second is non-existent, it likewise is not a cause and condition. Therefore, since all phenomena possess intrinsic nature, they do not arise from causes and conditions.
The Buddha said: “Good son!
As you have stated, that all dharmas should be like the nature of the five great elements—this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? Son of good family!
In your dharma, the five great elements are eternal; for what reason, then, are all phenomena not eternal?
If worldly objects are impermanent, for what reason are the natures of these five great elements not impermanent?
If the five great elements were permanent, then worldly objects should also be permanent.

Therefore, your claim that the nature of the five great elements possesses intrinsic nature and thus does not arise from causes and conditions, and that all phenomena are therefore identical to these five great elements, is impossible.
“Good son! As for your statement that because the locus of activity is fixed, there must be an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), this meaning is not so. Why is that?
Because all names are obtained through causes and conditions.
If a name is derived from a cause, its meaning is likewise derived from a cause.
What is meant by "a name being derived from a cause"?

Just as that which is on the forehead is called a crest-jewel (maṇi), that on the neck a necklace (hāra), that on the arm a bracelet (kaṭaka), and that on a chariot a wheel (cakra); or as fire in grass and wood is called "grass-fire" or "wood-fire."

Good son! When a tree first grows, it has no inherent nature as an arrow or a spear. Due to causes and conditions, a craftsman fashions it into an arrow; due to causes and conditions, a craftsman fashions it into a spear. Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature.
"Good son!
As you have said, it is like a tortoise born on land whose nature is to enter the water;
or like a calf that, once born, has the capacity to drink milk."
This argument is not tenable. Why?

If you claim that entering water is not due to specific causes and conditions, then since both [entering water and entering fire] would equally lack causes and conditions, why does one not enter fire as well?

Once a calf is born, its nature is to suckle milk; if it were not due to causes and conditions, and both [the milk and the calf] were devoid of causes and conditions, why would it not suckle from the horns? Good son!
If one claims that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such that they do not require instruction or cultivation and do not undergo increase, this argument is incorrect. Why?
Because we now observe that there is instruction, and through the conditions of instruction, increase occurs; therefore, one should know that there is no intrinsic nature.
"Good son!

If all phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the various brahmins would never have to slaughter sheep as sacrifices to purify their bodies. Since they do perform such bodily sacrifices, you should know that there is no intrinsic nature."
“Good son! There are generally three kinds of worldly linguistic conventions:
first, the intention to act; second, the time of acting; and third, having already acted.”
If all phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature, why would these three expressions exist in the world?
Because these three expressions exist, we know that all things lack an intrinsic nature.
"Good son!

If one says that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), one should know that each phenomenon would have its own fixed nature. If there were such a fixed nature, for what reason could a single substance like sugarcane be made into syrup, rock honey, honey wine, bitter wine, and so forth?"
If there were a single nature, for what reason would such various flavors emerge?
If such things as these emerge from within a single entity, one should know that all phenomena cannot be fixed as having a single, determinate nature each.
"Good son!

If all dharmas possessed a fixed nature, why would the noble ones drink sugarcane juice, rock honey, and black honey at times when they do not drink wine, yet later, when it has turned into bitter vinegar, drink it again? Therefore, one should know that there is no fixed nature."
If there were no fixed nature, how could things not exist without causes and conditions? Good son!
Since you say that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature, how can you provide an analogy for this?
If there are metaphors, one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there were an intrinsic nature, one should know that no metaphor would be possible.
Since the wise of the world all employ analogies, one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and lack a single nature.
“Good son! As for your statement that the body comes first or that the afflictions come first, this meaning is not so. Why is that?

If I were to claim that the body exists prior [to consciousness], you might object, saying, "Your case is the same as mine in that the body does not exist prior [to consciousness]"; for what reason, then, do you raise such an objection?
Good son!

The bodies of all sentient beings and their afflictions exist simultaneously, without one preceding or following the other. Although they exist at the same time, it is because of afflictions that a body comes to be; it is never the case that afflictions exist because of a body.

If you think that it is like a person’s two eyes, which are obtained simultaneously and do not depend upon one another— where the left does not depend on the right and the right does not depend on the left—
and that afflictions and the body are likewise.
This meaning is not so.
Why is that? Good son!
In the world, people see that although the wick and the light exist simultaneously, the light must depend upon the wick; it is never the case that the wick exists because of the light. "Good son!
If you think that because the body does not exist prior [to its causes], one knows there is no cause, this argument is incorrect. Why?
If you claim it is called "non-existent" because there were no causes and conditions prior to the body, then you should not say that all dharmas possess causes and conditions.

If you say that [the body] is not mentioned because it is not perceived, yet we now perceive that jars and other things arise from causes and conditions, why do you not state that the body likewise arises from prior causes and conditions, just as a jar does?
"Good son!
Whether one perceives them or does not perceive them, all dharmas arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature.
Good son!"
If you claim that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and are devoid of causes and conditions, for what reason do you speak of the five great elements?
The very nature of these five great elements is itself cause and condition.
"Good son!
Although the five great elements have such causes and conditions, one should not say that all dharmas are identical to the causes and conditions of the five great elements.

It would be like worldly people saying that because all those who have left the household life diligently uphold the precepts, even caṇḍālas and others should likewise diligently uphold the precepts."
“Good son! You say that the five great elements possess a fixed and solid nature; however, I observe that this nature is subject to transformation and is therefore not fixed. Good son!”
Ghee, wax, and lac are termed "earth" in your own system; yet this earth is not fixed, as it may resemble water or resemble earth. Therefore, one cannot say that its intrinsic nature is solidity.

Good son! White tin, lead, pewter, copper, iron, gold, and silver—in your teaching, these are called fire. This fire has four natures: when it flows, it is the nature of water; when it moves, it is the nature of wind; when it is hot, it is the nature of fire; and when it is solid, it is the nature of earth. How can you say that its nature is definitively fire?
Good son! The nature of water is called "flowing. When water freezes, it is not called earth; thus it is named "water. For what reason, then, when the water is in motion, is it not called "wind"?

If movement were not called "wind," then when it is frozen, it likewise should not be called "water. If these two meanings arise from causes and conditions, why do you say that all phenomena do not arise from causes and conditions?

“Good son! If you say that because the nature of the five faculties is able to see, hear, perceive, know, and touch, they are all inherent natures and do not arise from causes and conditions, this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? Son of good family!

The nature of intrinsic nature cannot be altered. If one were to say that the nature of the eye sees, it should be able to see at all times; there should not be moments when it sees and moments when it does not. Therefore, you should know that seeing arises from causes and conditions, and is not without causes and conditions.
"Good son!
Your statement that greed and liberation do not arise from the five sense objects is incorrect. Why is this so?

Good son! The arising of greed and liberation, although they differ in their causal conditions regarding the five sensory objects, both arise from mental reflection: through unwholesome reflection one gives rise to greed, while through wholesome reflection one attains liberation.
"Good son!
Greed arises through internal conditions and is liberated through them; it increases through external conditions.
Therefore, your claim that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature and that greed and liberation do not arise in dependence upon the five sensory objects is impossible."

“Good son! You say that those who possess all their faculties yet lack wealth and do not attain mastery, while those with impaired faculties who abound in riches and attain great mastery, demonstrate that there is an intrinsic nature which does not arise from causes and conditions.
This meaning is not so.
Why is that? Good son!
Sentient beings experience retributive fruits according to their karma; such retributive fruits are of three kinds:
first, retribution in the present life; second, retribution in the next life; and third, retribution in subsequent lives.

The poor and the immensely wealthy, those with intact faculties and those with impaired faculties—these karmic conditions are each distinct. If the possession of all faculties were due to an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then those who possess it should necessarily be abundant in wealth and treasures; and those who are abundant in wealth and treasures should necessarily possess all their faculties.
Now it is not so; therefore, we know for certain that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and that all things arise from causes and conditions.

As you have said, even infants in the world, who are unable to discern the causes and conditions of the five sensory objects, both cry and laugh; therefore, the claim that everything possesses an intrinsic nature is incorrect.
Why is this? If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then laughing should be constant laughter and weeping should be constant weeping; one should not laugh once and weep once.

Since one laughs once and weeps once, one should know that all things arise entirely from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and do not arise from causes and conditions.
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas arise from causes and conditions, from what causes and conditions does such a body arise?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The causes and conditions of this body are afflictions and karma."
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!
If this body arises from afflictions and karma, can these afflictions and karma be severed?"
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
The brahmin spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will analyze and explain this for me, so that upon hearing it, I may completely sever [these afflictions] without even shifting from this place.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If one knows that there is no obstruction in the middle between the two extremes, such a person is then able to sever the karma of afflictions. [The interlocutor asked:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have already understood and attained the eye of the true Dharma.
The Buddha asked,
"How do you know this?"
“World-Honored One!
The two extremes are form and liberation from form; the middle way is the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
"Having well understood the two extremes, he has severed afflictions and karma.
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and receive the precepts."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu. Immediately,
he severed the afflictions of the three realms and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, there was another brahmin named Hongguang (Mahāgovinda) who spoke again, saying:
"Gautama! Do you know what I am thinking now?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Nirvāṇa is permanent; conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Curvature is false view; straightness is the Noble Path.”
The brahmin said: “Gautama!
For what reason and by what cause do you speak thus?”

“Good son! You have always thought that begging for alms is permanent while special invitations are impermanent, and that being crooked is like a door-key while being straight is like the imperial banner.”

Therefore, I say that nirvana is permanent and conditioned phenomena are impermanent; "crooked" refers to false views, while "straight" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—it is not as you previously conceived it to be.
The brahmin said, "Gautama truly knows my mind: does this Eightfold Noble Path cause all sentient beings to attain complete extinction?
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
The brāhmaṇa said: “Gautama!
You already know my mind; why do you remain silent and not answer what I have now asked?”
Then Kauṇḍinya spoke these words: "Great Brahmin!
If there are those who ask whether the world is finite or infinite, the Tathāgata always remains silent and does not answer."
The Eightfold Noble Path is straight, and Nirvana is eternal; if one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, one will attain extinction, but if one does not practice it, one cannot attain it.
Great Brahmin!
It is like a great city whose four walls have no openings whatsoever, with only a single gate.

Its gatekeeper is intelligent, wise, and capable of discernment; he allows those who should be let in and bars those who should be kept out. Although he cannot know the exact number of those entering or exiting, he certainly knows that all who enter or leave must do so through this gate.
Good son! The Tathāgata is also like this:
the city is a metaphor for nirvāṇa, the gate is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path, and the gatekeeper is a metaphor for the Tathāgata. Good son!
"Although the Tathāgata has not yet answered you regarding whether there is an end or no end, those for whom there is an end must certainly cultivate this Eightfold Noble Path.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Venerable Kauṇḍinya!
The Tathāgata is truly skilled at preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma. I now truly wish to know the city and the path, so that I may act as the gatekeeper myself.
Kauṇḍinya said:
“Excellent, excellent!
You, O brāhmaṇa, have been able to give rise to the unsurpassed and vast mind.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Stop, stop, Kauṇḍinya!
It was not only today that this brahmin first gave rise to such a thought."

"Kauṇḍinya! In the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. This person had previously, in the presence of that Buddha, resolved upon anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi; he shall become a Buddha within this Bhadrakalpa. Having long ago thoroughly penetrated and fully understood the characteristics of dharmas, for the sake of sentient beings he manifests as dwelling among non-Buddhist paths, appearing to possess no knowledge."
"For this reason, Kauṇḍinya, you should not say, 'Excellent, excellent! You are now able to give rise to such a great mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this, addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying, "Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?"
Kauṇḍinya said:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is outside the śāla grove, twelve yojanas from this great assembly, where he is being harassed and disturbed by sixty-four trillion māras.”
All these hosts of Māras each transformed themselves into the likeness of the Tathāgata;
some proclaimed that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, while others said that all phenomena do not arise from causes;
some declared that all causes and conditions are eternal dharmas, whereas those born of conditions are entirely impermanent.
Some may say that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are real, while others say they are provisional; the same applies to the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
Some may say there are twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), while others say there are precisely four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
Some may say that all phenomena (*dharma*) are like illusions, like transformations, or like a mirage in the heat; others may say that one attains the Dharma through hearing.
Some say that the Dharma is attained through reflection; some say it is attained through cultivation; others speak of the meditation on impurity;
others speak of the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation; others speak of the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness;
and others speak of the three types of contemplation and the seven kinds of skillful means. Furthermore...

Some say it refers to the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*); the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*);
the Bodhisattva’s first stage through to the tenth stage. Others say it refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Still others say it refers to the *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, and *nidāna*.
Whether it be *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, or *upadeśa*;
or whether it speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Alternatively, it is said: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, detached emptiness, dispersed emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristics,

signless emptiness, emptiness of the aggregates, emptiness of the sense-bases, emptiness of the elements, emptiness of the wholesome, emptiness of the unwholesome, and [emptiness of the] indeterminate...

He records the emptiness of recollection, the emptiness of bodhi, the emptiness of the path, the emptiness of nirvāṇa, the emptiness of practice, the emptiness of attainment, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of emptiness, and the great emptiness.
Alternatively, he may manifest supernatural transformations, emitting water and fire from his body;
he may emit water from the upper part of his body while emitting fire from the lower part, or emit water from the lower part of his body while emitting fire from the upper part.
He emits fire from his left flank while water flows from his right, and he emits water from his left flank while fire issues from his right;
from one flank there resounds thunder, while from the other there falls rain.
Furthermore, he may manifest various Buddha-worlds, or again, manifest the Bodhisattva’s birth and his walking seven steps, or his dwelling in the inner palace while experiencing the five desires.
When he first left home to practice asceticism; when he went to the Bodhi tree and sat in samādhi;
when he destroyed the hosts of Māra and turned the wheel of Dharma; and when he displayed great supernormal powers and entered nirvāṇa.
“World-Honored One!
After the bhikṣu Ānanda saw these things, he thought to himself:
‘Such a miraculous transformation as this has never been seen before; by whom was it performed?’”
"Could this not have been composed by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni?
Yet he was unable to rise or speak as he wished; because the bhikṣu Ānanda had entered the snare of Māra, he further thought:
"The teachings spoken by the various Buddhas differ from one another; whom should I follow now?"
"World-Honored One!
Ānanda is now undergoing extreme and great suffering; though he thinks of the Tathāgata, there is no one who can save him. For this reason, he has not come here to this great assembly."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within this great assembly there are bodhisattvas who have already, in a single lifetime, resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...”
Having generated the bodhicitta from three lifetimes up to immeasurable births, they have already been able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
their resolve is firm, they are fully accomplished in the practice of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*,
they have perfected their merits, and for a long time they have drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas to purely cultivate the *brahmacarya*.
In their conduct, they attain the non-retrogressive bodhicitta, non-retrogressive patience, and non-retrogressive upholding;
they attain patience in accordance with the Dharma and immeasurable samādhis such as Śūraṅgama.
Such individuals, upon hearing Mahāyāna sūtras, never give rise to doubt, and are well able to discern and proclaim that the Three Jewels are of one and the same nature.
Their marks are eternally abiding and unchanging; hearing of the inconceivable, they do not give rise to alarm or wonder;
hearing of the various kinds of emptiness, their minds are not terrified or anxious; they clearly and thoroughly penetrate the nature of all dharmas;

they are able to uphold all twelve divisions of the scriptures and extensively explain their meanings; and they are also able to receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures of immeasurable Buddhas.
"Why do you worry about being unable to receive and uphold such a Mahāparinirvāṇa scripture?
For what reason and by what causes do you ask where Kauṇḍinya and Ānanda are?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, son of good family!
After I had attained Buddhahood, twenty years passed while I resided in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, I addressed the bhikṣus, saying: 'Bhikṣus!'"

"Now, within this assembly, who is able to receive and uphold for me the Tathāgata’s twelve divisions of the scriptures, provide whatever necessities may be required for my service, and furthermore ensure that they do not lose their own spiritual benefit?"
At that time, among that assembly, Kauṇḍinya came forward and said to me:
"I am able to receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures, to attend to you on your left and right, and not neglect my own duties for my own benefit."
I said: "Kauṇḍinya!
You are already advanced in years and ought to have an attendant; how then can you wish to serve as my attendant?"
Then Śāriputra spoke again, saying:
"I am able to receive and uphold all the Buddha’s words, provide whatever is required, and not neglect the practice of my own benefit."
I said: "Śāriputra!
You are already advanced in years and ought to have an attendant; how then can you wish to serve as my attendant?"
In this manner, even when five hundred arhats all offered themselves as attendants, the Buddha would not accept them.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, amidst the great assembly, had this thought:
"The Tathāgata now refuses these five hundred bhikṣus to serve him; whose service does the Buddha intend for them to perform?"

Having reflected thus, he immediately entered meditative concentration and saw that the Tathāgata’s mind was directed toward Ānanda, like the sun first rising, its light illuminating the western wall.
Having seen this, he immediately arose from his meditative concentration and said to Kauṇḍinya:
"Venerable One!
I perceive that the Tathāgata wishes to have Ānanda serve as his attendant."
At that time, Kauṇḍinya and five hundred arhats went to where Ānanda was and spoke these words: “Ānanda!
You should now serve as an attendant to the Tathāgata; please accept this task.”
Ānanda said: "Venerable sirs!
I truly am not fit to serve the Tathāgata."
Why is this? The Tathāgata is as venerable as a lion king, a dragon, or a fire; I am now defiled and weak—how could I possibly accomplish this?
The bhikṣus said: “Ānanda!
Accept our words and serve the Tathāgata; you will obtain great benefit.”
A second and third time he spoke likewise.
Ānanda said,
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I do not seek great benefit for myself; in truth, I am not fit to serve as your attendant.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke again, saying: "Ānanda!"
"You do not yet know this. Ānanda said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I only pray that you will explain this.
Maudgalyāyana said, "The other day, the Tathāgata sought an attendant from among the Saṃgha; five hundred arhats all requested the position, but the Tathāgata did not grant it."
"I have immediately entered meditative concentration and perceived that the Tathāgata intended for you to perform this; why then do you now refuse it?
Having heard this, Ānanda joined his palms, knelt down, and spoke these words:
"O Great Virtuous Ones!..."
