"If such a thing were possible, and if the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, would grant me three wishes, I would comply with the Sangha's command and serve at his side.
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What are these three wishes?"
Ānanda said:
"First, even if the Tathāgata were to offer me his old robes, I ask that you permit me not to accept them.
Second, even if the Tathāgata were to accept a separate invitation from a donor, I ask that you permit me not to go."
Third, that I be permitted to enter and exit at any time without restriction.
If the Buddha would grant these three matters, I shall comply with the Sangha’s command and serve the Tathāgata.
Then the five hundred bhikṣus, headed by Kauṇḍinya, returned to my presence and spoke thus:
"We have already exhorted the bhikṣu Ānanda to request only three wishes; if the Buddha grants them, he will comply with the command of the Saṃgha."
"Mañjuśrī! At that time, I praised Ānanda, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
"Ānanda Bhikṣu!
You are endowed with wisdom and can foresee censure.
For what reason?"
If someone should say to you, "You provide for the Tathāgata with food and clothing; therefore, first seek not to accept worn-out robes, nor follow separate invitations," Kauṇḍinya!

The Bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with perfect wisdom, yet because he enters and exits [his dwelling] only at fixed times, he is unable to extensively benefit the fourfold assembly; for this reason, he desires to enter and exit without restriction as to time.
“Kauṇḍinya! For Ānanda’s sake, I have opened up these three matters according to his wishes.
Then Maudgalyāyana returned to Ānanda and said to him:
"I have already requested three matters on your behalf, and the Tathāgata, out of his great compassion,
has granted them all. Ānanda said,
"Venerable One!"
"If the Buddha permits, I request to go and attend upon him.
"Mañjuśrī! Ānanda has served me for over twenty years, and he is fully endowed with eight kinds of inconceivable qualities."
What are the eight?
First, for more than twenty years since he began serving me, he has never accepted separate invitations to meals on my behalf.
Second, for more than twenty years since he began serving me, he has never accepted old or worn-out clothing from me.
Third, since he came into my service, he has never arrived at my place at an improper time.

Fourth, since he came into my service, although he was possessed of afflictions, whenever he entered or left with me the palaces of kings, kṣatriyas, or noble and wealthy clans, and saw women or daughters of devas and nāgas, he did not give rise to thoughts of desire.

Fifth, since you came to serve me, you have held the twelve divisions of the sūtras I have taught; not once has a single sūtra passed through your ears without you asking about it again, like pouring the water from one jar into another, with the exception of only one question.
"Good son!
When Prince Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Śākyas and destroyed the city of Kapilavastu, Ānanda was at that time filled with grief and distress; he wailed aloud and came to where I was, saying:
'I and the Tathāgata were both born in this city and belong to the same Śākya clan; why is it that the Tathāgata’s radiant countenance remains as usual, while I am so emaciated and haggard?'"
I then replied:
"Ānanda! Because I cultivate the concentration of emptiness, I am not like you."
After three years had passed, he returned and asked me:
"World-Honored One!
I went to that city of Kapilavastu and heard there that the Tathāgata practices the samādhi of emptiness; is this matter true or false?"
I said: "Ānanda! So it is, so it is, just as you have said."

"Sixth, since he has served me, although he has not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he constantly knows the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) into which the Tathāgata enters.

Seventh, since he has served me, although he has not yet attained the wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), he is able to discern that such-and-such a sentient being has come to the presence of the Tathāgata, and whether they will presently attain one of the four fruits of the śramaṇa, or will attain it later, or will obtain a human body, or will obtain a celestial body."
Eighth, since he has served me, he is fully able to understand all the secret words of the Tathāgata.
Son of good family!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with these eight inconceivable qualities; therefore, I designate the bhikṣu Ānanda as the Treasury of Much Learning (Bahuśruta).
"Good son!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with eight qualities, enabling him to fully uphold the twelve divisions of the sūtras.
What are these eight?"

First, the faculty of faith is firm and solid; second, the mind is upright and sincere; third, the body is free from the suffering of illness; fourth, one is constantly diligent and energetic; fifth, one is endowed with mindfulness; sixth, the mind is free from arrogance; seventh, one has accomplished concentration and wisdom; eighth, one is fully possessed of the wisdom born of hearing.
Mañjuśrī! The attendant disciple of Vipaśyin Buddha was named Aśoka, who likewise possessed these eight dharmas. The attendant disciple of Śikhin Tathāgata was named Kṣemakāra;

the attendant disciple of Viśvabhū Buddha was named Upaśānta; the attendant disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Bhadrika; the attendant disciple of Kanakamuni Buddha was named Suti; and the attendant disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha was named Yaśomatī—all of whom also fully possessed these eight dharmas.
"Ānanda, I am now likewise endowed with these eight dharmas; for this reason, I designate the bhikṣu Ānanda as the 'Treasury of Much Learning' (Bahuśruta-kośa).
Good son!"

As you have said, although there are immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas within this great assembly, all these bodhisattvas bear a heavy responsibility, namely that of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Because of such causes and conditions of compassion, each is busily occupied with subduing their own retinue and adorning themselves.
Due to these causes and conditions, after my parinirvāṇa, they will be unable to propagate and explain the twelve divisions of the sūtras.
If there are bodhisattvas who might occasionally be able to preach [the Dharma], people do not believe or accept it. Mañjuśrī!

The bhikṣu Ānanda is my younger brother; he has served me for more than twenty years, and whatever Dharma he has heard, he has fully received and upheld, just like pouring water from one vessel into another. Therefore, I now ask: where is Ānanda?
I wish to cause them to receive and uphold this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Good son!

After my parinirvāṇa, that which the Bhikṣu Ānanda has not heard shall be propagated by the Bodhisattva Hongguang, while that which Ānanda has heard he himself shall be able to proclaim and disseminate.

Mañjuśrī! The bhikṣu Ānanda is currently in another place, twelve yojanas outside this assembly, being tormented and distracted by sixty-four trillion māras. You should go there and raise your voice, saying:
"All you māras, listen attentively, listen attentively!"

The Tathāgata now proclaims this great dhāraṇī; all devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as mountain deities, tree deities, river deities, ocean deities, household deities, and others—upon hearing the name of this dhāraṇī, there are none who do not receive and uphold it with reverence.
This dhāraṇī has been proclaimed by as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers; it can transform the female body and enable one to know past lives.

If one observes five practices—first, pure conduct (brahmacarya); second, abstaining from meat; third, abstaining from alcohol; fourth, abstaining from pungent vegetables; and fifth, delighting in solitude—and having observed these five practices, receives, believes, recites, and transcribes this dhāraṇī with a sincere heart, you should know that such a person will immediately transcend seventy-seven billion wretched and evil bodies.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:

“Amāṭe | Vimāṭe | Nemāṭe | Maṅgāṭe | Haimarajye | Samantavati | Saprathasatani | Bramathasatani | Manasapute | Viraje | Amalate | Varame | Varamaśāṭe | Purane puranamānulate. Then Mañjuśrī, having received this dhāraṇī from the Buddha, went to where Ānanda was and, standing amidst the host of Māras, spoke thus:
“All you Māra followers, listen attentively as I recite the dhāraṇī mantra which I have received from the Buddha.”
Upon hearing this dhāraṇī, the Māra King gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, abandoned his demonic activities, and immediately released Ānanda.
Mañjuśrī and Ānanda came together to where the Buddha was. Upon seeing the Buddha, Ānanda paid his respects with a sincere heart and withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Outside this Śāla grove, there is a brahmin named Subhadra; he is extremely old, being one hundred and twenty years of age.”

"Although he has attained the five supernormal powers, he has not yet abandoned pride; having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he gives rise to the thought of omniscience and conceives the notion that he has entered nirvana.
You should go to him and say to Subhadra:

'The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. This very night, at midnight, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. If there is anything you wish to do, do it now; do not let yourself harbor regret on a later day.'"
"Ānanda! What you have said, they will certainly believe and accept. Why is that?

In the past, during five hundred lifetimes, you were the son of Subhadra; because the habitual tendencies of his affection for you were not yet exhausted, he accepted your words out of that very cause and condition.
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s command, went to Subhadra and spoke these words:

"Venerable sir, you should know that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. This very night, at midnight, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. If there is anything you wish to do, you should do it while there is still time; do not harbor a heart of regret on a later day."
Subhadra said: "Excellent, Ānanda!
I shall now go to where the Tathāgata is."
At that time, Ānanda and Subhadra returned to where the Buddha was. When Subhadra arrived, he paid his respects and spoke these words: "Gautama!
"I now wish to ask a question; please answer according to my intent.
The Buddha said, "Subhadra!"
"Now is precisely the time; according to what you ask, I shall answer with skillful means to suit your intention.
"Gautama! There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak as follows:"

"All sentient beings who experience the retribution of suffering or pleasure do so entirely in accordance with the causal conditions of their past karma. Therefore, if one maintains the precepts with diligence and undergoes physical and mental suffering, they can destroy their original karma. Once that original karma is exhausted, all sufferings are extinguished; when all sufferings are extinguished, one attains nirvana."
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who speak in this way, out of compassion for them, I shall always go to and come from such persons; having arrived there, I shall ask them:
"O worthy one!..."
"Did you truly speak in such a manner?
If he replies, "I did speak in such a manner," [one should respond:]...
"Why is that? "Gautama!
I see sentient beings who practice various evils, yet possess abundant wealth and treasures, and enjoy mastery over their own bodies."
Furthermore, one sees those who cultivate goodness yet remain poor and destitute, lacking autonomy;
one sees others who exert great physical labor and effort in their pursuit but fail to obtain anything;
and one sees others who obtain things naturally without seeking them at all.
Furthermore, one sees some who, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, nevertheless meet an untimely death;
one sees others who take pleasure in killing yet live out their full natural lifespan;
and one sees some who purely cultivate the brahma-faring and diligently uphold the precepts, among whom there are those who attain liberation and those who do not.
"Therefore, I say that all sentient beings who experience the retribution of suffering and pleasure do so entirely due to the causal conditions of their own past karma.
Subhadra! I shall further ask you this:
"O Benevolent One!
Do you truly see past karma?
If such karma exists, how much of it is there?"
How much can present asceticism destroy?
Can one know whether this karma has been exhausted or not?
Once this karma is exhausted, is everything exhausted?
If he should answer,
"I truly do not know," I would then provide an analogy for that person:

"It is, for example, like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow; his family members seek out a physician to extract the arrow, and once the arrow has been removed, the body attains peace and security."

Ten years later, this person still remembers it with perfect clarity: "This physician extracted the poisoned arrow for me, applied medicinal ointments and bandages, and enabled me to recover, so that I may dwell in peace and receive happiness."
"Since you, O Benevolent One, do not know your past karma, how can you know that present asceticism will certainly destroy past karma?
If he should further say: "Gautama!"
You yourself also possess past karmic deeds from former lives; why do you alone reproach me for my past karma?

In the sūtras of Gautama, it is also said that if one sees someone who is noble, wealthy, and powerful, one should know that this person was fond of giving in previous lives—is this not called past karma?
I replied again:
"O worthy one!
To know in such a manner is called inferential knowledge; it is not called true knowledge."
Within my Buddha-dharma, there are those who know the effect from the cause, and there are those who know the cause from the effect.
Within my Buddha-dharma, there are past karmas and there are present karmas.
You, however, are not so; you possess only past karma, but no present karma.
In your doctrine, karma is not severed through skillful means, whereas in my doctrine it is not thus—it is severed through skillful means.

"When your karma is exhausted, your suffering will be exhausted; it is not so for me. Once my afflictions are exhausted, my karma and suffering are then exhausted; therefore, I now reprove you for your past karma."
If that person should say:
"Gautama! I truly did not know it; I received it from my teacher, and my teacher made this statement. I am truly without fault."
I said: "Virtuous one! Who is your teacher?"
If he should answer,
"It was Pūraṇa," I would further say:
"Why did you not previously inquire one by one whether the Great Master truly knows past karma?
If your teacher had said, 'I do not know,' how would you have accepted his words?"
If one says, "I know," one should further ask: "Does the causal condition of lower suffering lead to middle or upper suffering?
Does the causal condition of middle suffering lead to lower or upper suffering?"
Does one who experiences superior suffering also experience middling and inferior suffering?
If you say no, then one must further ask: why does the Master say that the retribution for suffering and pleasure is solely past karma, and not present karma?
Furthermore, one should ask: "Does this present suffering exist in the past?
If it existed in the past, then all past karma has already been completely exhausted; if it were completely exhausted, how could one receive a body today?"
If the past does not exist and only the present exists, why do you further say that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings are all due to past karma?
O Virtuous One!
If you know that present ascetic practice can destroy past karma, by what then would you destroy that present ascetic practice itself?
If it were not subject to destruction, suffering would be permanent;
if suffering were permanent, how could one speak of attaining liberation from suffering?
Furthermore, if there were other formations that constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), since those of the past have already ceased, how could there be suffering?
O Benevolent One!
Can such ascetic practices cause those who perform pleasant karma to experience bitter fruits?
Or can they cause those who perform bitter karma to experience pleasant fruits?
Can karma that is neither painful nor pleasant be made so that its fruit is not experienced?
Can karma that is to be experienced in the present life be made to be experienced in a future life?
Can karma that is to be experienced in a future life be made to be experienced in the present life?
Can these two types of retribution be made non-retribution?
Can determinate retribution be made non-retribution?
Can non-retribution be made determinate retribution?
If he should further say: "Gautama,
I cannot."
I shall further say:
"O virtuous one!
If you are unable [to attain it], for what cause and condition do you undergo these ascetic practices?"
O virtuous one!
You should know that there certainly exists past karma and present conditions; therefore, I say that karma arises from afflictions, and retribution is received because of karma.
O Benevolent One!
You should know that all sentient beings possess past karma and present causes.
Although sentient beings have the karma for longevity from the past, they must rely upon the conditions of present food and drink.
"O Benevolent One!
If you say that when sentient beings experience suffering or pleasure, it is invariably due to the causal conditions of their past karma, this is not so. Why is that?"
O Benevolent One!

It is like a person who eliminates an enemy for a king; by reason of this cause and condition, he acquires much wealth and treasure, and through that wealth and treasure, he experiences happiness in the present life.
Such a person creates the cause for happiness in the present and experiences the retribution of happiness in the present.

For example, if someone kills the beloved son of a king, they lose their own life as a result of that causal condition; such a person creates the cause for suffering in the present and experiences the retribution of suffering in the present.
"O Benevolent One!

All sentient beings currently experience suffering and pleasure due to the four great elements, the seasons, the land, and other people; therefore, I say that it is not necessarily the case that all sentient beings experience suffering and pleasure solely because of their past karma."
"O Benevolent One!
If liberation were attained through the power of severing the causes and conditions of karma, then all noble ones would not attain liberation. Why is this?"

Because the past fundamental karma of all sentient beings has neither beginning nor end, I therefore say that when one cultivates the Noble Path, this path is able to obstruct karma that has no beginning or end.
"O Benevolent One!
If one were to attain the Way merely by undergoing ascetic practices, then all animals would likewise attain the Way.
Therefore, one should first subdue the mind rather than the body. For this reason, I have said in my sutras: 'Cut down this forest; do not cut down the trees.'"
Why is this? Fear arises from the forest, not from the trees.
To subdue the body, one must first subdue the mind.
"The mind is likened to a forest, and the body is likened to a tree. Subhadra said,
"World-Honored One!"
"I have already previously tamed my mind.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"How is it that you are now able to first discipline the mind?
Subhadra replied,
"World-Honored One!"
I first reflected that sensual desire is impermanent, without bliss, and without purity;
I then contemplated that form is indeed permanent, blissful, and pure.
Having made this contemplation, the fetters of the desire realm were severed and the sphere of form was attained; therefore, this is called "first taming the mind."
Next, one further contemplates form: form is impermanent, like an abscess, like a wound, like poison, like an arrow; one perceives the formless as permanent, pure, and tranquil.
Having observed in this way, the fetters of the form realm are exhausted and one attains the formless states; therefore, this is called "first taming the mind.
Next, one further contemplates perception as impermanent, a festering ulcer, and a poisoned arrow.
Having contemplated in this way, I attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is omniscience, tranquility, and purity; it is without falling away, eternal, and unchanging. Therefore, I am able to subdue my mind.
The Buddha said, “Good son,
how are you able to subdue your mind?”
The state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that you have now attained is still called "perception.
Nirvāṇa is without perception; how can you say that you have attained nirvāṇa?
"Good son!
You were previously able to reproach coarse perceptions; why now do you become attached to subtle perceptions and fail to reproach them?
This sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is therefore called 'perception,' yet it is like an abscess, like a wound, like poison, and like an arrow."
"Good son!

Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra possessed sharp faculties and great intelligence, yet he was still unable to sever such states as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and consequently received an evil body; how much more so for others?"
“World-Honored One!
How can one sever all forms of existence?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If one contemplates the true mark, such a person can sever all forms of existence.
Subhadra said:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘the true mark’? “Good son!
“The mark of the markless is called the true mark.
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘the mark of the markless’?”
“Good son! All dharmas have no self-characteristic, no other-characteristic, and no characteristic of both self and other;

they have no characteristic of causelessness, no characteristic of an agent, no characteristic of a recipient, no characteristic of a doer, and no characteristic of an experiencer; there is no dharma that is not [thus].”

The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are: the absence of the characteristic of male, the absence of the characteristic of female, the absence of the characteristic of a person (puruṣa), the absence of the characteristic of atoms, the absence of the characteristic of time,

the absence of the characteristic of self-nature, the absence of the characteristic of other-nature, the absence of the characteristic of both self and other-nature, the absence of the characteristic of existence,
the absence of the characteristic of non-existence, the absence of the characteristic of arising, the absence of the characteristic of one who arises, and the absence of the characteristic of causes.

There is no characteristic of cause or causelessness; no characteristic of fruit; no characteristic of fruit or fruitlessness; no characteristic of day or night; no characteristic of light or darkness;
no characteristic of seeing; no characteristic of a seer; no characteristic of hearing; no characteristic of a hearer;
no characteristic of cognition; no characteristic of a cognizer; no characteristic of bodhi; and no attainment.
Enlightenment has the characteristic of being without action, without a master of action, without affliction,
and without a master of affliction. Good son!
Such characteristics as these, according to the point at which they are extinguished, are called the characteristic of reality. Good son!

All dharmas are merely provisional; that which corresponds to their point of extinction is called "real," and is termed the characteristic of reality, the dharma-realm, ultimate wisdom, the ultimate truth, and the emptiness of the ultimate meaning.
"Good son!
These marks, the dharma-realm, ultimate wisdom, the ultimate truth, and the ultimate emptiness—by observing them with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
by observing them with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
"Because those of superior wisdom contemplate thus, they attain unsurpassed bodhi.

When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of one more birth; fifteen thousand bodhisattvas attained the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of two more births; twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained ultimate wisdom (*atyanta-jñāna*); and thirty-five thousand bodhisattvas realized the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This primary truth is also called the emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and it is also called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Forty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the samādhi of space; this samādhi of space is also called the samādhi of vastness, and it is also called the samādhi of the seal of wisdom.

Fifty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained non-retrogressive patience (*avivartika-kṣānti*); this non-retrogressive patience is also called "patience in accordance with the Dharma" and is also called "in accordance with the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*).
Sixty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained *dhāraṇī*; this *dhāraṇī* is also called "great mindfulness" (*mahāsmṛti*) and is also called "unimpeded wisdom" (*asaṅga-jñāna*).
Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the Lion’s Roar Samādhi; this Lion’s Roar Samādhi is also called the Vajra Samādhi, and it is also called the Five Wisdom Seal Samādhi.
Eighty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the samādhi of equanimity; this samādhi of equanimity is also called great loving-kindness and great compassion.

Immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha; and immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka.
Twenty-two trillion human and celestial women manifested the transformation of their female bodies to obtain male bodies, and Subhadra attained the fruit of Arhatship.
